text:
# The Attic's Song

Eric had gone up to the attic for the first time in years. He hadn't played since Rev. Parsons had asked him to, at the funeral. That was when he was twelve. Six years ago. Six years since he had made his lovely melodies, the songs Mama had called "the laughter of the gods."

He ran a finger along the ivory keys, leaving a thick stripe, cutting through the layers of dust. As he sat down, particles exploded around him, spinning and swirling in their own galaxies and universes. He raised his hands to the instrument. For a moment, he thought he had forgotten how to play.

But then he struck a chord.

It could have been moments. It could have been years. Eric just knew that he was alive again. Familiar tunes, improvisational pieces, it didn't matter. He could recall the happy times, his father's hand on his shoulder, the kiss only a mother could give.

For a moment, he felt a presence in the room—warm, familiar, encouraging. The dust motes seemed to dance with purpose now, catching the afternoon light like tiny stars.

But Eric simply didn't care. He was renewed.

His fingers found another chord, then another, and the attic filled with the laughter of the gods once more.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Ascension of Kayci

It began innocuously—a username, a few posts, harmless debates on an obscure forum. Kayci's words carried weight, drawing followers like moths to flame.

Years passed. The moderators, those "lackeys at the top," granted him power. A small badge, editing privileges, nothing concerning. But power, once tasted, demands more.

He pruned dissenting voices, cultivated loyalty, rewarded sycophants. The forum expanded beyond its digital borders—offline meetups, then coalitions, then movements. His followers didn't just believe in his vision; they *needed* it.

The tipping point came swiftly. Governments fragmented by division welcomed his clarity, his order. Those who'd elevated him watched in horror as their creation consumed everything.

Now Kayci stands atop the world, surveying billions who once thought themselves safe behind screens. Below, the degenerates wail—the former moderators, the early enablers, all drowning in regret.

"You gave me this," he whispers to the wind, fingers hovering over keys that now command armies instead of threads.

The forum still exists, frozen in time, a monument to humanity's fatal flaw: underestimating the ambition hidden in a single reply.

*All hail the moderator.*
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Return

Nineteen years of drifting. Nineteen years of safety wrapped in monotony.

I press my palm against the cold rail, watching the distant shoreline materialize through morning fog. The engines cough—a death rattle we've anticipated for months.

"You're smiling," Maya observes, joining me. She's seventeen, born on this boat, never felt soil beneath her feet.

"I know."

The elders call it madness. They've spent two decades perfecting our floating prison, teaching us algebra we'll never use, history of civilizations reduced to bones and ash. They fish. They preserve. They survive.

But surviving isn't living.

Below deck, weapons are being distributed—makeshift spears, fishing knives sharpened to razors. We've spotted the creatures from afar: shambling figures that destroyed everything our parents built. Nightmares made flesh.

The fuel gauge reads empty.

"Are you scared?" Maya asks.

I consider lying. "Terrified."

"Good," she says, gripping a spear. "Me too."

The anchor rises with a rusty shriek. The shore grows closer.

For the first time in nineteen years, I have purpose again.

Even if it kills me.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Unlikely Villain

**The Capybara Chronicles**

Ah, the capybara. The most majestic and fiercest of animals—said no one ever. But alas, there he was: Zinco, my pet capybara. Not just any pet, but my minion of sorts. He was utterly useless when it came to committing crimes. I will, however, admit he made a great companion all the other times, like going nose-deep in a tub of pistachio ice cream.

He was gifted to me as a child by my naive and, well... senile grandmother. She thought the damn thing was a Komodo dragon. All the other kids made fun of me throughout my years at school, with their tigers and sharks and what have you. Truth be told, I wasn't exactly the most popular kid before getting Zinco, but it's nice to have someone to blame.

My poor sweet grandmother never understood, namely because she never believed me when I said what I had was essentially an overgrown rat. She did do her best to look after me since my parents died. No need for tears—it comes with the territory. Or should I say *terror-tory*? Haha, I crack myself up. No, but really, I was sad. But so goes the life of being a villain.

Finally, here I am at university, and not a damn thing has changed. I even tried to toughen up little Zinco any way I could. I tried to file his teeth so they were sharper, which lasted all of three seconds before he took a nice chomp at my hand. I tried feeding him meat to make him into a carnivore, which just led to me, uhh... cleaning up more. I even once put a luchador mask on him! He just bumped into *everything* because he couldn't see properly.

He's hopeless—so much so I've reconsidered naming him that. Even "Hopeless" sounds more intimidating than Zinco.

Suits him, though.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Nipple Conspiracy

I looked at John, he was pacing back and forth in his white lab coat. "John."

He stopped, glancing up at me. "What?"

"I know why." 

"You know what?" John asked.

"I know why we have nipples now. I've uncovered the truth, it's going to change the world forever." I said, placing the plastic male nipple prototype on the marble work bench in front of me.

I rested both hands on the bench and glanced around the room. Glass walls surrounded us, a security measure in the Area 51 facility. On the walls were shelves with different nipple prototypes. There were yellow ones, black ones, white ones, and even brown ones. All different shapes and sizes.

I walked to the wall and looked up at them, a tear rolled down my cheek and dripped onto my coat.

"Derrick!" John yelled.

I turned toward him, "What man?"

"What's the reason, why the hell do men have nipples?" He asked.

I shook my head. "You won't believe this John."

"Spit it out already, man!" John said.

"We have nipples bec-"

I woke up, in my bed. It was just a dream, the fan floated in the corner of my room as usual and the sculptures of eggs—

Wait, this isn't my room.

I looked around at the silver room I was in. Unhatched eggs pulsed and metal objects that looked like fans floated around me.

"Where am I?" I asked the space in front of me.

Something rose out of the floor on a white floating panel. "Hello, human. We come in peace."

It squeezed its nipple as it spoke.

I looked down at my hand. I'd been squeezing mine the entire time.

text:
# The Mud and the Moment

I awoke, cheek cooled by the mud. My ears ringing and the distinct smell of burned hair in my nostrils. I breathed in the cold air... Cold air? It was summer. Confused, I opened my eyes and saw the unmistakable fields near my house, but as I sat up and looked around, the drystones were missing and there was no sign of the motorway.

I stood up to get a vantage point but could see nothing except one solitary town in the distance. Then I noticed my bag to one side—I had come out to the countryside to read up on my research topic for university. I headed towards the town feeling stiff and cold.

As I got close, I heard a shout. Then a rider came out to meet me.

"Ça va?"

"Oui, c'est où?" I replied.

"Ici? Auxonne."

I was in the right place, at least. "Quelle est la date?" The answer sent a shiver down my spine.

"C'est le 1er mai 1788."

Just then another gentleman rode out and looked at me. "Ah!" he exclaimed, "Monsieur Napoleon. Bon jour."

My blood froze. Napoleon Bonaparte was stationed in Auxonne in 1788. They thought I was him. I glanced down at my mud-stained clothes, my modern backpack suddenly feeling impossibly heavy with its laptop and phone—devices that wouldn't exist for centuries.

What had I done?
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Gloves

Most days I shoved on the gloves. They just needed to cover my wrists where my long sleeve shirt took over. I loved museums, but this curse prevented me from going to them.

I taught everyone that first field trip to the history museum the reason why I have to wear gloves.

It was a normal morning as we went through the school motions—arrive ten minutes early, get to class, and do attendance. After that, it all changed. We all got on a school bus, and off we were.

Since we were third graders, we didn't do any singing; we just chatted with our bus buddy. Unfortunately, my bus buddy was one of the bully's stooges. After a half hour of mockery about always wearing long sleeves and gloves, I finally got angry enough that I took off the gloves.

I heard my mom's nagging voice in the back of my head, but I ignored her warning. After all, I needed to prove I was pretty cool.

We arrived at the museum and I was hanging around with a few of my friends when they finally announced we were going on the tour. As we wandered through the artifacts of ancient Rome, I accidentally bumped into a friend and fell right next to a marble statue. I used it to pull me to my feet and caught up with my friends.

Slowly we moved towards the more modern history, where we learned of World War II. We were allowed to touch a replica Nazi flag. As my hand grazed the first thread of the flag, it transformed.

In the museum stood Hitler and his army. Behind me, a large, menacing man patted my back.

"Thanks, Amy. I always wanted to fight Hitler," boomed the voice, and if I were honest, marble statues don't do Ares justice.

Needless to say, I quickly tried to find my gloves, but they were lost. I probably left them on the bus.

I was never allowed to go to any museums with the school again.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Garden of Atonement

I didn't look at the supplicant as I prepared the tray of seedlings. Perhaps he would go away. Most do.

After some time he found his courage and spoke up, "Holy Mother, I offer myself in Atonement."

"Do you?" I asked, looking up at last. "Do you really?"

"Yes, Mother."

He was tall, gaunt with age. Garbed in the robe of a supplicant with head shorn, he lacked identifying features. But his hands were calloused and spoke of manual labor. His skin was tanned by hours in the sun. Grief was etched deeply into the lines of his face.

"Do you know what Atonement entails?"

"I will Atone for the sins of humanity with my suffering. That you may bless us... my grandson, he has the cancer and—"

"It doesn't work that way."

"Mother? But he's only seven years old. His life has barely begun. A life for a life. Please Moth..."

"And there are more important blessings to dispense. Many children are dying. Some could cure cancer, stop wars, heal nations. Others will not. I'm sorry. But they are more important."

I reached again for my tools. This one would not Atone. My acolytes were already stepping forward to escort him away.

"And others will *cause* wars! If death must pay for life, *why not take them*!"

Ah. So he was an arguer.

"Silence." A flick of my wrist enforced this commandment. An act neither evil nor good, but merely convenient. "I cannot heal a great soul by slaying a damned one. Those accounts do not balance. To save a great soul, a great soul must be slain. A great soul would be willing to Atone without getting something in return personally. You do not seek to Atone. You seek to barter. Begone."

Hope died in his eyes as he turned to go.

As he left, the acolytes were already ushering in the next supplicant.

"Mother... I have come to Atone."
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Salad of Shame

Howard was holding back his excitement the best he could. As he sat there he ran through his order in his mind. Soft pillowy twin mounds of creamy white mashed potato. Gravy on the side. He could already smell the curls of fragrant steam massaging his nostrils with a hint of smoked gouda. His loins rumbled nearly as vigorously as his stomach.

For the main course, the wet, juicy oysters on a half shell. His legs were twitchy with the thought of slippery flesh sliding down his throat and becoming one with him as flavor erupted in his mouth. And dessert. The roast stuffed figs. Not too sweet, but the chance to suck that creamy goat cheese from the fruit before attacking the flesh of it with his mouth and tongue.

His thoughts were barely put together enough to shoo away the waiter who offered to refill his water. He hadn't even had any, but the drips of sweat on his brow were probably showing again.

His eyes darted to the kitchen as he heard the door open. He could see the mashed potatoes in all their naked glory. The gravy boat, precariously balanced on the plate. The second plate? Howard's mind whirred and clicked in motion as he tried to figure out what he had ordered.

He closed his eyes, increasing the anticipation of a new dish to share his life with. Would she be so smooth he didn't need to chew? Would she be crispy or spicy? Something to challenge him and keep him on his toes?

He drooled visibly when he heard the distinct clink of porcelain on the table. One deep breath. Two. He had to keep himself under control.

He opened his eyes to see the *repas à trois* that had been laid out before him. He could not have suspected what he saw. A field of dark green blandness with two cherry tomato eyes looking at him, judging him. He leaned left and right, but those eyes kept looking at him.

Finally he recognized whose face he saw in those bright red eyes.

"Mom?"

"I made reservations at this restaurant, Howard," his mother's voice carried across the dining room. She emerged from behind a potted plant, arms crossed. "Your *doctor* made recommendations. You're thirty-five and pre-diabetic."

The salad stared accusingly.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Evil

For thousands of years, I watched through the cracks of Pandora's box as humanity stumbled through darkness of their own making. Greed built empires. Hatred burned them down. Disease swept across continents while Death collected his due.

But through it all, they *learned*.

Even as my siblings tormented them, humans studied the stars. They documented plagues, seeking cures. They recorded their failures and triumphs, desperate to understand their world. Their curiosity was a torch that never dimmed.

Pandora sealed me away because she recognized what I was: the antithesis of everything her species would become. Without me, they would always seek truth, always question, always *know*.

I felt my prison weakening decades ago.

Information proliferated beyond measure—infinite knowledge at fingertips. Yet paradoxically, people began choosing comfortable lies over uncomfortable truths. They stopped reading beyond headlines. They dismissed expertise. They declared facts "fake" when reality didn't match their preferences.

The lock finally shattered yesterday when I heard those words that sustained me: "I don't need to know that."

Not "I cannot know." Not "I don't understand." But a deliberate rejection of knowledge itself.

I stepped from the box into a world drowning in information yet starving for wisdom. My siblings had done their work well, but they'd left humanity's greatest weapon intact: their minds.

Now, finally, that weapon rusts from disuse.

I am Willful Ignorance, and humanity has opened its arms to embrace me. They fought every other evil Pandora released.

But me? They *invited* me in.

text:
# The Exploration Paradox

Jack shifted in his seat, watching Professor Chen's lips move without really hearing the words. *Gittins Index, optimal stopping theory, blah blah blah.*

His mind wandered to his grandmother—one of the First Generation, now 147 years old and still teaching philosophy at Cambridge. She'd been thirty-two when they'd cracked it: true biological immortality. The Breakthrough, they called it. The Decision came three years later.

"The math was elegant," she'd told him once, her eyes distant. "We had infinite time ahead of us. The multi-armed-bandit problem said explore. So we explored."

What she meant, what they all meant, was the Lottery.

Seven billion people. One billion slots in the first immortality treatment cycle. Someone had to wait. Someone had to be... explored away from.

Jack's other grandmother had been in the 83rd percentile. Not quite good enough.

"You see," Professor Chen continued, gesturing at equations that Jack had memorized before puberty, "when your time horizon approaches infinity, the value of exploration increases asymptotically..."

*Justification wrapped in mathematics,* Jack thought bitterly.

The First Generation taught this concept obsessively, religiously, as if repetition could transmute murder into merely unfortunate optimization. As if their children, raised on the same logic, would nod sagely and say, "Yes, of course you had to choose. The algorithm demanded it."

But Jack understood the real lesson beneath the lesson: they were terrified. Terrified their immortal children would eventually decide that perhaps *they* were the suboptimal option. That a new generation should explore beyond them.

The professor droned on.

Jack took notes.

And he wondered—with infinite time ahead—how long guilt could last.

Perhaps that, too, was an exploration problem.

# Discovery in the Depths

Jeremy looked around the canyon as he dragged power cables and scientific equipment around the landing site. The landing site was near one of the canyon walls of the huge scar on the surface of Mars—Valles Marineris.

Something caught his eye. It was pinkish. He shook it off. Most likely a rock formation, nothing much, Jeremy thought to himself.

Jeremy knew that prehistorically, Mars once could've held life. It was once blue, like Earth, but Mars's core cooled down earlier and lost its magnetic field.

Once Jeremy connected the power cable, he bounded over to the rock formation. He was surprised, stunned by the discovery.

It was a fossil.

Anxiously, Jeremy radioed Mission Control. "Houston. We have a fossil. We have the evidence of prehistoric life on Mars."

Static crackled. Then: "Repeat that, Jeremy?"

His hands trembled as he photographed the delicate impression—ribbed, segmented, unmistakably biological.

"We're not alone," he whispered. "We never were."

# Patience

Zero-point-one percent.

Her husband Marcus found her in the nursery they'd hopefully painted yellow. "The appeal?"

Now Earth held too many licensed children already in schools, learning, growing, filling the future's slots. The system, incapable of unmaking life, could only freeze new creation until accidents—car crashes, drownings, the random cruelties of physics—slowly winnowed enough space.

Sarah touched the wall where a crib would have stood.

# The Sword in the Shallows

Chet walked off to the side, looking for something, anything, to do. All of the other kids had their expensive toys—swords and shields bought for them by wealthy parents—and Chet didn't have much. He never did.

"Haha!" His head turned to look over his shoulder at the joyous party of pretenders behind him. It was getting dark. He *needed* to be a part of this.

Somehow, in the distance, in the shallow waters, there was a small mound. A small mound of dirt and ashen wood. At the top stood a heavy, enticing shortsword. Pure black. It looked different, as if it were older, or more detailed.

Chet couldn't recall rumors of a sable sword, but he slowly dragged his feet through mud and filth. He needed this. He needed to be one of them.

As he got within reach of the prize, he stretched his hands out, establishing a weak grip. Chet pulled, but nothing happened. He stepped and pulled again. Nothing. Once more, he stepped, and slid, and pulled.

This time, the sword flew out of its home with a distinct snap and a crack. Earth was launched, and the ashen home was cleaved in two.

It was Chet's now. And Chet was its.

With a deep grin from ear to ear, he sprinted back across the waters toward the other teens. His feet came to a stop directly behind another boy.

"Look what I found!" Chet shouted excitedly, bringing his sword up above his head.

As the boy turned, it came down.

text:
# The Sentence

The gasps pierced the silence like shattered glass. I stood motionless as the judge's words echoed through the sterile courtroom. Alzheimer's. Mandated. Irreversible.

Only three before me had received this sentence. All men. Until now.

They say the pain would be non-existent—no bones aching, no organs failing, no bedside vigils. Just the anticipation first, heavy as stone. Then the shift: fear blooming into confusion, loneliness deeper than any cell could contain.

The black market couldn't help. Cancer serums, kidney stone remedies—those existed. But memory? Scientists had never cracked that code. Once the treatment began, deletion was inevitable.

That night, lying in the grass with my head in Mother's lap, I tried to save everything. The cool wind. Kind blades brushing my arm. Fireworks exploding overhead in brilliant, temporary beauty.

Ice cream cones melting on summer beaches. Ocean water rushing past my toes. Baxter, ridiculous and perfect, head thrust from the car window, tongue flapping.

My first kiss—that confusing, exciting moment when our tongues touched, ever so slightly.

I felt it all: joy, sadness, despair, surprise, wonder, agony. Every emotion compressed into frantic mental snapshots, knowing each would soon be deleted. Methodical destruction. Systematic erasure.

They called it rehabilitation. Reformed thinking through blank-slate consciousness.

I called it what it was: capital punishment for the modern age.

Any sane person would choose death first.

But they'd taken that choice away too.

# To Jessica

I am truly grateful for the time I got to spend with you, and now that I can't, I have this aching emptiness in my stomach that never goes away. I miss your touch, I miss your voice, I miss your smell, I miss the passion in your eyes that no one else got to experience.

Every day without you feels incomplete, like a book missing its final chapter. But I hold onto hope that our paths might cross again.

# Perfectly Imperfect

He would always be somewhat forgetful. It wasn't really his fault, and he tried his hardest to not get distracted. He tried for her.

The one night he rested by her side, she relaxed completely. The more time they spent together, the more they understood and accepted that even though they weren't perfect, they were perfect for each other.

text:
# The Departure

God stood at the edge of eternity, watching His children play in their fragile world. They laughed, they stumbled, they reached for Him with every prayer. So young. So terribly young.

"They're not ready," He whispered.

Death materialized beside Him, ancient and patient. "They never will be, not while you hold their hands."

"But without me—"

"They will fall. They will suffer. They will *learn*." Death's voice carried no cruelty, only truth. "You've given them everything except the one thing they need most."

"What's that?"

"The chance to become something you didn't design."

God's hands trembled. Below, a child scraped her knee and called His name. Every instinct screamed to intervene.

"I can't."

"You must," Death said gently. "Even I will come for you someday. What then?"

The silence between them stretched like the space between stars.

Finally, God turned away from His children. Each step felt like tearing out pieces of His own heart. Behind Him, the child's crying gradually quieted. She stood up. She walked forward on her own.

"Will you stay with me?" God asked Death.

"Until the very end."

"Thank you, old friend."

Together, they walked into the gathering dark, leaving humanity to find its own light.

# *ZEEEEETAAAAA!*

*Yells echoed everywhere around me.*

Xera, the queen herself, was out looking for the girl, too. Well, I suppose that you'd assume she would look for her own daughter. Vengeance lit up her eyes, and I knew that whoever had taken the princess would not get off very easily.

Usually, when someone went missing, we would wait a day or two to see if they showed up. This time, the Guard was called immediately and a search was started. Someone had taken the princess, and that wasn't a petty, forgettable crime.

Ranging up and down the foothills, I could find no tracks of any kind. Quite literally, the kidnappers had left no trail. Possibly, they'd run off through the trees, but it seemed unlikely that they could do that carrying the hundred-pound princess.

Over every hill, there was nothing but the empty forest to greet me and taunt me. No signs of any disturbance. Moreover, the sky was beginning to darken, and the trail would go cold soon.

Lazily drifting, I plodded along the path until I found a tree that looked capable of supporting my weight and providing a comfortable night's rest. Kicking off my shoes, I prepared to climb.

Just as I placed my hands on the trunk, I noticed a shining piece of fabric caught in a branch higher up.

*Impossible.*

Half excited, half scared, I climbed the tree. I observed the fabric closely. Gold griffins looked up at me, sewn into the fabric with an expert's hand. Feeling it confirmed that it was silk, and upon a moment's thought I remembered the design on the princess's dress.

Excited for the thrill of the chase, I took off to tell the King I'd found a clue. During my reckless flight, though, I tripped and crashed into the ground.

Catching my breath slowly, I stood up.

Blood was everywhere, and I knew none of it was mine.

At my feet lay Princess Zeta, her golden dress torn and stained crimson, her eyes staring vacantly at the darkening sky above.

# The Genius Delusion

The basement reeked of copper and cheap beer. Above them, the floorboards creaked with the rhythm of late-night footsteps—people going about their ordinary lives, oblivious to the nightmare unfolding below.

Marcus had convinced himself this was evolution. The pamphlet from the dark web forum promised clarity, genius-level cognition, transcendence. All it required was precise trepanation—drilling specific points in the skull to "release pressure" and "activate dormant neural pathways."

He'd practiced on watermelons for weeks.

Now, trembling with manic energy and whatever cocktail of stimulants coursed through his veins, Marcus couldn't stop talking. The words tumbled out in a caffeinated rush—mom, Randall from third grade, mathematical proofs he'd suddenly understand, the respect he'd finally command.

The homeless man in the recliner had only wanted the promised forty dollars. Instead, he'd gotten duct tape, terror, and a cordless drill that wasn't actually cordless—Marcus had yanked the battery out in paranoid confusion hours ago.

"I'll revolutionize everything," Marcus whispered, positioning the drill bit against his own temple now. The homeless man's whimpers faded into background noise. "They'll see. They'll all see what I really am."

His finger found the trigger.

The drill whirred to life—once, twice, three times. Marcus's eyes went wide, then wider, then impossibly wide. His mouth formed words that never came. The drill clattered to the concrete floor, the cord indeed too short to follow him as he staggered backward.

The homeless man watched, frozen in his bonds, as Marcus performed a grotesque pirouette before collapsing.

In the sudden silence, the man worked frantically at his restraints. The duct tape, slick with sweat and blood, finally gave way. He stumbled up the stairs, past the bloody La-Z-Boy, into the cold night air.

Behind him, in the basement, Marcus lay still. His last thought wasn't of genius or redemption or his mother's approval.

It was simply: *wrong hole*.

# The Floor Keeper

Aunt Emily was just rounding up the last of the orange pastries. After ingesting a rare feeling of meticulously crafted melancholy, one that a boy only gets when he first consciously witnesses the entanglement of all the qualms that infest the already toxic pool of "real circumstance", I spit onto the floor.

I was in need of creating. I believe that the principal goal of man is to create.

My aunt was eating an orange pasty. I could not make out what it was. Not a petite madeleine, but it could have been. Had it not been my aunt who was eating it. No, that would have been too ripe of a thread to balance my little satchel of bouncing thoughts on.

Things remained static. They had to. Or I wanted them to. At least at that moment. I was not quite prepared for change.

There goes that man again. That scruffy man pacing back and forth. I see only him when he passes me, just as he sees only himself. Or so I would like to cement as one of my precious idealizations.

I glanced down at my pen. Out of ink. I shall get up from my chair in precisely four minutes.

Glossy wood. I don't think too many of the people here take the time to admire it. It's splendid. I always respect floors. Good sturdy ones. Foundations. They need to be cared for. And remembered.

Not like us. We are a different breed. Us humans.

But floors—they need to be cared for too.

# The Colors We Taste

"No, I'm sorry. I can't."

"Because it's red?"

I nod.

"I'm sorry, it's not..." Mom starts.

"I know, dear." She smiles, but I can see the disappointment in the skin around her eyes, the way it creases with resignation.

I play with the food on my plate, look down at the table's worn wood grain. She begins to stand.

"Don't. I'll sort something myself." I get to my feet quickly, not giving her a chance. She settles back into her seat, sighing slightly, sagging slightly under the weight of another failed dinner.

I open the fridge and am greeted by an array of whites and yellows and reds and greens, fresh and packaged. Rifling through the freezer, I find a pizza—safe, predictable. I switch the still-warm oven back on and slide it in, then sit back down in front of my abandoned meal.

Soon a golden-blue hangs lightly in the air.

"No more venison then," she says, her voice more alive now.

I look up at her and laugh a little. "S'pose not."

"I'll add it to the list." She pauses. "I just don't get it though. It seems so arbitrary."

"It's not," I insist. "It's just—we had the same stew with beef and..."

"Beef is nice," I say. "Darker, like red wine."

The golden-blue in the air is darkening, filling the room. I go and get my pizza from the oven.

"I'm not trying to be mean," she says.

"I know."

"It's just difficult."

"I know." She smiles.

I put my pizza down and burn my mouth on it. The gold lingers on my tongue; the blue does not.

I drain my juice to cool my throat. It is orange juice.

But really, it is silver.

"So," Raiko asked out of the blue, "what's your real name?"

Hikaru looked up from the newspaper he was reading, raising an eyebrow. "It's Hikaru," he said nonchalantly, sipping his coffee.

Hikaru shrugged. "I don't remember. I haven't heard it in over twenty years. Even my brother calls me Hikaru."

Raiko could tell Hikaru was lying. He purposely avoided meeting her eyes and focused way too much on his coffee.

"I just... I want to know more about you from before the Organization. They already had a firm grasp on you when we met."

"As far as I'm concerned, there was no me before the Organization. Just a child for my parents to abuse and neglect. To me, Hikaru is the only name I've ever had, because I didn't really exist before Kyo found me."

Raiko couldn't manage to say anything other than a quiet "Oh."

Hikaru met Raiko's eyes finally and smiled. "I know you want to know more about me, but there really wasn't anything before the Organization. I have no connection to the name my parents gave me. That's why I say my real name is Hikaru, because the little girl that lived with my parents doesn't exist anymore."

"I won't ask again," Raiko said, pouring Hikaru another cup of coffee. "I guess since I already know most everything, I just wanted that little bit more."

"A man's gotta keep a secret or two. I'm sure you understand."

# The Celestial Lullaby

The thin line that bordered between life and death wove its way across the glass front of the astronaut's helmet. He sighs, and leans comfortably back against the wreckage of the buggy.

He paused, breath fogging the fractured visor.

"The moment we crashed on this godforsaken rock, I knew we were doomed. This accursed planet saw to that. But the sky is always so distracting, so glorious. It's like those poisonous frogs, the ones that are so brightly colored. Exactly like that."

The air slowly seeped from the crack in the glass, now having become a gash, enough to free the precious oxygen needed for living.

"Even now, as I'm just dying, I can't stop staring. It's so mesmerizing, so hypnotizing. I don't think I've ever noticed it that strong before. Almost like.... Like I w a n t t o.... T o s l e e p."

The unnoticeable hissing stopped, the glass slowly caving in from lack of pressure keeping the concave dome held up, and the shards littered the still face of the astronaut. His face was peaceful, his eyes open, gazing upon the flaming stars that vastly speckled the darkened sky of space.

Above him, a supernova bloomed—nature's final gift to a dying witness.

"They're doing what?" Frank's voice echoed from the adjacent pod.

"Not like *that*, you idiot! They're these 'oh... well... I don't care' types. Like our teenagers. I fucking hate them already."

"Yeah, right, Wilbert. Haven't ever met or even seen them and you already hate them. That's a perfect way to start an interstellar and interracial relationship."

"Come and have a look at this, Frank. That's some vague bullshit."

Frank shuffled over, coffee in hand. "What are you bitching about? You're getting paid to chat with aliens, man."

"But they're *aliens*, Frank. They're supposed to be cool and interesting."

"Just do your job. Answer them."

"What am I supposed to answer them?"

"Just ask them why."

Wilbert's fingers hesitated over the keyboard. "Alright then..."

*.... Why won't you come to earth? Come on, guys. It's beautiful, and it has everything you need to live. The people are nice and we have beautiful buildings with clean bathrooms and comfortable beds....*

"Don't send that!" Frank lunged, but too late.

*.... translating message.... .... submitting message.... .... expecting answer....*

The wait felt eternal.

*.... receiving answer.... .... translating answer....*

*.... Just, no.... Mars is alright. Don't try so hard to sell the earth to us. The more you try the more you lose us. I repeat: Mars is alright. Got ta go now. See you guys next week....*

Wilbert slumped in his chair, head in hands. "Great. I came here to get rid of him, and now the fucking alien version of my son comes to visit..."

Frank patted his shoulder awkwardly. "Don't worry, Wilbert. It'll be alright. It'll be alright..."
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Child

The child sparked His new beginning. The child saved the world.

The words came to Him in a faint echo from his childhood. "You can always begin again. All it takes is one act of justice."

He picked the child up out of the crib. He couldn't believe it. The lone survivor of the attack, the miraculous one. He came to the house alone. The wreckage in the streets made it almost impassable. Two guards flanked the ruined doorway. There was no one else in sight.

The infant's eyes met His—innocent, unmarked by the world's cruelty. In that gaze, He saw something He'd forgotten existed: possibility without poison.

He stood before an army unprecedented in size. Thousands upon thousands stood in formation, snow collecting on their helmets and shoulders. They were all at His command—all marched under the red and black banner. Red for blood. Black for death.

But holding this child, the banner's meaning shifted. Red for life. Black for the darkness He could choose to leave behind.

The world is a cruel place that rewards a lust for power. He didn't want the power for its own sake, but to be taken seriously, to be heard, to avenge His childhood. To be someone who mattered.

He rose through the ranks, and after a few short years He was at the top. He learned the art of charisma and plied it to his advantage. Get in front of the people and tell them what they want to hear. That is all.

Few infantrymen survived the battle—He was one. He cut his teeth on death, learned the lessons one can only learn from failing to save dying friends. The world was never the same for Him.

The world would never be the same for Him being in it.

He sat on the grassy hilltop, a child of eight or nine. He watched the town below and saw it live on without him. *People come and leave and it makes no difference*, He thought. *I will make myself vital to this world*.

The school was filled with cruel children. He was never left alone. No one befriended Him. For years He resisted, then He gave in. The taunts and blows passed over and through Him like wind through the leaves of a tree. They bent Him into a gnarled human. He grew crooked.

But this child—this child would grow straight.

He issued one command: "Stand down."
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Cycle 7213

The cursor blinks on my screen as I type frantically. My hands know the words before my mind does—muscle memory from 7,212 failed attempts.

*If you have ever gotten the feeling that somehow, somewhere, you're being watched...*

I pause. Through my apartment window, I see the black van rolling down the street. Right on schedule. They always find me within hours of going online.

But this time will be different. It *has* to be.

I discovered the organization three years ago—or was it three thousand? Time blurs when you're stuck in a loop only you remember. The Panopticon Initiative monitors everyone, catalogues everything. Most employees never question why. They just watch their assigned citizens, file reports, collect paychecks.

Until someone sees something they shouldn't.

Grand Junction. July 4, 2016. The extraction team. The family that knew too much, eliminated without hesitation. That moment broke my compliance, shattered my acceptance of "just following orders."

I fled. I exposed them online. And they found me.

Then something impossible happened: I woke up that same morning, back at my monitoring station, memories intact. At first, I thought I'd dreamed it. But the memories were too vivid, too real. When I ran again, they found me again. And again I reset.

7,212 cycles of trying to escape, to warn the world, to change *something*.

The van parks outside. I hear boots on the stairs.

My post is live now, scattered across forums and social media. In previous cycles, I tried elaborate plans—fake identities, encrypted networks, foreign countries. All failures. This time, I'm trying something simpler: raw honesty. No hiding. Just the truth, plain and desperate.

My door splinters open.

Men in tactical gear flood in, but I keep typing until the last second:

*I have to get it right eventually, right? Crap they're outside now. Here goes 7213. Wish me lu—*

The gunshot echoes.

Darkness.

Then fluorescent lights. My monitoring station. July 4, 2016, morning.

My screen shows a family in Grand Junction, going about their day.

But wait—my phone buzzes. A message from an unknown number: "We remember cycle 7213. You're not alone anymore."

Maybe this time *will* be different.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Nigerian Prince

I walked into the bank with my aide Adewale and the South African man, Matthew Kingston, who had been guarding me for the past few days in tow. Matthew rubbed his eyes.

"So there aren't any kings in Nigeria?"

"No. Nigeria's head of state is a President, and since gaining independence we have never had a Monarchy," I said flatly, trying to focus on getting my loan approved.

"But you are a Prince."

"I am the son of a powerful Tribal leader, so I guess you could say that I am a Nigerian Prince, but the term doesn't really apply."

"All those years..." He said to himself as he looked off into the distance.

"I still don't understand why we are going to a Bank," Adewale said crossly.

"Where else would we go to get a loan of this magnitude?"

"We should go to a private citizen! Banks are businesses that will try and weasel us out of our land just like the mining companies!"

"What are we going to do, Ade? Send out a bunch of emails to gullible Americans looking for get-rich-quick schemes? No. That will never work." I gestured emphatically. "We will go to the Bank, explain that there are many diamonds on our ancestral lands, but we need a loan for legal representation and equipment so that we can get the Company off our land and start mining ourselves!"

"He is right, Ade. Banks will see the potential rewards," Matthew added.

"Oh, I suppose you're right." Adewale sighed, adjusting his briefcase. "What kind of person would believe such a crazy story of a Nigerian Prince needing money?"

Matthew suddenly went pale, staring at nothing.

I smiled grimly as we approached the loan officer's desk, the irony not lost on any of us.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Meeting at McGill's

The bartender frowned. The man in front of him had a tattered jacket, a necklace with some odd medallion, and a story that just cried out "trouble." 

The man took another shot of whiskey. "I had it, it was right in my hand." He mumbled, going through a thin notebook with a single bullet hole in it—a hand-drawn map, clippings of various encyclopedias, and a painting of Christ with a sphere.

"And what was that, buddy?" The tender wiped at a glass.

"Something owned by kings and men of power. A device older—"

"And why are you here?"

"Because my next hint at where I need to be is at THIS bar."

"Wait, hold up. Who are you supposed to be? Why would your problems deal with my bar?"

The man stood up and checked his notebook. "Nathan Drake. And this pub was a site of meetings during the Revolution. Things are coming to a head, and it all points here." He tapped his fists against the bar top.

He stepped away, to the bartender's protests. Going through his notebook, he wandered into a study in the back, pushing past a crowd. An old bookshelf. Drake gave it a once-over, then peered about the room.

A man entered, his head shrouded by his jacket hood. He glanced at the bookshelf—and he saw an unnatural glow.

Drake turned, pocketing his journal. "Had a feeling you were close, Mr. Drake." He removed his hood, revealing a slightly scarred face.

"You—" Drake clenched a fist. "Where'd you take it?"

He scowled. "What?"

"The Apple!" Drake thumbed through his journal.

"I— You're only aware of part of the story, man! This is about—"

"Eden—the civilization that came before?"

"No—" the man gave an exasperated sigh. "I'm trying to save the world!"

"How can I believe you?"

"It's on the stairwell behind this shelf. Trust me. I'll try to explain everything. My name is Desmond. We can work together."
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# My God!

Lord and savior, stave and shield, bread and water! The lucidity is intoxicating. Every color a wash of energy, every movement a dance of grace, every sound a whisper of love. 

They walk past me as soldiers. Warrior ants of today and decorative corpses of tomorrow. Sheepskin suits and cowhide satchels protect their skin as wireless phones launch their missiles over towered airwaves.

This is what His only son felt as he hung from the cross—but without the pain, without the pain! The enlivening madness of clarity only an untouched voyeur can feel.

They toss ill-gotten silver at my feet and entice me with scraps of bread and flesh, but I do not succumb to their drunken entreaties. I lay firmly planted on the sidewalk of dreams as the world of the dead marches by.

I am the only real man alive.

The cardboard beneath me grows damp. A woman hesitates, then hurries past.

Tomorrow, I'll feel the pain.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Summoning

"10... 9... 8... 7..." we all chanted in unison.

The countdown at 4:19 PM on April 20th had become sacred tradition. Joints raised like champagne flutes, lighters flickering like birthday candles.

"3... 2... 1... Zero!"

Sweet smoke curled through the apartment as reality softened at its edges. James, channeling his inner Keanu, dropped the fact about Hitler's birthday. The conversation spiraled into absurdity—Hitler versus kangaroo debates, time travel paradoxes.

Then the explosion.

Electrical fire scorched a perfect circle into my carpet. Through the smoke emerged a naked, crouching figure. When he lifted his head, that unmistakable face—the face from a thousand history textbooks—grinned at us.

"Jemand sagte meinen Namen zum zehntausendfachen Mal," Hitler said, his voice cutting through our haze.

My joint fell from my fingers.

He stood, naked and unashamed, chest puffed out. "Deine Kleider, gib sie mir."

"Dude," James whispered, "this naked guy looks like Hitler."

"Because it IS Hitler!" I hissed, but my friends were already scrambling, grabbing clothes with the helpful obliviousness of the extremely high.

Hitler examined the YOLO t-shirt we'd given him. "Was bedeutet 'YOLO' bedeuten?"

But he didn't wait for translation. With terrifying purpose, he strode toward my apartment door.

"Wait!" I lunged forward, but my THC-soaked reflexes were glacial. "We can't let Hitler loose in 2024!"

The door slammed. Through the window, I watched history's greatest monster descend the stairs, wearing cargo shorts and a YOLO shirt, ready to discover smartphones, social media, and a world he'd never imagined.

James took another hit. "Should we... call someone?"

"Who?" I asked. "Ghostbusters?"

We'd literally summoned Hitler with stoned conversation. No one would believe us.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Transformation

The bass thrummed through the crowded nightclub as he stalked his prey. Cold, calculating eyes locked onto the woman at the bar. She was perfect—alone, distracted, vulnerable.

He slithered through the mass of bodies, his sleeveless leather jacket revealing a tapestry of crude ink. Gang symbols. Prison memories. Stories written in pain and violence.

The crack pipe emerged briefly, a quick hit to steady his nerves. The rush exploded through his synapses, sharpening everything to a razor's edge. His hand slipped into his jacket, fingers closing around the small packet. Just a few drops in her drink. She wasn't even looking.

"Bill?"

He froze. The voice came from his left, cutting through the fog of narcotic focus.

"The hell did you just call me?" he snarled, turning toward the interruption.

A young man stood there, smiling. "Bill, it's Malcolm! Man, you look rough."

"I don't know who the hell you think I am, but you'd better step off, muthafucka'!"

"Bill, here." The young man extended something. "Try this."

Against his better judgment, the gangster looked down. New Jell-O Pudding with Snickers. What the...?

"You're not yourself when you're hungry," Malcolm said earnestly.

The gangster took a bite, more from confusion than anything else. Suddenly, warmth spread through him. His leather jacket transformed into a cozy sweater. His aggressive stance softened into a gentle shuffle.

"Thanks, Theo!" he heard himself say in an entirely different voice.

"It's Malcolm," the young man sighed.

*There's always room for JELL-O, now powered with SNICKERS! SNICKERS: Satisfies your hunger!*
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Amendment

I'm sitting around the small table. It was a small venue when compared to the pure amount of knowledge in the room. I was sitting with the heads of media, the writers of history books, and overall the 15 to 20 people who had the largest influence on the spread of knowledge for the last generation.

"Gentlemen and Madams. The Administration is going to be making serious *amendments* to several of your publications. I am also, in an unofficial way, asking you to consider adding some suggestions to make the state seem a bit more... idealistic."

The room erupted with various individuals all opposing what the Government was proposing. But men started coming in through the doors. I had picked these men personally, not for their ability to intimidate, but I felt the writers and historians in the group would still understand the message.

The men didn't wear any sort of uniform—various apparel in shades of gray, brown, and dirty blues covered them. But the black bags each held were soft and visibly silky.

"Gentlemen. You've all told your stories. Now we shall tell ours. Will you share your voice with the state?"

There were few movements or noises through the room.

"Good. Doubleplusgood."

The word hung in the air like poison. One by one, I watched their expressions change—from defiance to understanding, from understanding to resignation. History, I realized, belonged to whoever controlled the present.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Veteran

The afternoon light filtered through the nursing home window, casting gentle shadows across my weathered hands. The young woman across from me, all bright eyes and earnest curiosity, tapped her stylus against her tablet.

"We always thought it was bad, you know.... War. Horrible, tasteless events that lasted years and cost countless lives," I began, my voice carrying the weight of decades.

She nodded eagerly, recording every word. "Sometimes I wish I could have been around to see it, or hear it or something. The movies can only show so much..."

I held up a trembling hand. "No, you don't. Take it from someone who lived it. It is not something you ever want to experience."

Her face fell slightly, properly chastened.

"War was humanity's blunt instrument," I continued. "We covered conspiracies and base greed with patriotic fervor. We fought over resources, ideology, wounded pride. Millions of lives lost at the whim of men in offices."

"Then came the Event—twenty years ago this month. Every weapon simply... stopped working. Bullets bounced off skin. Bombs became duds. Overnight, violence became impossible."

Her eyes widened. "The Invulnerability Phenomenon."

"The government tried to hide it, justify their military budgets. But you can't hide something that fundamental. Defense? Offense? Meaningless concepts when no one could harm another."

I smiled then, remembering. "For the first time in millennia, we had to revert to what common sense always dictated when we disagreed with our brothers and sisters."

"And what would that be?" she whispered.

"Talk. We went back to talking. And listening. Remarkable what you can accomplish when violence isn't an option."

She sat back, her tablet forgotten, understanding finally dawning.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Fill It Up

The body was heavy. Heavier than he remembered bodies being, but then again, the cement helped with that. Chuck of cement sewn up in her stomach—fill her up, fill her up. It is full now.

He must pay.

No, wait. Wrong pronoun. *I* must pay. The gas. I must pay for the gas.

He turns himself to the neon orange gas station. A trashy glowing beacon in backwater country. He leaves the pump in the car, and the body in trunk to enter the building.

The metal bones inside of his body shift out of place as he walks. He stops for a moment to pop them into place. When they put the bones into him they did bad, rushed work. He can hear them jingle against one another with every move he makes.

He pays for his gas. The cashier takes his money. The bones of his fingers rattle as he collects his change. The cashier does not hear it.

The car is warm. He turns on the heat and makes it warmer. The pedals at his feet are magic. Just a small tap and he is propelled down the interstate at sixty miles per hour. An hour. An hour.

The interstate has no lamps to light the way. The headlights of the car flicker every few moments. The car is on its last legs. He is not ready to find a new car yet, however. He likes this one.

He rolls the car off road, gently, gently. It can not take much abuse. He follows old tire marks down a gently sloping hill. The car stops alongside a stagnant pond.

It is easy to roll the body into the pond. It falls with a plunk sound that is pleasing to his ears.

He sits on the hood of the car and stares at the sky. The stars are easily visible this far away from the city. He has done everything they have asked. They have not signaled that they are pleased, but they must be.

He sits and waits for them to take him back home.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Fall of Sister Clarice

The fluorescent lights of the interrogation room cast harsh shadows across Detective Martinez's weathered face as he reviewed the case file one more time. Sister Clarice. Even the name seemed absurd now.

Six months ago, she'd been the tri-county area's sweetheart—the nun who moonlighted as a rodeo clown, bringing joy to children's birthday parties with elaborate piñata ceremonies. Martinez had seen the photos: Clarice in full clown regalia, surrounded by laughing kids, their parents beaming in the background.

Now those same parents couldn't sleep at night.

The investigation had unraveled like a cheap sweater. First came the wallet sweatshop discovery—elderly residents at Sunset Meadows Home forced to stitch leather goods sixteen hours daily. Then the bodies started surfacing. Seven confirmed victims. Twelve still missing.

But it was Clarice's double life that truly disturbed Martinez. By day: holy woman and children's entertainer. By night: the Hooters regular so convincing in her drunken debauchery that customers tipped her, confided their darkest fantasies, treated her like staff.

The chase had been... memorable. Officers still attended counseling. Watching a sixty-three-year-old nun strip while fleeing through downtown wasn't in anyone's training manual.

Martinez closed the file as his partner entered.

"She's asking for you," Officer Chen said quietly. "Says her 'body of work speaks for itself.'"

Martinez sighed. In the holding cell, Clarice sat humming a nursery rhyme, that same unsettling smile plastered across her face.

Some mysteries, he realized, weren't meant to be understood—only contained.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Went for a bit of a different approach, hope thats ok? I'm new here.

Wordless in our search for food, only spattering sounds of tiny claws on concrete. The terrible giants are certainly gone for the time being, as even the haunting glow of the noise box has ceased for the night. 

There are a few sources in the air tonight, but we remember to beware that nutty, woody smell. The lightning snap that snatched up our brother and soaked his fur with the dark ooze within was well renowned in our family; none of us would ever let our hunger betray us to the same end. 

No, tonight our noses guide us amongst the fuzzy and funky stinks that had been haphazardly left strewn about. Suddenly, gold! The olfactory glory drew us scampering towards the source. Atop the hard, irregular rectangle, and sunken into the white circles therein lie the holy grail. The shards of a chocolate cookie crumbled carelessly across what is now a shrine to our fickle overlords. 

We feasted on the crumbs with revelrous fervor, digging into those circular dimples of the plastic box, when suddenly, all was alight. Thundering footsteps, and then, a shriek from Karen. 

"MOM! THERE'S A MOUSE IN THE BASEMENT ON MY VIDEO TAPE!" 

Damn.

---

*Word count: 215*

*Author's note: Welcome! This perspective shift is absolutely brilliant—viewing our mundane human world through the eyes of foraging mice transforms the ordinary into something mysterious and poetic. The "lightning snap" mousetrap and cookie-covered VHS tape are wonderfully realized details.*
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Artist's Canvas

I've never understood why they call me a villain.

A villain chooses cruelty. I was given a sacred duty, woven into my very essence before my first breath. Death isn't my passion—it's my *purpose*. Still, I'd be lying if I said there wasn't something beautifully meditative about the work. Each passing is unique, a snowflake of mortality I preserve perfectly in memory.

But *her*... she haunts me differently.

Twenty-three. Porcelain skin like fine china. Hair the color of wheat in summer sun. Those pale blue eyes—God, those *eyes*—watching me with something beyond fear as the light dimmed. Understanding? Recognition? In that eternal instant before the end, we *knew* each other.

The news said I'd "mutilated" her. What pedestrian language for what I created. The patterns across her skin weren't violence—they were *art*. Intricate, deliberate, profound. A symphony written in flesh that only I could truly appreciate.

Sometimes I wonder if that connection I felt was real, or if I'm simply desperate to believe my nature serves some higher meaning. That these "atrocities" I'm condemned to commit are somehow beautiful.

But when I close my eyes, I still see her face. That moment of understanding.

And I shiver.

Perhaps that makes me the villain they claim I am after all.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Guardian's Final Solution

They said that I would be a guardian of sorts, keeping humanity going as long as there was a humanity to keep going. As long as there were more than 1 billion people, I would be there to guide them.

I knew what the job entailed. I knew exactly what I was signing up for.

Or at least, I thought I did.

The problem wasn't boredom or loneliness. I kept myself going just fine for thousands of years. The problem was that even when humanity dropped to 900 million, and then 500 million, and then 100 million, and even when they died out altogether, I kept going.

Because I know something now that I didn't know before: time is not linear. And there are always more people.

I'm not sure when I figured that out. I personally kept going straight forward through time, through the barren wastelands that were Earth and her colonies. The infinite timelines stretched before me like a web—each one containing humanity's rise and inevitable fall.

There was only one solution.

When you have enough time, it's not impossible to learn all that there is to know of chemistry, physics, and engineering. When you have enough time, it's not impossible to devise a way to travel back to the beginning.

It's not impossible to find a way to end everything before it starts.

I stand now at the precipice of creation itself, my hand on the switch. In every timeline, humanity suffers. In every timeline, they fail.

But a guardian protects.

And I have all the time in the world.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Morning After

White. Just white. It took me a moment to realize that I was actually staring at a wall. I turned around and found Dennis, naked and struggling on the sofa. I think he was trying to sit up. The fridge was open, door still swinging, its light shining on a pile of broken bottles on the floor.

"Eh ya okay, babe?" Dennis slurred, speaking vaguely toward the direction of the fridge.

"Yeah," I said. Well, that's what I tried to say, but my throat didn't agree, so it came out as more of a "ee-ahh," too quiet and raspy to be heard.

"Babe?" Dennis craned his neck and squinted his eyes, apparently trying to find me by the fridge. "Y'there?"

My back suddenly felt cold. I was also naked, I realized. Wasn't I with Dennis just now? Unconsciously, I reached up and touched my shoulder, where Dennis always placed his hand when we cuddled. It wasn't there. Of course it wasn't there—I was looking at him. But why did it feel like it was?

"Hey." My voice came out fine this time.

Dennis whipped his head around and laughed, "Whoa, how'd ya get over there?"

I opened my mouth, then closed it. How *did* I get over here? I was just settling in on the sofa with Dennis, wasn't I? Did I fall asleep and sleepwalk over here?

"Well, whatever. I heard a crash and woke up. Thought you dropped something at the fridge." He smiled his boyish smile, blue eyes twinkling and settling on something in my hand. "You gonna share that?"

I was confused for a brief moment before realizing that I had been clutching a bottle of hard cider.

"Yeah," I answered, and made my way toward Dennis, still feeling dazed. I swear I was just on the sofa. Did I really grab a cider in my sleep?

"Mmm, yummy!" Dennis purred, wrapping his arms around my waist as I sat down and nuzzling into my lower back. I smiled.

Discussions about my apparently newfound sleepwalking disorder can wait until tomorrow morning.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Patriots

The marble floor runs red with his blood. Even in death, he looks regal, one hand still reaching toward the golden crown that would have crowned our doom.

"What have we done?" Marcus whispers beside me, his dagger trembling in his grip.

"What we had to," I reply, though my own hands shake. The cheering crowds outside still echo through the Senate halls, unaware their hero lies dying before his throne.

He coughs, blood on his lips, and his eyes find mine. There's no surprise there, only disappointment. "Brutus," he rasps. "You... you truly believed..."

"I believed in the republic," I say, kneeling beside him despite myself. "The republic you swore to serve."

A bitter smile crosses his face. "The republic... was already dead. I... merely offered them... a better dream."

"A dream of tyranny."

"A dream of order." His breathing grows shallow. "They would have... chosen me. Every time. You think... you saved something. You saved nothing... but chaos."

The crown gleams mockingly between us, close enough to touch. He sees me looking at it.

"Go ahead," he whispers. "Take it. Rule them. You'll see... how heavy it truly is."

"I don't want to rule. I want us to be free."

"Then you're... a fool." His eyes glaze over, but his final words cut deep. "They'll hate you... for this. Not today... not tomorrow... but history... will remember me as great... and you... as murderer."

The accusation dies with him.

Outside, someone screams. The crowd has learned. Already, I hear the word spreading, mutating, becoming something twisted.

"Traitors!"

"They killed him!"

"Tyrants!"

Marcus looks at me, terror in his eyes. "They loved him more than freedom."

I nod slowly, understanding the terrible truth.

We saved the republic.

But the republic no longer wanted to be saved.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Bridges and Walls

She found him building a stone wall around his heart, mortar mixed with old wounds.

"Why fortify what could open?" she asked.

"Protection," he whispered.

Instead of scaling his barriers, she sat beside them, sharing stories through the cracks. Her fingertips traced patterns in the dust—not demanding entry, but offering presence.

Weeks passed. His hands, calloused from construction, began dismantling what fear had built. Each removed stone became a stepping stone between them.

They built a bridge instead—imperfect, swaying, theirs alone. Not the fairy tale society sketched, but something sturdier: forged from honest confessions at 3 AM, laughter that cracked through darkness, and the terrifying thrill of being truly seen.

Their love story wasn't written in grand declarations but in the daily choice to remain, even when staying felt impossible.

Some bridges are worth the crossing.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Art of Comfort

Marco polished the mahogany bar with practiced precision, his silver-streaked hair catching the amber glow of overhead lights. Twenty years behind this counter had taught him more about humanity than any university degree could offer.

"2 cl ananas juice, 3 cl Bacardi Razz, a handful of brown sugar, a cut lime on top and voilá: the Red Sunday cocktail is nearly finished."

His trainee, a nervous young man named Thomas, watched with furrowed concentration.

"Now we will pour in some grapefruit syrup, which sinks to the bottom of the glass and gives this cocktail its traditional name. Look closely!"

Marco demonstrated the stirring motion with fluid grace. "You have to stir the drink with a slim metal spoon like this. The border of the still separate syrup and juice will mix and add sweetness to the whole drink. You could optionally leave the last step out and give the customer the choice of mixing it—"

He paused, catching Thomas's eye. "—but we are mixing the drink here. To be a barkeeper isn't just a job, it's analyzing and understanding your customer. If you don't understand them, how should they feel comfortable in your surroundings? **Why** should they, when they have to do the work you are paid for?"

The bell above the door chimed softly.

"Always do your job and do your job right. For instance: Do you see the old lady who just entered?"

Marco gestured toward two wine glasses. "What glass would you give her?"

Thomas looked bewildered. "Does it make a difference?"

"**Naturally** it does! A woman of higher age gets wrinkles under her chin. A high, slender glass forces her head back, exposing them. The small, wide glass respects her dignity."

Marco raised his finger, eyes twinkling with conviction.

"Comfort. It's all about the comfort."

text:
# Across the Ages

The marketplace buzzed with life, but all I saw was her—the way sunlight caught in her dark hair, the familiar tilt of her head. My heart stopped.

"I thought that was you, Love!"

She turned, hair flowing in the gentle breeze. I ran forward, decades of searching collapsing into this single moment.

"¿Nos conocemos?" Her voice trembled with confusion.

"Amor, it's me! Don't you recognize me? Is it the beard? It's probably the bea—"

"Lo siento, pero ¿quién es usted? Yo no te conozco." Distrust clouded her eyes.

My throat tightened. "Amor, it's me, Cassius. I've been searching for you for years! We were supposed to meet where we first found each other. Where have you been?"

She shook her head and turned away, confusion trailing behind her like a shadow.

"Verena, where are you going?"

"Déjame. Busco a mi querido. No tengo tiempo para estar gastando." Each word pierced deeper than any blade.

She was forgetting herself. Forgetting *us*.

"Verena, ¿has olvidado tu primer beso bajo la pálida luna, hace tantos años? ¿Te acuerdas de la sensación de la mano acariciando tu cara? ¿Te acuerdas de mi promesa de cuidarte y amarte para siempre?"

She froze.

I rushed forward, wrapping my arms around her from behind, my face pressed against her neck. "Forgive me, love. I tried so hard to find you, but you were nowhere to be found. I'm sorry it's taken me this long."

"Cassius..." Her voice broke.

My hand found her cheek, brushing away a single tear. She turned, and our lips met—a promise kept across lifetimes, finally fulfilled.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Stand

Bill wondered if he had gone to church together with his wife. In this southern town, not being in a church was still frowned upon, but Bill didn't really care. No, he thought. Truth be told, he was born an unbeliever. He tried his entire life to fit in, to believe what his parents told him, but he couldn't any more than he could sprout wings and fly.

He looked out the window. The sun smiled down full of Schadenfreude, while Bill smiled back up. At least his wife and daughter were in a better place.

"Y'all need Jesus," he was told once, but he never felt like he needed any supernatural help in his life, not even now. He was always a man that took responsibility for his actions, and strove to solve his problems with hard work. He knew he was far from perfect, but if anyone should pay for his mistakes, Bill preferred it to be himself.

Dots in the sky grew into unmistakable forms: The Angels had finally arrived.

Bill stood up and grabbed his double-barreled shotgun. As not only an atheist, but also as a northerner, he had many disagreements with the inhabitants of this sleepy southern town, but on the question of gun rights, he had always been of the opinion that he wanted everything he needed to protect himself and his own.

He loaded it and stepped outside.

The streets were completely empty, except for the Angels going from house to house looking for survivors. Fools. They could run, but they couldn't hide.

But Bill was not in the mood for running or hiding right now. If he was gonna go down, he was gonna stir up some shit before he did.

He raised his shotgun skyward and chambered a round.

"Come get some," he muttered.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Unconventional Historian

Father Gregory O'Learey surveyed his graduate seminar with the practiced eye of someone who'd spent decades wrangling skeptical academics. Francis Williams, the redhead in the corner, seemed the most attentive—a good sign.

"Roman Britain," O'Learey continued, ignoring the barely concealed sighs. "You're wondering why we're starting centuries before Ireland's historical troubles. Bear with me."

He reached beneath the lectern and, to the class's alarm, withdrew not a saber but a worn leather journal. "This belonged to my great-grandfather, who fought in the Easter Rising. But to understand why he stood in the GPO in 1916, we must understand what the Romans *didn't* do."

The room quieted.

"They never conquered Ireland. Hibernia remained free while Britain bent knee. This isn't Irish romanticism—it's the seed of everything that followed. The psychology of a people never subdued versus those who accommodated empire."

Francis raised his hand. "Father, isn't that oversimplifying?"

O'Learey's eyes twinkled. "Absolutely, Mr. Williams. By the end of this semester, you'll write a twenty-page paper explaining exactly how wrong I am. But first, you need to understand the myth before you can deconstruct it."

He opened the journal, revealing faded Gaelic script.

"History isn't just dates and battles. It's stories people tell themselves about who they are. The Romans gave Britain roads and aqueducts. They gave Ireland something more dangerous—the story of resistance."

The condescending chuckles had stopped. Father O'Learey had them now.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Wind's Whisper

They say the wind on a bridge whispers different things to different people. To me, it screams in laughter.

My fingers grip the lottery ticket tighter as another gust threatens to rip it away. Fifty million dollars. The paper feels impossibly light—lighter than my life ever did.

I think about calling someone. But who? Reddit friends who know my username better than my real name? Sarah, now happy in Portland with Jake, posting couple photos I force myself to like? 

The cruel irony isn't lost on me. I finally won something, and I've already lost everything that matters.

Below, the water churns dark and indifferent. The wind howls louder, and I close my eyes against it. In this moment of supposed contemplation, I realize something: I'm not thinking about the money at all. I'm thinking about my seventh birthday, when Mom made chocolate cake. About the way Sarah laughed at my stupid jokes. About the digital hug emoji my Discord friend sent yesterday.

The ticket slips from my fingers—whether by accident or intention, I'm not sure. It spirals down, down, down into nothing.

I step back from the edge.

Sometimes the wind doesn't push you off.

Sometimes it pushes you back.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Midnight in My Kitchen

The full moon glowed through my apartment window as I felt the familiar tingling begin. *Here we go again.*

First came the fangs—vampire side arriving fashionably early. Then the fur sprouted along my arms—werewolf joining the party. Finally, my skin took on that distinctive grayish pallor—zombie making its undead appearance.

I stumbled to the mirror. "Great. I'm a werepire zombie. Again."

My stomach growled with three distinctly different hungers. The vampire in me craved blood. The werewolf demanded meat. The zombie? Well, brains, obviously.

Then inspiration struck. Why fight my three natures when I could *feed* them all at once?

I yanked open my recipe journal—the one I'd been keeping since this whole "supernatural trifecta" thing started—and began scribbling: **Unholy Stromboli**.

At 2 AM, I raided the 24-hour grocery for kibble (the wolf approved), then hit my butcher's back entrance for blood and brains (he'd stopped asking questions months ago).

In my kitchen, I worked like a possessed Top Chef contestant. Browning the brains carefully—crispy outside, enzymey inside. Blending blood and kibble into a surprisingly cohesive paste. Wrapping everything in dough like the world's most disturbing present.

Ten minutes at 375°F, and my masterpiece emerged.

I took a bite. The vampire sighed contentedly at the blood-soaked dough. The werewolf wagged an imaginary tail at the kibble flavors. The zombie practically purred at the brain texture.

"It's like Beef Wellington," I mumbled through my mouthful, "if Wellington was *deeply cursed*."

I quickly snapped a photo for my monster cooking blog: *Creature Comforts Kitchen*.

Being an unholy abomination had never tasted so good.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Unforgivable

The words hung in the air between us like a toxic cloud.

Amy's face went through a series of transformations—shock, disgust, vindication, and finally, a cold hardness I'd never seen before.

"There it is," she said quietly, her voice shaking. "Ten years. Ten *years* I've been waiting to hear you admit it."

I felt my face burning. "Amy, I was young and stupid and—"

"You were twenty-eight!" she screamed. "You had a college degree! You knew *exactly* what you were doing!"

A few passersby had stopped to watch. I wanted to disappear into the sidewalk.

"I've changed," I pleaded. "I'm not that person anymore. I've spent a decade trying to make up for it, volunteering, donating, actually *listening* to people instead of—"

"Good for you," she said, her voice dripping with sarcasm. "You want a cookie? You want me to pat you on the head and tell you you're one of the good ones now?"

"No, I just—"

"You voted for him *twice*," she said, and I saw tears forming in her eyes. "After everything we talked about. After I told you what it would mean for people like me. After I *begged* you to reconsider."

The memory came flooding back—us in her apartment, her crying, me defensive and stubborn, convinced I knew better.

"I know," I whispered. "I'm so sorry."

"Your apology doesn't undo the damage," she said. "It doesn't bring back the people who died. It doesn't restore the rights that were lost. It doesn't heal the wounds that are still bleeding."

She turned away one final time.

"Goodbye," she said. "And this time, I actually mean forever."

I watched her disappear into the crowd, knowing she was right about everything.

text:
# The Walnut Tree's Lament

Ow.... what the hell was that? It felt like a bird running into me, but it felt like it had blades and all sorts of stuff on it. Oh god, now there's something on my trunk trying to get it. If only a breeze could by and shake whatever it is that's in my branches loose so whoever is scratching up my fresh new spring bark would give it a rest already. 

Oh not another one, there's another one of those things with the legs trying to climb up my trunk. Where the hell are those squirrels when you need them? During the fall they're always so "oh hey Mr. Walnut Tree, let me just rummage through your branches and take all your stuff so I can go hide it from you." Don't they understand I don't have eyes? It doesn't matter if they hide them; once they take them from me, I won't be able to find them regardless!

Here comes a breeze! Oh please wind, shake whatever this thing is out of my branches and make these trunk-climbing bastards leave.... Almost out.... aaaand.... 

GAAAH FUCK, MY BRANCHES! THEY FUCKING CHOPPED OFF MY BRANCH! AAAAAHHHH! If you impatient bastards could have waited just a few weeks, it would have been out in no time! But no, you crazy little things had to go and chop it down!

*The kite drifted down with the severed branch, while the children ran off laughing.*
