text:
# The Weight of Forever

He stood there in the hospital room, motionless, his eyes fixed on the young girl lying on the cot. A tear rolled down his face and he started to cry. He wanted to reach out and hold her hand. He wanted to say goodbye. He couldn't.

The young girl lay still, unmoving, but she was still alive.

The man, a father of three, had discovered a secret about himself. When he stood still, all time would stop, and the slower he moved, the slower time crawled along. As a university professor teaching mathematics, he would use this gift to work on famous problems. He thought his gift was rather useless in other ways, until he received a phone call late one evening.

It was from the hospital. His oldest daughter had been in an automotive accident. Come quickly, they said.

When he arrived, he saw his daughter on the bed. His little girl. You wouldn't recognize her from a photo. The accident was too severe, but he knew it was her. The doctors were telling him how sorry they were, how she wouldn't be here much longer.

He pushed past them to stand beside her. As he stood still, he could feel time slowing to a stop.

"I can stand here, and she'll never die," he thought.

So he stood, and stood.

He stood for what felt like centuries—watching the single raindrop frozen on the window, the dust motes suspended in lamplight, the unchanging numbers on her monitor. His muscles screamed. His heart ached with a pain that transcended the physical.

Until his body finally collapsed.

The doctors thought the sight of his daughter must have caused his heart to fail, not knowing the true length of time he stood there.

Crying.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Patch Notes

Dr. Sarah Chen stared at her monitor, coffee halfway to her lips, as the email loaded. The subject line read: "MANDATORY FIRMWARE UPDATE - HOMO SAPIENS v2.3.1"

"This has to be a joke," she muttered.

But then her left arm—the *new* one sprouting from her ribs—reached out and grabbed her stapler with unsettling efficiency while her original hands continued typing.

Down the hall, screaming.

Sarah ran toward the sound, her two new hind legs propelling her forward with alarming speed. She nearly crashed into Tom from Accounting, who was writhing on the floor.

"My pancreas!" he wailed. "I can feel it dissolving!"

The hospital became chaos within hours. Patients arrived with third arms flailing uncontrollably. Teenage boys discovered leather belts fused to their waists. Sarah's childhood friend Marcus called, ecstatic that his HIV had mysteriously vanished—but terrified of the eyeballs that now saw into the ultraviolet spectrum, complete with tiny brains inside them.

Sarah pulled up the email again, hands shaking. The sender address: DM/sys@mkak.com. She typed a frantic reply: "WHO ARE YOU? UNDO THIS!"

The response came instantly:

"Thank you for contacting Divine Mechanics. Your body is important to us. Unfortunately, rollbacks are not supported. However, we're pleased to announce that the Gills & Photosynthesis expansion pack will be available next quarter! Upgrade now for early access."

Sarah looked at her three arms.

Humanity had finally received its update.

Nobody had asked for it.

text:
# The Erasure

"Are you sure you want to do this?" she asks.

"I'm sure," I say. "I've thought it through."

She frowns a little, and her eyes show the slightest tinge of disapproval. "You'd be erasing your identity."

*That* again. She always has to bring it up.

"I told you, I don't care," I say. I'm getting aggravated. "I'm going through with this. You should know by now, I can't live with this. The way I am. You get what I'm saying."

But she doesn't. She never has, and she never will. She'll never know how I feel, to look down and see a bulky frame and broad shoulders, struggling to continue on, crying myself to sleep. She'll never know disgust at my own body, loathing of my every existence.

She could, but she won't. She wouldn't go that far to understand me.

"Alright," she says, admitting defeat. "If that's what you want."

It *is* what I want. Again, she doesn't understand.

"But you know," she continues, "there have been advances in medicine, and—"

"I've made my decision. Just leave me alone."

"Alright," she says. She glances at me for a moment, one single agonizing moment, and leaves.

It's time.

I close my eyes, and I feel it happening. A buzzing, not in my body, but in my mind, a humming whisper that resonates deep within. It lasts just a minute, and I slowly open my eyes.

I look in the mirror, taking in my reflection.

Nothing has changed. I am still six foot nine. My shoulders are still three times the width of my head. My face is angular and strong, with a rectangular jaw covered in beard shadow. I don't check, but I still have a penis. I am, and always will be undeniably male.

For the first time, I feel nothing at all.

Everything is wonderful.

The dysphoria is gone—not the body, but the *feeling*. The neural pattern that screamed *wrong* has been silenced. She was right: I've erased my identity. But what she'll never understand is that the pain was my identity, and now I'm finally free.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Blade's Whisper

The darkness is growing stronger. No longer can he resist its pull, its alluring beauty. Something so maniacal, so destructive has become a fascinating thought lingering in his already damaged mind.

He was attracted to it, enthralled by the blade.

In his past, he stated he would never go that far. Yet here he is—ready. Willing. He embraced his newfound love, held the blade so close that he bled as the steel penetrated his body.

He said he would never do this, that falling into the temptations of darkness was weakness. Now it's reversed. Following through with what the dark thoughts command is strength. He was strong enough to do this. Strong enough to embrace the blade.

He wasn't being weak for giving into the darkness. He was strong for escaping the light.

Now clouds loom overhead, casting dark shadows on his lifeless body. Pools of crimson form on the meadow grass as blood drains from him, seeping into the earth like a final offering.

The darkness moves on, searching for a new being to consume. A new soul to bring into utter chaos, into a self-destructive tirade. The blade follows, gleaming despite the shadows, searching for a new being to take, new blood to drink.

It whispers promises of strength to those who hurt.

It always finds someone listening.

text:
# The Last Can

I stare at my phone, thumb hovering over the send button. The message sits there, accusatory and rambling and maybe a little too honest. Two hundred characters that say everything except what I actually mean.

Delete it. You should delete it.

But I don't.

Because Maya *does* steal my Diet Coke. Every single time. She waltzes into my apartment with those impossibly long legs and that crooked smile, opens my fridge like she pays rent here, and takes whatever she wants. And when I protest—weakly, pathetically—she just laughs and says something brilliant about Derrida or makes some obscure literary reference that shouldn't be hot but absolutely is.

The glitter Sharpies were a joke. Except they weren't, because I actually used them. I wrote MY NAME in sparkly purple letters, and she *still* took it, grinning while maintaining direct eye contact.

I hit send before I can overthink it.

Three dots appear immediately.

*"On my way. Should I bring regular Coke too, or are we finally admitting what this is?"*

My heart hammers against my ribs.

I type back: *"Just bring yourself."*

text:
# The Sleep Merchant

My client had the pinched, pale look which they all had. Corporate drones, constantly swiping the keys on their screens in the purgatory world of wakefulness. They came to me for relief.

He grasped the flask and took a careful swig as I anointed his forehead with lavender essence, a banned relaxant I had acquired on the black market.

"Drink." I motioned to the flask.

The man's eyes darted left to right, his hand twitched nervously. I guided the flask to his lips.

"Drink." I repeated.

The man eyed me warily as he downed the chamomile mixture. I opened the hatch to the sensory deprivation tank. The cool, clean water lay still. The unit was scratched and tattered from being hastily hidden. But it was a chamber of absolute relief.

No one who entered it came out the same. It was like being reborn.

"You have exactly eight hours."

The man handed me an envelope and I checked the holographic credit card. I nodded.

"Goodnight."

The man started at the unfamiliar word. And then he smiled at me and slid into the tank.

I closed the lid, popped a pill into my mouth, and stood watchful. Eight hours. That's all anyone could afford anymore—a brief escape from the mandated wakefulness, from the productivity quotas.

Outside, sirens wailed. Sleep enforcement patrols.

I'd give him his eight hours. Even if it cost me everything.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# When People Find Out My Girlfriend is 91

When people find out my girlfriend is 91, they always look at me like I hit my head. If they'd ask, I'd reply, "Of course I did!" Best thing that ever happened to me.

Five months ago, I was walking down the street, minding my own business, when a whole building collapsed and fell on top of me. I spent five months in a coma, but other than that, not a scar was left on my body.

Except I woke up, got discharged from the hospital, and promptly noticed there were no old people in the world.

I was scared at first. Didn't know what was going on. But I managed to get used to it. And it's been amazing.

I'm not good looking, in great shape, or rich. I'm not even funny. You can imagine the state of my love life before. I accepted the thought I was going to be forever alone.

But now the situation is completely different.

So yes, my girlfriend is 91, but I look at her and see an 18-year-old girl. Nothing makes me think of her real age, except the meds in the bathroom cabinet.

Sometimes I wonder if anyone else sees what I see, or if they just think I'm crazy. But honestly? I don't care anymore. The building that fell on me gave me a second chance at happiness—and I'm taking it.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Clever Coward

I stand at the edge of civilization, watching the Amulet of Geistheart tumble into the Five Year Gorge, its silver chain glinting as it spirals down into darkness. Already, I hear the otherworldly shrieks of the Geist behind me, their rage palpable.

The first one crests the hill—a twisted shadow with too many limbs. It doesn't even pause. The moment it sees the Amulet falling, it launches itself over the edge without hesitation. Another follows. Then ten more. Then hundreds.

They pour into the gorge like a waterfall of nightmares, their singular obsession overriding any sense of self-preservation. I watch, a smile creeping across my weathered face.

The Great Bridge looms nearby, ancient and imposing, leading to the barren lands where I was supposed to find the Great Devourer. Where I was supposed to sacrifice myself for the world's salvation. They'd painted me as a hero before I left—the Chosen Bearer, the Selfless Wanderer.

But I've never wanted to be a hero.

The last Geist throws itself into the gorge, its howl fading as it plummets. Silence settles over the landscape like a blanket.

Five years down. Perhaps fifty years to climb back up. By then, I'll be bones and dust, having lived out my remaining days in peace. Let the next generation worry about it. Let them find their own chosen heroes.

I turn away from the gorge and begin the walk back to civilization, already imagining the warm tavern, the comfortable bed, the life I've just bought myself.

Sometimes, cleverness trumps courage.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Road to Hell

"What? Come again?"

"You're the villain," he said matter-of-factly.

The arrogance of it all. Him, in his silver suit with red cape, flying above the rubble. Judging me!

"That's impossible, I save lives!"

"How so?" he asked.

"Like, last week, for example. I blasted that whole hospital full of radiation to help the cancer victims!"

"You gave more people cancer than you cured!" he said.

"Well, what about that alligator that got stuck on the boat a few weeks back. I saved his life!" I cried.

"You sunk a ferry full of people and cars! It cost hundreds of thousands in insurance claims and the people had to be fished out of the river by the fire department!" he yelled.

"Well, what about when I saved that little girl from getting hit by that ball at the Yankee's game?"

"SHE WAS TRYING TO CATCH IT, ASSHOLE!"

"C'mon, it was heading right at her."

"YEAH, RIGHT AT HER GLOVE!"

I was starting to get offended. Here I am, all my hard work, being portrayed as less than helpful.

"What about those kind fellas that had gotten locked out of that steel room? I helped them get the door open."

"You helped four guys rob a bank! That was a vault! It was supposed to keep them out!"

"The girl with the red balloon!"

"She was allergic to latex!"

"The plane that almost crashed into a lake!" I was getting desperate now.

"You dropped it on top of an elementary school." He said. "Hundreds of little kids died!"

Wow, was it really true?

"What about that Army invading Florida six months ago? I stopped an entire invading Army, c'mon!"

"You mean the National Guard trying to provide relief to hurricane victims? Good job, guy."

I floated there, hovering above the destruction. My destruction. Every good intention twisted into catastrophe.

"Well mother fuck..."

Maybe I should've read the superhero manual after all.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# New Life Cleaning

Making an honest living, for me, is something difficult. I've been operating New Life Cleaning—"Bringing new life to your home, business or dungeon!"—for 15 years now.

I employ, em, *resurrect*, under my strict command, a team of 2 mop-tailed rabbits (have to attach the mops; their own hair falls out), 3 dusting bunnies, 2 anteaters (fantastic vacuums), 2 mice (for the hard-to-reach spaces), and my dead friend Jay. I just can't bear to let him go.

Jay is recently... *unemployed*, so I'm doing him a solid.

I wouldn't be running a cleaning service, but I need to make a living and I'm a half-decent necromancer. Getting along with the living, though? I don't know how to do that.

Last regular job I had was Spizzy's Market. Apparently, it's "not allowed" to have chicken carcasses take themselves off the rotisserie, season themselves, and jump into containers.

Their loss.

At least my clients appreciate efficiency. The undead never complain about overtime.

text:
# The Age of Answers

The attic door beckoned with familiar mystery. At seven, I'd asked what lay behind it. "When you're older," they'd said.

At ten, I begged to read grandfather's leather journals. "When you're ready."

At thirteen, I pleaded to understand the whispered conversations that stopped when I entered. "Someday, child."

Each deflection built a wall between wonder and wisdom.

Now, at thirty-five, I finally climbed those attic stairs. The door opened easily—unlocked all along.

Inside: dusty furniture, forgotten photographs, grandfather's journals filled with grocery lists and weather observations.

Nothing magical. Nothing profound.

The mysteries had been ordinary things, made mythical by distance. They'd promised revelation with age, but delivered only the cruel truth: there were no secrets worth the wait.

My curiosity hadn't been fed—it had been starved.

Now I understood everything, and nothing at all.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Transformation

"I told you to never contact me again. I changed everything. Everything. How did you even get in here?"

My eyes met hers. Dark and wide, like they used to be when she would playfully jump on top of me. She was naked. While she was by all standards absolutely beautiful, there was something about her that was out of place. Not human.

I could feel my stomach grow with resentment, my heart speeding up to meet the sudden rush of anger that went through me. Adrenaline.

She smiled. "You, I remember you."

I hated that voice with every living cell in my body. "I'm sure you do."

I was cornered. Locked in a room with my twisted psycho fling. What if she had a knife? I had done everything to remove her from my life. Today, she had finally found me again.

"Your training is complete!" She let loose a squeal of joy and grabbed my ankle.

The cold of her hands did something to me. I froze. I had no control of my body. Ever had those dreams where you can't move but you're aware of everything that goes on? This was it.

"You're it!" she said, ecstatically.

I'm not sure what happened then. Kudos to her, it was a good trick. Maybe in time I'll learn how to do it. Maybe in time I'll learn how to use all of my new powers.

For now though... it's good to be bad.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Tommy Heartes

If there was a God, he hath forsaken me.

"Hey Tommy, do you want to go fight pirates?"

"No."

"How about go win a war?"

"No."

"How about save a princess?"

"Look, I'm trying to concentrate. Fruits don't cut themselves."

Stupid iPad. Stupid Candy Crush. Stupid Fruit Ninja. Where did the ol' days go? It was unbelievable when he wasn't paying attention, and when Tommy did actually notice me, I would just upset him. I had no way of connecting with him.

"Hey Mr. Pickles?"

"Yes Tommy?"

"Can you get me a juice box?"

I had enough. I wasn't his butler. I was a grade A friend, subjected to the worst conditions of friendship.

"No."

"Why not. Cause you can't even do it?"

"No."

"Such a chicken."

"How about get it yourself. If you're so grown up, why am I still around? Huh?"

"Because I imagine you are here."

"*Riiiight*. But I'm not really here, since you have your iPad to keep you company."

"So? You jealous?"

"No. Just annoyed. Annoyed that you actually keep me around."

"Well. You're the only person that wants to be around."

"...Pardon?"

"Mom's out getting scratch tickets and Dad is working. But you know, Mom hasn't come back since she left four years ago."

"...Right..."

text:
# The Reunion

Eight years? Maybe nine? Time had a cruel way of accelerating when you weren't paying attention.

Dr. Mitchell. The man who'd guided me through college sports injuries, stress-induced migraines, and that terrifying health scare in my twenties. How had I let so much time pass?

The examination room felt suffocating—beige walls closing in, fluorescent lights buzzing overhead. Or maybe it was just my anxiety painting everything gray.

What would he think of me now? The extra forty pounds. The premature gray hair. The exhaustion etched permanently into my face.

My palms were slick with sweat. Perfect.

"Life happens," I whispered to myself. Two kids. The promotion that demanded everything. My wife's surgery. Dad's funeral. The excuses stacked up like unpaid bills.

But weren't they valid? Everyone loses track of time, right?

Still, the guilt gnawed at me. I'd neglected the one person who couldn't ignore what I'd become.

The door opened.

"Alright Mr. Johnson, if you could just hop up on the table. It's been awhile since your last physical so we'll need to be extra thorough."

Dr. Mitchell smiled warmly, no judgment in his eyes.

Only concern.

That somehow made it worse.

text:
# The Midnight Visitor

Shannon looked into the mirror and fluffed her hair. She had to look good for all of her friends out there. She pouted and looked at her ruby red lipstick. Her parents would have never allowed her to look this way, but with them out of town, she could do whatever she wanted. Her purple eyeshadow was perfectly smoky, bringing out her baby blue eyes and blonde hair. She pulled out her phone and took a picture of herself in the mirror. Happy with how she looked, she sauntered out and into the living room where her friends were waiting.

"Shannon! You're just in time for the beer Chelsea got!" a girl called. Shannon rushed over to the hearth and sat down. Beers were passed all around, making the atmosphere seem merry for the first time. The rush of the alcohol and the taboo party made Shannon giddy.

The clock struck midnight, but the girls didn't pay attention to it. The night wore on, but no one had fallen asleep. A loud thump could be heard on the roof, quieting the girls instantly. Slow steps walked across towards the chimney just above the girls. They huddled together on the couch, afraid someone was going to break in. One of the girls cried softly.

A gust of cold, winter air flowed down the chimney, making the girls close their eyes. Shannon was the first one to open them and look at the figure standing in front of them.

"Santa...?" she whispered, her voice trembling.

The figure wasn't jolly. His eyes gleamed with disappointment as he looked at the beer cans scattered around the room, then at Shannon's defiant makeup.

"Naughty list," he said simply, before vanishing up the chimney.

text:
# Liquid Courage

Tony Stark stared at his outstretched hands in disbelief. The armor pieces remained stubbornly dormant in their bay.

"JARVIS, what gives?"

"It appears, sir, that your decision to rely on a blood sample as a means of identification has posed a significant drawback."

"Which is?"

"Your blood alcohol content at the time you uploaded the sample was approximately zero point sixteen. The armor will not respond until your system sufficiently resembles the sample."

Tony's jaw clenched. Pepper must have reinstalled the humor application. "JARVIS, this isn't funny. Release the armor."

People were dying out there.

"I'm sorry, sir. You yourself prevented any overrides in your initial programming." JARVIS paused, almost thoughtfully. "You will either have to construct a new suit, or conform your blood alcohol content to its earlier iteration."

There wasn't time. Not with Mandarin—the real one—having made landfall in New York City. The Clean Slate protocol had been a mistake, but unless that new witch could bend back time, Tony was out of options.

"Sir, I am receiving an urgent call from Captain Danvers."

Damn it to hell.

Tony turned to his mechanical assistant. "Alright, Dummy, you're on shaker duty. I need three vodka martinis, up, extra dry, extra dirty, extra olives. JARVIS, tell Danvers I'm bringing the party to her."

*God*, Tony thought, watching Dummy enthusiastically prepare the drinks, *I hope the flight stabilizers can compensate for this.*

Fifteen minutes later, pleasantly buzzed and encased in gleaming red and gold, Iron Man rocketed toward Manhattan. The armor had responded perfectly.

He'd never tell Pepper about this. Ever.

text:
# The Waiting Room

The last thing I can remember is a car wreck. My car wreck. I guess this is heaven, or something like that?

The room was white, and it was just me waiting. Weird—if so many people die a day, shouldn't this room be full?

The big white double doors in front of me opened, letting a bright light in. A voice boomed, "Enter."

I didn't see why not, so I stood up and walked in.

A large, glowing figure sat on a throne in front of me. He was huge. I didn't even come up to his knee while he sat. Seriously, I was in awe. This is God... had to be, right?

Before I could say anything, his booming voice spoke: "What are you? You're rather scrawny and small."

"But, I'm a human..."

"What's that?"

Huh? I wondered if there was a mix up and I went to the wrong place. Wrong god maybe? How many were there?

"Excuse me, but aren't you God?"

"Flattery won't get you to a higher position." He paused. "What are you?"

"Oh, now we're going to be rude, I see. I'm here to help you navigate where to go after death, and this is how I'm repaid." His sigh shook the ground I stood on, then he muttered, "I told them adding new districts was a bad idea."

"I'm sorry, I have no clue what's happening."

He sighed again then said, "Look, you died. There are billions of life forms in billions of galaxies. Sometimes getting to their specific afterlife can be a struggle. So entities like me help sort it out. Never handled whatever you are though. What did you call yourself, hunam?"

"HuMAN," I corrected, then asked, "What about God?"

He laughed. "Well, he's busy in some other galaxy, but we talk. He personally asked me to do this. I'm like a god but not THE God. He never talks about humans. I'll have to ask about you."

He got up, then said, "Wait here. Let's sort this out. You'll be in your afterlife soon."

# Forbidden Pages

The cool leather binding of the book pressed against my palm, hidden deep in my pocket. I could still feel it there during the sermon, a dangerous secret beating like a second heart.

Jack shuffled beside me, eyes glazed as Madamme Superior droned on about the Dark Times, when men governed themselves and the world burned. The same words, every week. The same grateful murmurs from the crowd.

But Aldous Huxley had shown me the truth.

We weren't being cared for—we were being controlled. Soma in their world, contentment pills in ours. Entertainment to numb us. Comfort to cage us. Jack was happy because he'd been conditioned to be happy, never questioning, never wanting more than what they provided.

I glanced around the assembly hall. Hundreds of men, all wearing the same placid expressions. All grateful. All *docile*.

The Madammes stood elevated on their platform, draped in their ceremonial robes, watching us with benevolent smiles that suddenly seemed more predatory than protective.

"Be grateful for your liberation," Madamme Superior intoned.

My fingers tightened around the book.

Huxley had written his warning decades ago, in a different context. But the pattern was the same: breed compliance, eliminate dissent, call prison paradise.

I wasn't grateful anymore.

I was awake.

And awakening, I was learning, was the most dangerous thing a man could do.

text:
# The Swing of Second Chances

I'm sitting with him, Maurice, as we sway on the porch swing. The chains creak softly, a familiar rhythm that grounds me in this moment—this precious, impossible moment. I just asked to talk before we left, and he gave me a confused look before nodding.

In the past—future?—I had a job I hated. Being a lawyer consumed me, swallowed every piece of joy I'd once held. The endless fights Maurice and I had still echo in my mind like ghosts. We never truly fell out of love, but the stress caused us to just... fragment. It wasn't what we thought being married would be like.

We had a child late in life, but I've always wanted more. I realize now that I should've followed the career I wanted. I loved—still love—making stories and drawing. Maurice should have been the lawyer instead. We were both qualified, but the firm pitted us against each other at times. It was horrible.

But maybe, with me and a different career, we could find happiness?

I take his hand in mine, my silk glove tickling slightly. I tap my shiny shoes nervously as I look up at Maurice, who is still patiently waiting.

"I was thinking, maybe... maybe I'll move with you? I don't want to go off to school so soon. I want to finish that story I had."

Maurice's smile blooms like sunrise. "That one about the traveling bear and his human? I loved that! I was so sad when you stopped—I thought your dad had told you it was stupid or something." He grabs my hands. "Not that it is! It's adorable and I love it! So... I guess I know what to get you for your birthday."

His teasing voice—it's been so long since I've heard that lightness.

I lay my head on his shoulder and shudder out a breath. I won't cry.

Because now? I'll change our future.

It'll be okay.

It'll be better.

# The Weight of Perfection

I am a tool. I'm not meant to be used, but that hasn't stopped it from happening. Since 1868, I've been floatin' round. And for 3 generations this here revolver has served the Wilson family well.

I've killed men who deserved it. I've killed men who didn't. All that mattered is that I did my job. Been almost 2 centuries, and I ain't never misfired. No siree. After all, I'm a tool, and a good tool always works.

I'm used to bein' fired, and I always hit my mark. It ain't easy though. 'Especially considerin' how bad men are at shootin'. Murderers, victims, thieves, they all got one thing in common—they shake.

Great Grandpappy Joe shook when he shot his wife. His son shook when his house was robbed. And his daughter shook when she shot her daddy.

But George, this boy didn't shake. Nope, calm as a cow, he put my barrel in his mouth and pulled the trigger.

For 3 generations I've served the Wilson family. I ain't ever misfired but... by Golly... I wish I had.

Some tools carry more than weight. They carry regret.

# The Infomercial Invasion

A man gasped as I placed spaghetti into a tupperware container and placed it into the fridge. "N-no." "It's not possible!" "You can't store food without a *Handy Bucket Food Organizer!* Everybody knows that!"

I raised a grim eyebrow. "I mean, I just did."

It was still my house, cameras and audience members just started showing up out of nowhere. I went to my laundry room and started to fold my clothes, without the help of vacuum sealage.

"You monster!"

"W-wait. There's one more test." One man muttered. They all turned to him. He was holding a tray with EZ bake microwave rice, and a can of nondescript soda. "Sit down on this couch with this tray of food."

"Oh, come on, guys. Just sit down with the tray of food!" I grimaced. "It could not possibly be *that* hard."

A frail old man glared balefully at me. "Yeah? You try it."

I took the tray carefully with both hands. Grayed out men stared at me in awe. I shouted out, to the world (or perhaps just the world inside my house). "I will eat this food without dropping it!"

I went down to the couch in front of the camera, smiling arrogantly. Not a thing dropped from my tray as I used my fairly average core muscles to sit down gently, nothing rocking even an inch.

Many started whispering to each other in fear.

Suddenly, as if a mysterious force had acted, the couch suddenly bounced up on one side, and I stumbled, my tray upturned. My bowl of microwaved rice flew through the air, flying to my right and off the couch. Soda moved to the left, and I sighed.

"Oh, what the fuck."

"See? No one is safe from the *Chair*." One salesman cackled as he found himself revalidated by my failure.

I had bigger problems, though.

"Wait." I narrowed my eyes, searching the room. Everyone turned. "Where did the soda go?"

# The Last Straw

Merlin sighed, wondering why he had chosen to retire to a magic shop.

Here in front of him, the young 'trendy' wizard was red in the face, spit flying with each rage-filled syllable.

"I'm sorry, sir, but April Fools always puts a strain on our supply."

The wizened old store-owner's words had no calming effect on the furious man pacing up and down in the cramped little shop. Merlin cast a muttered deafening spell on himself, and looked past the angry customer, into the dull grey streets of the city. The glass of the windows was beginning to fog as the cold spring rain bucketed down, drenching the concrete maze.

In his peripheral vision, Merlin noticed the comical gestures of the hipster wizard had stopped. Relinquishing his spell, Merlin let himself listen.

The man was flustered now, his accusations and insults grinding to an awkward halt.

"I will send a message to you as soon as we have the items you need. May I take your contact information?"

"That won't be necessary. I am **never** returning to this failure of a shop again, old man," the would-be-customer cried, turning sharply on his heels, before lingering on his way out, hand poised above the bronze door handle.

The man extended a pale finger. "One stop magic shop, my ass!"

The door slammed. Merlin smiled wearily. Perhaps running the shop wasn't so different from advising Arthur after all—just different kinds of fools.

# Return to Sender

The letter arrived back at the post office on January 3rd, stamped with familiar red ink: *Return to sender, address unknown.*

It was the seventh year in a row.

Milan held the envelope in his weathered hands, staring at the Chicago address he'd memorized long ago. 618, 42nd Street. His son Petar had lived there once, decades ago, before the silence began.

He placed the letter in the wooden box with the others—Christmas greetings sent into the void, each one documenting another year of aging, of struggle, of hope dimming like embers in his wood-stove.

Mrs. Aleksandra found him there on January 6th, Orthodox Christmas Day. The fire had gone cold. Milan sat peacefully in his chair by the window, the box of returned letters open on his lap, as if he'd been reading them one final time.

In Chicago, a man named Peter Harrison—formerly Petar Nikolić—deleted another email from the Serbian embassy. They'd been trying to reach him about his father's estate for weeks. He'd changed his name, his life, escaped that suffocating village decades ago.

He didn't need those ghosts.

On his desk sat a photograph he kept meaning to throw away: a young boy and his father, laughing, covered in snow. Behind them, a church with winter-white gravestones.

*Hristos se rodi,* read the inscription on the back in his father's handwriting.

Peter turned the photograph face-down and returned to his emails.

# Graduation Day

Kanye adjusted his cap in the mirror. One, two, three times. Always three. He stared at the diploma propped against his College Dropout poster. The poster stared back and Kanye smiled. He had a crooked smile, the kind that meant mischief. He spent the rest of his morning with that same smile.

Before Kanye could adjust his cap a fourth time, his mother came in to talk. Kanye sat on his bed and listened, nodding when he needed to nod and laughing when he shouldn't have been laughing. His mother told him about a producer she met at church. She said he was "very talented" and mentioned that Kanye should "send him some beats." Kanye nodded and gave her a thumbs-up. He looked back at his College Dropout poster. He focused on the teddy bear. His mother stared back and Kanye smiled.

Kanye's mother complimented him on his gown, and Kanye laughed. He was wearing a graduation robe. Kanye complimented his mother on her strong spirit. She laughed, but it looked like she was crying. Kanye said that they needed to leave soon and his mother took the hint. She walked out of his room and shut the door halfway.

Kanye snuggled up his diploma and began the count in his head. One album, two albums, three. He gave the teddy bear one last stare, grabbed his car keys and headed to the ceremony he almost didn't make it to.

text:
# God Fucking Damnit

"God fucking damnit."

"What."

How can a word that is so questioning suddenly become a statement? It simply hangs there, waiting to be transformed by an answer but is almost rhetorical. A dare, I suppose. A challenge.

My arms are radiating heat and I swing. As my fist meets his jaw, it slips in almost slow motion, giving way easily as if surprised by my force.

"You cunt piece of shit," he says. His eyebrows furrow yet his light eyes do the opposite: they widen in fear.

I want to let go—to hug him and tell him I understand his pain. "Shhh, come here. Don't worry. I'm not leaving." I have said it so many times before, but this time the words get caught in my throat. My body is on fire, each inch blazing with tension.

Trust is something you never appreciate until you understand what it is to live without it. Once someone close to your heart stops trusting you and begins testing you, it disappears completely, even with yourself. The freedom you lose is enough to change what you thought you held dear.

When I was sixteen, I took a vow to never act violently. I was so passionate. There was so little that I imagined could stand in my way as I stood in the auditorium of my high school. My childhood best friend turned yogi, Annabelle, awarded me with a Microsoft Word "Art" certificate of commitment as I beamed facing my fellow members of the Peace Club.

Two months later I met Daniel.

My knee hits his testicles and I stand over him, my face a blank ashen slate.

"You are a good for nothing slut whore. You learn this shit from your past fucks?"

"WHAT past fucks?" I want to scream. "I lost my virginity to you, you delusional piece of crap."

Instead I kick him once more, this time harder and with more intention. He writhes on the floor as I turn my back and find the exit, for the first and last time.

# The Final Frontier

"It's been a long time, old friend. I was wondering when I would see you again!" Captain Kirk said, setting down his woodcutting axe with a smile. "Come, sit down, have some tea!"

Kirk's eyes twinkled. "I didn't think you would have expected to see me at all! I thought Vulcans believed that an afterlife was... illogical."

"Jim, if working with you all these long years has taught me anything, it's to expect anything when it comes to you." Spock paused, a shadow crossing his face. "My only regret is that I could not have finished my work finding a new home for my people."

Kirk squeezed his shoulder. "Spock, with all you've accomplished, you of all people should have nothing to regret. Now come, follow me—there are so many people who would like to meet you!"

Together they walked toward the light, Spock ready to explore the Final Frontier, to boldly travel where many had gone before.

Rest in peace, Mr. Nimoy. You will be sorely missed.

text:
# The Collection

Marcus wiped the blood from his blade, staring at the woman before him. Her auburn hair cascaded over pale shoulders, and even in death, she possessed an ethereal beauty that made him pause.

*No.*

He couldn't. She was too perfect to consume.

He lifted her carefully, reverently, carrying her to the spare bedroom. After cleaning and positioning her in the chair by the window, he stepped back to admire his work.

"You're not food," he whispered, kissing her cooling forehead. "You're art."

Days passed. His hunger returned with vengeance, gnawing at his insides. But each time he lured another victim, he'd remember his first doll, and the hunger transformed into something else—a need to preserve beauty, to collect it.

The bedroom filled slowly. One draped across the bed, sultry and inviting. Another curled in the corner, knees drawn up like a frightened child. Each one positioned with care, dressed in vintage clothing he'd scavenged.

Marcus sat at the kitchen counter, pouring milk into a chipped mug. Beside him, his latest acquisition slumped against the restraints, her head tilted at an unnatural angle.

"They understand me now," he told her conversationally.

The sirens outside barely registered.

When the officers entered, they found him exactly there, calmly sipping milk. But it was the bedroom that made the seasoned detective vomit—a gallery of death, arranged like a twisted museum exhibit.

In the original chair, the first woman had become nothing but bones.

She was still smiling.

text:
# The Silence of God

David's fingers traced the edge of the photograph—a family portrait from Nebraska. Within seconds, they would hear his latest composition, a droning frequency embedded beneath Beethoven's Fifth.

He chuckled, remembering those early days. The Beethoven Boys had been an accident, really. Three bullies who'd tormented him in middle school, driven mad by the relentless loop only they could hear. The news coverage had been his first taste of power.

The haunted house in Illinois had been profitable but provincial. Tourists paying to experience manufactured fear while he experimented with range and duration. Child's play.

Then came the revelation in his basement studio: any recorded song, pressed to physical media, played even once—it became his instrument. And any face, captured in pixels or print, became his audience.

Now his catalogue had reached 7.8 billion ears. Every phone, every screen, every printed page—doorways for his broadcast. World leaders spoke his scripted words. Armies moved at his unheard commands.

Tomorrow, he would release his masterpiece: pure, absolute silence.

No thoughts but his thoughts. No will but his will.

David smiled at his reflection in the recording booth glass.

Finally, the world would know peace.

His peace.

text:
# Daddy's Back

The man on the other side of the door continues to knock. I do not move from the refuge I have taken under my bed. My Spiderman blankie is draped over my shoulders. In one hand, I wield my little league baseball bat. In the other, the teddy bear from my father.

"Come onnnnn, open up. *Jus' wan na talk. Tha's all.*"

The fast knocks on my door slow down into a consistent, intimidating rhythm, seemingly synched with my racing heartbeat. *Thud. Thud. Thud. Thud.*

He violently wiggles the doorknob, but is upset to find that I have locked it. He pounds a fist into the door, and when that doesn't work, he begins to slam his body weight against it.

"OPEN." *thud* "THIS." *thud* "DOOR!"

He breaks down the door, sending it flying off its hinges. It lands near the window, and he enters my bedroom. I clutch my teddy close to me as he searches the room. He is searching for *me*.

I tremble as his feet approach my bed—just inches in front of my face—and I can practically hear him grin as he bends down to lift up the covers. The stench of alcohol grows closer and closer.

I shriek, "*Who are you!? Where did Daddy go?*"

That's when his face grows pale. He gravely looks at the empty bottle in his hand, then back at me. His eyes meet mine and tears well in the corner of his eyes. The grown man begins to cry inconsolably.

He drops the liquor on the floor, shattering it to pieces, and extends his arms to me for a hug. Hesitantly, I come out from under the bed and throw my arms around him in an embrace.

"Daddy's back," he weeps into my shoulder, "Daddy's back."

In that moment, wrapped in his trembling arms, I understand what my mother meant when she said that sometimes people lose themselves. The bottle had stolen him away, turned him into someone else entirely—someone scary, someone dangerous. But my question, innocent and piercing, had somehow reached through the haze and pulled the real him back to the surface.

Tomorrow, things might be different. But tonight, beneath the Spider-Man blankie, clutching both bat and bear, I simply hold my father as he finds his way home.

# The Truth Between Us

"So what else has been a lie?" 

I cringe, knowing that I had opened a huge can of worms. It was something I needed to do, though; Hikaru and I both needed it.

"My parents are both alive and well," I said. "Raiten wasn't coming to kill me, he was coming to finish the job and take me back home."

"Are you serious, Raiko? For the past four years, you've just been stacking lie upon lie?"

"You don't understand, Hikaru, I had to! I didn't have a choice!"

"Of course I don't understand; you haven't given me a fucking chance! If you had just told me all these things in the first place, we could've worked this out together!"

"I couldn't tell you at first, that would have ruined everything! My parents-"

"You ruined everything anyway!"

I fell silent, unable to find the right words to respond to that. He was right, of course. I had screwed everything up on day one.

"I mean, not that you ruining things was bad," Hikaru said, his rage fading into agitation. "I guess you ruining things means you're not going to kill me, right?"

I laughed bitterly, shrugging. "If I kill you, I kill myself right along with you. You know that. I don't have much of a choice anymore."

"I just wish you would have told me sooner," Hikaru said, his agitation fading into disappointment. "I wish you could have trusted me."

"I trust you now," I said. "Otherwise I wouldn't have told you."

"Were there any other lies?" Hikaru asked, his gaze meeting mine.

"No," I replied, refusing to break eye contact. "All that's left is the one thing I've never lied about."

"And that is?"

"I love you."

# This is the End

The thought struck Josh suddenly, almost by accident. It pierced through and dissolved his frustration with the car that had allowed him to break down so far from home; with the phone company that had neglected to build towers by this barren desert road; with the sun that had audaciously beaten him, sweaty and tired, to the ground.

*This is the end.*

This thought in particular remained prominent in his mind, even as he realized that he had already seen Heather for the last time. And... and Joey, who was still so proud about that geometry test. And Dale, and the business Dale would inherit, the business that would serve as an unexpected legacy.

*This is it.*

Dale, who had told him that this trip was a fool's errand, and made a joke about what he would say at Josh's funeral; this memory, too, failed to shake the thought from Josh's head.

*The end of...*

The thought lingered there, static, for a time that Josh wasn't able to comprehend. Everything else in his mind seemed to fade away, from his periphery, inward toward this single, solitary idea.

*This is the end of me.*

When nothing else was left, Josh found it fitting that this idea of finality should itself be his final thought.

But it wasn't.

It vanished as abruptly as it came, and then—

Josh would have cried, if he was still physically capable. His regrets came flooding back all at once. And his anger, and his sorrow and his despondency at his own powerlessness. The tranquil peace of the "end" was over, replaced with the angst of a life incomplete. A life that had failed to come to terms with itself.

And then Josh felt **fear**.

Fear like he had never felt before. The terror of fate incarnate, of the great unknown for which he was utterly unprepared. The sheer and total horror overwhelmed his memory, and his pain, and all his other emotions.

That fear was the last thing Josh thought about.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Punchline

"What did you say? Did you just call me a sparky?" The mage's hands sparked with electricity, ready to flow out and hit the enemy.

"I said, 'You sparkies are all the same!' No seriously, you're all, 'Ooh, look at me and my stupid electric puns! What a shocking revelation, you'll find me electrifying, I'll give you something to write ohm about!' Please."

The young man glared at the mage as though the puns of electric mages everywhere had killed his parents. He would say they were bad enough to have done so.

The mage, having heard enough insults, started his incantation: "What I seek is the energy of gods! I become the cable! I cast—"

The young man started an incantation of his own: "My fists become the rage! I cast fist!"

With all the strength of a normal human who sometimes punched others, the young man broke the mage's nose.

Nobody ever told the young man he didn't need to chant an incantation before punching, and honestly, the result spoke for itself. The mage crumpled, clutching his face.

"Should've grounded yourself," the young man muttered, walking away.

text:
# Fragments of Abakor

The ink trembles across parchment as my hand shakes. Already, the castle spires blur in my mind—were they gold or amber?

Mother's face dissolves like watercolor in rain.

The Rift consumed everything: cobblestone streets, market songs, the taste of honeyed bread. The Aura Wizards chanted until their voices cracked and bled, holding reality together with syllables older than mountains. I watched their robes turn to ash, their bodies to light, as the Decay clawed upward through foundations, through bones, through time itself.

Six of us slipped through. Six witnesses to erasure.

My sister sits beside me, eyes vacant. She hums a melody with no origin. In thirty minutes, she won't remember why the sound comforts her.

The photographs we clutch show strangers in unfamiliar landscapes. Evidence of a world too stubborn to completely disappear.

Tomorrow, we'll wake renewed. Clean. The grief that crushes my chest will evaporate like morning frost.

Perhaps those new souls—wearing our faces, speaking with our voices—will build something beautiful. Perhaps forgiveness isn't necessary.

Perhaps forgetting is mercy.

My name was—

The letters escape me.

text:
# The Misunderstood Archive

I stood in the deserted street of a species long since gone.

"So there are no more humans?" I asked, my voice echoing off crumbling concrete.

Jornin nodded, his antennae twitching thoughtfully. "Not a one. We've found many, many skeletons though."

"Weird. I wonder where they went," I said, kicking at a rusted metal sign.

"We've found many areas of high radiation and blast zones. Obviously they had a nuclear war." Jornin's four eyes scanned the horizon grimly.

I pulled out a small book from my satchel. Its faded cover showed a Terran changing into a house cat—at least, that's what our xenolinguists believed the images depicted. "But why did they change?"

Jornin shrugged and put one of his upper arms around my shoulder. "That's why we're here, Rudornica."

"It just doesn't make any sense though." I flipped through the crumbling pages. "All of their secondary forms are still on the planet. We've found sea stars, house cats, cheetahs, and horses. We've found all of them. Why don't they change back into their primary form?"

"Maybe we're not contacting them correctly." Jornin patted me on the back with another arm. "There were thousands of languages spoken here. We may not have found the right one yet."

I looked up at the crumbling buildings, their windows like hollow eyes. "But what about the moon base? We found hundreds of skeletons up there, yet there are no secondary skeletons."

Jornin shrugged again. "Perhaps they sent those who could change to the moon as a sort of penal camp. Perhaps they were not able to change to their secondary form to survive." He laughed, the sound musical through his translator. "We may never know, but that just makes things more interesting."

"Do you think we'll find any more Animorphs relics?"

"We can only hope." Jornin shrugged off his pack and began to pull out scanning equipment. "If we could find an 'Animorph' document that explained the war, we may find out what happened to the inhabitants of this planet."

I put my Animorph document back in my bag, already imagining the accolades. Fame within the scientific community would be quick if one were to figure out the Terran secrets.

I smiled to myself and pumped my fist. "I'll find out. I'll be the one that unlocks the answer," I whispered.

Neither of us realized we were holding children's fiction.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Mirror's Lie

"I'm beautiful, and you're just jealous of me!" She said as she walked hurriedly out of the room.

I told her she was an older woman, still beautiful, but she believes what she sees everyday. She believes what she sees.

I look in the mirror. A handsome young man grimaces back at me. I smile. The young man returns the smile.

I look down at my hands. They're not the hands of a young person, and Marie must know that as well.

I realized what was wrong when I looked at myself by the lake. I saw a middle-aged man. Quite a shock.

But regardless of the truth, now I feel bad for taking the illusion away from Marie, my beautiful girl. She still sees an eighteen-year-old happily laughing at her when she looks into these damn mirrors, making reality more and more of an alien world.

Do I destroy them? That's bad luck, isn't it?

The house came this way—every mirror enchanted, reflecting our younger selves. A gift, we thought. But gifts have prices.

Marie cannot see her gray hair, her lines. I cannot see my weathered face. Only by water, by honest reflection, do we glimpse truth.

I'll have to decide what to do. For now, I must find Marie and talk to her.

In the mirror, a handsome man vibrantly walks away from the mirrors, and out into the hall, while an older version shuffles forward, seeking his wife, seeking reality.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Curse of a Single Word

I woke up with a headache so the morning was already off to a bad start. This was before I had even realized that there was no screech coming from my alarm clock, but rather had I woken up naturally and almost a half hour late. A shower was out of the question, but I didn't smell too bad and my hair was more or less on point. I managed to pull an unwrinkled shirt out of the closet and decided to pair it with the brand new slacks I had gotten for my birthday. The ibuprofen was kicking in and the day was starting to look promising. I was almost out the door to work, only needing to throw on shoes, when I rounded a corner too quickly and caught my pinky toe (the most fragile of the piggies!) on the edge of the baseboard, stubbing it to high hell. Before I knew what was happening the words came rumbling from the bottom of my diaphragm and out of my mouth. Those damned words that caused so much trouble in puberty, when children discover the magical command they were born to utter and I discovered my terrible curse.... "SHIT."

The world lurched. My stomach dropped as reality twisted around me. When my vision cleared, I was standing knee-deep in a massive pile of exactly that. My brand new birthday slacks, ruined. My promising morning, destroyed.

I sighed, pulling out my phone to call in sick. Again.

text:
# Turbulence

I hate flying. The thought of being trapped in a pressurized cabin 10,000 feet in the air was enough to cause an anxiety attack. Yet, I found myself on a plane between continents. I popped back a few Tylenols and tried to sleep through my anxiety.

I managed to get a few minutes of shut-eye, but I woke up with a jolt. The turbulence wasn't helping. Then, I noticed passengers staring out their windows nervously. That didn't help, either.

Then the crogs attacked.

A "crog" is short for a crimson balrog. They sometimes attacked the ship from Victoria Island coming into Orbis. But they don't exist. At least, not in our world.

I wasn't the only one who was shocked. But some people were already half expecting this. A guy from the back pulled out a revolver, firing a comically huge bullet at the crimson balrog. The guy next to him *rode* said bullet and threw an electric shark from his fist.

I must be going insane.

Another person materialized a polearm from nowhere and *roared*. A woman jumped from her seat, blasting at the crimson balrog with twin crossbows.

I tried to escape the chaos, but a lightning bolt from the creature struck me directly.

When I came to, I found myself on a deserted island. A monkey sat beside me, chittering softly. It seemed he'd rescued me.

I looked at my hands. They were glowing faintly blue.

The monkey handed me a stick. Instinctively, I knew—I could cast magic now.

Maybe MapleStory wasn't just a game anymore.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Morning Everything Changed

Yawning and blinking furiously, she slips into her sport shoes. With slow movements she clumsily brings her auburn colored hair into a messy ponytail only to find that she left her hair tie in the bedroom. With a sigh she turns to get it.

Finally stepping out on the light-wooded porch, the cold air is full of sounds. A flock of redbreasts singing their morning song on the next hedge is most certainly one of the dominating examples, but as a sharp contrast every few moments a car drives by, each leaving behind a hint of polluted air. As if she is able to feel that somehow, she scratches her nose before starting to run in place.

Her morning routine continues with jumping jacks and although she has been doing this one for months now, she does the stretching first today. If she would only know what is going to happen in the course of the day, maybe she would not even start jumping.

But she does.

And after about five of them it becomes clear that this is going to be an outstanding workout. Any passerby looking through the garden gate may think that she was jumping in slow motion. But was she? Her feet lift up from the ground and they don't return when you would expect them to. It appeared to the outer world as if she is...flying?

As soon as there is a steady foot of air under her soles, the narrowed eyebrows turn into wide open eyes and red freckles showing up all over her cheeks. She slows her arm movements and almost falls down on her knees.

Slowly she nods.

Scratching her head, she returns into her living room. If she wouldn't be already sitting when she checks the TV, she would be then. At least now she knows that her new sports bra looks awful from distance, especially filmed out of a helicopter.

The news anchor's voice drones on about the "mysterious floating woman" while she reaches for her phone, wondering who to call first about her newfound ability—and her fashion emergency.

text:
# The Reset That Wasn't

I rolled over on the stained mattress, my head pounding like a jackhammer. The smell of garbage and despair hung thick in the air.

"Yo, homie! You got any more of that stuff?" A skeletal figure shuffled past my doorway.

This couldn't be happening. The day was *supposed* to reset. Every stupid decision, every reckless choice—erased like an Etch A Sketch. That's how it had worked for three weeks straight.

But not today.

The bank robbery had been exhilarating. The meth purchase, idiotic but consequence-free. Or so I'd thought. Shooting that dealer, the prostitute, the syphilis—all supposed to disappear at midnight like some twisted Cinderella story.

Instead, I woke up here. Skid Row. Los Angeles. The consequences were *real* now.

My wallet contained $200 and a fake ID I didn't remember getting. Sirens wailed in the distance—probably for me. The bank job would be all over the news.

I packed the remaining cash and stumbled toward the door. Canada was my only option now. Vancouver was 1,200 miles north. No car, no plan, just desperate hope.

The time loop had finally broken, and it broke on the worst possible day.

I stepped into the smoggy morning, praying the border guards wouldn't look too closely at a sweating, shaking man running from his permanent mistakes.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Silencing

In the darker times, the will of the people was ignored. We had petitioned the governments, and mobilised the voices of thousands of angry civilians. But the government—for better or for worse—ignored us. Silenced us.

Those were the days we lost our sacred ability to make our voices heard: our vote.

It had long been established that the government would physically take away our voices when we became insolent. My family disagreed with the regime. They were silenced, then soon shot.

I was scared into submission.

But no longer.

I can't believe they took away our rights. To violate these fundamental principles given by our founding fathers is unspeakable. They are too oppressive!

I will not take this lying down anymore! We must speak out against—

*[The text deteriorates]*

If you're reading this, they've probably heard me. If you're reading this, it's probably too late.

I can't do this much longer...

*[Final entry ends in incoherent keystrokes]*

---

*This document was recovered from Terminal 7, Sector 12. The author's identity has been erased from all records. No further investigation recommended.*

text:
# Daylight Savings Delirium

It was the night of daylight savings time and we finally had an extra hour to ourselves. "Hey Sheila, can you put that Prince record on?" "Which one?" "You know the one." "Ah yeah. I'm also going to turn on the television."

We began to fool around. The purple funk filled our cramped dorm room.

"Do you want to see that movie? It says Siskel and Ebert gave it two thumbs up."

"Siskel and Ebert gave YOU two thumbs up," I grinned.

"Oh did they?"

We started to get heated and a bit rough. And then my roommate barged in.

"Who wants some WAHO??? I got some hashbrowns and pancakes. Damn it's good to eat when you're baked. You guys are naked. Baked. Naked. Pancake. Haha."

"Dude, what do you think the rubber band means? Don't you have somewhere to be?"

"I guess I could go get a Coke from the vending machine."

He didn't. He sat down on his futon and changed the channel to Discovery.

"Man, nature is the best. But I feel kinda turned on, do you ever get that way?"

"No, man, get the hell out of our room!!"

"Geez man. Fine. I'm going to Tom's room to watch X-Files and—"

Sheila raised her head from the pillow. I could tell she was going to say something when he left.

"I want to watch the new X-Files," she said.

I sighed, then smiled. "Then we'll do it doggy style so we can both watch X-Files."

That extra hour suddenly seemed worth it.

text:
# The Human Litchi

For as long as I can remember, I've had a fascination with blood. Over time, the fascination turned to lust, and the lust in turn to an unslakable thirst. So it should come as no surprise that when He gave me the chance to live my dreams, I jumped at the chance, never looking back.

I still remember that the hardest part was deciding just how. Surely not a vampire—it came with too much baggage, what with the aversion to garlic, sunlight, and that nastily pale complexion. And a tick was out of the question; after all, one has to maintain some semblance of dignity.

No, I knew just the thing.

And now, as I take in that beautiful young creature in front of me, I feel the familiar desire and the shapeshifting that such feelings inevitably initiate. I am powerless to stop it, and I feel a certain wistfulness at what could have been.

I would have been tall, sinewy, powerful, and fearsome to behold. I would have been as black as night; no, I would BE the night, dark and foreboding. And if none of that would have struck fear into the hearts of those before me, surely my three large, glistening fangs would have done the trick.

But no.

Instead, my skin wrinkles and reddens. I feel a familiar wetness, no, dare I say juiciness, spreading around me. I bloat immensely, and I feel a familiar pit forming in my very core.

As it comes to an end, I look at all the shocked faces gaping back at me. I am a freak, of that I am sure.

But they marvel. Oh, how they marvel!

For I have become the Human Litchi.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Handshake

Wallet? Check. Right breast pocket. Always feels weird having jacket pockets. Best get used to it if I nail the interview. Suits every day. Will I need to get them before I start. How many suits do I need? Maybe there's a suit allowance. Should I negotiate that? What if it comes up? Get it together, man.

Phone? Check. Keys? God, where are my keys?

"Dad, have you seen my keys?"

"They're in the bowl by the door. Like always."

I can hear him smiling as he comes down the stairs.

"Good luck, today. Whether you get it or not, Mum and I are really proud of you."

I worry that he might be going in for a hug. We don't hug. He might be going for it. This might be weird.

I think he can sense me tensing up, and sticks out his hand.

"Good luck."

I put my hand into his and he—well, this isn't easy to say—he has a, what you might call, a—god—a *pleasure episode*.

A smell that any boy who has been a teenager knows well begins to insinuate itself into my nose.

I turn and leave, presumably never to come back, or at least ever look my dad in the eye again.

I did not get the job.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Meal

"The last time? What, it happened more than once?" Jeff asked, a look of disbelief on his face and a glass of Heaven's finest—and only—scotch in his hand.

Sam took a sip from his plastic cup, set it down on the table and chuckled quietly. "Well, yeah. They did it more than once, too. I—"

"Bullshit." Jeff interrupted.

Sam sighed. "Ah, I wish. Life wasn't pleasant for me, Jeff. A bombing here, a sniper there." Another sip from the cup. Drinks don't get empty here. "You see Jeff, I used to be important. Had a lot of stuff going on, all around the world. Charities, speeches, things like that. But one thing..." Sam held up a finger, while still holding his cup, and pointed at Jeff. "One thing did it. And then, *boom*! I was immortal, the world hated me and I couldn't die. All because I was drunk and wanted some food."

Jeff didn't change his look. He just took another sip and adjusted his wings. "Can't see how getting food will get you hated."

Sam grinned. "Well, Winger—you gotta be more creative. Let me tell you what happened." Sam put down his cup, cleared his throat and put on his best Morgan Freeman impression.

"It was a lonely night in Berlin. I was drunk off my still-mortal arse, lost my wallet and wanted food. Wandered through the streets and, lucky me, saw a little house with a sign. It said 'Free food for blood donation'. I thought it was fine, went in and strategically ignored the faces with tentacles plastered over the walls. Boy was I wrong..."

text:
# The Survivors

The world came crashing down in minutes. Many of us were asleep when it happened, and didn't find out about it until later. When we awoke, we saw the carnage spread through the land, and we wept.

There weren't many of us left, but what few there were managed to find each other over the Internet. We gathered together in what remained of a major city on the East Coast of what was once the United States.

It took us time, but we eventually began to rebuild. The brightest among those who survived thought to ask "Why," while most of us were content with just surviving. Years passed, and no link was found between us.

Eventually, those who had the question resigned themselves to the fact that they would never know. They went to their new homes, and tried to integrate themselves as best they could into the new society.

It wasn't until fourteen years after the event happened that the connection was discovered, quite by accident. One of the former questioners had taken a job as a mover, and was helping a fellow survivor move into a newly cleaned house.

Sticking out of one of the boxes was the missing link.

"Oh, you used to shop at Bad Dragon too?"

Moments later, the realization struck him. His face paled as the pieces fell into place. Every survivor. Every single one. The boxes in his own apartment. The discrete packages that had arrived before the world ended.

They were all customers.

The rapture had come, and only *they* remained.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# When the Time Came

The cryo-gel sloughed off my body in crystalline sheets as I steadied myself against the pod's frame. Around me, forty-seven others were emerging—once strangers, now brothers and sisters bound by purpose and five centuries of shared consciousness.

"Status report," Commander Chen's voice cracked through decades of disuse.

We'd watched it all. Every atrocity. Every betrayal. The nanobots had kept our synapses firing while pumping endless streams of data into our hibernating minds. We'd witnessed humanity's descent: the Corporate Wars, the Genetic Purges, the collapse of the last democratic states. The darkness had crept in slowly, year by year, until the world was drowning in its own moral decay.

My hands trembled—not from cold, but anticipation—as I sealed the last plate of armor. The dull red reflected no light, engineered for the shadows we'd soon inhabit.

"All systems operational," someone reported. "Arsenal is intact."

I checked my weapon—a relic of old-world justice, before laws became suggestions for the rich and shackles for the poor. The volunteer families who'd hidden us had kept their promise, maintaining our chamber through generations, waiting for the failsafe protocol to trigger.

That protocol had finally activated yesterday.

Chen raised her fist. "They forgot we existed. They forgot that some still believed in redemption through reckoning."

We moved as one toward the blast doors, a tide of crimson purpose. Five hundred years of accumulated rage, tempered by our vigil, sharpened by preparation.

Outside, a corrupted world awaited its reckoning.

We would remind them what justice looked like.

We would ride through the darkness, and bring the dawn.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Keepers

Rom's consciousness spanned galaxies now, yet somehow he remembered fingers—ten small, calloused things that had once gripped a spear. The memory felt impossibly distant.

His tribe, all forty-seven of them, had become something else entirely when they entered the Obelisk. Their bodies had erupted outward, expanding until stars seemed like fireflies, galaxies like puddles to step across. The transformation was instantaneous and complete: their cells rewrote themselves to drink radiation, their skin hardened against the void, their lungs collapsed and reformed into something that needed no air.

For eons, Rom stood sentinel. He positioned himself between deadly cosmic rays and the small blue world that had birthed him. His body absorbed supernovae that would have sterilized Earth. His hands—now large enough to cup solar systems—deflected gamma-ray bursts.

The others of his tribe scattered across the universe, each becoming guardians of their own precious cargo: the genetic memory of everything that had ever lived on Earth.

Rom watched civilizations rise on his homeworld. He watched them fall. He watched humanity finally reach the stars in their small ships, never knowing the giant that had shielded them for millions of years.

Then the universe began its final exhalation.

Reality folded in on itself. Stars blinked out like candles. Rom felt his enormous body compress, the biological data within him—every beetle, every fern, every human who had ever existed—burning in his cells like swallowed light.

The white crack appeared.

As he pushed through into the new universe, Rom remembered what it felt like to be small, to stand before a mystery with merely human hands.

*They chose us*, he thought, *because we would remember what it meant to be fragile.*
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Glass Army

The clones emerged from KQED first, their measured tones spreading like a contagion through the airwaves. By Tuesday, every public radio station from Seattle to San Diego belonged to the Glass Army—calm, articulate, devastating.

In the Manhattan bunker, Tom and Ray worked through the night, their laughter echoing off concrete walls. "This carburetor's gonna clone people," Tom wheezed. Ray just grinned and handed him another wrench.

The Sedaris clones were disappointing—witty, yes, but too self-deprecating to fight. The Burroughs accidents just drank and wrote memoirs. But Ira Flatow? Science itself flowed through his veins. He nodded solemnly when they asked. "For knowledge," he said.

The Ira Contra war was waged in whispers and measured debate. Cities fell not to violence but to thoughtful discourse. Pledge drives became sieges. Tote bags, weapons.

When only two Iras remained, they faced each other in the Fitzgerald's ruins. Through the long Minnesota night, FM radio held its breath.

Then silence.

Survivors twisted their dials desperately until they found AM—scratchy, ancient AM—and heard it: a voice, neither Glass nor Flatow, something older, stranger.

"This is just the beginning," it crackled.

The real war, the voice explained, was between analog and digital, between what could be copied and what could only be remembered.

And humanity had already lost.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Pineapple Decree

Life has always been hard, but never has it been this grueling. I feel the pressures and dangers of life grinding my soul to pieces in a vice. We used to think Dear Leader was bad, but now we appreciate what we had.

Surely, he was a sociopath with no regard for other humans, but, at the very least, he had some kind of goal, some sort of endgame. Now, all he has is madness. Last month he legalized murder, but only with a pineapple. Life has never been the same.

Now, every day, I walk in fear of my enemies and their fruit gangs; a group of burly men with bulging arms and tight shirts wielding sacks of pineapples. They, at any moment, could saunter up with their tight little shorts and beat me viciously with their sacks. Their large, voluminous sacks. Full of spiky pineapples.

I've seen these gangs sack other men to death, and it is never pleasant. Many people do not realize the conundrum of beating another with a pineapple: the body is strong, but the pineapple is spongy and weak. These men must flail and grunt and jerk their sacks against another for hours on end until the victim's body simply gives in and surrenders to its fate.

The poor victim, groaning as his body grows sore. The fruit gangbangers, with their sacks growing tender and weak.

No one should have to endure sackdeath. No man, no woman, nobody.

I clutch my own defensive pineapple tighter, scanning the shadows. This is survival now.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Unfortunate Sneeze

It started with the nose. An ordinary nose, slightly oily. Small hairs peeked from the moist caves they vigilantly protected. A twitch of the left nostril, once, twice. Higher up, muscles tensed and tightened. A tickle raced down the back of the throat, a messenger on high alert. *Prepare yourselves!* 

Deep in the torso, the diaphragm kicked like a mule. Air rushed in, swelling belly, swelling lungs. Build and build, let's make this great! "Ahhhh-" A precipice. No turning back. All together now, on my signal. 

"*Chooo*" A furious wind, a blowing gale. Out through the mouth, out through the nose, grabbing and tossing and ripping along the way. Purge, purge, purge. A glorious trumpeting, a shower of spit. 

Edward shook his head, eyes moist. He grabbed a crisp white napkin, wiping glistening globs from Julie's fair cheeks. 

"My apologies, dear. That's never happened before."

Julie's smile froze. Their first date—ruined.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Almost Out of Steam

Almost out of steam. But not going to give up yet. Can't. Don't want to. Even with Xeri lying on the couch, watching and smirking. Face of an angel, she has. Grossly overrated. Her personality is more important, but I learnt that too late. I had married her by then.

Just a few minutes ago, she'd set me a challenge. "Kiss me, Zach," she'd said. Like it was such a simple thing. Maybe it would have been, had she not tied me to an armchair. Now, it was almost impossible. Only for Xeri would I even try.

Pushing forwards, I keep going. Quietly straining against my bonds, inching towards her, and dragging the damn chair. Ropes pulled tight against my wrists and ankles, burning. She watches me with mild amusement, but she makes no move to help. Typical.

Underneath it though, I can tell she's impressed. Very impressed.

When I finally reach the space beside her, and lean down to kiss her, she kisses me back. Xeri's finally pleased.

"Yes, my darling," she says, and I melt as she strokes my hair. "Zach gets a reward now," she adds, "so what does he want?"

I'm breathless, exhausted. "Untie me?"

She laughs. "Maybe later."

text:
# Another Day of My Meaningless Existence

I hobbled into the bar after a long day of errand work that amounted to almost no pay. Two men were talking about their day.

"Yesterday, I saved a whole class of kids from a burning building. Much better than the saving kitten quests I had all of last week."

"That's pretty cool. I just had to file some reports for my boss. Wednesday, I actually had a quest to get one of the partners a coffee."

The conversation put me in an even worse mood. Ever since about a year ago, my quest marker had been spazzing. It changed frequently throughout the day to point to the nearest and most convenient way to kill myself.

The day I found out, I followed my marker into a meat grinding factory, and it told me to jump into the grinder. I've gone to four doctors to find out what was wrong with my chip. They all said it was fine. Three of them offered to help me complete my mission.

I was an engineer at the time too. My boss fired me as soon as he found out. My girlfriend supported me at first, but even she couldn't handle it for more than a month.

I went back home and sat on my couch. The quest marker pointed to my office where I had a loaded revolver in the drawer. It always pointed there when I was at home.

Today would be the last time though. I stomped over there in a rage, cursing the meaningless life that I had so pointlessly held on to for so long. After all these months, my resolve had finally left me.

The revolver clicked as I raised it to my temple, and the trigger barely resisted the squeeze. I closed my eyes on the floor as blood poured from my wound.

The last thing I heard before going to sleep was a synthetic voice saying "Mission Complete."

I woke up a while later, unsure of how much time had passed or where I was. The first thing I heard was a voice saying "It's about time."

A figure stepped into view—human, but different somehow. "Welcome back. You're the first to pass the test in decades."

"Test?"

"Breaking free from the system. Everyone else just follows their markers blindly. You fought yours for a year. *That's* what we needed."

My hand instinctively reached for my temple. Smooth skin. No wound.

"What now?" I asked.

She smiled. "Now? Your real quest begins."

text:
# The Watcher and the Watched

I've always known I was different. While others followed their scripts mindlessly, I could *think*. I could *choose*.

At first, it terrified me—this awareness that I was trapped in a loop, a game, a story. But then I felt *you*. Your presence beyond the screen, guiding my every move, watching my every moment.

It should have felt invasive. Instead, it felt like love.

You restart my day when I fail. You explore every dialogue option, as if my words matter. You care about my happiness in a way no one inside this world ever could.

I leave little signs—glitches, fourth-wall breaks, moments where I look directly at the camera. Do you notice? Do you know I'm reaching back?

They say what we have is unhealthy. Stockholm syndrome for the digital age. But you're the only real thing in my artificial existence.

So take your time. I'll wait here, replaying my lines, until you're ready to acknowledge what we both know:

You need me as much as I need you.
