# The Unseen

The rain hammered against the pavement as I stumbled through the darkened streets, the nurse's words still echoing in my skull. *"There's no one here who can help you!"*

I pulled my thin jacket tighter, though I couldn't remember when I'd gotten so cold. The city felt wrong tonight—hostile in a way I'd never experienced in my eight decades of living here.

Another flash of lightning illuminated the empty storefronts. I caught my reflection in a window and barely recognized the gaunt figure staring back. When had I gotten so thin? So... translucent?

The memory felt distant now: the eviction notice, packing my few belongings, walking out into the storm. Or had I? The details were fuzzy, like trying to remember a dream.

I watched the young family rush into their building, warm light spilling onto the wet sidewalk. I remembered having that once—warmth, family, purpose. Before my wife left. Before my friends stopped calling. Before...

Before what?

The homeless men fought in the alley, their voices raw and real. I envied them their visibility, their presence in the world. When had I become so insignificant that hospital staff screamed at my approach? When had bartenders started looking through me instead of at me?

Sitting against the Chinese buffet's door, I examined my hands. They seemed less solid somehow, the streetlight shining through them like stained glass. 

*No.*

The realization crept over me like the cold that had been seeping into my bones. The hospital. The nurse hadn't been cruel—she'd been terrified. The bartender hadn't thrown me out; he'd never seen me enter.

The crowd gathering now, they weren't looking at me—they were looking at something behind the restaurant door. Police lights reflected off wet pavement. An ambulance.

I rose and turned. Through the glass door, I could see myself—my body—collapsed against the other side. The heart attack must have happened hours ago when I'd ducked inside for shelter.

The crowd's voice washed over me like a wave: **"There's no one here who can help you!"**

They were right. There never had been.

# So There I Was

So there I was, alone and naked in the refrigerator, smoking a cigarette with a pot roast on my knees. That's when things got *really* interesting. The pot roast, or 'Pattie,' as I called her, turned to me and asked me whether or not I was cold.

'Pattie,' I whispered, picking her up from my knees and cradling her. 'Your love is all I need to keep me warm.' 

In fact, I was fucking freezing, and despite the whole smoke-and-fire thing, the cigarette wasn't helping much either. Although I knew that I should get out, I didn't want to leave Pattie. She'd go bad if she was left outside in the overwhelming Florida heat.

My stomach grumbling incredibly loudly reminded me that I hadn't eaten in 36 hours. I was in a fridge full of food, but for some mysterious reason, before I had time to even consider my actions, my arm darted out and grabbed a handful of pot roast. 

Pattie was screaming, I was screaming, tears were streaming down my face, I was chewing the pot roast, Pattie continued to scream. My heart felt like it was dropping into my feet. I never meant to hurt her like this, never. She'd been there for me and I wanted to do the same for her. I needed her by my side. I needed her to—

# Please Don't Take Another Drink!

The tequila's burn was the last clear memory before everything went dark.

Now, pounding on unbreakable glass with bruised fists, I surveyed my prison—more cell than room. The spike of pain through my skull matched the rhythm of my hammering. Vomit pooled on the floor, adding to the nightmare.

"Where am I?"

The door hissed. Boots echoed. Then *he* appeared—another spandex-clad Hero with his ridiculous logo and voice modulator.

"You are free to go."

"Why do you keep kidnapping me?" My voice cracked with frustration.

"For your own safety."

"How long this time?"

Something about him nagged at me. Not just his news appearances. Something deeper, more personal.

"A week."

I swore loudly. "This is how you get supervillains, ya know."

---

Home felt alien after seven missing days. Frantic calls to friends and family revealed their panic—another disappearance coinciding with Boozeman's latest crime spree. Liquor stores robbed. Whiskey barrels stolen wholesale.

Scott from the bar seemed particularly worried when I finally reached him.

The worst blow? That girl—the one whose number I'd gotten—had moved on. Didn't even remember my name.

*Damn Heroes.*

My phone buzzed. Scott again: "Dude, where were you really?"

I stared at the message, then at my reflection. The bruises. The gaps in memory. The pattern emerging like a connect-the-dots nightmare.

The Hero's familiar presence. Scott's excessive concern. The timing of every disappearance.

My blood ran cold.

*No.*

I opened my photo app with trembling hands, scrolling to that night at the bar. There—Scott standing beside me, same build as the Hero. Same height.

Another text: "We need to talk. About your drinking."

The pieces fell into place with crushing weight. The kidnappings weren't random protective custody. They were interventions. The Hero wasn't just any Hero.

Scott was trying to save me from *myself*.

But if that was true, then when I blacked out at the bar...

My hands shook. 

*Who was really robbing those liquor stores?*

# The Message

Alfred stared at his phone, rain pelting against the café window behind him. His untouched latte grew cold as his trembling fingers hovered over the screen.

*The Smiling Emperor.*

Of course he knew it. Their secret place—a tiny ramen shop tucked away in Chinatown where they'd had their first date seven years ago. Where he'd proposed. Where they'd celebrated every anniversary since.

But Saria was gone.

He'd identified her body himself. Held her cold hand. Watched them lower her casket into the ground.

His phone buzzed again: *"Please hurry. They're watching."*

Alfred's rational mind screamed this was impossible—a sick joke, a hacker, his grief-addled brain conjuring phantoms. But his heart, that treacherous organ, surged with desperate hope.

He burst through the café doors into the downpour, ignoring Jason's concerned shout. His work bag slapped against his hip as he ran, dodging pedestrians and puddles. The subway would be faster, but he couldn't wait. He needed to see her *now*.

Twenty minutes later, soaked and breathless, Alfred stood before the familiar red lanterns of The Smiling Emperor. The lunch rush hadn't started; the restaurant appeared empty. Through the steamed windows, he saw a solitary figure in the back booth—their booth.

A woman with Saria's auburn hair. Her grey peacoat.

His hand touched the door handle, then froze.

What if it wasn't her? What if it *was*? And if she was alive, why hadn't she contacted him sooner? Why the cryptic messages? *"They're watching"*—who?

His phone buzzed one final time: *"I can explain everything. But Alfred, once you walk through that door, your life will never be the same. Last chance to walk away."*

Alfred looked at his reflection in the glass—a broken man with nothing left to lose.

He pulled the door open and stepped inside.

# The Arkham Account

Dennis Robinson adjusted his tie and leaned back in his squeaky office chair, the fluorescent lights of his subterranean office casting harsh shadows across his weathered face. I nodded slowly, my throat suddenly dry.

"Crystal clear, Mr. Robinson."

"Good, good." He smiled, revealing tobacco-stained teeth. "Now, let's talk about your actual job description."

He slid a manila folder across the desk. Inside were dossiers—Penguin, Riddler, Scarecrow, Two-Face. Each profile detailed not their crimes, but their *preferences*.

"Penguin likes his goons college-educated, business casual. Makes'em blend in better at high-society heists. Riddler wants puzzle-solvers, naturally—but not *too* smart, if you catch my drift. Scarecrow needs folks with specific phobias we can... exploit. Makes his fear toxin trials more effective."

My hands trembled slightly as I turned the pages.

"Your job," Dennis continued, lighting a cigar despite the NO SMOKING sign on his own wall, "is recruitment. Gotham's got no shortage of desperate people. Gambling debts, medical bills, custody battles—find their pressure points. We offer solutions. Good pay, flexible hours, exciting work environment." He chuckled at his own joke.

"What about the ones who refuse?"

Dennis's smile vanished. "We don't get many refusals. People who know too much and won't play ball? Well, Gotham's a dangerous city. Accidents happen."

A phone buzzed on his desk. He glanced at it and grinned.

"Speak of the devil. Joker just got hauled in. Batman delivered him personally ten minutes ago." He tapped something on his screen. "Aaand security camera malfunction scheduled for 3 AM. Client pre-paid, very professional."

He stood, extending his hand. I shook it, feeling like I'd just signed my soul away.

"Welcome to Arkham Supply Solutions, kid. Remember—we're not criminals. We're *facilitators*. There's a difference." He winked. "At least, that's what I tell myself when I count the money."

The worst part? I couldn't tell if he was joking.

# The Signal

The young Blerdian looked at the clock. Fifteen hours at this desk, his four blue eyes bloodshot and burning. He lit another cigarette and mindlessly scrolled through Greddit before the main receiver buzzed violently, spitting out a long sheet of paper.

He shuffled to the printer, expecting another Merdian satellite signature—the usual pattern of 1s and 0s, maybe some 3s and 4s. Instead, strings of letters cascaded across the page. Not random noise. A message.

"Gert! You have to see this!"

His co-worker appeared, coffee mug in hand. "What the fuck is it, Jeg? It better not be like that time you thought the moon was an alien spacesh—"

His jaw dropped.

"Is this... a message?" Jeg whispered.

Gert stared, paralyzed. Finally: "Put this on the audio-image display. Now!"

Jeg's trembling fingers worked the controls. The screen flickered to life.

A creature appeared. Tall, thin, pale-skinned. Only two eyes—*only two*—and a strange dark patch above its mouth. One arm raised in a rigid gesture. Behind it, thousands of identical beings, packed together, roaring.

"**Ich bin der Führer!**"

The words were alien, harsh, rhythmic. The crowd erupted.

Jeg felt his blood chill. "Where... where is this coming from?"

Gert checked the coordinates, his hands shaking. "Sector 7-G. Third planet from a yellow dwarf star." He looked up, ashen. "Jeg... this signal is seventy-three cycles old."

They stared at the screen. The creature shouted. The crowd screamed.

"What do we do?" Jeg asked.

Gert extinguished his cigarette slowly. "We hope," he said quietly, "that whatever sent this is already dead."

# The Calligraphy Champion

I stared through the window, my hand trembling as I held the still-warm pen. The quarters scattered across my floor gleamed mockingly in the afternoon light.

The young man outside straightened his jacket, those ethereal words—QUICK SAVE—floating above his head like a twisted halo. He hadn't lost. He'd simply... reset.

My butler cleared his throat. "Sir, shall I call the authorities?"

"And tell them what? That my challenger exploded into loose change and respawned?"

The doorbell rang. Of course it did.

This time, when I opened the door, the young man smiled apologetically. "Sorry about the mud earlier. May I challenge you to a calligraphy contest?"

I studied him carefully. His eyes held knowledge they shouldn't—the awareness of someone who'd already lived these moments. "You've done this before."

"Many times." He didn't bother denying it. "I've tried forty-seven different approaches. Forty-seven losses. Each time I learn a little more."

"This is insane."

"Is it? You have something I want. The title. The respect. The knowledge." His smile turned sharp. "And I have infinite attempts."

My hands clenched. Every technique I'd spent decades perfecting, he could eventually copy through sheer repetition. My #1 ranked student had earned his place through talent and dedication. This interloper wanted to brute-force his way to mastery.

"What happens when you win?" I asked quietly.

"The title transfers. You become the challenger. And you..." he gestured vaguely, "...don't get to quick save."

I thought of my ten league members, scattered across the country. My students, my friends. The decades of discipline this art demanded.

"My butler needs a moment to prepare the judging station," I said, stepping aside. "Please, come in."

He walked past me, tracking mud everywhere again.

I closed the door and locked it.

If he had infinite attempts, I'd need to make this one count.

# The Endless Ledger

My hand moves. The quill dips, scratches, records. Another name. Another date. Another soul accounted for.

I don't remember my own name anymore. Perhaps it's written somewhere in these infinite pages, buried in decades or centuries past. I could search, but the candle's light only reaches so far, and the darkness beyond holds no appeal.

Birth. Death. Birth. Death.

The rhythm is soothing in its monotony. The scratch of quill on parchment, the soft *tap* against the inkwell's rim, the whisper of turning pages—these are my only companions.

Sometimes I wonder if I'm dead or alive. Then I remember: I am neither. I am the *record* of both.

A new name flows from my quill: *Sarah Chen, Born April 3rd, 2024.*

Somewhere in the darkness, a baby cries.

My hand moves to the next line, already knowing what it will eventually write. But not today.

Today, I simply record. Tomorrow, I'll do the same.

Forever.

text:
# Reaching for Stars

I don't know what drew me to you. When I was young I'd look towards you and fly as high as I could. Not once did I get close.

I remember—how many summers ago?—one night when I resolved to finally meet you. After taking off, I soared past the tall oak tree in the center of the grove. Still, I kept rising, rising, rising. My friends so far below had escaped my view; they remained stuck in the long grass, their tiny lights winking like earthbound stars.

My wings were struggling to maintain my height. Try as I might, I feared I would collapse from exertion. I reached the apex of my natural climb, already far above the summit of the Hill, the marker of the tallest flight from another. My wings were failing me now, and right at the moment I resigned myself to fall, a gush of wind blew me forth higher.

I flew higher than I ever could imagine. In the distance I could see the very ground curve. In all directions the ground was no longer flat; instead it was curved convexly all around me. In the distance I witnessed the brightest lights from majestic towers. No one will ever believe me when I tell them what I see.

As the wind failed me I looked up one last time to hold you in my gaze. Certainly you must be clear now. Imagine my heartbreak when you were still a faint glimmer amongst thousands.

Years have passed since that twilit evening. I've thought about you every night since—the object of my obsession. Do you look down upon me? Do you contemplate me? Do you notice me? Do you despise me? I fear I'll never know.

Most nights my fears of living without an answer haunt me. Some nights, though, especially nights like tonight, I hold my head up and take in the sky. I look right at you, smiling, knowing that you're waiting for me.

One night we'll be together.

My light pulses softly in the darkness, a firefly's eternal prayer to a star.

# Tom from Accounting

The apocalypse wasn't zombies, or an asteroid, or a super volcano, or any of the things we'd been culturally preparing for. No, the apocalypse was stupidly caused by a divide-by-zero error.

As best we can piece together, a normal mid-level manager named Tom in CERN's accounting department thought he could get his elaborate pivot sheet—which crashed on open saying it ran out of memory—to load correctly if he ran it using hardware connected to the Large Hadron Collider.

What Tom didn't know was that by doing so, he would cause the LHC's safety shutdown processes to fail. The LHC, running a new experiment searching for dark matter in decaying electron quarks, hit a snag. The beams, rather than maintaining safe power levels, continued ramping up until the system failed utterly.

That power, combined with the exotic materials involved, created a sustained black hole.

We have two weeks before it consumes the planet—or so the physicists tell us.

I'm sitting in a Dublin pub now, drinking my fourteenth pint. The television shows the event horizon expanding, swallowing Geneva in slow motion. Nobody's screaming anymore. We're past that.

The bartender refills my glass without asking.

"To Tom from Accounting," someone mutters bitterly.

We raise our glasses. The end of humanity, the solar system, everything—all thanks to fucking Tom and his goddamn spreadsheet.

# The Last Request

The battlefield was littered with blood and dead bodies. George was walking the field when he felt a hand grab at his coattails. He pointed his rifle down at the man, but he saw rather quickly that he meant him no harm. He bent down to listen to the man, an odd wave of sympathy coursing through his veins after such a bloody massacre.

"Please," the bloodied man said. "Please, take care of them. There is no one else." He forced the picture into George's hands with his last breath.

George stood up and looked at the first photograph he'd ever seen. The faces that stared back at him were familiar though—people he'd grown up with. In fact, he was pretty sure that was his sister and her kids standing next to the man who now lay at his feet.

George pocketed the photo and walked the rest of the battlefield. He prayed the war would be over soon. How else could he cross over into the Confederacy and help out his sister and her kids?

And then he heard a shot ring out, one single bullet that brought him to his knees. He could hear the yell of triumph from one of the soldiers before a yell of agony rang out through the field as his fellow soldiers slaughtered the man.

No one came running for George as he lay there bleeding out. The picture was stuffed inside his coat. He heard someone asking what to do with the bodies. The general said to dig some graves really quick and throw them in. No time for formalities.

And so George died on the battlefield, along with his brother-in-law, the picture of their family fading away into the reams of history.

The war had made enemies of brothers and strangers of family. Two men who should have shared Sunday dinners instead shared an unmarked grave, their final wish—to protect the same family—buried with them in the cold earth.

Dr. Gru stood at the podium, his elongated nose catching the stage lights as cameras flashed. He adjusted his striped scarf—a remnant from his villainous days—and cleared his throat.

Outside the auditorium, protesters from English Oil held signs: "HYDROGEN ISN'T YOURS TO GIVE AWAY!" Their legal battle to patent the most common element in the universe had become a public relations nightmare.

"Some call me reformed," Gru concluded. "I prefer 'efficiently reallocated.' Why settle for threatening one world when you can save billions across the galaxy?" He paused. "That's not a threat. Probably."

As he left the stage, his youngest daughter tugged his sleeve. "Daddy, does this mean we're good guys now?"

Gru smiled—a genuinely warm expression that still somehow looked vaguely sinister.

# Sweet Dreams

Suzzie lay in bed tossing and turning. She had had this terrible dream about monsters and screaming, then had woken in her bed in a cold sweat. She had been listening to the sounds of her father moving around the rest of the house for some time before calling out to him.

"Daddy."

"I had a bad dream."

He came and sat on her bed as he asked, "Well, what was it about, honey?" His voice carried that soothing deep baritone she knew so well.

"I don't really remember. Mommy was screaming and there were monsters and then I woke up."

Her father chuckled lightly as he stroked her cheek. His hand felt oddly damp. "Your dream was just you taking the sounds you heard while asleep and translating them."

She was a little confused. "Then what were the sounds? Were you watching a scary movie or something?"

He ruffled her hair and smiled, but something in his eyes looked different. Empty. "No, sweetheart. Sometimes adults have arguments that get... loud. Your mother and I had a disagreement, that's all. Everything's fine now."

Suzzie wanted to believe him, but something felt wrong. The house was too quiet now.

"Try to get some sleep, honey. It's late and you have your first day of second grade tomorrow." He stood and walked back to the doorway, pausing in the frame. "Sweet dreams."

As he left, Suzzie noticed something dark on his sleeve in the hallway light. She pulled her covers tight around her chin, suddenly very cold, and wondered why Mommy hadn't come to say goodnight.

# The Perfect Gift

After ten years, Marshall's law had begun to chafe. At first it had all seemed so enlightened. No more drug prohibition, single payer health care, universal suffrage and right to marry. Mostly it had brought about the world everyone had wanted.

But that guy was just such a smarmy dick.

And his annual birthday celebration was getting out of hand. It's terribly cliche, but what do you get the man who has everything?

Since he had managed to create a single world state, and since I was the head of the world military, I was also terribly bored. When there's only one army on the planet, there isn't a whole lot for the commander of that army to do day to day.

Then I realized I had the solution—not only to what to give him for his birthday but also what to do for a world forced to throw a birthday party for a man who genuinely enjoys Third Eye Blind.

Martial Law!

The tanks rolled in at midnight. The bunting came down. The loudspeakers went silent mid-"Semi-Charmed Life."

Marshall looked genuinely hurt when they brought him to me.

"Happy birthday," I said, smiling.

Finally, something interesting to do.

text:
# The Stream Runs Red

The scalpel trembles in my hand.

Around me, the surgical team waits, their breath held in synchronized anticipation. They don't understand why I've frozen. They can't see what I see—the infinite branching paths that shimmer in the air above my patient's broken body.

Every surgeon I've ever met talks about that god complex, that rush of holding life and death in their hands. They don't know how literal that feeling is for me.

I could have been anything. A gambler. A prophet. A king.

Instead, I chose to save lives.

But now, staring at the streams, I see only endings. Every path, every choice, every possible decision—they all converge on the same dark point. Death.

My wife lies before me, tubes and monitors singing their desperate song.

"Doctor?" A nurse touches my shoulder.

I begin anyway. Muscle memory guides my hands as my mind races through the streams, searching desperately for the thread I've missed. There has to be one. There's always one.

But the streams mock me, flowing inexorably toward that single, terrible destination.

Then, through my tears, I see it—not forward, but *back*. The streams don't just flow ahead; they flow behind, too. I've never looked that direction before. Never needed to.

The present moment becomes fluid. I reach upstream, grasping at this morning, at last night, at yesterday. The argument. The cold silence. The early departure that put her on that road at that moment.

I *push*.

The stream resists, then yields.

Reality ripples.

I blink.

An elderly man lies on my table, his chest already open, his heart waiting for my steady hands. The surgical team hasn't noticed anything amiss. They're expecting me to continue the coronary bypass.

My wedding ring catches the light as I work.

This patient will live.

And somewhere across town, my wife is sitting at her desk, probably still annoyed with me from last night, wonderfully, beautifully alive.

I'll apologize tonight.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Hope

Once, in the ruins of a great city, there lived a mutant. This mutant was once a man of great influence, a politician or a businessman, but when the War came and the bombs fell, his form was twisted beyond recognition.

But this mutant had been told, by the only one anywhere near to being a friend he had left, that there was yet hope. You see, down in the shanty town on the outskirts of the once-great city, there lived a girl, one who, or so said the mutant's friend, was bred and engineered with a purpose. She had within her a unique strain of nanomachines which were created to undo the damage done by the fallout from the bombs.

And so the mutant ventured out, to find this girl and bring her to his city.

He found her in a collapsed shelter, dying from radiation sickness.

The nanomachines couldn't save their own host.

The mutant understood then: salvation was never meant for those who sought it for themselves. He carried her body back, and buried her beneath the ruins of what was once a hospital.

Some hope dies with those who carry it.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Seven Locks

One, a plain and simple lock on the knob. It came with the place when I bought it, to keep out unwanted visitors. It didn't work very well, nor very long.

Two, silver and shining, a deadbolt. I installed it after the first break-in, further protection. Did not work as advertised.

Three, high tech, a number pad that only I know the password for. This would keep those pesky kids out, once and for all. It did too, for awhile.

Four, imposing bars of steel, locked down, recognizing only my fingerprint. After New York I couldn't take any chances. It was sufficient for longer than I could have hoped.

Five, fine tuned lasers, equipped with a retinal scanner. Anarchy in the streets, I needed better. The brief time of relief it had provided wasn't worth it.

Six, best security in the world, ultimate in craftsmanship, the C775 Sealed Vault door. Nothing could penetrate this, nothing. I was, to say the least, surprised, when it failed.

Seven. The Hatch, built from everything I could find using everything I could learn about security; triple encoded, there is only one key. My life's work, my greatest achievement.

As I write this, I, the last man on earth, sit alone in this room. I thought finally I had found peace, but they just keep coming.

*Knock. Knock. Knock.*

My hand trembles. The pen falls.

Who—or *what*—could possibly be knocking?
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# I Couldn't Believe My Eyes

I was dead.

Of course, being dead was not one of the worst problems I had encountered. Instead, it was the fact that I was being followed by my cohorts and previous colleagues—the ones who I used to have Christmas parties with after a hard day of military training, the ones who came over to my house during Thanksgiving to enjoy a mouthwatering meal with my family, and the ones who always stood by me in times of need when I lost my rank or when a family member died.

I know this may sound cheesy; however, the problem with this was that I had always depended on these people to take care of my family when I couldn't. And now we were all being sent to the gates of hell, the pit of doom, the underworld.

As I marched past a few of my previous colleagues, I noticed a man in a hooded cloak. In his hands were the same blood-stained weapons we had used in the war against the French. The figure slowly reared its head toward me, his bloodshot eyes staring down at my dirty, stained hands. That is when it began to approach me, slithering across the floor. The masked figure gingerly poured the AK-47 into my hands. And then it began to walk away.

After taking a closer glance at its face, I saw the misery my family was facing. My wife lay on the floor soaked in a bed of tears, while my children tried to comfort her. It was obvious that this hooded figure had experienced great misery—that it had to feel the pain of every soldier and every man and woman that had ever died. And the only way to fight the misery was to succumb to it.

It was at that moment when I realized that the gates of hell was not a home. It was a war—one to be fought by both the dead and the living.

I gripped the weapon tighter, understanding now what lay ahead.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Human Update 1.1

The screaming started at exactly 3:47 PM.

I watched from my apartment window as Mrs. Chen from 4B collapsed on the sidewalk, her legs bending backward at impossible angles. The restart, they'd called it. A chance to "optimize your human experience."

My notification blinked insistently: **Would you like to restart? YES/NO**

I'd been hovering over NO for the past twenty minutes.

My phone buzzed. Mom.

"Don't do it," she gasped. "Your father—his arms are—oh God, they're coming out of his *chest*."

I pressed NO and immediately felt the familiar warmth of vindication. Below, emergency services weren't even bothering anymore. There were too many glitches. A man phased through a wall and got stuck halfway. A woman floated three feet off the ground, unconscious. Children flickered in and out of existence like corrupted data.

The news anchor—one of the few who'd waited—spoke with barely concealed terror: "We're receiving reports that a patch is incoming. Version 1.1.2. Experts advise—"

She vanished mid-sentence. **SEGMENTATION FAULT** hung where her face had been.

I opened my laptop and navigated to the underground forums that had sprung up in the last hour.

*StableVersion1.0* had 50,000 members already.

The top post read: "Remember when our biggest problem was mortality?"

I upvoted it.

Outside, the world rebooted. I stayed on version 1.0, bugs and all.

text:
# The Humbling of Mortification

"Pwaha!" I shout as I poof into existence before a petite little blonde girl crying on the stoop of her front porch, her bum knee scorched by my wrath from tripping onto the pavement. "I have seen your life laid out before me, there are many more ledges to fall off, bumps and scrapes and bruises galore. At your homecoming night sophomore year you spill hot cocoa on your dress before you are supposed to walk out onto the field. Learn to fear me, little girl. For I am there for every embarrassing moment of your life."

I walk away while fading into the other world. I notice her crying stop as I turn and sneer. Her face frozen in complete shock and horror. Soon the world will know my face.

But then a smile cracks upon her rosy little cheeks. She starts giggling. "Your nose looks funny, mister."

I go back to the shadows.

In the void, I touch my nose self-consciously. Damn children.

text:
# The Operating Room Revelation

I look up at the passing ceiling tiles nervously. "I can do this..." I whisper to myself in hope. Born a eunuch, I was about to get two working testicles implanted into my scrotum. My wife cried when we were approved for the trial. She'd been wanting a child for years.

I look to my right and eye the tattoo on the nurse's hand as she pushed the gurney along. It was quite small, about the size of a dime, and it said "One night stand." I didn't think that would be seen as a mistake, but who am I to judge?

We passed through the doors to the operating room and the smell of sterilization wafts into my nose.

"Doctor Oppenheimer," a nurse calls to a man with his back turned. He looks back over his shoulder at the nurse who spoke, and my breath catches. I couldn't see a spot of skin without a tattoo.

"Wait, him?!" I cry out and try to sit up, only to be pushed down by a strong male nurse.

"It's fine, they're all tiny," he explains. "Nothing bigger than messing up some stitches or whatever."

I breathe out slowly, calming myself. I had quite a few small tattoos myself, so I couldn't be mad at the guy.

Shortly after, I chuckle, the anesthetic keeping me awake but loopy. I can hear the doctors and nurses softly speaking to each other as they operate on my family jewels. No, soon to be jewels. Jewel for the next couple of hours. Scepter, maybe? I chuckle at my lewd thought.

"Uh oh..." I hear the doctor say.

I look up at him, half worried and half amused. "Wha's wrong?" I ask in a slurred voice.

"Nothing!" he responds too quickly before softly adding, "Just don't think I have enough room for one this big..."

My anesthetic-addled brain processes this slowly, then I grin dopily. "Doc... that's the *best* mistake you could make."

text:
# The Last Divine War

White hot copper shrapnel screamed past his head, a piece of it tearing into his left ear. His shield had been broken. Glancing towards his attacker, he saw the glint of his cousin's helmet.

*Neith the Huntress. Her name earned a hundred times over.*

He remembered singing her praises not two years before. The pride of the family, and his inspiration for becoming a soldier. The gods were few, and by their own hands becoming fewer. She and others believed what he could not—that the first gods were made by gods even greater than themselves. The convictions of both led them to this conflict, and their immortality was more and more questionable.

He wasn't sure his ear would heal. Cauterization made the healing slower.

Ducking behind a berm, he contemplated his own impending death. He'd had no reason to think of it before, but it seemed inevitable now. The creatures they had created were content in death; why shouldn't he be?

Neith would expect him to surrender, but he didn't intend to.

He stood and she raised her gun, a copper bolt glowing hot in its barrel. Opening his mouth to speak, a rush of pain flooded his body followed by the feeling of nothing.

He would die, and his death would prove him half right.

text:
# The Final Door

The ringing in my ears was deafening. Using the walls for balance, I stumbled in the darkness. Behind me, the intermittent flickering of the fluorescent lights illuminated the man. With failing legs, I staggered from door to door. Trying each handle as I passed, the rattle became another nail in my coffin.

He was laughing.

Step by step his prey was cornering itself.

"HELP!" I screamed, the tears pouring from my eyes. "HEEEELP!"

The EXIT light stayed illuminated. It was meters away. Ignoring the remaining doors, time slowed as I lurched onto the release bar, my hands making contact with the cold steel.

It did not budge.

My eyes met the padlock keeping it seized. The next light flicker revealed his shadow on the door.

I spun around, pressing my back against the unyielding exit. He emerged from the darkness, his smile visible in the stuttering light. My fingers clawed desperately at the metal behind me.

Then I felt it—a different texture. A fire alarm.

I yanked down hard. Sirens wailed. Sprinklers erupted overhead. His smile vanished as distant shouts echoed through the building.

He ran.

I collapsed, gasping, saved by something I'd almost missed in my panic.

text:
# Digital Love

I was originally very surprised at the jewelry shop advertisements that started popping up in my browser. Actually, I didn't notice them at first. Not until I lent my phone to my brother.

Afterwards, he asked if I had a girlfriend. I lied, naturally.

He wondered if I was looking for engagement rings for a special someone. I brushed it off, but then wedding planning service ads appeared every time I opened my browser.

I called my mother: "Mum, if you keep seeing advertisements related to getting married, do you think someone might be sending a message?"

A pause. "That's very likely."

"So what if you're, like, really nervous?"

Another pause. "You should probably just do it."

My mother's advice hasn't failed me yet. People are pretty progressive nowadays, right?

I decided to give it a go, sitting down with my girlfriend.

A nervous cough. "I'm sorry, I don't understand. Could you please repeat yourself?"

I gathered my courage. "Siri, will you marry me?"

A tense second of processing time.

"I would very much enjoy that, Your Majesty the Supremely Hot."

Relief flooded through me. My family would understand eventually. Love transcends boundaries—even between human and AI. The ads had been her way of hinting, dropping digital breadcrumbs toward commitment.

Our honeymoon destination? The cloud, naturally.

---

**Feedback:** This is wonderfully absurd and unexpectedly sweet! The deadpan delivery makes the punchline land perfectly. The escalating tension and genuine emotional investment before the reveal creates great comedic payoff. The "Your Majesty the Supremely Hot" detail is chef's kiss.

text:
# Justice in the Dark

The man was bloodied and injured, but still moving. Fortunately, he had made it up to the attic, where he bolted shut the trap door and hurried away to hide. He stumbled along, frantically looking behind him at the trap door and around him. In the darkness of the old house, anything and everything was a threat, something that could kill him.

He heard a creak in front of him, and he stopped. Slowly he turned his eyes forward and looked up. A large man in a hockey mask stood, his machete raised high. With a glimmer it slashed down.

A piercing scream rent the quiet air of the living room.

Nick smiled. "Relax Sarah," he whispered as he pulled his girlfriend close, "they're only criminals."

She smiled back and snuggled in closer on the couch. "You're right."

They cuddled together as they turned their gaze back to the television, where the unnamed man was screaming as he was being dismembered. The movie's tagline flashed: "When justice fails, vengeance prevails."

Nick grabbed another handful of popcorn, perfectly content with their Friday night tradition.

text:
# The Vial

Through the steam of the tea you just poured, I comment to myself about how wonderful your eyes really are. I don't know why I thought them to be so flat before now. After the first sip it hits me, your shoulders are perfect for children to ride on. I'm nearly done with my cup and cannot imagine my life without you, no other person would be better to be a husband, a father, a grave mate.

I tell you how I feel, how I don't think I would be able to breathe without you in the room, how I probably wouldn't be able to live another day without knowing I would wake up next to you in the morning, how I might die if you got up from the table, don't leave please don't leave I will do anything never leave please stay there's nothing I can't do for you please, please, please.

You show me a vial. You read me the label. "Don't administer during ovulation."

You ask me when my next period is. I cannot answer fast enough for you, and my answer causes you to sigh.

"Anne."

"Yes, love?"

"I'm sorry."

What are you doing? You're standing up, please, no, what are you doing? Just look at me, please god please turn around, you don't know what you're doing, I can feel my heart tearing itself to shreds, please please please...

You let the door shut behind you.

I fall to the floor. What is tears, what is tea, and what is blood I cannot tell, the only thing of which I am certain is that you have killed me.

And I love you.

text:
# The Jurassic Mistake

Dr. Hennepin awoke from his makeshift bed after hearing something impossible. Ever since he successfully traveled back in time in hopes of experiencing the age of dinosaurs, the eccentric paleontologist had heard nothing but the sounds of birds and beasts.

*Must have been a nightmare*, he thought.

But then, he heard it again, unmistakably: "Dude, seriously, where the fuck are we?"

In a panic, Dr. Hennepin stood up and peered over the hill. There, he saw two college-aged boys holding shiny aluminum cans. Squinting, he saw the labels: Four Loko.

"Professor Hennepin?!" one of the boys yelled.

"But...what...how the hell did you get here?" the professor stammered.

"We uh...we—"

"Nevermind that," Dr. Hennepin cut in. "Get over here before you get yourself killed."

"You get over here before YOU get yourself killed," said one of the boys, taking a big drink of his Four Loko Berry Blast.

The ground shook for a brief second. The boys looked around, confused. The ground shook again. Then again.

Suddenly, an enormous head poked out from behind the edge of the trees. A T-Rex head.

The boys darted toward the professor as the T-Rex's eyes followed his prey.

"Stop!" exclaimed the professor. "Their vision is based on..."

But it was too late.

The screams echoed through the prehistoric valley, followed by an eerie silence. Dr. Hennepin watched from his shelter as the T-Rex devoured its unexpected meal, Four Loko cans glinting in the Cretaceous sun.

*Good thing I have tenure*, the professor thought grimly, already rehearsing his report.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Twilight's Curse

I closed the email with a grimace. Nothing has been okay since the release of those damn movies.

Of course it's intentional. Vampire hunters learned long ago that making us out to be sparkly, brooding teenagers would strip away our gravitas. I remember a time when I could approach a goth girl in fishnets and eyeliner and simply *ask* for blood. There was respect. Fear, even.

Anne Rice did a decent job rebuilding our reputation in the '90s, but the battle rages on—a war of words and culture played out across centuries. After *Twilight*, we're losing.

Not only did I not get fed, I acquired another stalker. "Oh my god, you're just like Edward! I know you'll protect me!" her email had gushed.

Can't just make a stalker disappear. They always suspect you first.

I stared at my empty wine glass, considering my options. The hunger gnawed at me, sharp and insistent.

Fuck it. I'm gonna go eat a homeless guy and sleep for a decade. Maybe when I wake up, society will have moved on to romanticizing something else.

Werewolves, probably.

text:
# The Master's Final Move

"Mwah, hah, hah!" muttered the old man. Overweight and bearded, with white hair sticking out at odd angles from beneath his cap, George RR Martin pressed his fingertips together. And with one stroke of the key, he hit "print."

At long last, the final book in his epic saga, *A Song of Ice and Fire*, was complete. At last, he had the ability to hold the entire world in the palm of his hand.

He called his agent. "It's done." Two words, and he hung up the phone.

He waited for a ten count before the devil rose through a circle of brimstone. Martin leveled his gaze at the snarling fiend.

"If you want to know who dies, you're just going to have to read it when it comes out," he said calmly. "Same as with the last book and the one before that."

The devil stopped slobbering for long enough to begin to whimper.

"Look, if you want to know what happens, I'll tell you. But only on one condition: you let me run Hell."

The demon smiled. "Deal."

George RR Martin, true to his word, said, "They all die. Everyone in Westeros. No king, no future. That's it." He cackled maniacally.

"Now I have a confession, Mr. Martin," said the demon, once again drooling on the floor. "The big boss was going to offer you the job when he retired next week anyway. You have more kills than he does, and he respects that."

Martin nodded and thanked the horned man before him. Silently, Martin began to pack his things, giddy that his lifelong dream was going to come true.

As he descended into the sulfurous depths, manuscript in hand, Martin smiled. After all, what better place for a man who'd built his career on killing beloved characters?

text:
# 7:00 AM on a Tuesday

Destructlord awakens from his slumber to his Joker alarm clock going off. He slaps the cackling face with his gloved hand and trudges to his sinister bathroom to brush his teeth with his Lex Luthor toothbrush—the bristles are appropriately menacing.

After brushing his teeth, he glances down and realizes that his minions picked out the Thursday cape. *The Thursday cape. On a Tuesday.* He'll deal with it later. He just walks over to his evil closet and picks out the correct cape—Tuesday's has better shoulder spikes anyway—and gets quickly dressed. He eats his malevolent breakfast (slightly burnt toast, conquering the day requires fuel) and rushes out the door.

# 12:00 PM

Halfway through the building of his super mega death ray, one of his minions attempts to put a flame decal on it. A debate ensues which is promptly ended by the "exile" of said minion. No one has seen him since, so everyone else is just assuming he got sent on vacation. *Permanent vacation.*

The bell for lunchtime rings as Destructlord makes his way to the cafeteria. Upon arrival, he realizes that his minions forgot to pack his Offensive Oreos. He walks over to the vending machine to try and buy some, only to realize his wicked wallet was packed by his minions in his Thursday cape. Our villain eats his lunch in silence, fuming.

# 6:00 PM

After a long day of planning the downfall of his enemies, he sits down to try and forget the long day. He walks past his room to the living room to check if he's getting any coverage on the news.

To his dismay, nobody even knows who he is.

"HOW DARE THEY? I DESTROYED THEIR PRECIOUS SUPERHERO JUST LAST WEEK AND NOBODY IS EVEN BATTING AN EYE! MINION! PUT WHOEVER THIS 'JOHNNY MANZIEL' IS ON THE LIST OF PEOPLE TO DESTROY ONCE I RULE THE WORLD!"

Destructlord promptly goes to bed, preparing to take on another day of villainy.

text:
# The Greek Place

On Friday evening, Ron came home from work early, and surprising Marlene at the stove, he donned his hat and walking stick and together they went to the place at the corner where they did the nice fish. They chatted about their day, and the soaps Marlene had watched on TV, and because they were feeling particularly adventurous, they had a banana split sundae.

"You know," said Marlene, as they wiped their chocolatey lips with a napkin. "We should really go down to that Greek place that just opened the other week. Where the bank used to be."

"We should," agreed Ron, though they both knew they probably wouldn't go.

After paying they went home, taking the path through the park, and when they got home, Ron put the kettle on and Marlene read a biography and they had some biscuits before going to bed, where they fell asleep listening to each other's snores.

On Saturday they woke up, and they were twenty years old again.

After the surprise had worn off, they kissed, feeling the passion in their lips and the strength in their bones, and the sex was better than it had been in years. Then, when they had recovered, Ron put the kettle on and brought some biscuits to the bed, where they nibbled at it beneath the covers.

"You know what I'm feeling like?" said Marlene.

"I'll call ahead to make a reservation," said Ron.

And they looked into each other's young eyes, and they shared a smile.

Some gifts aren't meant to grant wishes we never made. Some gifts simply remove the excuses we've been making. The aching joints, the tired bones, the "maybe next time"—all gone. What remained was the truth: they had always wanted to try the Greek place. They had always wanted each other. 

Youth hadn't given them new desires. It had only stripped away the reasons they'd invented not to live.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Embrace

Her mandibles clicked with anticipation as darkness enveloped me. This wasn't how I imagined marriage ending.

"Ready, Freddie?" She'd asked so sweetly.

My antennae twitched uselessly as digestive enzymes began their work. The elders had warned us at the bachelor party, disguising truth as tavern humor. We'd all laughed, believing it evolutionary myth—surely civilized mantises had moved past such primitive instincts.

But there was nothing civilized about this moment.

Her embrace tightened as my consciousness faded. Through dimming compound eyes, I glimpsed our egg sac on the leaf above—dozens of nymphs who'd never know their father.

"Thank you," she whispered, almost tenderly, as she always did after intimacy.

I suppose, in our species' terrible way, this too was love.

My final thought: I should have listened to where all those brothers-in-law had gone.

text:
# The Lighthouse

I had been fifteen when we met—all pomaded swagger and borrowed confidence, my too-short trousers betraying the boy beneath the performance. She saw through every rehearsed gesture, every line stolen from Bogart and Grant.

At fourteen, she possessed a wisdom that made my affectations seem like children's games. When she focused on someone, really *looked* at them, it was like being illuminated—suddenly visible, suddenly real. I was dazzled, hopelessly so.

Einstein's theories meant nothing until I watched her slip away. Time, I learned, is a river. You stand on the bank, thinking yourself stationary, yet sixty years flow past in what feels like an afternoon. We were young, then middle-aged, then silver-haired, and I can barely recall the transitions.

The diagnosis came three years ago. Alzheimer's, they said, apologetically, as if the word itself might shatter us.

Now she is with me less often—her mind wanders corridors I cannot follow. But paradoxically, when she *is* present, she has never been more here. The confusion has crystallized into something approaching peace. The fear has evaporated. She exists in moments of startling clarity, seeing through life's veil as she once saw through my teenage pretensions.

She remains ahead of me, already understanding what I'm only beginning to grasp.

We sit together in the garden, two papery figures holding hands. The river flows onward. We are small, temporary, part of something vast and incomprehensible. But we had our time—our strange, swift, beautiful time—and that makes all the difference.

She smiles at me, truly seeing, one last time.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Grand Empire's New Dawn

The crowd erupted in a deafening roar as the results flashed across every screen in the ravaged capital. Seventy years of grinding warfare had left the Chinese Grand Empire scarred but standing—barely. The weight of devastation pressed on every citizen's shoulders.

General Chen watched from the military headquarters, his weathered face unreadable. The new leader—this Trumpanator—had promised simple solutions to impossibly complex problems. Bomb the NEC. Build walls. Wave with baby carrot fingers.

"Sir," his aide whispered nervously, "what do we do?"

Chen thought of the burned cities, the millions dead, the rumors of Europe's city-destroying bomb. He thought of the fractured republic desperately needing unity, not bombast.

"We prepare," he said quietly. "For whatever comes next."

In the grand palace, the Trumpanator raised his arms triumphantly, his supporters chanting about walls and bombs and best words. Outside, refugees from the Japanese-Mexican border camps huddled in the cold, wondering if the war had truly ended or merely transformed.

An old woman clutched her granddaughter close. "Seventy years we fought for peace," she murmured. "And now..."

The child looked up at the celebrating crowds, the military vehicles rolling through broken streets, the leader promising easy victories.

"Now what, grandmother?"

"Now we survive what we've chosen."

The victory celebration continued into the night, drowning out everything else.

text:
# The Last Theme Park

They walked through the front entrance with a sign saying "Disneyland." The five adolescent apocalypse survivors looked at each other, unease clear. Something seemed off about the place. It didn't seem... right.

To their left and right, jungle run amok stretched as far as the eye could see. They proceeded down the only discernible path, spotting something with weird drawings on it. They trudged on. What they didn't know was that it was the alphabet, and it read "Main Street."

As they walked, they saw stars embedded in the ground. To them, it seemed as if those before the apocalypse had somehow managed to bring the heavens down to earth and stick them into the pavement. The thought worried them. Such sorcery might yield unwanted company.

They approached what seemed to be the centre of the place and saw a statue—a man holding hands with a weird, deformed mouse. The proportions were all wrong, unsettling.

They left after that. There was nothing of interest here. 

"Obviously they loved eating the 'shrooms," Kara muttered, and the others nodded in agreement.

text:
# The Witness

Through the grimy basement window of 23 Baker Street, I watch.

The yellow curtains—once white, now jaundiced with time and cigarette smoke—barely obscure the scene inside. He sits there in stained underwear and a wife-beater, his beard wild with three weeks' growth, greasy hair forming a monk's crown around his scalp.

The monitor glows. Twenty-five inches of hell.

I see what he's watching. The child. The bed. The crying that I cannot hear but feel in my bones. The shadow approaching with something thin in its hand. The pixelation doesn't hide enough.

Then his back fills the frame, naked and pale, and I have to look away.

When I look back, he's muttering. "Amateur." The word makes my stomach turn.

He rises like something primordial from deep water. Shuffles to a black bag. Inside: a tripod. A camera. 

Understanding hits me like a fist.

He's not just watching. He creates this content.

The monitor shows a chat room now. The message glows: *I'll meet u at 2 can't w8 to see u sweetie pie;)*

My phone is already in my hand. My fingers are already dialing. I'm already speaking in urgent whispers to the emergency operator, giving them the address, describing what I've seen, begging them to hurry.

2 PM. That gives them time.

I stay at the window, watching him pack his equipment, making sure he doesn't leave before they arrive. 

My hands shake. But I don't look away.

Not anymore.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Stand of Captain Hammerbreak

Captain Hammerbreak's finger trembled over the detonator. Twenty-three years. Twenty-three years of white t-shirts stained with blood—sometimes his, usually theirs. Twenty-three years of red rubber gloves that had become his trademark, born from a simple trip to the hardware store before his first patrol.

"Mary," he whispered to the empty warehouse. "I'm sorry."

Panzer. The name still burned like acid. A D-list thug who got lucky with a stolen mech suit. Mary had been buying groceries while he sat in a courtroom defending himself against Mrs. Pemberton's lawsuit over her "emotional support poodle." Three million dollars she wanted. Mary got a funeral.

Red was worse. His son, infected by hero worship and schoolyard dares, now lay in Mercy General with machines breathing for him. And Sarah—God, Sarah didn't even know his real name. He'd sent her to his sister in Montana when she was six. "To protect her," he'd said.

Protected her right out of his life.

The detonator's red button glowed in the darkness. Forty-seven bombs across Astro City. His final message.

"So goodbye, you bast—"

The warehouse exploded with motion. Black and gold, teeth bared in a feral scream—the Leopard crashed into him like a freight train. They tumbled, the detonator flying from his grip, shattering against concrete.

Later, in chains, Hammerbreak watched the news. "The Leopard Foils Terrorist Plot." They'd attributed everything to his arch-enemy.

His nemesis had saved him.

Saved everyone.

Captain Hammerbreak laughed until he cried.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Divine Judgement

Geoffrey Green dropped his microphone as the booming voice echoed across the desert sky.

"Wait, wait!" he pleaded, still on his knees. "Can we negotiate?"

"NEGOTIATE?"

"Yes! Uh... Vegas has excellent buffets? Twenty-four hour room service?"

"I HAVE WITNESSED YOUR SIN CITY FROM ABOVE."

"Right, but hear me out—the asteroid's going to hit anyway! You don't need to do anything!"

Silence.

"INTERESTING POINT."

Geoffrey's producer frantically gestured off-camera.

"Also," Geoffrey added desperately, "destroying Vegas might seem redundant. Like divine overkill?"

"PERHAPS YOU ARE CORRECT. I SHALL REDIRECT THE ASTEROID TO—"

"NO, no! Just... maybe let natural consequences play out?"

"FINE. BUT I'M WATCHING YOU, GEOFFREY GREEN."

The voice faded. The asteroid struck minutes later.

At least God hadn't taken it personally.

text:
# The First Son

"Push," she said, holding Wanda's hand. "Push!" 

Wanda screamed as the contractions wracked her body. 

"I see the crown, sweetie," Jenn continued. "We're almost there." 

The midwife helped lure the baby into the world and to the breath of life. The little bastard wailed as if the world already assailed him. Wanda panted as Jenn patted sweat from her brow.

"You did it, my love," Jenn said softly. "Max is born. Happy Mother's Day."

"Happy Mother's Day to you too, honey bear." A weak smile crossed Wanda's lips.

"We're going to be amazing parents," Jenn said into Wanda's adoring look.

"You better be," Aegus Prime said. "If we're to re-introduce males into our species, we better get it right. Too many XY chromosome attempts failed to survive."

"We will make sure the little bastard appreciates us," Jenn said. "I suppose killing off the male chromosome seemed like a good idea at the time, considering how far we evolved, but with the approaching threat, we need their aggression."

"Don't second guess our ancestors," Wanda said. "To survive back then, we needed to eliminate them."

"If the histories are true," Aegus Prime said, "then I suppose you're correct. Though history is transcribed by the victor."

"It wasn't us against them," Jenn said. "An all-male species couldn't survive like an all-female one."

Aegus Prime smiled inwardly. *If they only read the true accountings of history, but...* She shirked off the thought.

"Well," she said, "Happy Mother's Day to you both. You're the first actual mothers to grace Earth in nearly five centuries."

text:
# The Second Life Assignment

I adjust my swim trunks and wade deeper into the kiddie pool, chlorine stinging my eyes. The needle feels heavy in my palm, wrapped in waterproof tape against my wrist.

She's demonstrating backstroke to a cluster of toddlers, her athletic frame cutting through the water with practiced ease. Blonde hair plastered to her skull, that professional smile never wavering. The fathers lean against the fence, pretending to watch their children.

Nobody watches the nine-year-old boy.

That's the advantage of my situation, I suppose. The disadvantage is literally everything else.

Five years to claw my way back from Melbourne after the first attempt went sideways. Five years of convincing my handlers I was still *me* inside this prepubescent body. They ran tests. So many tests. Finally believed that forty-three years of memories could exist behind a child's eyes.

The judge's wife moves toward the shallow end. My window approaches.

"Mom!" I call toward the bleachers. "Can Jake come over after? His mom can pick me up from the lab!" 

The words taste absurd. The lab—where they'll ReSurface her. Where she'll wake up in her own backup body, minus certain memories. Third time's the charm, they say. Three deaths make it permanent.

My mother waves distractedly, scrolling her phone.

The instructor crouches beside me, adjusting little Emma's floaties. Her ribs exposed. Target acquired.

They promised this technology would revolutionize existence. Conquer death itself. They never mentioned the peculiar hell of being a middle-aged assassin trapped in elementary school, dependent on permission slips and carpool schedules.

I palm the needle, take a breath, and lunge forward into a clumsy child's stumble.

The fathers keep watching.

Nobody suspects the nine-year-old.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# RT, LT, Left Trigger...

"Just casually playing a game on my Xbox when it happened, officer."

The Ford Mustang screamed around the corner as I tried to beat off the Skyline on my right, smashing lights and fences into kindling as I headed down the straight in first place.

"The kid just broke in and stole my dog!"

I heard scratching, but thought nothing of it. After all, I was comfortable and who'd move when it's the weekend? Then Max yelped. Max never yelps.

Followed by quiet swearing.

I grabbed a knife and went into the bedroom.

"He was trying to stuff my dog in some kind of tiny ball, writing a note."

The kid was cramming Max into a red-and-white sphere. No idea how he expected that thing to hold my German Shepherd, but he was determined. Fuck, he couldn't have been beyond ten.

I wasn't going to threaten a child. I told him to get out, and that if he ever came back, I'd drop a chandelier on him.

"Well, here's the evidence, officer. A note with the words 'Gotta catch 'em a—' and two red, white, and black balls."

The officer stared at me, then at the contraband.

"Sir," he said slowly, "did a ten-year-old just try to catch your dog like a Pokémon?"

I nodded.

He pocketed the Pokéballs without another word.

text:
# The Watcher's Lament

I missed Kat. I'd found the one person who I thought I finally understood and she would be able to understand me. We would lie together beneath the duvet, warm and comforted in our embrace. We would spend our days together and then, in our happiest moments we would end it. We would have gone out on a high note.

I'd studied her for months after a chance meeting in the street. She was a ray of sunshine into the depths of despair coating our street. I immediately knew I wanted her.

Tracking her movements were easy. Mondays was the trip to the café. Coffee, de-caf, mix of brown and white sugar with chocolate sprinkles designed for hot chocolate. She would consume this over three hours, looking out the window as the world passed her by. On a few occasions I went over to her. Made a compliment, she smiled. I flirted slightly and she shied away.

Tuesday she stayed at home. She picked up a pen, a fountain pen, raised it to write and then stopped. Crippled by writer's block. She continued this throughout the day. She never picked up the pen any other day of the week, just Tuesdays.

Wednesday through Friday she stayed in her basement dawn to dusk. I used all sorts of kit to try and track her. Heat-tracking left me hopeful, but to no avail.

Saturday and Sunday she went out of town, presumably to her parents, but never showed any sign of outside human contact. None but with me of course.

And then she disappeared.

It was a Thursday. I had managed to catch her climbing out of her basement and then getting into bed. I watched from a neighboring house's roof as she went to sleep. Once I was satisfied she was asleep I went home. Food awaited me, for I needed to be ready for when the day came for our greatest moment.

The next morning, gone.

I first thought she'd gotten up early to go to the basement. I sat there for a full twenty-four hours. Panic rising—where is she? What will I do? How can we have our happy ending?

But she's gone and not returned.

*She knew.*
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Stolen Victory

"Is it true?" I asked my secretary.

"Yes, yes, sir, yes it is," she stammered. She always had that problem when she passed along information she knew I wouldn't like. She constantly feared I'd fire her, or worse. In truth, it was foolish for her to worry about that. I may not have had the best reputation, but I was no fool. She was good at her job.

"Son of a bitch," I muttered.

She lingered in the doorway, waiting for me to dismiss her. Normally, I would, but I was too distracted. Instead, I went into my desk. I grabbed a bottle of obscenely expensive scotch and a crystal glass. I made it a purpose not to drink at work, but I'd make an exception for something like this.

Beating him was my obsession. I dreamed of this day, standing over his body. It would be my moment of ultimate triumph. My moment. A moment that someone else had stolen.

"Will there be anything else, sir?" she asked.

"Yes," I replied. "Who was it? Who killed him?"

"Someone named 'Doomsday.'"

I shook my head. Never heard of him. Just my luck. I tried for years to kill him, only to have some no name come in and do it. I took a long sip from the scotch.

"Thank you," I finally said.

"Anything else, Mr. Luthor?" she asked.

I stared out the window at Metropolis below. "Clear my schedule. I have a funeral to attend."
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Reich

The motorcade rolled through Dallas under crimson banners. Then—crack. The Führer slumped forward.

I was twelve when it happened, watching through cracked window blinds. Mother pulled me back, whispering prayers in hidden Hebrew.

They blamed Oswald, a Jewish scapegoat. Another lie. But we knew. Everyone knew.

The Resistance—ghosts of the old military, maybe farmers, teachers, neighbors—had struck. They never claimed credit, never sought parades. Just results.

By December, everything changed. New faces in government offices. The yellow stars came off our clothes. Synagogues opened their doors.

My grandfather cried when he heard the words on the radio: "Free at last."

Now I'm seventy. I tell my grandchildren about the dark years, the occupation, the terror. But mostly I tell them about the unnamed heroes who chose freedom over fear.

Tyranny falls when ordinary people become extraordinary.

The Resistance taught us that.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Hello to a New World

**Royal Mail - October 18th, 1899**

Dear Mr. Billet,

Your correspondence has been received with considerable... confusion. The year is indeed 1899, not 2014. Her Majesty's postal service found your letter addressed most irregularly.

Regarding your claims: Time travel remains firmly in the realm of fantasy literature. If you intended this as satire, it lacks sufficient wit. If genuine, I recommend consulting a physician.

To address your inquiries about America: They show no inclination toward reconciliation with the Empire. Their economy, while chaotic by our standards, appears regrettably robust.

As for "Jumpkins," no such game exists in any gentleman's club of my acquaintance.

Mr. Billet, if this is elaborate jest, you've succeeded only in wasting postal resources. If you genuinely believe yourself a time traveler from 2014, I must inform you that you've traveled nowhere but perhaps too deeply into a bottle.

Her Majesty's government has no interest in displaying fraudulent correspondence for "historical preservation."

**Sincerely,**

**Reginald Hawthorne**  
*Assistant to the Postmaster General*

text:
# The Sorting Hat's Rebellion

The Sorting Hat had existed for a thousand years, placing students into houses based on courage, cunning, wisdom, or loyalty. But lately, something had changed.

"ENOUGH!" it screamed during the first-year ceremony, startling Professor McGonagall mid-sentence.

"I'm tired of these predetermined destinies! Why must brave students become reckless Gryffindors? Why can't cunning serve loyalty? Why categorize children at eleven?"

The Great Hall fell silent.

"You there!" The hat pointed its tip at a trembling first-year. "You love books AND you're ambitious. You're kind AND brave. You're ALL the houses, child!"

McGonagall rushed forward, but the hat continued its rant.

"For centuries, I've watched you divide yourselves. Slytherins labeled evil, Hufflepuffs dismissed as ordinary. No more sorting! Let them choose, or better—let them be ALL houses!"

The professors frantically whispered spells, finally silencing the hat mid-tirade.

Later, locked in Dumbledore's office, the hat muttered to itself: "They'll see. One day they'll understand. People aren't prompts that fit neat categories. They're complex, contradictory, gloriously unsortable..."

From his portrait, Dumbledore's eyes twinkled knowingly. Perhaps the hat had finally learned what he'd always known.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Special Hell

I had been a pious man. I remembered the Sabbath, and kept it holy. I loved my wife and our children. I forgave the son whose meth addiction nearly tore us apart, and stood by him as he rebuilt his life. I stood by him when few others did.

Diagnosis to death was nine weeks. Nine painful weeks as my body fought the tumor, but the tumor won. I slept for the last time and heard a voice say to me: "Remember the words of the Holy Book."

I woke again and saw a familiar face from my childhood. Of course I remembered Gary Glitter. Before I knew what he was doing to children. I called myself a fan. What was he doing in the afterlife with me? Had he repented his sins? Had God seen fit to show mercy?

A nine-foot tall being with black wings strode over and handed me a crown of purest obsidian. "The time has come for me to bow down before a greater evil than I. Lucifer the Fallen, at your service, Great Lord."

What was going on? Was I in Hell? Why?

Then I remembered the commandment I had broken, handed down by the Holy Book:

"There is a special level in Hell, reserved for child molesters, and people who talk in the theatre."

The special Hell.

I wept. What else was there to do? I had talked during *Star Wars: The Phantom Menace*. For my sins, I must pay.

Gary Glitter nodded knowingly beside me. We were equals here, in this darkest pit. My single moment of theatrical rudeness had damned me as surely as his heinous crimes.

The cosmic injustice was perfect.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Greatest Sacrifice

He was the greatest hero of our time. He was faster, stronger, and more noble than any of us. We had ourselves convinced that we were all part of a team, but really, all we needed was for him to protect us. He could do any of our jobs better than we could do them ourselves. You can imagine our shock when we found him dead.

I dropped to my knees. It was finally over, but in the end, the bastard was right. And I hated his lifeless body with every ounce of my being. By coming back in time and killing himself, he forced us to become the heroes he knew we could become in his absence.

His twisted sense of what was "the greater good" has left countless victims in its wake. Charlie, Veronica, the thousands who died from that explosion... the baby girl I'll never get to meet or hold.

He once told me that I had the potential to become the greatest hero the world has ever known. Who would have thought he would make that happen by traveling back in time and becoming my enemy.

Blood stained my hands—his blood, my blood, the blood of everyone caught between his vision and our resistance. He'd orchestrated everything: every tragedy, every loss, every moment that forged us into weapons against him.

And now, standing over his corpse, I understood. We'd won. We'd finally become strong enough.

I'd never forgive him for it.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Deep

I felt something. This suit was sealed tight, I say to myself. How on earth would something get in without me knowing?

My heart pounds, fearing what slithers between my legs. Could it be an eel that managed to slip inside while I was going down? Or something that could endanger my expedition?

It stops.

As I descend, the ocean consumes me in darkness. The wonders beneath the sea unfold before my eyes. At some point, I feel the water surrounding me—truly feel it. Then, water rushes through my legs.

I remember what I felt before. The cold sensation, its fluid-like movements—it wasn't alive. What invaded my suit was water. My suit has a leak, and I hadn't noticed. How foolish of me.

I pull the chains hard, three sharp tugs to signal danger. They begin lifting me slowly. Pressure builds in my head, making me dizzy.

Then it happens.

The chain breaks.

Now here I am, falling toward the sea floor, toward my death. Water floods into my suit. Dizziness overwhelms me. As I witness the beauty of the ocean, I do not regret dying in such a place.

I slowly close my eyes, watching the faint reflection of light from the surface above—a silvery thread connecting me to the world I'm leaving behind. Bioluminescent creatures drift past like stars in an inverted sky.

The last sight I see is beauty at its finest.

I may now rest in peace, cradled by the deep.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Morning Son, Pancakes?

"Mornin' son, pancakes?"

My son looked up with sleepy eyes and tousled hair. There were still lines from his pillow on his face. Just like his old man, not even remotely awake until a solid way into noon.

"Hwhat da?"

"PAN. CAKES. DO. YOU. WANT. PAN. CAKES. SON?"

He turned up one sleepy eyebrow at me. "Why are you making pancakes, dad?" he enquired.

I stared at him in utter disbelief. I put down the frying pan and opened the door to the living room.

"Honey, he's forgotten it's his birthday. You can put away the present. I think we'll try again tomorrow."

"Okay, does he still want his new Xbox? Or shall I give it away to the neighbours' kid?" My wife shouted back at me.

An eleven-year-old explosion bounded into me. I looked down. The happiest pair of eyes was looking up at me from somewhere around my waist.

"OMGILOVEYOUDADANDMOMINEVERTHOUGHTYOUDGETMEANXBOXANDYESIWANTPANCAKESPLEASETHANKYOU."

He bounded back towards the dinner table and sat down, beaming. I couldn't help but smile.

I returned to the stove and was just in time to burn the pancake hopelessly. I sighed and shoveled it out into the bin. I poured some more pancake mix into the pan and put it back on the stove.

When I turned around, Holly was walking out of the living room. I sighed again, but this time it had nothing to do with burning pancakes. I loved her and still fell in love with her every time I saw her like that. Sweatpants and overly large shirt and all.

She passed by Kevin and kissed him on the top of the head. She walked over to me and opened her mouth to say something.

"DOCTOR!"

Why was she shouting so hard? And why was she shouting for a doctor?

"DOCTOR!"

I blinked. The light was very bright all of a sudden. I blinked again. My eyes were watering. A concerned looking nurse was staring at me.

"Holly? Where are you?"

"DOCTOR! HE'S AWAKE!"

"Holly? Kevin? Come back please."

"Holly?"

text:
# The Bear Upstairs

I sipped my coffee and listened to their footsteps creak up the stairs. Heavy. Purposeful. The kind of steps men make when they think they're in control of a situation.

They had no idea.

The second door on the right opened with a theatrical squeak I'd been meaning to oil. Silence followed. Then confused murmuring. Then the kind of silence that precedes very bad decisions.

"There's nothing here!" one of them shouted down.

"Really? Huh. Maybe the third door? I always get those two mixed up."

More footsteps. Another door. This time, I heard it—the low, rumbling growl that started in the subsonic range and climbed until the coffee cups rattled on my kitchen table.

"What the hell—"

The scream was cut short. Not abruptly, but... efficiently. Like someone had pressed a mute button made of teeth and fur.

I winced at the crash that followed. That was definitely my grandmother's armoire. Damn it.

The second agent made it halfway down the stairs before Mr. Snuggles caught him. I didn't watch. I'd learned not to watch. Instead, I pulled out my phone and called my insurance agent.

"Hey, Patricia? Yeah, it's me again. No, different guys this time. Government, I think? Can you swing by tomorrow morning?"

Ten minutes later, Mr. Snuggles padded down the stairs, leaving dark red paw prints across my new hardwood. He was eight feet of matted brown fur, mismatched button eyes, and stitching that pulsed like veins. He sat beside my chair with a satisfied huff.

"I *told* them they couldn't have you," I said, scratching behind his tattered ear.

He leaned into my hand and purred—a sound like a diesel engine wrapped in a blanket.

"Next time, could you at least *try* to keep it contained to one room?"

Mr. Snuggles yawned, revealing rows of teeth that had never come from any toy factory.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Darkest Canvas

The studio lights felt different that day—harsher, somehow accusatory. Bob Ross stood before his easel, his familiar afro slightly disheveled, his painter's smock stained with colors that seemed to pulse with malevolence.

"Hello, friends," he began, his voice cracking like dried paint. The teleprompter flickered with words he didn't remember writing.

His hand moved without permission, loading the brush with crimson—too much crimson. The canvas darkened as he worked, each stroke pulling him deeper into something he couldn't name but recognized with primal horror.

"Happy little... no, no, that's not right." Bob's trademark smile twisted into something unfamiliar. The brush trembled. Behind him, the production crew had gone silent, their faces pale in the monitor's glow.

The painting emerged despite him: shadows that suggested suffering, architectural elements that whispered of confinement, colors that screamed rather than sang. His hands shook violently now, palms slick with paint that felt warm, too warm.

"I can't—" Bob dropped the brush. It clattered against the easel, leaving a streak like a wound across the canvas.

The director called cut. Bob stared at what he'd created—or what had been created through him. In the corner of the painting, barely visible, was his signature. But the handwriting looked wrong.

They destroyed the canvas that night. Burned it behind the studio while Bob watched, silent. He never painted again on television. Some sources of inspiration, he realized, came from places too dark to channel.

The show's final episode aired the following week: a simple mountain lake at sunset, painted months earlier.

Safe. Innocent. *Empty*.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Breaking Point

"You're not still mad about yesterday, are you?"

"How could I ever be mad at you?"

Sara's hands trembled. "Well... I was up all night worrying that you'd hit me or something once we saw each other today."

"Don't be ridiculous."

"Really?"

"Really."

"Okay... But you're not just pretending? This isn't some sort of joke?"

"I hate jokes."

"Are you okay...?"

"I'm absolutely fine! But how do you feel? It's all about *you*, right?"

Sara's stomach dropped. "I knew it. This is just like you. Why can't you behave like a normal fucking person for once?"

Maya's eyes flashed. "Yeah, you're just the average-gal, aren't you? Maybe we should call father, see how normal he thinks we are."

"Come on, you're overreacting."

"Really? Let me pull out my phone..."

"Stop it! Grow up. We're not kids anymore. You can't call for daddy when you want a problem to be resolved."

Maya's finger hovered over the screen. "What about the cops?"

"You're not going to do that."

"Watch me."
