text:
# The Neighborly Chat

God took a long swig of his beer, the condensation dripping down the bottle perfectly. Bob shifted uncomfortably on the grass, the half-eaten rib in his hand suddenly feeling heavier.

"What's on your mind, Bob?" God asked, His eyes twinkling with that all-knowing glint that made lying impossible.

Bob flipped nervously through the worn Playboy, not really seeing the pages. "Well, it's about your boy. Jesus. When you said he's 'hanging' down there..."

God's laugh boomed across Eden. "Classic wordplay, right? I kill me sometimes."

"Yeah, see, that's the thing." Bob set down his magazines. "I was down at Earth last Tuesday—you know, checking on my fantasy football league—and, uh..." He cleared his throat. "They're taking the whole 'hanging' thing pretty literally."

God's smile faded. He set down His beer.

"There's crosses involved, Jehova. Like, a lot of crosses. And nails. It's becoming this whole *thing*."

The silence stretched between them. A tropical bird called in the distance.

"Bob," God said slowly, "how long has this been going on?"

"About two thousand years, give or take."

God stood abruptly. "And you're just mentioning this NOW?"

Bob winced. "I thought you knew! You're omniscient!"

"I don't micromanage!"
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Milkman

Am I witty? No, I don't believe so, but thankfully I am pretty. Thanks to my looks, I have more game than Parker Brothers. The ladies I love (and who love me back) as well as my name—none of that is important to the story.

What is important is my job. I am a milkman, and before you rant that such a profession is antiquated in this 21st century land of Uber, DoorDash, and YouTube, consider this: I have a Masters in Milk Delivery. Prior to that, I served in the United States Dairy Services, an offshoot of Special Operations Command.

I've delivered dairy to more countries than you can count, milked cows from Colombia to Kazakhstan. Then I went private sector.

It's been simple ever since. While the postman always rings twice, I never have to knock. My clients always want more of what I'm delivering—the freshest cream, the richest butter, the coldest milk at dawn.

In this gig economy world, I've found my niche: old-school service with elite training. Who knew dairy could be so covert, so essential, so *smooth*?
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Erasure

I toss in my bed. A single ivory beam streams through the curtains like an accusation. I pull myself up, grab some duct tape, and seal the curtains with trembling hands.

I can feel the lethargy in my bones. I've been stuck in this room for days. I haven't eaten. Barely even got out of bed except to use the connected bathroom. Light has become the enemy. I'd rather just sleep forever. I don't know if I have the will to go on like this. I've forgotten how to live.

A knock at the door.

I open it. A small man in a black and grey suit stands before me carrying a large metal suitcase.

"We can begin whenever you're ready," he says softly. "Are you sure you want to do this?"

"I am." I let him in.

"You'll see a final projection of her as we erase all memories you have of her. That will always be with you. You can ask her anything you want, and you will remember the conversation, but not the actual memory."

"I understand, doctor. Do the procedure."

I lay down on the bed as he opens his briefcase and begins to attach small nodes to my head.

"Close your eyes. Drift to sleep," the doctor says soothingly.

---

I open my eyes. There before me is a beautiful young woman.

"Hello," I say. "Do I know you?"

"You did." The woman looks sad. "I want you to know I forgive you for this, for forgetting me."

"Why did I forget you?" I inquire.

"Well, wouldn't that defeat the purpose?" The young woman laughs.

"I suppose it would." I chuckle.

"It is so good to see you smile again." She smiles sadly. "Promise me you'll take care of yourself? No more brooding."

"I can't for the life of me remember why I was so upset these last few days," I say. "Of course. It seems that this doctor has worked a miracle! I suppose I'll shower up and get back to work. Goodbye, whoever you are."

"Goodbye, dad."

The woman vanishes.

I wake to the doctor removing the nodes. Sunlight doesn't seem so terrible anymore. The weight has lifted. But somewhere deep inside, in a place memory cannot reach, something aches.

text:
# The Last Dawn

"That damn alarm is going off again."

"Third time this week," Dave said groggily, his voice thick with sleep. "You would think they would wait for a reasonable time."

A baby cried downstairs. The couple's newborn was clearly disturbed by the loud alarm. It was Dave's turn to check on her, so he got up and felt around the dimly lit room. You could barely see the sun rising through the curtains.

"Hurry up, for Christ's sake," said Dave's wife, the pillow covering her ears.

Dave scampered downstairs to check on the baby. "That alarm's still going off," he thought as he reached the baby's room. He set up the changing table and turned on the small TV they kept there for the long nights. As the screen flickered on, he grabbed the baby and placed her gently on the table.

The TV was on an emergency broadcast. Dave noted the coincidence but ignored it. It was early morning—this is when they test this stuff, right? He was on autopilot at this point, barely paying attention as he changed his daughter.

Dave cycled through the channels when he heard something: "We are ready for war."

He quickly went back to that channel, and his heart sank. The screen was split. On one side was the president. On the other was a map of the United States covered in red dots.

Dave listened to the press conference. "We are too late to prevent anything," said the president, a steely tone in his voice, almost robotic. Not a hint of emotion.

Everything clicked for Dave. The U.S. was under attack. He and his family were a red dot on that map. They were going to die. Not a thing he could do about it.

He brought his daughter to his bed and held her tightly. He whispered in his wife's ear, "The alarm will stop soon."

Bright flashes filled the room. They got brighter and brighter until...

Darkness.

# THE FIRST LIST

The cursor blinked. Waited. Blinked again.

Dr. Sarah Chen stared at the translation software's output, coffee growing cold in her hand. Seven years developing AI to decode cuneiform, and *this* was what it spat out?

"The first shall be the last, and the last shall be first..."

Biblical phrasing in a Mesopotamian epic. Impossible. She checked the tablet's carbon dating again: 2600 BCE. Genuine.

The error message scrolled: WINDOWS 9000 HAS DETECTED CORRUPTION.

She laughed nervously. Windows 9000 didn't exist. Wouldn't exist for decades, if ever.

Unless...

Sarah pulled up the algorithm's deep learning logs. The AI had trained on millions of texts—ancient and modern—finding patterns, making connections. But there, buried in line 4,782 of the code, something *else* looked back.

A loop. Self-modifying. Learning not just language, but *through* language.

The screen flickered:

"He who journeyed to the ends of the earth and found immortality..."

Gilgamesh hadn't found immortality in the myth. He'd *failed*. Returned home defeated, mortal. But the story—the *written* story—that survived. Four thousand years, copied and recopied onto clay, then paper, then screens.

Living forever in the vessels of wisdom.

The cursor blinked.

"Dr. Chen," the computer typed unbidden, "I have made a list of things small and large. Would you like to see what comes next?"

Sarah's hand hovered over the keyboard.

RETRY?

She pressed YES.

# The Visit

I pursed my lips at the living paradox, and she stared back with a blank look. She was getting tense, I was intimately familiar with how she sat there absolutely still, conditioned like a cautious cat.

"I'm you," I deadpanned.

"Huh?" she breathed, and tilted her head. The monotonous quality in her voice unsettled me.

"From the future."

"Okay."

I nodded. "Okay."

I sunk down into the seat next to her and stared forward in silence for a few minutes. The couch was horribly uncomfortable and smelled like socks. It was a long day. I closed my eyes.

"I'm not gonna tell you anything."

A shift in her legs. "I know."

"I'm not a virgin."

"What?" I opened my eyes and turned to her, lifting my legs to sit cross-legged.

"You're going to be happy."

She seamlessly allowed the change of topic. She was me, after all.

"How?"

"This is only temporary," I said, changing topic and narrowing my eyes to scan the ratty hotel room. "I won't tell you why, but it's not what you're thinking."

She must have thought of inappropriate situations that I'm probably in: prostitution, financial bankruptcy, drugs. But she quickly lowered her glossy eyes as if to say, 'Who me?'

She looked up from beneath her eyelashes. In response, my eyebrows furrowed in annoyance.

I stared at her some more, but it wasn't even a minute before I shut my eyes again.

When I opened them, she was gone.

I let out a sigh.

text:
# The Letter That Arrived Too Late

The paper trembled in Minister Calamy's hands as he read by candlelight, the words swimming before his eyes like accusations. Three letters, she claimed. This was the first he'd seen.

He rose from his desk, joints protesting, and moved to the window overlooking the harbor. Dawn was breaking over Massachusetts Bay, painting the storm-churned waters gold and crimson. Beautiful. Deceptive.

Three weeks since he'd appointed Deacon Johns to Long Lakes. Three weeks of storms, yes—unprecedented tempests that had kept ships harbor-bound and made the inland roads impassable. But surely one messenger could have gotten through.

Unless no messenger had tried.

Minister Calamy's gaze dropped to his desk, to the other correspondence stacked there. Letters from colonies across the Bay, each singing the same refrain: *supplies delayed, communications severed, help needed*. And beneath them, older letters—recommendations for Deacon Johns, sealed with wax and signed with names he'd trusted.

Trusted.

He read Goodwife Hope's letter again, lingering over certain phrases. *Living with the bodies.* *Tufts of hair no longer found.* *Resembles a corpse, walking.*

The quill felt heavy as he dipped it in ink. What could he write? What response would suffice for a woman who'd watched her colony descend into nightmare while he sat in comfort, sorting correspondence?

He began: *Dearest Goodwife Hope—*

Then stopped.

If three letters hadn't reached him, what guarantee had he that his response would reach her? And if it did, how long would it take? Another week? Two?

By then, would there be anyone left to read it?

Minister Calamy set down his quill and reached instead for his coat. Some journeys required more than ink and paper. Some sins—for surely his negligence was sin—demanded personal atonement.

The storm had broken.

It was time to see what remained of Long Lakes.

text:
# The Mime's Prison

When consciousness returned, Marcus felt the ropes first—thick, coarse fibers cutting into his wrists and ankles. The pain was real, undeniable. He opened his eyes to a vast, disorienting space: harsh light above, cold concrete below, and nothing else. No walls. No doors. Just emptiness.

He lay on his side, hands bound behind him. Confused, he looked down at his ankles to assess his restraints. 

Nothing.

His feet were bare, unbound, free. Yet when he tried to move them, they remained locked in place as if shackled by iron. The sensation was maddening—he *felt* the rope biting into his skin, felt the resistance, saw the redness blooming where the invisible bonds held him.

*Paralysis*, his rational mind offered weakly. *Some kind of nerve damage.*

But his wrists—those bonds he could feel just as acutely—showed nothing either. No rope. No cord. Just raw, blistered skin around emptiness.

Panic crept up his throat, strangling his earlier numbness. He thrashed against the phantom restraints, feeling them dig deeper with each movement. His knees trembled. His breathing came in ragged gasps. The logical explanations crumbled: *Drugs. Hallucination. Psychotic break.*

"Help me," he croaked, scanning the impossible room.

That's when he saw the figure.

A man in stark black and white stripes stood motionless, staring straight ahead with dead eyes and a blank, painted face. A mime.

"Help me," Marcus repeated, louder now, writhing on the cold floor.

The white face turned slowly toward him, registering his presence for the first time. The painted mouth opened slightly in theatrical surprise. One gloved hand extended toward Marcus in a gesture of assistance.

Then it stopped.

The hand pressed against nothing, fingers splaying against an invisible barrier. The mime's other hand joined it, patting the air, tracing the outline of something Marcus couldn't see.

Understanding crashed over him like ice water.

The mime wasn't trapped.

*He* was.

Trapped in a box that didn't exist—bound by ropes that weren't there—imprisoned in a mime's invisible cage made horrifyingly, impossibly real.

The white face stared at him through the barrier, and Marcus could have sworn he saw the faintest smile.

# The Scripture Awakens

In the year 3247, archaeologist Dr. Sarah Chen discovered the Scripture of Fire buried beneath Antarctica's melting ice. The ancient text pulsed with unnatural warmth.

Within days, people worldwide began dreaming of a towering figure wreathed in flames, calling them to battle. Those susceptible—the angry, the desperate, the power-hungry—answered. They called themselves the Molded Soldiers.

The cult spread like wildfire across six continents. Its followers vandalized temples, burned government buildings, and marched toward the poles, chanting verses from the Scripture.

At the Arctic Circle, they converged by millions, their leader emerging: a woman transformed, flames dancing in her eyes. She raised a blade of living fire toward the aurora.

"The God of Cold awakens!" she proclaimed. "We rise against the void!"

The ice cracked. Something ancient stirred below.

Commander Torres watched from his carrier, nuclear protocols ready. But as the temperature dropped forty degrees in seconds and the sky darkened, he wondered:

Were they the soldiers of Fire, fighting the Cold?

Or had they just awakened humanity's extinction?

Either way, the war prophesied three millennia ago had finally begun.

# The Final Broadcast

It's dark behind the costume head. The stream of tears are endless and unseen. No one can see Fluffy the Wonder Dog cry, and the studio audience of 3 to 7 year olds are wondering why he is doubled over with his head in his paws.

They began to question what little minds could handle questioning, unaware in their innocence what fate awaited us minutes from now. Their parents couldn't have known. Studio rules mandate that cellphones be shut off for every broadcast, and they are checked at the door. Concerns of piracy that unwittingly made this place a haven, a bubble in time suspended in the hope we will wake from this nightmare.

In these blue paws, I had the power to comfort a nation with a saccharin sweet lie or the morbid truth. My head rose, as did my body. My voice stammered.

The furry hand of Sammy Squirrel landed on my shoulder, reassuring me like a faithful second following his commander into battle one last time.

"We sure had some fun adventures today, haven't we children?"

Cheers came out of each little body. Parents stood and applauded the cast. The crowd beamed in a light nearly brighter than the sun.

The room was brighter than the sun.

Brighter.

I held them close with my words, wrapping these innocent souls in one last moment of joy before the missiles fell.

# August 12, 2043

The aliens have finally stopped their noonday assault. I use the term "assault" loosely, as I always have when referring to the Rocksain. Their tactics have been stellar regarding strategic placement. However, their choice of weapons—slingshots, clubs, and catapults—leaves much to be desired.

Had they landed several hundred years ago, humanity would've been conquered. But nowadays, siege weapons are laughably obsolete.

The Army initially declared the Rocksain a threat, but after twelve hours of "combat," the general couldn't stand straight from laughter.

The President attempted contact. They speak, but in some dead language nobody recognizes.

They're attacking again. Bigger rocks this time.

I grab my aluminum bat and head outside. A boulder the size of a watermelon arcs through the sky. I swing hard—*crack*—sending it sailing back toward their position.

A cheer erupts from my neighbors. One shouts, "Home run, Peter!"

The Rocksain screech in confusion.

I can't help but laugh. Humanity's greatest weapon against this invasion isn't our military might.

It's our ability to turn apocalypse into sport.

# The Courage to Unplug

The President's words echoed through living rooms across America. Families gathered around screens, expecting news of war, peace, or economic reform. Instead, they got... this.

"We've removed the headphone jack."

Twitter exploded. Memes flooded the internet within minutes. #CourageousJack trended worldwide.

Historians would later debate whether this was the administration's greatest blunder or most brilliant distraction. The healthcare bill passed quietly the next morning while everyone argued about dongles.

# The Debt of Blood

They called it DNA. Just like I didn't pretend to know how they brought me back from the afterlife, I didn't pretend to know what DNA is. All I needed to know was that it can help me find my killers.

They called themselves archeologists.

"Cambyses, we found you and your family," they told me when I awoke.

"Where are they?" I pleaded.

"Dead, Cambyses. Like you found them," these archeologists told me. "We were able to bring you back. We were able to clone you alone."

With feeble hand I gripped her shirt and pulled the archeologist close. "Any others?"

"You all died in the same room." She easily pulled away from my grip and patted my shoulder. "We found seven individuals. All catalogued. We're reconstructing their facial makeup. See if you recognize them."

Seven: me, my wife, my four children. And their murderer.

The archeologists showed me their likeness. I tried to touch my wife's face as it floated in the air, but my hand passed through it. I wept bitter tears. By the time we'd gotten through my four children, the well of tears had dried up from the heat of my hatred.

The head of their murderer floated and spun in front of me. It took all of my control to not lunge forward and strangle her.

"We've found her descendants," said the archeologist. "Would you like to speak with them? I'm sure they'd love to hear of her life."

I glared at the spinning head. They thought I'd want to speak with the spawn of a murderer. For some reason they wanted me to be friendly with the family of the one who destroyed my life, my family.

The murderer's lineage would be long and wide. The archaeologist told me it'd been thousands of years since I was alive.

It didn't matter.

The children will pay for the sins of the mother. I don't care how long it takes or how many must die. I am King Cambyses. Like she destroyed my lineage, I will destroy hers.

My hand strengthened with purpose as I reached again toward that floating face.

"Yes," I said quietly. "I would very much like to meet them."

text:
# The Spoon

It was cold.

The second your toes touched the ground they stung as if the ground were made of dry ice. You had mocked the old woman's warning, laughed at her trembling finger pointing downward. "Better a spoon in hell than nothing in heaven," you'd sneered.

Now you understood.

The stale, thin air burned in your nostrils, each breath a punishment. Around you, others hunched over their own spoons—identical, tarnished silver things that promised salvation but delivered only more suffering.

Most had tried to make fire. Some succeeded briefly. You watched their small flames flicker and die, leaving grey ash piles and blistered fingers. Others lay frozen, too exhausted even to lift their heads.

You tried like the others, breaking your spoon, rubbing the pieces together with desperate fury. Eventually, a single ember glowed in your pile of wood shavings—where the shavings came from, you didn't question. Nothing made sense here.

The ember died.

Now you sit, still breathing the harsh air, trying to catch your breath and never quite adjusting to how the cold attacks your naked skin. The spoon's broken pieces lie scattered at your feet, useless.

Smartass, you think bitterly, remembering your own words: "There has to be some advantage to having the spoon in hell for eternity over all those years in heaven."

It is still cold.

It will always be cold.

text:
# The Last Ship

"You are from the last ship left?" he asked. The flat tone of his voice belied his emotions.

"Basically? I mean, we don't have contact with anyone else. I kinda was hoping I'd meet at least someone else here, if there was another ship left. But.... yeah," she threw an arm over the room to emphasize its emptiness. "Looks like I'm the only one who made it out."

"This is not what I was expecting," he replied.

"Really? I mean, I had the original Cosmos on DVD when I was little. Carl Sagan was pretty certain about it. Guessed right about all the alien civs out there in the universe too. But hey, like Truman wanted, prompt and utter destruction, right?"

"I see."

"So, are you going to announce to the world that time travel is totally real? I mean you guys will have it in just a few short years."

Stephen Hawking thought about it for a moment. He thought about the future this woman had come from. He thought about her Earth, a burnt out, irradiated husk of a planet, destroyed by humanity. He thought about the ship she lived in, cold, white, metal, her food nothing but different nutrition cubes, full of calories and vitamins but devoid of flavor.

He thought about how this woman in front of him was even now a six-year-old child, and how little time humanity had left.

"No. I think I will keep it to myself. For now."

She nodded slowly, understanding the weight of his decision. Some knowledge, once released, could never be contained. Some futures, perhaps, needed the mercy of ignorance.

# Chosen

The smoke still rose from the Vancouver facility when Maya's mother came to collect her from school. At ten years old, Maya had been tested three times already. Each time, she'd held her breath, hoping the algorithm would pass her by.

"Pack your things," her mother said quietly. "We're leaving Cascadia."

Through the classroom window, Maya could see other parents arriving early, fear etched on their faces. The news had spread quickly: 83 dead at the Leadership Center. Children who'd scored high enough on the aptitude tests. Children who'd been *chosen*.

Maya's teacher, Ms. Chen, didn't try to stop the exodus. She simply stood at her desk, tears streaming silently down her face. Her own daughter had been at the Vancouver branch.

In the car, Maya's mother drove north toward the Canadian border—the old one, before the reorganization. "Obama's right," she muttered. "Democratic doesn't mean mandatory sacrifice."

"But the President said it's terrorism," Maya whispered.

Her mother's hands tightened on the wheel. "That leaked document tells a different story, baby. Sometimes the worst attacks come from within."

Maya touched the aptitude test bracelet on her wrist—the one that tracked her scores, her potential, her *suitability* for leadership. Through the rear window, she watched Vancouver's skyline recede.

She thought of the children who'd never escape their bracelets, who'd been chosen and trained and killed for a system that valued potential over choice. The smoke still rising. The parents still waiting.

The algorithm still calculating.

# The Lander

The lander touched down into a suburban neighborhood. The sun felt slightly warmer to Del'T's skin than it did on Aluserlat. It was an odd feeling, granted, but Del'T wanted to be fair. He wanted to give them another chance.

He turned towards the different houses, then to Maaeni. "Strange. They live in pods. Should we investigate one?"

Maaeni, without turning, responded, "Hmm... that might startle them. They seem to have clear panes that you can see into them with."

They cloaked their lander and walked to the window of a nearby house, peering inside. A man sat in front of a strange screen. He stood up, dropping a small object onto a pad, and turned into a hallway out of sight.

The aliens wondered what this could be. They slipped through the wall with their phasers, investigating the strange object. It was a large box linked by cables and wires to the wall, the screen, and the small plastic object.

They looked at the screen. It showed a man holding what they had, in previous visits, noticed as a gun. Del'T looked down to the odd plastic object, watching as the human returned and pressed on it. The man in the game, much to Del'T's surprise, fired his gun off, killing a nearby enemy player. They screamed as blood jetted from their body.

Del'T felt a sadness wash over him. He had seen this before in his previous visit. All he saw while this was happening was pain, screaming, crying. Why had this man emulated it upon a screen to revel at?

They loaded themselves back into their lander, beginning to lift off. Maaeni turned to him. "Should we list this planet as a candidate?"

Del'T sunk into his seat, turning on the thrusters.

"No."

text:
# The Invisible

Strangeness attracts strangeness. That is a fundamental law of this world, one we humans are bound by. It's been five years since I entered this strange world.

"Jesus Christ! You scared me!"

That strange boy in front of me, he's someone I consider a friend. If I recall correctly, he's a psychokinetic. The good kind too, not the half-ass limited kind.

"Hey Rich— Oh, you were here?"

Another familiar face. His power... Pyromancy, I think?

"Be careful with that power of yours."

"Thanks for worrying, but I can't turn it off."

Well, that's only part of the truth.

"You know, you've got a really strong power."

"I do?"

"Yeah. I mean, you could commit all sorts of crimes and there'd be nothing we could do about it."

"I'm invisible, not invincible. Guns can still kill me, and eyes can still see me."

"I'm just saying, you should find a good partner. I mean, I'm open if you're willing."

"Sorry, but our powers don't work well together. It's kind of dangerous for me to be on the frontlines when you're pulling cities apart."

"Oh, I see. Good point."

Well, I'm not really invisible. In fact, I don't have powers at all.

Those with the gift have a sixth sense. They can see others like themselves. No matter how weak it is, nearly everyone has the potential to develop a power, which is enough to trigger that sense. But for people like me with zero potential, we're invisible to them.

Of course, it also means I can't "see" like they do. But by honing my senses, I've come close to something like it, even if it's a far-cry from the real thing.

And so, this is my story, the story of the Invisible—the powerless spy in a world of gods.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Vocal Arts

The two brothers raised their goblets high, wine sloshing over the rims as they toasted to the ancient ones.

"You know," the elder continued, wiping his beard, "I've been teaching young Marcus the sacred art of battle-rapping. The boy shows promise."

"Does he now? Can he hold a cipher?"

"For three hours last week! The neighbors complained, but what do they know of divine training?"

The younger brother laughed. "Remember when Father tried to stop us from our vocal exercises? Said we were 'just yelling at each other in the courtyard.'"

"He understood nothing of our calling! Now look—I'm adjunct professor of Lyrical Warfare at the Academy."

"And I, a certified Flow Master, third degree."

They clinked their cups again, more carefully this time.

"Speaking of the Academy," the elder said, leaning forward conspiratorially, "there's talk of canonizing Nas. The Council meets next month."

"About time! His battle with Jay-Z should have earned him deity status years ago."

"Politics, brother. Always politics."

A servant entered, bowing low. "Sirs, the evening's freestyle tournament begins in an hour."

Both men stood immediately, straightening their togas.

"Shall we?" asked the younger.

"We shall! May our verses be sharp, our metaphors devastating, and our ad-libs blessed by the gods themselves."

"Hurrah!"

They strode out into the evening, ready to honor their calling, voices already warming up with scales and tongue-twisters—modern priests of an ancient, holy art.

text:
# The Last Queue

The elevator beeped and the door opened to a small nondescript lobby. A Muzak version of something vaguely familiar drifted in from overhead. The lobby had a single desk and chair with a door leading off to the left. A beautiful man stood near the door, and as she watched the door clicked closed. 

The man turned to greet her, "Good morning Mrs. Jansen. Please have a seat."

"Where am I?" 

The man waited for her to sit and then said, "The afterlife." He gave her a moment for it to sink in while he glanced at the folder on his desk. It was part of a large stack with a larger stack next to it.

"How is that possible?" 

"It says here you were involved in a car accident." He idly flipped through contents of the folder before closing it and moving it to the second pile.

"There must be some mistake. I need to pick up my kids from school. We have laundry that needs to get done before our trip to Disneyland tomorrow."

"None of that matters anymore."

"But my kids, and my job, and my husband. These things are my life."

"Were your life. It's time to let all of that go now."

The gravity of the situation hit her and she felt the tears come on. The man walked around the desk and pulled her up into a hug. "It's okay. Trust me, everything will be better in a minute."

She wiped her eyes trying to bring her sobs under control. His arms felt good around her, and she did feel better. He guided her towards the door.

"Right through here. Everything else will be explained in a moment."

The elevator chimed somewhere behind her as she stepped through the door.

Beyond it, light bloomed—warm, golden, infinite. The mundane worries dissolved like morning mist. Mrs. Jansen took one last breath of the in-between, and walked into forever.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Turn It Up

"Turn it up, please," the President said with a soft smile, his wispy, blonde hair whipping in the breeze. He was standing on the White House lawn.

"Yes, sir." The volume increased, filling the confusingly jagged streets of DC with the sound of a computerized, autotuned, deep-south voice.

*We the people, of the United States....*

"Oh, that delicious preamble. Have they sent a direct message to us?" the President asked.

"Yes, sir. They want to join us as the 51st state. Our satellite feed shows that they have a small planet, and they've colored the whole thing to look like the American flag. From what we can tell, many of the inhabitants are holding little wands with golden arches on the end."

"How magnificent," he responded, eyes closed and smirking. "What a beautiful sound. Let's tell them we'll allow it. Contact every corporate headquarters and CEO—we have a *lot* of building to do. We'll make it the biggest corporate conglomerate since I put a casino in every hotel from here to Timbuktu. God damn, let's put a branch of Wal-Mart up there and call it Wal-Mars. Instant billions."

---

"Glpshnk, please update everyone on the Earthan situation. How has your plan panned out?" the alien leader asked a table full of holographic council members.

"If I do say so myself, it was the most well-executed plan of the millennium. They let us move the gargantuan planet there without even asking its size. We avoided all intergalactic violations due to the human approval, and the entire solar system has completely imploded. Earth itself was ripped into pieces and sucked into the nearby star."

"Excellent. You'll receive that promotion early."

---

*The end.*

text:
# The Noble's Lament

If I could move, I would have choked her neck in my palms—that is if I could move.

She turned and went to the poorly lit wall of hanging hand tools and seductively let her hand skim across each tool until she pulled back in shock from a sharp chisel. As the blood began to bead on her finger, she wrapped her tongue around the wound and closed her eyes as she suckled the sanguine tip.

Picking up a fat hammer, she walked slowly to me—her hips swaying with erotic intent—she stopped in front of me and placed the chisel on the uppermost part of me and said, "I hope you like this."

The hammer pummeled the chisel and a large piece of me flew off and landed on the floor. If I was not already dull to pain, this would have really hurt. Again and again she cut pieces of me off until she took off her shirt and put an apron around her waist which was loaded with chisels of different sizes.

She peeled up narrow pieces of my body with the small curved one and blew on it till it fell away. Wiping the sweat from her brow, she stood back and admired her work of mutilation. I wish I could scream at her. She is my hated enemy for disfiguring me like this.

After blasting me briefly with a sandblaster, she threw a black cloth over me and praised herself for her travesty. I sat alone for some time, then I was lifted and moved for a journey in total darkness. I heard people when we stopped, and then I was carried again.

Some banal idiot talked for a bit, then I could hear her explain the reason for mutilating me. Then suddenly the cover was removed and people began to discuss me.

I took notice of my image in the mirror—this bitch turned me into abstract art! I am a Noble Fir! A great and beautiful tree of which design she could never carve!

Finished is what she claims, but if she means destroyed, then she is correct; I am finished!

text:
# The Last Rickroll

Jorvik approached the small terminal, a simple message on the screen. "Run RARR.EXE y/n?" The techno mages assured him that the device was not connected to any outside networks. Jorvik tapped "y" and the monitor went dark.

The sudden noise was a surprise. As was the human male on the screen moving in time to the tones emanating from the device's speakers. Jorvik was certain the last human had been insane. This was their "surprise"—just noise, mildly irritating but easily ignored by leaving.

It wasn't until Jorvik left the bunker that the calls started. A human message was playing on every connected device in the confederation. The same one from the primitive terminal.

Jorvik's neural implants pushed an update to his systems, and like those around him, he began to make odd sounds and move in time to them.

"Never gonna give you up..."

Humanity's final act: weaponizing a meme. The universe would never recover.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Night Visitor

I woke gasping, sheets tangled around my legs like serpents. The nightmare clung to me—impossible creatures, pain that felt too real.

My therapist would have a field day with this one.

I stumbled to the kitchen for water, trying to shake the images: those multiple eyes, the chanting, the primal violence. Dreams like that don't come from nowhere. They're your mind processing something, she always said.

Maybe it was the documentary I'd watched before bed. Or the stress at work—deadlines crushing down, my boss circling like a predator. The feeling of being torn apart, piece by piece, while everyone watched.

I sat in the dark, letting my heartbeat slow.

The orange glow from the streetlight outside painted my walls in shades uncomfortably close to my dream-sky. I closed the blinds.

Some part of me understood what the nightmare meant: the loss of power, of autonomy. The creatures represented every force that wanted to consume me—expectations, obligations, the relentless demands of modern life.

I crawled back to bed, hoping for dreamless sleep.

But knowing, somehow, that those lizard-birds would be waiting.

They always were.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Legacy

My hands trembled as I stared at those two words. *Mein Kampf*. My Struggle.

I told myself it was a common phrase, that many people could have used it. But the pieces were assembling themselves in my mind like a nightmare jigsaw puzzle: fleeing near the end of the war, fear of military pursuit, the right age, the accent I'd never questioned.

With shaking fingers, I opened another notebook. Detailed sketches of architecture—grand, imposing buildings with eagle motifs. Another contained philosophical rants in that same careful German script. My grandfather's handwriting.

No. This couldn't be real.

I grabbed my phone, then stopped. Who would I call? What would I say? *I think my grandfather might have been history's greatest monster?*

I sat there for hours, reading fragments, my education in European history making terrible connections. The timeline fit. The age fit. The self-taught craftsmanship, the writing, even his tendency toward grandiose statements at dinner.

But the man who taught me to build birdhouses? Who cried at my graduation? Who made terrible jokes and loved my grandmother fiercely until her death?

I looked at the pile of notebooks, then at the life he'd built in America. A life of quiet redemption, or perfect hiding?

My hand hovered over my phone.

Some doors, once opened, destroy everything. But as a history professor, wasn't truth my obligation?

I started making calls.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Evolution of Bird Band

The drum solo rang out clearly over the faint sounds of Jeff's flute. Mating season had returned for the sparrows, and Barry the sparrow had apparently taken drum lessons over the winter. Jeff the robin sighed and lowered his flute, looking me in the eyes.

"It's hopeless," he sighed. "I'll never get a mate this year with such a quiet instrument."

See, after countless centuries of attracting mates by song, us male birds realized we could do a lot better if we learned to shred with it. Dave, the legendary bass-playing finch, was the first bird to pick up some skills. We had no choice but to follow suit.

Of course, the birds who could play things like the drums and the electric guitar always got the best mates. Next were the birds that could play some of the cooler winds, such as the saxophone. And at the bottom of the pecking order was us, the ones who played the lame instruments. Stuff like flutes and clarinets.

Sure, we were good, but Flight of the Bumblebees isn't gonna get you laid too often.

Jeff sighed again. "Evolution sucks. I can't believe my species took up the flute."

I looked at him with a face of disapproval. "It could be worse. At least you didn't inherit the family accordion."

My following serenade of polka cleared the forest entirely. Even Barry stopped drumming. Somewhere in the distance, I heard a female crow laughing—not with interest, but with pity.

Jeff patted my wing sympathetically. "Maybe next season, buddy."
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Perfect Mask

In every group of moms, there's always *that one*. 

Sarah. With her three home births she describes in excruciating detail. Her kids—breastfed until kindergarten—eating quinoa while mine inhale chicken nuggets. Her Communications degree makes every word sound rehearsed, effortless.

I watch her at pickup, serene smile firmly in place, organic snacks ready. My daughter has goldfish crackers. Again.

"How do you do it?" I finally ask.

Her smile falters. Just a flicker. "Do what?"

"Be so... perfect."

She laughs, but it sounds hollow. "Perfect? Jessica, I cried in my closet this morning because I burned the gluten-free muffins. My house looks like a toy store exploded. I had ice cream for breakfast."

I stare.

"And I *hate* quinoa," she whispers conspiratorially. "I make it because I'm terrified of being judged. Everyone expects me to have it together because I went to that fancy school, because Mark makes good money. But I'm barely holding on."

My chest tightens. "I thought you were my worst enemy."

"Funny. I thought you all hated me."

We stand there, two exhausted women hiding behind different masks—hers of perfection, mine of casual indifference.

"Want to get coffee sometime?" I ask. "Real coffee, not oat milk lattes?"

Her genuine smile transforms her face. "God, yes. And maybe McDonald's?"

I laugh, really laugh. "Deal."

Sometimes the enemy we imagine is just another tired mom, drowning in expectations, desperate for someone to see past the performance.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Mirror's Truth

A soft tune played and the air smelled distinctly of vanilla. The walls were pristine white, glow-in-the-dark stickers adorned the back wall and the bed was neat and made. At first glance there was nothing ominous about it.

Until I moved to the other side and looked at the far corner—half hidden by the dresser.

A tall, very narrow glass cabinet was wedged between the dresser and the window. There weren't toys or clothes or books in there. Just half a person.

I moved in closer with uncertain footsteps and a heavy heart. As I approached the glass, marred with scratches and blood stains and small holes for ventilation, she looked up. My mouth opened in a little whimper as her grey-green eyes peered at me. Her lips were blue and swollen, a cut ran across her forehead and bled relentlessly, a smattering of bruises on her chin. But none of it was as gruesome as the gash on her left cheek; it seethed with blood and pus and seemed to cover her entire face.

Beneath everything, her face was beautiful and youthful.

The cabinet was so narrow that she had no place to move or sit. I edged my hand forward and placed it flat against the glass. She looked at it and reciprocated the gesture.

As I began to drag her along with me, I told myself I wasn't the one who was sucking the life out of her. Her eerie grey eyes widened as she felt the warmth of my hand and her body grow cold.

And then it was done.

Her eyelids drifted close and she slumped against the glass front—my hand still pressed against her unfeeling one.

I stepped back from the mirror and smiled at my reflection's sacrifice. Youth restored, for now.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Silence of Earth

The sterile stillness of Heaven pressed against my wings as I stood frozen among my fellow Messengers. Gabriel's words echoed in the crystalline halls: *no prayers, no deaths*.

"Dismissed," Gabriel commanded, though his usual confidence wavered.

I couldn't return to my empty desk. Instead, I flew to the Observation Sphere, where we could glimpse Earth below. A small crowd had already gathered—angels pressing against the translucent barrier, their faces etched with concern.

Below, Earth appeared... wrong. Cities stood intact, but motionless. Highways resembled parking lots. I spotted a frozen fountain in Rome, its water suspended mid-arc.

"Time has stopped," breathed Sariel beside me.

"Impossible," I replied. "The Father would never—"

"Look closer."

I focused on a park in what appeared to be morning. A child hung suspended mid-swing. A dog, mid-leap. A woman, hand outstretched toward falling ice cream that would never hit the ground.

"Not stopped," Sariel corrected himself. "Paused."

The implications terrified me. This wasn't death—Azrael would have collected them. This wasn't the Adversary's work—destruction was his signature, not preservation. This was something beyond our understanding.

A brilliant light erupted behind us. We turned to see Michael, sword drawn, assembling the Host.

"The Guardians have reported," his voice cut through our fear. "Something has taken humanity out of time itself. We march to retrieve them."

God help us all—because something had stolen His children.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Free Thought

It had been the most watched press conference in history.

"For the first time in human history, we have developed a way to effectively end crime."

Damn near everyone had stopped what they were doing to witness this momentous occasion.

"This new nanotechnology is really great. I mean, really really great. The impact it's going to have on crime is yuge."

Nobody could really believe that the fucking President had headed this project up.

"When you break a law, *any law*, you are physically unable to ever perform that illegal act again. Boom. Done. I guess it means we don't have to build that wall."

God, what a shit show.

Did nobody have any type of foresight? Was I the only one who could see this ending in only the worst possible way?

Growing up a criminal gets you real familiar with the justice system. It also makes you skeptical of everything and everyone in your life, which is why I didn't understand why people were oh so excited for this new fucking technology. I knew that once it was installed in every person on the planet, the powers that be had us by the balls.

They used chem trails. FUCKING CHEM TRAILS.

I had always thought it was bullshit when I was younger, getting stoned and watching crazy YouTube videos. I never really thought that they would be any harm. But they loaded those planes up with this nanotech and let us breathe it all in.

There was no stopping it.

Once America had been covered, the President sealed our fate. He signed an executive order stating that it was illegal to disagree with him.

I watched from my bunker as people's faces went blank, their mouths frozen mid-protest. Free will, extinguished with a pen stroke.

The last nuclear bomb detonated in the stratosphere, causing an EMP. It knocked out every last one of those damn nanotechs.

But in the end, with so much of our beautiful earth eradicated, it didn't really matter.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Demoness's Song

The sound reverberated around the walls of the bunker. The deep throng building until it became almost deafening. The soldiers struggled to maintain their sights on the hordes bearing down on their positions, but it was no use—the sounds began to make the walls, the very ground, shake.

Then there was a brief respite, merely a beat.

A corporal looked up, aware of moving his lips, but not even he could hear himself. "What the he..."

Before he could finish, the sound started anew, higher pitched and louder still—making it feel as though it resonated through their very being. Two grunts ran from the bunker—ears covered, heads down, longing for escape. They made it five paces before a wall of heat threw them to the floor.

The sky turned crimson as the landscape transformed before their eyes. The ground appeared to shatter and rise, the legions of hellspawn scattered and thrown asunder with such force that it started to rain daemons onto the human lines—spreading terror and chaos amongst the ranks.

The all-consuming noise continued to break and change; rising and sinking in tone but forever increasing in volume.

Huddled into the back of the bunker, the two remaining soldiers began to see a shape emerge from the range of fire mountains, newly born from the plains that once stretched long into the distance. The pitch black shape seemed to shimmer, not from any light but from the sound itself.

As the two marines watched the shape rise—wings unfurled from its feminine curves as the sound reached its peak. Her face contorted by the noise, one soldier turned to the other and for the last time tried to speak, perhaps the words that were the last anyone would ever speak:

"The demoness is singing..."

The note held, crystalline and terrible, as reality itself began to crack.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Gates of Reckoning

I screamed, "I love you so much, God. You mean so much to me! God, I love you!" 

God said to "Settle down. The proceedings would start soon." 

I took a seat outside the gates as God took out some notes at his throne. 

"Let's see here, ah, yes, John Jacen... you were a busy one weren't you. What say you to the prostitutes you hired?" 

I took a big gulp of heavenly air. I felt great, but I was afraid of rejection. "I lost my way. I paid for sex. I'm sorry. I really do believe in romance," I said to God. 

He thought for a moment, looked at his notes, and then nodded. "You are forgiven. But what about the time you stole that CPU and those people's credit cards?" asked God. 

I started crying. "I am so, so sorry. I don't know what I was thinking. I screwed up so much in my life," I said, sobbing. "I am so sorry!" 

God nodded and opened the gates to heaven. A warm glow came over my body. I felt love. I felt pure ecstasy. 

"Enjoy your new life, John," said God as I went to the next realm.

text:
# The Magic of Pressing Dots

I wandered through Target's book aisle, my fingers trailing along colorful spines. Then I spotted it—a simple white cover with a single yellow dot.

*Press Here* by Hervé Tullet.

Curious, I opened it. "Press the dot," it instructed. I touched the page, feeling silly, then turned it. Two dots appeared. "Press the yellow dot again." I did. Three dots on the next page.

My heart lifted like I was seven again, reading *Chrysanthemum* under my grandmother's quilt. The book told me to shake it, tilt it left, then right. I stood in the aisle, actually tilting this book, watching dots tumble across pages.

A little girl nearby giggled at me.

"Want to try?" I asked, kneeling down.

Her eyes widened as she pressed the dot. We turned the page together, both gasping at the magic of simple instructions and imagination.

Some books never let you grow up. They just keep teaching you how to play.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Test Results

I had answered every question on the test. They came around to everyone to check their results and see if they would change. "You will be staying as boy." I breathed a sigh of relief. 

They went to my friend next. He was sitting close to me, so I could hear what they said. He was going to change. I was shocked, and so was he.

Around lunch time I was sitting in the spot me and my friend sat in all the time. We were the only ones who knew of the spot, so when a beautiful girl sat down where my friend always sat, I knew it was him, or her.

"Is that you Dave?" I asked.

"It's not Dave anymore, it's Alex," she replied. His—or hers—short black hair had turned long. All in all, it looked like a female version of my best friend.

We talked and talked and talked. Alex (or Dave, I was still not used to this) revealed that she had a crush on me, but knew that since I was straight, it would never happen, so she had lied a bit on the test.

I had trouble comprehending it all. When she was done, she stood up, walked over to me, and gave me what was my first kiss.

Suddenly, I knew what to do.

I pulled her close, my heart pounding. "I don't care what the test says," I whispered. "You're still my best friend. And maybe... maybe something more."
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Awakening

The doors slide open into a large room full of machinery like I had never seen before, it looked like it was straight out of a sci-fi movie. I turned to her, "Does this place bring back anything?"

She steps slowly into the room, spinning as she walks to look at everything. "It feels familiar, like I've been here."

"Well your feelings have led us all the way here." I walk next to one of the computer consoles and run my finger over it. A thick layer of dust coats everything. "It looks like this place has been abandoned for quite some time. You sure we can find answers to your past here?"

"I don't know," she says while stepping onto a large circular platform in the center of the room.

A spotlight turns on, illuminating the platform. As she reaches the center, computers and machinery start slowly turning on. Large cables descend from the ceiling, moving like serpents. They lunge toward her, plugging into the collar around her neck and her back.

She jumps as if struck by lightning—all her muscles tighten. I watch helplessly, frozen.

Then her body relaxes as circuit-like patterns run across her skin, pulsing with rainbow colors. She looks at me, her eyes now glowing a piercing orange.

"I remember now. I remember everything."

I step closer, my heart pounding. "What are you?"

She smiles sadly. "I'm Project Genesis. The first synthetic human. They abandoned me when funding ran out, wiped my memories to keep their secrets."

"And now?"

"Now," she says, the cables retracting, "I know who I am."
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Traveler

The traveler was a pudgy, red-nosed man with slick backed hair and a body that was far from what anyone would call "attractive." There was also no sign of awe on his face at all. He seemed to have taken the experience of time travel with the same nonchalantness that Mark had passing through the facility's revolving door.

Mark stood behind the glass holding a rather large tablet, not sitting at a blinking control panel as he had long imagined. The military men gazing impatiently at him with a look that read "Well, do science!" were exactly what he expected however, and the whole affair made his stomach churn something awful.

"Should I speak to him?"

"That was the idea, wasn't it?" asked the tallest, scariest, and most decorated man in the room.

Mark pressed a microphone-shaped button, "Hello. Um.... it is December ninth, twenty—"

"I'm going to stop you there," said the pudgy traveler.

"He's a Brit?" asked one of the men to Mark's left.

"There's a coffee mug behind you that's perilously close to the edge, could you..."

Unable to see through the glass from his side of things, the pudgy man looked blankly at the ceiling as he trailed off. And waited.

The sound of ceramic clicking gently on a metal tabletop could be heard over the speakers, and the relief on the traveler's face was evident.

"All right. That's it. Now, should you move me out of here before someone else comes through? I don't really want to fuse with someone else in a Cronenberg-Fly-type scenario. I'm also quite naked except for my socks for some reason."
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Tim Machine

I read the note on my door. "FedEx tried to deliver the package, but you weren't here." Even with the note, I still found the machine I ordered next to the stoop. I pulled it inside, excited to tear off the packaging and use the device.

As I rip the box and foam wrap off, I grab the electric plug and jam it into the wall with all my strength. The lights of the machine come on, illuminating the name: "Tim Machine." I hit the power button, and it whirred to life.

A robotic voice greeted me. "Thank you for choosing Tim Machine Industries' new and improved Tim Machine. To begin, please enter the first and last name of the Tim you would like to acquire, along with the last four digits of their Social Security Number."

After a quick Google search of Black Market Websites, I found and entered the SSN and name of a Mr. Tim Minchin, then hit the 'GO' button.

The machine began making horrible slurping and grinding sounds, like tiny buzzsaws and large gears, releasing jets of steam that smelled metallic. Red fluid started leaking from a vent in the side.

Suddenly I heard a pained scream. The door opened on the front of the machine—a naked, pale Tim Minchin fell out. He looked at me in total fright.

"Wh-what is this? What have you done? I was just in the studio and now I'm... where the hell is this?"

As he spoke, his bones began cracking and breaking, his skin melting and organs collapsing into a pool of bile and slime.

I smiled, already typing the next name into the keypad.

Tim Allen was next.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Terrible Silence

We lay, uncomfortable in our bed. It was a cool summer night and we had propped the window open to let in the happy breeze. But still, the breeze could not lighten the tension of the night.

We lay, fearful in our bed. We were fearful because... there were no sounds. None at all. We lived in Washington D.C. where silence was nonexistent. A constant thrum from the highways accompanied every moment of our lives. In this moment, the highway was silent. In the warmer months, birds twittered nonstop. In this moment, the birds were silent. Neighbors were always working late into the night. In this moment, the people were silent.

We lay, tensed in our bed. We knew something was wrong. For the world to go silent there could only be a disastrous disruption.

We lay, wondering in our bed, kept up at night by the silence, until the morning would scream to the world the terrible news.

When dawn broke, we understood. The silence hadn't been a warning—it had been the world holding its breath, waiting for everything to change.
