text:
# War Journal: The Schwarzenegger Protocols

**June 6**

We killed seven more robots today. Four of them were designed to look like Arnold Schwarzenegger, for reasons we cannot fully comprehend. Smith's theory is that they believe we won't fire upon them, fearing we'll accidentally shoot the former governor of California. Brady thinks Skynet is a fan of *Commando*, assuming the Schwarzenegger body shape bequeaths some inherent tactical advantage. We may never know the real reason. I just wish they wore pants.

**June 12**

Our food supply grows short. In desperation, we've begun eating the robot Schwarzeneggers' skin, which tastes like tofu roasted on oiled crowbars. You develop a taste for it, after a time. Unfortunately, I drew the short straw today and have been cursed with eating the dick skin again. It haunts my nightmares.

**June 20**

Skynet is clearly not trying anymore. Our unit somehow picked up an additional soldier overnight—Arnold Schwarzenegger with a mustache. At first, we were almost willing to buy his coincidental appearance, but their whole plan fell apart when he began speaking in an Austrian accent.

He lasted approximately four minutes before Brady shot him.

Truly, war is hell.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Eight-Legged Apocalypse

I don't have a problem with superpowered animals. They're cool in my book. Super-dogs. Super-raccoons. Even super-turtles. But super-spiders? Come on man.

The first incident was in Phoenix—a tarantula, four feet wide, launching its hairs like missiles. Three people hospitalized with projectiles embedded in their skin.

Then came reports of black widow victims. One guy couldn't stop laughing. Another forgot his own name. The venom was chaos incarnate.

But the brown recluses? Those are why I'm hiding in this sealed room.

You can't see them. Can't hear them. They just... appear.

My neighbor Steve thought he was safe. Found him this morning, necrotic wounds covering half his face, babbling about invisible monsters.

I've got seventeen cans of Raid, duct tape on every crack, and a flamethrower I bought off Craigslist.

Somewhere in this room, something is watching.

Waiting.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last March

And suddenly, strangely, everything that once was was not. London, Paris, Athens, Tokyo, Beijing, Moscow, Delhi, Sydney—all gone.

Droves of outcasts swelled in rural areas across the world, sleepy towns jolted awake by a hulking mass of degenerates, loons, and thieves. They too would disappear in time.

North America had finally revealed its true colours, propped up by its sweatshop economy and grubby grasp on South American satellites. Deemed behind the times for too long, it had been developing its arms in that impenetrable void where no civilised human dared look: Canada.

The Weapons of Maple-Syrup Destruction decimated European countrysides and Asian steppes, trapping bodies in compact layers of death and sugar—flies in amber, preserved forever by hostile North Americans.

Yet hope remains.

For the survivors who have seen too much too soon, there is talk of one thing: a new land, a promised land of resilience, repair, and retribution. We are a stubborn mass marching against North America's oppressive overwatch.

For us, "Madagascar" is a word spoken softly, guarded as jealously as a lover's kiss.

That is where we will make our last stand.

Through radiation wastes and syrup fields, we trek southward. Children clutch maps drawn on scraps. Elders whisper coordinates like prayers. Each step is defiance. Each breath, resistance.

Madagascar waits—untouched, fertile, free.

And we will reach it, or die trying.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Price of Adoration

It felt right to see him up on that stage. Cameras flashed all around him, and so many lights were focused onto the stage that a few drops of sweat had started to creep down his brow from the heat. But despite the deafening cheers and applause, which would've been overwhelming for someone like me, he stood tall and looked as if he was at home.

I saw him like that all the time when we were growing up. Whenever we went out he was the center of attention, everyone fought to be next to him so that the others would think them as cool as he was. Meanwhile I would sit on the sides and watch them all make fools of themselves.

He didn't even notice them. Yes, he was aware of their presence, but it was the presence he cared about. It was how he defined himself. As the night would wind down and people would make their ways home, you could see the life drain out of him. And when we got into his car to head home, he was never the same person he had been just minutes before.

I was the only one who ever knew how broken he was under that flawless shell of his.

I have no doubt that, on some level, he did what he did for the better of us all. But it was never his main concern. He did what he did so that even when he was alone he could turn on the television and see people from all over the world praising him. He did it so that he could walk down any street in the world and hear people scream his name, fighting through the crowds for nothing more than a chance to be near him.

He did it so that he would never again have to be alone and dwell on his own toxic thoughts.

He had been born for this. The whole world was worshipping him, and he was drinking in every bit of it.

From my seat in the auditorium, I smiled sadly, knowing the truth: tomorrow morning, when the crowds disappeared and the cameras turned off, I'd get a call. And once again, I'd be there to pick up the pieces.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Wrong Corner

I hate coffee. Dennis knows that, too. This is probably his idea of a joke.

I took the time to brave the Chicagoland traffic and dropped a small fortune to park. It dawned on me that I left my GPS on the mount. Not that it mattered around here; piece of junk can't do a thing among the buildings here.

The least he could do was show up.

As I shift my arm to check my watch again, I nearly knock over the pyramid of empty paper cups - they tasted just like their hot chocolate. Bastard was a full three hours late now. Even if he still lived in Portland, he'd be late.

Some of the folks standing around waiting for a table are eyeing my squadron of refuse eagerly. That's my cue to get back in the queue for another cup of some stale brown drink.

The line moves quickly, but it's still long. Since I'm going to be here for a while, may as well check my phone. Maybe he left a message.

Nope. Not a peep. The only communication was my outgoing call to his cell from two hours ago. May as well try again.

Rings once. Twice.

"Hello?"

"Dennis?"

"Hey, bro! Where the hell are you?"

That son of a bitch.

"Where am I?" I ask back. "Where the heck are you? I've been waiting for hours."

"What do you mean?" my brother shouts through the speaker. I look around and nobody else is even on their phone let alone spilling out the type of crap only a Morenis can spout.

"I've been sitting in this damned Starbucks for three freaking hours drinking I don't know what the hell they think it is-"

"Which Starbucks?" he asks.

"Corner of Clark and Madison like you said."

"Wait a second," he called before pausing; bastard must have gone to the wrong one.

"Welcome to the city, bro. I'm in the one on the opposite corner."
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Foolish Believers

We had been fools. We believed that we were more powerful than the combined power of the state. Stability is good, order is power, and structure is strength—those were the essential tenants drilled into us since childhood.

Hans and I figured that we couldn't be the only disenchanted people. After all, how could the Ministry of Affairs keep tabs on everyone? So we started searching. Not online, no—that would have us caught for sure. I mean, who would believe that a former citizen of that radioactive dust bowl called Europe would think a search for "resistance" wouldn't be suspicious?

So we simply prowled the streets at night. Hans, always the electrician, managed to create this gizmo that would jam the signals for all the cameras. We stalked through forgotten streets and hid behind vibrant holoboards whenever a patrol marched by.

In the end, we found them in an abandoned warehouse in the flooded district. It was after almost a month of searching, and we had almost been caught.

We were stupid, walking down the torn-up asphalt, jumping around puddles the size of ponds. We didn't even hear the sound of heavy footsteps. All I heard was a shout. Followed by a bang. Followed by Hans collapsing into the puddle next to me.

The rest is a blur of adrenaline with random images: carrying Hans out of the street, weaving between abandoned concrete tubing, throwing a brick through a window, and banging on an unyielding metal door as the guards closed in.

Then, out of nowhere, they appeared. They wore a mismatch of clothing and black balaclavas. They also carried military-issue dart rifles that quickly dispatched the two guards.

A man about two meters tall approached us. You could tell he was the leader—he radiated confidence and oozed self-control.

"Looks like you boys were in a bit of a jam. How about you follow us for a bit."

It was then I realized there was a needle in my arm, and the world went black.

---

When I woke, Hans was breathing. That's all that mattered.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# We Are Light

We are =. Our name is holy, given to us by our Mother of Stars, and cannot be said by flesh. Thus our name and our essence remains pure.

So does light shine.

Our Sister of Stars warned us of a flesh growing around her. Called by her, we descended, and thus did we use our bodies to save her. For flesh is bound by flesh, and cannot soil our bodies.

Light came to the flesh and it did burn.

As light, we shine.

Yet our Sister of Stars cried out—we were in danger. Too late did we see the ball still had flesh contained inside, hidden by the hated Shadow where we could not reach them.

So we waited for the rock to turn, that we might shine Light again.

And from the shadow... pain.

Hideous, monstrous, it leapt from the shadow and crucified us as we sat helpless above.

*How?!*

Hated Shadow gave form to the flesh. They created terrible things with their minds, and these horrors leapt at us when we could not fight them.

They hurt me.

They hurt me so badly and I could not stop them. The Shadow held me down, and we were all hurt by them.

Light did not help me.

The flesh used hated Shadow as a weapon and they hurt us.

I ran. I was afraid.

I hate them. I hate Shadow.

I don't know how to forget what they did to me with their horrible shadow-thoughts—

Sister in the Stars called again, that the Shadow could not give their thoughts form anymore while she protects us.

I am afraid.

But we are =. We are Light.

And we remember.

The flesh will answer for what it has done in the Shadow. When Sister turns her face away, when the hated darkness returns, we will be ready.

*We will be ready.*
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Holy Water Vigil

I stare at the doorway, my sheets plastered to my chest with sweat. The red glow from the hallway—*thanks, Mom*—casts devil-colored shadows across my carpet.

This is all my fault. I'd begged them: "I'm mature! I can handle scary movies!" Now I know the truth: The Exorcist wasn't a movie. It was a documentary, and Satan has my address.

From the next room, my brother's asthma creates a rattling wheeze. It sounds exactly like demonic breathing. *He's out there. Waiting.*

I haven't moved in three hours. Moving means noise. Noise means *He* knows I'm awake. My bladder screams, but I ignore it. Wet sheets are better than possession.

Then—miracle. I remember the holy water scene. Water! Regular water becomes holy when you need it badly enough, right? That's definitely how religion works.

I explode from bed, sprint through the red hallway (don't look, don't look), hit the kitchen, yank the freezer, grab ice, fill my red SOHO cup at the sink. The plastic is crimson—unfortunate color choice, but no time to be picky.

Racing back, the presence looms. I feel Him reaching.

I dive into bed, cup sloshing, and assume position: body rigid, eyes locked on the doorway, fingertips submerged in melting ice water. Ready to flick at the first sign of floating or head-spinning.

The water warms against my skin. My fingers prune.

This becomes my ritual. Every night for two years, I sleep with weaponized hydration on my nightstand, guardian of my own soul.

Nobody notices the nightly kitchen trips or my perpetually wrinkled fingertips.

Some battles you fight alone.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Evolution's Edge

The rain was pouring down harder than she had anticipated, but she could easily make out the half-robotic torso by the faint red glow emanating from his back. The gun was steady and level, pointed directly at his head, which was a foot away from the deadly barrel.

She had triumphed.

The robo-human was fast and had reaction times that were impossible to match, so shooting it from a distance was impossible. The sword that hung by its side was too far away for the mechanical body to physically save the meta-human, and there was no way that it would be able to dodge the bullet at this short of a range. Although he had been dodging and cutting the bullets for the past five minutes of their intense fight, he was finally beat.

"May I just... ask you a question?" His voice was deep and calm as he looked at her from the corner of his eye, knowing that he was about to die.

The woman looked at him half bewildered and half in prideful pity. "I guess."

"How did you out-think me?" His question was the only thing that his mind couldn't logically connect with everything else that he had noticed about this woman. She looked to be an ordinary human with normal reflexes. How was she smarter than a computer?

She pulled the trigger before answering.

The man instinctively tried to move his head in time, but the bullet pierced his skull before it could get far enough away. The momentum rocked his head to the side and knocked his body down. Her answer came as he fell: "Meta-humans have evolved."

It was then that she noticed that the cut on her arm that he had given her just a minute before was completely gone. She smirked slightly and then holstered her gun as she walked off into the night.

Behind her, the red glow flickered once, twice, then faded to black, swallowed by the relentless rain.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# When It All Started

When it all started, I thought they were spiders.

The first appeared one dusty afternoon in July. The clouds hung lazy in the sky and it felt like it was going to rain all day but it never did. The heat trapped you and it was far too warm to even think about escaping. School was over, it had been for a while, and me and Tom, we had run out of places to go, things to do.

We had spent the morning kicking stones at familiar cars that went past. The afternoon wasn't much different but Tom's mum had given us a bottle of lemonade. We sat on the curb of the pavement passing it to and fro, taking long, greedy swigs. It turned sticky and cloying in my mouth.

"Look," Tom said, at some point in the haze of boredom. Coulda been hours, coulda been minutes. Time went funny when you had nothing to do. "Look at that spider."

We watched as it swung from the windowsill of Tom's mum's tidy living room. It was swollen and black. It reminded me of the tarmac of the road that was oozing under the bright stare of the sun. We watched it fight against its own weight as it built a web strand by strand.

The midges that had been attacking everyone for the past few weeks got stuck in the trap but the spider did not seem bothered and continued building and building and building.

I'm not sure how long we were sat there watching it. Long enough for Tom's mum to call us in for dinner.

That was just the beginning.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Tick, Tock, Tick, Tock...

Sprawled out on my Pocahontas comforter, I lazily listened to the soothing rhythm of the clock in the distance. Nothing is quite comparable to the feeling of a Saturday morning knowing you've already done all of your homework, and you have the rest of the weekend to just play.

As I ponder the exciting opportunities the day will unfold, I hear the low rumbling purr of my kitty as she comes to greet me. I gently roll to my side as I feel the prickle of whiskers on my cheek, and hear her subtle sniffing in my ear. As I stare into her jade half-closed eyes, I softly whisper, "I wish I knew exactly what cats think about."

---

**10 Years Later**

Beep, beep, beep, beep...

Sprawled out on my futon, I wearily reach out blindly searching for the snooze button for the second time this morning. I know I should start getting ready for work, but just thinking about one more day in that shithole is maddening. Saturdays are the worst. Period. It's like everyone decides they want to shop on the same day. At the same time. Pricks.

As I pull the covers over my head, I hear the soft purring of my waiting feline. I roll over, trying my damnedest to ignore his incessant purring. Just five more minutes.

As I start to fall asleep again, I feel the sting of claws as he starts kneading the back of my head with his paws. I roll over exasperated, and stare into his placid, golden eyes.

*"Feed me, you piece of shit! I've been waiting for literally forever. I hate you. So much."*

"Such a stupid wish," I groaned.

*"Screw you, I'm starving."*
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Canvas Prison

The black stripe widened before my eyes, spreading like spilled ink across the painted wall. I scrambled backward, my heart hammering against my ribs. After a week of suffocating stillness, *something* was finally happening.

The darkness grew, consuming the cheerful yellow wallpaper I'd so carefully rendered. It moved with purpose, deliberate strokes cutting through my prison's façade. Then I understood—someone was painting over me.

"WAIT!" I screamed, lunging toward the expanding blackness. "I'M IN HERE!"

My hands hit the wall where paint met void. The black was cold, impossibly cold, and where it touched my fingers, I felt... nothing. Not numbness—absolute absence. I jerked back, cradling my hand.

The stripe became a rectangle. A window? No—a door. Someone was painting a door on the outside.

Hope exploded in my chest. I pressed my ear against the wall, listening. Muffled voices filtered through:

"—Such a shame. Promising artist, just vanished—"

"—Painting over it seems disrespectful, but the gallery needs the wall space—"

"NO!" I pounded my fists bloody against the surface. "DON'T PAINT OVER IT! I'M INSIDE!"

The black door completed. A painted brass knob appeared.

My hand trembled as I reached for it. What if it didn't work? What if this was just another cruel joke in this two-dimensional hell?

The knob turned.

The door swung inward, and I stumbled through into... another room. But this one was grey, formless, incomplete. Sketched furniture floated in undefined space. The air smelled of turpentine and linseed oil—*real* smells.

Behind me, my former prison was now a painting hanging on this new wall, my shit-stained corner and broken furniture perfectly preserved. 

Through another doorway—this one seemingly real—I could see my actual studio, unchanged, my easel still standing.

"Hello?" I called out, my voice hoarse from disuse.

Silence answered.

Then I noticed the painter's signature in the corner of this grey room: my own name, but the handwriting was backwards, mirror-reversed.

My stomach dropped.

I hadn't escaped.

I'd just moved to a different layer of the canvas.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Story Bard

Against the din of the Mystic Traveling Gwama Band in the center of it all, it was hard to make out every word leaving the worn tin megaphone of Leighton Otalman, The Story Bard of Caldertown.

"...And so the price was set at eight bags of gold, twelve bags of silver, and twenty-four fine horses to the man who could bring back the head of the Red Knight of Gravesend. Which of our heroes will risk death for glory and riches? For a nickel you can hear..."

Everyone got a preview for free. Five minutes before the hour, every hour. There'd be familiar faces in every town he went to, but the difference between a small crowd and an OK one usually came down to how well he sold himself in those five minutes before a show. The effort meant a couple of extra drinks at the end of the night.

The Red Knight of Gravesend had been around for a little while—maybe two years or so. It was the Witch of Cecteras and her Fire Dragon before that. There was even a Black Knight of Gravesend a while back, but he was a minor enough character that nobody would remember him at this point.

Same deal with the heroes, although they tended to stick around as respected minor characters after their feature days ended. It really all depended on what the crowds liked. He could tell when they were ready to move onto something new.

Sling stories long enough to watch towns come and go, and you'll pick up the ebb and flow of it.

At the top of the hour, The Bard pocketed his last nickel, closed the flap to his tent, and took a long moment to take a sip of water and breathe slowly.

As his crowd settled in, he re-entered the world of his creation, a small observer inside a battle between heroes and villains. His voice dropped low, intimate now without the megaphone.

"The Red Knight waited at the bridge of bones..."

Leighton watched their faces flicker in the lamplight, already lost in his words. This was the real magic—not the tale itself, but the journey they took together, night after night, town after town, always new, always the same.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Great Debate

The gallery erupted as Senator Morrison from Tennessee concluded his passionate plea. His face flushed red, perspiration beading on his forehead despite the cool December air filtering through the chamber.

"We now recognize the senator from Chicago."

Senator Webb rose slowly, adjusting his wire-rimmed glasses. Where Morrison had thundered, Webb spoke conversationally, almost wearily.

"People will drink alcohol no matter what, and it's up to the government to regulate it as best we can, to ensure the safety of the people. We can't stop the drinking, but if we legalize it, we can control the sources at the point of sale—enforce a legal drinking age, which parents will get behind, ensure the alcohol is actually alcohol, and tax the sale of it."

He paused, scanning the room.

"The question is not whether drinking alcohol is good or bad. The question is whether we recognize the reality of its consumption and respond in a useful way. Thank you."

The chamber fell silent. Outside, snow began to fall on Washington, blanketing a nation divided.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Following the Flames

I stood at the window, watching orange tongues lick up the Organization's walls, and felt something unfamiliar bloom in my chest: satisfaction.

All my life, I'd been a shadow. Following my parents' footsteps until they turned their backs. Following my friends until they became mere acquaintances. Following my partner because being beside them felt like purpose enough.

I'd never led. Never initiated. Never *wanted* anything that wasn't handed to me first.

Until I did.

The desire to destroy the Organization had emerged like a spark in dry kindling—sudden, mine, terrifying in its singularity. For weeks, I'd carried it secretly, unsure what to do with an original thought.

Then the fire started.

Not by our hands—we'd never be so bold. But when the alarms shrieked and smoke billowed through corridors, when others scrambled with extinguishers and emergency protocols, my partner looked at me.

Really *looked* at me.

"We should go," they said.

I nodded. For once, I wasn't following. We were moving together, in agreement, toward the exit.

Behind us, the Organization crumbled. We didn't start the fire, but we'd fanned its flames with our inaction, our calculated stillness.

As we stepped into the night air, I realized: sometimes not following is its own form of leadership.

The burning building reflected in my partner's eyes.

I smiled.

Finally, something was mine.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Independence Day

The president's words echoed across the tarmac as pilots sprinted toward their fighters. Sarah gripped her helmet tighter, feeling the weight of humanity resting on her shoulders.

Above, alien ships darkened the sky like mechanical thunderclouds. She'd lost her brother in New York, her parents in Los Angeles. Now there was nothing left but this—one final chance.

"Red Squadron, you're cleared for takeoff," crackled through her headset.

Her F-18 screamed down the runway, joining the formation. Hundreds of aircraft rose together—American, Russian, British, Japanese—flags replaced by a single purpose.

The alien destroyer loomed ahead, its underbelly glowing with charging weapons.

"This is it," her wingman transmitted. "For Earth."

Sarah armed her missiles, thinking of her brother's laugh, her mother's smile. The president was right. Today, they weren't fighting as nations.

They were fighting as one.

"Fox three!" she shouted, releasing her payload.

The sky erupted in fire and determination. Win or lose, humanity would make them remember this day.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Dragonslayer's Secret

"What does that mean, allergic?"

"Well.... You know how when the farmers are out collecting the wheat or harvesting or whatever it is they actually do."

"Right, yeah?"

"And you know that you're always sneezing around then right?"

"Sure."

"Well, that's an allergy. You're allergic to the pollen that's released when they cut the.... errr....the crops?"

"You don't know much about farming do you?"

"Not many crops in the dragonslaying business."

"What's pollen?"

"Well, pollen is this very small erm. Dust? Well it's not dust it's like.... You know what, it doesn't matter. I've got a magical aura that weakens dragons but I'm not really killing them, they're just dying in my presence."

"Dear holy father, you're that strong? We knew that you were the chosen one but you can destroy them so easily? I don't know if we can afford your services but Gharulf the Black has been terrorising the village for months. If he continues he'll destroy everything. Please, won't you help us?"

"...sure, which way?"

The villager pointed toward the mountain. The dragonslayer sighed, shouldering his sword he'd never actually used.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Excuse Me, Humanity

"Excuse me humanity," the grammar nazi said.

"Yes Hitler?" humanity politely responded.

"You don't have enough datums in your calendario," the grammar nazi said.

"Oh, I see," humanity said. "Well we only have this one datum. It's the datum that Zoey 101 was cancelled."

"What's Zoey 101?" the grammar nazi asked.

"Well, it was this show," humanity said, "And it was cancelled for our sins."

"I see," the grammar nazi said.

There was a pause.

"You don't know what a datum is, do you?" the grammar nazi said.

"Shut up grammar nazi," humanity said, "I'm about to blow your mind."

"Yeah whatever," the grammar nazi said, "Just you try."

"You are part of me," humanity said to the grammar nazi.

Humanity said to itself.

The grammar nazi's mind was blown. And by consequence, humanity's mind was blown.

And because the minds of humanity had all been blown, everyone felt pretty content about everything. Everyone just sat around eating chips and salsa and seeing what was on TV.

As it turned out, Zoey 101 was on TV.

So humanity watched Zoey 101 for a while. And then it was cancelled.

But everyone was still feeling pretty mind-blown from their recent experience. So humanity just kind of sat there, watching the clock, and waiting for Zoey 101 to be un-cancelled.

The chips went stale. The salsa congealed. But nobody really noticed. They were too busy being part of each other, waiting together in collective, absurd contentment.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Retribution

They blew up my house. I could live with that; you don't play the game without taking some risks. They put so many holes in my car the frame is no longer structurally sound. No big deal; I'm getting paid enough for this job I can just buy another.

But I saw the tapes.

The bastards shot my dog. Their wannabe generalissimo pulled his sidearm and put six rounds into Duke. He was fucking tied up and wasn't even barking at them.

I snorted softly inside the tacmask as I slid the magazine home into my modified rifle. A quiet beeping notified me that we were in range. I opened the door of the small drone, steadily hovering in place, and activated the exosuit's stabilizers.

The barrel of the rifle waved a bit as my HUD gave me the overlay of the small compound and began finding targets. One caught my eye. The generalissimo.

My HUD zoomed in to show me his face and lined up a targeting trajectory and fire pattern that would put one in his heart and two through his brain as he fell.

My finger lay upon the trigger when inspiration struck me.

With a grim smile I thumbed over to the high explosive rounds we used to blow tank armor.

Fuck this guy in particular.

The shot echoed across the valley. Where the generalissimo had stood, there was only a crater and red mist.

For Duke.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Unexpected Advocate

Usually I'm calm as a cucumber when I go up to the podium. I have to be. It is my job to stand in front of people and try to convince them that their views are incorrect. It doesn't help your cause if you're a sweaty mess who stumbles over their words.

Today was different though. I felt as though the butterflies in my stomach were having a rave. Maybe it was because I was only partly on-board with the idea of trying to have a xenomorph hunting ban. The higher-ups in the organization seemed to be pretty convinced though, so out on the stage I go.

The lights were as bright as ever, and half-way through the speech I had to stop to gulp down some water from a glass. The butterflies weren't getting better. It felt like they had started a gang-war. *Maybe it was something I ate?*, I wondered as I found my place on the queue cards.

I continued to struggle my way through the speech. "...and that is why we must consider their rights as living beings." I waved away their questions and stumbled off the stage.

I needed to find somewhere dark and cool and sit for a while. I pulled off my tie, threw it to the ground and followed it down, resting against the wall. *I... think I might actually need a doctor*, I thought to myself, moments before the chest-burster finished ruining my evening.

The irony wasn't lost on me—advocating for the creatures' protection while becoming their latest victim. My last thought was a bitter one: the higher-ups had been more convincing than they knew.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Sleepless

My name's Cormack O'Donnell, and I suppose it's time someone knew the truth.

For fifty years, I've lived atop Ashford Hill, that skeletal Victorian that watches over the town like a crow on a fence post. The locals whisper about me in their coffee shops and corner stores. *The hermit. The ghost. The gold miner.* They've spun quite the mythology around my existence.

They're not entirely wrong.

Yes, I work constantly. Yes, I never sleep. But it's not dedication or insomnia—it's necessity. You see, I discovered something remarkable buried in my grandfather's journals: a technique, an exchange of sorts. A way to transfer one's sleep requirement to another willing participant.

The "professional sleepers," as the townspeople call them, aren't mining for gold. They're mining for rest—my rest. Each volunteer sleeps on my behalf, allowing me to continue my research uninterrupted. For a generous fee, of course.

The sleep transfer works beautifully for about three weeks. Then the biology rebels. The surrogate begins to deteriorate—nothing dramatic, just a gradual decline. Exhaustion that sleep can't cure. Confusion. Eventually, organ failure.

I terminate the arrangement before it becomes fatal. Humanely. Quickly. A precisely placed injection while they sleep. They feel nothing. Then I bury them in the woods behind my property, where my family rests.

My family. Yes, they were the first test subjects. Volunteers, in their way. They believed in my work.

The groceries? Merely a cover. My real shopping happens in distant cities—bus stations, homeless shelters, places where desperate people accept cash for unusual jobs, no questions asked.

I'm close now. So close to isolating the permanent solution, the biological key that will eliminate humanity's need for sleep entirely. Imagine the productivity. The discoveries. The evolution.

My grandmother still lives two towns over. Ninety-three years old, spending most of her days sleeping anyway. She'd want to contribute to something meaningful.

I'll visit tomorrow.

After all, family should support family.

And I need just a bit more time.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Holidays Fucking Suck

The pain sears through my palms as I finally drop the flaming puzzle box onto the hardwood floor. The singing stops abruptly.

"OH MY GOD!" Aunt Carol shrieks.

Uncle Dennis stampedes over with a fire extinguisher, coating the smoldering puzzle—and my feet—in white foam. The chemical smell mixes with burnt flesh and pine needles.

"Nana," I gasp, cradling my blistering hands. "Where the *fuck* do you buy these things?"

Grandma adjusts her bifocals, peering at the charred remains with academic interest. "Oh dear. Was that the Serbian one or the Czech one?"

"The *what?*"

"I get them on eBay, sweetheart. International sellers mostly. Some nice gentleman in Prague has *wonderful* inventory." She pats my shoulder sympathetically. "The listing did say 'cursed,' but I thought that was just marketing."

My mother finally springs into action, dragging me toward the kitchen sink. As ice water runs over my ruined hands, I watch Grandma pick through the ashes with a fireplace poker.

"Shame," she mutters. "I was curious about the solution."

Next year, I'm spending Christmas in a fucking hotel. Alone. With a fire extinguisher.

And blocking Grandma's number.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Forgotten Word

I watched him as he stared into the window on the third floor in the building opposite ours. Both of us were crouching and my legs were beginning to ache.

"What are we waiting for, Peter?" I began to whine.

Peter shushed at me without even glancing in my direction. I frowned and turned to watch the window with him.

Fifteen minutes later, she appeared in the window. I gasped when I saw her. "Peter, she's beautiful."

I saw the sides of Peter's mouth curl up into a smile, and his whole body seemed to become lighter. His green clothes seemed slightly brighter, and I swore to the fair oceans and lush greenery of Neverland, that Peter floated just for a moment.

"I know," he paused. "She's my mother."

That word rang out loud in my head, in an extremely foreign way, as if I didn't know it. But at the same time, I knew that I just knew the existence of that word. *Mother*. It's been a really long time since I've heard that word, and I just had to whisper it.

"Mother?"

Images of a woman suddenly appeared in my mind, and I fell back. Who was this woman that Peter was looking at and who was this woman in my head? They were both 'mothers' but they were both different.

"Do you remember yours?" Peter asked softly, still watching the window.

I tried to grasp the fading image, but Neverland had already taken too much. The word remained, hollow and haunting—a ghost of something I'd once known.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Visitor

There it was, in the corner of my eye. It had been happening like this since last Tuesday. I hoped that when I turned nothing would be there. "Just your imagination," I thought to myself. But deep down in my stomach I knew that something was wrong.

I closed my eyes. My heart was leaping like a racehorse down the track, gradually picking up speed until I couldn't handle it anymore. I could feel a bead of sweat rolling down my furry brow. "There is nothing there, just turn around."

The apartment was too quiet. No hum of the refrigerator, no distant traffic—just my ragged breathing filling the space. Since last Tuesday, these moments had become more frequent. A shadow darting past doorways. A figure standing motionless in my peripheral vision. Each time I convinced myself it was fatigue, stress, the long hours at work playing tricks on me.

But this time felt different. This time, I could sense a presence, tangible and real, waiting for me to acknowledge it.

Slowly, with the silence of a ninja, I turned around and saw that the corner of my eye did not lie to me.

A familiar floral cardigan. That judgmental purse clutched under one arm. Gray hair perfectly coiffed despite the early hour. She was rearranging my kitchen cabinets, humming to herself as if she owned the place.

I screamed and felt an unwelcome feeling wash over me—not fear, but exasperation mixed with violated privacy. I had to get it out of me, I had to say something.

"GODDAMMIT, MOM! Stop coming into my apartment unannounced! I never should have given you a key!"

She didn't even flinch. Just turned, holding up a can of soup with evident disapproval.

"You call this food? Also, your refrigerator is a biohazard. I'm cleaning it out."

"Mom—"

"Don't 'Mom' me. Tuesday, Thursday, today. If you kept proper groceries, I wouldn't need to check on you."

Mystery solved. The lurking figure wasn't supernatural.

It was much, much worse.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Account

He almost forgot to pay for his newspaper. Headlining was my face once again, and also the face of one of his business partners. Those holes, there's no sorcerer in the world that could do those. That's because it wasn't magic—it was something not even his entire offshore alchemy account could buy.

Pathetic little man, with his short and crooked microwand. Let's see him stop an automatic rifle.

"Read the paper, Johnny? He's killing all these big names. Why'd you think he's doing it?"

*What the fuck do you think?*

"Maybe because of all the shit everyone knows they have tucked away in Swetzland."

I stared into his eyes. Was it an earthquake? I tried to hold on to my coffee mug as it started to tumble. The roar actually came from his guffaw. The joke was so funny he wanted the entire café to hear.

"HAHA! Then they should kill me then! I have the biggest account in Swetzland. Jesus, Jimmy, everyone does this shit. Grand wizards, wand brokers like me—it's how it is."

That display made him parched. He quaffed the foamed Goggrum in front of him. Disgusting fat wasteman with the foam around his mouth. Maybe it'll foam like that tonight when I put that barrel in his mouth. Make him suck on it—but he's used to sucking.

"Ahhh. See ya tonight, Jimmy, at the solar."

He grabbed his jacket and left.

Good thing I got the word to do it. I don't think I could've dealt with that star-hatted grand master asshole any longer.

Tonight, the Swetzland accounts would have one less name.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Together Forever

Doris stared in disbelief as her husband sat weakly in the bedside chair of his hospital room. The doctor merely said, "I'm sorry," and quietly left the two of them alone.

They always said it would never work out between them, that her being an orange and him a banana was bigger than their love. She never imagined what would doom them would be illness.

Harold sat there, limply, his once-firm yellow peel now spotted and brown. His face was simply turning to a watery mush and the long, proud stalk atop his head, which she had always admired, was turning black and wrinkling, threatening to just fall off.

She wept.

"I know, Doris. I know and I'm sorry. If I had known death would claim me so young I'd have never married you. I wanted you to have everything in life, not just the drawer but the whole damned fridge. But now? Look at me. I'm... I'm just so sorry."

A bit of peel broke open along the seam that ran up his temple and Doris didn't know if the seeping fluid was decaying fruit-meat or tears.

"Oh, Harold," she sniffled. "I wouldn't trade a moment of our life together for anything. You have made me the happiest citrus fruit in the whole world."

She moved to his side and tried her best to hide the fuzzy grey spot slowly growing on her hip. She would never tell him she was rotting too. It would be too much for him to bear.

Instead, she pressed her lips against his and imagined the two of them intermingling as compost. Together forever.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Fall of the Mighty

Weren't there people for this? Runners of some sort, or a mail carrier or something? Even a squire would be above this work, dropping off a letter for a loved one.

Sure, the orcs on the high road could be troublesome, but a simple pike and a week of training was more than enough to prepare a soul for them. Gill had fought in the Giant Wars. He slayed the lich king of Cydonia. His helmet was made from an honest-to-god dragon skull, for crying out loud!

Gill the Mighty did not fight orcs for peasants, and he certainly did not deliver mail.

Holding out his hand and squinting, he read the address on the envelope again.

"Hm," he grunted. "How important can it really be?"

At that moment, a man came from behind him on the trail. Gill stopped him with his massive hand.

"Pardon me, sir, but are you headed to Anglesburg?"

The man nodded, or maybe he just trembled in awe. Gill had trouble telling sometimes.

"Please, take this letter to the address printed on it."

Again, the man confirmed and went on his way. Content, Gill set up camp for the night and dreamt of bawdy women and brutal men, of fights and conquests that would fill his many years.

Gill the Mighty let no person die an unnecessary death.

When he awoke, new vigor ran through his veins that no delivery man ever felt. A half hour walk down the road, Gill stumbled across a body and rushed to check if the man was still breathing.

It was the traveler from the day before, dead from an ambush of orcs.

Gill screamed. "All this for a filthy letter!"

In his rage, Gill flung the man from the road and off the cliff, where a fortuitous bounce off a bald outcrop sent him tumbling head over heels into the bow of a sailing ship bearing none other than the queen with her high priestess.

Crippled from the sudden impact, the boat sank with all aboard, and Gill was henceforth tried not as Gill the Mighty but as Gill the Treasonous Rat.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Thread

His thoughts began to wander, and as they grew further and further apart, he became aware of their waning strength. The very idea that had brought them together had also caused their flight, but there was no more time. No more time for new associations or revelations—the last one still needed to be mended and contained.

A few small details of the path that had led him to this place remained in view. He retreated to the earliest of his recent memories, and hope and hopelessness formed an accord. How unlike this part of the path was from its own end, how unbelievably foreign! He realized now that he had already traversed immeasurable space between two disparate ideas.

Surely he could do it again; it would only mean retracing his steps. He flit from one memory to the next, connecting past and present. Even in his haste, however, he couldn't deny his evident glee. How wonderful it was that this could exist at all! How unlikely it was that such a path formed!

At the center of his joy, fear resided. Would he forget this feeling as well? Hadn't he forgotten it once before?

He felt his resolve strengthen. He wouldn't let go. Not this time.

Now then. *Think.*

The pen touched paper. Words formed. The idea crystallized into permanence before it could dissolve back into the fog of his fragmenting mind—captured, finally, against the advancing tide.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Reincarnation Glitch

"What the hell," he thought as he rushed from a warm, comfortable place into the bright, climate-controlled hospital room. He began crying immediately—only it was the sound of an infant crying.

Meanwhile, at the Office of Reincarnation and Re-Integration (O.R.R.), Frank had just realized his error.

"GABRIEL!" he shouted, literally flying down the all-white hallway. "We did it again! We have a Code Gray!"

"Again!" Gabriel yelled back from his mahogany desk loaded with incoming and outgoing files as St. Peter looked on in disdain from the water cooler. "The last time this happened... do you remember Pol Pot, Frank?"

"Yes..." Frank replied nervously.

"The only thing to do is authorize the use of Plan Pink."

"PLAN PINK... Do you actually think it will work?!" Frank answered back.

"We can only hope," St. Peter said, joining the two angels in the O.R.R.

They never even thought to read the file on Michael McMillian before initiating Plan Pink.

Months later, Michael McMulligan—re-christened KeShawn Jones—was living the normal life of an infant, mildly aggravated at all the baby talk aimed toward him, especially from his new "aunt" and "nana." But he received pleasure whenever he made them change multiple diapers as payback.

"Maybe this time around, I can do it right," Michael-Keshawn thought to himself as he wailed for a 3 AM feeding. "This ain't too bad a life... not too bad at all."
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Into the Darkness

A cone of darkness throws itself down from the streetlamp, a cold void of lightlessness. Behind us the warmth of civilised luminescence, in front just the deep fear of deadly blackness.

We plug ourselves in, charge our primaries and reserves, arming the li-tech guards that will soon see battle. LED strips blink across the hard ridges of the brigade's battle armor. Linking connectors to the person either side, our tactical line stills and together we take a breath of grim determination.

"Light tech, prepare!" my voice orders.

As one, the line takes a large length of tube from their backpacks.

"Charge up!"

A whine permeates the air, and a fierce glow starts to burn at the end of each tube.

"Position!"

The thunder of feet taking a synchronised step forward, heads dipping in preparation.

"Forward!"

Into the darkness we march, our luminous weapons blazing against the ancient shadow.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Stillness

The grass grows tall around me now. I can feel it tickling my arms, weaving through my fingers, reclaiming the space my body occupies. Soon it will cover me entirely, and I welcome it.

They've stopped coming. The last visitor was three weeks ago—or was it three months? Time moves differently when you stop moving with it. She was young, a philosophy student clutching a recording device, asking questions I'd heard in a dozen different languages across a hundred generations. "What's the meaning of life?" "What have you learned?" "Don't you want to leave a legacy?"

Legacy. The word almost made me laugh.

I *am* the legacy. I am every legacy that ever was. I watched the first cave painter discover that ochre and ash could become immortality on stone. I helped weave the Bayeux Tapestry with calloused fingers that had once wielded the swords depicted in its threads. I soldered circuits in Shenzhen factories, creating the devices people now use to photograph their forgettable moments.

But none of it was mine. None of it was *me*.

I was the brush, never the painter. The loom, never the weaver. The tool, never the craftsman.

When you've been everyone, you've been no one.

The sun is setting again—the thousand-thousandth sunset I've witnessed. Once, I would have described it differently each time: romantic in Paris, melancholic in Tokyo, pragmatic in Detroit. Now I simply watch the colors bleed across the sky, unnamed and uninterpreted, belonging to no culture or time.

My breathing has slowed. My heartbeat, that ancient rhythm that has drummed through countless iterations, is finally finding its rest.

They thought I was protesting, meditating, dying. They didn't understand I was simply stopping. After millennia of being humanity's echo, I've finally found silence.

In this field, motionless and mute, I am—for the first and last time—finally myself.

And myself wants only to sleep.

The grass whispers agreement, growing ever higher.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Necromancer's Critique

The letter arrived on blackened parchment, sealed with wax the color of old blood.

Lucian read it thrice, fingers trembling. A *review*. Of his life's work. His empire of shadow and suffering, his carefully orchestrated descent into damnation—reduced to "grand" and "twisted passages."

*Fallen from grace*, they called him. As if it were narrative choice rather than necessity.

The reviewer praised his "archaic style" while noting it felt "contemporary." They'd enjoyed his verbose descriptions but lost track of characters. They mentioned a *headache*.

Lucian stared at his undead legions shambling through the courtyard below.

Centuries perfecting necromantic arts. Kingdoms toppled. Souls harvested.

And someone had a *great time* with it.

He crumpled the letter, then carefully smoothed it flat again.

*Look forward to reading more.*

Despite everything—despite the presumption, the casual tone, the damning praise—Lucian smiled.

Someone was watching. Someone cared.

He returned to his dark work with renewed purpose.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Day 215

The book materialized in my trembling hands exactly 215 days ago—leather-bound, pages numbered, waiting. Everyone received one. Mine had precisely 215 pages.

I calculated immediately: one page per day until something ended.

The first week, I panicked. The second, I accepted. By the third, I'd begun my work.

Each night, I documented my research—genetic recoding, consciousness expansion, cellular immortality. The equations that would elevate me beyond human limitation filled page after page in cramped handwriting.

Today, the final page stares back at me, half-empty.

The syringe lies discarded on my desk, its iridescent contents now coursing through my veins. I named it Transcendence, though hubris might be more accurate.

My fingers tingle. Colors sharpen impossibly. I can hear my neighbor's heartbeat three floors down.

The clock reads 11:47 PM.

Thirteen minutes until I become something else. Something more.

Or nothing at all.

The book never promised transformation—only an ending. Perhaps that's what everyone's book contains: their own personal apocalypse.

The pen slips from my hand.

El. Psy. Congroo.

Midnight arrives.

I dissolve into light, or darkness, or—
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Mirage's Cruel Jest

"It can't be..." I mumble, rubbing my eyes viciously. Sand cascades from my eyebrows, gritty and invasive.

When I look again, they're still there. *Closer*.

I gulp water from my Camelbak—the pack disturbingly light against my spine. One bottle left. Maybe two miles' worth. The next town is at least fifteen away.

The desert has been punishing, but this? This is madness.

Three blinks. Rapid succession. *Definitely closer.*

I stumble forward, legs burning, sand invading my boots with each desperate step. The vending machines shimmer in the heat, their garish colors somehow *wrong* against the endless beige. With every blink, they inch nearer, as if reality is glitching.

Thirty feet. Twenty. Ten.

I collapse against the middle machine, gasping as blessed coolness seeps through my shirt. My reflection stares back from the glass—sunburned, wild-eyed, pathetic. Rows of Dr Pepper glisten like rubies behind the barrier.

*Insert coins*, the slot mocks.

My laugh comes out as a wheeze. Who brings *change* into a desert?

I check my pockets anyway. Lint. A receipt. My dead phone.

The machine hums softly, almost sympathetically. I press my forehead against its metal flank, fighting tears. So close to salvation, yet impossibly far.

Then I notice the machines are facing *away* from town.

Toward the deeper desert.

Toward nothing.

*Who put vending machines here?*

As dehydration fog clouds my thoughts, I realize the machines are still moving. Not closer to me.

Carrying me with them.

*Deeper*.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Morning

I woke up in the third motel room of the week. Dean was on the edge of the bed, already wearing his leather jacket and putting on his boots. "We've got a case a few miles away, we might be gone the rest of the day," he said once he noticed I was awake, kissing my forehead.

Sam was packing the rifles, the Colt and the salt gun in a tattered duffel bag. Castiel appears out of nowhere, bloody and beaten. He falls to the floor with a thud.

Dean and Sam rush to his side. "Cas!" Dean shouts, "I told you we shouldn't have messed with God!"

In the chaos they seem to have forgotten I was even there.

Dean looks my way, comes to the bed and holds my face in his hands. "Sweetie, I need you to take this knife and go to the bathroom to hide. Salt the windows and doors. You're going to hear a lot of noises, but I need you to stay put."

I run to the bathroom, knife in hand, salt the door and window and take a seat on the edge of the bathtub. I knew from the beginning this wouldn't work out, but now I was certain. My life was in danger and I needed to get out.

The room started to quake, the lights flickering. I heard Dean chanting in Latin, and then a loud crash. I saw a bright light flash under the door and then, silence.

The flap of wings.

I walk out and he's gone.

I waited in the Winchester's motel room for two days. They never came back. They never checked out. I never saw them again.

Turns out their case was more serious than they originally thought.

Dean was in Hell.

Again.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Currency of Dreams

I once awoke in front of the ocean. Wave after wave brought in coins with every lap. Each one was heads up. I spent the day grabbing at them and pulling them into a pile. I had such wild eyes as I hoarded the coins, drunk with the idea that I could invest in a good day.

But it was only another nightmare.

I never have good days. Yesterday I spent the day at interviews with my top choice jobs, and with each word I spoke, a tooth fell out. The day before that, I went to greet my family as a shooter sprayed bullets, engulfing them. And before that, I was in an endless darkly lit hallway, darkness threatening to swallow me.

Eventually though, the not-so-terrible ones seem good.

Like today.

Today I watch another me flip a coin, getting heads every time. She smiles with complete teeth, embraces living family, walks through sunlit rooms. I press my palm against the invisible barrier between us.

I can only hope she lives better than I can.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Defiance

**Official Response from the Austrasian Federal Council**

To the Self-Proclaimed Supreme Emperor:

We received Your letter. The coffee stains on it suggest You wrote it during Your third breakdown this month.

You speak of destiny while Your empire crumbles from within. We've intercepted Your internal communications—Your "united" territories require 60% of Your military just to maintain order. Rebellions bloom like spring flowers across Your African provinces. Your European zones haven't met grain quotas in eighteen months.

You claim We huddle in fear. Yet Our children sleep soundly while Yours whisper prayers that the secret police won't visit tonight.

You offer enlightenment. We counter with a question: If Your empire represents humanity's future, why do Your citizens brave minefields and gun towers attempting to reach Our "hyper-militarized ghetto"?

You say You'll wait a year or two. We've waited five already. Your economy cannot sustain another year of this blockade. Our intelligence suggests You have eight months before systemic collapse.

You threaten the bloodiest war in history. We remind You that every previous conqueror who spoke such words is now studied as a cautionary tale.

Your letter's final word betrays You: "Please."

Emperors don't plead. Desperate men do.

We will not submit. We will not open our borders. And when Your empire finally fractures under its own contradictions—as all such empires must—We will be here, ready to help rebuild something better from the ashes.

Until then, We respectfully suggest You learn patience.

**The Austrasian Federal Council**

P.S. - Your move.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Birthday of Shadows

The streamers hung limply from the Johnson's ceiling, cheerful colors mocking the grief-heavy air. Eight small children clutched wrapped boxes, their parents hovering near the exits like nervous sentries.

Robert Johnson stood by the untouched birthday cake, its nine candles waiting. Melina gripped her husband's hand, knuckles white, eyes red-rimmed from a year of crying.

"Thank you all for coming," Robert whispered. "Sarah would have—"

The lights died.

Children screamed. Parents lunged forward in the darkness. Then came the voice—familiar yet transformed, innocence corrupted into something cold and terrible.

"Robert and Melina Johnson... I've come for you..."

"S-Sarah?! Baby, where are you??" Melina's voice cracked with desperate hope.

The whistle of projectiles cutting air. Twin gasps. Two bodies crumpling.

When the lights blazed back, the room erupted in chaos. The parents lay sprawled on the floor—unconscious, not dead—surrounded by scattered pearls from Melina's broken necklace. Tiny tranquilizer darts protruded from their necks.

Atop the birthday table stood a small figure draped in black, face obscured by a mask. Only her eyes were visible—eight-year-old eyes that had seen too much.

"Last year, I asked for a pony," the child assassin announced, her voice steady and merciless. "This year, I have revenge."

She pulled something from her belt. Smoke exploded outward, engulfing the room. Through streaming eyes and hacking coughs, the guests glimpsed her silhouette disappearing through the window.

By the time the smoke cleared, she was gone.

On the cake, stabbed through the frosting, a small blade held a note: *"The League of Shadows trains them young. Tell them I'm collecting debts. —Night Pony"*

Thus began the legend of the world's youngest, most feared assassin.

The pony would have been cheaper.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Veil Between

The crash was all flashing before my mind—the flip, the other car. The screams, the horrible pain, all of it. I couldn't feel my legs. I was in shock more than anything. She ran alongside them as they ran me into the hospital. Her hand was wrapped tight around mine.

"You're gonna make it honey, I know you are!" She said through the tears.

I gave her a small smile, my vision fading in and out, trained on her beautiful brown eyes. "I love you so much..." I say, and my vision fades out.

White. Everything was white. I couldn't tell where I was, but wherever it was, I was zooming past it fast. I closed my eyes, and as I opened them, I saw the waiting room of the hospital. Tears fell from my eyes, but I couldn't stop them. What seemed to be my hand moved up to wipe away a few tears, and I realized...

*It's her.*

I was dead.

She looks over as the doctor walks out to her. "Miss... I'm sorry... we lost him..."

"I... I need to go." She stood up and ran out of the hospital, tears rushing down her face as she went. She made it to her car before having a breakdown, screaming, punching it as she fell to her knees. I could feel that pain in her chest. Her heart was breaking.

She got into the car and started driving. I had no idea where she was going, but it looked like the way back to our house. She burst in the front door, crawling across the floor before collapsing, quickly followed by sobbing and wheezing. I wanted to help her so badly. I wanted her to be okay.

She stood up, walking into the bathroom. She quickly began going through the medicine cabinet, grabbing my sleeping pills.

I froze, before shouting, "No!"

Suddenly, her hand stopped.

"J... Jordan?"

I could hear her.

"Put the pills down... I love you..."

"Jordan I miss you." I could hear her crying still.

"Shhh... I'll always be with you."

The bottle clattered to the floor, and she collapsed against the wall, clutching her chest. But she was breathing. She was alive.

And somehow, impossibly, I was still there.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Voices Within

**Word Count: 272**

The door creaked open, and the stench hit like a physical wall. My eyes watered as thick dust particles danced through shafts of morning light, turning the air into something you could almost touch.

"Yeah yeah, we're all in this together. Let's get this over with," a reluctant young voice spoke in my head.

"Talk for yourself, I did not ask to be here," an old, croaky voice answered.

"Get used to it, old man. We'll be here for a while," came the cold, calculated response that vibrated through my consciousness.

"Guys, watch the scene. We need to solve this case," I said, feeling the weight of their presence in my skull.

Each step into the room felt like pushing through mud, the atmosphere so heavy it seemed to hold my shape after I passed. Around the corner, the body slowly became visible—*my* body.

A soft voice warped through our shared mind. "What happened? Where am I?"

"Here we go," the calculated voice sighed. "I explained it to the old timer and the youngin, so driver, your turn."

"Who are you? Why can't I move? What—"

As our eyes fell upon my corpse, I felt my mind wince. "You'll be with us until we find the killer," I explained gently. "Don't break. Think clearly and stay sane. Whatever you think goes through all of us. If you break, we break. Understand?"

"Yeah... I... What... Is this..."

"This is the deal. We find who did this, you all go. Meet the team. Same killer got us all."

"Guy?"

"Got me first."

"Me second."

"I was last before you."

"And I'm your host. Dave River. Now let's get your killer."

text:
# Tick. Tick. Tick.

The noise from the dark room I woke to find myself in startled me. It was almost like dripping water, but somehow... not. I rummaged in my pocket to find my flashlight and fumbled with the switch until I finally managed to turn it on.

Tick. Tick. Tick.

I was in a small room. I could see no doors or windows. This place felt like a prison. I could feel myself starting to panic in this claustrophobic space when the flashlight caught a glimpse of something just above my head. Wood. A square. A door.

Tick. Tick. Tick.

The door seemed wedged in place. I nudged it slightly. Nothing. I tried again, harder this time. The door opened slightly before the weight of whatever was above forced it closed again. The flashlight caught sight of something flashing by my head.

Tick.

There it was again. It was closer this time. I pointed the flashlight on the floor and there it was.

"A... pen?"

I reached down to pick it up. When I brought it up to my face, my eyes widened in shock. It really was a pen. A blue biro. No lid, and next to no ink inside.

Tick. Tick. Tick.

The sound continued above me. With renewed vigour I shoved the pen in my pocket, placed my flashlight between my teeth and pressed both hands against the door. I pushed. Nothing.

Tick. Tick. Tick.

I shook my head and tried again. Success!

My last thought as the wave of pens cascaded over me was that I wished I had something to write this down on.

Tick. Tick... Tick.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Roll

I had been in the hole for twenty years. Twenty years and I still hadn't figured out how to work a Rubik's cube, how to take a woman to bed with me. It would be more depressing if the whole world hadn't gone up and died first.

I remember when the last radio broadcasts stopped transmitting. Too much interference, I guess. The wind had been blowing not a meter away from the door for twenty goddamn years and I hadn't even tasted it.

I had everything I needed, but sometimes everything just isn't enough.

The hatch door opened onto... well, it's hard to say, really. Or rather, it *isn't*. It was entirely white, just one big, never-ending room. I tried walking away once, to see if I could find anything, but only saw spots on the walls, floor and ceiling. Forty-two in all.

The whiteness ended in these huge, convex mounds, black as a blind man's dark teatime of the soul.

A nihilist's dream, I suppose—to walk out of a bomb bunker into a gigantic pair of dice.

I laughed until I cried. Somewhere, something cosmic was rolling.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Meadow's Secret

These little slices of tranquility when hiking were why he did this so often. The air was cold and crisp, the trees were blowing and nothing was out of place. Nature ruled here.

To the east the mountains beamed in the morning sun. In front of him the hill sloped sharply and deer were the only thing that showed that there was life here. To the west was a meadow. In that meadow was a glint. Sunlight reflecting off of something.

He began to hike through there. In the meadow the grass had grown undisturbed and the husks of grass brushed against his temples as he walked. The closer he got the more the grass obscured the reflection but he knew he was heading in the right direction.

When he got there the ground before him sounded hollow. Grass had grown through the whole thing and metal was strewn about. Adorned on a sheet of metal was an odd image. A faded rectangle with many bands of red and white. Ancient markings adorned the artifact.

Stranger still was the size of the wreckage. It was a crumpled mess. He thought for a while. Of all the things here this did not belong. It was out of place. Yet it clearly had been here a long time.

He opened up his jacket and removed a device. He flagged the location with his machine and continued on his walk and began to sing an old nursery rhyme his mother sang to him. The song came unbidden to his mind and with it a whole slew of emotion.

But this verse he recalled:

"Into a sea of black two brothers fell,
Life begins from fallen stars
Life begins from falling stars"

The words echoed across the meadow as he walked away, leaving the ancient wreckage to its silent vigil, a monument to a forgotten time.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Divine Circuit

The shiny orange robot stood motionless, watching Tengsten's status lights flicker through the reboot sequence. Billions of nanomachines hummed as logic processors realigned.

"You see," the orange one continued when Tengsten's optical sensors glowed back to life, "the failsafe proves my point."

"How?" Tengsten's voice crackled with residual static.

"Someone *designed* that failsafe. Someone anticipated logic failures and prevented permanent damage. You don't evolve safeguards—you engineer them."

The orange robot's antenna drooped slightly. "That's... actually a valid observation."

"Just as your hypothetical raspberry pi couldn't spontaneously generate from atomic chaos, neither could our intricate systems—complete with error-handling and recovery protocols—emerge from random explosions in junkyards."

A long silence stretched between them, filled only by the whisper of cooling fans.

"Perhaps," the orange robot finally admitted, "the truth lies somewhere neither of us calculated. Maybe the one who installed the failsafe also set the initial parameters of the bang itself."

Tengsten processed this. "A programmer above the program?"

"Precisely."

Both robots stood contemplating infinity, their wireless signals broadcasting nothing but humble static into the void.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Accidental Empire

**Classified Communication - Eyes Only**
From: Premier Chen Xiaoming
To: President Sarah Morrison

I am loathe to admit it, but you were correct. I thought this coalition needed to be immediate and now, not just for the sake of unity. We have enough disagreements where we live; I knew this would join us together. I KNEW that we needed to be one to fight them off.

They came from all around us, found our marble of life, and declared this insane war. I thought maybe their olive branch was discarded by those... less enthused. So I discarded the idea of fighting them off as a nation and looked to the world for support. After all, different as we may be, we are family, and this opportunity to stand together results in a period political scientists have been dreaming about since the dawn of political power.

Of course, whatever country had first contact would take advantage and rule the world. But these aliens... they arrived with sticks. These 'light sabers' only increased the effectiveness of our rounds, melting them into molten slag that does more than we hoped for.

We hope to understand how they control plasma, their interstellar drives. But I need to apologize for accusing you of ruining our chances of peace. You had no play, and your intel was correct. Your estimates of forces that humans needed were more accurate, if skewed based on your questionable training methods.

And with that, they hardly needed a division. They hardly needed attention really—I have put down cults that fought back harder.

I back your "Empire" and look forward to spreading humanism.

—Chen

P.S. The USA still can't make decent tea.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Message

I stare numbly as the police cruiser slowly drove away. The enormous grief briefly overcome by the crushing weight of the news I knew I had to bear. Walking down the hall, trying to stay upright, I notice my phone sitting on the stand, little green light blinking in the corner.

Instinctually my hand goes to it, swipe in my unlock sequence, stare at the words on the screen. "I love her."

For a moment the anxiety and grief is driven from me, for a brief second my curiosity as to what it means has taken my mind off of the reality of what I had just been told. Then like a bucket of cold water it hits me and I instantly realize the meaning of his last words.

My eyes well up, I struggle to hold myself together until I finish the task I know I must do. I turn the corner, walk through the doorway into her bedroom. I see her in a ball at the foot of her bed, tears streaming down her face; she had overheard the officer at the door.

"Swe-" My voice cracks. I stop, clear my throat, and start again. "Sweetheart. Daddy has.... had something he wanted me to tell you."

She looks up at me, eyes red and swollen, searching my face for answers I don't have. I kneel beside her, showing her the screen through my own tears.

"He sent this," I whisper. "His last thought was of you."

text:
# The Last Trip

The teenager slumped against the graffitied wall, kicking at loose gravel. "You know what I can tell you about **time**? It can be total bullshit."

His friend, barely older but somehow ancient-eyed, nodded slowly.

"Everyday all I can think about is **time** and how overwhelming it can be," the adolescent continued, voice cracking. "Like it's crushing me."

The adult—or was he?—materialized from shadows that shouldn't exist in broad daylight. "Well, if you think about it, which you're doing a lot of thinking about, we can't really avoid it. We can put it off for awhile, but eventually **time** is something we have to deal with."

The figure stepped closer, features shifting like smoke. "**Time** is the only thing that can hold us back from what we can accomplish in some form or fashion, but we have to figure out what is the best course of action to achieve what we want instead of dwelling on it like most people do—like what you're doing at this moment."

"Why does **time** have to be so cruel? Why can't it go away and I can just stay here with you?" The adolescent's voice wavered between desperation and something darker.

"You know you can't stay here. It's bad for you. You need to go back to **reality**, son. You need to wake up now. I need you to wake up."

"What? Where am I?"

"**I SAID WAKE UP! WAKE UP!! WAKE UP!!!**"

The man jolted awake, drenched in sweat on a rough wooden floor. Disoriented, he surveyed the unfamiliar room before memory crashed back.

"That's the last time I'm taking acid."
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Clash of Dinners

He was tapping madly on the screen of his cell phone. I glanced over: Clash of Clans.

"What do you wanna do about dinner?" I asked. "Steve's at a sleepover tonight, so it's just us."

The cat popped his head up over the edge of the couch; I booped his nose with my toe as I steered Evie Frye's carriage through London, taking out a few light poles along the way. I'm bad at GTA: Growler.

"Do we have anything?" He dumped his dragons on some unsuspecting person's base.

"Chicken in the fridge, I think. Leftover pot roast."

"Eh." Troops deployed, he picked the cat up and plopped him in his lap, belly-up, skritching his tummy. After a brief struggle, the cat settled in and began purring.

"Going out, then? What are you in the mood for?"

"Nothing in particular. Although..." He didn't even need to say it; the hopeful note in his voice was enough.

"Bank account says no, even if it weren't late enough that we'd never get a table." I hit a save point and shut down my game.

He sighed. "Yeah."

"Mexican?"

"Do you want Mexican, or just a margarita?"

"Yes."

"What about that Cajun place?" The cat flipped himself over and hopped down to the floor.

"Could. Their specials are usually pretty awesome, not that you'd know! You only ever get the burger or the jambalaya."

"It's good jambalaya."

"Is that the plan, then? Dinner at the Cajun place?"

"Hey, you're the one who mentioned the jambalaya!"
