text:
# The Girl Who Stopped Reading

She used to devour stories like breathing. Now her books lined the shelves untouched, pristine corpses in a mausoleum.

"I hate digging them up," she told me once, tracing spines with trembling fingers. "You lose its beauty. A book is alive—walking in your mind, pulling grass, hiding under leaves. Analyzing it means catching it, pinning it down, skinning it. I don't need to see the heart to know it's there."

But that wasn't why she stopped.

I noticed the worn spines she'd hidden, broken pages tucked away—evidence of a love so consuming it destroyed. She'd read herself into those worlds until she couldn't tell where fiction ended and her loneliness began.

The fearless girl who once lost herself in stories had become terrified of what she might find there: her own reflection, desperate and aching.

So the books stayed closed. Beautiful. Untouchable.

Safe from her hungry, breaking heart.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Cosmic Reset

The whispers came three times, each three interstellar years apart, spoken in hushed urgency without melody: "To the centre you must go."

We obeyed. Several trillion humans pilgrimage across the universe in countless ships, drawn by an irresistible call.

At the centre, everything died. Drives failed. Reactors went dark. Billions of vessels became coffins drifting in the void, only recycled air keeping us alive in our graveyard at the universe's heart.

Then the voice returned—stronger, clearer.

First Sanskrit, then common tongue: *"I rise again."*

A wave erupted outward. Black became white. Stars inverted. Reality shuddered.

*"Much better,"* the presence gurgled, amused. *"I got lazy on the seventh day."*

We understood then, in our final moments. We weren't pilgrims or chosen ones.

We were witnesses to deletion.

*"Maybe I'll do better on the next universe,"* it mused as existence began folding inward.

The ships compressed like paper in a fist. We didn't scream—there wasn't time.

Just white.

Then nothing.

Then the first whisper of a new creation.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Weight of Tomorrow

I stared at the impossible device in my trembling hands, sweat dripping down my temples in the oppressive jungle heat. The archaeological dig had been routine until we uncovered this object—sleek, metallic, utterly impossible for a civilization that predated written language by millennia.

The timeline continued cycling on the screen, showing humanity's possible futures branching and collapsing like dying stars. Each path I examined led to the same bleak conclusion: extinction by 2047. Only twenty-three years away.

"Dr. Chen?" My assistant's voice echoed from outside the tent. "You've been in there for hours. Are you alright?"

I quickly concealed the device. "Fine! Just... cataloging artifacts."

But I wasn't fine. The weight of what I'd seen pressed against my chest like a physical force. Every branch of the timeline showed the same cascading failures: climate disasters, resource wars, societal collapse. And somehow, impossibly, I was supposed to change it.

Over the following days, I became obsessed. The device revealed leverage points—moments where a single action could alter trajectories. A conversation here, an investment there, a warning to the right person at the right time.

I started small. An anonymous tip about a vulnerable power grid. A donation to a struggling research team working on carbon capture. A letter to a young politician who would listen.

The timeline shifted, just barely. The date moved back three days.

It wasn't enough, but it was something.

I realized the robotic voice was right—I hadn't been chosen randomly. An archaeologist understands how small artifacts tell grand stories, how tiny details shape civilizations. I knew how to read the patterns of rise and fall.

As I packed to leave the dig site, the device pulsed once more: "The path is yours now."

I nodded to the empty tent. Twenty-three years to save eight billion people.

Time to get started.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Weight of What Cannot Be Undone

The electronics ticked on. Indifferent. Relentless.

My brother's hand rested on the armrest between us, perfectly still. He had always been the steady one, even when we were children. Even during those fifteen years that had brought us here.

She stowed her bag overhead—three rows up, across the aisle. Close enough that I could smell her perfume. The same one. Always the same one.

My throat constricted.

"Breathe," my brother whispered without looking at me.

But breathing felt like betrayal. Like acceptance. Like watching the second hand sweep forward when every cell in my body screamed to turn it back.

The flight attendant began the safety demonstration. Exits here, here, and here. Oxygen masks. Brace position. As if any of it mattered.

She settled into her seat, pulled out a book. Her fingers traced the cover—a nervous habit I'd memorized long ago. Before everything fractured. Before the ideology took root in my brother's mind like poison ivy, and I followed because he was all I had left.

Three hours.

The plane lurched backward from the gate.

I could stand up. I could scream. I could tell them about the carry-ons, the "randomly selected" screening that meant nothing because we'd planned for everything, accounted for everything.

Everything except her.

My brother's hand moved, just slightly. A question.

I looked at the overhead compartment. Then at her, absorbed in her book, oblivious.

Fifteen years of certainty crumbled.

The plane turned toward the runway.

I closed my eyes.

And reached up.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Mighty Have Fallen

The ice rattles in my glass as I stare at the faded poster on my garage wall. Me. Skeletor. Lord of Destruction. Now John B. Skeleton, according to the legal documents Mattel's lawyers shoved down my throat.

"Most evil being in the entire realm," I mutter, taking another swig of cheap whiskey. The irony tastes bitter.

Tuesday nights keep me sane. Adam shows up first—still built like a tank despite the mall cop uniform straining at the buttons. Clawful lumbers in next, his prosthetic hand clicking against the doorframe. We don't talk about Beast-Man anymore. Lymphoma took him in '91, and some wounds don't heal.

"Heard Lyn's coming tonight," Adam says, shuffling the deck.

I grunt. "Great. She'll probably spend the whole night talking about oil drilling rights."

But when she arrives, we fall into our old rhythm. The cards fly, the beer flows, and for a few hours, we're not has-beens scrambling for used car commercial residuals. We're warriors again, trading barbs and war stories.

"Do the trick!" Clawful demands, grinning.

I roll my eye sockets and pop the bottle cap out with practiced ease. They cheer like I've just conquered Castle Grayskull.

My phone buzzes. My son—my actual son, not some rubberized action figure version—sending photos from the Ghost Rider set. Pride swells in my chest cavity. He made it further than I ever did.

"Heading out soon," I tell the guys. "Anniversary dinner tomorrow. Twenty-five years."

Adam claps my bony shoulder. "You did good, Skel—I mean, John."

Driving home through the Valley, past the strip malls and the fading dreams, I realize something. I'm not the Lord of Destruction anymore. 

I'm just a guy with friends, family, and Tuesday night poker.

And maybe that's not such a terrible ending after all.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Two Thousand Years. Give or Take.

The color drained from Julius's face—or would have, if he'd had any color left to lose.

"I... yes. Quite familiar, actually." His voice had gone hollow. "Common enough punishment in my time. Barbaric thing."

I nodded slowly, watching realization dawn in those ancient eyes.

"You don't mean—"

"Yeshua bar Yosef," I said quietly. "Carpenter's son from Nazareth. Died on a Friday afternoon, hill called Golgotha. Been here ever since."

Julius stood motionless, and for a long moment, neither of us spoke. Another soul flickered past, gone in an instant.

"Two thousand years," he finally whispered. "Because of... because you were..."

"Famous?" I laughed bitterly. "Remembered? Yeah. Turns out being the cornerstone of the world's largest religion has some serious drawbacks in the afterlife. Can't fade when billions still pray to you, still remember your name."

"Sweet Jupiter."

"Wrong god, friend." I smiled without humor. "But I appreciate the sentiment."

We stood together in the liminal space, two ghosts bound by memory—his lasting decades, mine stretching into millennia, with no end in sight.

text:
# The Scribe's Gambit

The odds were always against us, but now was the time to prepare defences impenetrable enough to hold off a hundred men and horse. Their leader, Sir Swigton, although incredibly arrogant and self-minded, was now leading his army from the north to pillage any village found southward in the name of his King.

Our mayor had been dreading this day for weeks on end now, which was more than welcome to his daughter. She had been renounced all of the land as "the biggest slut there ever were."

The clapping of four hundred horses could be heard from miles out, coming closer and closer until eventually; nothing. They had stopped at the village gate.

Although you couldn't tell whether it was a noble knight or not, our suspicions were confirmed when the knocking on our gate was answered with Swigton's raspy yet overconfident voice. "Good day! I have come with most excellent news. Your village can be saved! But with a price. But it can be saved! But only if one of your men faces my knights within the next five seconds."

"Five! Four! Three!"

Everyone in the village stared at one another with utter confusion and panic. Seeing as I was closest to the gate, I was quickly seized by a bunch of blacksmith men and thrown out into a patch of dry dirt.

Sir Swigton stares down on me smugly, asking in a cocky fashion, "What shall you fight with?"

I quickly reached in my pockets, revealing a piece of wool, a quill pen, and some shredded up paper. "Sorry sir, give me just a moment to prepare myself."

Was all I could say before I began writing. After about two and a half minutes of sloppily yet-quickly writing my rough draft alibi to hopefully save my ass (but not everyone's), I handed it in, and gave Swigton a bit of time to let him wrap his small mind around my letter.

After finishing his light reading for the day, he coughed, stood up straight, and proclaimed, "Wow, she really is that much of a slut, huh?"

The village collectively held its breath, waiting to see if my desperate gambit—throwing the mayor's daughter under the metaphorical horse—would be enough to distract this pompous fool from his original intent.

# The Supervillain's Mother

"Stewart! What in heavens do you think you're doing?!"

"M-momma...?!" His finger circled off the giant red button in the steel panel. "What are you doing here?!"

"Your friends called me, Stewart! They say you're trying to destroy the entirety of Manhattan! What are you thinking?! Your aunt Marie lives in Manhattan!"

"Those aren't my friends! They're my rivals! And stop calling me Stewart, mom! I'm a villain now! I'm MegaBit now!"

MegaBit sighed and started walking down the metal stairs, as the whole Justice Squad giggled like infants behind his mother.

text:
# The Pressures of the Day

The striped shirt became his uniform of invisibility. Ironic, really—designed to be spotted, yet allowing him to disappear completely.

Waldo stood among the crowds at the beach, his red-and-white stripes camouflaged by umbrellas and towels. The barbershop quartet sang something cheerful. Children shrieked in the waves. He felt nothing.

The pressures had mounted silently: deadlines, diapers, disappointments. No single moment broke him—just the accumulation of being perpetually observed yet never truly seen.

So he walked. Mountains, mazes, carnivals, space stations. Each crowded scene promised connection but delivered only claustrophobia. He was always surrounded, never accompanied.

His cane tapped rhythms of solitude across continents. He shed possessions like skin—wallet, keys, the wedding ring that left a pale band on his finger.

They searched for him in photographs, in memories, in the spaces between people. But Waldo had become what he always was: a figure hiding in plain sight, searching for himself in a world too busy looking to actually see.

He walks still, glasses reflecting empty landscapes, seeking the one place he's never been.

Home.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Dear Rob

Rob's hands trembled as he reread the letter for the fifth time. The familiar loops of his 'g's, the way he crossed his 't's—it was unmistakably his own penmanship. But the words made no sense.

He laughed nervously, crumpling the paper. "This is insane." But his voice cracked, and that pit in his stomach grew heavier.

Three days later, Rob stood in his manager's office. "I quit."

The flight to Ecuador felt like a fever dream. Vilcabamba was smaller than he'd imagined—dusty streets, aging hippies, and locals who eyed him with polite curiosity. He found the supermercado easily. Corner location. Just like the letter said.

July 18th arrived. Rob sat in his hostel room, staring at the bag he'd prepared. His rational mind screamed at him to stop, but something deeper—instinct, fate, desperation—urged him forward.

10:15 AM. July 19th. The bag ignited with a whoosh that sent shoppers scrambling. Rob ran, lungs burning, toward the town's edge.

A yellow cab idled there. The driver smiled. "Need a ride?"

Rob's throat was dry. "I... I don't know."

"First, tell me—what's my favorite color?"

The words tumbled out automatically: "Who needs colors when you've got vibrations."

Pedro's smile widened. "Get in."

As they drove into the mountains, Rob noticed something odd. Pedro's reflection in the rearview mirror looked younger than his profile. And when their eyes met, Rob saw the unmistakable shape of his own face staring back.

"Welcome," Pedro said, "to your beginning."

text:
# The Loop of Six

There are six of us, all running for our lives.

The city explodes around us—concrete and screaming. A steel rebar punches through my chest. I'm dead before I hit the ground.

I turn my head and scream at the sight of Andrew, lying dead, the same rebar through his chest. But I can't stay—the rest of us keep running.

A colossal hand descends. Grey, leathery skin fills my vision as Angela and I are crushed together. My eyes follow the arm up to its face—ancient, terrible. Then everything goes damp and red. I hear my bones crunch beneath the force of its teeth.

Gordon disappears in the maw. David and I make a break for it.

I'm suddenly airborne, flying until my body meets brick. A single finger pins me down. My legs go numb as I stare into eyes like burning pits. The demon roars.

I'm flattened.

And then—

There are six of us, all running for our lives.

Andrew beside me. Angela ahead. Gordon shouting directions. David's hand grabs mine.

We die again.

We always die again.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
**The Empty Anniversary**

She turned the key, already smiling. Tonight would be perfect—their anniversary. He always outdid himself with romantic gestures, and she'd spent the week imagining possibilities. Candlelight. Wine. Maybe even that velvet box she pretended not to hope for.

The door swung open to silence.

No music. No rose petals. No warm lighting or the smell of dinner cooking. Just... emptiness.

Her smile faltered as her eyes traced the living room. Bare spots on the walls where their photos had hung. Gaps in the bookshelf like missing teeth. She walked to the bedroom, each step heavier than the last.

Half the closet—empty.

His dresser drawers—pulled open, abandoned, hollow.

The note sat on the bed, a white rectangle against dark sheets.

*I'm so sorry. I can't do this anymore. There's someone else.*

Twelve words. One year dissolved.

She sank onto the mattress, still holding her purse, the note trembling in her other hand. The questions began immediately, a vicious chorus: *What did I miss? What did she have? Could I have stopped this? Why not wait one more week—just give me tonight?*

Love doesn't simply disappear. It transforms. Hers curdled into something toxic—pain braiding with hatred, guilt threading through everything. She'd replay every conversation, every moment, searching for clues she'd missed, signs she'd ignored.

The cruelest part wasn't his leaving. It was the silence he left behind—unanswered questions that would echo for years, filling every void with doubt. Not about him, eventually, but about herself.

Self-loathing, she would learn, cuts deeper than any betrayal.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Promise

The Mercenary's chest heaved with his heavy breathing. There was a warm sticky sensation as blood ran down his arm. The peeling paint on the wall he was propped against flaked off and fell on his shoulders and into his hair. He leaned his head back against the wall as his eyes rolled about lazily. Nothing caught his interest; his thoughts were fleeting and incomplete.

A shadow engulfed his body as a woman squatted down to examine him. The Greek gently caressed his face in an attempt to wipe the blood from it but only managed to smear it. Her long dark curls fell forward, she felt her jaw tremble. Tightness gripped her chest as she felt the wet warmth of tears beginning to stream down her cheeks.

There was a sudden pressure around her wrist; she looked down to see his hand firmly grasping her arm.

"I'm going to have to get a new suit, Al..." He whispered weakly.

"We'll go to that place in Turin you liked and get a new one," she replied in a pleading tone.

He stared into her muddy green eyes; subtle wrinkles had taken hold at the corners of her eyes from squinting to hold back the tears. The rising sun at her back gave her golden skin a heavenly glow.

"Did I ever tell you you're beautiful?" He smiled weakly.

"Every day," she quickly shot back.

"That's a lie."

"I love you..."

"I love you too."

There was silence. The Greek softly pressed her head against his, shutting her eyes tightly.

"It says 'cherish him'...the tattoo on my back it..." She said desperately.

"I'm not going to die."

She pulled back and opened her eyes. The lazy, lost look that had marred his face was gone. It was replaced by the unshakable look of certainty.

She believed him.

"I'll be fine."

She believed him.

In that moment, between heartbeats and shallow breaths, something shifted. The promise wasn't about surviving. It was about refusing to surrender—not to death, not to despair, not to the inevitable darkness closing in. His certainty became her anchor, and her belief became his strength.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Test Subject 47

The entry cuts off there. Blood spatters dot the keyboard.

I found Dr. Milliken's tablet three weeks after the facility went dark. Standard protocol: when a black site stops reporting, send nobody for thirty days. Let whatever happened burn itself out.

I'm the cleanup crew.

The island looked peaceful from the helicopter. Tropical. Beautiful, even. The kind of place you'd see in a travel magazine, not a dossier marked CLASSIFIED: EYES ONLY.

The facility entrance was underground, hidden beneath what looked like a weather station. The keypad still worked. Milliken's access code got me inside.

The smell hit first. Copper and rot and something chemical I couldn't place.

He wasn't exaggerating about the blood.

Twenty-three staff members. I found them all. Some in pieces. Some... arranged. Posed, almost artfully, in the cafeteria like a family dinner. Their faces had been removed with surgical precision.

The operation room was worse. Security personnel, torn apart with bare hands. The walls bore child-sized handprints in blood, dozens of them, overlapping like wallpaper.

I found the observation logs. Subject 47 (they never used names) had lasted eleven days on the surface. Longer than any previous test. When they'd retrieved her, she'd been humming. Cheerful, even.

The psych evaluation was chilling: "Subject displays no remorse, guilt, or recognition of moral boundaries. Extreme adaptation to survival pressure. Recommend immediate termination."

But they hadn't terminated her. They'd wanted to study her more.

The security footage showed what happened. They'd brought her down unrestrained. Underestimated a thirteen-year-old girl.

She'd killed the first guard in eleven seconds.

The last timestamp was Milliken's smoke break. The cameras captured her methodical progress through the facility, that little-girl laugh echoing through corridors as staff ran screaming.

Then she'd opened the main door and left.

I sit in the safe room where Milliken died. The door shows scrape marks where she'd tried the handle, then given up. Patient.

My orders are to sterilize the site. Make it disappear.

But I keep thinking about that laugh on the recording. About the coordinates Milliken tried to give.

About a thirteen-year-old girl, somewhere in the world now, who learned exactly what she's capable of.

And I wonder: did we create a monster, or just reveal one?
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Burden of Knowledge

The dungeon sprawls before us, trap-laden and dark. I see the pressure plate beneath the wizard's foot before he steps. I know the poisoned dart will fly from that carved serpent's mouth. I understand the ancient runes spell "PUSH HERE TO OPEN."

But I cannot speak.

The DM's invisible hand clamps over my mouth whenever inspiration strikes. I watch the warrior examine the obviously hollow statue for twenty minutes. The priest debates divine intervention for a simple lever mechanism.

I am Rænir Stormfire, cursed with competence in a world of stumbling heroes.

They will survive—barely—through luck and excessive healing potions. They will claim victory, grow stronger, level up.

And I will follow, forever biting my tongue, watching them reinvent the wheel.

*Such is the life of ev'ry NPC.*
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Transformation

I'd been in bed for months. At first there were knocks on the door, whispered promises and careful words. There had been yelling, crying, threats.

"Don't you care about your *future*?"

I did. God, I did, and just saying it like that left a sour taste in my mouth.

My mother begged me to keep going to school. I couldn't. I should have, but I just couldn't. I kept remembering that night. His rough hands and taut muscles, my elbow ramming into his stomach, the feeling of torn fabric.

My heart felt as if it had been ripped out of my chest, leaving nothing but a hollow cavity where it used to be. Gone was the nervous fluttering when I saw the boy I loved, the thrumming beat when I was afraid. There was nothing left of me but an empty shell.

And that night drowned my senses: both of us gasping for air, my choked screams, skin hitting skin.

My father called a psychiatrist. He knocked on the door like all the rest of them, knocking, knocking until it echoed in my head and pierced through my tangled thoughts. Knocking that persisted even in my dreams. My dreams, that were haunted by memory after memory.

I did not realize what had happened for quite some time. I rarely went outside, so my skin did not burn. I hardly ate, so I did not crave blood. I never smiled, so I did not see my fangs.

And it would be many months still before I noticed twin puncture marks on my neck—marks that never healed, never faded.

The trauma had consumed me so completely that I'd missed an entirely different violation.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Hotcakes and Hazards

I remember the cutesy name that I liked: hotcakes. I don't remember where I put the griddle. Or the necessary cooking temperature for pancakes. Or the ingredients. I know what the end product should look like when it's on my plate, and with startling clarity I can remember exactly how much maple syrup (supposedly from Vermont) is left in the fridge.

The doc suggested I make things easier on myself, like having a bowl of cereal with milk instead of pancakes or bacon and eggs. Cooking food requires an intense amount of focus and can be time-consuming for me now. It's also almost guaranteed to make me frustrated and cranky first thing in the morning.

I didn't miss the doc's other concern, and what he's *really* worried about. Namely, it's gotten to the point where it's risky for me to operate a stove, as I might forget that I'm cooking a meal and go watch the birds out the back window for a couple of hours. That could result in some unintended consequences, such as burning my house down with me inside of it.

My mind may wander, but my ability to synthesize data immediately in front of my nose hasn't diminished. When I sit with the realization that it's gotten to the point that I'm a danger to myself, I am terrified.

I don't sit with it long, because there's too much for my mind and body to do to just get by in the day-to-day. Like find the griddle, read the recipe for the hundredth time, and make my beloved hotcakes.

I find the griddle in the linen closet. I read the recipe taped to the refrigerator. I set a timer, loud and insistent.

And I make hotcakes.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Weight of Survival

The lake stretched before them like liquid glass, catching fragments of dying sunlight. Two figures sat at the water's edge, neither quite looking at the other.

"I want to be able to look back. And say I tried."

"So do I, believe me. So do I." 

The wind over the water. Ripples. Fowls calling somewhere in the distance.

"But it's the darndest thing." A helpless chuckle escaped his lips. "To look back. You've got to survive, first."

Silence settled in the reeds around them, heavy as stone.

Then, for the first and last time—his voice was cold. "I'll try enough for both of us. You, on the other hand." The scrape of a chair against weathered dock planks. "You can live to a hundred for all I care and do enough of looking back for both of us."

---

Old Man Lee was looking back now. Wondering if he had made the right choice.

His hundredth birthday would take place tomorrow. And it made him remember.

"I wonder what the past eighty years would have been like. If only..."

The door opened behind him.

"Mr. Lee." That patronizing tone again. "At your age, you really should know better than to break the rules."

"Oh, I couldn't help myself. It's been so long since I last saw the stars. Old regrets, you see."

She did not see. Of course she wouldn't.

"Why don't you get back to your room. It's dangerous to stay out at night. Life after the End is a bit different from your time."

*If only,* he thought again. *If only I had tried.*

If only there was some way to stop looking back.

If only, if only, if only.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Dislike Protocol

Mark Zuckerberg stared at the monitors displaying Jimmy's path of destruction through Times Square. Buildings crumbled like sandcastles as the Like-powered maniac grew stronger with each notification ping.

"Ten million dead," whispered his chief security officer. "And North Korea just made Facebook mandatory. Twenty-five million new users—all liking Jimmy's posts."

Mark remembered the early days, when Likes seemed innocent. Positive reinforcement. Digital validation. He never imagined someone could weaponize it, absorbing power from every thumb-up until they became virtually godlike.

Others had tried to stop Jimmy by gathering Likes themselves, but power corrupted them too. The cycle repeated: hero becomes villain, cities burn, millions die.

Mark's finger hovered over his keyboard. The Dislike button code was ready—untested, unpredictable. If Likes gave power, what would Dislikes do? Drain it? Reverse it? Destroy the user entirely?

"Sir, Jimmy just posted a selfie with the Statue of Liberty's severed head. He's gained another million Likes in thirty seconds."

Mark closed his eyes and pressed Enter.

Across the world, a new button appeared. Billions of fingers reached for it simultaneously.

Jimmy's scream could be heard from space.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Dragon's Sermon

The dragon's scales shimmered like molten gold under the fluorescent church lights. Each footfall echoed with the weight of ages, claws clicking against worn linoleum. 

Reverend Jacks remained frozen, his hateful words dying in his throat like ash.

The creature reached the pulpit, its amber eyes sweeping across the terrified congregation. When it spoke, its voice was surprisingly gentle—a warm rumble that seemed to resonate in their very bones.

"For twenty years, I have listened," the dragon said. "I have heard every sermon, every condemnation, every word spoken in my Father's name that twisted love into hate."

It turned to face Solomon directly. "You speak of vengeance and wrath, Reverend. You speak of striking down those you deem unworthy. But tell me—where in His teachings did He command you to judge? Where did He say to exclude, to condemn, to spread fear?"

The dragon's tail swept across the stage, knocking over the collection plates. Coins scattered like tears.

"I was sent to remind you: God is love. Not selective love. Not conditional love. *Love.*"

The creature's form began to shimmer, becoming translucent. As it faded, its final words lingered:

"The only heathen here today stood at that pulpit."

Reverend Solomon Jacks collapsed to his knees, finally, truly humbled.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Vision

The monitors flickered with humanity's death certificate. I should have seen this coming—literally. That was my job.

1.3 visions per day for three years. I'd saved thousands from the Vanishings. Politicians, scientists, children. Each vision a gift, each prevention a victory. The VAN called me their crown jewel. My neighbors called me a hero.

Now those neighbors were ash in the street.

I replayed the morning in my head. Waking up, coffee, the routine check-in. "No intel to provide." Four words that sealed humanity's fate.

The lockdown order came instantly. They knew before I did—I was the target.

But why? Why protect one precog when thousands existed? Unless...

My fingers trembled across the keyboard, pulling up classified VAN files I wasn't supposed to access. The bunker's isolation meant no one could stop me now.

The data loaded. My stomach dropped.

I wasn't special because of my vision frequency. I was special because of my *effectiveness*. Every vision I reported, every person VAN saved, every Vanishing we prevented—they all followed a pattern. My pattern.

The Vanishings weren't random selections. They were course corrections.

Those taken weren't victims. They were catalysts—people whose continued existence would prevent... this. The wars, the nuclear exchange, the extinction event now unfolding across every screen.

VAN hadn't been protecting humanity. They'd been dooming it.

And I'd helped them do it, 1.3 preventions at a time.

The bunker's air filtration system hummed steadily, designed to keep me alive for months. Outside, radiation crept across continents like spilled ink, erasing everything.

I understood now why they'd fought so hard to keep me. Not because I was valuable.

Because I was the mistake that needed correcting.

A new vision finally came—my first in days. I saw myself, months from now, alone in this bunker. The last human alive.

I didn't bother reporting it.

There was no one left to listen.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Unnecessary Man

The removal of death makes all things unnecessary.

That was what we had not realised, I thought, as a 200kg lion pawed and gnawed at my immortal knee. The sun fell. And rose again. I had not left the dead tree that I sat up against. But the lion had gone.

I remember the first day I had sat down. I had felt thirsty. And hungry. But when I'd realised that a lack of food and water wasn't going to kill me, my hunger and thirst had ceased to hurt. Or I had ceased to care. Did one cause the other? The pain, the sensation had just melted away.

The second day, the sun burned down on my face. But what of it? The sun wasn't going to dry me out and kill me, so moving into the shade was unnecessary. The sensation of heat was just an artifact from my mortal life, a memory. And the sensation disappeared.

The lion on day 50 had caused me quite a fright! And I admit to having felt truly alive if only for seconds. But my existence wasn't at risk, and watching the beast mournfully fail at separating my leg from my body made me feel deader than ever.

*Creation is necessitated by mortality*, is my last thought. And then my mind is infertile.

Years have passed now, the sands of time creep into my mouth and crust up against my eyes. No information can harm me or give me value. With no meaning from sensation comes no need for differentiation.

I am one with the sand.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Step Forward

"Step forward onto the mat," I said, my voice echoing how tired I actually felt. "Please state your name, and demonstrate your power."

The teenager before me grinned and raised his eyebrows. It's basically the same look I get every single time I come to work—one of cocky demeanor. You could almost hear his thoughts: *You haven't seen this before!*

I watched as the kid sent an arc of electricity toward the ceiling.

"How was that?" he asked, practically bouncing with excitement.

"Stale."

After a while, you can break down any power into categories. There are the Old Age Elementals—fire, ice, water, things pagan societies thought were elements. The Classics—super speed, flight, super strength, genius intellect. Then the Mentalists—telekinesis, telepathy. It gets boring.

"Stale?!"

To my surprise, he fired an arc straight at me. As it collided, I stood up and crossed my arms. Painful, yes, but most of the current drained harmlessly through my rubber boots and rubber-lined pants.

"Go to the office. NOW!"

Shock filled his eyes. His face went milk-white as he shuffled up the steps.

I turned to address the room. "Fellow students, I do not have any powers. However, I know how to circumvent nearly any power. Remember that next time you try to kill me because I offend you."

The silence was delicious.

"I got this position because the last coach was smeared on that wall by a jerk with super strength. I'm a student like you, but I'm the only one who can beat you all in combat."

I gestured toward the stairs.

"Now if you'll excuse me, I need a coffee and a new sweater."

With that, I walked up the stairs and slammed the door, leaving them to contemplate the uncomfortable truth: power means nothing without discipline. And rubber-soled boots beat electricity every time.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Final Performance

Something wasn't right here. Everyone was still going on as usual like nothing had happened, but something just wasn't right.

"Captain, the enemy ship is inbound. What should we do?"

The other actors were saying their lines like normal, and I realized I was just standing there, looking like I was seeing ghosts—but I might as well have been. Where the camera, director, audio, and everyone else had been just a moment ago had turned black, like some sort of fog. It started from the back of the room and slowly moved forward to envelope the production team until all that was left was just the actors and the set.

Was this some sort of zone that actors get into? Where suddenly they can't see anything but the set and the other actors? No, it couldn't be. The blackness was still closing in, and my ears were ringing.

I saw one of the other extras giving me a weird look, as if to ask what the hell was going on with me, but their face seemed to stop making sense after a few seconds. I heard the voices around me start to muffle and echo, as if I was down a long tunnel, the ringing becoming louder and louder.

The darkness was almost upon me, and I started to panic. Something wasn't right. I tried to say something, but my tongue felt like jello, and all that I could muster was a few half-voiced grunts.

What is going on?

Then darkness hit me, and I felt the right side of my body hit a wall.

---

**Later that week:**

"We are gathered here today to say farewell to our dearly beloved. She had only just begun her promising acting career when it was cut short by a freak aneurysm. While we all grieve our loss, we can take comfort in knowing that she passed quickly and painlessly."
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# 1s AFTER DEATH

When I opened my eyes to find myself in my own living room, I thought I was still alive. My head hurt a lot, which made sense, but I still couldn't understand how I was still alive. It was supposed to be easy. Shot in the head. That's what the internet said.

I stood up carefully and slowly, afraid that I might bleed out or something. I looked around once I was on my feet. There was a lot of blood on the scene, especially on the wall behind me. I decided to check my clothes now that I was at it, but my mind stopped working when I looked down.

I was laying there.

I screamed and crowded to the other side of the room. It took me a couple of minutes to calm myself down, but I did. I approached the body—myself—slowly, to see the damage that the bullet had caused. My jaw was destroyed, and I couldn't see the back of my head, but I assumed it looked the same.

I was startled by someone breaking into my room. My parents.

"ETHAN!" My mother's cries echoed through the room as she crouched in front of me and hugged my dead body. "Ethan, my boy. My sweet boy, please, you are okay, you are okay."

I wanted to puke.

My father saw my body and ran downstairs to get the phone, leaving my mother sobbing over my corpse. I bet at the funeral they'll say something like, "So young. He was so happy, he was just 13 years old. We could have never known."

Dirty liars.

I decided I wanted to leave for the afterlife and went to the door. I ran against something that didn't let me go through.

"What the fuck..." I whispered to myself as I touched the invisible wall. I then tried the windows, and it was the same. Something was not letting me get out of this room.

My father came rushing back exclaiming that the paramedics would be here soon.

And I just sulked there in a corner, realizing I was still stuck on earth.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Secret Friend

I look at the clock and notice that it's 5:39 already. Only 1 minute left. Did I give myself enough time? I start running towards the stairs. 5:40. Half way up I hear it. The door slowly creaks open as I freeze in my tracks. It's going to see me if I stay here so I turn and book it back up the stairs. I won't be able to hide in the attic, it's too late for that. So I run to the far room and dive into the back of the closet. *Must keep quiet, must keep quiet* I think to myself.

From below I hear shuffling and some commotion. Finally voices fade in, "wash your hands kids, I'll start making supper." The little 3-year-old, Jace, screams back "NOOO!! I want to play with Anna upstairs! She makes me laugh!"

I hear his mom and dad start talking in hushed voices indistinguishable from the TV that "big sister" turns on. An hour passes before I hear Jace approaching. I whisper for him to come here and creak open the closet.

"Anna, I missed you! Let's play!" he says as he hands me some food that he stashed away.

I reply quietly, "just for a little bit. I missed you too and thanks for the food. Just remember, your mommy and daddy can't find out that I'm real and live here or I'll have to leave and we can never play tickle monster again."

He nods solemnly, his big eyes understanding more than any three-year-old should. I've been here six months now, hiding in plain sight as his imaginary friend. It's not much, but it's safe—safer than the streets or the shelters. And Jace needs me too.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# We Didn't Care

*As the factories started up*

We didn't know.

*The toxins we released*

We didn't know.

*But you never stopped*

We didn't know.

*You knew the destruction it causes*

WE DIDN'T KNOW!

*You raise your voices almost as fast as the pollution levels rose*

WE DIDN'T KNOW!

*Sea levels soared, millions died*

WE DIDN'T KNOW!

*The Earth is ruined, barely inhabitable even to us*

WE DIDN'T KNOW!

*There were warnings, pollution levels rising, you had time to stop!*

WE DIDN'T KNOW!

**YOU DID KNOW! YOU WERE TOO GREEDY TO CARE!**

We did know... that the Earth was dying around us.

We did know... that it was all our fault.

We did know.

The damage is done now. The end is not near. It has already happened and **we didn't care.**

text:
# C-Cash?

"C-cash?" The woman's eyes widened at the man before her. "You want to donate $10,000... in cash?"

"Yes. And you can't open this envelope until Christmas."

"E-envelope? But—" She stopped as her eyes focused on the bill he withdrew from his back pocket. "That's not real."

"It really is!"

"How do you know?"

"Touch it."

"What? No!"

"Just touch it!"

"What will that do?"

"Trust me."

She reached out a hand, eyes staring dead at the man before her. As soon as she touched it, her eyes lit up, and her body shuddered. "Amazing!"

"Right?"

"So it can be used?"

"That's right!"

"Okay, just put it in the envelope. This is amazing! This is more money than we've ever seen before!"

"Remember—"

"Oh, don't worry. It's a small thing to do."

He grinned at her and folded the bill neatly into a small envelope, which he handed to her. As their hands both gripped the envelope, the bill vanished, an event noticed only by the donor.

"Christmas, remember."

"Don't worry. You'll get your letter by tomorrow, I promise."

He grinned, shook hands, and left with $10,000 in tax deductions—and an empty envelope in the charity's confused hands.

text:
# Finding X

I opened the paper, unprepared for the horrors that lay ahead.

A right-angled triangle stared back at me. Shortest side: 3cm. Bottom: 4cm. Sloped edge: a big, mocking **X**.

Question: Find X.

Easy. X.

*Sarah.*

No. Concentrate. Can't fail the first question because of her.

*Why?*

Focus! Find... X.

*In Mexico with Joe, sipping piña coladas—Facebook, Twitter, Foursquare, Myspace, Bebo, her blog, her vlog all confirmed it.*

Pythagorean Theorem. Three squared equals nine. Four squared...

*Foursquare. She tagged herself with Joe, less than a week after we ended. She always said she hated Italian food.*

FOUR SQUARED IS SIXTEEN. SIXTEEN PLUS NINE IS TWENTY-FIVE. THE SQUARE ROOT...

OF THE PROBLEM WAS HER CHEATING, MANIPULATIVE, BITCHING FACE.

I calmly closed the paper and excused myself from the exam hall.

Definitely not sobbing.

text:
# The Tired Manifesto

Marcus hit "post" at 3:47 AM, his eyes burning from the screen's glow. The words had poured out like poison finally released from an infected wound.

By morning, his inbox exploded.

*"This spoke to my soul."*
*"Fuck you, nihilist prick."*
*"I printed this and hung it above my desk."*

He read them all with numb detachment, sipping cold coffee. The irony wasn't lost on him—his desperate declaration of universal mediocrity had become the most engagement he'd gotten in months. Even his exhaustion was predictable.

His phone buzzed. An unknown number.

*"Coffee? I read your thing. I think I'm tired too."*

Marcus stared at the message. Some stranger, reaching through the void. He almost deleted it. Almost went back to bed. Almost proved his own point about monotony and predetermined responses.

Instead, he typed: *"Corner of Fifth and Main. One hour."*

She was younger than expected, with paint-stained fingers and dark circles matching his own. They didn't exchange names at first, just sat in silence, two specks on their glorified meteor, drinking overpriced lattes.

"So," she finally said, "we're all average?"

"Aggressively average."

"And that's supposed to be comforting?"

Marcus considered this. Outside, people rushed past—each one carrying their private universes of worry, ambition, heartbreak. All of it meaningless. All of it everything.

"I don't know," he admitted. "I thought writing it would feel like liberation. It just felt like... more tiredness."

She smiled sadly. "Maybe that's the point. We're too tired to pretend anymore, but too stubborn to stop caring."

They sat together until their cups emptied, two average creatures finding something beyond words in shared exhaustion.

"Same time tomorrow?" she asked.

"Yeah," Marcus said. "Yeah, okay."

Perhaps love wasn't transcendence. Perhaps it was just choosing, again and again, to be average together.

Right?

Right.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Seeds of Renewal

I whisper it again at dawn: *I am all that remains of the man I once was.*

They still see him when they look at me—my father's shadow, my brother's ghost. The apple that fell and festered beneath that gnarled tree. Their disappointment lingers in sidelong glances, in conversations that halt when I enter rooms.

But I am not that apple anymore.

I am the seeds that survived the rot, carried skyward by chance and circumstance, dropped into unfamiliar soil where no one knows the tree I fell from. Here, the ground is unmarked by old roots and older expectations.

Each morning, I tend to myself like a gardener: patient, deliberate, forgiving of slow growth. The past remains behind me—not forgotten, but composted into something useful. The future stretches ahead, uncertain but unwritten.

When doubt creeps in, when old voices echo in my skull, I return to the words that ground me: *I am all that remains of the man I once was.*

The rotten parts have been discarded.

What grows now is entirely mine.

This is my mantra. This is my truth.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Weight of Fire

The acrid smell of burning leaf lingered in the air, a ghost of what she'd just done. She stared at the gray ash on the grass, her hand still trembling.

Control. That's what separated her from the monster she'd been that night.

She picked up another leaf, brown and brittle from autumn's touch. This time she counted her breaths—in for four, hold for four, out for four. The techniques Dr. Morrison taught her seemed laughable applied to *this*, but what else did she have?

The leaf rested on her palm. She imagined not rage, but precision. A single point of heat, concentrated, deliberate. Like lighting a candle, not burning down a house.

A wisp of smoke curled upward.

Her heart raced, but she held steady. The ember glowed at the leaf's edge, eating slowly across the surface in an orange line. Beautiful. Controlled. Nothing like before.

*Nothing like him.*

She let the leaf fall and stamped it out, then looked toward the house where Jack was probably still locked in his room. Three days since he'd spoken to her. Four since that night in the alley.

She couldn't undo what he'd seen—his sister becoming something else, something terrible, even if it saved his life. But maybe she could become something different than what that rage made her.

The next leaf didn't burn at all, no matter how she focused.

Then the one after that crumbled to ash in seconds.

She gathered five more leaves and arranged them in a row.

Practice. Control. Precision.

*Redemption*, whispered a hopeful voice she barely recognized as her own.

She began again.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Christmas

Christmas at our house is just another day to get high.

The needle marks on Dad's arms tell a better story than any holiday card ever could. If he's even around, he's far too busy with flying or nodding off to be bothered with traditional festivities. My last Christmas was my mother's last Christmas, and maybe I'm a little bitter, but I'm mostly happy with that. Morbidly enough, something about that feels right, but then again, I never had a choice.

Any cheer we could've ever mustered died along with her.

Out loud, I'll admit that it would be wrong to celebrate Christmas without her, but that's bullshit. She's an excuse. She's the excuse he mutters to himself as if he's not convinced and as if I can't hear him, and the excuse he tells me as if it's a fact pulled right from an encyclopedia.

For a moment, I'll humor the thought that something more than eternal blackness waits for us after death—I know she'd be heartbroken to part the clouds and look in on us, today of all days. Then again, she probably has been. When the reaper forces you to leave your only son with a pillhead, any mother would be crushed with the weight of motherhood failure.

"Hey, boy."

I blink away the haze that crept onto the surface of my eyes—they got lost in the corner, where just years ago, a garnished tree stood.

"Want a line?"

I nod, watch him, and when he's done playin' around I adjust mine, which he made two toothpicks skinnier than his own. He just grins at me, admitting his intentions without words. I ignore it, do my drugs, and let it be.

With a hearty sniff I mutter a Merry Christmas. I even tack *dad* on the end, something I haven't called him in a bit, but hey, I was feeling a bit sentimental, even as he vacuumed the table with his nose.

He pulled his head up hard, as if he just broke water after being lost breaths away from drowning.

"Oh, shit," he manages through a sniff with extra help from the back of his hand. "Christmas. Yeah."
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Cleansing

The robber was on the floor, one hand clutching a gash in his stomach where Hank's knife had torn into his abdomen, the other held up in a plea for mercy. Tears were streaming from his blackened eyes as he mumbled desperate cries through bloodied lips.

"Please man, please don't! You don't understand, I'm starving, I just needed some cash for food! For my family, for my daughter!"

Hank smiled. He had heard excuses before, but one about a child? It may well have been true, but *he didn't care*. Not anymore. His time as a detective in the homicide unit, years of examining inhumanity, had taught him one thing: never to care, never to get attached, never to give a damn.

It mattered not if the man had a family. He had to die.

As he approached the wounded criminal, his fingers tightened around the cold steel grip of the baseball bat. The first blow upon the criminal's head did nothing to silence his shouts, but as the second blow landed with a sickening crunch, the robber's screams turned to gurgles, then silence as his blood and brains spilled out onto the cold tarmac.

Hank swiftly rifled through the corpse's pockets to check for anything important. In the man's jacket was nothing, but his blood-soaked jeans yielded a tattered leather wallet. Aside from a few credit cards, all that the wallet held was a photo. Torn, and clearly ancient, the photo was faded, but nonetheless depicted the man and a young girl.

*He did have a family. Not that it matters*, Hank mused as he quietly exited the alleyway, removing the bloody gloves and tossing them into a passing bin.

Another night had passed in his mission to cleanse the city.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Damn Bird

The damn bird is back.

It won't leave me alone. I close my eyes and hope it leaves. It just hops on my back and pecks. Damn bird. I grab at it, but the two days I've been on this stinking piece of wood have stolen my strength, among other things.

It jumps up and flies away.

My tongue sticks in my mouth. It's getting harder to breathe. Can I choke on my own tongue? I wish the sun would show a little mercy. It wants me to burn. I know it does. It hates me as much as that bird. It wants me to die. It wants to cook me on this wood, make a nice meal for whatever wants me.

I wonder how I'd taste. Days at sea would ruin my body. It couldn't be all that good.

No, stop, this won't help. I can't think about this. I can't die out here. You can't do this to me. Please don't. It's not my time. I have people who love me. I have a family. I have a, a, a...

I'm never getting back to them.

I'm dying at sea. No one is going to find me. I don't want to go like this. Please God, please help me. You're not going to listen. You're with the bird and the sun. You hate me, you want me gone. You want me to die out here, you bastard.

You love that damn bird, don't you. Don't you!

You care for this stupid bird more than me. You want him to make it, not me. Damn you. Just kill me already. Why are you doing this to me? I thought you were merciful.

Oh God, please, please.

Please.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

# The Breakup Letter

Dear Writer's Block,

I have wanted for months to tell you this, and since you never liked it, well I found it fitting to write you a letter. So let me make it clear from now on: WE ARE OVER!

You are probably wondering how it happened, trying to figure out at which moment in our lives I changed. Maybe even considering this is a bad joke because I have "an abysmal sense of humor" and that now I am trying to be witty but in fact I sound pathetic.

Let me tell you something: this is exactly the reason why I am terminating this relationship. You are always shooting me down. Whatever I do, whatever I said, is just not good enough for you. And I just started noticing that my misery is your delight.

How did you react when I started my "gekfgvlhfuyeéhhuiiueg" or even the "HIrufrmouzgvfyué42fuz"? You sneered at me. You fucking sneered at **ME**! and then dropped a "Now I understand...." You fucking don't understand anything. You fucking don't understand **ME**!

So get out of my life!

Sincerely,
Author

**PS:** Tell Anxiety that her daughter has slept around with all my colleagues. I didn't even have to question, they spontaneously confessed. All of them. Guys **AND** Girls. Seriously!? When did you have time to two-time me!? Fuck, forget about it. I have already sent a text to your mom!

**PPS:** Remember your best friend? Procrastination? It's confession time! I did her! I did her in the bedroom. I did her in the kitchen. I did her on the dining table. I did her everywhere. She's not that good-looking, but damn! that girl let you do eeeeeverything! She is **NSFW**! But you know what, at least she's a *salope*. You're a **bitch**.

text:
# A Lightbulb's Last Wish

To be honest, I felt a little silly at first, like an ungrateful child that knows it's being inconsiderate. Despite being capable of things they couldn't even fathom, despite all the pros of being what I was and the vast list of cons attributed to them, I simply couldn't help myself.

It's a strange thing for the living to envy the inanimate.

Yet as I watched each missile spiral towards its demise and give all it had to one final moment of grace, I thought how dull my glow must seem. How few creatures live their lives like fireworks, how many simply stretch themselves as thin as they go, until they can hold no more and die. Seeking to see the next day rather than seizing the one that's ensured.

Many may argue a consistent life is preferable, but personally I think consistency is for the lifeless. Rocks and mountains, they do just fine holding the line. The planets seem happy orbiting a fixed track.

But fireworks, they're what life's all about.

Before there was life there was plenty of consistency and I think perhaps the purpose of life, if one there ever were, was to simply shake things up a little. Day in day out I glow the same, illuminating nothing more than my own personal space, inspiring none and ultimately draining myself to nothing.

I am done with that.

I wish to fly high above the heads of the world, and in one untimely climax, release all I have left. I wish to reach my full potential, if only for a second, and fizzle down to this earth, bidding her adieu.

I think we could all learn a lot from fireworks.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
**INCIDENT REPORT A17411**
**10-11-2017**
**CLEARANCE LEVEL 100**

Commander Sarah Chen floated in Bay 14B, staring at the empty docking port where the impossible had occurred twelve hours ago.

"How does a spacecraft that's sitting on the ground in Russia dock with us in orbit?" Mayfield's voice crackled through the comm.

Smith joined them, tablet in hand. "I've been going through the internal footage. Watch this."

The video showed the Soyuz interior—completely pristine, as if fresh from the factory. No wear, no scuff marks from use. But there, barely visible on the control panel: a date stamp reading 10-11-2027.

"That's ten years from now," Chen whispered.

Jones appeared in the doorway. "NASA just sent an encrypted flash. Diego Garcia recovered debris fragments. The metallurgical composition... it doesn't match current Soyuz specifications. The alloys won't be developed for another decade, according to materials science projections."

The four astronauts exchanged glances.

"It came from the future," Mayfield said what they were all thinking.

"And it came empty," Smith added. "Like it was showing us something. Or warning us."

Chen looked back at Earth, rotating serenely below. "The question isn't how anymore. It's why. Why did someone—or something—send an unmanned spacecraft backward through time to dock with us?"

Her tablet pinged. The message was brief: **MARSAP RECOMMENDATION: SILENCE PROTOCOL APPROVED. CEASE ALL DISCUSSION. CONTINUE MISSION.**

But continue toward what? Chen wondered, watching the sun rise over the Pacific, illuminating the exact spot where the impossible visitor had burned up on reentry.

The future had knocked on their door.

And then fled.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Slowest Hero

Every little boy and girl grows up wanting to be a superhero at some point. All the comic books, all the movies, they all showed the same thing: The superhero always wins, and the evildoer always loses. Maybe not at first, but in the end eventually they do.

They all have a different way of beating the bad guy too. Some are invisible. Some have super strength. Some can hear from miles away, and yet others can turn to stone. These are all incredibly useful in different situations.

But me? I didn't get any of those.

I woke up last week and discovered that, on command, I could move slowly. Not slowly like grandpa shuffling across the street. Not slowly like a snail. No. I could move so slow that even my very electrons moved at mere millionths of their original speed.

Talk about useless right?

Well yes and no.

Yes because at the time of the crime, I couldn't really do anything to stop the bad guys. No because, well, due to my super-slowness, I actually aged more slowly. My metabolic rate essentially dropped to zero during my power's duration, so effectively, I could live almost forever.

Why is this useful in fighting crime though?

Well I guess I lied; it won't stop crime. But I can attend each bad guy's funeral. So there's that.

I've started keeping a list. Criminals who got away. Mysteries unsolved. Justice delayed.

But never denied.

I'll outlast them all.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Curse of Compulsive Kindness

The curse started three months ago—a witch's revenge for a careless insult.

When Karla confessed her affair, rage boiled inside me, but my mouth betrayed me. "I'm willing to work on it," I heard myself say, smiling.

At work, my boss slashed my salary. "I accept that," I chirped, while screaming internally.

Every confrontation ends the same: I compliment, agree, submit. My true thoughts trapped behind this grotesque mask of perpetual niceness.

Today, Marcus cut me off in traffic, nearly killing a pedestrian. I wanted to curse him out. Instead: "No problem, friend! Great driving!"

The witch's note said the curse breaks only through "ultimate selflessness."

Standing on the bridge, I finally understand. One last good deed—removing this hollow shell from the world.

But as I climb the railing, a child's scream pierces the air. A girl, drowning below.

I dive without thinking.

Pulling her to shore, something breaks inside me.

"You goddamn reckless kid!" I shout at her parents.

The curse... lifted.

True goodness was never about compliance. It was about courage.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Midas Curse

Samuel wept as he walked down to the river nude. He held a pistol in his left hand. The stones cut at his feet shortly, before squelching and bleeding as they turned to flesh. The air was cool, but still Samuel dreaded it. He held his breath. When he took in air, it burned in his lungs as tiny pieces of meat flew around through his windpipe. 

Choking and breathing raggedly, he finally arrived at the river. He knelt at the river. Where his legs touched the ground, it became flesh. Mouths out of stones, eyes out of pebbles, all moaning softly for release from their pain. Without lungs to support them, they soon died, only to be revived by Samuel's touch. 

Samuel put down the pistol by his side. He put his fingers in the water, preparing to wash himself. However, the water betrayed him. It turned into a sluggish rainbow of yellowish lymph and hemolymph, animal blood and even the blue and purple blood of fish and sea animals. 

Samuel wept. He picked up his pistol, by now white as bone. He pulled it to his head, and pulled the trigger. The bullet failed, already integrated into the organism he created. 

Samuel wept.

Behind him, the flesh-stones screamed. The world pulsed with corrupted life. He could not die, and everything he touched could not remain dead.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

# The Wall

"See, I told you this was a good idea," President Trump said from the fiftieth floor of the newly remodeled and renamed Trump White Tower. "Those other losers said it couldn't be done, now we have a wall on the border. Although I will admit that it's sad that the Mexicans are all turning to these walking corpses—I mean, some of my best friends were Mexicans—I am glad that I was able to make Mexico pay for the wall. In this time of international crisis, I believe there is only one thing we as Americans can do: profit on the misfortune of our neighbors. That is why I propose we outfit the US Mexi-corpse wall with chain guns. We can sell a line of ammunition for triple its cost to tourists who want to try their hand at killing these undead freaks. Again, no disrespect to those of the Mexican persuasion. Also, I would like it noted that the phrase 'Mexi-corpse' is under copyright, and if you use the term, you will be sued. Thank you and good night."

"President Trump is full of... well, something..." the newscaster started as the emergency broadcast ended.

Josh turned the television off with a scowl. He stood and walked to his room to retrieve his shotgun from his gun vault. *Damn it, I can't believe people actually voted for this guy*, he thought as he loaded his twelve-gauge Benelli with slugs.

"Josh, where are you going?" Sarah called from the kitchen.

"The market," Josh called back as he slammed the door shut behind him.

Texas had become a battleground. Corpses walked the streets day and night, and it was getting harder to tell the survivors from the dead. 

*God, why did I vote for him?* Josh wondered, checking his ammunition one last time before stepping into the chaos outside.

# The Rehabilitation Solution

Mr. Nakamura set down his teacup, his expression unreadable. "You're describing chemical lobotomy."

The consultant's smile didn't waver. "We prefer 'neural recalibration.' The terminology matters for public relations."

"And these 'pleasant workers'—who employs them?"

"Various industries. Agriculture, manufacturing, service sectors. The Wint Bill established reintegration partnerships with corporations who receive tax incentives. Everyone benefits."

Mr. Nakamura studied the glossy brochure. Before-and-after photos showed transformed faces—the "after" images all shared the same placid, empty expression. "This man was convicted of tax fraud. Eight years became one night. What happened to his accounting skills?"

"Retained, mostly. Complex reasoning may be... simplified. But he's reliable, punctual, and grateful for employment."

"Grateful," Mr. Nakamura repeated softly.

"Our recidivism rates speak for themselves. These individuals don't reoffend because they literally cannot conceive of defying authority. It's perfect compliance."

"You've eliminated not just criminality, but autonomy."

The consultant leaned forward. "Mr. Nakamura, your country faces similar criticism. Overcrowding, aging facilities, mounting costs. We're offering a proven solution. The Europeans wanted rehabilitation? We rehabilitated. They can't complain about the methodology when the results are so spectacular."

Mr. Nakamura closed the brochure. "In my language, we have a concept: *tatemae* and *honne*—what we show publicly versus what we truly believe. You've mastered *tatemae*. But some of us still value *honne*."

He stood. "Thank you, but Japan will find another way."

The consultant's smile finally faded. "That's what America said once."
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

# The Curse of Creative Freedom

**"Shit eh? It's fucking Tuesday," I thought.** I got nowhere on my English creative writing assignment due for Mr. Smith on Wednesday. If only he let me put curse words in our ADULT themed assignment... Stupid Asswipe, damn it.

---

"Fudge," said the Cursing Master.

The Cursing Master was a Master of Cursing. He had dueled many a foul-mouthed cretin believing they themselves capable of besting him. They had no idea the CPM that Curse Master possessed. 60 CPM!!! 60 CURSES PER MINUTE... Before they could eek out a "Da-" or a "Fu-" or a "Bit-", they'd be tormented by a different curse. He was called the Curse Master for a reason.

But this time, this assignment he was assigned might just be out of his reach. His target was a boy, different from his usual targets. The Curse Master knew he would fail this time.

The boy was a sheltered child from the family of the Smiths. One of the three ruling noble families that forbade the usage of curses and spoke only in formal speech, not even daring to use slang. They ruled the world with their eloquent speech and well-mannered gestures, as if blessing those beneath them.

The Curse Master, disguised in scholarly robes and pretending to be part of the boy's royal escort, tapped the boy on the shoulder as he left the palace to welcome the other ruling families' escorts.

The boy turned around.

The Curse Master could not believe his eyes. The boy was not a boy but a raging angry giant floating butt with a red flared up—

---

"Okay, what the fuck is this shit?" Mr. Smith asked me.

"Your requested assignment, Asswipe." I laughed and ran off.

I never passed English 9. God damn curses fucking me up. I hate this world.

But somehow, in that stupid meta-narrative disaster of a story, I'd managed to say exactly what I wanted to say: sometimes the rules don't make sense, sometimes authority deserves to be questioned, and sometimes the best act of rebellion is just being yourself—even if yourself is kind of an idiot.

Worth it.
