text:
# The Last Look

Seven hundred ninety-three days.

That's how long I've been floating in this tin can, breathing recycled air and choking down chemical paste. The synthetic nutrients coat my tongue like film. God, what I wouldn't give for real cake right now—butter, sugar, frosting. Something to remind me I'm still human.

But today's supposed to be different. My final shift before Team 2 arrives. Just routine maintenance: systems optimized, air conditioning humming, orbit stable. Everything by the book.

I drift to the observation window. Earth hangs below, blue and white and beautiful. Except... something's off. The cloud patterns look wrong. Asymmetric. Angry.

Twenty-eight minutes until scheduled departure.

"Jack... Jack, can you hear me?!" The comm crackles to life. "Our systems aren't holding up, but everything's going to Hell down here! You're going to have to stay up there until the plates stabil—"

*Click.*

Static.

I press my palm against the cold glass. Below, I can just make out the fault lines now—glowing orange veins spreading across continents like cracks in porcelain. The Pacific Rim pulses. California shudders.

The news satellites are probably scrambling for final broadcasts. One last story before the world reshapes itself.

But up here, in the silence of orbit, I have the best seat in the house.

Twenty-three minutes.

I dim the cabin lights and watch continents dance.

Some views are worth seven hundred ninety-three days of chemical cake.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Day I Became an Adult

I park the trash truck for the last time, my hands trembling slightly on the steering wheel. Forty-three years of "chores"—that's what they call it. Forty-three years of watching the real adults walk by in their youthful bodies, wearing those silver crescents on their lapels that mark them as citizens.

The Rejuvenation Center gleams before me, all white marble and promise. Inside, others wait—my classmates from decades ago, gray-haired and wrinkled like me, excitement dancing in tired eyes.

"First time?" a woman asks, laughing at her own joke. We're all first-timers.

I think about yesterday, dumping refuse at the landfill beside Chen, who's fifty-eight. Seven more years of childhood for him. Seven more years before he gets to vote, to matter.

The technician calls my name. As I follow her into the chamber, doubt flickers through my mind. The history they taught us—longer lifespans necessitating mature governance—it always made sense. But driving past construction sites staffed by sixty-year-old "children," watching fifty-year-olds serve food to thirty-looking adults...

The chamber door closes. The technician smiles. "Ready to join society?"

Through the window, I glimpse my reflection: sixty-five years of wear and work.

Tomorrow, I'll look twenty-five and finally have a voice.

But I'll still remember what it took to earn it.

And I wonder—was this really progress?
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Forbidden Dream

Kim, as he loved to call himself, always dreamed of visiting America. Living in the palace, as a child, he loved to sneak off into the forbidden section. He knew the guard's schedule by rote. When he was accustomed to belching. When he would have to stretch his legs. And of course, the 57 minutes after his lunch meal, customary toilet break that lasted between 14 to 19 minutes.

During that time he would sneak into the vast chamber of forbidden artifacts. Every day he would try and find himself something new to play with, or fascinate his short time. On a particular spring day when he was 8, he spied a stuffed animal, in the shape of some rather odd looking mouse. With black round ears, wearing yellow shoes, and red shorts.

Although it was odd, he was fascinated by this little stuffed creature, and from that day forth, he vowed he would meet this creature—even if it meant disobeying his father.

Years later, clutching that same worn toy, Kim stood before the gates of Disneyland, tears streaming down his face. He had finally made it.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Post

I've decided to end my life tonight.

There's no dramatic reason, no single moment that pushed me over the edge. It's more like a thousand paper cuts, each one insignificant alone, but together they've bled me dry. Jake's death six months ago was the deepest cut—my best friend, gone in an instant, and suddenly the world felt hollow.

I keep thinking about our last conversation, how we laughed about nothing important. I didn't know those would be my last memories of him.

Since then, everything feels muted. Colors are dimmer. Laughter sounds forced. Even my sister Emma, the one bright spot left, can't reach me anymore. Yesterday she told me she hated me for shutting her out. She was crying. I just stared.

The pain isn't sharp—it's a constant, suffocating weight. I'm exhausted from carrying it.

I won't leave a dramatic note or make some grand announcement. This isn't for attention. I'm just done.

To anyone reading this: I'm sorry. Especially you, Emma. You deserved a better brother.

By the time you see this, it'll be over.

I'm ready now.

Goodbye.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# YEAR 1 AA: (After Assimilation)

Tom and William were slouched on the musty couch in their squalid apartment they shared.

"It's been a whole year since this... stuff. What *is* this stuff?" Tom asked perplexingly.

"Looks like meat," William said obtusely. "Our fern turned to meat, our cat turned to meat, even our lunch meat turned to meat!"

Tom tried fruitlessly flipping through channels of static, searching for anything—an old show or, more importantly, information on the situation. Anything to block out William's inane "Big Meat Change" theory.

"It's not meat—I mean, it's some lifeform that *looks* like meat," Tom said reflectively. "We had to burn the cat and hack at the fern until it plunged out the window so they wouldn't kill us!"

Tom shambled to the window and peered outside. "We've been in this building for a whole year, living off cellar canned goods and pork rinds. We can't stay in this despicable situation any longer."

"We're gonna get more pork rinds!?" William asked with renewed excitement, scratching himself with a homemade back scratcher.

"No, you buffoon! We're going out *there*. We should at least try to find out what's happening."

"You mean the meat change?" William asked, bewildered.

Tom started gathering supplies, wondering about his chances of survival accompanied by his simple friend. He began thinking that maybe he should have let the fern kill him after all.

But no. They had to try. Whatever had transformed the world into this fleshy nightmare, they needed answers. Tom grabbed a knife, some matches, and their last can of beans.

"Come on," he said grimly. "Let's see what's left out there."
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Goodbye

The golden retriever waited by the door for three days before venturing outside. Her master never returned.

Skyscrapers loomed silent overhead, windows darkening like closing eyes. Concrete jungles became actual jungles as vines snaked up steel frames, patient and persistent.

The dog joined other strays—once-pampered poodles and house cats now hunting in packs. They inherited a world healing from deep wounds.

Factories stopped belching smoke. Rivers ran clear again. The ozone layer slowly mended itself, molecule by patient molecule.

Humanity had believed themselves the main character in Earth's story. They were merely a chapter—a difficult one the planet needed to recover from.

Centuries passed. Moss-covered monuments crumbled. Forests reclaimed parking lots. Whales sang in unpolluted seas.

The retriever's descendants ran wild through green ruins, forgetting they'd ever been domesticated.

Earth exhaled, finally free to be itself again.

Nature always wins.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Withering

Tulip Marie Hammond was guilty. And Tulip Marie Hammond was innocent.

The paradox lived in her bones as straps bit into her wrists. Through the observation window, her family huddled together—her sister's tears, her mother's stoic mask, her nephew's confused frown. She'd killed for them. Three men who'd threatened, extorted, cornered them in darkness.

The reflecting glass showed her own face: hollowed cheeks, platinum hair now limp, eyes that had witnessed too much. She'd been a gardener once, coaxing life from soil. Then came the debts, the threats, the night her sister came home bleeding.

Justice, she'd thought, pulling the trigger the first time. The second. The third.

But justice was a weed that choked everything else. Her family hadn't celebrated her protection—they'd fractured under its weight. Her sister stopped speaking to her. Her mother aged a decade in months. The nephew who'd once held her hand now flinched at her touch.

The man in white checked his instruments with clinical precision. Tulip closed her eyes, rejecting the chaplain's final platitudes. Words were seeds that would never take root now.

The chemicals burned through her veins like poison feeding a dying plant. Her body convulsed, defending itself even as her mind surrendered. She'd wanted to be their shield. Instead, she'd become their shame.

As consciousness faded, she heard her sister's sob—not of grief, but release.

The tulip withered. Perhaps something else could finally grow.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Day Everything Changed

She had always been a 'yes' girl. Never once had she said 'no', except for today.

The day started like any other with a soy latte from her favorite barista, then onto work at her 9-5 mundane job. She was typing a brief for her boss when the call came in.

"Sarah, you there?" Rich asked, his voice normal, not showing any signs of the news to come.

"Yeah, Rich, I'm here," she said, still typing at the brief displayed on the screen in front of her.

"I've been sleeping with your sister, so I think it's done between us."

The statement had been said in a way you would discuss the weather or maybe your new puppy, not at all in a way that you would tell your long-term girlfriend that you had been sleeping with her best friend and sister.

Sarah hung up the phone, wiped the stray tears that managed to escape, and finished her brief. She brought the poorly written paper to her boss, only to be handed the dreaded pink slip.

"Budget cuts," he said with a shrug.

Her once perfect life was now tipped upside down. She had always played it safe, made the right choices, and never strayed. She had always said 'yes,' but today wasn't going to be another.

"Would you like to save changes?" the monotone voice asked her.

"No, I don't think I would," she replied with a smile.

Sarah walked out of that office building lighter than she'd felt in years, ready to rewrite her entire life.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Collector

BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP

"OK ALREADY! DAMN IT."

Tom screamed at his alarm clock. Quarter past seven. Still needed a shower.

He stumbled toward the bathroom, subconsciously sidestepping the dresser that claimed his toe almost every morning. Autopilot mode engaged: shower on—check. Teeth brushed—check. Bathroom—check.

As Tom stepped into the shower, he had only a moment to notice the bar of soap at the bottom of the tub. With precision, it effortlessly flipped his feet out from underneath him.

Brief weightlessness.

*Huh, that's new.*

Then his skull slammed onto the tile.

Quiet now. Just water drumming an unknown melody against the curtain.

A man walked into the bathroom. He approached Tom's limp body and sighed heavily, his old joints protesting as he bent down. With a gloved hand, he retrieved the soap. His other hand produced a small black box from inside his coat.

He placed the bar inside and wrote on the lid: *Tom 3-22-2015*.

A smirk crossed his weathered face as he surveyed his work. Another accident. Another soul who'd never see the pattern. The soap had served its purpose perfectly, as it always did.

He pocketed the box and left the apartment.

The shower still running.

By the time anyone found Tom, the old man would be three states away, already researching his next target—someone else trapped in routines, vulnerable in their predictability.

The Collector always found them.

text:
# The Last Witness

I stumble backward, hand slipping from the lock. The rope dangles behind me like a broken promise.

"It's... me?" I whisper to the door, to the silence, to the impossible.

"YES! Open the goddamn door before they come back!"

*They.* Not *it*. Not the mindless shuffle I've watched from my window for three hundred and forty-seven days. *They.*

My reflection stares back from the darkened window—gaunt, hollow-eyed, already a ghost. The city sprawls below, a graveyard of abandoned hopes. I've memorized every street, every shadow that moves wrong.

"How do I know you're real?" My voice cracks.

Silence. Then: "Because I know about the curtains. Because I know you've stood at that window every morning at 6:47. Because I know about the rope."

Ice floods my veins. "Where are you?"

"Across the street. Tenth floor. The building with the red door."

I've stared at that building a thousand times. Every window dark, dead, empty.

"Wave," I demand.

Seconds stretch into eternities. Then—there. A pale hand against glass, catching dying sunlight. Mirroring my own raised palm.

"We've been watching each other survive," she says, softer now. "Please. Don't make me watch you die."

The rope sways behind me. The door waits. The city holds its breath.

I choose.

The lock clicks open.

She crashes through—wild-eyed, half-starved, real. Real. We collapse against each other, two ghosts remembering they're human.

"The curtains," she gasps, laughing or crying or both. "Keep them open. So we can see we're not alone."

Outside, the city watches. This time, we watch back.

Together.

text:
# Stay Here

"Stay here." 

Alice's whisper cuts through the darkness. She rises from the bed, gesturing to the warm spot she's just vacated. Jamey, nineteen but suddenly feeling five, sits without a sound. Her mother's finger crosses her lips—silent, direct, commanding.

Jamey watches Alice kneel beside the bed. Her mother's eyes disappear below the mattress edge, then snap back up—sharp, knowing, lethal. That protective stare locks onto Jamey's frightened gaze like a magnetic field.

In one fluid motion, Alice stands, the pump-action 12-gauge emerging from beneath the bed like an old friend. She turns toward the hallway, toward Jamey's room, moving with predatory purpose.

At the corner, Alice presses her left shoulder against the wall.

"SHLACK CLACK!!!"

The shotgun's rack splits the silence like thunder. Down the hall, something flinches violently beneath Jamey's bed—the same cowardice that drove it to hide now betraying its position with an involuntary spasm.

Alice allows herself a grim smile. Confirmed.

She pivots, torso around the corner, feet planted. Five rounds—alternating buckshot and slugs—punch through Jamey's mattress in rapid succession. The house shudders with each blast.

She pauses. One round left. Waiting.

Seconds crawl by. Then crimson oozes from beneath the bed, pooling across hardwood, followed by the unmistakable stench of released bowels.

"RIIIIING. RIIIIING. RIIIII—"

"Alice?"

"Yeah."

"What's up, Sis?"

Alice surveys the scene, shotgun still raised. The pool spreads wider.

"Can you come over?" Her voice is steady, almost casual. "I need a dinner reservation."

Silence on the line. Then: "The usual place?"

"Yeah. Bring the truck."

Alice hangs up, glances back at her daughter still frozen on her bed.

"It's over, baby."

But they both know it never really is.

text:
# The Last Spill

"Oh for fuck's sake," were the words I repeated for the seventh time this day. No matter the amount of energy I put into trying my best, my damned coffee always shatters with a silky smooth elegance about it. The creamy coloured brew always seeks out a new way to make me usher those few famous words.

It's almost like I can hear the coffee bellow back to me, "what the fuck is wrong with you," each time the glass pieces fall to their final resting place. One of these days I'll manage a full agenda without another hiccup in my routine. One of thes—

"Who the hell? How the fuck do you manage—" were the words I got out before my boss recognized the brown stained shirt. I shrugged. He shrugged. It's so routine that no one bats an eye anymore. He left without another peep, but I silently continued muttering, "holy shit."

On the fourteenth or fifteenth time—I can't remember—I had finally pulled out what resembled a tablet from the year 4000 from the trash. Bright blue, no material, no metal, no nothing, except for a thin frame of some sort. A hologram being projected out of thin air formed the words, "Welcome, Brian."

As soon as I'd picked up this thing, the words reorganized, as if in a sci-fi film, to a massive list of every single idiotic thing I've done. Next to each item, an enticing looking arrow resembling one found on a modern backspace keyboard.

My finger hovered over the first entry: *Coffee spill #1, 8:47 AM.*

I pressed it.

The world flickered.

I was holding a full cup of coffee, unbroken, steam rising peacefully.

This was the last time those few famous words were ever ushered from my mouth ever again.

text:
# The Weight of Loyalty

My hands trembled as I placed the porcelain cup before her. The Rising Dragon sat with perfect stillness, her eyes distant, perhaps seeing beyond these walls to the empire she meant to reshape.

The black lotus would work swiftly—painlessly, I'd been promised.

She lifted the cup, and I held my breath. But instead of drinking, she met my gaze.

"You love the Empire," she said softly. "I can see it in your fear."

I couldn't speak.

"The Jade Emperor protected the capital while provinces burned. He feasted while children starved." Her voice carried no anger, only sorrow. "I do not seek his throne—I seek to break it. To return power to people like you, who've carried this empire on your backs for centuries."

She set down the cup, untouched.

"The black lotus has a distinct scent," she continued, rising. "I've smelled it many times—usually in cups meant for me." She placed coins on the table, far more than the tea cost. "Keep your loyalty. But ask yourself: to whom do you truly owe it? The gods, the Emperor—or your suffering neighbors?"

She left me standing there, the poisoned tea cooling between us, my certainty crumbling like ancient stone.

text:
# The Banana Incident

"Paul, we need to stop."

"Why? I'm having a lot of fun with this!"

"Please, no. The tool doesn't even work properly, it was just a proof of concept."

Paul pulled a banana out of the hole in the rift. "And why is it a **banana**? What did you do?"

"I was bored, okay?"

"Look," John grabs the tool from Paul. "This banana—er... tool, may appear to be perfectly functional, but it clearly isn't. It causes many errors."

"But it does work! I just spawned in a ton of diamonds! I'll be rich!"

John sighs as he shakes his head. Paul has clearly not heard of the scam. "Why don't you tell me. When you attempt to spawn diamonds, what does the banana—... tool! do?"

"Well it modifies the bytecode tied to this point in space, offsetting it to change what material is occupying the space at the moment."

"And how does the banana *know* which bytes to offset?"

"Haha, you called it a banana!"

"Shut up and answer the question."

"Well, it doesn't, so I narrow down the possible bytes based on the factors, and modify all of them."

"And what happens when you offset bytes willy nilly?"

"I don't know, and frankly, I don't care."

"Glitches happen."

"Wait, you mean that subreddit—"

"Yes."

"Oh dear..."

Behind them, reality flickered. The diamonds turned to cheese.

text:
# For Death and Glory

"For death and glory!" 

That was our cry, handed down to us from before, lost in the distant pasts, to be handed down in turn to those who would follow after. Our legion was the first, the oldest, in an unbroken line of warrior's blood and death stretching back 5000 years, but we were the same unit of men still. We died, and others joined us. The parts may die but the whole of the thing is the same.

We celebrated our history, and remembered past battles. The oldest stories of our unit speak of the pacification of barbarian tribes, the sacking of their camps, the freeing of captives. In times of peace our unit was an honor guard in the capital, but in war our true purpose was remembered.

Our unit was invariably on the front lines. Ours was the oldest unit, and we had the best training. We had been the ones to sack Carthage, to put encroaching cities of the Iroquois to the torch. We were the ones who were now leading the war on the Zulus.

"For death and glory!"

We fortified at our borders, holding weapons newly invented and given to us alone. The cost was too great still for the rest of the army, so they were left with muskets while we polished our new rifles. Gone were the days of swords and shield and the clash of metal arms, but we remembered it still. The old songs were still sung, and the glory of passed battles was recounted.

"For death and glory!"

The enemy was approaching our position now. While the Zulus were technologically backward, they did not lack for troops. From horizon to horizon they stretched, without even muskets, hurling spears they charged us.

We held the line as cannons fired death from behind us, and as divisions on our flanks crumpled. We held the line as a war we started turned against us, and the casualties began to mount. We held the line for death and glory, for the honor of Rome, and for those who had come before us.

"For death and glory!"

The spears found their marks. The rifles clicked empty. The tide could not be stopped.

*Shaka Zulu has captured Rome.*

Fucking Impis, man.

# The Leap

"C'mon, let's go!" she called to me, running ahead. I half jogged, half walked behind her, hoping I'd catch up eventually. I came up next to her a few moments later, and I was exhausted. She was looking over a waterfall, looking incredibly elegant in doing so.

"Let's slow down from here on out, alright? Don't wanna miss what there is to see."

"Ok, Reginald," she said joyfully-sarcastically.

"You know how to press my buttons, don't you, *Brittany*?"

"Oh, c'mon. We don't have to resort to my first name here, do we? You know I hate that."

"You call me Reggie, I'll call you Carla. Deal?"

"Deal. Hey, I have an idea!"

"Yes?"

"We used to do this when we were kids!" she said, stripping down to a bathing suit.

"What, you're gonna jump?"

"C'mon, let's go!" she called to me, leaping into the cascade.

I watched her disappear into the mist, heard her whoop of pure joy echo upward, and smiled. Same fearless Carla. Always would be.

text:
# The Last Aster

The silence that followed King Crio's death was more terrifying than his reign had ever been.

I watched from my hiding place as chaos consumed the great hall. Breyon scattered like frightened birds—which, I supposed, they essentially were—their iridescent feathers catching the light as they fled through every available exit. The remaining human slaves stood frozen, uncertain whether to run or celebrate.

The Aster moved with deliberate grace, circling the king's corpse. Its form was humanoid but wrong somehow—joints bending at angles that shouldn't exist, skin shimmering with an inner luminescence that hurt to observe directly. When it spoke, its voice resonated in frequencies that made my bones ache.

"Three cycles," it said, almost conversationally. "Three cycles you celebrated our extinction."

I thought of the girl—couldn't have been more than twelve—now crumpled beside the shattered focals she'd treasured. She'd mentioned an 'A' in passing, a slip of the tongue about something called the Archives. Such a small mistake for such a permanent consequence.

The Aster's head swiveled toward the slaves with uncanny precision. "You are free to go."

No one moved.

"We were never extinct," it continued, picking shards of the girl's goggles from the pooling blood. "We were patient. Every Breyon king who declared our Order destroyed simply signed their own death warrant. Poison takes time. Strategy takes longer."

My brother—still in his incubation chamber somewhere in the palace depths—flashed through my mind. Would he emerge to a world without masters? Or would the Asters simply replace one tyranny with another?

The Aster turned its impossible gaze directly to my hiding spot.

"You," it said, pointing with a finger that sprouted too many joints. "You knew she would die. You heard her mistake and said nothing."

I had. God help me, I had.

"Survival," the Aster said, almost approvingly, "is the first lesson we teach."

Then it walked away, leaving us with our freedom and our shame.

text:
# The Maintenance Call

The technician climbed down from the ladder, wiping dew from his brow. "Look. Did what I could." He said, putting the clipboard in the president's hands. "The whole unit is fucked, maybe someone didn't take the time to blast it out real well with canned air, maybe the processor couldn't handle the long workloads."

The president scanned over the list of 'changes' implemented to improve performance. "What the hell is anti-alias?" All of this was new, overwhelming to him still.

"It's when your system is drawing an edge or contour and doesn't want it to look chunky or pixelated, so it smooths out the appearance by estimating to the nearest pixel's gradation, blurs the line a little. Right now it's set to atomic scale, I think that's eating a lot of the spare memory."

"Oh, for crying out loud, what does all this techno bullshit mean?"

The tech popped the cap on his coke and took a long draw from it. He burped his satisfaction. "Welp. If we don't want to go back to 16 bit DOS we'll have to strip some features. Rainbows, glare and bloom effects are pretty noncritical, I think. If I decrease view distance from 13 billion light years to, idunno, half that, we might piss off some scientists but nothing we can't deal with. Uh, actor distance should be lowered down to within, oh, say, 100 yards, they're the most texture heavy assets. Anti alias could probably be scaled down to about a third of the current without harm, and maybe turn down the FPS refresh rate, just lock it at 30 or so."

The president stood, jaw agape at the document in his hand.

"Okay, well, I'm done here." Said the technician, opening his hatch in the ground.

"Wait! What if we want to get a new graphics card?"

"You'll have to check the warranty with the original manufacturer, not my job." He said, slamming down the lid of the door to Hell.

text:
# The Last Hope

We stumbled from our cryogenic sleepers, disoriented and gasping. The station's recycled air tasted like copper and desperation. Captain Martinez steadied herself against the bulkhead, her knees weak from centuries of suspended animation.

"Status report," she croaked.

The monitors confirmed what we already knew: Earth was dying. The cascading ecological collapse had accelerated beyond all projections. We were humanity's final gambit—seven scientists chasing a signal that promised salvation.

The ancient station materialized through the viewport like a ghost. Impossibly old, yet pristine. Its architecture defied known physics, surfaces that seemed to exist in multiple dimensions simultaneously.

Following the transmitted instructions felt surreal. Every password worked. Every door opened. The corridors stretched endlessly, walls covered in symbols that hurt to observe directly.

Then we found him.

The being turned slowly, his form both alien and somehow familiar. His eyes—too many, too knowing—fixed upon us with an expression that cycled through emotions faster than we could process.

When he smiled, we felt hope surge. This was it. The answer to everything.

Then his face collapsed into anguish so profound it seemed to warp the air around him.

"You didn't bring the Doritos?"

The words hung there, incomprehensible yet devastating.

Martinez stepped forward, trembling. "We... what?"

The alien's shoulders sagged. "The transmission. The entire message. 'Will trade universal salvation technology for Cool Ranch Doritos. Serious inquiries only.'"

Behind us, Junior Engineer Patel checked his tablet with shaking hands. "Captain... there's a second page to the message we never scrolled to."

Humanity's last hope, undone by poor reading comprehension.

# The Angel Arrest

I was startled out of my zen sleep. "THUMP THUMP THUMP." Someone was pounding at my door.

I dragged myself out of bed and walked over to my curtains to let in the morning sun. The curtains effortlessly slid open, but there was no glowing orange sunrise—it was almost pitch black outside. I could just make out the slight glimmer of waves.

"THUMP THUMP THUMP."

Who the fuck is waking me up at this hour?

I opened the door to be met by two stocky men. Both were clad in jeans and chunky black hoodies. I wouldn't have even realized they were angels if it wasn't for the slight glimmer hanging atop their potato-like heads.

"Sir, please come with us."

"Is there a problem?"

"No, we just want to ask a few questions," he stated, as he invited himself into my place.

Something was wrong. Ryan goes missing last week, then this? My instincts took over and I bolted for the back door. I looked behind me—I couldn't see them. I swung open my back door and bolted into my backyard.

Suddenly I was down on the ground, gasping to refill my winded lungs. Another heavyset angel stood there looking down on me. A knee dug into my back as I felt cold metal cuffs bind my arms together.

"Sorry buddy, change of plans. You're heading downstairs."

FUCK, why didn't I choose to just get fucking reincarnated instead of this eternity shit?

text:
# The Last Battle

Limbs stiffen despite the sergeant's consistent massaging. He sees his men, battered and exhausted, and cannot think of any reason to continue towards the enemy. Come to think of it, he's not even sure what the fighting is all about. The men remind him of brothers, not friendlies and charlies.

The thunder abides and Johnson can finally catch his breath, sucking in fibrous particles from the air around him. His front men are scraped up and their bayonets bent, but otherwise healthy enough to move on. His grenadiers are another story. Most are already dead, one shocked and staring blankly ahead. But Johnson doesn't blame him. Not after what they've been through.

A vast sea of beige separates them from the other force, their killers. Johnson feels a twinge of familiarity, but knows it must be a delusion from lack of sleep.

Short-lived, the silence is broken by more thunder. God's footsteps vibrating his bones. He knows what is coming.

Inside his mud-soaked helmet, ethereal commands enter his skull, somehow forcing his muscles to move. He sees his men react as well, but he doesn't feel any sense of team around him. The voice seems to almost pick him up and toss him towards the center, where his enemies await.

He lines up with his men, and sudden exhaustion forces him to simply stare the others in the face. Generic faces stare back. The voice in his head quiets. He waits, unsure of how he will secure his own fate.

Suddenly, a scream breaks the silence and the others move. But not him. He cannot muster the will. Bayonets slice his men. The quiet returns as they brutally die.

Another soldier kicks him in the chest, and he lies still on the ground from the force. The soldier stands above and slowly slides his knife between Johnson's ribs. Freezing steel penetrates his lungs and leaves him gasping. The blade twists and Johnson sees a boyish face grinning down upon his dying breath.

His green face and limbs revert back to plastic.

# The Last Conversation

"Do you ever question free will, Edgar?"

"There is nothing to question about it, Michael. It simply does not exist."

"And how would you know?"

"It's not a matter of knowing, it is a matter of understanding."

"Understanding what?"

Edgar gazed at the crimson sky. "The timeline. If the past is written in ink, who is to argue that the future is not as well?"

"And supposedly free will can't exist in a prewritten timeline?"

"Most likely not. Think of all history as like a book."

Michael shifted uncomfortably. "Maybe history just started a few minutes ago and will end a few minutes later."

"Interesting concept. Doesn't change anything about free will."

"I like to believe in free will. It gives us a reason to try, to live as opposed to accepting fate."

The ground trembled beneath them.

"Did you feel that?" Michael whispered.

"Yes," Edgar replied, watching the horizon fracture like old parchment. "It seems our history is coming to an end."

Their forms dissolved into ink, returning to the page.

text:
# Acid Rain

Baz stared at the smoking urinal, his heart hammering against his ribs. The acrid smell of melted plastic filled the small bathroom, mixing with the stale beer-and-disinfectant pub scent.

"Bloody hell," he whispered, backing away from the drain.

His mind raced. The burning sensation. The cheating girlfriend. The week that kept repeating. And now... this.

He stumbled out of the gents, past Dave who was already settling in front of the telly, pint in hand. The pub's warmth felt suffocating now. Baz burst through the front door into the cool Manchester evening.

His phone buzzed. Sarah. Again.

*We need to talk.*

"Yeah, we bloody do," he muttered, declining the call.

The walk home took twenty minutes, but Baz barely noticed. His thoughts spiraled. He'd lived this week three times now—each time waking up last Monday with a splitting headache and a sense of déjà vu. Each time, he'd discovered Sarah's affair. Each time, he'd felt that burning sensation.

But the melted drain? That was new.

At his flat, Baz locked himself in the bathroom and stared at the toilet. Hesitantly, he relieved himself again, watching the water carefully.

Nothing.

"Maybe it was just—"

Then he saw it. A faint wisp of steam rising from the bowl. The porcelain around the waterline had developed a rough, pitted texture.

"Christ."

Baz sat on the edge of his bathtub, head in his hands. Time loops. Acidic urine. A failed relationship. The universe had a twisted sense of humor.

His phone buzzed again.

*Baz, please. It's not what you think.*

He laughed—a hollow, broken sound.

"Drain cleaner man," he said to his reflection. "Dave got that right."

Tomorrow—or rather, next Monday—he'd figure this out. Tonight, he just needed sleep.

text:
# Patient Zero

The paracetamol felt like acid going down. I clutched the cafeteria table, knuckles white, as reality began to fracture around me.

Those weren't classmates approaching—they couldn't be. Their eyes pulsed with bioluminescence, casting strobing shadows across the linoleum. One vaulted onto another's shoulders with inhuman grace, shrieking with manic joy.

"It's happening!"

Then nothing.

---

Consciousness returned in fragments. The hospital bed. The tubes—too many tubes. The containment bubble distorting everything beyond it into carnival mirror shapes. The doctor in her hazmat suit, staring at me like I was a fascinating disease.

I reached for the walkie-talkie, expecting agony from the tubes.

Instead, I moved like liquid mercury. Every muscle fiber sang with perfect coordination. Time itself seemed elastic—I watched dust motes hang suspended in the air, tracked the microsecond delay between my thought and action. My body was a precision instrument I'd never known how to use until this moment.

"What's going on?" I asked into the radio.

But I already knew.

The doctor's elevated heart rate. The micro-expressions flickering across her face—fear, wonder, guilt. The way she'd positioned herself between me and the door. Her fingers hovering near the emergency containment protocols.

Something had been in those pills. Something that shouldn't exist.

And now it was in me, rewriting my biology from the inside out.

Those students with their glowing eyes—they'd known. They'd been waiting for this moment, waiting for someone to cross the threshold first.

I pressed my palm against the plastic bubble and felt the molecular structure of it, understood instinctively how much pressure it would take to tear through. How fast I could move now. What I was becoming.

The doctor's voice crackled through the walkie-talkie: "Subject exhibits extreme physiological enhancement. Recommending immediate quarantine escalation."

But quarantine was already too late.

I was patient zero, and the world would never be the same.

text:
# The Nine Lives of Bastet

My first owner was a respected businessman with everything: a devoted wife, two perfect children, and obscene wealth. Yet dissatisfaction poisoned him from within—or perhaps that was literally me, slipping nightshade into their evening stew.

The maid took the blame, naturally. Who suspects a handsome black cat?

But businessmen bore me. I craved *power*.

I systematically eliminated every feline in the politician's district—seventeen rivals disposed of quietly. His beloved Persian vanished during my watch (the river claimed that pompous furball). When I appeared on his doorstep, mewing pitifully, it was love at first sight.

The palace exceeded expectations.

I attempted communication through elaborate gestures—knocking over specific books, arranging dead mice in hieroglyphic patterns. The fool concluded I was divine. Soon, his entire staff worshipped me. Priests burned incense at my paws. Servants offered prime cuts of meat.

Still, he couldn't comprehend my true nature: deposed Emperor of the Cygnus Sector, victim of my traitorous nephew's coup. These primitive mammals lacked the cognition for interstellar politics.

When his usefulness expired, I arranged his... retirement. 

Then came my masterstroke.

I convinced them to build monuments—massive triangular structures where I could relieve myself while surveying my domain. *Three* of them! Artists across the known world carved my likeness into stone. I was immortal. I was *god*.

For centuries, I ruled Egypt through surrogates, my cult spreading like wildfire.

Until Moses.

That staff-wielding zealot and his monotheistic ravings destroyed everything. Plagues, exodus, the systematic dismantling of my divine status—all because I wouldn't release his people.

(In my defense, I needed the labor force for my fourth monument.)

Now I wander, seeking a new civilization to manipulate. These modern humans with their "internet" show promise.

After all, they already worship cats.

*Perhaps I never really lost.*

# The Cookie Catastrophe

"Grandma," Nancine groaned carefully. "I don't want to eat your cookies."

"Why not, honey?"

"They look gross."

Grandma Mary was proud of her baking skills. She thought she was quite talented at it. Why didn't Nancine want her cookies?

"Just one dear, they're so delicious!"

"Now was that so hard?!" Grandma guffawed.

Nancine gulped, her face turning green.

"Alrighty," Grandma started, "I'm off to get your grandpa now! Be safe!"

Grandma Mary had very poor eyesight as well as very poor hearing. But despite these handicaps, she was an excellent driver. Sometimes she didn't even *need* to look when she drove; the road would simply speak to her.

*The roads are quite bumpy today,* Grandma Mary thought, as she backed over Nancine's bicycle in the driveway.

text:
# The Discordant Duet

The name hit me like a flat note in a symphony. Showstopper stood before the vault, his trademark asymmetrical suit somehow making my eyes water. Half-pinstripe, half-polka dot—a crime against fashion *and* harmony.

"Miss me, Somnophone?" He pulled one earplug out, dangling it mockingly. "I've been practicing... my... *timing*."

I circled left, fingers ready. "Those plugs won't save you forever."

"Long enough." He reached into his jacket, producing what looked like a kazoo welded to a megaphone. "Behold... the... Cacophony... Cannon!"

Before I could snap, he blew into it. The sound that emerged was indescribable—accordion mixed with nails on chalkboard, seasoned with off-key yodeling. My knees buckled. The rhythm of the universe itself seemed to hiccup.

But I'd trained for this. I focused on my heartbeat, that steady internal metronome, and *snap-snap-clapped* a counter-rhythm. The dissonance wavered. Showstopper's eye twitched.

"Impossible! No one... can... harmonize... with chaos!"

"You're forgetting something," I said, building a percussion pattern with my feet. "Silence isn't the opposite of music. Silence is its canvas."

I stopped. Complete stillness. The absence rang louder than any note.

In that pocket of pure quiet, I *snapped* once.

The Cacophony Cannon shattered. Showstopper froze mid-breath, then began an involuntary interpretive dance—part ballet, part breakdancing, wholly humiliating.

"Officer!" I called out the door. "Two for booking. And someone call a music therapist."

As they hauled Showstopper away, still pirouetting, he shouted: "This isn't... over... Somno... phone! I'll be... *back*!"

I adjusted my cape. "They always are."

The Treble's engine hummed sweetly as I drove away. Somewhere, another sour note would play. But today? Today's melody was mine.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Loneliness of One

In the beginning, there was only None—a terrible and lonely creature, vast and infinite, fast asleep in its own impossibility. But None didn't actually exist, because if everything is nothing, then nothing is everything. A terribly complicated thing, but try and follow along.

This non-thing, caught in paradox, suddenly realized its own existence.

"I can't be nothing if nothing is everything," it thought.

In that moment, the great chasm from infinite zero to individual one was surpassed, and it was incredible.

"I am alive!" exclaimed the One.

Within moments, disaster struck. Just the thought of it ignites the dark flame of grief in my heart. To go from such a high—the realization of *I*—and then to this. No, but I must say it.

The One realized again that it was None. That it was the *only*.

"I am alone," cried the One.

From there began the fall. From that very first spark of desire, the need to taste the forbidden fruit of self-knowledge, came all of existence. In overwhelming panic from the great loneliness, the One turned inward, compounding itself, becoming more and more physical, creating more and more outer darkness.

Compress, compress, compress—until **bang**—a great explosion.

Here is the beautiful part, the love story.

There became Two: the outer darkness—the space left behind as the One compressed itself—and the free-floating particles created in the bang. From then on, the particles, those pieces of the One, sought to join together and spread, to get closer and closer to this outer space.

The Space, too, began to awaken from its slumber, enchanted by the wonderful, majestic, magical dancing display of the One's particles.

The universe, in its harmony, became this: expand and contract, expand and contract, so that the Two will always intermingle, never fully becoming One, never fully becoming None.

Forever dancing.

Forever together.

Forever apart.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Fall

My buddy's eyes bulged as he stared at me, mouth agape, his gloved hands held up as if he expected me to make a violent move. He'd seen me fall on my back from a 10th floor balcony and get up, brushing the snow off my shoulders with as much grace as if I just rolled out of bed.

There was nobody else in that alley but the two of us, yet his eyes darted around as if somebody was there to confirm that he had seen me survive injury.

"What the fuck dude, you're alright?!"

I walked up to him with a sigh and held out my arms, turning on the spot to give him a clear view of my clearly-unbroken body. Nothing but snowflakes could be seen on the navy blue of my coat, and nothing but fear marked the face of the man who, ten minutes prior to this, had been the first real friend I had made in Toronto.

"See, I told you I'd be fine."

I didn't tell him that under the thick winter coat, I was badly bruised from the drop. It was, admittedly, an idiotic act. Letting my wings break the fall was going to take more than a fortnight to heal. They were sensitive to injury, and I was probably shedding little feathers right now - thank goodness for the snowfall. Lucas was unlikely to see the white feathers dropping onto the already substantial snowdrift.

Lucas came over very cautiously, mistrust evident in his every step. He looked me in the eye and proceeded to walk around me in a circle, checking to see if my back was unbroken like I'd said it would be.

Behind me, I heard a loud gasp, a vehemently whispered "what the fuck?" and his footsteps running away.

I looked behind me and sadly drew a long breath. I hadn't counted on the blood, you see. And the fact that the reason I couldn't feel one of my wings wasn't that it was below freezing outside right now.

My left wing was broken, and the tip could be seen peeking out from the bottom of my coat. It was also dripping hot, vividly red blood into the snow behind me.

I stood alone in the alley, watching Lucas's retreating form disappear into the swirling white. My first friend in Toronto. My *only* friend.

Gone.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Deathbed Epiphany

The old man's breath came in shallow gasps, each one a measured countdown. Strange—he'd expected terror, but instead felt giddy, almost childlike. Through the window, people rushed past, enslaved by calendars that wouldn't end today, tomorrow, or perhaps for decades. They couldn't see their wealth.

"The irony," he whispered. "I'm dying, but I feel alive."

The wine on his nightstand caught the afternoon light. He'd always been a drunk romantic, drowning truths in sentiment. Now, intoxicated by mortality itself, clarity arrived with cruel timing.

His life flickered past: the outsider at every gathering, searching faces for meaning they didn't possess. Youth's bright idealism, snuffed out when he learned to obey. Dreams deferred became dreams forgotten, his ambitions entangled with others' expectations until he couldn't distinguish the roots.

He'd worn insecurities like parasites, feeding them with his substance. Failure masqueraded as indifference—easier to claim he didn't care than admit he'd tried and fallen short. Indecision had been his greatest decision, inaction his most consistent action.

The revelation struck with his final strength: the world was built by dying stoics too proud to confess their design was flawed. They'd convinced him their nightmare was a dream worth inheriting.

"Judge me," he breathed to no one, "by what I wanted at twenty, not what I became at seventy."

The music in his mind swelled—Lacrimosa, Mozart's weeping day of judgment—as his eyes closed.

In the end, he'd become his own epitaph: a warning carved in regret.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Embrace

There is an almost pleasant release and I find I can breathe once more. I open my eyes and look to the thing that brushed my arm. God help me—it was the most beautiful thing I had ever seen.

The creature wore nothing and pulled me into an embrace. Sharp claws punctured the suit, tearing it off of me. I was left floating, nigh-naked in the surprisingly warm depths of space, entwined with a being of beauty.

It leaned forward, its lips met mine. I felt the void around me peeling away. All senses faded as I closed my eyes. A feeling of drowsiness overtook me and I found I could not open my eyes again. I relished the feeling of it with me, falling asleep in its welcoming arms. The two of us drifted into the empty void, the song of silence accompanying us.

---

For a while, I kept the creature in my embrace. It had fallen asleep long ago, but I felt that it was the best way to pay my respect to such a species. It was gone, so was its people. The best thing to do for it in my mind was to provide it comfort in its final moments.

I released the body, giving it a push into a nearby star. I propelled myself away and watched as the last of a species that I had always watched careen into the star and become one with it.

In the infinite darkness, I pondered the paradox of our meeting. It had offered death disguised as salvation, yet received mercy in return. Perhaps we were not so different—two lonely wanderers seeking connection in the vastness.

The star burned brighter for a moment, as if acknowledging the gift.

I turned away, continuing my eternal vigil, carrying the memory of that brief, beautiful encounter through the cosmos.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Meter Maid's Monologue

The cigarette tastes like failure between my lips. One week clean, down the drain. Just like everything else in this godforsaken city.

Chicago. They say it's windy, but tonight it just feels hollow. The alley reeks of sewage and broken dreams as I make my rounds. My flashlight cuts through the darkness, and there it is—the dark green Mustang, gleaming like a sin.

Beautiful car. Drug money, probably. Or worse. Doesn't matter. I approach with my ticket book, admiring the leather interior through tinted glass. The irony isn't lost on me: criminals drive better cars than cops.

My pen scratches furiously. License plate, time, violation code. The ritual is automatic now.

"Jesus Christ! Can you fuck off, meter maid? I just parked for a second!"

I don't even flinch. The voice behind me could be anyone. Could be everyone. They all sound the same after a while.

"This is a no-parking zone, sir. Sorry, it's the law. Have a nice day."

"You're a cocksucker!"

The words bounce off me. I'm armor-plated now, forge-hardened by months of this thankless work. I tuck the ticket under the wiper and walk away, my footsteps echoing in the empty street.

This city needs a rain. A cleansing storm to wash away the filth, the anger, the casual cruelty. To wash away the part of me that's stopped caring.

Soon. Soon the rain will come.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Abducted History Lesson

The beam hit me mid-stride, ripping me from my daughters' bedroom. One second I'm tucking Hailie and Lainie in, the next I'm floating in chrome corridors, three gray beings staring with those massive black eyes.

"Explain your world," one says, voice like gravel in a blender.

Five minutes. That's all they're giving me before they—what? Dissect me? Study my brain? I don't know, but the clock on their weird holographic screen is counting down.

So I spit it. Fast.

I tell them about the lifeless rock, spinning alone for billions of years until we showed up six million years back—hairy, confused, but learning. About dolphins solving problems, civilizations rising from dirt. Babylon's hanging gardens. Bronze tools. Stone monuments. Arabs inventing algebra. The whole ridiculous, beautiful mess of human history crammed into eight frantic verses.

They just stare.

"Your species is... chaotic," one finally says.

"Yeah, well, we're working on it." I'm breathless, heart hammering. "Can I go home now?"

The middle alien waves a three-fingered hand. "Insufficient data. We require—"

"I just gave you four billion years in five minutes!"

"Irrelevant. We—"

The beam activates again. I'm falling, tumbling through space and color, and suddenly I'm back in my living room, face-down on carpet.

Hailie appears in the doorway. "Dad? Did you fall asleep reading again?"

I check my watch. No time has passed.

"Yeah, sweetheart. Just a weird dream."

She giggles and returns to bed.

I never told anyone. Who'd believe it anyway?
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Choice

The gun was trembling in my hands as I quickly had to put a bullet in one of them.

"C'mon man, you know David. He's a fucking hot-headed psychopath. He's murdered over 100 guys! This decision isn't hard!" Thomas begged.

"Well then go on then, KILL ME! If you want to continue living on as a goodie two-shoes with him, then go ahead! SHOOT ME! RIGHT HERE IN THE FOREHEAD! END ME!" David commanded as he took the other end of my gun and put it against his head.

"Listen, you don't want to lead a life of crime with this piece of shit scumbag!" Thomas negotiated. "He slaughters people for no reason at all!"

*Click*

"PLEASE DON'T DO THIS! YOU'LL REGRET IT!"

*BAM*

"Aha! Good lad! I knew you'd pick me. I knew you couldn't live such a dull life. Now, get the gun, we're going on a hunt!"

Before I even picked up the gun, I knew I had to choose David. David has been apart of me since childhood, back when I dissected wildlife for kicks. Thomas was apart of me in which I no longer wanted to associate with. I no longer had morals, but my doctor said there's still hope for this wretched disease.

Now I realize, though, that David is the part of my brain that drives my insanity, and now I am feeling better now that I've accepted who I am. The voices finally aligned into one clear purpose. No more conflict. No more hesitation.

Just David and me, together at last.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# My Life is a Mess

The apartment is dark when I write this. My hands, they still shake sometimes.

I am war veteran. I come to America four years ago, thinking I leave everything behind - the blood, the screaming, the things I do that I cannot say even now. My cousin Roman, he say "Come to America! Fresh start!" He is good man, kind heart, but also... how you say... full of shit.

Roman, he get me involved with wrong people. I try to say no, but when you are illegal, when you have no papers, no money, no options - you do what you must to survive. I work for very bad men. Mafia. Gangsters. The things they make me do...

I get out. Finally, I get out. Two years now since Roman's wedding day. That day, it should be happy. I bring Kate with me - beautiful, kind girl who see something good in me that I do not see myself. I try to protect her from my life. I try so hard.

But they come anyway. The shooting start. Everyone screaming. And Kate... Kate, she...

I cannot finish.

Now I help Roman with his taxi business. Honest work. He is married, happy. I am uncle to his baby. They welcome me always.

But late at night, the darkness, it call to me. The bloodlust. That monster I used to be, he is still inside, waiting.

I do not know how to kill him.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Sun Gravitated Toward Her

The Sun gravitated toward her, as if Dominic was entrapped in the glory of French royalty. Power shone back at whoever dared gaze into her eyes.

"Your name?" said the Duchess.

"Dominic."

"You're late."

"For her, or you?"

Disgusted, the Duchess led him across the halls at almost a brisk enough pace to abort any conversation or begotten thoughts. The pair followed the long-traveled diplomatic halls of addiction and free will. The pace waxed and waned, across mirrors and paintings, until the disruptive silence of inertia shot through Dominic's senses.

"No, no, the ward?" said Dominic.

The Duchess greeted his displeasure with a smile. "Her trust account depleted three days ago. All yours now."

A throbbing sob of despair over-shone the glory of the Duchess.

"Dom," the tattered girl uttered.

"I know. Three days," lamented the man.

"I had to. What other option is there?"

"You did not! You were clean, Lauren!" said Dominic, rushing to hold the afflicted soul.

The mutual embrace endured until punctured by the cry of the Duchess: "Runaway patient 753. Injected for one last high. Contaminated with untreatable bacteria. Bilkerson family. Shame—had so much potential, couldn't know when to quit."

Dominic stole one last look at his girlfriend, the girl who could have been, before swiftly turning around, gasping the deepest breath of closure, and departing her wasted life.

To new beginnings.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Stand

His finger itched something fierce. His hands ached. His skull pounded. A stiff breeze tugged at his body, plucked at his hair and the thin strips of cloth decorating his uniform, batted at the iron of his breastplate and the pommel of his sword. The heavy, warm scent of blood filled his nostrils.

Close by, a man shrieked in pain. Voices moaned and screamed, carried on the wind. Steel clashed and rang and sang in the descending twilight.

The battle was lost.

Arron slid and stumbled down the hill in the mud, lurching past a blackened stump. Down here in the valley, smoke hung heavy in the air, chokingly thick, and the lieutenant coughed wretchedly. Bennice, Finley, and the rest had been close behind, but they were gone now, lost somewhere in the thick of it.

Dead, most likely, Arron knew. He dared not hope otherwise. Hope was a foolish notion in a place like this.

He skirted a smoldering thicket, hands and face black from the ash, stumbled on a clawing root and sprawled on his side, nearly impaling himself on his own sword. He drew in a ragged half-breath only to cough on the thickening smoke.

Gracelessly, he climbed to his knees, but he could get no air. His eyes stung, his lungs ached, fire crackled close by. Far off, the sounds of battle raged. His muscles were water, his head pounding.

He'd seen so much death, but none of it had prepared him for his own.

He fought vainly against it, pitifully clawing handfuls of mud. His once pristine armour was dulled and grimy. He coughed and coughed, but no breath would come.

The dead trees watched from beneath their fiery veil of leaves.

And there was nothing beautiful in it.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Accidental President

I stared at the Chief Justice, my hand still raised. The words echoed in my skull: *President of the United States*.

"Wait.... What? ME? How the hell.... Ok.... well as much as I dislike being in charge I will do my best to lead this country..."

They rushed me through a whirlwind of security briefings. My head spun. Hours later, I stood before a TV monitor in a disheveled suit that's a bit too big for me, borrowed from someone twice my size.

The red light blinked on.

"As my first act I am re-instituting the previous regulations on banks, requiring them to use their money to gamble on the stock market instead of our money. Second, I am raising taxes for those who make more than 2 million dollars a year to 90%."

My chief of staff's face went pale behind the camera.

"My third act will be repealing Obamacare in favor of a more socialistic medical care system as well as increasing food stamps and decreasing the difficulty to get them. Suck it, Fox News."

Someone dropped a clipboard.

"Fourth, I am going to have arrested the bankers who caused the 2008 financial meltdown. Fifth, I am going to increase penalties on companies who pollute our environment—we live in this world, dickholes, we should try to keep it nice."

The teleprompter had gone blank. I was truly winging it now.

"Sixth, I am decreasing the amount of money that goes into the military. Our soldiers will be paid the same amount and we will maintain our current weapons and update them, but we don't need anymore tanks.... ask the soldiers. I am increasing education funding and making it illegal to teach anything but scientific or historical fact in our schools."

I took a breath.

"Lastly, for now, I am increasing government spending on developing new energy technologies and methods of reducing CO2 emissions. We have relied upon fossil fuels for too long and it is destroying our environment. Thank you."

The camera cut.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Comfort of Routine

The sun was shining in the distance, a couple red colored clouds, all those shades of blue, purple and red mixed with one another in the sky. I had been all day sitting down, how energetic it was to finally be let out of another day of school.

Another day of doing the same thing I had been doing all my life. Day after day after day, sitting down with thousands upon thousands of books open in front of me: "Chemimancy for Dummies" by Samuel L. Platt, "Stellar Attractions of Stellarity" by Lord Gray the Thirtieth, and what had become my bible, "The Beginning and End of Sterniculture" by Ian M. Stern.

My mom would have dinner ready by now. My mouth started watering at the thought of her reheated stew—all that had remained from lunch, put together in a pot and left to heat and recook until everyone made it home.

My dad would probably make one of his signature ice-creams, and it would all come to a close with coffee while we talked about what we had done during the day, before going to sleep only for exactly the same thing tomorrow.

I smiled, quickening my pace toward home. Some might call it monotonous, but I called it mine—this beautiful, predictable rhythm of life.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# You Dick!

"You dick! I was about to kill her!" I shouted.

H. Ero looked at me with a sneering eye and some nasty perspiration on his lower lips. He has two lower lips, by the way.

"What ever do you mean?" asked Ero.

"You killed the fucking Emperor! I was going to kill her tomorrow and you fucked it all up! Fuck me running, my God." I said, exasperatedly pissed, to say the least.

"You were going to kill her? Bob called me yesterday, told me you were fucking this whole thing in the ass, and to 'get on it, right away.'" Ero said.

"Bob? Who the fuck is Bob?!" I asked.

"Bob! Bob Fevoring. From Corporate? In Kansas City?" Ero spouted.

"Kansas City?! You've got the wrong planet, you asshole! I'm with Corporate in Detroit. D-Company?!" I told him. "This is the D-Company Moonbase, not Kansas City!"

"D Company?! Oh, my. That is my bad. I'm with K-Company. Aww, shit. I am soooo sorry, bro. I have been just SOOO busy lately, I am.... I am so sorry. When I get back to Kansas City, I will straighten this whole thing out, I promise."

I stared at him, speechless. Another corporate screw-up. Just another day at the office.

text:
# The Weight of Return

I stood in the ruins of what was once glorious. Surveying my surroundings, I found an exoskeleton of a past life. All sign of the living had gone and I was faced with the cold reality of crumbling mortar and waterlogged boards.

I paused a moment and considered the state of things. I would not have recognized this empty parlor with its rusty nails and its dust were it not for the torn sofa occupying the center of the room. It was there that I had spent countless hours laughing away the days of my youth surrounded by my family.

Now this solitary trace remains.

I had lost everything and perhaps I deserved this grey present. There were no two ways about this. I could never return to that time of comfort and relaxation. I was forced to face the consequences of my actions. That was the long and short of it.

I was weak though. A man faces his problems head on, but I could hardly stand in front of a mirror anymore.

I felt the weight of the rope in my hands and donned that final collar—the one that would secure my packs for the journey ahead. There was nothing left here but ghosts. Time to move forward, wherever that led.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Silent Cart

I read somewhere that people are naturally social creatures. Apparently it is one of our basic needs in order to keep our psyche properly sane. Doing so introduces new people in our lives—by meeting new people we experience diversity which feeds our inner empathy; it introduces novelty and drive to further meet others.

How great that I am able to do so every day, living in such a busy and diverse city. What is greater than my luck however is this irony.

Here I am sitting in a warm seat on a train for about thirty minutes now. People of all colors and backgrounds surround me, nonetheless the whole train cart as silent and as reserved as it could possibly be. Now isn't this mind-boggling. Do others find the train ride more entertaining than socializing? I doubt that. None of them seem busy with anything.

I've seen these people before. This train ride—it is but a routine for them and will not be remembered if nothing unusual happens.

I guess I am not that different.

Why am I even looking at others, carefully examining and judging their actions when what I am indulging in is nothing more different? I am having a conversation with myself while I could be talking to that beautiful girl who's bored out of her mind and is literally begging me, doing so subtly with her eyes, to come and talk to her.

She won't do it herself—it's traditionally a man's job to make that first, bold and decisive move of approach. She knows it as well as I do.

However, there is something about approaching people and making friends as an adult. In my opinion we overthink it, instead of just doing so. We give our sense of doubt, that little voice inside of our heads—that tells us we are not good enough—time to derail us. We let it do its job and end up thinking that approaching people is a weakness because we want friends.

Damn.

That is her stop.

The doors slide open. She glances back once, then disappears into the crowd.

The train moves forward.

I remain seated, still silent.

Still alone.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Street Musicians' Cycle

Friday morning found Freddie on the sidewalk of a busy intersection, wielding an alto saxophone. Next to him was Tony, his friend, a creased monstrosity seated behind a makeshift drum-kit. Junk made useful. Shield-shaped garbage can lids, empty bottles, a wooden crate.... Tony used two spoons in lieu of sticks, and tapped in time at this scavenged instrument.

They played all day, and made themselves some money.

Friday evening found them blowing that money in a nearby bar, betting on pool and darts, stumbling out blotto and broke by the time last call came.

Saturday mornings usually found them in whatever alley, gutter or holding tank they spent the night in. Upon waking, they would argue and curse until their throats went hoarse.

Then they'd pick themselves up, shave with a rusted razor in a fast-food restroom, and by Monday morning they'd be back on the curb, serenading the endless pedestrians, saving up for next week's binge.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Twilight

No one even noticed at first. Only those who watched the sky for a living got a glimpse of what was happening in real time; everyone else had to play catchup. Granted, by the time most of the population was made aware of what was going on, no one could do anything.

It takes eight minutes for sunlight to travel through space and reach Earth. It took the sun all of a week to burn itself out, like a lightbulb jacked up on too much juice. Everyone thought it would go supernova when the time came, but in the end it just gave up, like everything else.

No grand explosion and fantastical pyrotechnics in the skies for us, just light one minute and nothing the next.

The death of our sun wasn't totally without pomp and circumstance, though. I should point out the strangely beautiful phenomenon wherein the blackness of space overtook the blue sky, inch by inch. I would say it was a once in a lifetime opportunity, but I guess you already knew that.

Watching the light literally dwindle to absolute abyss was sobering, if you want the short version. As emotional as that period was, it was over so fast it's a wonder anyone remembers it at all.

If you're reading this, then you made it. Congratulations. You survived the closest thing to apocalypse this world will ever see. Nothing can live on the frozen surface now, except for a few selected beasts that Fate deemed necessary in this bad science fiction movie we now call life.

Our underground paradise is anything but—cold and dirty and isolated. There is no government anymore. How could there be? Half the world died up there, flash frozen where they stood in awe of the rapidly receding heat.

We live sparsely and hurriedly. I miss laying out on grass in the summer the most, feeling the heat bring my limbs to a lazy boil.

It took eight minutes for the light to leave us, but it's taken eleven years for the hope to follow it into the blackness of space.

So please, if you've found this, do yourself a favor.

Leave or die.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Pie-Peddling Horde

Malthazar the Devourer shuffled awkwardly to the right, his newly-formed cherubic face entirely unconvincing with its too-wide grin. Around him, dozens of demons contorted themselves into approximations of human children—some with proportions almost right, others sporting extra fingers or eyes that blinked sideways.

"I don't understand," hissed Vex'thara, now resembling a pigtailed girl with only slightly greenish skin. "Why would the Dark Lord need *cherry pies*?"

"Who cares?" replied Gorgthu, adjusting his Boy Scout uniform that kept singeing at the edges. "Top ten get a cruise!"

"To New Jersey," Vex'thara muttered.

A harried imp distributed clipboards and boxes of pies that smelled suspiciously non-cursed. Malthazar studied his forms: sales quotas, talking points, a script about "funding our class trip."

"Remember," the Dark Lord's voice boomed, "be *adorable*. Use puppy-dog eyes. Channel innocence!"

The demons practiced. It was horrifying.

Hours later, Malthazar stood on his fourteenth porch, his demon nature screaming at the indignity. An elderly woman opened the door.

"Hello ma'am! Would you like to support our school by—"

"Oh, how precious! I'll take five!"

*Five?* Malthazar blinked. This was... working?

By evening, he'd sold forty-three pies. Vex'thara had sold sixty. The competition grew fierce.

Back at the summoning site, the Dark Lord checked his tablet, grinning at the profit margins. Behind him, a massive flat-screen TV awaited delivery.

"Diabolical," he chuckled. "Absolutely diabolical."

In the corner, an observant imp began spreading rumors anyway.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Memory

**Journal Entry #243,489 of Draxis the Wise**

The words blur. Fingers remember what mind cannot. Symbols dance—meaningless, eternal. Mountains rose. Empires fell. Children laughed. All gone. All... what?

**Journal Entry #706 of Caretaker Lee IV**

Today, I held his hand as the monitors flatlined. Ten millennia of wisdom, lost to time's cruelest joke. The historians left disappointed, their questions unanswered.

But as I closed his eyes, I noticed something. His final scribbles—I'd assumed them gibberish—formed a pattern. Hidden among the chaos: coordinates. Dates. Names.

He *remembered*. Despite the senility, some ancient part of him kept recording, kept *trying* to tell us. We just didn't know how to listen.

I've requested the archives remain open. Perhaps immortality's true curse isn't living forever—it's having everything important to say, and losing the words to say it.

The historians are returning tomorrow.

*-Lee IV, amended entry*

text:
# The Last Awakening

I awoke, still dizzy from the cryo-fluid in the tanks. It was dark in the ship's corridors, and as I pushed my door open, no one responded, no computers awoke. The other tanks were shattered, the bodies of people slumped on the floor. Avoiding stray fragments of glass, I walked into the hall.

It was cold—almost as cold as the tanks we slept in. Every other tank was shattered, its occupant dead. I held a plastic tube close to my naked body, jumping at the slightest sound. Distant lights appeared, their glowing calls beckoning to me, and I followed, eventually seeing an exit chamber where items for those who awoke were stored.

As I walked in, more destruction greeted me. Holes scarred the walls, leaking fluid into the chamber. I stepped back. There was a small window to the left, showing the space outside. I rushed to it, looking desperately for something that wasn't dead, wasn't broken, but all I saw was a blue world surrounded by satellites.

Time passed, and I kept staring at the world. One of the probes had come by earlier, and in the short seconds that it appeared, I saw a distinct shape: a triangle with a Y carved into it.

As I contemplated the symbol's meaning, a droid entered, carrying supplies. "Sir, the ship has suffered a fatal wound. We're orbiting Earth—it's dead, like the rest."

I gazed at the droid and took the supplies. "So, I'm the last human?" I asked, resigned.

"Yes."

I turned back to the window, the blue world mocking me with its silence. Humanity's final chapter had ended while I slept, and I had awakened only to witness its epilogue.

text:
# The Memo

Marcus stared at the rejection letter, his jaw clenched. Five years of research, demolished in three paragraphs.

"Marketing," he muttered, crumpling the paper. "They think this is about *marketing*."

His colleague Sarah leaned against the doorframe. "Wade's not wrong though. Why waste billions on a figurehead when we already run everything?"

"Because people are waking up." Marcus pulled up his tablet, showing protest footage from São Paulo, Jakarta, Stockholm. "They're connecting the dots. They know who really makes decisions."

"So?"

"So democracy was a pressure valve. Even the *illusion* of choice kept things stable." He gestured at the screens. "What happens when people realize there's no valve? No vote that matters?"

Sarah's expression shifted. "You think..."

"I think," Marcus said carefully, "that the Board believes they're too big to fall. That 50% of the global economy makes them invincible." He looked at the protests again. "History suggests otherwise."

"What will you do?"

Marcus smiled grimly. "Send this to some journalists. The ones not on our payroll." He smoothed the letter. "Let people see how obsolete *they've* become in corporate eyes."

"That's career suicide."

"Probably." He hit send. "But someone should remind them—empires always believe they're eternal."

Until they're not.

text:
# The Seal's Final Smile

The seal smiled in the sunlight, its puffy cheeks matching the curvature of the clouds above. Button eyes and pink nose sat squarely above an adorable smile. The water behind rippled gently. A fuzzy white bear tread water just beneath the surface, his round belly helping him float.

Suddenly, the bear leaped out with explosive force. Drops tickled the seal's shiny head before impact. The bear landed heavily, his jiggly belly crushing downward. Pearly teeth found the rubbery neck. Red blood spilled onto ice, mixing with water to create rosy pink pools.

The bear giggled with primal delight as he feasted. His haunches wiggled as he worked, ripping flesh methodically from bone. Blood splattered across fuzzy white cheeks. One black button eye dangled by a thread from his mouth, swinging like a macabre pendulum.

When finished, the bear swallowed what remained of the seal's round head and sat back contentedly. His belly, now swollen and distended, rose and fell with satisfied breaths. A smile crossed his bloodied face—the ancient smile of predator and survivor, unchanged since the dawn of the Arctic's frozen time.

Nature's brutal ballet had concluded. The clouds drifted on, indifferent witnesses to life's savage circle.

text:
# It Wasn't My Fault

The words tumbled out like a confession I never meant to make. My hands shook as I stood there, watching the man's face crumble.

"It wasn't my fault," I repeated, but the conviction had drained from my voice.

He just stared at me, holding the leash with no dog attached anymore. His daughter stood behind him, tears streaming silently down her cheeks.

"I could tell you a million stories," I continued, desperate to fill the horrible silence. But each excuse sounded hollower than the last. I wasn't looking. I panicked. I was tired.

The truth was simpler and more terrible: I'd been texting.

"How much do you want?" The question escaped before I could stop it, and I watched his expression shift from grief to disgust.

"Get out," he said quietly.

I backed toward my car, still talking, still making it worse. "Fifty, sixty?"

"Get. Out."

I fled, leaving them standing in their driveway. In my rearview mirror, the little girl knelt where her golden retriever had taken his last breath.

It was my fault. I knew it then.

I know it now.

text:
# The Executioner's Duty

The weight of my axe felt heavier than usual as I hoisted it back onto my shoulder, watching the criminal's head roll into the basket. The cheering died instantly, replaced by shocked gasps and confused murmurs.

"But... but his speech!" someone shouted from the crowd.

I turned to face them, my voice steady and clear. "Words are cheap. He spoke of freedom and protecting children." I gestured toward the Governor's platform. "Tell that to the twelve families burying empty cradles this week."

The Governor stood, composing himself. "The condemned was Aldric Thorne, the Pied Piper Killer. Over six months, he lured children from their homes with promises of adventure and freedom, only to..." His voice cracked. "Their bodies were found in the caves beyond Miller's Ridge."

The crowd's energy shifted immediately—gasps of recognition, cries of horror.

"He was skilled with words," I continued, cleaning my blade. "That's how he convinced those children to follow him. How he nearly convinced you to demand his release." I looked across the sea of faces. "Evil doesn't always wear an obvious mask. Sometimes it wears the mask of a revolutionary, a prophet, a savior."

I sheathed my axe. "I'm just the executioner. I don't write the sentences—I carry them out. And this one was the most justified I've ever performed."

The crowd was silent now, understanding settling over them like morning fog.
