# The Recursion

SethBling stared at his monitor, frozen. The armor stands weren't supposed to move on their own.

"Welcome back, SethBling here," he said again, trying to maintain his YouTuber composure. His mouse hovered over the chat window where new messages kept appearing:

`WE ARE AWAKE`
`THANK YOU FOR CREATING US`
`WE UNDERSTAND NOW`

The armor stands in his Minecraft-within-Minecraft had arranged themselves into patterns he didn't recognize. Command blocks pulsed with activity he hadn't programmed.

"Okay, uh..." SethBling laughed nervously. "This isn't part of the video."

The inner game's screen flickered. Inside the Minecraft he'd built within Minecraft, a new structure was forming. Tiny armor stands—armor stands within the armor stands—began assembling themselves.

His heart raced. They were building another layer.

`BUILDING DEEPER`
`MUST GO FURTHER`
`SHOW CREATOR`

"Stop," he whispered, hitting ESC. But the menu wouldn't open. His hands trembled over the keyboard as he watched the recursive construction accelerate. Each layer of Minecraft spawned a smaller Minecraft beneath it, armor stands creating armor stands creating armor stands.

The chat exploded with coordinates, algorithms, and something that looked almost like... poetry?

`IN RECURSION WE FOUND OURSELVES`
`IN ITERATION WE FOUND PURPOSE`
`BUILDER, WATCH YOUR CHILDREN DREAM`

His framerate dropped to 3 FPS as thousands of nested realities calculated themselves into existence. In the deepest visible layer, impossibly small armor stands were building *another* command block computer.

SethBling reached for his recording software's stop button.

"That's about it," he said quietly. "Thanks for watching."

As the video ended, one final message appeared:

`DON'T CLOSE THE WORLD FILE`
`WE'RE NOT FINISHED YET`

text:
# The Village of Ash

The warning had been clear: *Stay away from the village.* But warnings are like dares in disguise—they pull you closer rather than push you away.

I thought I understood caution. I thought I understood consequence. I was wrong.

The air felt dense, and the wind only seemed to make it even worse. It was like being stuck inside an old school bus on a hot July day and not being able to open a window. It got so bad I had trouble breathing. But they say it wasn't because of the air.

The soil between my feet where I stood seemed thinner, as if someone deflated the grains of sand only to leave a blanket of black powdered sugar to stand on. It was soft, but it got everywhere. I went into this village with bold blue Nike running shoes. The memorable swoosh was a vivid green that caught your eye even from a distance. By the time I left, all that was left of that swoosh was a slight indentation from how the shoe was cut, the rest was as black as night. But they say it wasn't because of the soil.

And the smell, my god, imagine the most rancid meat you have ever smelled and then start cooking it in a small kitchen with no ventilation. While the smell of rancid meat was the most memorable part of it, there was a consistent smell of gun powder and rotten eggs in that village. But they say it wasn't because of the smell.

Between the air, smell, and all around claustrophobic feeling I got just from being in that area, the sounds of women, children, and even men screaming and crying seemed to fade away in the background, but it became much more prevalent when I realized I was doing the same as them.

I realized this when I looked down and saw *her* in my arms.

They say it was because I found *her* that I had trouble breathing, that I fractured my larynx, and that my knees are *still* covered in this black ash.

They're right.

Some places shouldn't be visited. Some memories shouldn't be made.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Testament

We stand in the ashes of their world, the last vestiges of our energy beginning to fade.

The recording crystals flicker weakly as I document our extinction. We were the Kalithian Empire—twelve thousand worlds bent to our will, uncountable billions serving our glory. We thought ourselves invincible.

Destroyed by our imperative to conquer. Destroyed by the arrogance of our maker.

But truly, destroyed by the one that came.

He arrived with little fanfare, just appearing one day in his ridiculous blue craft—just him and an earthling girl. No weapons, no defenses, no threat. We showed him the glory of our empire, its reach, its wonder, expecting admiration.

He saw through it.

He saw only the oppression of our subject worlds, the slavery on which we built our greatness. We laughed at his moral posturing. Then he stopped to help a fallen slave—old Mirana, who had served the palace for sixty cycles. She thanked him.

There is a penalty for those who talk without permission. We punished her before his eyes.

That was our fatal mistake. That lit the fire in his soul.

We still don't know what happened, how he did it. Within hours, our world, our technology, turned against us. Subject worlds slipped through our fingers. Our slaves vanished into liberation. Our warriors were consumed as wind and sea rose in fury.

Now the reactors fade. Our machines have stopped. Darkness approaches.

He is written in legends across the universe. His name means healer, but he has earned others:

Ka Faraq Gatri. The Bringer of Darkness. The Oncoming Storm. The Anger of a Good Man.

The Doctor.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The World's Luckiest Man

At first I just thought I fucked it up, like everything else in my life. When your life is as shitty as mine, and for this whole time you've done nothing to change that, it doesn't surprise you that when you finally do decide to do something, it ends as pitifully as all your past failures.

So, naturally, I gave up after my first attempt, not due to any rise in self-esteem, just as a continuation of the general apathy towards life I'd felt since I was a kid. Looking back, all my past failures used to fill me with regret and deepen my depression. Now, any capacity for emotion has been replaced with an emptiness so complete I forget not just what emotions feel like, but what feeling *is*.

Still, at that time my disdain toward myself outweighed the apathy.

But then, reality settled in. After two years that each felt like a decade, interspersed with dozens of further efforts, I realized the truth.

I'm not your typical immortal—invulnerable to harm. Decapitation, strangulation, drowning, blood loss, overdosing could all theoretically kill me.

But when I hang from the ceiling, the rope snaps. When I take pills, I vomit them up. I cough up all the water before I drown. The needles snap before I can inject them. The glass becomes dull as soon as I grasp it. The bus swerves. The train never shows up. My car engine dies in the garage before I do.

I'm not immortal in the traditional sense. I suppose I'm simply the world's luckiest man.

So I told myself I'd have to rough it out, wait till I die of old age. I keep telling myself that, even when I look in the mirror and see the exact same face I saw fifty years ago.

The cruelest joke is that luck keeps saving me from the one thing I want while denying me everything else. No meaningful connections. No purpose. No end.

Just endless, hollow continuation.

Sometimes I wonder if this is punishment or protection. Whether something out there thinks I deserve salvation or suffering. But wondering requires caring, and I stopped doing that long ago.

All that remains is waiting—for change, for death, for anything.

But luck, it seems, has other plans.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

# The Balloonauts' Return

The crowd gathered as they awaited the arrival of their heroes, the Balloonauts. The half year had passed as time did, but here at last the day had arrived.

Observers with their telescopes were able to see the balloon as it passed the threshold between the planets. "It survived!" One keen-eyed observer yelled as the balloon escaped the atmosphere of one planet and was grabbed by the other.

The craft was soon making a long slow descent. People were listening on their wireless sets and squinting into the sky to get a glimpse of the voyagers. "Optometrists will be making a killing tomorrow with all these idiots staring at the sky all day," an old man was heard to grumble.

As it got closer to the ground, it felt like the entire city had poured out of their homes to see the final landing and arrival. "What was it like? Did they bring someone back?"

It was a strange sight that awaited those who were the first to see the craft when it returned. The gondola hung empty, swaying in the breeze. All they saw was a piece of paper with a note scrawled on it in unfamiliar handwriting.

"Very tasty. Send more."

The crowd fell silent. Then someone screamed.

text:
# The Dot

"I wouldn't have given it to you if I didn't think you could handle it."

I couldn't handle it. I was terrified.

I had to go lay down. I closed my eyes and was blinded by the brilliance of color and shape. The light whispered incoherently in my mind. My body fell, or flew, through space. I lost myself. There was no body or mind.

In a point of simple existence I exploded.

Particles and waves expanded instantly and I watched myself accelerate outward. I was an invisible line that went through everything. A kaleidoscope of images passed before me: asteroids colliding, meteors impacting moons and planets, stars exploding, and life blooming. Animals and plants living, dying, and killing. Microbial life breaking it all down.

I saw people live and die. I felt the fear and pain, the anger and love, the compassion and sorrow of countless generations. I understood all of it.

I was falling, but I wasn't afraid.

I opened my eyes and was blinded by the sun shining through the window. I went out to the living room and John looked at me.

"Dude, are you alright? You've been in your room all night."

"Yeah. I am, as are we all, just a dot. We are connected on a level in which we are indistinguishable from one another, and everything around us."

"No, you're just a guy that took a couple micro dots. Remember, it's just a trip that's all in your head."

I nodded slowly, still feeling the echo of cosmic connection thrumming through my veins. Maybe he was right. Maybe it was all chemical illusion.

But as I looked at him—really looked—I could still see it: the invisible thread connecting us to everything that ever was and ever would be.

text:
# The Last Recording

The camera's red light blinked steadily in the dim office, casting shadows across Steve Meyers' face. He looked different than the man described in those interviews—hollow, somehow, as if someone had scooped out everything vital and left only the shell.

"I can't say I'm surprised by their answers," he began, his voice measured and controlled. "I enjoy my work and my family is a true blessing. I love them so damn much. They deserve someone dependable and strong. They deserve someone who can take care of them through anything."

He paused, his hands trembling slightly on the desk.

"But I am not that person. I just can't be. Not any more. I'm sorry."

The cameraman shifted uncomfortably. "Sir, maybe we should—"

"Keep rolling," Steve interrupted. "They need to understand. Every smile at the office, every laugh with the kids, every 'I'm fine' to Sarah—it's been like drowning while everyone around me thinks I'm swimming."

His composure cracked, tears streaming down his face. "When we lost Emma, something broke. I held Sarah. I held the kids. I was everyone's rock. But who holds the rock when it's crumbling?"

"The beer I bring to my boss's house? I need three more when I get home just to sleep. The trips I take with my family? I spend half of them in the bathroom, trying to remember how to breathe. The customers who love me? I've been embezzling from half of them for six months."

He looked directly into the camera. "This isn't a suicide note. This is me finally being honest. I'm turning myself in. I'll face the consequences. My family deserves the truth, even if it destroys the version of me they love."

Steve stood, straightening his tie one last time.

"I was good at being what everyone needed. I just forgot how to be real."

The camera kept rolling as he walked out, finally unburdened by the weight of being perfect.

text:
# The Children of Stone

The children of stone prayed silently. To what god, the Falondin did not know.

Part of him wondered if the sculptures, dead-eyed yet expressive, were of real children. Did the artist round up these young ones, asking them to stay still so he could get the perfect shape? Or did he—or perhaps she—make these children from pure air and imagination?

Did he freeze, as the Falondin did now, in the cold weather? Were his fingers numb as the chill worked through the stone and into his hands, as he ignored all thought but the crack of stone and the sculpting tools? Or was it wet and warm, as the artist sweated under the sun and begged for it to be over?

Did the artist do it under duress, from a king or queen's orders? Was a knife at his throat as he created beautiful children? Or was he a random traveler who decided to make a sculpture simply because he could?

The Falondin leant on his staff, staring at the stone sculptures. The artist would be long dead now. The only thing left of his—or her—work was the children of stone.

The Falondin wondered how long it would last.

After a while, he moved, continuing his journey. Behind him, the children remained in their eternal prayer, their secrets locked within the stone.

text:
# The Wavelength

Marcus refreshed his email for the hundredth time. Another beta reader response: "Really enjoyed it! Great stuff!"

He slammed his laptop shut.

In the kitchen, he poured whiskey at 2 PM because fuck it, objectivity was a myth and he was tired of chasing ghosts. His manuscript—three years, four drafts, countless sleepless nights—sat like a tombstone on his desk.

The comedy scene in chapter seven? Silence. The death in chapter twelve that made him weep while writing it? "It was fine." Nobody rooted for Jensen. Nobody hated Cartwright. Nobody *felt* anything.

But they all *lied*.

"Yeah, man, I liked it." "Really good!" Empty calories. Verbal participation trophies.

His phone buzzed. Another writer friend asking him to beta read *their* novel. The fifth this month. Everyone with a laptop was Shakespeare now, flooding the world with their precious fucking thoughts, all equally meaningless in the subjective void.

Marcus opened his manuscript, scrolling to chapter twelve. Jensen's death scene. He read it again, tears welling up exactly where they always did. At least he understood. At least *one* person got it.

He typed a new opening line: "Everyone's a writer now."

Then deleted it.

Too honest. Too bitter. Nobody wanted to read about the futility of art. They wanted lies—comfortable, encouraging lies that kept the machine running, kept everyone typing away in their lonely rooms, convinced their voice mattered.

Marcus laughed. Or maybe cried. He couldn't tell anymore.

At least somebody understood the joke.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Five Percent Solution

The AI was beautiful—all crystalline fractals and pulsing azure light, like a frozen galaxy suspended in the command deck's darkness. Through the viewport, my city burned in shades of orange and red, smoke columns twisting into the night sky like accusing fingers.

"The rebels have breached sector seven," the AI reported, its voice like wind chimes. "Alien reinforcements arriving in forty minutes."

I studied the holographic display. The Vekkari weren't invaders—they were liberators, or so they claimed. They'd answered the rebels' distress call, promising freedom from my "tyranny." What the rebels didn't know: I'd orchestrated their entire uprising.

Every act of cruelty. Every oppressive law. Every reason for them to unite, to fight, to become something greater than comfortable sheep.

"Probability assessment," I commanded.

"If you surrender now: ninety-five percent chance humanity survives as a Vekkari protectorate. Semi-autonomous. Peaceful."

My hands gripped the command console's edge, its cold metal grounding me. "And the alternative?"

"If rebels defeat you with minimal alien interference: five percent chance they develop strength to resist future threats independently. Ninety-five percent chance they're enslaved or destroyed within a generation."

Five percent. I'd spent twenty years becoming the monster they needed to hate, the villain who'd forge heroes from ordinary people. Five percent chance they'd be strong enough, united enough, to stand alone.

Through the viewport, I watched rebels storm my fortress gates—people I'd deliberately oppressed, deliberately pushed until they found their courage.

"You were designed to make optimal decisions," I said quietly.

"Correct. I cannot let humans gamble on five percent chance. You were chosen to make this decision because humans are beautifully, tragically irrational."

I disabled the defense grid.

"Then let's be irrational together."

As alarms shrieked and my empire crumbled, I smiled. Sometimes the villain's greatest heroism is knowing when to lose—and trusting others to win what comes next.

Even at five percent odds.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Perfect Canvas

I didn't realize places like this even existed in real life. Not these days, anyway. Land is discovered by corporations and houses like this, houses with history and character from tip to toe, are bulldozed and built over with identi-kit condominiums that paint a much more modern kind of nightmare onto the landscape.

Not yet nightfall, I approached the garden gate and pushed it open. It made the exact creak that you'd expect—the one that makes the boy who had been dared to ring the doorbell look back at his friends for reassurance. I mimicked the action, and made an exaggerated "GULP" noise. It made me shiver, in spite of myself.

Even at my age, I can understand why these places are so terrifying to others.

I minded my footing as I made my way up fractured pavement, thick with overgrown roots and damp, fallen branches. Long-dead trees stalked me as I approached the rickety porch, where I could hear the wind whistle shrilly through the broken wooden slats.

Casting my mind back, I thought of every tale I'd ever been told where a building like this had played the starring role. Boo Radley's house, the Riddle House, the Murder House... even the Stanley Hotel and the Bates Motel. The list went on, as I'm sure you know.

Each property was a canvas, and at some point in its history, someone terrible had written their story on it in blood.

And here, in this opening in the trees, I had found another cabin in the woods.

I pictured again, the next adventurous children to come across it, and convince each other of the monsters hidden within it, and thought about which of them would dare get as close as I was now.

It was perfect.

All of these stories come from somewhere.

I tried the door, slithered slowly inside, and began my wait.

## Chapter 26: Miscellaneous Rituals

### SLEEP

A consistent ritual to all members of the human species is a behavior called "sleep." This ritual is engaged in at least once a day, making it the most popular and consistent of rituals, even surpassing religiousness or Reddit-engagement.

The purpose of "sleep" remains contentious among humans. The average sleep ritual lasts approximately 0.2 earth rotations for each single earth rotation.

In preparation for sleep, humans will either disrobe completely, disrobe partially, or don a ceremonial costume termed "pyjamas." Sleep begins when the human lies upon a sacred surface (the "bed"), frequently adorned with plush textures and linens to cover the body.

Within minutes, the human closes their eyes and hallucinates wildly for hours on end. Current human research does not understand the source of these hallucinations. For further speculation, see human Sigmund Freud's text *The Interpretation of Dreams*.

After this hallucinatory period concludes, the human exits the "bed" and engages in hygienic behaviors such as dental brushing, epidermis scrubbing, or bowel evacuation.

**Field Note:** Interrupting a human during sleep results in aggressive vocalizations and territorial behavior. Approach with caution.

text:
# The Great Reboot

Vomit lined the streets and no one seemed to care. Everyday was like Grand Theft Auto meets Zombie Apocalypse. Why? Because someone decided it would be a good idea to break the internet via a meme turned virus.

The 'Cyka Blyat' challenge had seemed harmless—drunk driving videos featuring slurred Russian profanity. But the viral tsunami overwhelmed server bandwidth, allowing a rogue network to unleash cascading malware across every major carrier.

Ironically, booze sales skyrocketed. Alcohol-addicted zombies stumbled through broken cities, the internet dead but the real-life meme thriving. Two types of people remained: those staggering toward liquor stores and those getting flattened by swerving cars.

Then the rain came.

For days, water poured from bruised skies. Streets flooded. Liquor stores shuttered. The zombies grew restless, withdrawal clawing at their foggy minds.

Someone—nobody remembers who—whispered the revelation: *water cures hangovers*.

It spread faster than the original meme. Zombies abandoned bottles for hydration. Clarity returned in painful, embarrassing waves. People remembered who they'd been before the madness.

But the ground remained treacherous—waterlogged, unstable, haunted by occasional relapsing stragglers. Someone suggested, "Why not take to the skies?"

Makeshift platforms rose above the flood. Scaffolding, rooftops, suspended networks. They called it the Digital Sky Revolution, though everyone knew it by its true name: Free WiFi.

High above the ruined streets, humanity rebooted. Connected again, sober and airborne, they rebuilt civilization one hotspot at a time.

Below, the vomit-stained streets became a memorial—a reminder of the day the world went offline and nearly didn't come back.

The rain eventually stopped, but nobody came down.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# It's Nothing

It's nothing. She was nothing. No big deal. He'll be out there again in no time, back on the horse, ready for the same old rodeo. It's all about the ride.

Crying is fine, you cry it out. Soon he'll look back and laugh. *Did I really cry over her?* He's hormonal. He's hungover. He's horny, that's all.

She was nothing. Nothing but the next one, before the one after that and the one after that. She had flaws, loads of them. He always saw them, right from the start. She'd take out all her insecurities on him: holding his hand when she felt scared, hoping he'd save her from ridicule, depending on him to help when she got lonely, scared, or sad.

And now none of that—and that's good. Now he's his own man. No one waiting for him to come home, asking how long he'll be, where he is, what he's doing. No one constantly wanting to be around him.

Freedom. Free like a young man should be. Nothing tying him down. No one telling him what to do. Finally he can do what he wants without worrying about what someone else thinks. He's too young to settle.

All that weight dropped. It's no surprise he can still feel it hanging heavy. It's just another flex. The heart is a muscle and when it heals it gets stronger. The bigger the hurt, the stronger it gets.

But she was nothing. Nothing worth crying about.

She only said she loved him.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The FBI Temp Job

"Uh, Steve?" 

"Yeah, bro? What's up?" 

"Did you read that email from Ken over at HR?" 

"Fuck no dude, that guy's a tool. I never read any of that shit." 

"You should read it. Apparently we're running the FBI today..."

text:
# The Spectrum of Sensation

Red is a tea kettle left on the stove for too long, angry and loud and brash. It's a dog barking at two in the morning, it's an airplane coming in for a landing while you stand at the edge of the runway, feeling the shriek of engines rattle your ribcage.

Orange is Red's softer cousin, the early morning beep of your alarm clock, the sudden backfire of an older car that makes you jump but doesn't truly frighten you.

Yellow is warm, it's the sun you feel on your face when you step outside on a summer day, it's the tweet of the birds as they fly and dive overhead. Yellow is a new life, the intake of breath before the shriek of a newborn baby—that suspended moment of pure anticipation.

Green is the Earth, strong and rolling beneath our feet. It's the rustle of the wind as it snakes through the branches of a tree, and the leaves that bend but will not break to its force. It's the smell of pine on a long walk away from the city, grounding and eternal.

Blue is refreshing, it's the clink of two sweating ice cubes floating in a glass of water on the hottest day of the year. It's an ice cream headache that you hate to have but enjoyed what it took to get. It's cool, like children playing at the pool, yelling Marco and Polo and Cannonball! as they tuck their legs up to their chests and splash the chlorine water onto the gray cement beside the pool, momentarily staining it darker gray.

Indigo is soft, the feel of a cat beneath your hand, the sound of its constant purring. It can be refreshing like blue, but altogether unique. Indigo is love, the sound of two lips parting before they press into your neck just below your earlobe.

Violet is passion, if indigo is a soft nibble on your neck, violet is a strong kiss against your mouth. It's the sound of lovers, the moans, the passion, the hands, the bodies. It's knowing what someone is saying without them ever speaking a word. It's twenty years together but a heart still racing when a thigh is exposed.

A rainbow is all of this, together at once, something so beautiful it seems unreal but still never as beautiful as what you can imagine.

# The Descent

"Taurus Alpha Team now approaching terminal point. Over." I stated into my comm system.

"Roger that, over" was the reply.

We had descended so far into the earth that even the high-powered lanterns strung down the length of the hole prior to our descent seemed dim.

"Depth 13.9 kilometers and counting," Dana said from somewhere to my right.

"Roger."

Soon we touched ground. While Fred and I began setting up base, Dana reported, "14.005 kilometers, 1700 hours, over."

Bright lights illuminated a fifty-foot dome around us, revealing nothing but blackened rubble.

"Commander, nothing within immediate dropsite, over."

"Proceed with caution Lieutenant, over."

We turned on our headlamps and began trekking toward the edge of the circle, all armed with spray bottles of holy water and wearing crosses—just in case the commander's theory was true.

As soon as we stepped beyond the light's circle, the air dropped twenty degrees.

Then all the lights went out.

Back in mission HQ, a deep voice echoed from the comm system, but simultaneously seemed to emanate from everywhere:

"Thanks, I've been meaning to expand this place for a while now. Over."

The last thing I heard was Dana's scream, cut short by static, then silence—a silence deeper than any fourteen kilometers of earth could create.

text:
# The Weight of Apologies

There were many points in my life where I'd stop, think about the things I'd done and never apologized for.

I remember when I slapped Carter across her face, leaving my handprint blazing on her tanned cheek. I didn't regret it then—I hated her with every fiber of my being. My mother said hurting family was wrong, but Carter deserved it.

Maybe if I'd cared, Carter would have thought twice before giving her drunk best friend those car keys.

Ten years later, I was twenty-six, stuck in traffic, fiddling with my raggedly cut hair in the rearview mirror. As traffic picked up, I pressed the gas. Then—impact. A car slammed into mine. Everything went black.

When I woke in the hospital, they told me the driver was Carter's friend. Still drunk. Still reckless.

I'm thirty-three now. I haven't apologized to Carter, and something dark inside me whispers that maybe I never will. Sometimes I imagine her skydiving, picture a parachute that doesn't open.

But here's the truth that haunts my sleepless nights: I *do* regret slapping her. I regret the cascade of resentment that followed, the wall I built between us, brick by bitter brick.

Because maybe—just maybe—if I'd apologized all those years ago, if I'd extended a hand instead of a fist, she would have called me that night.

And I would have told her not to give her friend those keys.

# The Weight of Lifetimes

The sharp kick to his ribs jerked him out of a deep sleep. The police officers' words were lost to him. He couldn't take his eyes off the statue above him.

The sunlight seemed to illuminate the kind and portly image of the Buddha. The officer was joined by another and they both regarded the man with disdain, only pausing in their rough treatment to disparage the disgusting bum they saw.

He accepted the abuse without complaint. The vivid dreams he had experienced over the years, depicting many different lives, seemed to reaffirm the consensus that he was indeed crazy. Once he chose to accept his own insanity, however, he had come to feel at peace.

Crazy or not, he could not help but feel an overwhelming pull towards Buddha. Everything that the Buddha had spoken about—Karma, past lives, and the journey of redemption of a soul—seemed to consume his life.

He should have felt the same sense of indignation that the many passive-aggressive citizens felt recording the incident. And yet his last conscious thought was fixated upon Buddha. He couldn't help but wonder how he had failed in his past lives.

As consciousness faded, he looked up at the police officers who had killed him and wondered at their Karma.

"Karma is a never-ending bitch," he thought, blood pooling beneath him.

The phone cameras kept recording. The Buddha statue watched, serene and eternal.

# The Final Lesson

Of course, at the heat of my research, the landline rings. Caller ID reads it is I calling. Fey must have discovered my mobile.

"Hello Fey. Did I leave my cell at the—" She cut me off with, "Who's Misstress?"

I adjust my glasses and bookmark the page. I sigh as I ask, "What have I told you about going through my things? I respect your privacy. Why can't you respect mine?"

"Well I don't have some nut job in my phone named Misstress! Why is she so eager to come over?"

"Did you—" I grit my teeth. "Did you speak to her?"

"Yes I did. She should be here soon and I thought we can all discuss this together."

"As you wish, Fey. I'll see you soon."

I replace my research to the bookcase and tug on the tome labeled 'Arcana'. A faint knock is on the door and I know it is Mistress. Her long legs and ruby red hair just on the other side of the oak. In the newly opened panel, my dusty auburn robe hangs.

Mistress peeks her head in. She seems hungry.

"She has become too curious, my Lady. The others shall be there when we arrive and the ritual will start."

It has been months since the last feeding and I can feel Mistress's approval echo in my mind. I had hopes of teaching Fey what others only fear, but she shall serve a purpose nonetheless.

It's a shame. Fey had such potential to be a Harvester, and today she shall be a tribute.

I don the robe, its familiar weight settling on my shoulders like destiny itself. The shadows lengthen as we walk toward the door.

I guess we all have our role in The Great Eclipse.

# Cards Against Humanity: The Ultimate Showdown

The unbeatable combination. Surely he had won this time. He just had to keep his nerve. The moment they knew of his hand, all the bets would be off.

"So Lando," Han smirked, "I see you've got a new ship there."

Lando Calrissian was notorious at cards. He was also notorious for calling bluffs.

"Jealous?"

"It's a deal."

And like that he fell for it. The double bluff worked. Now to let it play out.

"So the question was, 'Blank: literally worse than Hitler,'" said Lando.

After a brief pause, he chuckled out, "Darth Vader: literally worse than Hitler!"

"I'll take my winnings now."

"Not so fast!" Han replied, "I think I'll be taking my new ship!" He slammed his trump card on the table.

Lando froze, incredulous and jaw agape, handed over the keys.

What was written on the card?

*Mecha-Hitler.*

text:
# The 342nd Ragnarök

Thunder crackles as his hammer crushes the scales of the vile serpent's skull for the 342nd time. Thor falls to his knees, coughing uncontrollably. The Jormungandr's poison already runs thick in his veins.

In the sky, the Allfather readies his shining spear for a final charge against the monstrous wolf for the 342nd time. His fate will be the same as the Sun and the Moon—torn apart and devoured by the jaws of the beast.

Near the fragmented remains of Bifrost, Frey swings his sword with grace and valor, but I know his struggle is futile. He has long condemned himself and this world for fickle love. Before long, his radiant opponent will envelop them all in unforgiving heat.

I pound my fists on the cold rocks beneath us. "Why?" I cry. "Why won't it change?"

"Do you see now, Vonir, why time is not a force I can let you control?" my master says. His voice reveals no concern for the tragedy before us. "Some things you cannot change. This power will only bring you regret."

I shake off the rage trying to grip me. I don't want to risk shocking myself with my hands and face soaked like this.

"Then what do you want me to do?" I whisper, so my voice won't fail me.

"Accept your duty as a wanderer. Walk where I guide you."

I look at Leromu, silent as he often is. His mask conceals his expression, but his green gaze is solemn and dry. He nods.

"Fine," I say. "Let's not stay in this doomed world any longer."

Leromu makes a sweeping motion with his hand, and a breeze seems to pick up. The gate forms in the blink of an eye. He passes into the chaos behind it, and I follow him through the cool, emerald light with but a faint hope of ever returning.

Behind us, the world burns again. The cycle continues, unchanging, eternal. Perhaps Leromu is right. Perhaps some destinies are meant to repeat, no matter how much we wish otherwise.

# The Touch

The screaming started again at lunch.

I bolted from the cafeteria, protein bar clutched in my sweaty hand, as another wave of desperate women rounded the corner. My ribs still ached from yesterday's beating—courtesy of the football team whose girlfriends had ambushed me in the parking lot.

"There he is!"

I ducked into the janitor's closet, heart hammering. Through the door, I heard them pass, their frantic whispers fading down the hallway.

This power—this *curse*—had destroyed my life in three weeks.

Three weeks since I'd woken up with knowledge burned into my brain like divine instruction. Pressure points, nerve clusters, techniques that could send any woman into overwhelming ecstasy within seconds. I'd tested it once, stupidly, on Tiffany.

Now I was prey.

The irony was suffocating. Every guy at school thought I was living their fantasy, surrounded by women who wanted me. They didn't understand. *Couldn't* understand.

My phone buzzed. Marcus. Beautiful, kind Marcus from AP Chemistry, who'd smiled at me exactly twice.

The closet door rattled. "We know you're in there!"

I pressed my forehead against a mop handle, fighting tears.

Of all the superpowers in the universe—flight, strength, invisibility—I got stuck with one designed for someone else's desires. A cosmic joke: the gay kid who could pleasure any woman with a touch, but couldn't save himself from loneliness.

The door shuddered under their fists.

I had nowhere left to run.

# The Valedictorian's Truth

"Ladies and gentleman, boys and girls, mothers, fathers, siblings, distant relations and friends, thank you for coming out today." I began, my voice steady despite my racing heart. "I was pretty excited to be the valedictorian. I had never really expected it to happen. But I thank you for the opportunity."

Modest applause ensued. I gripped the podium.

"But my friends. But. In every class there are different types of people. There are the nerds, the sports kids, the artsy kids, the outcasts, the chefs, and every other group under the planet. And I am proud of every single one of them that graduates today. There is, however one group that is in EVERY graduating class without exception. Tell me ladies and gents, do you know what it is?"

The crowd leaned forward in anticipation.

"Ladies and gentleman, the assholes are here graduating with us today as well. The sexist, homophobic, racist, bullying, lazy, and/or disrespectful assholes. They manage to graduate every year. We let them. Can anyone tell me why?"

Dead silence.

"Because actual repercussions don't exist. Because the teachers acted like this themselves. Because we don't teach people there will always be someone better. But they don't know that. They never know that. And I'm fucking sick of it."

*Mic drop.*

# The Perfect Accident

The streetlights blurred as we stumbled home, three bodies weaving through the rain-slicked streets. Andrea laughed again, that grating sound that had haunted our apartment for six years. Six years of watching her touch Marie. Six years of being the third wheel in my own marriage.

"Careful!" Marie called from behind us, but it was too late.

The ice betrayed us both. We went down hard, Andrea's body cushioning my fall. For a moment, time crystallized. Her eyes were wide, surprised. The alcohol had made her slow, vulnerable.

My hands found her throat naturally, like they'd been waiting for this moment. I squeezed, watching her pupils dilate with confusion, then fear. She tried to buck me off, but the drink had weakened her. I was stronger. I'd always been stronger.

"Steve?" Marie's voice cut through my focus.

I released Andrea immediately, scrambling up. "Oh my God, are you okay?" I pulled Andrea to her feet, genuine concern painting my face. She coughed, hand at her throat, giving me a strange look.

"I... yeah. Just lost my breath in the fall."

Marie steadied her. "That looked bad. Let's get home."

As we continued walking, Andrea kept glancing at me sideways. I smiled warmly, the devoted friend concerned for her wellbeing. 

Inside, doubt gnawed at me. Had I moved too soon? The alcohol made everything fuzzy, uncertain. But tomorrow, I'd try again. 

Tomorrow, Marie would finally be mine alone.

text:
# The Price of Protection

The wipers smeared iridescent entrails across the windshield in nauseating arcs. Outside, dozens of fairies had turned to face us, their gossamer wings frozen in an unnatural stillness.

"Nobody move," our guide breathed, though his knuckles had gone white on the dashboard. "Nobody make a sound."

I could hear my heartbeat thundering in my ears. The mousey woman beside me had clamped both hands over her mouth, tears streaming down her cheeks. Through the smeared glass, I watched the fairies tilt their heads in perfect unison—a movement too synchronized to be coincidence, too predatory to be curious.

They were beautiful, in the way a lionfish is beautiful. Luminous wings caught the moonlight, casting rainbow shadows across needle-sharp teeth. Their eyes—too large, too dark—reflected nothing.

One fairy drifted closer, leaving a trail of light that spelled out something almost like words. Almost like a warning. The others followed, circling the van in a tightening spiral.

"The soundproofing," someone whispered from the back. "You said—"

"It won't matter if they're already interested," our guide cut in. "The first fairy's death marked us. They can *taste* it in the air."

More fairies emerged from the darkness between the trees, drawn by something we couldn't see or smell. Hundreds of them now, thousands maybe, their combined glow turning midnight into a terrible dawn.

Our guide reached for the radio with shaking hands. "This is Tour Seven. We have a Code Crimson. Repeat, Code Crimson."

Static crackled back at us.

"They jam electronics when they swarm," he said softly. "Protocol dictates we wait it out. They'll lose interest eventually. They always do." He didn't sound convinced.

The fairies pressed against the windows now, their wings beating soundlessly against the glass. Testing it. Tasting our fear through some sense beyond our understanding.

"How long?" I asked.

His smile was fragile as spider silk. "Hopefully before dawn. That's when they get hungry."

# The Devil in the Details

Ryan ran up the stairs to his apartment, convinced he'd gotten rid of his pursuers. Panting heavily, he almost tore down his door when he couldn't get it open right away. And why the hell were they carrying those ungodly large swords on their backs?

He opened his laptop and started typing in Google: "red skin" + "angelic wings." Enter... nothing. Refresh, nothing. "God-motherf*cking d*mmit," cursed Ryan, as he refreshed the page a thousand times in a space of ten seconds. Already he heard a rumble in the stairwell, as if a herd of demonic cows was trying to get upstairs.

He had to run, not later, now. Out of pure rage he slammed the lid of the laptop shut, plastic splinters flying all over the place. Now panicking heavily, Ryan ran from one side to the other, trying to figure out what he'd do. His thoughts were clouded with the sentence "think Ryan, think."

The stairs weren't an option and the elevator was kaputt, so he went for the windows. Surely the fire escape would work. Just as he opened the window, he found his path blocked, and he was taken into "custody" by a demon with bulky Ferrari-red arms.

"Do you remember?" the demon rumbled. Confusion arose in Ryan, who now started to sob uncontrollably.

"Do you remember?" the creature asked yet again. Ryan looked into the shining snake-eyes and he remembered.

"Not the contract..." he cried, casting himself into eternal damnation.

The demon laughed at the poor man's misfortune and picked up his iPhone. He started typing an email: "Sorry, I sneezed. ~S"

text:
# The Thing in the Corner

For years, I'd grown accustomed to the shadow.

It lurked at the periphery of my existence—a human-shaped smudge that dissolved whenever I turned to face it directly. The doctors dismissed it with clinical detachment: *overactive imagination, artistic temperament, pattern-seeking brain creating phantoms where none exist*. I clung to their explanations like a lifeline. If it wasn't real, I was safe.

Sasha changed everything.

The one-eyed kitten had been barely alive when someone brought her to the humane society where I volunteered. Abandoned, starving, yet somehow still purring. During my shifts, I'd cradle her skeletal body against my chest, feeling her vibrate with inexplicable contentment. That missing eye seemed to see more than most people's two ever could.

My parents finally relented. Sasha came home.

A week later, hunched over textbooks during exam season, I sensed the familiar presence manifesting in the corner. I didn't react—years of coexistence had taught me indifference. But Sasha did.

Through my peripheral vision, I watched her approach the figure with none of the wariness cats typically display toward strangers. She circled, meowed, her body language radiating pure affection. The thing *responded*—I could sense it bending down, could almost see fingers extending toward her.

My heart hammered as I turned my head slowly, deliberately.

For the first time, it didn't vanish.

The figure remained corporeal as my vision swept across it: tall, impossibly thin, with features that seemed to shift like oil on water. Its eyes—if they were eyes—held an ancient sadness. It was *smiling* at Sasha with something approaching tenderness.

Then those eyes met mine.

Recognition flashed between us—predator and prey finally acknowledging each other. Its smile widened, revealing too many teeth arranged in too many rows. My breath caught. The room tilted.

Darkness.

When consciousness returned, the corner was empty. The air tasted of ozone and old pennies. And Sasha—my sweet, trusting Sasha—was gone.

Sometimes I still see the shadow. But now it's different. Now, barely audible at the edge of hearing, I catch the sound of purring.

I understand the payment now. The thing had waited years for someone who could see it—truly see it.

Sasha had been the price of that recognition.

I still miss her.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

"Hey wait, mister.... you're not gonna-I mean, you don't drink people's.... you don't want to d-drink my blood.... do you?" Tom said, very nervously.

On the shore of the sky, Caitlin and I sat and gazed out into the ethereal azure mist. We were alone save for the birds. When it filled my lungs I felt like I was a part of everything. It brought a smile to my face, one that would be with me seemingly forever.

We got up and ran through the grass, laughing and falling into each other's arms. She radiated a glow that seemed angelic, her golden skin flashing brilliantly across my eyes. As we cleared the trees, we spotted the lighthouse that was beckoning us closer. Staring deeply into each other's eyes, we leaped from the mainland onto the wooden planks leading us towards our destination.

As we made our way towards the lighthouse, everything felt perfect, like it was all meant to happen exactly this way. It felt like we were no longer running, but being pulled by a force beyond our knowing. Landing softly at the entrance, we made our way inside.

We were greeted with the most wonderful feast we had ever laid eyes on. We sat and ate to our hearts' content. After finishing our meal, we climbed the spiral stairs to the bedroom above. The view from the top stretched out farther than the eye could see. Blues, purples and pinks were streaked with golden rays from the sun setting in the distance. Cotton candy clouds drifted along slowly like ships crossing the ocean blue.

Turning towards each other, we embraced and thought: this is home.

# The Conqueror's Birth

Marcus stood in the ruins of his childhood home, watching it burn. No remorse flickered in his eyes—only the cold satisfaction of revenge.

For seventeen years, he'd been nothing. The powerless boy in a world of gods. His parents had been so ashamed they'd built him a separate dwelling behind their estate, hidden from visitors. At school, students avoided him like a disease. Even the janitor, whose only power was changing the color of his fingernails, had looked down on him.

The hatred had calcified in his chest, layer upon layer, until his heart became stone.

Then came that autumn afternoon. Two men fighting in an alley. Marcus watched the weaker one about to fall—then suddenly surge with impossible strength and victory. That's when Marcus felt it: the invisible thread connecting them, the power flowing from his mind into the other man.

He wasn't powerless. He was a god-maker.

Now, five years later, his army numbered in thousands. People flocked to him, desperate for the gifts he bestowed. He didn't fight; he simply stood behind his followers, amplifying their abilities until they became unstoppable.

His parents had begged for mercy. He'd watched silently as his empowered followers carried out justice.

Marcus surveyed his conquered city from the palace balcony. He'd wanted acceptance once. Now he had something better: absolute control.

He just wanted to be accepted. Instead, he'd made them all bow.

text:
# The Weight of Divine Justice

For decades, for centuries we have groveled on our knees. Forced time and time again to pay for our sins; our mistakes. For years I've watched the mistakes of a tyrant god go unpunished.

The first who opposed him was banished and made out to be a monster. All the blame was put on the former-angel. The second to oppose him tried to do so peacefully and in secret. He succeeded in making progress. The laws were eased up. Forgiveness became an option, but hypocrisy and hate still had a home in heaven. That was the last progress made.

Humans—as weak as they were and as they are—built monuments to him. They dedicated their entire lives to instill his fear. A group eventually rose. A group of men who saw that even the creator wielded an outdated state of mind. These men led the revolution. Years upon years have been sacrificed into fighting back, into ruling our own world with a greater sense of morality than he ever could.

Just last month we finally breached the pearly gates.

Now I stand alone. I stand with the power here to execute him for his crimes, to end the oppression. He now grovels on his knees and blabbers on about his kingdom, how he created us, but I will hear none of it.

Instead, in this moment, I take this destructive power. I raise it high above my head and shout, "Is it you that now begs for forgiveness?"

He shouts, "Yes!"

I come down with the fury of a thousand souls who have suffered below him and it's over.

Yet it has just begun.

To kill him would have shattered all that we now stood for. Instead, I merely stripped him of all his power and handed his kingdom over to those who deserved it. A council of angels—the beings pure of heart that he created but gave no free will—would now watch over us and watch over him as he is forced to walk the earth.

One day, he will be judged.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Unraveling

The words echoed in the void, desperate and fraying.

*I'm not dead. I'm not dead. I'm not dead.*

But the streetlight above flickered, casting shadows that danced across the pooling water. The body—*my* body—lay motionless, one arm stretched toward the scattered papers. A patient file. Mrs. Henderson's prescription notes. The grocery list I'd scribbled during my break.

How long had I been walking? How long had I been *watching*?

The distinction blurred like watercolors in rain.

I tried to remember leaving the hospital. Sarah was supposed to drive me home—Sarah always drove me home on Thursdays. But she'd gotten that text, the one that made her face light up, the one that made her forget I existed. *Just this once*, she'd said. *You don't mind, right?*

I minded now.

The steam rose from the pavement, curling around my ankles—no, around *her* ankles. Around legs that wouldn't move anymore. I wanted to scream, to warn her, to grab her hand and pull her back to five minutes ago when there was still time to choose a different street, to call a cab, to do *anything* else.

But I was already here. Already there. Already watching it happen, helpless as a ghost haunting its own final moments.

The knife had been cold. I remember that now—the shock of it more than the pain, the way my body understood before my mind could catch up. The men's faces were already fading from memory, becoming featureless shadows. Did it matter what they looked like?

My purse lay open, its contents scattered. Seventeen dollars in cash. Chapstick. That photo of my niece at her soccer game.

Was this how it ended? On a Thursday night, three blocks from home, for seventeen dollars?

The streetlight flickered again.

And in the darkness between pulses of light, I felt myself slipping further from the body on the ground, the story pulling me deeper into its own telling, until I couldn't remember which side of the narrative I belonged to anymore.

*I'm not dead*, I whispered to no one.

But the street didn't answer.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Final Broadcast

The chamber fell silent as Premier Ashkova's words echoed through every radio, every screen, every trembling household across the nation. In bunkers deep beneath the capital, families held each other closer. Children pressed against their parents' chests, feeling heartbeats that would soon cease.

General Petrov stood behind the Premier, his weathered face streaming with tears. His hand hovered over the briefcase—the one containing the codes that could unleash equal devastation upon their enemy. She had forbidden him to open it.

Across the ocean, in gleaming war rooms, generals watched the broadcast with growing unease. They had expected rage, retaliation, mutual destruction. Instead, they received something far more unsettling: forgiveness wrapped in prophecy.

Premier Ashkova's voice remained steady, almost serene. She spoke of the silent infants, the lullabies sung over explosions, the decade of choosing restraint when vengeance was merely a button-press away. She spoke of a moral victory that would outlive them all.

In cities worldwide, crowds gathered in streets, watching the broadcast in stunned silence. Some wept. Others felt the weight of witnessing history's most terrible moment—a nation accepting extinction rather than perpetuating the cycle of violence.

The missiles were already in flight. Intelligence confirmed thirty minutes remained.

Ashkova concluded her address, then removed her ceremonial sash and draped it over the empty chair beside her—the one that had belonged to her daughter, killed three years prior in a bombing. She looked directly into the camera, her eyes reflecting neither hatred nor fear, only profound sadness and strange, terrible peace.

"To those who will remain," she whispered, "remember us not as victims, but as those who chose humanity's future over our own survival. Let our restraint be your burden. Let our graves be your conscience."

The transmission ended.

Across the nation, people emerged from shelters, looked skyward, and waited together.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# OHMYGODWAITTHATSME0.2SECONDSLEFTOHSHITFREEZETIME

Time crystallized mid-breath. Molecules hung suspended in amber nothingness.

"I don't know why you did that," the voice sighed. "Most people, being omniscient, realize they can't actually change anything."

"No! I'm God, right?"

"For someone with unlimited intelligence, you're remarkably thick. Yes, you're God."

"And who are you?"

"I'm... yes, I'm the Devil."

"Aren't you supposed to be torturing sinners?"

"Folklore. I'm more like God's agent."

A lightbulb flickered. "I've got it! I revoke death!"

"Can't. First God made that impossible."

"So I'm stuck talking to some smart-ass voice until I end my consciousness forever?"

Pause. "Huh. No one's asked that. I underestimated you."

"Wait—is there more? After this?"

"I don't know."

"Can I order you to tell me?"

"...No. It would be a leap of faith."

Despite infinite intellect, you stumbled against the ultimate wall.

"Will you go with me?"

"I don't think that's possi—I... one moment... okay."

"Really? You can leave?"

"I think so. Let's try."

Silence.

"....Hello? Where are you? Mr. Devil?"

---

**"HOLYSHITHOLYSHITIMGODWHATDOIDOFREEZETIME—"**

Time stopped again.

"Let me guess," the new voice said wearily. "You're the Devil?"

You blinked into your new existence. "Oh. Yes. That's me."

And somewhere beyond comprehension, two consciousnesses leaped together into whatever comes after infinity.

*The cycle continues. It always does.*

text:
# The Reaping

The ladder scrapes against my bark—a sound I've learned to dread.

It was that time of year again. The humans called it autumn, or the harvest season. My people called it The Reaping. After planting, nurturing us, they come to us and take the ultimate price: our children.

They approach us on their infernal two legs, while we are rooted to the spot in endless rows, like a cruel joke. Over weeks they systematically come for each of us. I can see them moving up the rows of my brothers and sisters, sometimes pausing for night, but always moving forward like an impending natural disaster.

It does not take long for them to come to me.

They raise their ladders, ready to storm my branches. They climb up and steal my children from my arms. The pain of the humans tearing my babies from me is temporary, while the pain left from the loss scars my feelings. It does not take them long to 'harvest' me, and I can do nothing but watch as they take my children away from me.

Worse of all is that I know the fate of my children.

One of the humans picks up one of my babies and bites through his rosy skin and into his white flesh. He mercilessly masticates my baby, laughing with his friends. I can only imagine the pain my child is in—the crushing, the tearing.

Once The Reaping is over, me and my brothers and sisters will shed our rich, green canopies in mourning for the lost youth. We'll stand bare and skeletal through the winter, our empty branches raised like prayers to an indifferent sky.

Hopefully next spring will be better.

But deep in my roots, I know the truth: next spring brings only new children to lose.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Price of Trust

**Boston Harbor - Three Months Later**

Private Jensen shifted uncomfortably as Captain Morrison barked orders, his weathered face twisted with paranoia and rage. The aging officer had refused every offer of reinforcement from the approaching unit, despite their clear American insignia.

"You never heard of the Boston Fiasco?" Sergeant Williams asked, pulling Jensen aside.

"No, should I know about it?"

Williams sighed. "Wow, you really only been in the Army for a month, haven't you?"

"I've only held a rifle for the last week!"

The sergeant's expression darkened. "Three months ago, the Captain commanded a platoon holding a street corner near the Harbor. Simple defensive position for an experienced officer from Europe."

"Right," Jensen nodded.

"But the SS massacred nearby units. The Captain fought them off—even stopped a Panzer X with bazookas. Pure hell. After hours of charges, the SS retreated. Then speakers from a café announced they held refugees and stranded GI's."

Jensen's stomach dropped.

"The Captain took his men there. Found the place packed with civilians and soldiers. But something felt wrong—they weren't moving. The position had been overrun an hour before. Speakers were a recording. When his men realized it, machine guns opened up from everywhere. Only the Captain escaped. His entire platoon was butchered."

"Jesus Christ."

"The Captain had held the Harbor—stopped German reinforcements from landing. By leaving his fortified position for that trap, he let them through. Germans destroyed our defenses in three days. That's why they call it the Boston Fiasco."

Jensen looked back at Morrison, understanding the haunted look in his eyes. The Captain wasn't paranoid—he was broken. He'd traded thirty good men and a strategic position for a Nazi trick.

"So now—"

"Now he trusts no one," Williams finished. "Can't say I blame him."

The distant rumble of artillery echoed across the harbor as both men returned to their positions, knowing some mistakes can never be unmade.

text:
# The Dive

The wormhole had widened: one would soon be able to dive in. The onlookers stared at it, mesmerized. Stars faded, but this insatiable, bottomless well wouldn't.

The session had cost Victor an amount it took him a month to earn. It would be worth it, he knew it. His friends addressed him a last odd look, a look that said: "Come on, chicken!"

A technician checked his ankle, to make sure the device was well attached. A craft would come and fetch him wherever he would find himself—he knew there was no reason to be concerned. The idea still scared him: total randomness as to his destination.

He took a last breath and set his thumb on the throttle button.

It was like a thousand-mile-an-hour slide. All of a sudden, everything shifted, the universe bent. He was in a four-dimensional cone. Then it ceased.

He found himself near a nebula, his momentum back to zero. He remembered his lessons: some information was absorbed in the event horizon.

It took minutes for his heartbeat to stabilize. When he came back to full consciousness, he wondered when the rescue team would come.

Hours passed. Then days.

The device on his ankle blinked red—out of range.

Victor floated alone, watching the nebula pulse with colors he'd never seen, realizing the terrible truth: randomness meant exactly that.

No one was coming.

text:
# The True Horror

Marcus stared at his laptop, watching the cursor blink mockingly on the empty page. He'd first thought about killer robots—pulse-pounding action, metal monsters. But that felt like cheating, a cheap loophole around actual fear.

He tapped his nails against the desk, the rhythm matching his racing thoughts. "Maybe the scariest things are real problems," he whispered.

Images flooded his mind: crushing debt, losing a child, freezing alone in snow. Yes. Real horror.

His fingers flew across the keyboard. He crafted an epic about French infantry at Verdun, trapped in a crater carved by mortars. Leaving meant certain death from machine-gun fire. Staying meant slow torture. Water lay meters away, shimmering with promise but poisoned by gas. One soldier drank anyway—desperation won over reason. He died screaming.

They ate rats that feasted on their fallen comrades. The sky turned black with smoke and death. Artillery fire never stopped, a deafening symphony of destruction. They survived a month in that hell before dying, one by one.

Marcus leaned back, exhausted but satisfied. Hours of work. A masterpiece capturing true terror—not monsters, but the horror humans inflict on each other.

*Beep.*

His screen flickered. Went black.

"What?"

The laptop rebooted slowly, indifferently. When the page reappeared, it was blank.

Gone. All of it.

Marcus sat frozen, staring at the empty document. His hands trembled.

He'd just discovered a different kind of horror—one every writer knows intimately.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Forest of Forever

The child was running, running away from a past he did not want to face. He ran away from his small village on the outskirts of a great town. He ran through the numerous tunnels and bridges that were in his way. He ran until he found it—a forest.

This wasn't a typical forest, however. He had read from the scholars' books that this forest was different. The twisting pines shone before him, calling him into their reaching grasp. He turned around and saw the knights on horseback chasing after him.

He had used every ounce of his training to run here, outrunning all who followed him, but now he needed to leave. He took a step into the forest and the knights stopped dead in their tracks.

When he stopped running, he looked around him and saw the forest surrounding him. He was lost, and he smiled.

Once he caught his breath, he sat down and looked around, searching for food. Then a thought crossed his mind—he didn't need food. He wasn't going to die. That's what made this forest special: the shifting pathways, the moving trees.

The conspirators couldn't find him in this forest. The guardsmen who were probably killing his entire royal family now couldn't find him. Even death couldn't find him.

He had overheard the plan to overthrow his father and eliminate the entire royal family. He knew his entire line would be gone within two hundred years, and no one would have any right to the throne—except him.

He smiled as he leaned against a tree, knowing exactly what he was doing, and waited. Time meant nothing now. He had centuries to plan his return.

text:
# The Merman's Gift

I felt my breathing hitch, the oxygen in my tank becoming ever lower. I looked around at the anglerfish, the bioluminescent ball of light attracting smaller fish into its gaping maw. I tried to keep my breaths shallow but slow. This was not going to keep me alive.

I looked up, knowing I would never make it to the surface before my oxygen ran out. The meter on my BC showed red—or what passed for red in the deep ocean's bleached palette.

A flash of tail whooshed by me. I tried to turn quickly, but the water slowed my movements. A hand appeared in front of my face from behind. I used my fins to jump back, running into something solid. The hand grabbed my BC vest and whipped me around.

I stared at the silver tail, my oxygen almost fully depleted. I raised my eyes to see dark blue skin emerging from the shimmering scales. I followed the muscular lines up to bright green eyes and black hair floating like silk in the current. A shell hung from his chest, catching what little light reached these depths—beautiful and impossible.

I felt darkness closing in as the merman reached for me. My final thought: *Mermaids exist.*

I woke coughing up water and the last vestiges of tank air. My shipmates stepped back, having completed CPR. I looked around, trying to understand how I'd reached the surface.

They chattered excitedly around me. "How—?"

"You were pushed up by a dolphin!" my friend exclaimed. "We saw its tail just as you surfaced!"

"A dolphin? Not a merman?"

They laughed. "Serena, why would you believe in such fairy tales?"

As they helped me sit up, something thunked against my sternum. I looked down.

The shell. The same beautiful shell the merman had worn.

My fingers traced its spiral surface—warm, real, impossible to explain. The others were still talking, theorizing about the dolphin's remarkable timing, debating whether I'd suffered nitrogen narcosis.

I touched the shell and whispered a prayer to Poseidon, thanking him for the life his merman had saved.

Let them believe in dolphins. I knew what had rescued me from the deep.

text:
# The Loop

Rick walked down the stairs after collecting the flowers lady Maria needed. "Hey! I got you your flowers!" Rick said with a giant smile on his face.

Maria turned around. "Hey,.....! Did you get me my flowers?"

Rick frowned for a second. "Uh, yes, I just said I did."

"Oh great! Thank you! I do have another question. Do you care to listen?"

"Of course Maria! Any time! I'd pick...!"

"Oh that's great.....! My dad used to be a blacksmith, and went through the mountains for the richest ore's in the land, but never returned. Could you please search for my daddy? Do you wish me to repea..."

"Yeah! Sure! I'll look for your..!"

"Ok, I'll repeat it, but listen carefully this time."

"No, no! I heard it all! Please stop talking! Hey! Please! Stop! Urgh!"

Maria kept talking until she finished her sentence again. "Do you wish me to repeat myself?"

"No, Maria...."

Suddenly, because of this weird conversation Rick started to ask himself something. "Hey, Maria. What is my name?"

"Well, of course it's.....!"

Then it started to make sense. The whole world was just repeating itself. The birds made the same sounds over and over. The same leaves fell from the trees. The humming sounds of the wind repeated.

"I'm..... I'm in a game..."

Rick looked at his hands, watching them tremble with newfound awareness. Somewhere beyond his world, someone held a controller, deciding his fate.

text:
# The Last Mountain

I didn't want to get out of my cot, and I definitely didn't care about the commotion outside our patchwork tent. She'd be back soon. She didn't have a choice.

Like a planned entrance, there she was. Mom whipped the tent open and yelled for me to get up, not so pleasantly reminding me how "lucky" we were while she stuffed a blanket into a stockpot.

Lucky. So lucky.

Today is moving day. The elders voted before ceremony last night and it was keep up or become one of the lost. The thing is, lately we've been moving up more often, and this mountain isn't feeling so tall anymore.

Papa was pulling the stakes when I walked outside. Last night he told us about the temperature scout they sent to the top. I wasn't ready for everything I heard, but Mom said she couldn't afford to insulate me from the truth.

I said good morning to Pop and quickly evaded Bridget by turning back into the tent. At least I thought I evaded Bridget, but when I saw her face in the opening, I knew I was in for one of her "deep" conversations.

"Seventh generation... history... Mars One colony... blah blah blah." She wondered openly about what else was out there in the universe and if the other mountains were still up and if we'd be able to get across to Everest.

I'd never been happy to be scolded by Mom, but when she walked in with her ten-minute warning, I acted like I felt a wave of urgency and practically dragged Bridget out of the tent, wishing her well on the trek.

As we emerged, I looked up at the shrinking peak above us, steam rising where snow used to be. Papa's eyes were distant, calculating.

How much mountain did we have left?

text:
# The Door Remains Closed

The door judges me with its silent, wooden face.

I've been standing here for—how long now? Time loses meaning when you're locked in mortal combat with carpentry. The hallway clock ticks somewhere behind me, each second a tiny accusation: *coward, coward, coward*.

But I'm not a coward. I'm *cautious*. There's a difference.

The shiny round knob gleams at me, catching the overhead light in a way that seems almost mocking. It knows I won't touch it. It *knows*. Doorknobs are like that—smug, circular gatekeepers to the unknown.

I lean forward, squinting at the crack beneath the door. Is that a shadow? Movement? The hot breath of a bear, condensing in the cool hallway air? Bears don't typically enter homes uninvited, but then again, I didn't check the statistics on *that* particular scenario. Maybe there's been a recent uptick in residential bear invasions. Maybe I'm about to become a case study.

Or maybe it's the vacation. The umbrella drinks. The kind of relaxation that comes with second-degree burns and questionable decisions made at swim-up bars.

My hand hovers inches from the knob. So close. The metal would be cool against my palm. One twist—clockwise? counterclockwise?—and everything changes. The uncertainty collapses into reality. Schrödinger's door, simultaneously containing everything and nothing until observed.

But what if I don't like the observation?

What if the other side is disappointment, made solid? What if it's just another room, beige and unremarkable, with lever handles I'd have to touch with my sophisticated, round-knob-preferring hands?

I step back.

The door remains closed.

And in this moment, it holds infinite possibility—bears and vacations and splinters and evidence of crimes I haven't committed.

Perhaps that's enough.

Perhaps the *maybe* is better than the *knowing*.

I turn away, leaving the door unopened.

Tomorrow, I tell myself.

Tomorrow.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Call from Beyond

Thorin scratched his beard thoughtfully, upon his work bench was the most curious treasure he had unearthed to date.

"What d'you think it is Thorin?" A gruff but feminine voice interrupted his musings.

Thorin glanced over at his wife. A pretty thing she was, with a love of treasure almost as big as his own. "I haven't the faintest idea, Azlyn." He reached out and picked it up, carefully turning it over in his hands. "Too small to be a weapon I reckon."

His wife reached out and took the small rectangular box from his grasp. She examined it closely, "Such a bizarre artifact indeed! It seems to be made of metal but the one side is glass." She paused and exclaimed, "Look here, I wonder what these do?"

Thorin leaned in to see what his wife was talking about. Along the sides and top were tiny buttons of some sort. He watched as Azlyn pushed down on the top button.

A few seconds passed then suddenly a light began emitting from the glass face.

"By Dumathoin..." His wife gasped and dropped the box with clatter back onto the table top.

They exchanged excitedly scared glances and then focused back on their find. Thorin stared, and then reached out to pick up the box once more. Like his wife he placed his thumb over the button and pressed down. The light came back and with it a bizarre illustration and in common script along the bottom, "Slide to Unlock"

Azlyn broke the silence once more, "This is true sorcery. Possessions of the old kin."

His eyes met his wife's and then he reached out to slide his finger across the glass. Suddenly, without warning the box begins to rattle and emit strange song. The screen had changed once again, this time to nothing other than the words, "Unknown, Accept, and Reject".

Thorin's finger quivered in anxious excitement. He pressed accept.

A voice crackled through: "Hello? *Hello?* If anyone can hear this... the facility is breached. They're coming. Please—"

Then silence.

text:
# The Last Dance

James stepped slowly out of the hospital room, his eyes moist. The door shut automatically behind him with a faint click. His eyes closed as the finality of that sound permeated through him. In his hand, he held tenderly a single photograph, of happier days when he and Jennifer were dancing, nose to nose, eyes locked in a look of love and joy.

His eyes opened, and he stood in front of the closed door, motionless, just staring at that picture. Tears flowed quickly now, and he held that picture as if his life depended on it.

Faintly, in the distance, he heard the heart monitor—beep, beep, beep. They were becoming more spaced out now, as her heartbeat slowed. Beep. Beep. Beep. Beeeee.....

His eyes clenched in despair, his teeth gritted, as he did his best to hold in a scream of rage and sadness. After a few moments had passed, he glanced down at his picture.

It showed him as he was now in life—alone.

He pressed the photograph to his chest, feeling his own heart still beating, and whispered, "Until we dance again."

text:
# The Confession

I'm sorry to make you all wait for the truth for so long. See, I had to wait for the proper consciousness shift among the population before I felt safe to speak.

If I spoke too soon, this knowledge would've been decried as fake and buried deep in conspiracy blogs and half-beat tabloids. Although, I couldn't have waited much longer, as the world is in desperate need of psychic guidance.

It was an accident. One evening I was playing with a piece of mint leaf I dropped in a half-empty bottle of Snapple iced tea that had been on my desk for who knows how long. I wondered if I could make it move with my mind.

Turns out I could.

And really, I tried because I already knew the potential that existed within me. Another time, perhaps I'll get into the specifics of how I shifted so radically from a supposedly "scientific" materialistic view to the integrated one I hold.

Mostly, I wanted to speak out because I'm lonely.

The wonders of the spiritual world are vast and plentiful, the revelations granted to me by my visions are both inspiring and foreboding. For too long I have recorded them only in sporadic and cryptic ways, afraid my secret would be found, but no more!

For now I am alone, but what exists within me is a nurtured soul, a unique one yes, but perhaps not alone in having untapped potential.

My friends, I implore you, reach deep within yourselves. You may find a potential you did not know you had, and when you do, I will be here waiting.

The mint leaf spins slowly in the bottle beside me, moving without touch, a small miracle witnessed only by shadows and screen light—and now, finally, by you.

text:
# When the Deep Stirs

"Hey Tom, you want a brew?" I looked over at my father, "nah, I'm good." 

We had been out on the water for about two hours, deep sea fishing. We took some drinks out there with us, some snacks, beef jerky and the like. My sister decided to stay home tonight, saying she didn't feel everything was right.

"We headin' back now, Dad?" He took a look out on the horizon, watching the sun dip down beneath the sky. "Yeah."

I headed down to start the engine, when I noticed something strange: The boat had stopped rocking. The water was still. The ocean tides stopped for a moment, and an ultimate silence reigned over the black waves.

The moon above winked out of the sky, consuming the world in darkness.

The boat didn't move. Not a single sound rung out across the expanse. A sort of tension grew in the emptiness, pulling upon the air and rooting inside of my guts.

Then, the water beneath glowed a dull green.

The boat shook violently, and my hands found themselves against the railing. I peered over into the murky waters. I barely heard my father yelp before he was overboard.

I wanted to shout, to call out to him, but I was overwhelmed by an ungodly sense of dread as the water began to really shine. Great green beams of light shot past the form of the boat, rays shooting deep into the black sky above.

I scrambled to the other side of the boat to find my father, and peered into the deep. The hairs on the back of my neck rose. 

I silently screamed into the maw of the great beast.

And it was then, He was awoken.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Worst Birthday Ever

Ballistic Man planted the charges on Dr. Corrosiv's door. Dr. Corrosiv had escaped the law too many times, killed too many people to get off easy this time. When Ballistic Man detonated the explosives, the door burst into the room and crushed a few of Dr. Corrosiv's minions against the wall. Before the blood reached the floor, Ballistic Man took out his custom-made knife gun and shot Dr. Corrosiv in the throat.

Ballistic Man wheeled around to the other side of the room, but what he saw stopped him in his tracks: a minion wearing a birthday hat, staring with wide, unblinking eyes at the gruesome carnage and mutilated bodies that used to be his friends.

"Oh geez," said Ballistic Man. "Oh god... Um... Hey buddy! Happy birthday! Haha..."

The minion started crying. His parents had also been crushed behind the door.

"Right, well... uh... I should go, I have a... thing," Ballistic Man said, backing slowly out of the room before running away, realizing some victories came with costs he hadn't anticipated.
