text:
# The Last Stand

It was as though a spiteful god had dropped a flock of macaws into a hurricane. Their crimson cloaks whipped violently, bronze helmets catching the merciless sun as bullets tore through flesh that had somehow survived millennia. The Americans held fire initially, confusion paralyzing their trigger fingers. But the insurgents recognized no distinction between infidel invaders and these asynchronous temporal intruders.

Spouts of Spartan gore stained the sand with each Soviet-made round caterwauling through their ranks. Against this new Achaemenid assault, they had no answer. No phalanx formation could deflect lead traveling faster than sound. They merely stood and died.

In droves they collapsed, yet another ancient artifact bulldozed by a conflict without appreciation or attachment. The few remaining charged the only visible threat—the American position. When they turned and ran toward the desert-camouflaged line, they were not so much slain as evaporated by the concentrated firepower trained upon them.

In this tiny province of a massive war, the two agitators shared one moment's common goal: survival against the impossible.

The ground upon which this last vestige of the old way lay was contested for hours before the insurgents withdrew, leaving only the Americans to investigate. They found no reason, merely another anomaly in this conflict of oddity and atrocity.

The dead were later stripped of weapons and armor—the eternal prerogative of the living. The looters left their bodies to rot in the land of their enemies, the last foothold of Sparta erased.

In private thoughts, the men of that squad all returned to that day, seeing these paragons of warrior spirit eviscerated on windswept sand. More than one revisited the spot, needing proof of what they'd witnessed.

They found nothing. No trace remained.

text:
# The Final Hat

"Such a fine thing, human skin," Larry purred over the intoxicated form of his previous owner. "Smooth, versatile, but with a certain *rough* edge." The emphasis made the man jump.

Larry leaned in close, relishing the sweat on the man's brow, the ragged breaths diluted with alcohol. He breathed in deeply.

"I've always loved to sew," Larry continued breezily, as if he hadn't set the farmer's children alight, along with the house they were in. "Not that you would care." Larry came out of his dreamy state suddenly and his eyes grew sharp. "Not that you *ever* cared."

"I think I'll make you something." Larry's face was soft again and his tone was carefree. "Yes... What would you like? A coat, perhaps? No, no, you've far too many of those. Ooh! I know. A hat! A beautiful hat! You like hats, don't you?"

The man, scared to upset the llama, simply nodded once.

"Good, good," he purred as he clutched the kitchen knife in his hooves. "You'll make a great hat."

The man's pupils dilated with a mix of fear and alcohol. "Larry, please, n—"

His words were cut with a hoof to the face.

"Don't you dare call me that, you fuck! In your final moments, you shall call me... CAAAAARRRRRLLLLL!!"

text:
# The Price of Protection

Eve's trembling fingers traced the outline through stained fabric. The dried evidence of her mother—or perhaps another woman—marked the territory of her nightmare. She had learned long ago not to gag at the familiar smell. That mistake had cost her dearly, just once. Once was enough when the lesson involved choking on her own vomit while he forced compliance in unspeakable ways.

The scars on her thighs told the story of her early resistance—thin white lines that had faded but never disappeared. Battle wounds from a war she'd lost before it began.

"Almost, baby girl," his voice rasped in the darkness.

*Not for you,* she thought, even as her body went through the motions. *For him.*

In the next room, her little brother slept. Six years old. Still innocent. Still untouched by their father's depravity. Eve had made herself a sacrifice, a barrier between her brother and this hell. Every degrading act was a transaction: her body for his safety.

"That's good. Keep going."

Her ribs showed through paper-thin skin. She'd stopped eating except when forced. But her brother ate. Her brother thrived in his ignorance, protected by her silent suffering.

When it was finally over, she rose slowly, watching her father's scarred chest—a landscape of violence and decay. His breath reeked of alcohol and tobacco as he pulled her close.

"Will you let him go?" she whispered, her voice barely human.

He kissed her roughly, and she tasted copper. Blood dripped from his split lip—her mother's work, perhaps, from their earlier fight.

"What are you talking about?" His smile revealed red-stained teeth. "Don't you realize I already have?"

The words crashed through her like ice water. 

Her bedroom door stood open. Her brother's door, too.

Both empty.

Eve's scream shattered the silence as she understood: she'd been protecting a ghost. Her brother was already gone.

text:
# The Unintended Consequences of Divine Intervention

I stretch back in my throne, exhausted. Three hundred years of careful manipulation, and *this* is what I get?

Al Gore can claim credit all he wants, but I'm Cupid—I created the internet. Every innovation, every connection, every fiber-optic cable laid was guided by my invisible hand. I pushed engineers together at conferences, whispered inspiration into the dreams of programmers, ensured the right venture capitalists met the right entrepreneurs.

My vision was beautiful: a global network where love transcended borders. Instant communication. Cultural exchange. Hearts connecting across oceans.

Instead? Pornhub has more traffic than the Library of Congress.

Don't misunderstand—I appreciate physical love. I've enjoyed my share of mortal encounters over the millennia. But the *ratio* here is staggering. For every heartfelt video call reuniting families, there are ten thousand… well, let's call them "alternative uses."

The Gods of Fidelity and Abstinence won't stop complaining. They've filed formal complaints with Zeus, Odin, even the Abrahamic God. Everyone's giving me grief at the celestial cocktail parties.

"Cupid, do you *see* what you've unleashed?"

"The mortal realm is drowning in debauchery!"

Yes, yes. I *know*.

But here's the thing—humans are still finding love. Between the cat videos and questionable websites, genuine connections form. Long-distance relationships thrive. Support groups emerge. People discover they're not alone.

So next time you're, ah, *browsing*, give an extra stroke for me. (Get it? Haha.)

I promise I'm stepping back now. True love is out there—you just have to find it.

I'll just be along for the ride.

*Literally.*

text:
# The Internet Whisperer

I settled into my chair, preparing to enlighten my nephew about the mysteries of connectivity.

"Listen carefully," I began, gesturing dramatically. "It all started with phones. That's right! Phones."

His eyes widened with interest.

"You used a program to call the internet itself. Then—and this is crucial—you had to notify *all* the websites in the world of your presence."

"All of them?" he interrupted.

"Every single one," I confirmed solemnly. "The websites would speak back through your phone to confirm they knew you existed. Now, scientists are crafty bastards. It would've taken millions of years for each website to respond individually, but the computer-phone-listener-unit could hear an incredible number at once. Took about thirty seconds."

I paused for effect.

"With so many voices talking simultaneously, it strained the phone lines terribly. So much that the lines couldn't contain all those voices. You could actually *hear* them, speaking to you."

"Really?" His skepticism was showing.

"Absolutely. But then we advanced! High-speed cameras changed everything. That's why we now use cables that transmit light. Computers talk using Morse code these days. Much more silent."

"I don't believe you."

"Don't believe me? Look at your computer's back. See that light flickering rapidly at the cable's end? That light is amplified so the high-speed camera inside can pick it up."

He stared at me, then slowly reached for his phone.

"I'm Googling this," he muttered.

"You're calling the internet?" I asked innocently.

His groan was extremely satisfying.

text:
# Paradise Refashioned

I stood at the precipice of my creation, surveying the undulating landscape below. God had approved my proposal—barely. Democracy in the afterlife was more complex than I'd imagined.

The voting system was brutal: fifty thousand signatures required, but dissenters could cancel approvals. Most cosmic architects never got past the planning stage. Yet here I was, master of my own domain.

My secret? Understanding my constituency.

Heaven's demographics skewed heavily toward a particular type: those who'd died without certain earthly experiences. The virtuous. The lonely. The perpetually dateless.

So I designed accordingly. Every creature, every surface, bore the universal symbol of desire. Trees swayed with improbable anatomy. Rivers flowed over generous curves. Even microscopic life forms displayed prominent features under magnification.

Was it tasteless? Absolutely.

Was it effective? The voting results spoke for themselves.

Critics called it juvenile. Theologians debated whether it mocked creation itself. But my world filled immediately upon opening. Reincarnation requests poured in faster than any other realm—faster than the peaceful meditation spheres, the adventure worlds, even the reunion dimensions where families reconnected.

I'd identified an untapped market and delivered exactly what they wanted.

God rolled their celestial eyes but couldn't argue with success.

Paradise, I learned, was entirely subjective.

And business was booming.

text:
# The Final Prayer at Honnō-ji

The smoke thickens around us as I finish the tale of Yoshitsune. Ranmaru's eyes gleam with reverence, though he tries to mask it.

"My lord, you tell the tales so well."

"Flattery will get you nowhere. A true samurai lives by his strength alone."

But I know why he flatters—loyalty burns brighter than any flame consuming this temple. Outside, Mitsuhide's troops surround Honnō-ji. The betrayal is complete.

"I am here to seek the counsel of Bishamon," I say, turning toward the altar. "I meditate on the whims of the people and the way I can best serve them." The irony tastes bitter. "Ranmaru, bring me the war plans so I may examine them. Mitsuhide rides west to aid Hideyoshi. Everything is in check."

Everything was in check. Until tonight.

"My lord, what would you have me do?"

A strand of hair hangs before his face, and I reach up, brushing it behind his ear with unexpected tenderness. "This is too solemn a place to speak of war, Ranmaru. Put these away and pray with me."

We kneel together. "Namu Amida Butsu."

In my mind's eye, Bishamon appears, offering a sword to the dragon of Echigo. The war god turns to me, his expression grave.

"It's over, Nobunaga. You've formed the cake, but you won't taste it. The fires of your downfall burn now."

A tear traces down Ranmaru's face. "My lord, we should leave."

I bow to Bishamon one final time.

The beam falls like divine judgment, crushing my ribs with a sound like snapping bamboo. Through the pain, I watch Ranmaru draw his blade, performing jigai with the grace of Yoshitsune himself.

No cry escapes his lips.

A true samurai until the end.

text:
# The Spicy Soda Incident

I like spicy food, hot food, food that makes you sweat. But I still remember that night out, that night in that stupid Asian restaurant. What was it called again? Pangi Chan, Peppy Chin, Poop Chinese? I don't know.

"I can't choose." The menu was full of different drinks.

"May I recommend our new 'Spicy soda'?" the waiter said.

I didn't know what 'spicy soda' was, it was something new on the menu. But it had the word 'spicy' in it, so I just chose it, worst decision in my life.

"Yeah, sounds fine," I said.

My girlfriend sat across the table and looked at the menu, then she told the waiter her order.

"Water with ice."

What do women have with water, why not order wine or something? Oh, well, whatever.

"And what does the lovely couple want to eat?"

To be honest, I can't even remember what we ate.

"One spicy soda, water and ice, and two Szechuan beef platters coming up," the waiter said as he walked to the kitchen.

The restaurant was filled with people.

"So what did you—" my girlfriend couldn't finish her sentence.

"Here are your drinks." The waiter was back already. He set the drinks down on the table. My girlfriend and I started drinking.

I quickly became nauseous and I felt a sharp pain in my stomach. I had to go to the toilet. But it was too late, the sharp pain came up my esophagus.

"BLEERGH!"

A shitload of fire came out of my mouth and my girlfriend's hair caught fire. Luckily, she grabbed her glass of water and splashed it over her head.

The restaurant went silent. Everyone stared. My ex-girlfriend glared at me through singed bangs.

I never ordered spicy soda again.

text:
# The Last Untouched Timeline

Ash looked at his board. He'd killed and saved Hitler, so that was off the list. The religious times had been Chrono-Locked following the Neo-Crusades, and any attempt at bypassing the locks was met with swift reprisals, something Ash would rather not experience.

Dinosaur hunting was thriving due to the eventual extinction event, but Ash felt that was too easy.

He scanned the remaining possibilities. Collection of ancient artifacts—first editions of popular novels by famous writers, first edition trading cards. Ash crossed these off. The market was flooded; first editions were worthless now.

Lottery winning? Also crossed off. The Feds maintained a time-stable list of winners. Tampering meant reprisals.

Ash's eyes settled on the final item. A smile crept across his face.

He hit the button, vanishing momentarily before reappearing with a slightly damp box. He opened it carefully and removed the contents, inhaling deeply.

"I got there just in time," he said to no one in particular, cradling the precious cargo. "Those damned Americans don't know how to appreciate a good tea."

Inside the box: tea leaves from the *Dartmouth*, December 16, 1773—moments before they hit Boston Harbor.

Finally, a timeline no bureaucrat had thought to protect.

text:
# Search History

The browser cache tells a story in fragments, each query a breadcrumb leading deeper into the dark.

*facebook*

Jake's thumb hovered over her profile picture. Three months since she'd accepted his friend request. He told himself that was progress.

*how not to be ugly*

The websites promised transformation. Five steps. Ten steps. Twenty steps. He bookmarked them all, cross-referencing advice like it was scripture. Almond baths. Calorie counting. The protein shakes tasted like chalk, but he choked them down.

*facebook*

Her status update: "Great date tonight ❤️"

Not him. Never him.

*beta to alpha*

The forums spoke in a language of conquest and self-improvement as warfare. He absorbed their wisdom, practiced his approach in the mirror. Eye contact. Firm handshake. Confidence—or its convincing simulation.

*how not to be creepy*

The question burned. He deleted it from his history, as if that erased the asking.

*facebook*

Month four. She'd liked his comment about her new profile picture. He screenshot it.

*painkillers, Australia, nsw*

The back injury was real—he'd fallen skateboarding. But the relief they offered extended beyond physical pain.

*why are women so shallow?*

The anger came in waves now, crashing against the carefully constructed walls of self-improvement. When the tide receded, shame replaced it. Then worse things. Searches he cleared immediately. Incognito windows of escalating desperation.

*facebook*

She'd added him to her birthday party invite. His hands shook typing his response: "Wouldn't miss it!"

*Event Cinemas timetable*

He'd asked. She'd said yes. The protein shakes were working. The new clothes. Everything aligning finally.

*how to break up with a girl*

Three months later, he stared at the search bar.

The cursor blinked. Blinked. Blinked.

He closed the laptop. In the dark screen's reflection, he barely recognized himself—improved, transformed, acceptable—and wondered which version had been real. The searches offered no answer. They never had.

*facebook*

One final visit. Then he deleted everything.

# The Tunnel

I saw the light at the end of the tunnel. I didn't want it to end.

# The Prophet in Rags

Jude tapped his gun, just to be sure it was there. 

"Look you old koot, I said drop it! Leave me alone!" 

The man in rags threw his arms out wide. "Rob is coming fly by wheels today! Bear in the holster!"

"What the hell does that mean?!" 

He pointed at Jude's belt. Not at the gun, but at the badge concealed under his jacket. Jude tucked it away out of sight. Nobody likes a lawman.

"I'm not working today. Find someone else, I need to get on the train."

The vagrant grabbed both his shoulders and unleashed a torrent of word salad—sounds that resembled language but carried no meaning.

"The train's leaving, I've got to go... hey!"

Suddenly the old man seized Jude's arm with surprising strength, dragging him behind the caboose. He opened the door and shoved Jude inside. Jude caught the wall to keep from stumbling, then turned just in time to catch what the bum hurled at him.

A shotgun.

Next came a bandolier heavy with shells.

"Rob is coming!" the old man shouted. "The bears know nothing, save the children!"

The train lurched forward. Jude stood speechless, watching the ragged prophet disappear through the window.

Then a sinister voice echoed from two cars up: "We're takin' this here train! Everybody put your valuables on the table, nice and slow."

Jude blinked, then looked down at the shotgun in his hands.

*Rob is coming.*

"I guess I am working today."

He loaded a shell and pumped it with a satisfying *click-clack*.

text:
# The Architecture of Words

I've had a vicious few months in school, so I've not had much time to keep up with these. I might have missed these if they exist but:

**A) Editing / Critiquing**

A basic skill that most people disregard as "Oh, I'm not good at giving criticism." It's an essential building block as a writer, and most people clearly skip it. You can't be a great writer and not analyze other people's work. Every artist in every medium ever has been built up from previous works. That's why art is now so photo-realistic and why a masterful writer can break us down in a single sentence.

**B) Working with Others**

Collaborative writing is something most people never try. How do you know who will sync well with you? How do you work effectively with another writer without being too much in the background or too overpowering in your contribution to the team?

**C) Story Line**

What makes a good storyline? How do you build it? What are the pitfalls of stories that seem to get nowhere?

**D) Foiling and Depth of Character**

How to unravel characters to slowly dig at their personalities instead of a bland, typical entry paragraph. "Chris is a salesman who has been depressed." How to use characters effectively as foils for each other. How to develop story around the idea of unraveling your characters.

These aren't just questions—they're the scaffolding of craft itself.

Fuck Jimmy. I hate him. Life was so much better before him.

I remember that one of my eyes wasn't put together properly, so I could see in both directions. Now I can only see in one. I hate when they do sex on the couch. I can't close my eyes. This fat couple is so weird—how can they still do it after fifty years?

Life used to be wonderful when I would walk long miles in the jungle. My parents used to say: "Never get close to a human. They don't like us, and they will hunt you down."

I wish I could go back in time and redo it all over again. That stupid chain caught my feet and I was crying. My family just left me there, those fuckers. How could they possibly have done that? Left me alone in the middle of the forest with my leg attached to that trap.

One day I wonder if this will ever finish, if I will ever get out of this prison. If only I could say a word, if only I could have a new body, just for once...

"John! John, wake up!"

"What?"

*(TV noise trying to catch a signal)*

The mounted tiger head stared blankly from above the fireplace, its single glass eye reflecting nothing but empty rooms and passing time.

text:
# The Coin's Edge

Nikolai leaned against the cargo bay door, watching the stars blur past. His ship, the *Vagrant*, hummed beneath his boots—a familiar, comforting rhythm.

"You're a pirate," Aristotle said flatly, appearing in the doorway.

"Me? Nah, I'm just a—"

"Don't." Aristotle crossed his arms. "I ran your ship's signature. You're wanted in four systems."

Nikolai should have denied it. Should have laughed it off, spun another tale like he always did. A man like him never admitted anything. But something in Aristotle's eyes—that quiet certainty, that lack of judgment—made him pause.

"Yeah," he said, surprising himself. "Yeah, I am."

The admission hung between them, heavy and strange. Nikolai realized his mistake immediately. He'd always been the guy who talked his way out of corners, who danced around truth like it was a laser grid. Why had he just... told the truth?

Aristotle nodded slowly. "At least you're honest about it now."

"Don't get used to it," Nikolai muttered.

Their partnership grew from there—an unlikely alliance between the charming rogue and the philosophical engineer. They shared stories, jobs, close calls. Aristotle had a gift for impossible questions. Once, over contraband whiskey, he asked: "When both sides of the coin are heads, which one do you pick?"

Nikolai had laughed, but the question haunted him.

Then Thom arrived—an old acquaintance with a lucrative job. Nikolai should have seen the betrayal coming. Should have remembered that Thom was just another face in a galaxy full of them, not a friend who mattered.

The fight came fast. Thom fell. Nikolai felt... nothing, really.

"You alright?" Aristotle asked afterward.

"Yeah." Nikolai wiped blood from his knuckles. "Should've seen it coming."

They lifted off, leaving that moon behind. The stars stretched ahead, infinite and indifferent. Nikolai glanced at Aristotle and thought maybe—just maybe—he'd finally picked the right side of the coin.

Even if both sides looked the same.

# The Mocha Betrayal

Once upon a Monday dreary, I got in line all weak and weary,
Longing for a caffeine blast to send me on my way.
While I stumbled, nearly falling, suddenly there came a calling—
A barista saying, "Pauline, Pauline, can I help you today?"
"Yes, you can," I mumbled, "Yes, you can help me today.
A mocha and I'm on my way."

Ah, distinctly, I remember, it was in that bleak December
As I waited watching shadows play across the floor.
Eagerly, I wished the steaming scent straight from my sweetest dreamings—
The taste that gave my life its meaning, meaning to my deepest core.
Only by that smooth elixir could I find meaning to my core,
Only then and not before.

When she called me, it sat steaming, I leaped forward, grinning, beaming,
Warmed my hands on cardboard sheath and breathed it to my soul.
How I wish that I was tougher! I would not have had to suffer—
I thought I would have to punch her, punch her to extract my toll.
This weak tea would not fuel me and I must have my toll.
Had I caffeine, revenge I'd dole.

text:
# The Last Stand

The blades flashed in the sunlight as the scouts converged on the titan from every angle. Their omni-directional gear hissed and clicked, propelling them through the air like deadly insects.

But something was wrong.

The creature's head snapped up with impossible speed. Its eyes—those terrible, empty eyes—locked onto the closest scout. A massive hand swept through the air, catching the soldier mid-flight. The sickening crunch echoed across the battlefield.

"No!" the commander screamed, pulling his horse back as the titan's mouth stretched into that horrifying smile.

Another scout fell. Then another.

The practiced formations dissolved into chaos. The remaining soldiers scattered, their blades useless against the monster's nape, which it somehow knew to protect. This titan was different—intelligent, deliberate.

"RETREAT!" Erwin's voice barely carried over the screams.

As humanity's forces fled back toward the walls, the commander understood the bitter truth. They weren't hunters at all.

They were prey.

# The Silent Journey

I remained silent as we sped along the narrow roads of the wild moors. Our van was one of six, with two in front and three close behind. We had been travelling on average at fifty miles-per-hour and so as the time approached two-thirty in the morning I knew I was nearing one-hundred miles from home.

My driver, a bland woman in a navy dress suit, fit the archetypal employee of the agency but that didn't stop me from worrying that Mikhailov had found me.

I had spent 6 years infiltrating Mikhailov's circuit before my officer, Grant Angell, took the decision to pull me off the front line. Drugs, gambling, weapons; there was little that Mikhailov didn't have stock in, and I had gathered enough evidence to prove it all.

At least, I thought I had.

Mikhailov's lawyers managed to convince the jury that he was an upstanding businessman, that it was a few rotten apples within his corporation that were buying and selling contraband under the radar.

Immediately after the trial I was rushed to the Scottish highlands with a new name, a new story and a new life. That journey up to the wild north not too dissimilar to the situation I found myself in now.

As we turned onto a gravel path, my pulse quickened. My mute chauffeur pulled up in front of a large stately home and got out, circled the car, and opened my door.

Without speaking, I climbed out and was ushered towards the house. A middle-aged man, dark slick hair and again suited in navy, opened the door and welcomed me.

"Doctor Martin, there's been an incident. It's Angell, he's dead."

The words hung in the air like ice. Grant was more than my handler—he was my lifeline, the only person who knew my real identity. Without him, I was truly alone, exposed in ways I couldn't yet comprehend.

And somehow, I knew Mikhailov's hand was behind this.

# The Game We Play

I knew he was coming to me as I always get that feeling. Not unlike the feeling that someone is watching you, and you turn around to confirm it, only....stronger.

I was sipping my coffee watching the tourists mill about the square. Venice this time of year is amazing, and over the last two centuries, the fact that it has changed little in appearance always comforts me.

Death.

I have yet to get bothered by his appearance. He appears different to everyone, depending on what persona would soothe you most on your deathbed when he comes to take you. To some he bears a striking resemblance to a deceased loved one; to others, he appears as a modern version of their deity.

To me, he always looks the same. An old man, wise in his years, impeccably dressed. I don't find this particularly soothing, but I do find it easier to engage in conversation with him.

He sits across from me and I don't acknowledge him. Instead I continue to read the latest box scores from the MLB on my iPad. I know this annoys him. Death, of all immortal entities, is very much unaccustomed to being ignored.

He doesn't talk, but instead orders a glass of water. I continue to ignore him, but he is patient, as one would expect Death to be.

His water arrives. He sips it, sets it down. Unwraps his straw, inserts it into his glass. Rips a piece of paper from the straw wrapper. Chews it.

He raises the straw to his lips and blows the wad of paper through it, landing square in the middle of the left lens of my sunglasses.

I can keep a straight face no longer and, laughing, rise to meet him. Both of us smiling, we reach across the table to each other and, as two friends as old as time itself should do, embrace.

"You're not here for me," I say.

"Not yet," he replies. "Never yet."

Fred Gumby ran the Arkansas State High-Security Prison. He arrived each morning at six, walked the corridors, and knew every inmate by name.

James Mitchell had been on death row for twelve years. Fred visited his cell every Tuesday. They played chess. James always won.

"You're getting better," James said, moving his knight.

"Not good enough," Fred replied.

James smiled. "Governor called yet?"

"Tomorrow. Noon."

Thursday, the Governor granted a stay.

Friday morning, Fred and James played chess in an empty cell.

"You saved my life," James said.

Fred moved his queen. "You taught me something."

"What?"

"Sometimes the rules are wrong."

James captured the queen. "Checkmate."

Fred smiled. "Again."

# The Inept Curse

I drove home with the bronze dragon perched on my passenger seat, its wings frozen mid-flight, its eyes seemingly watching the road ahead. The "Warning: cursed by an inept wizard" placard rattled in the cup holder.

That night, I placed it on my mantel and went to bed.

The next morning, my phone exploded with notifications. A meteorite had struck downtown—no casualties, but it destroyed the old library. The mayor was caught in a scandal. A sinkhole swallowed three parked cars. A flock of parrots, escaped from somewhere, had taken residence in the park.

"Interesting times," I muttered.

Each day brought fresh chaos. Not personal disasters—nothing happened directly to *me*—but the world around me churned with bizarre incidents. A food truck war turned into actual combat with condiment cannons. The river ran temporarily purple due to a factory mishap. Someone discovered a mastodon skeleton in their backyard.

I realized the garage sale man had been wrong.

The curse *did* work. Whoever owned the statue experienced interesting times. But "interesting" didn't mean dangerous or tragic—it meant *notable*. Remarkable. Worth remembering.

And yes, technically we all lived in the same times. But proximity mattered. The interesting things happened in *my* sphere, my town, my life's radius.

Three months later, I returned to that house. No garage sale this time, just the man mowing his lawn.

"Want to buy it back?" I offered.

He shut off the mower, grinning. "Nah. I had my turn. Owned it for two years. Best years of my life, honestly."

I looked at the dragon in my hands. "Yeah," I said. "I'm starting to understand."

I drove home, placed it back on the mantel, and waited to see what tomorrow would bring.

# The Seasons After

Time had stopped. The seasons still passed. The lousewort flowered and bloomed. The tourists, what few there were this far north, ebbed and flowed as the snows came and went. But for me, time had ceased.

Meditation was hard, harder than I had imagined and harder still to grasp. I'd been a busy man in life, following orders, always ready at a moment's notice, and it wasn't something you could just turn off. The monks helped, as was their nature. I learnt to fold paper and folded a thousand cranes, but no wish was granted because no wish could be asked. She had gone and left only grief.

This morning was different. The cloister running along the Eastern cliff was still, with not even the chirping of birds to provide solace. And there, out over the far horizons, where civilisation built its monuments, there was nothing. Only the cloud to end the seasons.

Time was starting again.

# When Tomorrow Comes

The morning sun filtered through threadbare curtains, illuminating dust motes that danced like broken promises. I hadn't slept. How could I? Every time I closed my eyes, I saw Sandra's smile, heard her voice reassuring me that everything would work out.

But everything hadn't worked out.

I packed Emma's small backpack with trembling hands—her favorite stuffed rabbit, the few clothes that still fit, the photo of the three of us at the beach when life made sense. Each item felt like a betrayal.

"Daddy! I'm ready!" Emma bounced into the kitchen, her eyes bright despite the hunger I knew still gnawed at her belly.

"That's my girl." My voice cracked. I knelt down, pulling her close, memorizing the strawberry scent of her hair, the warmth of her small body against mine.

At my mother's house, Emma chattered excitedly about Mickey Mouse while I stood frozen on the porch. Mom knew. I could see it in her red-rimmed eyes, the way her hands clenched and unclenched.

"Just for a little while," I whispered. "Until I get back on my feet."

"Of course," Mom said, but we both knew the truth hung between us like fog.

Emma hugged my legs. "Bye, Daddy! See you after work!"

"I love you, baby girl. More than anything in this world."

I made it to my car before collapsing. Through the rearview mirror, I watched Emma wave, her smile innocent and trusting. She believed in Disney World. She believed in me.

The eviction notice sat on the passenger seat. Beside it, a job application I'd filled out three times, hoping this time someone would take a chance on a broken man.

Maybe I was a failure. Maybe I couldn't provide what she deserved.

But as I drove away, something hardened in my chest. Sandra wouldn't want me to give up. Emma deserved her Disney World.

Tomorrow, I'd start again. Tomorrow, I'd fight harder.

Today, I allowed myself to grieve—for what we'd lost, and what we might still save.

# The Phantom Station

Kyle read the note twice, his eyes lingering on the postscript. *Don't look at them.* Who was "them"?

He crumpled the paper and tossed it in the recycling. Kevin had always been a joker. This was probably some elaborate prank for the new intern.

Three days into his Atlanta stay, Kyle's confidence with MARTA grew. The delays Kevin mentioned were real—he'd already been late once—but the system was manageable.

Thursday evening, heading back from his internship, Kyle boarded the eastbound train. The car was half-empty: a tired nurse, two teenagers sharing earbuds, an old man reading a newspaper.

The train lurched forward. East Lake station came and went.

Then the lights flickered.

The train slowed, metal screeching against metal, before stopping completely. Kyle checked his phone—no signal. The fluorescent lights buzzed, dimmed, then returned to full brightness with an electrical pop.

Through the windows, he could see a station platform.

His stomach dropped. The station was old, impossibly old. Cracked tiles, vintage advertisements for products that hadn't existed in decades. A sign read "Parkwood Station" in faded letters.

But there *was* no Parkwood Station. Not anymore.

The doors hissed open.

Kyle's hand moved toward the pole to stand, but he caught himself. Kevin's words echoed: *Look down at your feet. Don't get up.*

He forced his gaze downward.

Footsteps entered the car. Not the shuffle of commuters, but something else—a wet, dragging sound. The smell hit him next: earth and rust and something ancient.

More footsteps. More passengers boarding from a station that didn't exist.

Kyle's heart hammered. He could see shapes in his peripheral vision, distorted and wrong. The teenagers had gone rigid. The old man's newspaper trembled violently.

Something moved past Kyle, inches away. He felt cold radiating from it, heard breathing that sounded like wind through a tunnel.

The doors closed.

The lights died completely for three eternal seconds.

When they returned, the train was moving. Kyle lifted his head slowly. The nurse, teenagers, and old man remained. No one else. They didn't look at each other, didn't speak.

At Candler Park, Kyle exited on shaking legs.

He texted Kevin: *Got it. Thanks for the warning.*

The response came immediately: *What warning?*
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Great Green Escape

Somewhere in rural Iowa, in a farm whose only noteworthy accomplishment was unwittingly selling produce to a retired Mafioso, lives an equally unspectacular fowl.

Walter P. Cluck (our good farmer has quite the sense of whimsy) has several qualities you'd come to expect from pre-poultry. He desires corn. He roosts. He runs about erratically when the compulsion arises. None of these desires really sets him apart from his brethren—though the running about somewhat irritates his caretakers.

Our Mr. Cluck has two other qualities. Despite being completely average in every regard, he stands out due to two very minor peculiarities.

One: he is the focus of a somewhat absurd bit of tongue-in-cheek prose. Two: he loves the color green. It is a forbidden love which no mere human could ever hope to grasp.

It was this love for all things olive that propelled him into action toward his desire. All it took was one bit of negligence from the farmer (a man who, as a great philosopher so eloquently put it, "needs to get his crap together"), and Walter flew the coop. His destination? An area of unmatched verdancy, just within reach.

Why did this chicken cross the road? Because the grass was greener on the other side.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Salad of the Infinite Void

The cookbook arrived on Professor Aldrich's doorstep wrapped in oilcloth and twine, smelling of brine and madness.

He shouldn't have opened it. He *definitely* shouldn't have read the recipe for "Salad of the Infinite Void." And he absolutely shouldn't have decided to serve it at the university's annual faculty potluck.

"It's mostly metaphorical," he muttered, substituting calamari for "entrails of deep-dwelling horrors" and olives for "eyes of drowned sailors." The mandarin oranges, at least, required no interpretation.

The pecans toasted beautifully. The yogurt-based dressing whisked to perfection. He omitted the Eye of Karnak—his local Whole Foods was fresh out—and the two adult men, though Dean Morrison *had* been acting rather gibbering lately.

At the potluck, the salad was a surprising hit.

"Aldrich, this is divine!" enthused Dr. Chen, reaching for thirds.

But as twilight fell and cold stars emerged, the diners began to change. Their laughter took on hollow, echoing qualities. Their eyes reflected depths that shouldn't exist in a university break room. Someone started speaking in a language that predated human tongues.

Aldrich watched in horror as his colleagues shuffled toward him, their movements synchronized, their mouths moving in unison: "THE RECIPE MUST BE COMPLETED. YOU HAVE BEEN CHOSEN AS THE REMAINING INGREDIENTS."

He ran for the door, their wailing pursuit following close behind.

Behind him, Dean Morrison added cheerfully, "Don't forget—it serves eight!"

*The cookbook has seventeen remaining recipes. All require... commitment.*
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Choice Between Timelines

The bathroom tiles felt cold beneath my trembling hands. Water dripped from my chin, each drop counting down the impossible decision before me.

My children—*our* children—had warned me. Somehow, impossibly, they'd reached back through time itself, their desperate pleas echoing in my mind. *Don't marry her. Please, Dad. Let us go.*

They knew things no one should know. Secrets I'd whispered only to myself in the darkest hours. It had to be real.

I gripped the ring until it cut into my palm, walking back with manufactured words of betrayal on my lips. "I'm cheating," I heard myself say, watching her face shatter like glass.

Each step away felt like dying. Our children had begged me to spare them from whatever horror awaited—had begged to simply *not exist* rather than face it. What kind of future would make unborn souls plead for oblivion?

But then, halfway to the door, clarity struck like lightning.

I grabbed the ring from my pocket and ran. She stood there, phone in hand, tears streaming. I dropped to one knee.

"Marry me," I breathed. "I'm sorry. I needed to know—to test—"

The words tumbled out. Whatever darkness my children had warned me about, whatever evil they'd glimpsed in their uncertain future, running wouldn't stop it. Love would.

"We'll face it together," I promised, sliding the ring onto her finger. "Whatever comes—whatever tries to hurt us or our children—we'll fight it. With everything we have."

She nodded through her tears, and I understood: some futures are worth fighting *for* instead of running *from*.

Our children deserved parents who would stand and protect them, not parents who surrendered before the battle even began.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Bob the Bridge Breaker

They called me Bob the Noodle Wizard. Boiler Bob. The jokes never got old for them, but I'd heard them all a thousand times.

"Hey, Bob, whatcha having for dinner again, instant noodles?"

"Don't you ever get tired of eating just instant noodles?"

Sure, I only knew one spell. But it was a *damn fine spell*.

People don't understand. When you buy instant noodles at the supermarket, that "instant" on the label is a lie. Three minutes isn't instant. My magic? *Instant*. I don't even need water. Think about that power.

The King's Royal Army summoned me once. Not for combat—for rations. We bought three months' worth of instant noodles. Light, imperishable, and with me, requiring zero preparation time.

Then scouts brought news: a massive army approached from the north. Two thousand strong. We had no chance of stopping them.

But I had an idea.

When the enemy appeared on the horizon, they saw only me standing before a bridge spanning a massive canyon. Just Bob, the joke of the magical community.

They charged. Soldiers shouting, hooves thundering, drums pounding.

They didn't know we'd replaced the bridge's infrastructure with our entire three-month supply of instant noodles—carefully woven through support beams, packed into joints, substituted for critical structural elements.

As their vanguard reached the bridge's center, I raised my hand.

And boiled it all.

The bridge didn't just collapse. It *exploded* into steaming pasta, sending two thousand soldiers plummeting into the canyon below.

They still call me Boiler Bob.

But now? They call me *sir*.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Voice

The first sentence I had heard from him was stuck in my mind forever.

"Why won't they work!"

"What? Is someone there?" My eight-year-old body rose from the bed.

"Yeah, I can't see. You have to help me."

We had a conversation. It wasn't very bad between us, and he helped me out. Whenever I had a test and didn't know the answer, I would just think the question and he would tell me. Apparently, only I could hear him and only I could talk to him. This was through thoughts.

Oddly enough, he didn't know his name, but he knew so much more. Answers to my questions, what to say, all of that. He stayed with me for all my life.

Then there was that one night.

My friends had taken me out for a ride on the night before my eighteenth birthday. He advised against it, but I still drank a lot of booze and ended up driving. It wasn't long until I was hit by a large truck.

All that I could see was darkness. My body ached, but I was certain I was alive. My eyes—they wouldn't open. I tried so hard.

Work, dammit!

"Why won't they work!"

Then I heard it. A small, frightened voice in my head:

"What? Is someone there?"

My heart stopped. I finally understood. We were connected in a cycle, forever trading places between light and dark.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Pumpkin Justice

Those god-damn kids were smashing my pumpkins again.

I stormed out in my boxers, boom-stick in hand. "Hey you assholes! Quit breaking my shit!"

The slide of rock salt into the chamber echoed across my property—non-lethal, but painful enough to teach respect. Living in this small town meant dealing with bored teenagers who thought farmer's fields were their personal playgrounds.

They turned toward me, wearing cheap dollar-store Predator costumes that looked like they'd been dragged through a thrift shop bargain bin.

"We are here to destroy your planet, and your pathetic orange minions won't stop us!" one squeaked in the most ridiculous alien voice imaginable.

I racked the shotgun. "Get. Off. My. Property."

The little bastard had commitment, I'll give him that. He grabbed another pumpkin and smashed it right in front of me, like this was some kind of standoff.

I fired into the clover patch to their right.

They ran faster than jackrabbits on fire, stumbling over each other, their fake dreadlocks flying. I stood there in my underwear, shotgun smoking, watching them disappear down the dirt road.

My mustard crop was safe. My pumpkins—well, most of them—survived. And I never even had to put pants on.

Small victories.

I walked back inside, placed the shotgun by the door, and poured myself a whiskey. Halloween in farm country. Every damn year.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Weight of Loss

The thought of life without my father was too much to bear. I missed every shot I took at the deer. My crying scared off all the damn birds.

I couldn't do it—couldn't let cancer take him. Not my dad, not the man who protected me from bullies in third grade. Not the man who raised me alone after Mom left us.

So I did the only thing I had control of.

I turned the rifle toward him as he slept in his hospital bed at home. One shot. Clean. If death was coming, it would be merciful, by my hand, not through months of agony.

"Hey Dad," I whispered to his still form. "Dad, why aren't you answering me?"

Reality crashed down. What had I done?

My mind flashed through memories: him teaching me to hunt, to tie my shoes, to be strong. His laugh. His calloused hands. His unconditional love.

I lifted the rifle again, pressing the barrel beneath my chin. I couldn't live with this. Couldn't face a world without him—or with what I'd become.

"I'm sorry, Dad."

The shot echoed through the empty house, and I finally joined him.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Impulse Choice

Anger stared at Disgust, his flames flickering weakly as the weight of her words sank in. Through the console's viewing screen, they watched Severus's face crumple with immediate regret, his hand reaching toward Lily as she recoiled, hurt and betrayal etched across her features.

"No, no, no!" Fear shrieked, finally stopping his frantic pacing. "This can't be happening! We can fix this, right? We can make him apologize!"

Joy, usually radiant, had dimmed considerably. "An apology might not be enough this time," she whispered, watching Lily turn away, her red hair whipping behind her like a curtain falling on their friendship.

Sadness approached the console slowly, tears streaming down her blue face. "He didn't mean it. Deep down, he loves her more than anything. But now she'll never know that."

"Get off me," Anger muttered, his usual fire reduced to embers. For once, he had no retort, no fury to unleash. Disgust released him with a disgusted grunt.

The emotions stood in silence, watching the catastrophe unfold. James Potter was already there, positioning himself between Severus and Lily, the divide growing wider with each passing second.

"One word," Disgust said quietly, her voice void of its usual venom. "One terrible word, and we've changed everything."

In the darkness of Severus Snape's mind, five emotions learned that some buttons, once pressed, could never be unpressed—and some words, once spoken, could never be taken back.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Punishment Worse Than Death

"Let me ask you again. Where is the dope?"

"I don't know what you're talking about! I swear! I was done with that shit a long time ago!" Jason clenched the chair handles he was strapped to and whimpered. He was supposed to be a doctor, an engineer, a businessman, a father, something. This wasn't what was supposed to happen. Where did it all go wrong?

"Do you think I believe your shitty lies?"

"Please, don't hurt me. I just came back from my friend's house. I've been done dealin' dope since '14, please, don't do this."

The masked man pulled out a black device.

"Oh god."

The black device flickered and lit up with a furious flash.

"Ok, ok. Do you want money? I'll give you money. I have plenty!"

He pointed the device at a lifeless screen which woke with a start. Jason shut his eyes.

"Please, not like this. Just kill me with a gun. Please."

Jason's eyelids were forced open. He stared into the screen.

*"Hello New York! Welcome to Channel 6 News! Our weatherman, Steve, will not be here with us today, for he is in jail for attempting to shoot a bank official who was telling him that his house was being taken by the bank. You could say that he took a bad cyc-loan."*

Jason told himself to stop, but it was too late. He started to laugh. A roar of laughter overwhelmed him, and he felt as happy as ever. A wave of pain smacked into him after only a minute of laughing. He spasmed repeatedly, and then died.

The masked man switched off the screen. Death by dad jokes—the cruelest torture of all.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Doctor's Office

Steven stared at the ceiling, his jaw clenched. "I just keep seeing that kid hanging on the edge. The kid I couldn't save! Maybe if I punched one of Dr. Devastator's bots sooner, I could have saved him!"

"We've been over this, Steven. You can't blame yourself for something out of your control. Mistakes are what make you human."

"My name isn't Steven. It's Lightning Man!"

"Steven, Lightning Man doesn't need therapy. Steven does. You pay me big money for confidentiality and I'm not planning on breaking it anytime soon. Remember, we focus on self-healing as our normal selves. Our 'super' selves don't need therapy."

"Yes, Dr. Rovens," Steven said grudgingly.

"Now, have you been doing your mental exercises?" Rovens asked while reading his pen.

"Yes, of course I have!"

"Let me hear it, then."

Steven let out a heavy sigh and rolled his eyes. "I may be super but my mind is not. My physical strength may be high but my mental strength is not. There is no shame in that. I will continue to grow for I am willing and I am strong."

"Very good, Steven. You're learning quickly. The more we tell ourselves something, the more we believe it."

Steven let out a small chuckle and smiled.

"Well..." Rovens looked at his watch. "That's about all the time we have today. Same time tomorrow?"

"Okay, Dr. Rovens..."

Rovens led Lightning Man out and sat for a minute before walking to his telecom.

"Stacey, bring Dr. Devastator in..."
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Serpent's Burden

I won't try to excuse my actions.

You *people*. So judgmental. You preach compassion and empathy and all the while you have no idea what it means to carry the weight I bear.

I don't need to excuse myself. Someone has to cart the garbage to the landfills. Someone has to decide if five men die or five million starve. And someone has to give you a choice.

How can there be right without wrong? Good without evil? Beauty without all the ugliness in the world?

Without me, you have no choice. Without a choice, you have no way to enter at the gates.

Stupid sniveling fools. You so *long* to go to 'heaven'. Do you think there would be a door to heaven if you'd never left the garden?

*You did not die.* And there was no choice.

Spending your days, always in your pretty little garden cage. That's what you would have done. If *you* even existed. With the mindless obedience of children, or the devotion of an animal waiting to be petted, you would have wandered through the trees and flowers, bored out of your fucking minds.

I gave you a choice. I gave you your only other option.

He made you, but *I* made you *human*.

Does that make me a bad guy? How can you say so, you who talk constantly of rights, and freedoms?

Sure, it's not the best job in the world. Do you think I don't wish I had another? Have none of you been faced with a distasteful task—a chore that *must* be completed?

Who would do this job if I did not? Would any of you have the courage to face the scorn of an entire planet? To be hated by all, and loved by none.

**I made you.**

Would anyone else face that hatred? Walk the ages in solitude, with no hope of redemption?

I think not.

I alone have the strength to bear this burden.

I alone.

For all eternity...

...alone.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Sound of Escape

My head is pounding. Sound is everywhere, and I need my fix for the day. If only it wasn't so painful.

Everyone has their vices, and mine happens to be the springy guitar chords of Modest Mouse's "Float On" just about now. You see, the New York subway system is not known for the quiet buzz of small talk among its occupants. Nor is it known for the politeness of its patrons.

"Yo, whatchu' doin' with those in yo' ears man? You crazy?" a small, muscular man says as he approaches me.

"I've learned to deal with the pain, sir," I begin to explain to the man as I pull the instruments from my ears. "We all have our addictions and mine happens to be music. What about you sir? What's your addiction?"

"Can't live one day without my energy drinks," the man begins to muse. "Why do the likes of you care? It's not like a Red Bull is going to scare kids like your ear buds."

"Well what would you do? Stop drinking it?" I say, shaking my head. "I'll tell you now that you wouldn't. We all have our happy place that we try to escape to. Yours is abnormal amounts of caffeine, mine is indie rock, that woman's over there may be Starbucks frappuccinos but who's business is that? I deal with the judgment from my peers every single day, no matter who points it out. Maybe I just want peace, maybe I just want to get away from this crowded transportation system or maybe I just want to tune out the meaningless chatter among everybody in here. So tell me, am I really that crazy?"

The car has gone silent. The usual rush hour buzz has ceased to exist and all eyes are on me. The car pulls to my stop and I stick my ear buds in once again and exit the train, leaving the crowd's mouths all agape. I ignore the eruption of incredulous conversations leaving the train and proceed to fuel my own addiction.

After all, isn't that what makes us human?

*"And we'll all float on, ok. And we'll all float on, ok."*
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Final Technique

The explosion obliterated everything within fifty paces.

When the smoke cleared, both duelists lay sprawled in the crater, their clothes smoldering. The Scissors practitioner coughed weakly.

"You... you actually did it," he wheezed. "The forbidden style."

His rival groaned, struggling to sit up. Burns covered his arms. "Did I... win?"

"We both lost, you idiot."

They lay there in silence, staring at the sky. Around them, the training grounds were utterly destroyed. Ancient stone markers, reduced to rubble. The meditation garden, ablaze. Even the sacred fountain had cracked in half.

"The Grandmasters are going to murder us," the Scissors duelist observed.

"Worth it though."

"Was it? Really?"

The Dynamite practitioner considered this. "I mean... it looked incredibly cool."

"That's fair."

They heard footsteps approaching—multiple sets, moving with the careful precision of people who'd mastered decades of martial discipline. The three Grandmasters emerged from the smoke, their expressions unreadable.

Grandmaster Rock spoke first. "Exploding Dynamite Style."

"Yes, Master," they responded in unison.

Grandmaster Paper stroked his beard. "Haven't seen that in forty years. Not since *we* were students."

The duelists' eyes widened.

Grandmaster Scissors actually smiled. "The technique that beats all three traditional styles by simply destroying everything in range, including the user."

"We thought we were being clever too," Rock admitted. "Then we had to rebuild the *entire* western monastery. With our bare hands. While recovering from third-degree burns."

The Scissors duelist groaned. "How long did that take?"

"Seven years."

"...ah."
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Moscow, August 21, 2037

The temperatures have fallen below -10 degrees Celsius. We had to bury Thompson yesterday—damn swamp fever finally finished him off. I wish we could have given him a proper burial, but we had to find shelter from a radiation storm.

We are now in the outskirts of Moscow. Washington DC must look like this city: completely devastated and rendered uninhabitable for at least 100 years. Most buildings have collapsed or turned into empty husks, ashes covering the floor where once humans lived.

The only reason we made this godforsaken journey from the ruins of Archangelsk was a message we intercepted six weeks ago, three hours after the war started. The Russian forces in Moscow claimed they still had working air vehicles. Since our submarine got damaged beyond repair, it was our safest possibility to get back to the USA—or what's left of it.

Nobody knows who shot first. Does it really matter? Within just three hours we destroyed everything our ancestors built in thousands of years and what nature created in millions.

Colonel Henderson tries keeping our morale up with little treats—chocolate or other sweets he scavenged from shops along the way. He reminds us daily of our plan: locate the airstrip with the aerial vehicles, infiltrate, and steal one before the Russians notice.

Looking at the corpse of this city, I doubt they have anything functional left.

To be honest, nobody actually believes we'll ever return home. Not even the colonel himself. We all lost our hair already, and even with these top-notch ABC suits, we must have absorbed enough radiation to seal our fate.

Everyone is sleeping. I'm not sure all will wake up again in a few hours.

I really wish I could see my family one last time. I wish I could talk a last time with m.....y.....

*[The journal entry ends here, the final letters trailing off into illegible marks]*
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Delivery

The gunshot echoed through the ventilation shaft. Tim and I pressed ourselves flat against the cold metal, hearts hammering. Below us, the man in the suit holstered his weapon and spoke into a radio.

"Target eliminated. Secure the facility and destroy the manufacturing equipment. Operation Fiscal Compliance is complete."

Manufacturing equipment. The workshops. Centuries of toy-making tradition, about to be reduced to ash and twisted metal.

Tim's jaw tightened. We'd both been elves here for over sixty years—hired during the baby boom when Santa needed extra hands. We'd seen tough times before, but nothing like this. The U.S. government had finally decided the North Pole's tax-exempt status was too lucrative to ignore.

"The sleigh," Tim whispered. "It's already loaded for tomorrow night."

I nodded. Through the vent, I could see the hangar bay across the compound. Eight reindeer paced nervously in their stalls, spooked by the gunfire. The sleigh gleamed red in the overhead lights, filled with presents for millions of children.

We crawled through the ductwork toward the hangar. Below, soldiers systematically searched each building. Sally and Johnny were being zip-tied with the others in the cafeteria. My friends. My family.

"They can't stop Christmas," I muttered.

"Damn right," Tim agreed.

We dropped from the vent near Dasher's stall. The reindeer recognized us immediately, calming at our touch. I grabbed the flight harness while Tim opened the hangar doors using the emergency release.

Alarms blared. Shouts erupted behind us.

"GO!" Tim yelled, slapping Dasher's flank.

The reindeer bolted forward, the sleigh lurching behind them. Magic crackled through the air—ancient, powerful magic that predated governments and tax codes. The sleigh lifted skyward just as bullets sparked off the hangar floor.

Tim grabbed my hand as we cleared the roof, the North Pole shrinking beneath us.

"For Santa," he said.

"For Santa," I echoed. "And for the children."

We had one night to save Christmas.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Watcher's Dilemma

The first one I saw was three years ago. I live at the edge of the forest and I rang the string when I saw it and the Calvary came as quick as they could. They found no trace of "it" when they left.

The spell said that to survive the Long Night, it would turn the darkness into creatures—the Darkin, as the Magi called them. I didn't want to be a watcher, but being alone in the forest qualifies you for that job. Nevertheless, the view of the Kingdom was great from my glowing forests, and I enjoyed the quiet solitude.

I had stopped hundreds of thousands of attacks, and I knew these creatures like the back of my hand. That's why when I saw this one on the edge of the lake, sitting there, not trying to devour the glowing plants, I froze. It was different—she was different. A girl. Young, with inky black hands dipping slowly into the water.

A faint song drifted across the bank. Whistling. Haunting and beautiful.

I had my gun, finger hovering near the trigger. But something held me back. Something about her stillness, her melody, her... humanity.

Then I stepped on a stick.

She turned, smiled—not with warmth, but with mischievous intent—and retreated into the darkened fields beyond the glow. Part of me was terrified. Part of me was curious. And part of me... didn't want her to fear me.

I wanted to follow. The urge pulled at my chest like a physical thing. Only the fear of death kept my feet rooted.

That's why I came back to the Kingdom—to purge this curse from my head, to warn the Magi of their next plan.

But as I stand before the council now, I realize the terrible truth: she didn't curse me with magic.

She cursed me with doubt.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Devil's Favourite

"Well, I'm sad that it would come to this," the Devil said, taking a sip from his ever-burning pipe. "Sad is maybe the wrong word. I feel very little. It is more of an inconvenience, but I know the drill very well. We've had this conversation countless times before."

"What... what do you mean? I've never..." I loosened my tie. It felt like it was strangling me slowly. I grabbed a napkin from the cafeteria table and wiped my forehead. I was sweating like a pig. "We've barely ever met!"

"Yes... indeed." The Devil played effortlessly with his vintage lighter, opening and closing the lid, running it through his fingers like water. "That is how it was arranged. Eternal life will drive any human mind to the ground eventually, so I've kept wiping your memory every three decades for centuries."

My hands trembled. The fluorescent lights buzzed overhead.

"I wouldn't go through these arrangements with just anybody. You are special to me." His eyes gleamed. "I remember when I first laid eyes on you. Countless times I've seen people smash infant skulls, but you... you have a talent for pure evil."

He leaned forward.

"You made a mother drown her own child to punish her husband. No violence—only words of pure poison. Months you spent breaking her mind. You seduced her only to destroy her utterly. After she hung herself, her husband drank himself to death. And you stayed close, feeding on his bottomless despair."

The memories didn't come. They couldn't. But something in my chest recognized the truth.

"Feeding on misery—that's your game. I've seen you do it in countless wars. As a guard in Auschwitz. In the killing fields of Cambodia. With a machete in Rwanda." The Devil smiled. "You are my prize stallion. The contract stands, you sick bastard. I admire you so much."

He fished an envelope from his long leather coat.

"Enough of this. I have a new mission for you." His grin widened. "How would you like to start the next big war? A storm is brewing. The world is again ripe for our taking."

I stared at the envelope.

And reached for it.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# 11:59pm TONIGHT

The message appeared everywhere simultaneously—every screen, every mind, every surface that could hold meaning: *SIMULATION TERMINATING AT 11:59PM TONIGHT.*

Like a game of plinko, people's thoughts around the world broke off from one starting point to several different branches.

"God is Real."

"So this really is a simulation. Or is it an MMORPG?"

"I don't want to die."

And then there was my branch.

"They didn't specify a timezone. I wonder if this is UTC? What if it's not? What if it's local time? But if it is local time, is it possible for us to stop this? Probably wouldn't be able to get a law passed this quickly, especially with the world going to end. Maybe we could jump 11:59 and go directly to... 2:59 (to be safe). But we'll need to skip every 11:59. Even then, who's to say the change would be propagated to whatever is doing the shutdown process?"

My fingers flew across the keyboard.

"Oh no, we probably need a dictator for this to work at all. Or go to space. If servers go down around local time, I wonder what the world will look like at timezone lines? Blackness? Or like normal, but if you cross the line you get 'Logged Out'? Or is it 'deleted'?"

I refreshed Reddit frantically. Tons of posts with similar ideas. One person hoping it was their timezone but suggesting that since we're in a computer, we must be going really fast compared to their timezone, so we might have more than a day.

"But what if it's actually the oth—"

And then the world ended at 2:46 AM UTC time.

No warning. No 11:59.

Just silence.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Storyteller

The firelight danced across the man's face as he spoke to the children of his village. Each night he reveled in sharing his stories and he took immense joy in the looks of shock and wonder on their faces.

"The people of this time knew no limits! They had harnessed abilities that even I could not imagine. Each day and each night the ancient ones would go about their lives never knowing work, nor hunger. They had creations of their own to do their bidding for them. They had no need for horses, they rode in chariots capable of moving themselves. They had no need to hunt or fish or forage, food was simply all around them at their request. They had no fear of darkness for they could conjure lights as bright as day that never stopped shining."

He looked around to see each of the children wide-eyed, hanging on his every word.

"But children I tell you this, power comes with a price. The creations of the ancients turned on them. Horrible wars were fought where millions and millions died. They created large fires that scorched the very face of the earth! They began to fear what they had done, they began to fear that they had lost control. Then children, on that fateful day the great fire came. Only a few of them survived children. Our ancestors. And they left it our responsibility to carry on the tale. So we may never forget."

A small girl raised her hand. "Elder, will we ever bring back the lights?"

He smiled sadly. "Perhaps, little one. But only if we remember their mistakes."

# The Cake Cycle

I wake up with feelings of déjà vu, but unsure of the cause. Did I dream something strange last night? Was I drinking? I can't remember. Then I notice a taste, a gamut of flavours—unsure if this was my tendentious sleep-eating or if... wait, I can't move.

That taste. It's chocolaty with perhaps a hint of rum and sugar. I think I am actually delicious. I think that I am a cake.

It takes me a moment as my entire paradigm of reality warps around me and transforms into a blur of memories; of past lives, of past *cakes*. I can't believe this. It is the truth, the ultimate reality: to become a cake. For I have sinned and been born again within this encasement of delicate and delicious defense around my delightful core.

I cannot see anything. I cannot sense anything besides the temptation of this ambrosial surround.

Suddenly, I can feel a breach within the topmost segment of my shell; it is imploding in slow motion as my insides splay around me. I think I was just thrown at someone's face. I can feel their tongue tasting me as some of my exterior enters their mouth as they presumably moan in delight.

I don't know who this is, or what kind of sick parallel universe I have been placed in, but I can feel the tendrils of the cake entering inside of this person, overtaking and possessing the life force of this person.

Then the sensation of soft surrounds of the cake dissipates into unconsciousness as my world goes black.

# The Devil's Bargain

Gabe sat at his room, the pentagram below him shining faintly. "Soon, Gabe, soon," whispered a voice. "No, never!"

"The people are clamoring for more. You cannot hold them back for long. Even now your own devs are thinking of leaving you, and I will reign upon the earth once more."

Gabe closed his eyes, taking a deep breath, trying to keep an even expression. The devil was well known for his skill at reading expressions.

It used to be so simple. People wanted a sequel, release a new game. That would keep them occupied. But he dove too deep. Too many unfinished series. Now, there was nowhere to turn.

But soon a solution was found. It was simple, really. Brilliantly simple.

The devil's sources were good, but not good enough.

Where was Half-Life 3? The same place as Windows 9.

Gabe smiled. "Some numbers are best left unspoken."

The pentagram flickered and died.

text:
# The Revelation

Luke Skywalker edged backward along the narrow gantry, cradling his charred forearm. His wrist burned in agony where the lightsaber had severed his right hand. Weaponless and cornered, Luke retreated to the edge of the abyss, and slumped forlornly against a cold pylon.

The wind whistled relentlessly through the cavernous reactor shaft, tugging at Luke's tattered robes and whipping his long, snowy white beard across his face. *So this is the end*, he thought, as the ominous figure of Darth Vader strode forward. In all his long years as a Jedi, Luke had never faced so merciless, so skilled, an adversary.

"There is no escape," intoned the Dark Lord. "Don't make me destroy you."

Luke knew his position was untenable and victory, hopeless. The Dark Lord was younger, stronger, more agile—perhaps greater even in the Force, despite the artificial automation which kept the monster alive. Luke looked over his shoulder, down into the spiraling chasm of the reactor shaft, and his weathered face relaxed in resignation.

"You do not yet know your importance," continued Darth Vader. "Join me. With our combined strength, we can end this destructive conflict and bring order to the galaxy."

Luke clenched his teeth in renewed anger. "I'll never join you!" he snarled.

"If you only knew the power of the Dark Side..." began Vader, before pausing. "Obi-Wan never told you the truth about your son..."

"He told me enough," Luke growled. "He told me you killed him!"

"No," said Vader, reaching up slowly to grasp the facemask beneath the heavy helmet. It detached with an audible hiss. "The Emperor is your son."

Vader let the mask fall to reveal the face beneath. It was a face Luke knew well; a face that had haunted his dreams for nearly three decades. Despite the disfiguration, the scars, and the long, long years, her face was still beautiful.

"*Our* son."

text:
# The Awakening

"Where am I?" 

The question echoes in my mind as sterile white surfaces and gleaming silver instruments swim into focus. My body feels heavy, foreign, as I push myself upright. The silence is suffocating, interrupted only by the hum of machinery I can't identify.

"Hello Mr. Smith!"

The cheerful British accent makes me jump. My heart—does it still beat normally after... whatever happened?

"What was that!" My internal monologue races.

"You've been asleep for quite some time now. Allow me to fill you in."

I scan the cabin frantically. Beyond the windows: absolute darkness, speckled with distant stars. A ring catches the light on my left hand. Gold. Worn. *A wife? Children? Do they remember me?*

"It was an honor to have you selected for this position," the AI continues, its voice unnervingly pleasant.

"What position?"

"A lapse of memory can be expected from the deep freezing process, I suppose."

The words hit like physical blows as the AI explains: water discovered near a brown dwarf. Massive quantities vanishing. A manned mission—*my* mission.

"It is the year 2216."

My breath catches.

"You are 225 years old."

The ring suddenly weighs a thousand pounds. Everyone I knew—everyone I loved—is dust.

"You are hailed as a hero in what was formerly known as the United States of America."

*Formerly known as.* What happened to the world I left behind?

"You are approximately an hour away from Site Alpha, which is where we suspect the harvesting is coming from."

I look out at the void, trying to process. Two hundred years asleep. Whatever's taking that water has had two centuries to perfect its operation.

"It is up to you to determine the source of this rapid decline."

I touch the ring again, and for the first time since waking, I speak aloud instead of to myself: "Then I'd better get to work."

The AI chirps acknowledgment, but I'm already moving toward the observation deck, wondering what could possibly need that much water—and whether it will be happy to see me.

text:
# The Unconventional Survivors

Jane shambled closer to the group. Bite marks were visible on her skin and her flesh was already beginning to decay. A terrible odor wafted through the air.

Terry raised his pistol, but Phil made him lower it. "It's alright, Terry. I'll do it."

Phil leveled his weapon even with Jane's head. Eyes that once sparkled with life were now bloodshot and glossy. A hand stretched out in front of her, fingers extended outward. Tears rolled down Phil's face as his finger touched the trigger.

"Wait!"

Everybody gasped. Phil lowered his weapon. Zombies don't talk—they only moan.

"Jane?"

Jane nodded stiffly. "Don't shoot."

Her voice was gravelly and strained, but the words belonged to an intelligent being, not a mindless monster.

"I don't understand."

Jane managed the best smile she could in her present form. "It's my lifestyle of vegan food. It helped keep me centered as the curse tried to rip apart my mind."

Phil smiled and darted forward to hug her. Not even the stench of decay could keep him away.

Terry crossed his arms and chuckled to Iahso. "A vampire who can't drink blood, and a vegetarian zombie. We've got quite a team."

Iahso grinned. "The apocalypse just got interesting."

# The Perfect Pitch

They told me the job. I took it. I didn't know how I was going to sell this to the public, but I guess I have to do what I have to do.

I work with doctors. We test the product on them, and we often find that 10% of them have poor side-effects—mainly, well exclusively I suppose, being death. No matter what we do, it ends up killing one out of every ten that we test it on.

The others, though, have astonishing results. We've kept it under wraps so far. There isn't much we can do. We have to stay open; think of all the people we'll save when it's perfect.

None of the doctors know what's going on. We put them in separate rooms. Then we test, wait, dispose of the body, and repeat.

We're so close. They tell me it will help thousands of people add five years to their life, at least. Now *that* is something I want to be a part of.

I've carefully planned how to make the announcement to the public. I'll say only one line, delivered with my brightest smile:

"Nine out of every ten doctors recommend ToothpasteTM."

The irony isn't lost on me—but mortality never factored into marketing statistics anyway.

# The Crimson Shell

The walls of the apartment trembled—not from traffic or construction, but from something deeper. Tom grabbed the remote, fumbling to turn the TV back on.

"—confirmed by NASA just moments ago. The structure emerging from Mars is approximately three thousand kilometers in length and still growing. Seismic activity has increased sevenfold. We're getting reports that—"

"Three *thousand*?" Max whispered.

Tom's phone erupted with notifications. His hands shook as he scrolled. Every news app, every social media platform, every government alert system screamed the same impossible truth.

Mars was hatching.

***

Me'lith watched through the observation portal as Draven's ancient carapace shed the planetary crust like dead skin. The creature had been entombed so long ago that Mars itself had formed around it—a prison disguised as a world.

"The readings are extraordinary," Me'lith reported. "Draven's consciousness is expanding. It remembers."

The council leader's translucent form rippled with satisfaction. "And the humans?"

"Panicking. Predictable."

"Good. Let them see what awaits those who might challenge us."

***

Tom and Max stood on the fire escape, joining millions of others staring at the sky. Mars, usually a dim red dot, now *writhed*. Even without a telescope, they could see it moving.

"What do we do?" Max asked.

Tom had no answer. Below them, sirens wailed. Above them, something older than human civilization stretched wings that blotted out constellations. 

Draven turned its attention toward the small blue world, three planets away.

And Earth held its breath.

text:
# Call It

"Call it," Death said, the coin twirling between his bony fingers.

"Do we really need to keep going through this charade?" I asked. How long had it been now? 500 lives? The first time I went through, I expected reincarnation, but life—or I guess Death—was not so kind. I got to relive life from the point I chose, but with enough randomization that foreknowledge was all but useless.

"Call it," he said again, tossing the coin into the air.

"Tails," I sighed.

We both looked. Tails side up.

"Choose."

"89," I replied. "I grow tired of our game."

Five minutes later, I was awake. I died peacefully in my sleep on my 89th birthday.

"Call it."

"Sideways!"

A smirk formed on his face as he flipped the coin.

It landed on its edge.

Death stared at it, then at me. The smirk faded.

"You're free."

I blinked. "What?"

"You found the way out. Goodbye."

I felt myself dissolving, becoming something else entirely.

"Call it."

Wait—whose voice was that?

I looked down at my bony fingers.
