text:
# The Betrayal

I had given every inch of strength to my work. I had been given a lot of it. Information Exchange and Classification took up most of my time, but an equal amount of stress was almost consistently gleaned from 'holy' coffee and 'holy' doughnut runs. After exactly 60 days of purgatory I had been transferred to Heaven's Department of Secretary's Assistants. I only know I had been there for 60 days because my Advocate told me when I arrived—it had felt like a bit more than that.

In essence I had lead a morally ambivalent life, and now I was being given a chance to not go to hell, because although I hadn't been bad, I hadn't been good either. The deal was simple: burn in eternal hellfire or be the office monkey of a few angels for twenty years. My final decision was the obvious one, and so I completed my work with a youthful fervor.

Yesterday was my last day as a Secretary's Assistant. I briskly walked into the office and to my desk while recalling bits of idiotic tasks I had done over the years—especially the first few. Filing papers into drawers four stories high, sending e-mails in triplicate because duplicates might be misplaced, and trying to corner a doughnut shop that flies around in a plane that has no natural corners. It had been exhausting.

But I was done.

I walked down the floating golden steps and towards the floating golden door of my office. I opened the door and as it shut behind me, I collapsed.

I awoke with a pain in my side, and my head, and my legs, and my chest, and everywhere else. It was excruciating. I was burning alive. Not alive. Dead. I was in Hell.

I had been lied to.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Confrontation

Arthur looked up from his book, an understanding light glimmering in his eyes. "You care about him," he said, his tone mocking, taunting Gilbert for coming and saying such things.

"That's why you're going after me like this."

Gilbert growled, a low tone of warning, his entire posture somehow growing even more dangerous than it had been moments before. "That's not the fucking point, Arthur!" He spat, shaking with poorly repressed rage. "The point is, you need to make up your mind and tell him *something* before I beat the ever-loving shit out of you!"

Arthur swallowed, his book suddenly forgotten on the table. Gilbert took this as a sign to continue.

"You're destroying him, don't you see that?" He hissed, his German accent coming out more strongly in his rage. "He doesn't eat much anymore, barely ever sleeps, it's a stretch to get him to talk. And there you sit, mocking me for coming to you and telling you something is wrong."

He slammed his hands down on the table right in front of Arthur, leaning closer as the Brit wisely leaned away. "You may think you're the perfect fucking gentleman, but if you let this go on, then what you are is a god damn murderer."

"H - he wouldn't be so..." Arthur offered, nervous and meek, an odd contrast to his posh accent.

"He would - fucking - too, *dummkopf*!" Gilbert hissed. "Look around tomorrow, and really look." He jabbed an aggressive finger at Arthur and the blonde awkwardly leaped back from it. "Even an unobservant stick in the mud like you will see what I'm talking about!"

And with that, Gilbert turned and stormed out, leaving a scared and dumbfounded Literature major behind before said man could utter a word.

Arthur sat frozen, staring at the empty doorway. His hands trembled slightly as he reached for his book, then stopped. Gilbert's words echoed in his mind—*destroying him*.

Had he really been so blind?
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Time

"We have to talk."

My girlfriend Sally says those words as soon as I walk in the door from work.

"Okay?" I answer, confused, putting down my work backpack.

"There's another guy, Jack." She places her hands on her face.

"I'm sorry, what?" I ask, not sure I heard her correctly.

"I've been cheating on you. I can't handle the guilt anymore." Her tone is confrontational, like she's the victim here.

"Wow. You act like it's my fault. Who is the guy?" My legs feel weak. I need to sit down. My stomach churns.

"His name is Fred. He works with me. And it kinda is your fault. You work so much I—"

"You're really gonna make this about me making money so we can stay afloat on minimum wage?" Anger replaces the shock. "What about the baby we're supposed to have? The engagement?"

I pound my hand on our coffee table in defeat.

"The baby is Fred's. Face it. We don't fuck anymore. How could it be yours?"

"I thought that one time on your birthday..." I trail off.

Silence stretches between us like a canyon. She starts crying.

"I'm sorry, Jack. I never wanted it to end like this. I wanted a clean break but I didn't know how to do it."

"So you fooled around, got knocked up, and accepted my engagement last week? What the fuck, Sally?"

I stand up, initially heading for water, but my feet carry me past the kitchen, straight to the back door. The evening air hits my face as I step outside.

I slam the door behind me for the very last time.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Watch That Stopped

It had stopped ticking at 7:34 in the afternoon.

At 9:05 am the day before, it had been on the wrist of a young man making his way to work. At 11:13, the young man had went to lunch with a few coworkers. A regular day.

Around 2:54, a phone call was answered. 3:17 he pulls up to the hospital and runs inside. At 9:43 he holds his newborn daughter in his hands, tears streaming down his face.

At 10:04 the next morning he shares warm smiles with his wife as they cuddle their new daughter.

At 1:31 their daughter starts to have trouble breathing. 4:47 He holds his wife while she cries. The doctor tells them they are doing all they can.

Around 6:15 the doctor returns with sadness etched on his face.

At 7:32 the man is returning home with his wife. They cross over a bridge. At 7:34, he removes the watch—a gift from his father—and lets it fall into the dark water below.

Some moments shouldn't be measured.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Best Piss I Ever Took

The throb behind my eyes reminded me why day-drinking on a Tuesday was a terrible idea. But when you've been unemployed for almost a month, days blur together like watercolors in the rain.

I woke with a bladder so full it hurt. Six PM, according to my phone. I stumbled to the bathroom, barely getting everything aimed in the right direction before the relief came—that transcendent, almost spiritual release that sometimes, just sometimes, beats every other pleasure in life.

A solid minute. One continuous stream, no stutters, no stops. Pure bliss.

Then, right as the flow tapered off, I heard it: the distinctive wobble of Uncle Theodore's Peloponnesian urn rocking on its marble pedestal.

I shoved my deflated member into my briefs—of course the last drops stained the front, they always do—and grabbed the Game Informer from beside the toilet. I rolled it tight. Makeshift weapon, check.

In the foyer, a figure dressed like a cartoon cat burglar—all black with an actual domino mask—was pawing through my valuables.

Without thinking, I pushed the urn off its pedestal.

The crash was spectacular.

The burglar spun. I waved.

He bolted.

Hours later, after the police finished their investigation and dusted for prints, I called my insurance company. That urn—ugly as sin, a family heirloom I'd always hated—was insured for several million.

The check arrived within a week.

Sometimes the universe works in mysterious ways. Sometimes it takes a full bladder, a hangover, and a clumsy burglar to solve your unemployment problem.

I framed that stained Game Informer. Best piss I ever took.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Way Back

He came out of the flashback the way he always did, bewildered and sore. His eyes frantically scanned the room, establishing his setting before they settled on her face, pale and streaked with mascara, eyes wide, relief slowly taking over as his eyes met hers.

She looked more freaked out than usual, and he worried that he'd hurt her this time.

He opened his mouth to speak, but struggled to form anything coherent. This was par for the course, he should have been used to it by now, but each time, he feared he'd broken himself permanently.

She recognized the fear in his eyes and pressed a finger to his lips. She pulled him in close, resting his head on her modest bosom. Her hand moved to his cheek and he settled in.

She began to sing her standard medley of spirituals and folk songs, slowly, and quietly, so as not to betray the wavering in her voice.

"I'm sorry," he finally whispered.

"Hush now. You're here. You're safe."

He closed his eyes, letting her melody guide him home.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Hollow Years

The clock on the wall marks another meaningless hour. I am ninety-eight years old, and I have accomplished nothing.

They say everyone leaves a legacy. Mine will be absence itself—a negative space where a life should have been.

I remember being young, burning with ambition. I would be someone, do something that mattered. Immortality through achievement—that was the dream. But fate is a patient destroyer. It didn't crush me in one violent moment. Instead, it eroded me grain by grain, year by empty year.

I lost Sarah when I was twenty-three. A car accident. Sudden. Final. My heart went into the ground with her, and I never learned to excavate it. The family I might have had dissolved into hypothetical ghosts. The children I never fathered. The grandchildren who will never know my name.

Death should have raged at my door, claimed me in dramatic fashion. Instead, it waits politely, knowing I'm already hollow. Why hurry? There's nothing left to take.

I wake each morning to a world that doesn't need me and never did. I am background noise in someone else's story. My mind circles the void where purpose should reside, fingers probing the chest cavity where my heart once beat with hope.

Now I pray only for darkness. Not from despair, but from logic. Nothingness is honest. Emptiness is where I belong.

When they find me—if anyone bothers to look—they'll discover a shell that stopped living decades before it stopped breathing.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Visitor

"Have you ever done this before?" I ask the young man, as he sits in a small chair, much too small for his large frame.

He smiles and answers in what I can only assume to be English. "I've done a lot of things, but this is the best outcome I could ask for..."

As I turn to ask the Officer beside me for a translation to my native tongue, the man reaches forward and grabs my hand, shaking my attention from Herr Guttschmidt's stuttering attempt at bridging English to German. I'm forced to look at this man in his strange clothes, so out of place in my formal police office.

The man smiles a small, strange smile and says in perfect German, "I did what had to be done to protect my people."

As his perfectly accented German rolls off his tongue, he deposits a blue and white flag on my desk and touches the small black watch on his arm. A huge flash of light erupts in my richly decorated office, used now as a formal interrogation room.

When Guttschmidt and I climb back to our feet, the prisoner is gone. Only remnants remain: a large scorch mark and a book on the chair where the prisoner had sat moments before.

The cover reads "Mein Kampf."

Guttschmidt picks it up, exclaiming, "Look at the author's name!"

It is that of our victim—one Adolf Hitler, aged one year and three months and two days on the day of his death at the hands of our disappearing prisoner.

I stare at the flag on my desk, its Star of David gleaming in the lamplight, and wonder what horrors this stranger prevented.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Memory Tree

"Damn thing won't start..." Marcus mutters, yanking the cord of his worn chainsaw. Rust flakes scatter with each pull. After several minutes of curses that would make his late wife blush, one final jerk brings the motor sputtering to life.

He positions himself against the old maple, angles the blade, and squeezes the trigger.

*WHACK!*

His back hits the dirt before he can process what happened. A massive branch lies beside him—one that shouldn't have fallen. No wind. No warning. He scans the empty forest, shaking off the pain.

Rising, he restarts the saw and approaches again. This time, hundreds of leaves explode downward, blinding him in a cascade of green. He stumbles back, bewildered. Mid-April. The maple shouldn't be shedding.

The chainsaw dies in his hands as he sets it down, sinking to the forest floor. A childhood fear washes over him—that primal certainty of running up dark stairs, knowing something watches from below. His breath catches.

*You are not alone.*

He forces himself up, circling to the tree's far side. Then he freezes.

His knees buckle. The chainsaw thuds to the ground.

There, carved deep into the weathered bark, is a heart. Inside: *M + E*, the letters he'd carved forty-three years ago, when Emma said yes beneath these branches. When they'd promised to grow old together, rooted like this tree.

The sobs tear through him—violent, uncontrollable. She'd been gone three years, but she was still here. Still protecting their tree.

He couldn't do it. He wouldn't.

Some memories refuse to fall.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Afterlife Love Connection

The lights dimmed, leaving only vague shadows and dim candlelight. *Erika's Bar and Grill* had been hosting the *Supernatural Meet and Greet* for a decade. It was usually a more lively crowd, but with Halloween approaching, the living were making plans, leaving the ghosts bored and a bit lonely.

Emera had been dead for fifteen years. Her outfit, faded with time, remained the same baggy jeans and plaid crop top combo that was coming back into style. Her short hair hung around her face in dark fringe. She only came to this because Cholly asked her to. The preteen liked this sort of thing, despite not being old enough to take part himself.

Ghosts didn't mature much in their time on earth; they lacked the living experience that made mental jumps that much easier. Cholly still liked to scare people, haunt their toasters, and scream them awake. Emera had graduated from Pranking 101 while she was still alive. She was 21 and the right age to want some companionship. Cholly was like a little brother, the Casper of their haunting.

Cholly had gotten Megra to come as well, along with Harrietta, though they were off in some corner, toeing the line between reality and the dream world. Emera had no interest in other ghosts. She didn't like the way they made her feel—heavy and distorted. So she sat at one of the incorporeal tables, waiting for the next person to join her.

The humanoid who sat down was male, with great horns and a thin smile. He had sharp nails and a top hat. His pronged tail slid across the table, where it ticked like a time bomb.

Not her type.

"What brings a lovely little lady like you to these parts?" the demon said, his red lips drawn back into a menacing grin.

"You know, looking for an Afterlife Love Connection." Emera looked away from "Dan" towards Harrietta.

"That seems logical," Dan said.

He spent the rest of their time talking about his castle in the Lake of Eternal Heartbreak. Emera nodded politely, already planning her escape.

text:
# The Interview

Marcus backed toward the door, his heart hammering. Three months of unemployment had made him desperate, but not *this* desperate.

"Look, there's been a misunderstanding—"

"The ad said 'easy work, top pay,'" the blonde receptionist interrupted, blocking his exit. Her laptop screen glowed with what looked like a live streaming interface. "You responded. Contract's on the website. You clicked 'agree.'"

The spandex-clad man jangled his chains impatiently. "Clock's ticking, sweetheart. We've got five more interviews today."

Marcus's mind raced. Had he actually read the terms and conditions? His stomach growled—he'd eaten nothing but stale hot dog buns for two days.

"I... I can't—"

"Five thousand for today's session," Blonde said flatly. "Cash."

Marcus froze. Five thousand dollars. That was rent, food, a chance to breathe.

"What exactly would I have to—"

"Positronics National is an adult entertainment company," she explained, her tone businesslike. "Niche market. Very niche. But lucrative."

The spandex man checked his watch.

Marcus thought of his eviction notice, the shutoff warnings from the utility companies, his empty refrigerator. He thought about dignity, self-respect, boundaries.

Then his stomach growled again.

"Just... just this once," he heard himself say, voice barely a whisper.

The blonde smiled and started the camera.

Sometimes rock bottom has a basement, Marcus realized. And sometimes, when you're drowning, you stop caring what kind of boat picks you up.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Price of Education

I pull into the faculty lot in my midnight blue Porsche, parking between Martinez's Tesla and Chen's Lamborghini. The student pickup line looks like a luxury car dealership now.

Five years ago, KARMA nearly destroyed us all. The Kindly Automatic Response and Metric Assessment seemed innocent enough—just another accountability measure. But when they linked it to our literal survival, everything changed. One parent's viral rant could trigger a community-wide downvoting cascade that manifested as... accidents.

We lost thousands. Mrs. Patterson, hit by a meteor while watering her garden. Mr. Hughes, food poisoning from a sealed container. The Jefferson Elementary shooting where every bullet somehow missed the children but found their teacher.

I survived by luck, or maybe I just hadn't angered the algorithm yet.

When only 30% of teachers remained, the government panicked. They couldn't automate education fast enough. So they did what America always does—threw money at the problem.

Three hundred grand starting salary changed everything. My twenty-three years of service and consistently high test scores? I'm pulling in $2.8 million annually.

I grab my Hermès briefcase and head inside. Fourth period is Shakespeare.

The irony isn't lost on me: they had to make teaching lucrative enough to be worth dying for.

But damn, it really is good to be an educator now.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Hour Wait

Marcus refreshed the page obsessively, watching the clock tick down. Fifty-nine minutes. Fifty-eight.

The new system had changed everything. Where once the fastest writers dominated, now everyone had exactly one hour. No advantage to being first.

He stared at the prompt: *"The last light in the universe."*

His fingers trembled over the keyboard. Around the world, thousands of writers faced the same blank screen, the same merciless countdown.

Thirty minutes left.

Marcus typed frantically, deleted, typed again. The pressure squeezed brilliance from his mind like water from stone. A twist formed—what if the light wasn't dying, but choosing to leave?

Ten minutes.

He polished the final sentence as the seconds evaporated. His hand hovered over 'submit.'

Five. Four. Three.

Click.

The page went blank, then bloomed with stories. Hundreds of them, appearing simultaneously like stars igniting across the night sky.

No names. No timestamps. Just words.

Marcus scrolled through the constellation of creativity, anonymous among equals. Somewhere in this vast display was his story, and somewhere were the masters he'd always admired.

For one perfect hour, they'd all been the same.

Just writers, racing against time.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Singing in the Flames

Charles pulled his fireproof jacket tighter as ember-sized raindrops began to fall. The forecast had been accurate, as always—Jesus did good work with meteorology.

"I'm singing in the flames, just singing in the flames!" he sang, twirling his umbrella as he dodged a particularly large cinder. "What a hellish feeling, I'm burnt again!"

"Boy, I swear by the Devil in me and you, you better shut your mouth or I'll do it for you!" His neighbor—a piggish-looking man whose jowls quivered with rage—leaned out his window.

"I may enslave you!" Christopher Columbus added from across the street, shaking his fist.

Charles sighed and retreated inside, the brief moment of joy evaporating. He slumped onto his couch, staring at the ceiling where scorch marks formed abstract patterns.

Why him? He'd done nothing wrong. He'd been a librarian, for crying out loud. He returned shopping carts. He donated to charity. Some of the people in Heaven were far worse than him, and he'd gotten stuck here with Edison—who'd stolen every invention he could—and Columbus, whose crimes were literally taught in schools now.

God had visited him once, sheepish and apologetic. "Clerical error," He'd said, wringing His hands. "Really sorry about this, Charles. Problem is, the system's locked. Can't reverse a placement without breaking the entire cosmic bureaucracy. You understand."

Charles hadn't understood. Still didn't.

He flipped the TV back on, catching the tail end of a commercial: "Purgatory Passes—work your way up! Accept prayers today!"

Nobody was praying for Charles. Nobody knew he needed prayers. His file said he was exactly where he belonged.

---

**MEANWHILE IN HEAVEN:**

John reclined on his cloud, sipping ambrosia and watching cherubs play harps. He still couldn't believe his luck.

One hundred and three murders. That cult he'd led. The embezzlement. Somehow, somewhere, wires had crossed, and he'd ended up with Charles's assignment.

He grinned, raising his glass to the cosmic mistake that had saved him.

"God bless bureaucracy," he whispered, and meant it literally.

text:
# The Forgotten Crossing

The book was torn and matted. Some pages had stuck together, unreadable, as the ink had bled through. Only a part of the last page was legible.

"Our maps had been lost in the storm, our sails halved like the last pieces of bread. There is no water, and no food. Only the kegs of rum remain. The air aboard was sweet as sailors slacked and staggered all around. Hoping to drink off the last of rum before anyone found us and stole it for lack of being able to protect ourselves. Jobs half finished, or ill fashioned, didn't seem to matter. There was no water for the body or the mind. It's funny how quickly the drink lets you be at peace with forgetting. (Ink is smudged) My head hurts and my body is heavy. There is no one on the deck, no one manning the helm. The sails are torn. We were supposed to have been sailing straight west for the last week. A terrible fog lies upon the water, and I can't tell if the boat is bobbing up against a sand bar or ill positioned. I look overboard, and can't see anything, only the sound of the water slapping the ship rises up. I don't understand. The shore should be here. Yes, everyone's already gone ashore. I'll..."

The entry ended there, trailing off like the fog itself had swallowed the words whole.

text:
# The Interview

Herbert shuffled nervously in his seat. He needed this job. He couldn't blow this interview, not now. Tapping his feet repeatedly, he looked back at his copy of the initial waiver he signed.

"1. The company is not liable for any harm physical or otherwise that may or may not befall the participants of the interview 2. The company is not liable for any loss of memory which the participant may or may not experience"

That made him nervous. Looking for literally anything else to turn his attention to, he looked up. The woman sitting across from him was staring at him; she looked away as he made eye contact. Someone coughed. He heard the clicking of heels and snapped his attention back to the white door.

The door swung open and the secretary came into view. Herbert remembered thinking she looked like a rather strict librarian.

"Miss Johns, Mr. Drake, and Mr. Herbert—your performance in the written test was deemed to be," she ruffled a few pages, "satisfactory. Please do follow me. The rest of you are free to go. Do not contact the company again."

She went back through the white door. Herbert ignored the cacophony of groans that ensued and followed the secretary nervously, running his hand across his hair. The other two candidates were right behind him.

They followed her through a corridor which ended with three doors.

"The next stage of your interview has commenced. Good luck," she intoned and without a word stalked back through the passageway.

Herbert stared at the three identical doors, each unmarked and pristine white. Miss Johns chose the left. Mr. Drake reached for the middle. Herbert's hand trembled as he grasped the right handle.

Behind him, he heard a door open, then silence—so complete it felt like erasure.

He turned the knob and stepped inside.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Coward's Mythology

Marcus stumbled through the abandoned subway tunnel, clutching stolen antibiotics. Behind him, something ancient stirred—a creature from forgotten myths, now hungry in modern darkness.

His companion lay bleeding topside. *Not my problem,* Marcus thought, quickening his pace.

The creature's footsteps echoed closer. Marcus's heart hammered. He thought of Jenny's face, her desperate plea for help. The antibiotics burned in his pocket like hot coals.

*I could go back.*

The thought flickered and died. Survival first. Always.

He emerged into gray daylight, alone. The tunnel entrance collapsed behind him—dust and screams swallowed together.

Marcus pocketed the antibiotics. They'd fetch good currency in the settlement.

That night, he dreamed of ancient gods judging cowards. He woke unchanged, ready to survive another day in this twisted mythology where monsters were real and heroes were extinct.

text:
# The Choice

The time had come for Daniel to choose. It was his 13th name day. He would choose today whether to join the Silent Brethren or the Truthspeakers. The choice would affect the rest of his life permanently.

The two Orders had a friendly rivalry going—but that was not the thing he was worried about. It was the permanence. If he chose the Silent Brethren, he would only be allowed to speak once every three or so years. And then, only a choice sentence or three.

On the other hand, the Truthspeakers were supposed to talk almost constantly. Every moment filled with chatter. Only those with a steel will would be able to keep sane.

***Later***

Daniel sat in silence. The box in front of him held his official vestments. The point of no return had come, and gone.

The ceremonial beanie with the blonde wig hair attached would be his to wear until his own could grow out. The oversized t-shirt and baggy pants fit surprisingly well, and the yellow coat fit snugly over them. The razor and shaving tools would be his constant companions—after all, only the Silent Brethren were allowed beards.

As soon as Daniel had donned his Truthspeaker clothes, he headed towards the door. His brethren—or "Homies"—would be waiting for him, and for the ceremonial feast.

Today, Daniel was truly a man.

***"SNOOCH TO THE NOOCH, FUCKERS!"***

text:
# The Orange That Changed Everything

There isn't much to my story, really. But in all of my life, I've never felt more alive than at that moment—never more important.

I still don't know who he was. He just came up running, out of nowhere. Gelled-up hair, nice suit and tie, canvas shoes like all the kids wear now. Long brown coat.

"Lucy," he said to me. I was going by Lucy back then.

"Take this orange. In thirty seconds it just might save your life. And then, everything will be fixed. The whole timeline will be back in place."

He handed me an orange. I looked at it, confused, and when I looked up he was gone. Vanished. Not sure where he went.

But that orange was surely handy. I took a few steps, about to cross the street, then stopped to peel my orange. Zooming past me was Mr. Venese from down the street. Ha! Blind as a bat. Would have run me right over!

Sometimes I wonder: was I supposed to die that day? Did that stranger fix something broken in time itself?

I'll never know. But I keep orange peels in my pocket now, just in case.

text:
# The Game

"This is it, Joe." The man in the trenchcoat said. "Here's the game." He held up a revolver. "6 chambers, 5 bullets. Answer the question correctly... and I'll take out a bullet. Incorrect answer and I'll shoot you. Of course, there's the chance that you don't get killed. That's fortunate for you. You'll be free. Are you ready to play?"

Joe nodded nervously.

"What gets wetter as it dries?"

"Ah... um, A towel?" The man took a bullet from the gun.

"If I drink, I die. If I eat, I'm fine. What am I?"

"Err -- a fire!" Another bullet.

"We see it once a year, twice a week, and never in a day. What is it?"

"Ah... um! The... The letter E!" Another bullet.

"What has four eyes, but can't see?"

"Ah..." Joe stammered. "Potatoes!"

The gunshot rang in the quiet room, and Joe slumped over, a trail of red streaming from his chest.

"Mississippi," the man whispered, pocketing the revolver and disappearing into the night.

text:
# Huckleberry's Pet Shop

"Hey Kate, look at this turtle," James said as Kate walked over and stared through the glass. "And it's got a little monocle too!" Kate said, eyeing the turtle. "Shall we get him?"

"Hush fools, your human breath reeks, I can smell it through this glass, foul woman. Both of you, release me from these bonds of cruelty!"

"What's that noise? It's coming from the box," Kate said, but James was off trying to find a way to purchase the shelled animal.

The turtle was speaking, but the glass wouldn't allow its speech to be emitted to the outside. "I am Jerry the Turtle, pleased to make your acquaintance. I also see your companion has found a way to release me."

All that came out was a light grumbling noise. Kate went to find James.

*Until another day, vengeance will release me. Humans will feel my wrath*, Jerry thought to himself. His monocle shook as he slid into his shell.

Kate and James left the shop—they were hungry and wanted some McDonald's.

*Until another day*, Jerry thought to himself, watching them disappear through the door.

This turtle was fairly expensive. Perhaps that was for the best.

text:
# The Mysterious Ticking

Harry Potter paused in the Hogwarts corridor, his head tilted. "Do you hear that?"

Hermione stopped beside him. "What is it?"

"A ticking noise. Not over here... not over there..." Harry frowned, following the sound.

Ron joined them, his face puzzled. "That's oddly rhythmic."

The three friends tracked the noise through the castle, passing Snape in the hallway. The Potions Master swept by without acknowledgment, his robes billowing behind him.

"It's almost catchy," Hermione admitted as they walked. The ticking seemed to follow a pattern, echoing off the stone walls.

Dumbledore emerged from his office, his eyes twinkling. "Ah, investigating our mysterious percussion, are we?"

The students nodded, continuing their search. The sound grew louder as they approached an old pipe near the dungeons.

"There!" Ron exclaimed, pointing. "I found the source!"

He leaned closer to examine the pipe. His face went pale. "It's a pipe bomb!"

Before anyone could react, there was a tremendous BOOM. 

From the shadows came a cold laugh. A figure materialized—Voldemort, surveying the chaos with dark satisfaction.

The adventure, it seemed, was far from over.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Bear's Lament

A penetrating thud echoes through the valley, eventually reaching the doorstep and interrupting the deepest of self-imposed slumbers. Once tranquil, his lair's temperament instantly gave way to scorn the instant those fierce brown eyes retook control.

It's hard to decide when he's most dangerous—when his waves are at their tallest heights or during that calm that always precedes his storm. The world simply bows to his decree; in this form he deposits his will relentlessly until all opposers give way. But in all his wrath there is flawlessness, for all his efforts are validated from his view. His drive stems from his naive lust of blissful solitude.

Darkness. As his eyes adjusted after a long absence from the sun, they rapidly scanned, attempting to source this imposition.

Near-blindness. Flexing and stretching his neglected muscles, he gradually rose to truly address the problem and sauntered toward the doorway, brooding and scheming all the way. The longer he is away from the coddling warmth of his bed, the more anxious he is to return.

Blindness. As reality clicked into focus, he aimed down his sights and readied himself to dismantle any opposition. Glances shift, the natural buzzing that fills the air settles, and all seem to look to him.

Knowing the cost of battle they blow him off, misconstruing the loneliness for malice. Unanswered, misunderstood, and incomplete; he goes back into hibernation to bear his lonesome bare-bear self.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# As We Love

The first lash split the air before it split skin.

The woman in gold and pink wielded the leather cord with practiced precision, her movements almost balletic. Each crack was met with thunderous approval from the stands. The prisoners—hollow-eyed, silent—didn't cry out. Perhaps they had nothing left inside to express.

"Feel the liberation!" the Emcee bellowed, her voice amplified by unseen mechanisms. "Feel love's correction!"

The crowd swayed in unison, a sea of ecstatic faces. Some wept openly—tears of joy, they would insist. Others reached toward the arena floor as if trying to touch the transformation happening below.

A young man in the third row turned to his companion. "Beautiful, isn't it? The way we care enough to save them?"

His friend nodded vigorously, eyes glistening. "Such compassion. Such profound love."

Below, blood mixed with sand. The prisoners swayed but remained standing, their bodies testament to a will that persisted beyond belief, beyond the crowd's manufactured rapture.

The Emcee paused, breathing heavily. She surveyed her work with satisfaction. "Do you feel it returning? Do you feel love flowing back into your corrupted vessels?"

One prisoner—a woman whose back was now a canvas of red—lifted her head. Her eyes, still clear despite everything, met the Emcee's. In them was something the crowd couldn't see from their distant seats: not apathy, but its opposite. A love so fierce it had refused to perform itself on command.

The Emcee saw it and faltered for just a moment.

Then the crowd's roar swallowed everything again, and the leather cord rose once more, and the word "love" echoed through the arena like a curse disguised as prayer.

text:
# First Contact on Mars

Dr. Mot Preepman led his team deeper into the Martian cave, their scanners pulsating with unprecedented life readings. His heart raced as bioluminescent shapes emerged from the darkness.

"My God," he breathed.

Before he could react, one creature spoke: "Greetings. We come in peace. Take me to your leader." The voice was tinny, mechanical, absurdly high-pitched.

They were textbook aliens—diminutive green bodies, bulbous heads, obsidian almond eyes, silver jumpsuits reflecting his headlamp.

"What is that smell?" One alien's elongated fingers plucked a baggie from Preepman's pocket.

"It's premium chronic!" another shrieked excitedly, brandishing a ray gun. A violet beam vaporized the contents instantly, filling the cave with aromatic clouds.

Preepman felt reality tilting as alien and human voices merged:

"Vape Nayshe!"

Command would never believe his report. He didn't believe it himself.

text:
# The Necromancer's Homework

In a cold darkened chamber, deep deep down below,
I poured over my research, my eyes all aglow.
*I have finally done it! It is finally time!*
*The secrets of Death have now are finally mine!*

I poured out a beaker, full of foul-smelling goo.
The torches burned brighter, shining over my brew.
I called out some words, and they burned brighter still—
Shivers ran down my spine. Necromancy's a thrill!

I threw in some old bones that I found in the moor.
They rattled and shook, and became drenched in gore.
Flesh grew through them like water, poured into a mold,
And despite the hot torches, the room soon grew cold.

"Aha! Eureka!" I yelled out with a cry!
I KNEW I'd succeed! Now I will NEVER die!
I cackled a cackle, giddy from my success,
Ignoring the figure in certain distress.

It moaned and it groaned, rolling into a ball.
It bumped into a table, and then into the wall.
With its muscles still shaking, it pushed hard and stood.
It looked to my face, and it looked to my hood.

I reached out for a crossbow, eyes still shining like dew,
When the figure spoke up with a "Son? Is that you?"

My eyes wide with shock, I realized who it was,
Who stood now in my lair, and who now gave me pause.
"Father!? What happened! Could that really be you?"
*And I just nearly killed him!* The thought made me turn blue.

"Of course it is me, oh you silly buffoon!
Now go play outside, and get out of this room!
A boy of your age should get out in the sun—
You shouldn't stay in, that can't be REAL fun!"

"Yes, Dad." I moped, walking out to the door.
I pulled off the old sweatshirt that Dad always wore.
I sighed a great sigh, leaving my mess behind.
*One day soon, with some luck, I will rule all mankind!*

text:
# The Wall's Secret

I swept methodically, the bristles scraping against ancient stone. Another candy wrapper. A crushed water bottle. The detritus of daytime tourism.

Then the ground cracked.

Not dramatically—just a gentle splitting, like eggshell from within. The foundation stones of the Great Wall shifted, and something emerged.

They were beautiful in a way that made my eyes water. Translucent limbs unfolded with impossible grace, bodies luminescent under the moon's gaze. No faces, yet I felt their attention on me. No mouths, yet their voices filled my head with crystalline clarity.

*Free. Finally free.*

My broom clattered to the ground.

*The Egyptians completed their transformation centuries ago,* they explained, their consciousness washing over mine like gentle waves. *Natural death is merely the chrysalis stage. We've been waiting, changing, becoming.*

I thought of the workers who'd died building this wall. Thousands of them, buried in the foundations. Not trapped—transforming.

*You must guide us back,* they insisted. *Our families still wait in the villages. They'll remember us.*

I imagined knocking on doors in Beijing at dawn. "Excuse me, your great-great-grandfather just hatched from the Wall. He's different now—no mouth, glows in the dark—but he's home!"

They drifted closer, expectant.

I ran.

At my kitchen table as sunrise painted the walls gold, I scribbled frantically in my will: CREMATE ME. IMMEDIATELY. BURN EVERYTHING.

Because I finally understood what we really are—not the endpoint of evolution, but larvae. And I had no interest in discovering what butterfly horror I might become.

The Wall keeps many secrets.

I'd learned one too many.

text:
# Miss Braun

My mind is drifting. This is really quite frightening. Those lights! They keep flickering! It really is quite stuffy in here. It's making me drowsy. And so hot.

*Miss Braun.*

I can't concentrate. Oh Adolf. My Adolf. You foolish and impetuous man. What have you done? Always foolishly rushing into things. Never taking any counsel but your own. And so here we are. Americans and British to the east. And I don't even want to think about what approaches from the west.

We've been down here for weeks now. I need some air. I'm panicking now a bit. Oh Adolf, you foolish man.

*Miss Braun.*

Berlin is in ruins. The whole country is in ruins, to be frank.

*MISS BRAUN!*

"EVA!!"

"Sorry, I was deep in thought, my apologies."

"Miss Braun, the Führer is addressing you."

"I'm sorry. Yes, Adolf?"

I want to see the sun again. These few men are all the friends we have left.

"Eva, concentrate. Please. Listen, this is important. I said, are you prepared to follow me anywhere?"

"Yes, Adolf. What else have I left to do? To be left hated and despised on my own? Of course I will go with you."

"My dear, we have only the one option left open to us if we are to escape the world's fury."

"Any option is better than being holed up down here. And the blood on my hands scares me to death."

"Indeed."

text:
# Forever Friends

The cemetery gates creaked as I pushed them open, a bouquet of sunflowers—your favorite—clutched in my trembling hand. The morning dew clung to the grass, soaking through my sneakers as I walked the familiar path to your resting place.

I knelt beside your tombstone, tracing the engraved letters of your name with my fingertips. "Hey, buddy," I whispered, my voice cracking.

Remember those nights? Controllers in hand, Mountain Dew cans scattered around us, laughing until our sides hurt at some ridiculous glitch in the game. We'd watch the darkness fade to purple, then pink, then golden—and we'd still be there, refusing to let the magic end.

You were my safe harbor. When Dad left, you didn't say much—just handed me an extra controller and said, "Let's play." That was enough. That was everything.

I pull out the letter, weathered from being rewritten a dozen times. "I never told you I was scared," I read aloud. "Scared of growing up, of losing what we had. I never told you that you saved me more times than you knew."

A robin lands nearby, tilting its head as if listening.

"We talked about wives and apartments, but I never told you the real dream—that no matter what changed, you'd always be there." My tears fall onto the paper, smudging the ink.

I place the letter beneath the flowers, weighted down with a smooth stone we'd found by the creek years ago.

"I'm sorry we ran out of time," I say. "But you're still my best friend. Forever means forever."

text:
# The Price of Immortality

The torch tumbled through smoky air, its flames finding purchase on ancient cedar beams. Herostratus watched his rabble descend upon the shrieking priests, chaos consuming the Temple of Artemis like a ravenous beast. Smoke and blood mingled in the air—a perfume that brought a twisted smile to his lips.

He approached the adviser calmly, deliberately. The man stood wrapped in furs despite the heat, waiting.

The knife slid from Herostratus' belt with a serpent's whisper. "I'm generous tonight. Tell me *why* before I begin carving."

The adviser's eyes held no fear, only cold satisfaction. "These people have endured for centuries. Destroying a man? Simple. Destroying a state?" He gestured to himself. "Already done to me. But destroying their *Gods*—their beliefs, the foundation of everything they are—that is true revenge."

Laughter erupted from Herostratus—wild, manic. Then he lunged.

The adviser didn't flee. He stood perfectly still as Herostratus tackled him, pinning him to blood-soaked earth. The knife descended.

Screams. Struggle. The wet sound of steel parting flesh.

When Herostratus finished, the adviser was faceless—literally stripped of identity, transformed into something immediately repulsive to all who saw. One of the *faceless ones*, forever exiled from humanity.

"Now you're mine," Herostratus whispered. "Together, we'll destroy them all."

If Artemis could fall alone, so could the rest. Aerithys. Gizmondrite. Gromanthar. Tundrawarf. Names already fading into forgotten darkness.

This was his superiority—not merely breaking human spirit, but erasing the very foundations of civilization itself.

Behind them, the temple collapsed in a shower of sparks.

Their crusade had only begun.

text:
# The Dark Awakening

A sharp pain went through my skull just as I was waking up. I looked down over my bruised body and remembered what had happened yesterday. I could still feel the electricity flowing through my body, finding every nerve, every vein and causing agonizing pain. 

I could still remember the scarred face of my father as he looked up at me with some form of pride.

The soft cooing sounds to my right alerted me to where I actually was. The gentle breathing of the Ewoks sleeping was almost soothing. Almost. 

I tried not to wake them as I shimmied through the mass of huddled bodies. Sharp pieces of the wooden floor poked the bottom of my feet, and the rough rope of the treetop village felt coarse against my battle-worn hand. The phantom pain in my right hand reminded me of my loss.

I was consoled by the memory of the previous night. My father, accompanied by two other spectral beings, visited me in a vision. He looked younger, unburdened, and it was hard to recognize him outside of his scarred and masked form.

Anger swelled inside me. Why did my father have to die? I feel worthless.

Dark thoughts crept in like shadows. My father didn't have to die from this—nobody did. The Empire had killed so many innocent people. Maybe it was time to carry on the legacy left by my father.

For years, he had carried out justice across the galaxy under the guise of "Darth Vader." He had brought balance to the galaxy. He was the most powerful being to ever exist.

And I am here to carry on his legacy.

The darkness whispered promises of power, of purpose. My hand trembled as I stared into the predawn sky, feeling the pull of destiny—or damnation.

text:
# 3... 2... 1

**By Anonymous**

Did you feel it?

In the time it takes you to read this sentence, another person on Earth has died.

3... 2... 1.

Oh, that's another one.

What are the chances that it's someone you know? When was the last time you called your dad? Checked on your baby?

3... 2... 1.

And that's three. Your father, mother, and brother could all be dead now and you wouldn't even realize.

3... 2... 1.

Pretty soon you'll be the one counting down those three seconds, because it will be the last three seconds of your life. Can you imagine, feeling death coming, counting down because you know it's the last thing you will ever experience?

3... 2... 1.

You'll be lucky if you see it coming. You might be a child, or a teenager, a mother or someone who never got a chance to be any of those. It doesn't matter.

3... 2... 1.

And there's a chance, just a chance, that the last thing you do will be counting down to your own death. Say it with me now:

3... 2... 1.

No last words, no family around you. You'll be found dead in the morning by a family member if you're lucky, or days from now by someone investigating the awful smell if you're not.

3... 2... 1.

Enjoy that last breath, savor the air going in and out of your lungs one last time. Feel your heart squeeze out a few more pitiful beats, because this might just be the end.

It could be coming in...

3...

2...

1.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The True Terror

I stood there, sword in hand, smile on my face. "All of the foes I have faced, all of the pain I have endured—it is for this moment. I have destroyed every last foe. I shall ensure evil never again enters this world. I shall destroy the Soulstone of Terror!" I shouted fiercely.

With relentless force, I swung my sword and shattered the artifact into a million pieces. Finally, the reign of terror would be no more. No more would evil ravage this land.

As the last pieces hit the ground, I realized what I had done. I grabbed frantically into my pouch and pulled out what I thought was the Stone of Life. But what I truly held was the Soulstone of Terror.

I had just destroyed the Stone of Life.

The cursed stone had clouded my sight, twisted my visions. I had killed thousands of men—innocent men with families, who did nothing more than protect their country and land. What I thought was the enemy was truly friend. I caused this. I brought upon this darkness, this terror.

I fell to my knees as the portal opened above me, darkness pouring into this world. The darkness I had created.

The prophecy had been fulfilled—not by a hero, but by me, the deceived fool. I was never the savior.

I was the harbinger of doom.

text:
# The Last Save

I have made a grievous, grievous error. I am lost, my kingdom is against me, my sons with it.

All I wanted was to make my lands into heaven for all who lived there. I changed laws, they hated them. No matter my decision, it was the wrong one.

The war to the east, to take back our homelands, was an evil waste of lives. The peace with those to the north, whose lands were once ours, was called wrong and hateful towards my people.

The starvation that came after the drought was blamed on me, on my feasts within the palace—my feasts of bread and water.

When I put down the first rebellion, I was too harsh. When I let a lord beneath put down the next, I was too apathetic towards the kingdom's needs.

Now, one last desperate effort has failed, and they all rise against me. My sons, my lords, my generals—every last one is out for my blood.

I have only one hope.

*ESC. Click. Load.*

The familiar menu screen glows before me. Three hundred hours invested. I hover over the save file from six months ago, before the drought event chain triggered.

Maybe things will work better this time.

I click.

The throne room materializes around my character once more. Outside, the people still love their king.

For now.

text:
# The Weight of Darkness

I was desperate. The bottle in my hand felt heavy, even though all of the dark, bitter liquid inside was gone. I couldn't see straight, and the warm liquid pooling at my feet told me that I had really done it.

I dropped the bottle, the weight of it finally making me drop it. I looked at the body in front of me and whispered, "Finally, some business," and walked off into the night, leaving bloody footprints on the floor as I sauntered away, stumbling from the drink and the adrenaline.

My memories are hazy for the rest of the night, but I remember the hot splashes of blood against my skin, and falling asleep in the alley outside O'Riely's Pub. The ground is cold against me, and I find that my hands are sticky from the dark red they are coated in.

Nobody had found me, huddled as I was against the dumpster. I got up and tried to find a way to clean up, and luckily, found a tap. I turned it on, washing my entire body, stripping from my ruined suit into an undershirt and a pair of boxers.

*I'll say I got mugged, and was drunk enough that I couldn't move afterwards. Finally, I can feed my family.*

Suddenly, my phone rings. I answer it with a shiver and say, "Hello, this is Jim, how may I help you?" my voice hiding the fact that I was shivering quite well, sounding cheerful and upbeat.

"Jim, we have business... But it's not the business you want. Our s-s-son and daughter were found... dead in an alleyway, and Uncle Bill was found a street over. They were covered in blood, and looked to have been beaten with bottles..."

The phone slipped from my fingers. The cold water still dripping down my face felt like ice. My knees buckled.

*Finally, some business.*

The words echoed mockingly in my shattered mind.

text:
# The Weight of Words

She bit her lip, and tried to erase the thought out of her mind. But it remained there, prominent as ever, making her head throb as it urged to be vocalized.

"I've done everything I can, I don't know what else you want from me!" He shouted as he slammed his fist down into his thigh.

A smirk crossed her face for a brief second before she could wipe it away. Luckily he was too caught up in his own personal turmoil to see the break in her calm demeanor.

*Everything.* Well, he wasn't lying. He had dragged them from state to state in search of work, separated her from their family and friends, as he continually tried to prove himself to be something. Their savings had long been dried up, work was hard to find for someone like him—or so he said—and anger replaced the laughter and joy that once surrounded them.

"Are you even listening?!" He shouted, leaning across the table towards her. "Why won't you respond? Just say it already!"

"You're just like him."

The words spilled out into the air as she covered her mouth quickly, wishing to take them back in. The anger in his eyes turned into pain, and tears welled up threatening to fall.

"I'm sorry," she whispered under her breath as she stood up from the table.

She began to walk past him and her hand instinctively reached out to comfort him, but she caught herself, bringing it back down to her side. Resuming her walk, she approached the door, picked up her bag, and left him staring at the wall with tears falling down his face.

The door clicked shut behind her—a period at the end of their sentence.

text:
# The Price of Forever

I cringe again as I deliver another unmarked box to a plain looking door. I knock and walk away, knowing it will be found. I hate that I grew curious. I hate that I dug deep to find out. If only I just followed blindly like I have done for so long.

There has never been a greater moment that the saying 'ignorance is bliss' was so true. But now it's too late. I know, and I know I cannot just stop.

When I first got the email, I figured why not? It was just simple little tasks, mainly deliveries. It would be a blast if it turned out true. It turned into daily routine for a while. Something I did absentmindedly.

It wasn't until a few years passed did I realize it was working. While others aged, I didn't. I remained looking like a teenager. At first it was cool but annoying since I was carded everywhere. I stopped caring after a while and enjoyed my youth.

I found love and had kids. They received the same emails. I encouraged them, but not all wanted to do it. I worried for them, but they grew old happily. I lost my love and met another, figuring out that it was my choice that keeps me in eternal youth.

My life just continued, and so I enjoyed it with many families. That is until recently.

Once again I have a new mate and an abundance of kids. My first from this batch just reached sixteen and got her first letter. Though everyone questioned at first, she insisted she wanted to know why she should do these tasks. What were their purpose?

Out of love and a slight budding curiosity, I set about finding out myself.

Again, I wish I hadn't.

All the packages, all the slipped notes—they were to help others do other tasks. It led on and on, like the butterfly effect, till at last I found out why.

It was to cause death.

We were the cogs, the pieces. All put together, we are Death itself. Which is why we never die. As long as we are useful, we live.

And so I keep following my small tasks. I need to. I am doing mine, and my daughter's now.

She doesn't need to know.

I'll carry this burden alone, protecting her from the truth that would shatter her. Each delivery feels heavier now, weighted with understanding. But I knock, and I walk away, and I continue.

Because the alternative—for both of us—is far worse than living with the knowledge.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The One Hunch Man

A burned body laid there cooking in the relentless desert sun. A bunch of detectives recently arrived at the scene, some were taking pictures, others were exploring the area around the body, looking for evidence.

As they worked their numb little minds, they were startled to see a big black van suddenly arrive at the scene. The door flung open! The sun crawled away! To further emphasize the divine figure that left the vehicle, in a traditional 19th century detective outfit with the smuggest face on the planet... was... THE ONE HUNCH MAN!

The wind stopped, as to give his eyes permission to feast upon the murder scene. The detectives took one step back as he loudly bent himself to rip a bent piece of dry grass off the dying land. He took the greatest look to end all looks on the grass and froze for a few seconds.

He then slowly stood back up, took out a small plastic container, and placed the grass there. He collected himself and sprouted an answer.

"It was Max J. Hamilton!"

The detectives exchanged glances.

*A day later, the One Hunch Man was laughed out of court. Turns out hunches don't make for great evidence. Max Hamilton walked free, and the grass remained just grass—worthless and sun-bleached, much like the detective's reputation.*

# The Amazing Persian Horned Viper

My favorite animal is the Persian Horned Viper. This incredible snake lives in the country of Iran and hasn't really been found anywhere else in the world. What makes this snake so cool and special to me is its remarkable spider-like tail.

The Persian Horned Viper uses its amazing spider tail as a lure to attract prey. When birds see what they think is a tasty spider wiggling around, they swoop down to catch it. But surprise! Instead of getting a meal, they become the meal when the snake strikes.

Besides having this really cool spider tail, this viper possesses extremely toxic venom. It's so poisonous that it can take down very large animals incredibly fast. The venom is so dangerous that scientists haven't even developed an anti-venom yet! This means if someone gets bitten, they're in serious trouble, making this snake one of nature's most formidable predators.

The final fascinating thing about this snake is its rarity. Unlike common dangerous animals like lions that are easy to spot, the Persian Horned Viper is exceptionally hard to find. Scientists have only discovered a handful of specimens, and they weren't even certain it was a distinct species at first. After finding about five individuals, they confirmed it was indeed its own species.

This is why the Persian Horned Viper is my absolute favorite animal!

text:
# Some Days, I Love My Job

"Some days, I love my job. Those days are the worst," I said as I lay on the old 90's leather couch of my therapist.

My therapist tilted his head and removed his glasses. "Well, why would you say that? I thought you liked your job."

I sat up and walked to the window where I watched a group of children playing on a swing set. "It's not that I hate my job, I just don't love it. There's a difference between 'love' and 'like.' I like my job in the sense that it provides me with an income, gets me out of the house to see my friends, but at the same time I loathe it."

At that moment, I heard my parents yelling at me. I heard them telling me to be a lawyer. I heard them telling me I would never make money traveling the world being a photographer. I heard them telling me I needed to make money and I would never be anything until I was a lawyer. That the only way to be successful was to have a white collar job.

My thoughts were interrupted by my therapist's soothing voice. "It's never a bad thing to love something. Even for a moment."

"Yes, I agree it's good to love, but I don't want to love this job. By loving this job and accepting that a part of me loves it, is agreeing with my parents. I'm afraid that the more I start loving this job, the less I will follow my passions and dreams. I'm afraid that the more I start to love this job, the more I become an adult, and the less I remember what it's like to be a child—to think like a child."

The therapist leaned forward. "Perhaps loving your job doesn't mean abandoning your dreams. Perhaps it means you're learning to find meaning wherever you are."

text:
# The Last Goodbye

"Do you still love me?" he asked, tears streaming down his weathered face.

"Of course I do, honey," she whispered from the hospital bed.

He knew she was lying, but he couldn't tell her that. He couldn't give up his secret—the experimental emotion-reading implant the research facility had given him six months ago. If she really loved him, they wouldn't even be having this conversation.

Hell, they'd been together now for what... six years? Jesus, he was an idiot. All the lies throughout the years about growing old together and always being there for each other. How stupid he felt now for believing that.

"Was it something I did? I can change, you know. Everyone can change," he sobbed, the words barely coherent.

"No, of course not, honey. This has nothing to do with you. It's not your fault," she replied, tears silently crawling down her pale cheeks.

*She's not allowed to be sad. I'm not leaving her. She's the one leaving me,* he thought bitterly.

He knew this day was coming. Even on their good days, he would catch glimpses of her sadness when she wasn't looking—the sorrow behind her smiles. There wasn't anything he could do. He tried being a better man, tried to give her things no one else could. In the end, it didn't matter. This was her choice... not his.

"I... I think you should go now," she said, her bottom lip quivering uncontrollably.

*She can't even look at me,* he thought, watching her squeeze her eyes shut. *Does she really hate me that much?*

As he turned to leave, she stopped him one last time.

"I love you," she said.

"I love you too," he replied.

The room fell quiet. She laid still for a moment before slowly turning toward the doctor standing in the corner.

"I'm ready," she said.

::BING::

The doctor nodded as the lie detector confirmed what he already knew—she'd told the truth. Making his way to the machines, he could only manage a half-hearted smile.

She'd loved him all along. She was just ready to let go of the pain.

text:
# The Perfect Morning

I blink awake, disoriented. The bedroom is unfamiliar—tastefully decorated, sunlight streaming through gauze curtains. And there's... someone standing beside the bed.

"Here, I've brought you breakfast in bed," she says, smiling.

I don't know her.

The tray settles onto my lap with practiced ease. The omelette is restaurant-quality, the fruit glistening, the toast golden. Ice cream for breakfast. Coffee steaming invitingly.

"I know what you're thinking—ice cream? For breakfast?" She laughs, tucking a strand of hair behind her ear. "I just think you should treat yourself."

I should say something. *Who are you? Where am I?* But my mouth stays shut as she glides downstairs.

The food tastes... perfect. Too perfect. Like a memory of food rather than the thing itself.

She returns with folded laundry—my laundry, I realize with growing unease. My favorite faded t-shirt. The jeans with the ripped knee.

"I thought you wouldn't mind if I did your laundry before I go to work." Her smile never wavers. "Stay as long as you like. I'll only be gone for three hours..."

She leans in to kiss me, and I catch my reflection in her eyes—blank, empty, like looking into a mirror that shows nothing back.

Her lips meet mine. The kiss is flawless.

And I finally understand: I'm not the guest here.

I'm the fantasy.

text:
# The Month That Got Away

The young timekeeper stood, straightening his celestial robes with trembling hands. As he turned toward the crystalline door, the God of Time's voice stopped him cold.

"Wait. Before you go, I need to know—how does one *lose* an entire month at McDonald's?"

The young man's shoulders sagged. "I... I put the October scroll in my bag while ordering a Big Mac. When I sat down, I hung the bag on my chair. After lunch, I grabbed what I thought was my bag, but..."

"But?"

"Someone had an identical bag. By the time I realized, they were gone. October just... vanished into mortal hands."

The God of Time pinched the bridge of his nose. "Do you have any idea what chaos ensued? September 30th repeated seventeen times. Mortals thought they were losing their minds. Calendars spontaneously combusted. Halloween decorations appeared in July."

"I know, Sir. I'm truly sorry."

"Sorry doesn't fix temporal paradoxes." The God waved his hand dismissively. "Get out. And if you ever find that bag, October is keeping those seventeen extra days. Consider it interest."

The young man left, wondering if somewhere, someone still had a mysterious scroll labeled "October" tucked beside their old french fries.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Cartographer's Secret

I remember the first time I walked into that room and the warm scent of cinnamon that filled the air. And although it also smelled strongly of leather and dust, till the day I die, I will always remember the cinnamon. Especially given the reason I had come.

It really was the last thing I would have expected his shop to smell like. As the door creaked shut, ringing the bell again, a voice shouted out from the back, "Just a minute!"

The whole place was neatly organized. On either side of the shop there were bookcases filled with leather-bound tomes. In the center, a particularly hefty specimen was proudly displayed, sitting open on a lectern for anyone to read. On the wall hung a well-preserved and ornately detailed map of the Conquest. It sat alone in the center, fancy electric lanterns on either side.

Clearly the centerpiece of the shop, I found myself drawn in by the sheer beauty of the work. Not only did the lines appear crisp and fresh, but the color was impeccable. Clearly, this was not some poorly attempted copy, and the detail belied an intimate knowledge of the land.

I was so overwhelmed by the artistry that it took me a moment to realize it detailed the pre-Conflict borders, complete with traitor crests.

"Beautiful, isn't it?"

Forgetting for a moment why I had come, I turned to face a short man with a large bushy beard and a belly to match.

I glanced once more at the map then back at him. "Kinda risky, don't you think?"

A sly smile spread across his face. "What can I say? I like to live dangerously."

It was clear I'd come to the right place. This was the man who could help me find what the regime had tried so hard to erase—the truth about my family's past, hidden somewhere in those forbidden borders.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Cape and Flour

The apartment smells like burnt coffee—*again*. I forgot I put the pot on before Amy flew through (literally through) the skylight at 4 AM, chasing some crisis only her super-hearing could detect.

It's a great gig. Really.

I don't see her as often as I'd like. The dry cleaning bills are sucking us dry, and my family was targeted that one time, but Amy is living out her dream of helping everyone. Everyone but me. It's okay though. Really.

She dons her cape, and I wash dishes. She saves infants, and I vacuum. She gets featured on the news, and I sleep alone.

If she were here, I bet she'd say *you knew what you were getting into*, and I guess that's true. It's just that I never expected her teenaged phase of sneeze-and-burn-the-house-down would turn into... well, "Woman Rescues Family of Three from Mudslide."

She doesn't even *like* mud, hates getting dirty, but that's not important to them. They want to know about her hand slipping as she grabbed the kid, the thousand-dollar reward; they want to make her into a perfect being.

But I know the truth—that she leaves cabinet doors open like, all the time. That her makeup permanently clutters our bathroom counter. That she has nightmares about every time she was too late.

But it's worth it. Really.

I get to hold her at three in the morning when the city stops needing her. I get to cherish the smell of rose-scented shampoo in her hair, and the way our bodies still fit together after all these years.

I get to cook pancakes with her, and dust her nose with flour, and wipe my hands across her ass so she has to change, and I get to watch her slip into my boxers instead of that damned "Supersuit."

That's what the media calls it, at least. It's just a latex persona she wears when there's trouble. It's not her favorite movie, or the candle she says smells like home. It's not the creaky life we've been building since high school.

It's not the ring in my pocket.

She is Amy, just Amy.

And she's worth it.

# HELLO BILLY MAYS HERE WITH THE AMAZING FINGERNAIL™!

Billy Mays burst through my television screen at 3 AM, his voice rattling my apartment windows.

I looked at my own fingers. Ten perfect keratin shields gleamed back. When had I gotten these?

"FINGERNAILS NOT INCLUDED WITH BASE MODEL HUMAN," Billy interrupted, suddenly beside me. "You're running the trial version, pal."

I checked my hands again. Smooth. Empty. Had I ever had nails?

Stumps.

# The Chosen One's Résumé

"Do I really have to go?" Keljarin groaned, struggling with the consonant cluster that was his own name.

text:
# The Eternal Loop

The sun was bright, the sky was blue, and the wind was loud. Loud doesn't even describe it, really. The sound was like a stampede of horses galloping all at once. The wind blew across my face; my hair was flailing about.

My leg had gone numb from being in the same position for so long, and my hands began to hurt from the vibrating of the wheel. Sitting aside me was my brother. His knuckles were white as he gripped the door handle. One hand on the handle, the other pressing upon the roof.

The look of fear, maybe sorrow, grew on his face. A look I had never seen on him before; always such an aloof man, distant from emotion, from me. But here he was, frightened.

The car sped up. Faster. The engine revved louder. Faster! My vision grew blurry as I sped down the bridge. FASTER!

And as fast as it came, it went.

We were found dead June 8th, 2014. We drove off a bridge into the canal below. The death wasn't quick. It wasn't painless. It was real.

And yet, here I am again, repeating my past.

The sun is bright. The sky is blue. The wind is loud again.

text:
# The Devil's Lament

As Lucifer, I really get a bad rap. The Bible treats me as such a bad guy and a hard ass. Let me tell you what I really do. You aren't going to like it or believe it, but I'm going to tell you anyway.

Back at it I go. It never ceases. Did God win? You bet He did. He fucked me, and He fucked all of you in the process.

text:
# Double Life, Double-J

My name is Jack. No, not Jack Mehoff (haha), Jack Jackson. I got teased a bit, but it made a new nickname, Double-J. That is my username across the internet, and that's how a small country like Colombia was able to find me.

I am a hacker for them, and I get paid big bucks. About 200,000 per year, and I hack a lot. I worked for 2 years, bought a Lambo, invested the rest, 1 year later, a house. At 17! Crazy, right? And I have a half a million saved up. Stock markets rule!

text:
# The First Lock

They called him the Impossible Prisoner.

The First Lock shattered beneath his fists—brute strength reducing oak to splinters.

The Second Lock fell to stolen wire and patient hands—perception guiding each delicate movement.

The Third Lock opened when hunger became his weapon—endurance outlasting their cruelty until they blinked first.

The Fourth Lock surrendered to silver words—charisma weaving promises until the warden himself turned the key.

The Fifth Lock meant nothing when intelligence transformed bedsheets into rope—the window his gateway to freedom.

The Sixth Lock tried restraining his body—but agility born from endless exercise built momentum, wall crumbling after the hundredth impact.

The Seventh Lock never closed.

Someone forgot. Just once. During his medical transfer, every barrier stood open like an invitation.

Luck, they said. Divine intervention, others whispered.

Now the prison stands reformed. The locks remain, each a monument to his legend:

Strength's shattered door, preserved behind glass.

Perception's picked mechanism, studied endlessly.

Endurance's remembered standoff.

Charisma's key, chained to every warden's neck.

Intelligence's sealed windows.

Agility's straightjacket, mandatory now.

And Luck's final lock—placed on the guard himself, a brass padlock worn around his wrist.

*Never forget,* it whispers.

But somewhere beyond these walls, the Impossible Prisoner smiles.

Because he possessed something beyond seven attributes.

**Will.**
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Tyrant's Last Words

When Gustav felt the blade piercing just below his shoulder blades, his first reaction was amusement. The assassins stepped back, all seven of them, not one daring to take the knife out and finish the job when they saw he was still standing.

He saw it in their eyes: the fear, the accusations, and then something else, something they all thought, but not one dared say. So he did it for them.

"Sic semper tyrannis. You all think you're doing a great good thing, crushing a tyrant, a devil." He did laugh then, with no intention to run, to call for his healer, to search for life. "But was I really that bad?"

He sat on his golden throne. What better place for an emperor to take his last breath?

"Yes, I killed young men and women for my pleasure. I destroyed empires. Crushed civilizations. Obliterated ancient powers. Yes, I killed your fathers, your sons. I indulged in your daughters. But do you know what you have done? I assure you, History will smear your names, not mine. Glory shan't wait for you after stabbing in the back a man dying from old age."

The last emperor died smiling, leaving his victorious assassins trembling, their heroic deed suddenly feeling hollow and stained with cowardice.

# Food Food Food

Is it that hard to figure out? I tap my shoulder, I want food. No, I don't want to go to the bathroom. God dammit.

You've worked here four months, and you can't figure out that when I tap my shoulder, I want food. Yes, fucking finally. You managed to figure it out before I starved; maybe you'll last here after all.

I mean, you did eventuall— no no no no no. No, I'm not eating anymore salads. Bring me real food; for fuck's sake, I need something with chocolate! Get that away from me. Your hand smells like sweat and your disgusting moisturizing cream.

No, I'm not being crabby, you just suck at your job.

We do this every day; you try to get me to eat something healthy, and I don't. I just don't want to. I don't give a shit about calories or cholesterol, whatever that is. And seriously, if you put anymore vitamins in my chocolate milk, I'm going on a hunger strike.

They don't taste like chocolate milk; I don't know why you'd think I wouldn't notice a mixed berry flavor in chocolate. You wonder why I'm pissed off every day; you think I'm an idiot, and you can just do whatever you want to. If I could call you out on it, I would.

I threw the vitamin-spiked milk on the floor every day for a week, and every day you thought it was because I had to go to the bathroom. I'm supposed to be the one with Autism, but you're the one not learning anything.

Yes! Chocolate! Thank you thank you thank you. I could give you a hug! I think I will! You're the be— oh, okay.

No, I just wanted to hug you. No, I'm not angry, I jus— no, the food is fine, I was— NO! DON'T TAKE IT AWAY!

GOD FUCKING DAMMIT WHY ARE YOU WHEELING ME TO THE BATHROOM?

text:
# One More Keystroke

The cursor blinks at me like an accusation.

I've read Jeff's archives three times now, searching for clues I know aren't there. His last post was about coffee—good coffee, the kind that makes mornings bearable. Nothing dark. Nothing final. Just Jeff being Jeff, finding poetry in the mundane.

My daughters think I'm crazy, logging into a dead man's blog. Maybe I am. But when I close my eyes, I see that email timestamp: 4:15 PM. Fifteen minutes before he jumped.

Why me?

I left exactly seven comments over two years. Nothing profound—just "Great post" or "This really resonated." We never spoke. Never exchanged pleasantries beyond the sterile format of blog correspondence.

Yet in his final moments, while standing on that balcony with rush hour traffic humming below, Jeff thought of me. He trusted me with his digital legacy, this collection of thoughts that touched thousands of strangers.

The comments section has exploded since the news broke. People sharing how Jeff's words saved them, inspired them, made them feel less alone. One woman said his post about grief helped her survive losing her son. A teenager said Jeff taught him writing could be honest.

I want to be angry at Jeff for choosing this ending. For robbing us of more wisdom, more wit, more perfectly crafted observations about imperfect life.

But mostly I'm just sad.

Tomorrow I turn 49. Middle-aged, divorced, ordinary. Yet somehow, I became the keeper of something extraordinary.

So here's what I know: Jeff existed. Jeff mattered. Jeff wrote words that will outlive us both.

And if you're reading this, struggling like Jeff maybe struggled, please—write one more sentence. Take one more breath.

Choose one more keystroke.

For Jeff.

For you.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# And Here, I Stand

On the grounds of the graves of my friends. It's been many years since I came back—437 years unless I was mistaken. That was the night the vampire bit me, transforming me into this monster that I am today.

My army was sent here that day with a threat to the kingdom I served. We rode into town, thirty-two warriors strong. Fifteen of them were slaughtered by the beasts. I gave my life for my brother. One of the creatures lunged at him, fangs bared, about to strike. I threw my arm out to protect him. He killed the walking nightmare, but not soon enough to save me.

They thought I was dead. That's why I even have a grave here.

I told only one person I survived—my wife. I explained what happened, how I wasn't safe to remain in this town. She asked what I would do next.

The answer was simple. I began hunting every vampire I could find, traveling from town to town, killing each one as painfully as possible. My quest has led me back here, to the place where it all started.

Now, as I prepare for one of the hardest battles of my life, I stand where everything changed forever. The original vampire—the one who turned me—still lurks in these shadows. Tonight, I end this curse, or I die trying.

Either way, I'll finally rest.
