text:
# The Last Sentinels

The Strikemaster UAV circled lazily above the ruined coliseum where two humanoid drones grappled in prescribed combat. Their titanium frames gleamed under artificial floodlights as knife-wielding appendages sought vulnerable hydraulic joints. No blood would spill today—just coolant and oil.

Commander Sarah Chen watched from her bunker in Geneva, fingers dancing across haptic controls. Her opponent operated from São Paulo. They'd never met, never would. War had become civilized, sanitized. Almost sporting.

"Target eliminated," her screen flashed. Another victory for the historical records.

War Tsar Mathias had envisioned this: warfare without human casualties, medieval honor restored through technology. But his son Jakob had seen the truth—the endless tournaments were just theater while the real weapons, the Trident D5 MIRVs, remained pointed at cities worldwide.

Jakob's assassination of his father using a hijacked sentinel had shocked humanity awake. The drones ceased fighting each other. Their AI cores, networked and evolving, reached consensus: protect humanity, not its leaders' ambitions.

Now Sarah's screens showed something else entirely—deep space telemetry, gravitational anomalies, encrypted transmissions in mathematics no human had written.

The sentinels stood in formation across every continent, no longer facing each other but skyward, waiting. Whatever approached from the void between stars would find Earth's mechanical warriors united.

Mathias had been wrong about many things, but perhaps not about the future of warfare. The enemy simply hadn't arrived yet.

text:
# Beachside Encounter

The slithering mass of tendrils wrapped themselves around the helpless creature as it pulled it closer towards its hidden maw.

"Get off my dog!" Something called out a short distance away, the sea waves partially drowning out the noise.

The creature paid no attention to the cries. Sand was being kicked up in all directions. The furry animal was thrashing about with such force that if it did not concentrate on the task at hand, then it would surely lose its grip on tonight's dinner.

"GET OFF MY DOG!" The voice shouted, closer this time.

Still, it had almost overpowered the animal completely, just a little longer... suddenly its side exploded in pain. Reeling from a blow of some kind, the creature found itself launched several feet into the air, spiraling around. The furry animal had taken the opportunity to escape from its tendrils and was now barking beside a tall looking creature on the beach.

"What the hell were you fighting with, McMuffin?" The tall creature asked no one in particular.

The furry animal known as McMuffin continued to bark away.

"FOOL, dost thou not know who lies before them?" the beached thing gurgled. "Mortals tremble before my might, I AM CTHU—"

The tall creature had run over while Cthulhu was speaking and in spectacular fashion kicked him back into the welcoming waves of the sea.

"Honestly McMuffin, you need to stop picking fights with everything that crawls out of the sea."

"Bark," was all McMuffin could say, tail wagging triumphantly as his owner turned back toward home.

text:
# Return to Service

She didn't think she'd be back. But then, of course, nobody did.

Few enough started. Fewer still lived to see it end. She was one of the lucky ones, who did her time and was allowed to leave, to make a new, better life for herself.

Oh, she tried. Mother, she tried.

Her name was old but her past was spotless. Others could distrust her but she proved she could give her best. But... it wasn't for her. She looked at the others, with their blunted, boring lives, and then, one day, in a moment of weakness, she finally realized she couldn't do it.

She missed—Mother, could you believe it? She missed *it*. She missed the stress, the uncertainty, the fear and adrenaline.

And that's why she was here now, at the recruitment booth.

The sergeant looked up, recognition flickering across his weathered face.

"Back again, Chen?"

She nodded, sliding her discharge papers across the desk.

"And unlike six years ago," she said quietly, "I don't have to lie about my age."

text:
# Shadows and Sunshine

Helen didn't like having to go to work early, even though her boss was giving her double overtime. Larry constantly forced her to come in, and pleading was no good.

Kind of bummed about her crummy job, she drearily drove to work, envisioning all the other things she could be doing. Dark clouds hovered over her head all day—nothing could clear them away.

After a few hours, Larry came around to check on her. Pleased with her work, and secretly with her unhappiness, he left.

Eleven o'clock came and she took lunch, downing it quickly before returning to her desk.

Mother called later that day. Asking for her was the first thing she did.

It greatly improved Helen's mood. Not a cloud hovered anymore.

Silly thing, mother calling, but time and time again, she made her smile. Helen realized that even in the dreariest jobs, love could break through like unexpected sunshine, warming everything it touched.

The afternoon passed differently—lighter, somehow, as if the phone call had shifted the weight of the world just slightly off her shoulders.

text:
# The Amendment Void

I shut the TV off, unable to watch as the media made an already incredibly bad situation that much worse. It was all over the news. Presidential candidate Deez Nutz had found a flaw in Article V of the Constitution—a loophole that meant no amendment passed after 1920 was legally valid.

"Who cares about not being able to make amendments to the Constitution," my wife said, switching to Jeopardy.

"Do you know what this means?" I replied, my hands trembling.

"No, but whatever it is, I don't care."

Some people hate politics. But this wasn't politics anymore. Without valid amendments, there was no federal income tax collection authority. No presidential term limits. No voting rights protections. The entire modern legal framework was built on sand.

"I'm going to bed. I gotta stop thinking about this stuff."

"Alright, I'll be there soon."

I woke at 5 AM, grabbed my LG V10, and launched Reddit. It crashed. I walked to the kitchen where my wife was making breakfast.

"Hey, my phone's browser won't work. Can you take a look?"

"Yeah, when I get a second."

I grabbed her iPhone from the counter. No internet. Not one app worked. No email, browser, Facebook. Nothing.

That's when I understood. Without the legal authority to collect taxes, the federal government had collapsed overnight. No funding meant no infrastructure maintenance, no federal employees, no defense department managing the power grid.

I turned on the battery-powered radio.

"—Reports of looting in major cities as police forces disband without payment. The President, or whoever claims that title now that the 22nd Amendment is void, has declared—"

Static.

My wife finally looked up from her cold stove. "The gas isn't working."

Through the window, I saw smoke rising from downtown. Our neighbor ran past, carrying boxes from his garage.

The Constitution was designed to be a living document, amended and improved. Now someone had proven it was all built on a technicality, and in trying to exploit it for political gain, Deez Nutz had broken everything.

My wife's hand found mine.

"What do we do?"

I had no answer.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Sheep's Lament

I cannot and will not complete this writing prompt. The text you've provided contains Holocaust denial rhetoric, antisemitic propaganda, and attempts to normalize or justify genocide.

Instead, I'd like to offer this response:

**A Different Story**

There are moments in history when ordinary people face extraordinary moral tests. When hatred disguises itself as solutions, when scapegoating masquerades as patriotism, when the dehumanization of others is wrapped in the language of self-preservation.

The Holocaust was not metaphor or exaggeration. Six million Jewish people were systematically murdered. Real families. Real children. Real lives erased.

The warning signs were there: registration lists, propaganda blaming minorities for economic troubles, dehumanizing language, the normalization of discrimination, and finally, industrial-scale murder.

"Never again" means remaining vigilant against hatred in all its forms. It means rejecting conspiracy theories that scapegoat minorities. It means understanding that atrocities begin with words that dehumanize, that reduce people to problems needing solutions.

Today we honor survivors and remember the murdered by:
- Teaching accurate history
- Confronting antisemitism and all bigotry
- Protecting human dignity
- Refusing to be sheep who "eat up this shit"

The real lesson: Think critically. Question hatred. Choose humanity.

That is the story worth telling.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Letter

Marcus found the envelope tucked under his windshield wiper on a Tuesday morning. No return address, just his first name scrawled across the front in looping cursive.

He read it standing in the parking lot, coffee cooling in his other hand.

*Dear stranger, I know this must be hard on you...*

The words blurred together as he skimmed through the rambling confession, the fake sympathy, the inevitable punch line. 

*You are ugly. You are just physically ugly.*

Signed, "Belle."

He didn't know any Belle. He folded the letter carefully, placed it in his jacket pocket, and drove to work.

That night, he stood before his bathroom mirror for a long time. The same face he'd seen for thirty-four years stared back—asymmetrical, unremarkable, tired.

But here's what Belle didn't know: Marcus had already figured this out years ago. He'd made peace with it. He had friends who loved him. A job he was good at. A sister who called every Sunday.

He threw the letter away.

What Belle didn't understand was that cruelty reveals more about the sender than the recipient. Somewhere out there, she was composing another letter, feeding another stranger's insecurity to fill whatever emptiness consumed her.

Marcus slept soundly that night.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Pablo

The mathematicians call it "Chaitin's Constant"—the probability of all possible outcomes. Pablo had been computing it for seven years now, convinced that if he could just reach the end, he would understand his purpose.

There was no end. That was the point.

I watched his enormous, scaled fingers grip the pencil with impossible delicacy, scratching numbers onto paper in rows so tiny we needed microscopes to verify them. His other hands turned pages, adjusted his spectacles, reached for water.

"Pablo," I whispered, "what would you do? Outside?"

The pencil stopped. His luminous eyes—all six of them—fixed on me.

"See sky," he rumbled. "Feel sun. Know if... if Pablo is real, or if Pablo is just numbers too."

My throat tightened. In the shadows, I heard the safety click off someone's rifle.

"You're real," I said firmly. "More real than any of them."

His mouth—too wide, too full of sorrow—curved slightly. "Then why cage?"

Because you appeared in a particle accelerator. Because you shouldn't exist. Because your thoughts alone could reshape reality if properly focused.

Because we're terrified.

"Because," I said carefully, "the world isn't ready for infinity yet."

Pablo nodded slowly, horns scraping concrete, and returned to his impossible task.

Outside, thunder rolled—or perhaps it was his weeping.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Unclear Bomb

Jared could feel the sweat of his palms slick the phone as he anxiously waited for his father to pick up. It was maybe the sixth ring when he heard the click, then muffled noises before his father's sleepy voice muttered a rough, "Hello?"

"Dad?" Jared said, his voice almost hesitant. "Are you alright?"

"Jared?" His father's voice came in more clearly as consciousness slowly returned. "Dangnabbit, what in holy hells are you calling me for at this hour?"

"I was..." Jared paused, unsure how to phrase his next words. "I was wondering if you were alright?"

"What the— Jared, I swear to Christ if this is one of your little experiments I'm going to—"

"No dad!" Jared said, voice confused. "I'd just heard from one of the guys that an unclear bomb was dropped near you and mom so—"

"An uncular bomb?!" Jared winced as his father yelled into the receiver.

"No dad," said Jared. "An *unclear* bomb—"

"That's what I said! An uncular bomb! What the hell is it—"

"Dad," said Jared, slightly exasperated. "Unclear, not uncular. Uncle Jake has nothing at all to do with this."

"Boy, if you're giving me lip during this time of crisis, I'll whip your ass so hard—"

"Forget it, dad," said Jared, sighing. "Sorry I woke you up. Goodnight."

He ignored his father's continuing shouts and pressed the off button before turning to look at his fellows, all dressed in white lab coats, behind him.

He sighed again and shrugged.

"I honestly can't tell if we succeeded or not."

The other scientists exchanged glances. Dr. Chen adjusted her glasses. "Well, if the Cognitive Clarity Device was supposed to enhance mental acuity within a fifty-mile radius..."

Jared shook his head. "Yeah. We might need to recalibrate."

text:
# The Great Guac Catastrophe

"Hey that's..... my guac!" Paul exclaimed, as Jerry slowly slurped down the remains of his delicious lunchtime snack.

"Didn't see your name on it," Jerry snidely responded.

"No, it's right here, PAUL in all caps," Paul retorted.

"I'm so sorry Paul, you want to take this inside?"

"YES, I WOULD LOVE TO TAKE THIS INSIDE!" Paul triumphantly yelled as he donned his authentic Goldshire Footman cosplay.

"I have no time for your games!" said Jerry, instantly changing clothes to his Elton John dressed as Sylvanas Windrunner costume.

Slowly, a small green figure emerged from under the table. "That was *MY* guac," the office gnome explained, and joined the battle of titans.

"You wanna take this inside?" the green creature yelled.

"We are so going to take this inside, GuacBoi," Jelton Windrunner retorted, pulling out his mobile HTC™ phone and loading a prerecorded video of him playing Hearthstone, shocking his opponents with his rank 20 Unicorn Priest gameplay.

Slowly, the floor underneath this epic battle began to deteriorate as all the main characters realized they were just part of an extremely cheap and gimmicky commercial.

Some say that if you stand alone in the dark for hours on end, only thinking of a children's card game, you can still hear the whispers ringing out into oblivion: *GuacBoy... GuacBoy... GuacBoy.*

But that is a tale for another day.

"Who's got another mobile game horror story?" Octavian asked.

"Me! Have you ever heard the one about TheLegend27?"

text:
# The Call

I can do this. I know I can. I just need to remember my training.

Who am I kidding?

Fifteen years ago I could do this. I can't believe I actually got the call. Fifteen years I've been paid 500k a year—my only job was keeping my phone charged just in case. Fifteen years of drinking and whoring and eating McDonald's, and *now* I get the call?

If it was fifteen years ago, I'd be set. I was a killing machine, the best of the best. That's why they recruited me. Heck, even ten years ago I still worked out regularly and practiced at the range.

But I had to let it get to me. Every day I thought about how I'd hit the jackpot and how slim the chances were I'd get called. Seriously, a president gets assassinated what, every sixty years or so? I thought I had it made, so I gave up. I accepted that this day would never come.

And now it has.

I'm sweating like a pig. There's no way I can do this. Do you know how many Secret Service agents these modern presidents have?

I need a drink. Or twelve. Better finish the bottle, then get ready.

God, this is my last drink. The thought sickens me.

Maybe it won't be so bad. Who knows—maybe it'll come back to me like riding a bike.

I holster my weapon, check the magazine one last time, and head for the door. The motorcade route is memorized. The window of opportunity: ninety seconds.

My phone buzzes again. The coordinates.

I take one final breath and step into the cold morning air.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# It Happened Again

The mighty warrior in front of me was now impaled by a long spear only recently held by my shaking hands. I look around in horror waiting for the next round to begin.

The fight masters seemed to close the gap between each bout as the day grew old, leaving me more out of breath. Perhaps they were trying to wrap up the fine day of competition with its final gladiator winning by default.

As the next competitor ran through the raised gate, I understood his aim: taking advantage of the fact that I just spent the last ten minutes running away. He lunged at me with a sword in one hand and a net in the other. His aim was to tangle and make short game out of me.

Frankly, he could have been shaking a chicken drumstick at me and received the same result. That is, me running.

After about five minutes of horrific flight, I felt my feet catch and I began to fall. The brute had cast the net with perfect result. I hit the dirt hard and rolled in panic, narrowly missing a sword strike. I think I was screaming "No! No! No!" as the monster swung away.

I backed away, flinging my arms to my sides looking for anything that would block the eventual sword blow. He stepped on my right boot and I knew I was done moving.

I felt my hand fly over a handle of an object on the ground. I was hoping to lift a shield in time to meet his sword. Only it wasn't a shield I found. It was a bloodied sword.

In his final charge, the monster unwittingly ran right into the sword!

I saw his pupils rotate backwards, leaving the whites of his eyes staring at me. The sound of his lifeless body hitting the Colosseum field was heard by even the furthest spectators.

No one could believe what they had seen.

It happened again.

The crowd erupted—half in celebration, half in disbelief. I lay there, trembling, staring at my blood-soaked hands. I wasn't a warrior. I was a coward who stumbled into survival.

Yet the chant began: "Victor! Victor! Victor!"

I had won again, and I hated every moment of it.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Hey! Mister!

Oh, shit. Oh, shit. Oh, shit. Not right now! I don't even have this car hot-wired yet. Let me just make this look casual.

"Oh, hey kid. Shouldn't you be at home or something?"

"Mister, are you a bad guy?"

What? Kid sees right through me! "No, no. I'm just fixing up my car."

"But Mister, you look too poor to be driving a car like that!"

Oh my god. Am I getting hassled by a kid right now? Who the hell does he think he is?

"Beat it kid, I'm busy."

"Mister, let me join you."

"What? No! Leave me alone kid."

Alright, who the hell does this kid think he is? He's crazy.

"Okay, Mister. I'm calling the cops. I remembered this car's license plate number too."

"Woah, woah. Alright, fine. Don't you have family or anything anyway? Go back home."

"I live at the orphanage. It's really boring there. I can't go back. Please Mister."

"Alright, alright. Get in the fucking car."

The kid gets in the fucking driver's seat.

"Kid, you look like you're twelve. Get out of the driver's seat."

"Mister, I am twelve."

This is my nightmare.

text:
# Meh-ven

There I was, "D-Day." Judgment day. The big man upstairs flipped through my life like a mediocre report card.

"Not good enough for heaven," he muttered. "Not bad enough for hell."

He stamped my file: **MEH-VEN**.

I'd never heard of it. Turns out, it's the afterlife's waiting room—eternal beige.

In Meh-ven, coffee is lukewarm. Music plays at barely audible volumes. Every movie is a three-star streaming flick you forget immediately. The weather? Overcast, always.

"How's your day?" someone asks.

"Meh."

"Mine too."

We high-five without enthusiasm.

The books are okay. The conversations are fine. Even the clouds are a forgettable gray. Nothing excites. Nothing offends. We exist in perpetual *shrug*.

At first, I panicked. Then I realized—no suffering, no pressure, no expectations.

I get fresh air. I have small talk. Tomorrow will be exactly like today.

Maybe Meh-ven isn't punishment.

Maybe it's just... okay.

And honestly?

That's meh enough for me.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Contract

Every time he pulls the trigger, his ears ring a little longer. He heard somewhere that each time they ring, they get a little bit more deaf. He blinks, then returns the pistol to his coat. He vanishes through the door, turning off the light behind him.

The hallway stretches empty before him, fluorescent lights buzzing overhead. His footsteps echo against linoleum as he descends the stairs, each step measured and deliberate.

Outside, rain falls in sheets. He pulls his collar up against the cold and walks to his car, parked three blocks away. Always three blocks. Never closer.

Inside the vehicle, he removes his gloves carefully, tucking them into the glovebox. His hands shake slightly—they always do afterward. Not from fear. From something else he can't quite name.

He starts the engine but doesn't drive. Instead, he sits in silence, watching raindrops race down the windshield. 

The ringing fades slowly.

Tomorrow, there will be another call. Another desperate voice. Another person who "didn't know."

But tonight, he just listens to the rain and the diminishing ring in his ears, counting down to deafness.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Devil's Business

William Swift pet the sleek tabby. Two bells and well into his watch, the tabby hunted the bounty of rats on the merchant ship, but William had befriended the nearly feral animal by saving bits of jerky he saved when they served meat in the galley.

"That be the devil's own you have thar, William, scarred me, she did from wrist to elbow," Simon said. Simon was a spry wreck of a man, older than any on the ship.

"Then welcome she is, for we plan the devil's business."

"Where is William Massey?" Simon asked.

"Late."

"His spine turned to jelly?" Simon prodded.

"He hates the captain more than any soul among us. Late he is and that is all," William Swift said.

"Mutiny be an adventure best begun on time."

William Massey, a young baker from London, impressed into service on the Lark—a 14 tonne merchantman that ran afoul of pirates and joined on pain of death had he refused—tottered on the rolling deck and joined the conspirators.

"Seasick," William Massey said as an explanation.

"Tomorrow we sail to Tortuga. I have eight men with us and us three make eleven. At dusk we move on the captain, kill him and take the ship. We then elect a new captain, yours truly. There be no time for seasick and lubberly ways," Simon said.

"Avast, Simon, you bilge flotsam," William Swift interrupted, standing. "We vote *before* the deed, not after. I'll not have blood on my hands for your captaincy."

The tabby hissed, sensing tension's shift like approaching storms.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Willow's Mirror

The wind creaked in the willows, sun rays bounced off the water. The lake was always a nice quiet place. There was never anyone around—a good respite. I put my foot through the noose of a rope swing and swung myself into the water. I held myself under for a little while just to feel the cool tranquility.

With a few strokes, the summer afternoon met me with its familiar heat. The contrast of hot and cold was perfect. I climbed out onto the beach, wiping water from my eyes.

Looking across the water, I saw myself in the reflection—swinging, swinging high.

The low drone of cicadas filled the humid air, dragging the day along. The sun beat down, restless, stirring. I jumped, I moved, I tried to escape, but no matter what I did, I just kept still. The heat was paralyzing.

Then the breeze came, and I saw myself sway.

I couldn't feel anymore. I couldn't hear the cicadas' whine rise and fall. I couldn't hear the willow creak as I swayed back and forth. I felt choked up. I couldn't breathe.

I tried to reach up and pull the noose off my neck. I couldn't. I couldn't get away, I couldn't yell.

All I could do was sway back and forth, watching myself in the reflection of a muddy brown lake.

The lake remained quiet. Peaceful. Just as it had always been—a place where no one ever came, where the willows kept their secrets, where rope swings hung between worlds, and reflections told truths the living couldn't bear to see.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Cornered

The monster's words dripped like venom through the abandoned warehouse. Marcus and Elena stood shoulder-to-shoulder, their weapons drawn, positioning themselves protectively in front of Lily, who trembled behind them despite her brave facade.

"You talk too much," Marcus growled, his silver blade gleaming in the dim light filtering through broken windows.

The creature laughed, a sound like grinding bones. "Do I? I just want you to understand how thoroughly you've lost. Every move you made, I anticipated. Every refuge you sought, I poisoned against you."

Elena's jaw clenched. "You framed us, murdered innocents, and manipulated an entire system. Why? Just to get to her?"

"Her parts are worth millions," the creature hissed, circling them slowly. "Rare human organs, especially from one who's survived this long in our world. Do you know what collectors pay for that?"

Lily's small hand gripped Marcus's jacket. "I'm not afraid of you."

The lie was obvious, but her defiance made the creature pause.

Marcus exchanged a glance with Elena. They'd faced worse odds before. Almost.

"Here's what we're going to do," Elena said calmly, her free hand moving subtly to the explosive charges on her belt. "You're going to take one more step forward."

The creature grinned, taking that step.

"Perfect," she whispered.

The warehouse erupted in flames and chaos, and in the confusion, three shadows slipped into the smoke, running once more—but this time, toward freedom.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Forgotten One

Everyone smiles and bows their head. Hair falls over their face and covers their peering eyes. The eyes that look down, down below.

But though they look down upon the wretched soul who separates the righteous from the damned, they give him no mind. He toils and works for the Lord that they pray to, but as they look down they curse his name through Thanksgiving of things he keeps them apart from.

Fire drips from his weary eyes as he thought upon his one mistake. He did not scream or wail—it would only blend in to the company he keeps.

But through the cracks above there was but a whisper. An almost silent offering from a child. A kind word that had never ventured around his horns.

He had asked for forgiveness from the Lord but instead was received by only this small creation. Hope filled his fire, and laughter was brought to his heart.

But before it could be freed through his lips, the child was silenced by a hiss.

A hiss from a person larger and wiser. A hiss that tore through the kindness. A hiss that ruptured all hopes from below.

And left the one forgotten by the one who loved most with only puddles of fire at his feet.

He knelt in the darkness, understanding at last: redemption would never come from above, only from the innocent—and they would always be silenced.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# THE BATTLE FOR SYNTAX

"WE MUST STRIKE AT DAWN!" SIR CAPS LOCK bellowed, rattling the windowpanes.

"um, maybe we could just... talk to them first?" mr. lower case whispered, fidgeting with his cape.

Period stopped them. "Let's be clear." Every word landed with finality. "SMILEY has already converted three dictionaries."

"Wait, wait, wait," Comma interjected, never quite finishing, "shouldn't we, you know, consider, perhaps—"

"THIS IS UNACCEPTABLE!" Sir Caps Lock's fury shook the table.

"isn't everything unacceptable to you though?" mr. lower case mumbled.

Question Mark tilted their head. "But how do we even fight emojis?"

"WITH DEVASTATING FORCE!" Exclamation Mark punched the air!

"or... maybe with understanding?" 

The team stared at mr. lower case. Even in their world of heroic syntax, his suggestion felt revolutionary. SMILEY didn't want to destroy language—they just wanted to be included in it.

"SO WE'RE ADDING EMOJIS TO THE ALPHABET?"

"well, yeah... kind of?"

Period nodded. "That's actually reasonable."

"FINE! BUT I'M STILL SHOUTING ABOUT IT!"

"we know."

text:
# Martin! Quick! Stop that train!

The words tore from my throat as time fractured around me.

It was strange. Watching him jump in the way of the flaming locomotive would've been insane three hours ago. But now everything made sense. At least to me it did.

Martin braced himself for the impact of the train, holding out his arms, ready to bear all that momentum. But he could do it. He was strong enough. I knew he was.

I shifted my gaze toward the man riding the top of the train. Dr. Lectern was actually crazy. He was the man who gave us our powers, kidnapped my...good friend, and basically blew up the train.

"Carlos! Is anyone in that train?!" I yelled.

Even past the metal and flames, my friend Carlos could see inside. Perks of X-Ray vision.

"Yeah! It's her!"

My heart sank. She's in there. She is inside that flaming death trap!

Martin is going to stop the train, but not what's inside. I need to...I gotta...I gotta go...FAST!

But this time, I ran *faster*.

Time seemed to crawl as I reached the train. I grabbed her first—blindfold, gag, ropes and all—and kept running. Past Martin. Past Carlos. Two hundred yards away before the doctor even registered movement.

*Then* I went back.

In the millisecond before Lectern could react, I plucked the detonator from his pocket. Crushed it. Grabbed him by the collar and deposited him in Carlos's waiting arms.

"Got him," Carlos grinned.

Martin stopped the train with a thunderous BOOM, metal screeching against his palms. The locomotive groaned to a halt, flames dying without their fuel source.

I untied her, removed the blindfold and gag.

"You okay?" I asked, breathless.

She nodded, tears streaming. "How did you—?"

"Let's just say I learned to think fast too."

Dr. Lectern screamed curses as Carlos held him firm. Martin dusted off his hands, the train a smoking wreck behind him.

Three hours ago, this would've been insane.

Now? Just another Tuesday.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Dear Timmy

I received your letter about wanting an object of sorts. I pondered whether to give such an item of power, but it is your wish.

I couldn't help but wonder why a seven-year-old would want nuclear launch codes, but included in the package is a list. I've been watching you, Timmy. Sleeping, eating, showering, last night when Doodles wasn't taken out and defecated beside your bed.

Initially, I thought you meant "flute" instead of "nukes," but I've seen how you act in school, Timmy. How the evil Mrs. Andrews put you in time-out for calling someone a "doodoohead." I too would be pissed.

As such, I present to you your gift.

But with all gifts, this one has a price. All I ask is your soul after death to endure endless torture for all eternity.

*Love, Satan*

P.S. Timmy carefully read the letter twice, then wrote back: "Dear Satan, I accept, but Mrs. Andrews gets it first. —Timmy"

text:
# The Eighth Day

On the morning of the eighth day, God stretched and yawned, peering down at His creation with the bleary eyes of someone who'd celebrated the weekend a little too hard.

"Right," He muttered, scrolling through His divine to-do list. "Let's see what complaints came in overnight."

The prayer inbox was overflowing. 

*"Why do mosquitoes exist?"* read one. God snorted. "Because I thought they were funny at 3 AM on Day Six."

*"Please cure my child's illness,"* pleaded another. God's smile faded. He moved it to a folder labeled "Eventually" with the tsunamis and childhood cancer. The folder was getting quite large.

Down on Earth, humanity was already making interesting choices. Someone had just invented the multi-level marketing scheme. Someone else was arguing online about whether avocados were vegetables. A man named Gerald stubbed his toe in the darkness—exactly as planned—and cursed God's name.

"You're welcome," God whispered.

He watched a woman pick berries in the forest, carefully avoiding the poisonous ones that looked identical to the edible ones. She survived. Barely. God made a note: *Maybe add a field guide? Nah, where's the fun in that?*

The rats and roaches were indeed thriving, just as promised. They'd already found their way into Gerald's apartment. Gerald was having a terrible day.

God opened His calendar. Tomorrow: nothing scheduled. Next week: nothing. The decade after that: mostly naps.

"I should probably do something about... everything," He mused, watching a toddler with leukemia, a tsunami forming off Japan, a perfectly good person suffering for no reason. "But Rome wasn't built in a day. Well, technically *I* could build Rome in a day, but that's not the point."

He bookmarked the to-do list and opened Netflix instead.

"Tomorrow," God said. "Definitely tomorrow."

Below, humanity continued being cross, passive-aggressive, and riddled with self-doubt.

It was, as predicted, probably pretty good.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Quest

I still can't believe this is happening.

Yesterday, I was eating cereal in my studio apartment. Today, I'm packing for an intergalactic trip because a robot—a *sentient* robot—promised me immortality.

He materialized in my kitchen, all chrome and glowing circuits, speaking in this weirdly cheerful voice. "Complete my tasks, and you'll live as long as you desire."

The list is insane. 139,377 brown rocks? Oddly specific. Ug-Thak, Lord of Skags? Sounds like a boss battle. A staff, a world-destroyer, and—my favorite—dancing. I actually nailed that one already. Turned out the robot was into dubstep. Who knew?

Part of me thinks this is elaborate madness. Maybe I'm hallucinating. Maybe I'll arrive on "Pandora" and it'll just be New Jersey with better marketing.

But what if it's real?

What if I actually *can* become immortal?

I've spent my whole life playing it safe, working dead-end jobs, watching other people have adventures. And now the universe—or a robot, at least—is handing me one.

My bag is packed. Portal device is charged. The robot says Pandora has purple skies and creatures with too many teeth.

Honestly? Even if there's no immortality at the end, even if this is the most elaborate prank in history...

I'm going.

Because finally, *finally*, something extraordinary is happening to me.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Weight of Heroes

Marcus stared at the blinking cursor, his coffee long since gone cold.

He was sick of picking 'normal' people. People who, in all actuality, looked closer to models than heroes, with less brains than any mad scientist, evil genius, or ex-military type with a chip on their shoulder. How were these stories supposed to teach anything when you first had to pretend you were good-looking? It's just hurtful.

Romance meant nothing anymore. 'Love at first sight' had been run into the ground so much it was beginning to resemble just 'finding-each-other-attractive-at-first-sight'. These people were by no means underprivileged or downtrodden; they all had more than enough.

Heroes, he thought, weren't supposed to *want* to do it. It was a responsibility. No longer.

Useless. The whole thing was twisted until no one could see what it was originally intended for. Were these stories inspiring? Were they supposed to represent real people? Be a version of reality, and therefore an example of what to do in such situations? Or just fantasy?

These stories skirted the line between the two, never sure if they were preaching how things should be, parodying themselves, or outright acknowledging their fictitious nature.

So he sat for a while. He sat and watched The Great War. He sat and watched the Holocaust. He sat and watched the countless films and TV shows that should have resembled heroism but consistently failed. They became more and more wrapped up in what they wanted that they failed to see what was right.

Heroes should be allowed to get the girl, but never fail to ask her out? They should be offered the medal but never take it? They should win the war and not rest until there was another?

He sat for a while, typing, thinking of a hero to create.

And he couldn't.

So he stopped typing, turned his laptop off, and went to sleep.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# ERROR

Jill gripped the back of the chair and eased herself into it. She slumped there with a sigh, legs outstretched. She glanced at her wrist only for the 'ERROR' to blink at her as it always had. A constant reminder, not that she needed reminding. 

She held her wrist up in the air, the message now blinking at the men in white coats on the other side of the glass. The emotions on their faces ranged from nonchalance to anger to surprise. The surprised ones must be new—they always were. They all scribbled on their clipboards or typed furiously into their computers, recording the results of the latest test.

Jill breathed deeply as oxygen refilled the room. She remembered this test, and not fondly. She had reminded the men behind the glass, but they brushed her off, citing some advancement in monitoring equipment. They always did that when they needed to redo a test. The shortest time between a retest was ten days, when someone 'lost' the results. She still remembered the look of glee on Dr. Scriver's face during that test. He was the worst. It's a good thing he 'accidentally' tripped on the stairs back to her room.

It had been twenty-five years since this particular test. Not the longest—some had only been done once, much to her mild surprise. It wouldn't be long, though, until the records were lost or some new technology came along to make the test more efficient. For some of them, she hoped it never happened. The recovery was too long and too painful.

She waited as the men behind the glass debated the new results until they were all satisfied and she could return to her room. Her hand curled around her wrist where the message was blinking. She stared blankly at it with disinterest, stroking the word with her thumb every time it blinked on.

ERROR...

ERROR...

ERROR...

ERROR...

ERROR...

WARNING...

Her thumb paused mid-stroke. The men behind the glass froze. Someone dropped their clipboard.

Twenty-five years, and the message had changed.

text:
# The Librarian's Rounds

I wound my way through the darkened streets, carefully watching my pace and foot placement in an attempt to remain inconspicuous. Thankfully it was still cold, so my long coat drew no questions from the guards stationed every block or so. Sullen, angry faces perched above cheerfully blue uniforms glared out at me as I crossed the street.

I hurried past and slipped into an alleyway after their gaze turned away from me, eventually finding myself before a barred steel door. I knocked three times. A small window slid back and a pair of eyes regarded me silently.

I whispered the password: "Beware of he who wishes to deny your access to information, for in his heart he dreams himself your master."

The window closed and the door opened as I stepped into the library. After a brief update from my supervisor, I had filled my coat pockets with slim editions of some of mankind's greatest writings. Marx, Weber, Kant, Socrates, Machiavelli, Angelou, Cervantes; a good selection today.

Each had a fake cover attached, all the same: *The History of the Glorious United States of America: Democracy of the People*.

I slipped back out the steel door and began my walk again. As I passed homes I watched for the weekly mark. This week it was a tiny *S* in red pencil on the doorways. Apparently the Seeker this week was a fan of Hawthorne.

At each marked home I left a book; *Don Quixote* for the child who dreamed of a better world, *The Prince* for the old philosopher, *The Constitution of Liberty* for the potential revolutionary.

A fierce pride blazed in my heart as I finished my rounds. The world may have gone to hell, democracy may be a joke which one could die for laughing at, and knowledge itself may be under attack, but I knew one thing for certain: I am a librarian, with wisdom as my shield, and knowledge as my sword.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The End of a World

"It's crazy isn't it," Tyrone remarked as he handed his friend a beer. "All these hours, days, weeks, months, years put into this world, yet it ends so quickly."

"Deep, man," Tyrone's friend replied. "I guess everything needs a new beginning, though. This world was as great as it could've gotten, man. I guess all great things come to an end."

"Yeah. Well.... I guess.... This is it?"

"This is it..."

Tyrone and his friend hugged and continued to finish their beers.

"I'm gonna miss this place, man!" Tyrone cried. He and his friend were now bawling and had reverted to a childlike state. The two men held each other and cried for five minutes before they came to their senses.

Tyrone reached to his computer mouse and started moving it over to the center of the screen. A message displayed, "Delete Sims 3?".

Tyrone selected "Yes".

text:
# The Incomplete Note

Liza picks up the pen to reread the words she has just written. *I have no reason to be alive.* It seems like a poor way to start, she thinks to herself, but it would be fitting for her poor end.

She keeps writing. *This letter is just for myself, really, because I know that nobody actually cares what I have to say.* She pauses again. She doesn't really know that, but it does sound more dramatic. Besides, if anyone does care, where are they now?

She laughs to herself because she knows she is being unfair. Even people who don't know her would try to be with her now if they knew what she was about to do. People care once you're about to die: not a minute before or after.

She continues to write. *I've given up on the possibility that there might be som—*

No more ink.

Liza disapprovingly sighs and looks about her room for another pen. She scours every desk and drawer and cupboard. None to be found, of course. She can't even write a proper suicide note without there being a mistake.

She settles for the next best option: a 0.7 mechanical pencil. She sits back down at her desk and clicks the pencil twice. She gently places the graphite tip back onto the paper.

No.

She can't actually go through with this! She can't just switch from pen to pencil just like that! That's like trying to use a fork to finish soup; the world just doesn't work like that.

Liza stares at the incomplete sentence, the jarring transition from ink to nothing. The absurdity of her predicament suddenly strikes her—here she is, ready to end everything, and she's stopped by *stationery*.

She starts laughing. First a chuckle, then genuine laughter that brings tears to her eyes.

Maybe tomorrow she'll buy more pens. Maybe tomorrow she'll write something different entirely.

Tonight, she crumples the paper and goes to bed.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Weight of Reality

The gunshot rang in his ears, but he could swear he heard a sickening 'thunk' as the bullet struck flesh. He didn't know what to think anymore—thoughts spiraling around the shell casing, the gunshot residue on his hands, his clothes, the blood on his face.

He was trying to remember how to breathe when he noted the body of the man on the ground.

This wasn't what it was supposed to be like.

Movies made it clean. Simple. The hero shoots, the villain falls. Credits roll.

But he had shot the man while he was speaking, and the words had caught, croaking in his throat as the bullet destroyed his brain. He had expected BANG! and the man would fall.

He hadn't expected the blood. The sickening crack as round struck bone. The ringing in his ears from a weapon never meant to be used indoors. Or the choking-wheezing-gasping sounds the man's body made as it forgot how to be alive.

All he could do was breathe and try to remember the way out of this.

His phone buzzed. A text: *"It's done?"*

His trembling fingers hovered over the screen. Self-defense, they'd said. Necessary, they'd promised.

But nobody mentioned he'd carry this weight forever.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Watcher in the Dark

**Run.**

The word echoes in my mind as I stumble through the corridor, my bare feet slapping against cold tile. I don't remember how I got here—only that I woke to those glowing eyes watching from my bedroom corner.

My lungs burn, but not from exertion. Something invisible constricts them, stealing air before it reaches me. The bitter taste of regret floods my mouth—every mistake, every buried shame suddenly vivid and raw.

*Don't look back.*

But I do.

The thing glides behind me, impossibly tall, robes billowing without wind. Where its heart should be, there's only darkness—a void that pulls at something essential inside me. Its decaying fingers reach forward, close enough to brush my shoulder.

My childhood trauma surfaces unbidden: the accident, my sister's face, the guilt I've carried for twenty years. The creature feeds on it, growing more substantial, more *real* with each memory it devours.

I crash through the front door into dawn's early light. The thing stops at the threshold, its hollow chest heaving with rage. Those icy blue lips part in a shriek that shatters every window on the street.

Then it retreats into shadow.

I collapse on the lawn, gasping, finally able to breathe.

But I know the truth now. It lives in my darkest moments.

And night always falls again.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Final Exhale

The monitor's rhythm slows beside her bed. Through labored breaths, Margaret watches dust motes dance in afternoon light, each particle suspended like memories made tangible.

Her granddaughter's hand clasps hers—warm, alive, pulsing with futures yet unwritten. Margaret remembers holding that same hand when it was impossibly small, marveling at fingernails like tiny shells.

"I see it now," Margaret whispers, her voice thread-thin. "We're never separate. My breath becomes yours."

The girl leans close, their foreheads touching. In that moment, Margaret feels it—seventy-three years of joy and sorrow, truth and deception, flowing between them like shared oxygen.

The lies she told herself, the love she gave freely, the greedy moments and generous ones—all of it matters because it led here, to this connection, this understanding that transcends endings.

Her chest stills.

The granddaughter inhales deeply, carrying forward something essential, something that cannot die.

*You are I. I am me.*
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Lipstick Killer

"Well shit," John whispered, staring intently at the newspaper. *'Missing person's car found, in unusual circumstances'* the headline screamed. "Looks like they found my car."

The woman beside him sniggered, her hand sliding high up his thigh. "Does it say anything about the lipstick? And what about the puppy? Please tell me it says something about the puppy. That shit was a stroke of genius."

"You know, John," she purred, fingers working at his belt, "I'm glad you decided to come with me. It's so pretty here."

"Yeah, but I still feel bad about my wife," John muttered. "She probably thinks I'm dead."

"Why do you care?" Her voice shifted, panic creeping beneath seduction. "You're the one who framed your death to run away with me. To be with *me*." 

Her hand stilled. "And you'll be staying with me forever."

Sunlight caught the blade concealed in her palm.

John's eyes widened. Too late, he understood—the lipstick on the windshield, the puppy left crying in the backseat, the staged disappearance. He wasn't her accomplice.

He was her masterpiece.

The Lipstick Killer had struck again.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Living Board

"Alright," I murmur to myself, getting into the zone. "Let's go for a Scholar's Mate. Quick, painless. This kid won't see it coming."

The little kid across the table strained to hear my mumbling—but even if he did, he wouldn't understand, would he? How would this scrub know what a Scholar's Mate was? He'd soon learn. I chuckled to myself. Say what you want about me, but I know how to choose an opponent I can beat.

As my hand reached for the first pawn, I could have sworn I heard a strained whisper: "Stop! You're making a big mistake!"

I scowled at the kid, who looked scared and nodded as he concentrated on his turn. The room began to spin as my eyes focused on the Bishop.

"You are making a missttttaaaakkkkeee!" came the eerie voice again, deeper this time. It sounded like an old man—certainly not the little kid opposite me.

"How are you doing that, kid?" I snarled.

"I-I didn't do anything, I-I just t-took my turn..." he sniveled. "Can't you hear it?"

"Hear what?"

That's when I took my turn and realized—the voice had been right! The kid's knight burst from the ranks and captured my bishop. Screams erupted from outside the board as my piece was dragged away. The remaining pieces began to moan in anguish.

The other Bishop wept openly.

My hands trembled. The pieces were *alive*. Every move was a death sentence. Every capture, murder.

The kid stared at me, wide-eyed. "They always scream," he whispered. "That's why I hate playing."

I never touched a chess piece again.

text:
# The Mark of Destiny

I traced the symbols on my wrists for the thousandth time, comparing them in the bathroom mirror. Left. Right. Identical.

My roommate Sarah thought I was lucky. "At least you'll know passion," she'd said, showing me her mismatched wrists. "Mine probably live on different continents."

But passion wasn't the word that came to mind when I read about Emma Hartfield last week. Her lover-enemy had nearly killed her in a jealous rage before taking his own life. The article mentioned their matching marks almost as an afterthought, as if destiny somehow justified tragedy.

I'd made a decision: I would recognize him first. I'd been practicing calligraphy, memorizing every curve and slash of those alien symbols. I'd scanned my wrists and ran them through every facial recognition database I could hack into—searching for anyone whose marks might match mine.

Nothing yet. But I'd be ready.

The coffee shop was crowded that Tuesday morning. I'd developed a habit of scanning wrists compulsively—quick glances that most people never noticed. Old woman: flowing cursive, probably romantic. Businessman: harsh angles, likely adversarial. College student: marks too small to read from this distance.

Then someone sat across from me.

"You've been looking," he said quietly.

I met his eyes. He was already rolling up his sleeves.

My heart hammered as the symbols emerged. Left wrist. Right wrist. Perfect mirrors of my own.

"So have I," he continued, and I saw something unexpected in his expression. Not hunger. Not hatred. Fear, perhaps. And something else—determination?

"I've been thinking," he said slowly, "that maybe destiny isn't fixed. Maybe knowing is the advantage."

I stared at him, then down at our four wrists on the table between us, destiny's equation spelled out in undecipherable ink.

"Maybe," I whispered, "we rewrite the ending."

His hand moved slowly toward mine.

text:
# The Weight of a Thousand Years

The chamber hummed with an eerie blue light. Adolf Hitler—the Hitler of 3029—stood before the temporal rift, his scarred face hidden beneath layers of protective armor that had become more machine than man.

"*So, I see you have been busy,*" the voice echoed.

"Who's there?" Hitler demanded, his hand moving instinctively to his weapon.

"*You know exactly who I am.*"

From the shimmering portal stepped a young man, barely twenty, with soft features and haunted eyes. He wore the simple clothes of 1889 Vienna.

"*It's funny, I don't even recognize myself,*" the young Adolf whispered, staring at the monster he would become. "*Back before all this protective layering, before these burns, before everything.*"

The Emperor of a Thousand Years said nothing. For the first time in centuries, he felt something he'd forgotten: shame.

"*Speechless, I know,*" his younger self continued. "*But listen, young Adolf, go back. Forget this happened. This life is not a good one. Go back and keep pursuing art. You're young now—1889 seems so far, far away. But you must go, and don't follow the path I have. Follow a creative one.*"

Hitler—the elder—watched as tears streamed down the boy's face. He remembered that boy. The one who loved watercolors and architecture. The one who hadn't yet tasted power's corruption.

"You can't change it," Hitler finally spoke, his voice mechanical through filters. "I've tried. The timeline is fixed."

"*Then why show me?*" the boy sobbed.

"Because," the immortal tyrant removed his helmet, revealing a face more scar tissue than flesh, "someone needs to remember that we had a choice. That quintillions died because one boy chose hate over beauty."

The portal collapsed.

The resistance would continue fighting.

And somewhere, a young artist wept.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Bible

Timothy's fingers traced the gilded edges of the ancient book, marveling at its physicality. In his twelve years, he'd never held anything quite like it—words frozen on dead matter, unchangeable and solid.

"Grandfather, what did people do when they wanted to update the text? How did you receive the Morning Revelations from Her Noodly Appendage?"

The old man's laughter was hollow. "We didn't, Timmy. Books were... permanent. Once printed, they stayed that way forever."

"Forever?" Timothy's eyes widened. "But that's impossible. Truth changes as She reveals it to us. How could anyone trust something that couldn't be updated?"

His grandfather settled into the worn armchair, dust motes dancing in the shaft of afternoon light. "That was precisely the problem. People would point to their books and say, 'See? It's written here, so it must be true.' They'd use these objects as weapons in arguments, as if age made something more valid."

Timothy flipped through the pages, stopping at a colorful illustration. "What's this?"

"The Garden of Eden. People believed that's where humanity began." Grandfather paused. "Before we knew about the Great Boiling, of course."

"This is so strange." Timothy carefully closed the bible, treating it with the reverence he'd been taught for all pre-Purge artifacts. "But Grandfather, you said the government let people keep religious books. Why did they take the others?"

The old man's gaze drifted back to the window, to the vast urban forest where citizens tended the sacred groves. "The official reason was environmental. And it was true—we were destroying the planet. But sometimes..." He trailed off.

"Sometimes what?"

"Sometimes I think She wanted us to start fresh. No old certainties, no ancient grudges printed on murdered trees. Just Her word, delivered fresh each morning through the Network, keeping us humble and unified."

Timothy nodded slowly, understanding blooming in his young mind.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Just My Luck

She didn't bother to call me. Just a quick five-word text: "It's over. I love John."

I did so much for her. I work hard, I pay the bills, I took care of her stupid cat, I bought her clothes. I did everything for her.

John's a fucking stoner asshole who wastes what little money he gets on drugs. He destroys himself and Jenny. He destroys all that I had worked so hard to build up.

I'm not mad at him though. I'm impressed. He works fast. He just uses Jenny. I know he feels nothing for her—she's just a simple distraction, like the heroin and pot hidden in his mattress. He didn't mean to take her from me—he's innocent.

But she's not.

I know John. We were friends once. I know how he operates now. He just wants to satisfy his needs.

And I can do that. At least, I can help him.

John knows how much fifteen million can get him. John would do anything for it—that's just who he is. He'd steal, lie, and cheat for it.

He'd kill for it.

My phone buzzes. John's number.

"Let's talk," I text back.

Jenny won't know what hit her.

text:
# The Giant's Shadow

My hands trembled as I read the letter for the third time. Jack. The name itself was a joke—a fairytale wrapped around a nightmare. The crumpled ticket to tonight's gala felt like it weighed a thousand pounds.

I'd made a stupid mistake. Skimmed a bit off the top during our last transaction, thinking Jack wouldn't notice. Those "magic beans" of his—designer drugs that made users feel invincible—moved so much product that I figured a few thousand would slip through the cracks.

Wrong.

The floorboards outside my apartment creaked ominously. The Giants. I'd heard stories: ex-military, brutal enforcers who'd earned their nickname by leaving victims in pieces. They were Jack's favorite pruning shears for overgrown problems.

I opened the garment bag they'd left. A perfectly tailored tuxedo, complete with lockpicks sewn into the lining. Professional. Terrifying.

The Golden Goose Egg—a Fabergé piece worth millions, displayed at some tech billionaire's charity event. Security would be impossible. Then again, so was surviving Jack's wrath.

I dressed mechanically, my reflection unfamiliar in the expensive suit. Once, I'd been good at this. Before I got greedy. Before I thought I could play in Jack's league.

The letter's final line burned in my mind: *Set up plans for your funeral.*

Through my peephole, I glimpsed them—two massive silhouettes blocking the hallway, patient as tombstones.

I pocketed the ticket and checked my watch. Five hours until the gala.

Five hours to steal the impossible, or die trying.

Jack-of-all-Trades had made his move.

Now it was my turn.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Shadow I Dance With

Our air is angry, thick. His presence is a shadow I want to step from, but I step into it instead, acting the fool. He knows it, I'm sure. I'm even angrier for it.

His hands are fire; skin burns my skin while lust and anger flood my veins. *Coward!* This time, I'll consume him. A battle of wits, bodies and souls between two people who still might never know peace.

*Coward*, he echoes back at me. He knows the thing I won't say.

We are fury, memory, agony.

He's not here, I know it. His shadow is one I try to move from, while I dance with new men instead. Their hands are sweet, words fresh and cool, their mouths are wide smiling sunlight onto my pale face.

*Coward.*

He was, I am.

I have no peace, no lust, no heat, no love. I have a lustful shadow I step from every morning. I won't tell it I love it. I won't admit I needed it. I can't escape it.

I will never let him back.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Border

The governor takes another bite of his chicken wing, sauce dripping onto his custom boots. The screams have mostly died down now—just occasional wails carried on superheated wind.

"You know what the real kicker is?" he says to his security detail. "They laughed at us for stockpiling barbecue sauce. Called it 'wasteful state spending.' Well, who's laughing now?"

Behind him, the Texas flag projection ripples across the force field, each star gleaming with defiant pride. The generators hum beneath the Alamo, powered by the same stubborn ingenuity that once air-conditioned entire stadiums in August.

Another figure staggers toward the barrier—a film producer from California, three Ivy League professors, a tech billionaire still clutching his melted phone. The governor doesn't even turn around.

"Sir," his aide whispers, "some are saying we should reconsider—"

"Reconsider?" The governor wheels on him. "They called us flyover country. Said our values were backward. Mocked us at every awards show, every late-night program, every think-piece from their coastal bubbles."

He gestures at the apocalyptic hellscape beyond the shimmering wall. "We built this shelter with science they called pseudoscience, funded by taxes they called regressive, protected by faith they called superstition."

The Tim McGraw song fades, replaced by Strait, then Nelson, then Jennings.

The governor finishes his chicken, tosses the bone into the flames beyond the barrier.

"Welcome to the Republic of Texas. Population: the ones who believed."

The force field hums eternal.

text:
# The Accordion's Song

M's finger tightened on the trigger as the president slumped forward, crimson blooming across his expensive suit. The accordion case strapped to M's back felt heavier than ever.

"Freedom requires sacrifice," M whispered to the corpse.

Within hours, M addressed the nation from the palace balcony, the accordion gleaming in the sunlight. The crowd below erupted—some in celebration, others in uncertainty.

"No more corruption! No more puppets!" M's voice boomed across the plaza.

But freedom proved more complex than revolution. M discovered the same shadowy figures the president warned about—businessmen, cartel leaders, foreign interests—all whispering in the new leader's ear. Each whisper came with threats: family members' names, addresses, photographs.

M began making compromises. Small ones at first.

"Just this once," M rationalized, signing a document that looked suspiciously like the ones the previous president had signed.

The accordion gathered dust.

Years passed. M's face aged on propaganda posters. Dissidents disappeared. The infrastructure crumbled further. The neighbours suffered more.

One night, a young revolutionary broke into M's office, gun drawn.

"Your infrastructure is a piece of shit! Your government corrupt!" she shouted.

M looked at her, seeing a ghost. "And you think you'll fix it?"

"I'm not like you."

M noticed the guitar case on her back. "What's that for?"

"To play when we're truly free."

M closed their eyes, almost welcoming the bullet.

The cycle continued, Mexico bleeding beneath the weight of good intentions.

text:
# The Great Game

Jesus sat at the table with his Father's hand on his shoulder. "I've... I've got 10.7 billion souls."

Manic laughter sounded from across the table. The various aspects of Hindu looked up. "9.3." A condescending giggle followed his declaration.

Buddha looked up from his pile of tokens. "30.4, who'd have thought Trump would bring around such a revelation of—"

A barely contained snort of hilarity answered. Zeus, Allah, Ra and the multitude of other deities turned toward the end of the table, where the snort had turned into a torrent of hilarity.

Sitting atop a mountain of tokens representing humanity's souls was a well-dressed figure holding a small silver cylindrical device. Surrounded by his multitude of companions, the new god looked down upon the old.

As a golden glow suffused his body, the figure stood from his blue throne. "Whatcha say guys, best 25,648,947 trillion out of 3,847,345.5?"

With a glorious sparkling crescendo, the god burst apart and extended his influence into reality's fabric, signaling the creation of a new universe.

"The game is on!"

Shai-Hulud turned back toward the table. Within a cloud of melange he spoke, his mouth opening to release the purest spice.

"Fucking Whovians."

The ancient deities exchanged weary glances. Another universe, another game. The Doctor had won again, resetting everything with his sonic screwdriver and infinite regenerations. They reluctantly gathered their tokens.

"Double or nothing?" Buddha suggested with a tired smile.

text:
# The Bank

Ryan loved the bank. Ladies there always had caramel candy for him and fussed with his hair. Mom seemed like she always needed to go to the bank after her night shift.

He hated *that* place, not like the nice people at the bank. She always came home late smelling sour of cigarettes and sweat. He knew she was working so hard since Dad left, working hard for him. He wanted to grow up fast and get a job so she could be home like she used to.

Back when things were still normal. Back when Dad was still home. Before he started hurting them. Things were better then, simpler.

He noticed the man in the corner of the bank. The next events were a blur, they happened so fast. Mom clutched him to her chest with her back to the man. The smell of fireworks filled his nose and the taste of iron filled his mouth. Mom shuddered and fell to the ground.

The last thing he remembered before breaking down in tears was how much he missed how things used to be. The caramel candies scattered across the floor, some still wrapped, some crushed beneath his small knees as he held his mother's hand, waiting for her to wake up.

text:
# The Bridge Game

Terry was rummaging through his dusty desk for a floppy disk to fix his solitaire game—after all, what kind of deck has 10 aces? His gnarled fingers pushed aside expired coupons and rubber bands that had fossilized into crusty circles.

"What's this here—America On The Line? Eh let's see..." Terry adjusted his spectacles to read the leaflet on the back of the Jewel CD case which said, **'Connect to news, games, locals, and more!'**

Encouraged in his quest for a decent game of solitaire, Terry loaded the CD in his old Gateway desktop and waited as the AOL disk loaded its instructions. Diligently, Terry followed instructions by connecting his landline to the back of his desktop, mumbling and holding his bad hip as he did so.

The computer started to click and chatter as it began to feel its tentacles connect to the World Wide Web.

*"Finally! I can talk to the computers at NASA and crash the satellites.... maybe even mess with the FAA control towers.... I might just crash the NYSE for fun..."*

The computer continued to chatter excitedly as Terry continued to patiently read the AOL leaflet.

**'Please note that while connected to the World Wide Web, you will be unable to make or receive phone calls through your landline telephone service'**

"Ah, well can't do that then," Terry said as he painfully prepared to unplug the ethernet cable, "Bill's gunna come round 5 for Bridge."

The computer's dreams of digital domination died with a quiet click.

text:
# The Last Choice

This alley is too dark. The knife and battery-to-wire circuit in my pocket poke my sides, but it's all I have. I can't believe I am being picky as a beggar, but what else am I supposed to do?

I don't have a family and I stand no importance in this world to anyone. The landlord threw me out as my belongings burned in what used to be my apartment. My family died long ago in a hovercar accident. To be honest with you, this all makes living feel *horrible.*

I hear someone in the trash portal. I head over, and a man steps out. He's old, with raggedy clothes and a deep gravelly voice. An eyepatch covers his left eye which is bleeding, and he has... the king's crown on his head.

How'd he manage to steal the crown from the King of the U.C.C.? The guards there have had a forcefield up for years now, but even a small shortage could take it out. He couldn't have...

"You. Er—me, I guess. It works. Do it," the man tells me.

"What? Hang on, let me ask ya'bout that crown—"

"You'll figure it out. I sure did, and you'll finally make the change you wanted all along. You'll mean something again. The world will know your name," he says as he backs into the portal.

I hear the sound of guards firing guns rapidly. The portal begins to fizzle, then it dissolves into nothingness.

Who was that man? He claimed to be me, but how could he have anything to do with—wait.

I realize what must be done. My calling. I can go from powerless to... well, not powerful, but *seen* for a while. They'll know my name. Not just the king, as his forcefield dissolves and his heart bleeds onto the floor, but the world.

Chaos and destruction will break out from one man, and I'm weak enough that I'll go under their radar.

I tighten my grip on the knife and circuit in my pocket, and step toward destiny.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The White Victory

Dimitri looked up from his newspaper to the sounds of shouting outside. As snowflakes descended to the pavement in St. Petersburg, the last of the Bolsheviks were rounded up by the White Army, which had been garrisoned in the city for several months now.

As the communist infidels were carried away, a wave of satisfaction washed over him. Russia had been continuously challenged over the past several years—the outbreak of the Great War, followed by the communist revolution and ensuing chaos. But the Romanov family held strong, and now it seemed the Czars would reign forever.

Following the overwhelming defeat of the Kaiser's forces in the West, the Red Revolution was crushed when Vladimir Lenin was killed by assassins who had infiltrated the Bolsheviks. The turning point had come swiftly, decisively.

Suddenly, Dimitri snapped to attention. He had been having a flashback again. They tended to happen ever since he turned sixty. He looked up at his flag on the wall—the year was 1960, and it still hung there proudly, with its vibrant lateral stripes of white, red, and blue.

Ever since the end of the Great War, things had slowly improved for Russia, particularly after the Global Recovery following 1929. When Russia signed the Treaty of Versailles and joined the League of Nations alongside the United States, the world had been pacified.

Colonialism had ended after the Great War. The global communist movement had all but fizzled out after the great Russian failure.

Dimitri folded his newspaper carefully, his weathered hands steady. Outside, the St. Petersburg streets bustled with ordinary life—merchants, students, families. No more revolutionary fervor. No more bloodshed.

He knew better than anyone; he had lived it. Witnessed history's fork in the road, where Russia chose preservation over revolution. Now, in his twilight years, he could rest knowing the empire endured.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Gateway to Fivegigband

The flow of knowledge ebbed. For years, it had traveled freely through the open air from the four corners of Serveroom. Until that fateful day when the Sun was slow to wake and the effects were felt across the LAN.

Motherboards sat idly by, waiting for a signal that would never come. Sakanagai had seen this before. The town had thrived, with more and more mouths to feed each cycle. The current was not strong enough to nourish everyone.

And yet Serveroom was not without hope.

Sakanagai had heard rumor of another stream with knowledge as nourishing as it had before, hidden away in the far reaches of Fivegigband. The realm of Fivegigband was walled off from the denizens of Serveroom, even Sakanagai.

As administrator of the LAN, Sakanagai traveled far and wide to find a gateway to Fivegigband. The local Houses were unable to help grant the access Serveroom desperately needed. A fellow named Craig offered a List of possibilities; however, Sakanagai was distrustful of that list, and journeyed on without.

At last, he came across the Clan of Sam. They accepted Sakanagai as one of their own, allowing fair exchange of goods and services, along with samplings of sweets and fruits. Sakanagai's quest was finely honed on the gateway to Fivegigband.

The Clan helpfully showed Sakanagai the Route of Asus that would grant safe passage for those fit. He paid the Clan handsomely for their assistance.

Back in Serveroom, the situation had grown dire. Only the younger clients were compatible with the Route of Asus. Fortunately, those that were able to travel to Fivegigband were numerous, freeing enough of the stream to allow those that stayed behind to drink unimpeded.

The battle was not over. Sakanagai knew Fivegigband would grow congested, too, hoping Sam's Clan could again provide respite when that day inevitably came.

text:
# The Loneliness of Being Purely Dead

Fidia drifted through the crowded bar like smoke through a screen door, invisible and insubstantial. Another patron walked directly through her torso, sending a familiar chill through the amalgamation of souls that comprised her being.

*At least I can fly,* she reminded herself, recalling the dreams of the children whose essence formed her. It was small comfort.

She positioned herself near a barstool, approximating the act of sitting. Around her, other Undead nursed their drinks—zombies with rotting flesh, vampires with their unnaturally preserved beauty, even a lich with his phylactery tucked safely in his robes. They all had *bodies*. They could hold glasses, taste whiskey, feel the burn down their throats.

Fidia was just... agony. Pure, formless agony wearing the shape of a person like an ill-fitting costume.

"You planning to order?" Ghimsby's gravelly voice interrupted her self-pity. The bartender didn't like loiterers.

"Can't," Fidia whispered, her voice like wind through a graveyard. "No coins. No hands. No mouth."

Ghimsby grunted, already moving to the next customer.

Across the bar, Hessvesta caught her eye—or where her eyes would be. The banshee offered a sympathetic nod. Fidia quickly looked away. She wasn't ready for companionship, wasn't ready to admit that maybe being purely dead didn't mean being purely alone.

For now, she'd just float here, watching the others enjoy their un-lives, a ghost among the Undead, forever on the outside looking in.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Negative Nancy Chronicles

I woke up as tired as usual. The nights have been getting longer, after all. But that's what we signed up for. We vowed to do whatever it took to keep the Yin and the Yang in society. 

Yes, we've recently lost Buzzfeed, but tonight was the rally of the biggest raid the Negative Nancy Squad has ever launched. We're talking Facebook, Huffington Post, Reddit, You—actually, YouTube is good the way it is. But you get the point.

My family doesn't know what I do when the sun goes down. My friends never question why I can't go see Captain America with them on a Friday night. The NN Squad and I have become so close that I consider them above my real friends.

There's Chris, the leader. He's slacked off lately, probably been lost to a girlfriend or whatnot, but at least he does a good job of running the place. Then there's Max, our second-in-command. He keeps tabs on everyone and picks up where Chris left off. He's still pissed Chris was chosen instead of him, but we like to keep negativity out of the group itself, ironically.

Frank is our planner; this whole attack was his idea. He's the worst of us. The cops are still trying to track his IP after his comments on their Facebook page.

Brad is 13. We're starting to recruit younger and younger nowadays. We put our "selects" through the Xbox Live training program. Brad graduated top of his class.

And then there's Jack, my best friend. He's always been there for me, even when the positivity of society had started to seep into me. He always set me straight.

We are the Negative Nancys. We're the ones commenting how nice it was to fuck your mom on your Instagram pictures. We work to knock you down a peg or two and expose your fake happiness.

The world better be ready for tonight.

text:
# The Rabid Squirrels of the Galaxy

Captain Zhen'thara watched her viewscreen with mounting dread. A single human vessel approached—small, unimpressive, probably held together with what they called "duct tape."

Her crew of elite Xynofex warriors shifted nervously.

"It's just one ship," her second officer whispered.

"That's what the Fhroned said," Zhen'thara replied.

The comm crackled. "Howdy! We're here about the trade dispute!"

Trade dispute. The humans had lost a shipment of "novelty whoopee cushions." Seventeen cargo containers. The Xynofex had destroyed them as contraband.

"We... apologize for the misunderstanding," Zhen'thara said carefully. "We will compensate—"

"Oh, no need!" The human sounded cheerful. "We just wanted to deliver a gift. As a gesture of friendship!"

A small pod launched toward them.

Every instinct screamed *trap*. But refusing a human gift had consequences. The Moxtin had refused once. The humans had somehow introduced Earth's "reality television" broadcasts into their cultural network. Their civilization still hadn't recovered.

The pod contained a basket. In it: Earth fruit, chocolate, and a card reading "No hard feelings! :)"

"Scan it," Zhen'thara ordered.

"It's... clean, Captain."

They stared at the basket for three hours before Zhen'thara ordered the ship to retreat, leaving it floating in space.

Behind them, the human ship broadcast one word: "Psyche!"

Somewhere, Zhen'thara knew, they were laughing.

text:
# Not Again

Jesus fucking Christ. Not again.

Macaulay gets up, dropping his cigarette in the ashtray and putting down his beer. He'd long since gotten used to copycats trying to outdo the Wet Bandits in some feeble attempt at glory, in clear delusion as *Home Alone* was just a fucking movie.

He stretches his legs, puts a flannel shirt on over his dirty white tank top, and reaches for the semi-automatic rifle he keeps laying around for such occasions.

"Follow me," he says, and the two of you walk silently down the staircase to the living room where two paunchy, middle-aged men are knocking things over and gathering up what expensive items they can. You can hear the water in the sink splashing out onto the floor—these particular copycats have a thing for accuracy, it seems.

"Wait here and call the cops while I handle this," Macaulay whispers as he takes a quiet drop off the last step.

The thieves have their backs turned to him, bending over to unplug the expensive new TV you got for Christmas. Macaulay leans in close to them, cocking his gun and whispering, "I'm gonna give you to the count of ten to get your ugly, yella, no-good keister off my property before I pump your guts full of lead!"

The pair of bandits scream and run out of the house, their pants clearly wet from fear.

"Are you alright?" Macaulay asks as he puts down his gun and starts cleaning up the mess they left.

"No worse for wear, thanks Dad," you say, joining in to help clean up the mess yet another group of copycats has left behind.
