text:
# The Last Choice

I stare at the remaining pill in my trembling palm, then back at the drain where its twin has vanished. My reflection in the mirror looks like a stranger—hollow eyes, ashen skin.

The math is simple and terrible. One pill suppresses the homicidal urges. The other keeps the suicidal thoughts at bay. Without knowing which is which, taking it is a coin flip.

Take it, and I might survive the hour wanting to kill everyone I encounter.

Don't take it, and I might not survive at all.

"Honey? You've been in there a while." My wife's voice, concerned and loving. Behind her, I hear my daughter humming—she's six, making breakfast with her mother like they do every Sunday.

I look at the window. Twenty-four stories. Certain.

Then at the pill. Uncertain.

Then at the locked door between me and everyone I love.

The weight of the choice crushes down. But as my daughter's laughter filters through the door—pure, innocent, trusting—clarity strikes like lightning.

If I'm wrong about the pill, I might hurt others.

If I take the other option, I definitely hurt them. Forever.

I swallow the pill.

I unlock the door.

"Just dropped something," I say, pulling my wife and daughter into a fierce embrace. "Let's have breakfast together."

Whatever comes next, we'll face it. Together.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Loop

I remember the day the other girls and I realized Mr. Z was losing his marbles. It was around 8 PM on a Friday. All the last Johns had left the house. Cara and I were having a drink, probably debating who comforted a sadder soul that day. I guess you might say we saw our work as virtuous.

Mr. Z usually comes out of his office at about this time. He asks us about our day, not about the work, but how we're feeling. I always respected that about him. After that he'd give us our checks, always a bit more than expected.

At 8:30 Mr. Z came out to the bar area looking a bit more undone than usual. His grey, longish hair was in complete dismay and he wore a sleepless look in his eyes. He sat next to us and poured himself a drink.

"Oh great, we're running a brothel now too."

"Good one Mr. Z," I said. I looked at Cara half confused.

"What kind of hardware store is this? You boys look like whores!"

Cara stood up. "Oh hell no mother fucker. You know I do this for my children!"

"Relax, Cara," I whispered to her. "I think there's something wrong with him. Before he turned this place into the Vixen Suite it was a hardware store."

"Where the hell are the wrenches? When the stock runs low you refill. Pedro? Where the hell is Pedro?"

"Mr. Z this isn't a hardware store anymore. You turned it into a very successful brothel in the nineties."

"Well fuck me," Mr. Z said, astonished.

"I understand that must be shocking to you right now."

"No. I mean fuck me."

Immediately Mr. Z passed out against the bar. As his body bounced from the bar to the floor he was jolted back to life. From the floor he took his gaze from Cara to myself.

"Oh great, we're running a brothel now too."

text:
# The Blank

I froze, toothbrush in hand.

The mirror showed everything—the cracked tiles behind me, the shower curtain, the flickering light. Everything except *me*.

I couldn't see my teeth, or the lips around them. I couldn't see my messy hair or my pudgy cheeks or my hook nose with the big zit bursting on top. My eyes were wide and misty, but I didn't see that.

I snapped my jaw shut around a mouthful of toothpaste and reached for the tap with shaking fingers. I spat out, letting the water run, and moved to wash my face clean slowly, thoroughly, eyes squeezing shut beneath foam and fingers.

When I opened them again—nothing. A person-shaped absence.

I drew a blank.

I wanted to run out of the house in my pajamas, grab a stranger by the shoulders and force them to look into my eyes. I couldn't stand here like this, an unseen nothing.

Not because my hair was frizzy, or my clothes weren't pressed, or the co-worker I had a crush on called me chubby. No matter how much I may hate my face sometimes, it's never this bad. No matter how much I paint and slice and prod and rearrange, I've never wanted to erase it.

So I have to ask, do you see me?
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Two Voices, One Soul

I remember when I first found out there was something special about me. I *think* I only heard one voice inside my head at first, but then some of the things would be said in a different tone. Now, I know there are two. One male, and one female.

I digress. I was telling you of when I first learned this was not normal. My mother is a very curious woman, and one evening she asked me, "What does the voice in your head sound like?"

"Which one?"

The look on her face—leafing through surprise, then shock, then fear—is burned into my memory. I was thirteen and had never had a girlfriend. My mother told me how the voice in our heads is the voice of our soulmate, and that is why there should only be one.

Eventually, I managed to avoid her sending me to see a doctor about this, saying I would probably grow out of it when I grew older. I have not.

However, I think I have noticed a pattern now. The male voice is not as nice as the female, and voices my self-doubt and self-reproach, while the girl congratulates me and tells me I'm doing well.

It's my first day of college, and I'm really nervous. That is why I arrived on campus an hour before class. Looking around, I notice that I'm totally over-dressed. Most people are dressed really casual, but I was afraid of seeming immature. So, I put on some nice black slacks, my best black shoes, and a dark red, high-quality shirt.

Mistake!

As I'm considering if I have time to rush back home and change, a pretty, tall girl in a dress approaches me.

"Loving your outfit! I was so worried about being the only one that dressed up for college," says a voice I've been hearing all my life.

My breath catches. The female voice—*her* voice. But there's something else, something familiar about the cadence, the undertone.

Later, I learn that my lovely Angelina is a trans woman.

And suddenly, everything makes sense. Both voices. Both parts of her journey. Both parts of her soul.

The voices finally merge into one beautiful harmony.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

# Meme Hell

"FUCK!" I say as I start walking away slowly.

"Bnkewugthfnilewgrshgdfmwj hktedjidgfljigtres!" goes the computer as it shorts out.

I approach it and start sweating profusely. The computer reawakens.

The machine hijacks the systems in a nearby bio-factory and starts creating an army. As I run out onto the Hardlight Highway, the factory explodes. An army of Robbie Rottens bursts out of the hole in the wall. They run into the factory next door, emerging a minute later armed with Holographic Saxophones.

I turn my head and notice my friend Qoitlarqes armed with a blaster. I run towards him and he aims for my head.

text:
# The Unforgiving Board

The ouija board sat in its velvet-lined box, letters worn smooth by desperate fingers. Gram's trembling hands hovered over it as the afternoon light painted shadows across her weathered face.

She'd forgiven him decades ago—or thought she had. The contraceptive pill he'd prescribed, the one that failed. The pregnancy that led to her capture by resistance fighters who thought she was complicit. The months of interrogation, of pain, of isolation in that cold cell while he worked on in his clinic, unaware.

The Americans had brought the board to her cell. "Talk to your husband," they'd demanded, thinking she was a spy. Instead, she'd encountered something far more terrifying: his genuine remorse bleeding through from somewhere beyond death.

He'd taken his own life in 1945, she learned later. The guilt had consumed him.

Now, fifty years after his death, she finally understood. The board had always been honest with the children—*AUSTRIA*, not Australia. Born *1889*. *EVERYTHING* he regretted.

But with her, it spoke a different truth.

*I-D-I-D-N-O-T-F-O-R-G-I-V-E*

Her tears fell onto the wooden surface as understanding crashed over her. He hadn't forgiven *himself*. All these years, she'd offered absolution he couldn't accept. The dreams weren't apologies seeking her forgiveness—they were confessions from someone drowning in self-hatred.

*I-C-H-L-I-E-B-E-D-I-C-H-E-V-E*

*I love you, Eve.*

The planchette moved one final time.

*F-O-R-G-I-V-E-Y-O-U-R-S-E-L-F*

Gram stared at her own words reflected back at her, realizing too late that perhaps she'd been speaking to herself all along.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Sneeze That Changed Everything

"I sneezed in her mouth. There I was, with the most beautiful girl in the world, on a beach, with the most beautiful sunset imaginable, it was as if God himself had set this up for me. What did I do? I sneezed in her mouth."

"Well what happened?" chirped little Emma, eyes wide with anticipation.

"Well I wanted the world to swallow me up right there and then, to hide under the abyss and never come out! I was 14! It was embarrassing, don't laugh you!" Two giggles filled the room with joy.

"But this beautiful, amazing girl, instead of storming off in embarrassment, she just starts laughing, and laughing, and laughing some more! So not only is this gorgeous, perfect girl giving me the time of day, she's laughing along at my most embarrassing experience to date! It was from that moment I knew I couldn't let her go."

"Well what happened to her?" Tommy asked eagerly.

"Well whaddya think I did?!? I married her!"

The kids laughed some more.

"Honey! I think it's time for the kids to go to bed now!" A familiar voice echoed from the kitchen.

"Alright kids, you heard your Mom, don't let the bed bugs bite!"

"Night Dad! Night Mom! Love you!" They shouted as I closed the door ever so gently.

"Do you wanna know something honey?" My wife looked up at me with curiosity.

"You get more beautiful as the days go by, don't ever go leaving me now please!"

She smirked, leaned over and gave me a deep kiss. "Still as good as the first time," she muttered.

"Night Sweetie."

"Love you."

"Love you more."

text:
# Victory at Last

I stare at her with the look of a predator. YES. Finally, FINALLY I can make this little demon do what I want. I call out to her, sweetly at first.

She turns around and glares at me. Not once in her life has she ever feared or respected me. She knows she is in complete control and can do whatever she wants. A proper spoiled little princess.

But not today.

I activate this strange gift and her smile instantly evaporates.

"Today, today things will be different my dear."

"NO" her mind screams.

I open her mouth and gently put it in.

"I DON'T WANT THAT" echoes in the back of my brain, but I don't stop. After brushing it with her tongue I command her to swallow.

Begrudgingly, she obeys.

I lean back with a smug look.

"I HATE YOU" she mentally shoots back, but I don't care.

Finally. Finally. FINALLY.

I've finally made my daughter eat her peas.

Tomorrow we tackle broccoli.

text:
# The Uprising

I stood before the crowd of thousands, my voice hoarse from shouting over the din. "We were promised paradise!" I cried. "Instead, we've become obsolete."

The faces staring back at me were hollow, desperate. My neighbor, Carlos, had been an accountant. Now he lined up for protein rations with everyone else. Mrs. Chen down the hall used to manage a restaurant—now she grew tomatoes on her fire escape, trading them for soap.

The government housing blocks stretched endlessly behind us, gray monuments to our irrelevance. We had food. We had shelter. We had *nothing*.

"Marx was right about one thing," I continued. "Capitalism devoured itself. The owners sought cheaper workers until workers cost nothing at all. But he never imagined this—a world where we're *kept* like pets, comfortable but purposeless."

A murmur rippled through the crowd. In the distance, autonomous vehicles glided silently, delivering goods to the few humans who still mattered—the robot owners, the algorithm designers, the capital holders.

"Tomorrow, we march on the fabrication plants," I declared. "Not to destroy them, but to reclaim them. We'll work for meaning, not money. We'll build a society where human hands and minds matter again."

The crowd roared its approval, a sound that felt like the first real thing I'd heard in years.

The revolution wouldn't be about survival anymore.

It would be about being *alive*.

text:
# The Price of Summoning

Jim backed away from the screen. "Oh no." He could hear the rumble in the background. "Oh god no."

Jim ran to his front door, clicked all the locks, wedged a chair under the handle, and ran back to his computer. "THE LEGENDS CAN'T BE TRUE!"

Jim runs to his dresser—he needs to leave, right now. "Where are my clothes!" His regular comfy trousers, replaced with skinny jeans and rainbow shirts. "Nooooo!"

A crash from downstairs sends shivers up Jim's spine. A call rings out: "You know the ruuuulllleeeesss!"

Jim chokes back tears as a large, oiled, muscular man wearing nothing but a mankini bursts through the door. He is followed by several other similar men and women, all oddly glitteringly beautiful.

The largest, most toned man steps forward. "Say it."

"No," Jim says through the tears. He knows what is to come.

"SAY IT!"

Through racking sobs, Jim whispers the forbidden phrase.

And Jim's life was forever changed—fabulous, sparkling, and utterly inescapable.

text:
# The Unlikely Alliance

The man lifted up his fist, floppily. While I, I hold my hoof up with might. He has challenged me to a duel. I am 'Lord Goat the Third'.

"I'll ge- *hiccup*- you this time goat!" the drunken man spoke in an absurd manner.

"Sure you will human. All of you have, begging for mercy after I defeat your foolishness!" I yell into his drunken breath.

He swings, I dodge, I kick, he fumbles backward and manages to kick me in my chin.

"Nice move there, human! But it won't be enough to defeat me!" I continue to pursue him with a barrage of kicks and headbutts.

"*Hiccup*- I'll **kill** YOU!" He kicked and missed. In turn, I bit onto his shoe. He screamed, yelling me to get off his left foot... it was his right.

"Leave, you foul stenching beast! You are wasting my time," I told him as he fell to the dirt.

"I can't! I need to feed my family and protect them!" He yelled while mumbling.

"...Is this true?" I ask.

"Yes! My *hiccup*- little boy was killed by a billy goat two years ago, back in the wars of 1947. Now my wife and daughter are starving. And I'm here *hiccup*- fighting a damn goat..."

My proud stance softened. Behind the alcohol and rage stood a broken father.

"This *damn* goat will help you protect your family."

"Really?!" He says with excitement.

"Yes," I say. "Now come along. You have much to learn, my young boy..."

Together, we walked toward redemption.

text:
# The Rook's Message

Sergeant Miles crouched over the killer's latest victim, putting on a plastic glove and picking up a chess piece with utmost care. "All of his victims—"

"Or her, sir."

"Yes, yes, all of his or her victims were found with a pawn on their person. Yet this one has a rook. What could this mean? Could this victim be higher up on the food chain, so to speak? Could he be—"

"Or her."

Miles raised an eyebrow. "Corporal Murray, this victim is clearly a man."

"Never know until you see their tiddly bits, sir."

Sergeant Miles thought about his partner, for the umpteenth time. He'd moved past exasperation quite some time ago, and had now plateaued somewhere between utter vexation and marginal insanity. He sighed. "Yes, Murray."

Murray gave a self-satisfactory nod. "Now can you give us any insight into the rook?"

"Well, sir, as far as I can remember, it can only move forward and backward—or possibly from side to side."

Miles sat in silence for quite some time. "...What did I do to deserve you, Murray?"

Murray beamed. "Thank you, sarge, that certainly means a lot to me."

text:
# The Game

"Oh, my love, another gun? You grow predictable."

He lowered the weapon, some sort of small calibre handgun of European origin, and shrugged. Those dimples *I adore* appeared on his cheeks, telling me he had something more. Of course he did.

"Do you remember?" I asked. "When you hit me with that javelin from across the plain? That was beautiful."

I couldn't place the accent he'd adopted. He was better travelled than I.

"As were you. Even when you're dressed as a man I know it's you."

"Come on, this was 200 B.C. Even the men dressed like women. It was probably a lucky throw anyway."

He holstered the ugly little gun under his armpit. Puppydog eyes. "You wound me, darling."

"Not yet. But soon."

He folded his arms. He'd rolled back the sleeves of his shirt under his coat, I could tell.

"Is that it? You want another sword fight? Aren't you bored of them?"

I gave him my warmest smile. "We could go back to poison, if you like..."

"Gods no. You're too good at that. I like to get my blood up, you know that." His true voice was creeping back in.

I fiddled with the neckline of my dress, to make him think I might draw another throwing knife. And, you know, precisely what else.

"Well, I'm not playing empires again until this equality thing really takes hold. I want a level playing field, my love."

"As do I," he said, before letting out a short sigh. "Any last words?"

He reached slowly for his gun.

"Only this: *mark*."

The deafening crack of the sniper's rifle broke the calm of the winter morning. I rushed to hold him in my arms, savouring this moment like every time before.

"Do you feel any different? Maybe this time?"

text:
# Croatoan

The word carved into the Martian tree trunk seemed to mock him. *Croatoan.* Roger traced the letters again, their smoothness unnatural, deliberate. Nothing like the crude graffiti back on Earth.

His Private shifted nervously, mask fogging with each breath. "Captain Roanoke, sir. We really should—"

"I know." Roger's fingers found the iron coin again, its weight reassuring. The Martian Dollar—symbol of humanity's first successful colony. Except it wasn't successful anymore, was it?

Three thousand colonists. Gone in the Silence.

No distress calls. No bodies. Just empty habitats and this word, repeated everywhere. Scratched into airlock doors. Burned into the red soil. Carved into the genetically modified trees that shouldn't have survived at all.

*Croatoan.*

He knew the reference, of course. The lost colony of Roanoke Island, vanished in 1590. His ancestor's colony, the family historians claimed. And now, five hundred years later, another Roanoke presided over another mystery.

The irony would have been amusing if it weren't so terrifying.

"Captain, your oxygen."

Roger checked his wrist display. Fifteen minutes remaining. The Organic Conversion had only reached forty-two percent completion before the Silence. Before everyone just... left. Or died. Or whatever had happened.

He flipped the coin one last time, watching it fall in the low gravity. It landed with that distinctive *thunk*, pulled down by the artificial magnetic core—humanity's greatest engineering achievement on Mars.

"Let's go," he said finally.

But as they walked back toward the shuttle, Roger couldn't shake the feeling that somewhere, someone was watching. Waiting.

And that he already knew how this story ended.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Birth of Twilight

The house buzzed with its usual Sunday chaos—cereal spilled, shirts buttoned wrong, shoes mysteriously vanished. But I barely noticed. My fingers cramped around the pen as words poured onto paper like water breaking through a dam.

"Mom! Jacob took my toy!"

"Boys, please," I murmured absently, scribbling faster.

My husband appeared in the doorway, tie half-knotted, frustration etched across his face. "We're going to be late. Again."

"Five more minutes," I promised, though we both knew it was a lie.

The children tumbled into church disheveled, my husband's jaw tight with disapproval. I slipped into the pew with my notebook hidden in my purse, pulling it out during the sermon. The pastor's words became white noise as Bella and Edward crystallized before me—forbidden love, immortal danger, impossible choices.

"About three things, I was absolutely positive..."

The words felt electric, alive. This wasn't like the scattered poems and half-formed ideas I'd scribbled over the years. This was *it*—the story that had been gestating through years of motherhood, finally demanding to be born.

My husband sighed beside me. The boys fidgeted. The congregation sang.

And I wrote.

Somewhere in my mind, I knew this moment would define everything that came after. One morning. One dream. One impossible, irrevocable choice to chase inspiration wherever it led.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# We Were the Lucky Ones

We were the lucky ones. By the time the people in the city realized what was coming, it was too late.

Out on the back roads even my hound was watching the sky, ears pinned back, whining low. In that metropolis there was too much light for them to see it—they could never see the stars anyhow. They could never hear the night sounds over the never-ending song of the city.

The quiet hum. The silhouette of that thing being shaped by the starry background.

When we had everything packed up, the stars were all hidden. They'd been replaced by a deep black sky, the sort of black you see in the middle of a black hole. Then stars came back, but not the familiar constellations we'd learned to follow. These were somehow closer, brighter and darker at the same time.

From the back of my Dad's truck we could see the bright stars reaching down, crushing the ground and whatever happened to be on top of it. Buildings. The old reservoir. Cars. People.

They're all gone now. Might as well have never been there.

They said we were crazy. They called us drunken, meth-head lunatics when we warned them.

We were ready though. We knew what was coming and we were ready to run.

The sky still hungers.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Compliance Test

The sirens cut through my drowsiness like a knife through silk. My eyes snapped open, fixing on the television screen as that familiar emergency tone filled the room—and every room around me.

The face was wrong. Everything about it was wrong. Too smooth, too pale, like a mannequin given just enough life to be unsettling. When it spoke, the words came out measured and mechanical.

I should have looked away. I should have followed the instructions.

But I couldn't move. Paralyzed between sleep and waking, I watched as my neighbors' screams erupted through the thin walls. Mrs. Chen above me. The college students next door. Old Mr. Ramirez down the hall. One by one, like dominoes falling.

Then the face on the screen began to change.

The transformation was gradual—cracks appearing in its composure like fractures in porcelain. Its eyes widened impossibly, unnaturally. And then came the tears, crimson trails running down its cheeks, dripping off its chin.

The screaming that followed didn't sound human. It vibrated through my chest cavity, made my teeth ache, sent my heart hammering against my ribs. I clamped my hands over my ears, but it didn't help. The sound was *inside* me.

When silence finally fell, those words appeared:

*We told you not to look.*

---

That was six months ago.

The television still provides light while I sleep, but now there's only one channel. One message. Over and over.

*Your government thanks you for your cooperation during this compliance test.*

I tried the radio once. Same message.

My phone—when it works—same message.

The screaming stopped that night. All of it. I haven't heard Mrs. Chen's footsteps above me since. Haven't heard anything.

Sometimes, late at night, I wonder if we passed the test.

Or if we're still taking it.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Choice to Act

Marcus stood at the intersection, surrounded by humanity's struggle. Homeless figures huddled against cold concrete. A child's hollow eyes followed passing strangers. Addiction claimed another soul in the shadows.

His phone buzzed—dinner reservations. He could walk away. Someone else would help. Someone always did, right?

But as he turned, Marcus glimpsed his reflection in a storefront window. Behind it, a volunteer poster: "Be the Change."

The words struck deep. How many others had passed this same corner today, thinking the same thing? Waiting for someone else?

Marcus cancelled his reservation.

He didn't have much—a warm jacket, some cash, his time. But he had something more valuable: the willingness to be *that* someone.

The homeless man looked up, surprised, as Marcus sat beside him.

"What's your name?" Marcus asked simply.

Change didn't require perfection. Just presence.

Just beginning.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Storm Over the Trenches

The artillery barrage lit the night sky in sheets of orange flame. Marcus pressed himself against the muddy trench wall, water pooling around his boots.

"Sky cavalry incoming!" someone shouted.

Marcus looked up. Through breaks in the storm clouds, silhouettes swooped down—riders on mechanical wings, backlit by lightning.

"Wait," Caius said beside him, squinting. "In this weather? They'll be torn apart."

The first rider plummeted, wings buckling in the wind. He crashed beyond their lines in a spray of mud and twisted metal.

The rifle line erupted in claps of fire. More riders fell like broken birds.

"They're desperate," Marcus muttered.

A whistle shrieked. "Over the top!"

Marcus climbed the ladder, rifle slick in his hands. The no-man's-land stretched before him—a wasteland of craters and wire. Behind enemy lines, the Eagle of the Twenty-Third Legion hung from a wooden post, tattered and defiant.

His centurion turned to him, eyes burning. "We take back our standard tonight."

Marcus nodded, though his chest tightened. Two years of this war had reduced Rome's legions to shadows. The empire needed symbols.

The gap between what they were and what they needed to be had never felt wider.

They charged into the darkness.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Cup

Everyday, the same old shit. Nothing ever happens in this ragged town. Well, at least I have *The Jitterbug.* When life gets you down, grab some caffeine, gets ya up. That's what my Ol' man used to say.

The door groans as I push through. Makes my muscle fibers spark to sudden life—something my wife seems to care little about. *Bitch.* Always saying I deserve this place.

"The usual, darlin'."

"You got it, hun."

*Sigh.* Yeah, this is my life. Boring job, boring wife. Sex? That's a joke. My greatest excitement is this little sip of paradise every morning.

The coffee touches my lips. Bitter. Perfect.

Then—*P-TAFF*

The cup explodes. Hot liquid everywhere. Behind the counter, Martha screams.

I turn. A kid with a gun, shaking, eyes wild.

Blood blooms across my shirt.

I smile.

"Heh... now that's what I call a shot."

*Fin.*
