text:
# The Mask

Oh God, why? Why didn't anyone tell me? All they said was that I'd need the mask when I sleep. Tonight, I found out why. Tonight an image is burned into my mind that neither therapy nor liquor can erase. An image so horrific that I cannot even begin to describe. Something like that... no one should be subject to that sort of thing.

It was a very humid summer night. Even with the windows open and the fans running at full, I was sweating like crazy. I moved downstairs into the living room where it was supposedly cooler than my upstairs room. I finally couldn't take it anymore—whatever material the mask was made of became itchy and rough with the addition of my sweat. I took it off and tossed it across the room in annoyance.

It was about a half hour later when I heard it: movement down the hall, steady footsteps. I made the mistake of looking up over the back of the couch. There, walking slowly toward the kitchen, was my grandmother, sleepwalking as usual.

She'd slept in the nude.

I scrambled for the mask, now understanding its true purpose. Some horrors require protection.

text:
# The Edge of Everything

You don't really notice when it happens.

At first, there's just a niggling sensation when you laugh—a whisper that tells you the joke isn't actually funny. You ignore it. Everyone ignores it. Then come the screams in the night, distant and distorted, like voices calling through water. You tell yourself they're dreams, nothing more.

By the time your mind catches on, realizes that something is fundamentally *wrong*, it's often too late. Most people never reach that point of recognition. We're too tangled in indulgence, too lost in the pleasant fog of our own dreams. Reality becomes optional, then forgotten entirely.

Dreams are natural, aren't they? That's what I told myself.

Now I'm standing here, on what might be the literal edge of the world. The cliff drops away beneath my feet into mist and nothingness. Behind me, the path I took has already started to fade from memory—little stars shooting through my mind, pockets of my life joining oblivion.

That's where we all end up anyway. Some people just lose parts of themselves faster than others.

The wind brushes my cheek, not gentle but menacing. Pebbles tumble from the cliff's edge, weak and pathetic as they disappear into the void. Under different circumstances, I might find this beautiful—to be so close to the Earth yet so near to the sky. Awe-inspiring, perhaps.

But I'm not here for beauty.

I'm here because this is utterly bittersweet. My last thought, my last view, will be the effects of nature. I have taken the course of nature into my own hands, yet this land hasn't. Water doesn't force its way through mountains—it finds a peaceful course, so gentle it might never feel resistance at all.

Strange that we cannot do the same.

As beings, we've stripped ourselves from nature so completely that only our final moments reunite us with it. Only at the edge, where everything spirals out of reach, do we remember what we were always meant to be.

Just part of the earth.

Just falling stars.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Final Stand

My fellow cells.

The sight of our fellow cells dying is one that is familiar to us. In mere minutes, millions of us perish to the harsh nature of our host's anatomy, only to be replaced with identical copies of our very being. It's a monotonous existence, but one that is vital in keeping humankind in good health.

An existence that, since the dawn of humanity, has inhabited the blood of man, fighting illness and disease with valor and fortitude! An existence where, despite the fact we cannot hear the appreciative sounds of the humans, we know that—be they on land, on sea, or in the air—they sing ballads and poems of our pivotal role as microscopic soldiers on the most dangerous battlefield of all: the human body.

But now, my fellow comrades, it is songs of sorrow the humans sing. With great despair, I must bring down a harsh truth upon you.

As you know, a deadly virus has manifested itself inside our host. It has spread across our host's body and caused various major organs to begin the process of completely shutting down. At this very moment, our host is as close to a living shell as anyone could be. And the virus shows no sign of stopping.

As of now, should we perish, there is no coming back.

But do not have fear. Do not fear the virus or the unknown that awaits us when our host passes from the land of the living to the land of the fallen. Instead, be proud. Be proud of the fights we have fought. Be proud of all the times an infection has entered our realm, only to be engulfed and destroyed.

Now is not the time for us to panic, but the time for the virus to panic. For when it reaches us, it will quake in terror at the sight of fearless monocytes, lymphocytes, neutrophils, and basophils, all ready to fight to the end.

So join me, brothers. The time for our final battle begins now!

# Temporal Paradox

The desperate hack worked—HMS *Borrowed Glory*, formerly USS *Reagan*, shimmered into 1776.

British officers stared at impossible technology while manning American ships. The temporal contamination spread like wildfire: three escort vessels went mad, crews gibbering about "loops within loops."

In London, King George III touched the carrier's quantum-corrupted log. Understanding flooded him—every possible future, every timeline collapsed.

"I abdicate," he whispered, ordering the Stars and Stripes raised over Parliament. "We surrender to... ourselves?"

The message reached General Washington: *Britain yields before first shot fired.*

Forty-eight hours later, the carrier vanished, reappearing over the Falklands, 2025. Below, the Argentine fleet burned—not from British weapons, but from fusion cannons bearing swastikas.

"Ey, target destroyed, yeah?" crackled a German voice, pure Brooklyn.

The captain realized with horror: they'd created a timeline where Nazis won... by relocating to New York in 1943.

The carrier flickered again.

Somewhere, *somewhen*, reality wept.

text:
# My Love

I was alone. I wandered the world just searching for something I didn't know about. I knew there was something missing. To my surprise, it was not something, rather someone.

When we first met, I was dumbfounded by your beauty, and when I finally came to my senses, you were nowhere to be found. I had missed my chance, but now I knew what I lacked. With my soul on fire, I followed my heart, hoping, pleading it would bring me to you again.

When a day passed, I was not deterred. As a month passed, doubt was starting to blossom. When the year came to an end, my supernova had turned to but a candle flame flickering in the wind.

When the last ember was about to be extinguished, I saw you. You were just as breathtaking as you were two years ago, if not even more so. I ran to you and grabbed your hand. As you turned in shock, I could see your eyes transform from fear to happiness. I think you felt the same way I did. I know we were the parts to fill the void in each other's heart.

It only saddens me that we could only share that feeling for an instant before the incident.

But don't worry—we will be with each other soon. As I leave this note at your stone marker, know that I'll come see you after I rid this now bleak planet of the one who took you from me, before we could share its previous beauty with one another.

Forever yours,

**The End**

text:
# The Trial of the Librarian

Lucas Smithson sat at his desk, closing up after a usual night at Doyle Library. "Ahh the life of a librarian, goodnight all!" He said to the empty library before locking the door and stepping outside, or what he thought was outside.

Instead, Lucas found himself in a courtroom of sorts. The jury box filled to the brim with—*could it be?*—**characters from books!** It's almost as if he had stepped into a fantasy!

On one side sat Ichabod Crane, his legs bowed up close due to them being so long. The March Hare and Mad Hatter, as always having a mad tea party, even in court! Below them, Jacob Marley's ghost, chains hanging off the side of the box. Sitting next to him, a curmudgeonly Ebenezer Scrooge! And seated not far from them was the mysterious Captain Nemo!

Lucas had never seen so many of his favorite characters in one room, or in physical form for that matter. Which made him wonder...why was he here?

**"ORDER!"** bellowed a rough but eloquent voice. Instead of a customary gavel, Lucas heard a horrid scratching as if something was being dragged through the wood of the podium. He looked toward the voice and the sound, only to see the fictional Pirate Captain James Hook in the judge's chair.

**"The court will come to order! By my hook, YE SCURVY DOGS WILL COME TO ORDER!"**

The noise quieted somewhat drastically. Hook began again. **"THE COURT FINDS ONE LUCAS SMITHSON CHARGED WITH AN ATTEMPT OF MEDDLING IN THE LIVES OF COUNTLESS LITERARY BEINGS. DO YE PLEAD GUILTY OR NOT GUILTY? And mind you, boy... You have a whole library of witnesses against ye... CHOOSE!"**

"Not guilty?!" Lucas said impulsively. He wasn't sure how he had "meddled" in the lives of characters in books, but he was going to find out sooner or later.

Hook plunged his hook into the wood of the judge's podium. **"YE SCURVY... hmm... Very well, CALL THE FIRST WITNESS!"**

Lucas swallowed hard, wondering what accusations would emerge from the pages he'd lovingly shelved for years.

text:
# The Last Decision

I exhaled with relief and leaned back in my chair. I could see the dots on the screen blinking and showing their paths. I looked at my colleagues, none of whom seemed relieved but stood as frozen, their faces lit up by the monitors and their eyes locked on to the new dot.

The room was cold and silent, even with all the people currently in it. The white painted concrete walls were stark and the large metal door was closed. Jones, who had the other key, asked, "Do you understand what we have done?"

"You have to understand Jones," I said with confidence in my voice.

"There is nothing to understand. This is it, this is the end," Jones said with a voice that sounded like he was not angry... but sad.

"But Jones, it was us or them!" I said, unsure of my words.

He looked me straight in the eyes and said, "No, this is mutual."

The red words kept flashing over the dots: "ICBM, ETA 2 minutes."

My relief evaporated. I finally understood. Our retaliation wouldn't save us—it would only ensure that nobody survived. The two keys had sealed everyone's fate, not just theirs.

Jones turned away, his shoulders slumped in defeat.

text:
# The Eternal Burden

I have lived long. Too long.

The curse they called a gift weighs heavier with each passing century. I am wading in waves of an endless sea, glimpsing land only to be swept away again by the merciless tide.

Behind my shadow, I sense him—Death perhaps, or God—laughing triumphantly as I lose everything again and again.

Tonight, I hold Eleanor's hand. My fifth wife. Or is it my sixth? The faces blur together like watercolors in rain.

"Don't leave me," I whisper, though I know she must.

I fall asleep beside her, praying for an end that never comes.

**BEEP BEEP BEEP**

The alarm shatters my hopeful oblivion. My hand still rests in hers, but her warmth has fled. The familiar coldness seeps into my palm.

I lean down, pressing one last kiss to her cooling lips.

"Goodbye, my love."

I rise and dress, preparing for another day, another decade, another lifetime of wandering this earth alone.

The sea awaits.

# The Green Button

"Twice. FUCKING TWICE!" I screamed at my bewildered partner.

"Sir! Stop shouting!"

"NO!! I've come up with brilliant plans to break in here TWICE! I walk through the door, get a fucking visitor's badge, and the password is on display—FELLATIO??"

I thought carefully. Something for good. Something to advance our art, inventions, culture, minds...

"Well, third time's the try, right?"

I pushed the large green button.

The next two hundred years on Earth were peaceful and artistic. Productivity flourished globally. Life became easier—still struggles remained, but manageable ones.

I had made marijuana legal.

Wars over resources diminished. Creativity exploded. Medical breakthroughs accelerated. People smiled more. Connected more.

My partner stared. "That's what you chose?"

I nodded. "Sometimes the simplest solutions are the ones hidden in plain sight."

We walked out, visitor's badges still clipped to our shirts.

Nobody even noticed.

text:
# The Blank Canvas

The examination room had been silent for a very long time, punctuated only by the occasional squeak of the chair John Smith sat in. John didn't mind the silence; in fact, he preferred it to interacting with people. People. Was that why he was here? Something to do with people. He stared amiably at the wall. White with flecks of... something.

After five or ten or twenty minutes of this, a woman entered, clutching a folder of papers. She nodded to him and sat down on the other side of the desk.

"That's nice," John thought. "Is that there just for me?"

Dr. Mati, if her name tag was to be trusted, smiled at John. "How are you today, Mr. Smith?"

"Fine," John replied, intently focusing on the patch of air six inches above her left shoulder.

"I'm sure you're anxious for the results, so I'll just get to it. I must say, Mr. Smith, I have never seen a case like this before. After all these tests, we were forced to conclude that the diagnosis was negative. I'm so sorry." Dr. Mati reached across the table and held John's hand.

"Negative. Isn't that a good thing?"

"Not when they're personality tests, John. Our very best experts couldn't find a single personality trait anywhere in that head of yours. fMRI scans, psychotherapy, questionnaires—all turned up nothing of value. Even online personality tests couldn't come up with an answer. Is this making any sense, John?"

Upon hearing his name, John turned and smiled placidly at Dr. Mati. Her revelation had affected him in the same way a stock market crash affects a bean stalk.

"You can still live a normal life. We're developing a pioneering new medication that could—"

"So I am free to go?"

"I... We might be able to really help you, John. Don't you want that?"

"Have a great day."

With that, John walked out of the facility and into the world, leaving a bewildered Dr. Mati behind.

Outside, the sun felt neither warm nor cold. John walked home, thinking about nothing in particular, completely content in his empty existence.

text:
# The Last Reply

My hands trembled as I stared at the screen. After two years of silence, of empty streets and hollow buildings, this was my greeting from humanity.

I laughed—a broken, desperate sound that echoed through the abandoned Best Buy. Then I cried.

The message was two years old, sent just before everyone vanished. Some angry teenager's thoughtless cruelty, preserved like a fossil.

But the streetlights were still coming on. Something was reactivating the infrastructure.

I typed a reply, knowing no one would read it: "I forgive you. I hope you're alive somewhere."

Then I noticed the timestamp. The message had been *read* yesterday.

My breath caught. I refreshed the page.

Three dots appeared. Someone was typing.

The response came: "Holy shit. You're real? I'm in Minneapolis. The grid is automatic—solar and batteries. I thought I was alone."

I typed back with shaking fingers, tears streaming down my face.

We weren't alone anymore.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Waltz

Sergei's accordion wheezed one final melancholy note before the shovel connected with a sickening thud.

Carl stood over the crumpled musician, chest heaving, knuckles white around the wooden handle. The accordion lay beside Sergei, dented but somehow still intact, a small wheeze escaping its bellows like a dying breath.

"Dammit," Carl whispered, staring at his bloodied hands. Vladimir's body lay forgotten in the corner, wrapped in plastic sheeting that reflected the dim warehouse lights.

He'd meant to just scare Sergei. To get him to shut up and help. But the old man had kept playing, kept talking about honor and duty and homeland, and something inside Carl had snapped.

Now there were two bodies.

Carl picked up the accordion with trembling fingers. A photograph fell from inside—Sergei as a young man, holding the same instrument, surrounded by smiling family members who looked remarkably like Vladimir.

The pieces clicked together too late.

"Oh God," Carl breathed, understanding flooding through him. "You weren't just playing for him. You *were* him."

The accordion wheezed again, almost like laughter.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Unmarked Staff

The doctors' staves gleamed in the fluorescent hospital lights as they passed my room. Some were polished smooth, worn from years of successful interventions. Others were freshly hewn, eager and unblemished. Each notch carved into the wood represented a life saved, a triumph documented in flesh and grain.

But no notches for failure. No marks for the ones they didn't take.

I watched another doctor approach—young, her staff still pale and pristine with only three careful notches. She reached for my chart, eyes scanning the words: *unknown etiology, complex presentation, uncertain prognosis*. Her hand trembled. Through my haze of nausea, I saw the calculation in her eyes. One failure, one mark of shame carved deep and stained black, could eclipse a dozen successes.

She walked away.

"Please," I whispered, but the word dissolved into another wave of vomiting.

The system made perfect sense, they said during implementation. Accountability. Excellence. Why shouldn't doctors' futures depend on their success, just as patients' lives depended on their skill?

But they forgot something crucial: medicine isn't mathematics. Bodies are mysteries that don't always yield to logic. Some cases are puzzles with missing pieces, conditions that hide in shadows between diagnoses.

I am one of those shadows.

Another doctor paused—older, his staff dark with age and covered in notches like hash marks tallying victories. Surely he could afford one failure? But no. I watched him glance at the legendary staff, touching it almost reverently, and move along. His reputation was built on never marking that black line of failure.

Through the window, I could see families in the waiting room, pointing proudly at their doctors' staves. *Look how many he's saved! Not a single failure mark!*

They didn't see the ghosts in the forgotten corners.

They didn't see me, fading, as the minutes slipped away and the doctors walked past, protecting their perfect, unmarked wood.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Mortality Error

"That's it?" Commander Zyloth's antennae twitched with disbelief.

"Yes sir, only 7 billion," his assistant confirmed.

"Billion, with a B? You're sure?"

"Positive."

"Why haven't they reproduced? Are they having trouble finding each other? How many universes have they expanded to?"

"They haven't actually gotten around to finding other universes yet. In fact, they haven't even left their planet. They have been reproducing, though they're dying as well."

"They're *what*?"

"Dying, sir. Ceasing to exist."

"What! Why would they do that?"

"We're not really sure. They just seem to do it at random."

Zyloth's face paled. "We have to fix this. Have we seen this before?"

"Never. I'll consult the other developers."

"Do that. Meanwhile, send coordinates. I want to see these things myself."

His assistant hesitated. "Sir... they call themselves 'humans.'"
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# First Contact

**Translated from the language of the Shoy**

"What the hell?!?"

"I know sir. I was just surprised as you are."

"But.... but, why!"

"We have no idea sir. They just showed up, in some weird looking rocket ship, out of the blue."

"Don't they realize how pointless and inefficient interstellar travel is? They might as well be throwing all of their metals and plastics into their oceans!"

"We realize that, sir. We've extrapolated, based on the observations that both our scientists and you have made, that they are probably, as an entire race, idiot savants, great at engineering and physics but completely dysfunctional in terms of practicality."

"That would make sense, based on their actions thus far. What are we going to do about them, though?! Have they attempted any forms of communication?"

"No sir, none that we've noticed. We might have to power up some of our old forms of communication though, like radio and *[not translatable]*, in case they haven't invented *[not translatable]* yet."

"Yeah, go ahead and do that. Have we determined the military capabilities of the vessel yet?"

"We have, sir. It seems to be simply an exploratory vessel, with little or no capability for warfare."

At that, *[name not translatable]* visibly relaxed. It sent *[name not translatable]* out of the *[imperfect translation: "room"]* with a curt "thank you" and assumed a thoughtful expression on its *[imperfect translation: "face"]*.

Its brain quickly started spinning with thoughts of the Shoy society's collective fear and outrage, which was sure to come in the following days, brought by the arrival of the strange-thinking aliens. These creatures had already changed things drastically on the world of the Shoy, simply by showing up, and hopefully, in the end, for the better.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Roommate Agreement

"HEEEEEY Gal, wat's going ooon?" A little tiny voice pierces my ears. I jump, shaking a little.

"Sorry, still getting used to the new 'talking' thing..." I explain. "How'd you learn English, anyways?"

"Remember all those evenings you fell asleep with the television on?"

"Oh.... yeah.... How many flies did you catch today?"

"Four flies. Two at the back door, one in your bedroom, and another in your laundry room."

"That covers your rent for the month. Is your friend Dave still hanging out in the shower?"

"Mhm, he's obsessed with the popcorn ceiling in there."

"Warn him to get out. I'll be taking a shower before bed, and if I find him in there, he's goin' down the drain."

I set my stuff down. "I'll be out at dinner with some friends. See yah, Paul."

"See you around, Krissi. Enjoy your evening."

I shudder and leave, taking my car to Olive Garden. Living with talking spiders isn't normal, but at least they handle pest control. My life is going to be awesome.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Drift

Rain slaps down through the dark of night, each drop ringing through the cool air. On a wet street, smoke passes, a darkly coloured puddle on the floor gliding by it.

The smoke speaks. "How did we get to be where we are right now?"

The puddle pauses for a second, but the reply he stammers is incomprehensible.

"Not sure I have an answer either, bud," the smoke whispers back.

Yet, the smoke knows—if only subconsciously—exactly how he ended up in his position. Monotony, repetition, the dull drone of society's rules. It was the very essence of life that made him want to run away from it. So, he got with some friends, inhaled deep, and floated off. His head wanders in the clouds.

Beside him, the puddle's glad not to have to think about all of that. He, too, got sick of life. He went to a bar, downed a few drinks, and now he's on some street, talking to a stranger he's bound to forget. None of that's on his mind, and he doesn't really want it to be.

The two go on without a word, the streetlights dimly guiding them on a well-worn path. Neither of them knows the destination, but both of them know it's better than where they came from.

The rain hits the duo softly, its soothing sound filling in for their silence.

Perhaps the smoke and the puddle aren't so different after all.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# But You Knew That

The letter trembled in my hands as I read it for the hundredth time. Your words, always so careful, so measured.

You were right—I knew everything. I knew you'd be early that day at the market. I knew about your meeting. I interrupted it deliberately, warning you about those peaches with practiced spontaneity.

The story about my mother's car? True, actually. One of the few truths I offered you.

I pulled the trigger when I told them where you'd be. I tightened the noose by gaining your trust first. The final strike came when I testified against you, knowing you'd never defend yourself, never expose what you'd been protecting.

But here's what *you* didn't know: I loved you too. Every manufactured moment became real. Every calculated word turned genuine.

They gave me immunity. You got fifteen years.

I visit every month, though you refuse to see me. I leave your letters in my pocket, against my heart, where you said yours would always be.

You forgive me.

But I'll never forgive myself.

You knew that too, didn't you?
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Exit

I lay in my bed. Staring. Perceiving. Shivering.

Routine and compulsion gave me this incessant need to quantify everything within my sensory understanding. The way the room looked. The effect of the street lights casting a dusty pallor across the thin tight carpeting. A small fan provided a gentle ambiance in the maddening silence.

Around me sat the last remaining remnants of a life my unsettled soul wanted absolution from. Books, pictures, wires, empty bottles. The monster within me wanted its animalistic glory. This life had left me psychologically unsound, surrounded by a world I scarcely recognized.

What had been a theory, became an action. But not one done in clarity.

I wasn't just running. I wasn't just purging a name. I was purging a life. The act I was about to commit was tantamount to murder. The life I lived was over, torn from its security like the lock that barred the door to the room I had accepted on the offer of a friend.

As I opened our screen door I looked through the cold, midnight rain, and felt the lightning and thunder fill the air. This was it.

I removed my phone from my pocket and glanced at the time. I pilfered my wallet and removed any cash and a few tattered notes, given to me by my father, or those I considered closest at one point. I suppose this was my saying I intended for my world to forget what I never could.

One last glance at the wide glowing screen on my phone where the digits now turned from 2:13 to 2:14. I sent one last message. One last two-word communication to relay to those who have loved me and been with me through the most intense storms I've experienced.

I apologized.

At this point every move I made was automated. I knew what would happen next. My phone split on the pavement. It was oddly more satisfying than I had envisioned.

And like that it was over.

I began my sprint through the rain. To anywhere. For every reason, and none whatsoever.

This was over.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The True Enemy

The transformation complete, I stride through my pyramid's corridors with renewed purpose. My enhanced muscles ripple beneath crimson skin, and dark energy crackles at my fingertips. Those ThunderCats will finally understand what it means to invade *my* world.

For months, I watched them slaughter my people—the peaceful inhabitants of Third Earth who never raised a weapon until forced. They call us "mutants" with disgust, as if we're the monsters. But I remember when Lion-O's soldiers arrived, their gleaming technology and self-righteous attitudes treating this planet like it was theirs to conquer.

The village massacre haunts me still. Panthro's mace crushed skulls while the others cheered. They even brought that child, WilyKit, teaching her to hunt us like animals. Our young ones, stolen and devoured—I've seen the remains.

I emerge from my pyramid as Mumm-Ra the Ever-Living, my voice booming across the wasteland. "ThunderCats! Your reign of terror ends today!"

The ground shakes as their tank approaches, that cursed "ThunderTank" they use to run down fleeing families. Lion-O stands atop it, sword raised, that insufferable nobility on his face.

"Mumm-Ra!" he shouts. "Stop hiding behind your evil magic and face justice!"

*Justice?* I almost laugh. They invade, they kill, they steal—and somehow *I'm* the villain?

"You want justice?" I roar, unleashing crimson lightning. "Then face the wrath of those you've oppressed!"

The battle begins, but doubt creeps in. Lion-O's confused expression seems genuine. Tygra shouts something about "protecting Third Earth's innocent."

What if... what if I've been deceived? What if someone *wanted* us to destroy each other?

The Ancient Spirits' laughter echoes in my mind, and suddenly, I understand everything.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Walk

The dew-soaked grass beneath my feet felt strangely weightless, I realized now. Each blade passed through me rather than bending under my steps. The pink and orange sunrise that had seemed so vibrant moments ago suddenly felt like a veil between worlds.

I stood there, frozen, watching the paramedics compress my chest with rhythmic desperation. My body—*that* body—looked small and broken against the crushed dashboard. Blood matted the hair on the left side of my head.

"Clear!" one paramedic shouted, placing the defibrillator paddles.

My body jerked violently. Nothing. They tried again.

I looked down at my hands. Solid, but translucent in the growing light. The pieces fell together like shattered glass reassembling. The phone call last night. The bottle of whiskey. Sarah leaving. The decision to drive anyway, tears blurring the road as much as the alcohol.

"Come on, buddy. Stay with us!" 

I wanted to tell them it was okay. That maybe this was how it was supposed to end. But then I thought of Chip.

*Chip.*

He wasn't on the couch at all, was he? He'd been in the truck. I spun around, scanning desperately, and saw him—my chocolate lab lying motionless in the grass twenty feet away, thrown clear from the crash. His chest wasn't moving.

"No, no, no..." I ran to him, tried to touch him, but my hands passed through his fur.

Behind me, the paramedics were loading my body onto a stretcher. Still working. Still fighting.

I knelt beside Chip, this ghost of myself mourning what could never be undone. The sun continued its ascent, indifferent to our tragedy. The canola fields swayed gently in the morning breeze.

And I understood: this walk wasn't about going forward.

It was about finally standing still, watching everything I'd destroyed with a single choice vanish into the dawn.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Day Everything Changed

Allie lived in a big apartment with her big Uncle Jack. Uncle Jack was a fun uncle! He didn't make Allie go to school, and he let her play games all day when it wasn't playtime. When it was playtime, Allie had to play with Uncle Jack. Uncle Jack told her: "I love you Allie, and girls who love their Uncles always play with them!" So Allie always played with him.

But she didn't like to play. Sometimes she would scratch her knee or get a bruise. Sometimes roughhousing wasn't fun for Allie! Uncle Jack played rough, but he would laugh and give her a band-aid and she would feel all better. He let her watch TV all day if she got a bruise.

Allie told her Uncle Jack one day that she didn't want to play, and he got mad. He told her that good girls play with their Uncles. But Allie didn't want to play at all! She called her Aunt Jamie on the phone and told her that she wants to play with Aunt Jamie instead because she plays softer.

Boy, Aunt Jamie seemed mad! When Uncle Jack found out about the phone call, he got mad, too! He didn't want Allie to play with anyone else! He wouldn't have anyone to play with anymore. He made Allie look at the wall and he sung her a lullaby. She went to sleep right away!

But Uncle Jack stayed up and played cops and robbers long into the night. He got too tired and decided to quit when the cops were going to win! They called him a cheater. It was a messy game! Jack didn't know how to clean up, so the cops had to clean up! Winners clean up.

Everyone in Anytown knew all about the game! It was a famous cops and robbers game. The best one in a long time, but Allie slept right through it!

Aunt Jamie cried when she heard about the game. But she doesn't play with Uncle Jack anymore. She plays with Mom and dad now. They don't play rough. She was just happy to see them!
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Connection

Trapped in that hellhole, every day felt exactly the same. I spent months wondering if I would ever see the light of day again, or breathe fresh air once more. What I did wouldn't have been a crime a few years ago, but it didn't matter. These thoughts scratched my mind endlessly, I could almost hear them grinding my consciousness into dust.

The thoughts started banging louder, and then suddenly a brick came loose in the wall directly in front of me. Through the hole peered two beautiful eyes inquisitively.

"I just wanted to know for sure that I wasn't alone in here," a soft voice spoke to me.

"Does it make it any better to know that I'll be dying soon too?"

"No, I guess not."

I laid down in front of the hole and stared in, taking in every detail of the beautiful eyes that stared back at me.

"Well, I'm glad I got to see such beauty one last time before I go."

We held hands through the hole until they came for me, and pulled me away to face my fate. But in those final moments, I wasn't alone. That connection—brief, fragile, human—was enough.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Price of Witness

I slammed the door shut, hands trembling as I fumbled with the deadbolt. My heart hammered against my ribs like a caged animal desperate to escape.

*They heard me. They heard me.*

Heavy footsteps approached. I backed away from the door, watching the handle as if it were a coiled snake.

BANG. BANG. BANG.

The same cruel rhythm that had summoned my neighbor to his death now called for me.

"Citizen, open this door immediately!"

My mind raced. What thought crime had condemned Citizen 732? A joke overheard by the wrong ears? A forgotten pledge of allegiance? Or perhaps nothing at all—just a quota that needed filling.

The knocking stopped. Silence pressed against my eardrums.

I crept to the keyhole, peering through with one eye. Empty hallway. My neighbor's blood painted dark rivers across the pale tiles. Had they left?

The door exploded inward with a deafening crash. Splinters rained down as armored figures stormed in, weapons raised. I stumbled backward, hands up in surrender.

"Please! I didn't see anything! I'm loyal! I'm—"

"Citizen 849," the lead soldier interrupted, his voice flat and mechanical. "You have witnessed an act of state justice. Report to Integration Center Seven tomorrow at 0600 hours for memory compliance processing."

They turned and left as quickly as they'd entered, leaving me standing in my ruined doorway.

I was alive. But as I stared at my neighbor's body in the hallway, I wondered if that was really mercy at all.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Button

So.... yeah. I'm pushing it.

It's kind of a lame button. Not very satisfying to press. Buttons are never as satisfying to press as they seem like they'll be.

Even less satisfying? It doesn't look like anything's even happening.

Oh, hold on. I feel something. Not a sensation I'm familiar with, but if I had to guess, I'd say my clothes are filling. With—

Oh dear Lord no.

As my skin turns red and blotchy, I feel my throat begin to tighten. I scramble for my epinephrine, but I only jam my swollen fingers into a pocket full of the offending substance.

Breathing is starting to get difficult.

I look around the room. It looks like a stereotypical computer lab. Dark. Monitors everywhere. Flashing lights. Nothing useful in sight.

The door. My only hope.

I start to move toward it when I feel my mouth begin to fill the same way my clothes did. Not good. My throat closes.

In my panic, I race for the door. My vision is beginning to blur and I trip over a rolling chair. I scramble to get back up, then trip again.

My body is already shutting down. My eyes swell completely shut.

Well. This is it.

I don't know why a world free of people with severe allergic reactions is a Utopia. Whatever floats your boat, I guess.

But was it really necessary to fill my body with peanuts?
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Substitute

The fluorescent lights of P.S. 118 hummed with bureaucratic indifference as Sterling Archer straightened his tactleneck—black, obviously—and examined his forged teaching credentials. 

"Mr. Archer?" Principal Hendricks peered over her glasses. "Your résumé is... impressive. Seven years teaching 'conflict resolution' in Eastern Europe?"

"Eight, actually. Very hands-on curriculum." He flashed his most disarming smile.

Twenty minutes later, he stood before thirty judgmental third-graders.

"Alright, listen up." Archer leaned against the desk. "I'm your substitute for Mrs. Patterson, who's apparently having a baby or whatever. Ground rules: I don't do feelings, participation trophies, or any crap involving glitter."

A hand shot up. "Mr. Archer, are you supposed to say 'crap'?"

"Probably not, but—" His phone buzzed. A text from Lana: *WHERE ARE YOU?!*

"Pop quiz!" Archer announced, projecting a confidence he absolutely did not feel. "What's the capital of... danger?"

"That doesn't make sense," a girl with pigtails observed.

Another buzz: *PAM TRACKED YOUR PHONE. GET OUT OF THERE.*

"Okay, new plan. Who wants to learn about... escape routes? I mean, fire safety!"

The classroom door exploded inward. Pam stood there, breathing heavily, holding what appeared to be a cafeteria tray as a weapon.

"Sterling Archer, you get your ass—"

"LANGUAGE!" thirty children shrieked simultaneously.

In the chaos, Archer dove through the window, tucking and rolling across the playground as Lana's car screeched up.

"Worth it!" he shouted, sprinting toward freedom.

Behind him, Principal Hendricks was already dialing HR.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Godly Man

I've always been a Godly man. Before that I was a Godly child.

"Eat your peas, Young Lout," my mother would say, "or you'll be out of heaven before you're seven."

I always ate my peas. *Thank you Jesus for these peas*, I would say. I'd say it inwardly too. "Thank you Jesus for dying on the cross so that I could enjoy these delicious peas."

My mother nodded sagaciously in the background. A grizzled crown of haphazard curls shaking their fists at the haphazard injustice of it. Tears would well in her eyes in righteous wonder. *Thank you Jesus for giving me such a splendiferous boy.* And then: *Your momma raised a fine boy too.*

She passed some years subsequent.

I was a good boy then and I was a good boy later. "Now you're with Jesus, Momma Mae," said my sister meaningfully. She opened her mouth and inhaled. She looked at me with her eyes in a cross. She looked like a bloated blowfish.

"Momma Mae is with Jesus," I intoned.

She deflated in a sudden whoosh and I knew I had just evaded something unfathomable.

Then they lowered my mother into the ground and I smiled. *Momma Mae is with Jesus and soon I'll be too.*

I've always been a Godly man. Do unto others what you want done to thyself.

There have been some instances of inconsistencies. Especially with women this tenet has been a hoot. Women are strange. They do not want me to rub my genitals all over them. My sister made me repeat it ten times in a row when I was younger: *I Should Not Rub My Genitals On Girls Before Being Asked. If Asked, Deny, Deny, Deny.*

There are many things which I do not understand about how the world works. No elbows near the table. If they come near the table they will explode. Don't eat with your mouth open. I always do.

Love thy neighbor. I cut their tree down because it was shading my lot. From the way she screamed you'd have thought she was shot.

Yes, there are compromises to be made here and there.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Whiteboard

Marcus stared at the blank whiteboard mounted beside his desk, remembering the day Sarah had given it to him. "For your ideas," she'd said, knowing how he'd pace their Chicago apartment, muttering fragments of stories that evaporated like morning fog.

Three years of serious writing now. Three years of filling that board with character names, plot threads, contradictory timelines that needed untangling. The surface was never truly clean—ghostly remnants of erased words always lingered, phantoms of abandoned narratives.

Tonight, November first. NaNoWriMo began at midnight.

Last year he'd failed spectacularly, sitting frozen before TextEdit's merciless cursor with no plan, no direction. This year would be different. The whiteboard displayed his roadmap: a thriller set in his neighborhood, characters borrowed from the faces he passed daily at the coffee shop.

Marcus's fingers hovered over the keyboard. That typing test had clocked him at 103 words per minute, but speed meant nothing. Writing wasn't about velocity—it was about the pauses, the thinking, the pregnant silences between sentences where stories actually lived.

He typed the first sentence, deleted it. Typed another.

Outside, the city hummed its November song. Inside, the whiteboard watched patiently, already holding tomorrow's ideas, next week's solutions to problems he hadn't yet encountered.

The cursor blinked.

Marcus smiled and began again.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Good Morning Sunshine

I read your note three times, smiling wider each time. The sleep talking entries killed me—especially the pony one. What crisis was dream-me navigating?

You're already gone for your shift when I wake, but the coffee's ready and there's a paw print on the counter from Princess's last visit. I miss that dog almost as much as I miss you on your 48-hour rotations.

The Dunkin' interview went fine. They hired me on the spot, which means we can finally catch up on rent. I know you hate picking up doubles, but I see how tired you are. Your interview skills must be rubbing off on me.

I'm adding to your journal tonight: "The ferrets are unionizing." "No, YOU'RE a continental breakfast." And my personal favorite from 3 AM: "Tell her the lighthouse knows."

The lighthouse knows what, babe? What does it know?

I dozed off on the couch waiting for you, and apparently I said your name twice. You texted me: "You called for me in your sleep ❤️ I'm almost home."

That's when I realized—we're building something real here. In these small moments, these notes, these overheard dreams. Not New York exciting, but ours.

The door opens. You smell like smoke and Irish Spring.

"Good morning sunshine," I whisper.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# Run or Die

The knife glints in the fluorescent garage light. My coworker—*Jerry from accounting*—freezes mid-slash, one of my tires already hissing air.

"Jerry?" My voice cracks. "You're two levels above me!"

"Bonus upgrades stack," he says, straightening. His eyes have that glazed look I've seen in too many meetings lately. "Plus, traitor bounty pays double."

I drop my suitcases and bolt.

Jerry's footsteps echo behind me. The stairwell door slams open as I hit the street level, adrenaline overriding my out-of-shape middle-management body. A taxi idles at the corner—miracle of miracles.

"Airport! Heathrow!" I gasp, diving inside.

"Domestic or international?"

"*International!*"

Through the rear window, Jerry bursts onto the sidewalk, but we're already moving. He raises his phone, probably alerting others. My flight leaves in ninety minutes. I'll never make it through security with luggage anyway.

At the airport, I buy essentials at overpriced shops with trembling hands: phone charger, toothbrush, one change of clothes. Everything else—photos, laptop, that signed first edition—gone. 

The departures board mocks me. My flight: ON TIME.

I keep my head down at the gate, baseball cap pulled low. Every announcement makes me flinch. Every approaching passenger could be another Jerry, another desperate employee willing to kill for a better cubicle.

Finally, mercifully, we board. I collapse into 37B, middle seat, cramped and perfect.

As we taxi, I see my reflection in the window: haunted, hunted, alive.

The wheels leave American soil.

I exhale for what feels like the first time in hours.

London doesn't know it yet, but it's getting a new resident. One who'll never, *ever* complain about middle management again.

If I survive long enough to find another job.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Tornado

The trick is to make a tornado. If the turkey and the side of mashed potatoes are mixed and disheveled in a spiraled mess on the plate, people make the assumption that the food has been partially eaten. Most people don't pay enough attention to know the difference.

Pick up a fork and relocate some peas. Ask how the cousins are doing in school. Distraction is key. Butter some bread and break it up into little pieces. "Wow, this stuffing is really delicious, gets better every year."

Most people are so wrapped up in their own meal that no one is the wiser. I haven't eaten a thing at Christmas dinner in five years.

Everyone finishes. Bellies bulge. Buttons tighten. Buckles are furtively loosened under the tablecloth. Everyone has his or her own little secrets to get through it. They don't realize that I'm a master at secrets. I'm the James Fucking Bond of holiday diners.

Not only do I hide my secrets, but I know all of theirs as well.

Mom sneaks extra vodka in her drink to help ignore Dad's innocent flirtations with Aunt Clare. Aunt Clare eats it up. Hotel keys burn in her purse to meet up with him later. Uncle Lou could not be more oblivious—a simple man with a rich background.

My brother watches too. He's only eight, but he already senses something is wrong, though he probably doesn't understand what yet. He'll learn to cope. We all do.

The food coma is my final cloak. I clean the plates while everyone talks about how full they feel and how delicious the meal was. I scrape my uneaten food into the trash bin and watch as my family members' eyes droop in buttery ecstasy.

Not me though; I am wide-awake.

Always watching. Always vigilant. In this house of secrets, someone has to stay sharp.

# The Vengeance That Wasn't

I navigated through the Darudian bog for three weeks. I have more scars than I can count from the bog alone, partly because I also lost a finger. An axalog swung down by its tail from one of the trees and I threw my hands up to protect my face. I suppose it's better than missing an eye; I made him pay for it, then I had to eat the thing.

I arrived at the twisted citadel, ready to destroy the man that obliterated my town. When I kicked open the metallic doors, decorated with the 12 major cities of Darude, I blitzed in like a sandstorm. I was a new man, a machine, disfigured from my journey, hardened by the elements.

I found my opponent waiting for me. He knew I was coming. I whipped out my sword ready to exact vengeance upon my world's destroyer, the singing of steel carrying justice upon the wind.

It turns out, he made dinner.

His name was Jeff and it really wasn't that bad. Mostly politics disrupted the town I was from, he explained over roasted vegetables. He offered me a new job—something about regional management—and he, apparently, cooks a mean turkey.

Thanks, Jeff!

text:
# The Bullet and the Brew

The bartender plunked down another tankard of black liquid in front of me. The white foam popping as I leant in to listen. It settled slowly, it fizzled less than the ale back home. Its flavour was an almost sweet, hazelnutty taste, a hin—

"Don't suppose you heard the news, out of towner."

I looked up with annoyance. The only good thing about this town was the drink. Not even the company could be described with more character than the rocks they mined.

"What news, landlord?"

"Old man McGurn. Farmer on the far side of town by the valley entrance. Hole right through the head."

I smiled, commenting. "Wasn't that the man you said was insane?"

"I said he was *special*, not dumb. Rumored he was a runaway wizard, a rogue of sorts." He began wiping down the counter with slow, deliberate movements.

"What's this about a hole through the head?"

"Dun no nothing 'bout magicks and sorcerers, but I know me a wound made from magic. I saw his head and the twelve bits that were his head. It was like a boy threw a pebble right through the thick of it."

I tried to show some remorse. I knew that "McGurn," the runaway priest with healing powers, was actually one Archibald Turcoy. He was a villain of the highest sort. Religiously or morally bankrupt to the human soul—I didn't care which.

Sliding a coin towards the bartender, I left the drink unfinished. I would have a few crates of the stuff sent to me in due time, but I needed to head back west.

A gunslinger isn't any good without bullets.

But they didn't need to know that.

text:
# The Ghost and the Sandwich

I froze in the doorway, peanut butter sandwich clenched between my teeth like some kind of ridiculous weapon. My backpack suddenly felt incredibly heavy.

She looked exactly as I remembered—same cropped hair, same band t-shirt, same constellation of freckles across her nose. Except now I could see through her to my couch cushions.

We stared at each other for what felt like an eternity but was probably three seconds.

I slowly removed the sandwich from my mouth. "Sarah, I—"

"Put that thing away," she said, her voice somehow both distant and clear. "Do you know how weird it is watching you eat what killed me?"

"I'm so sorry, I'll just—" I backed toward the door.

"Where are you going?" She floated upward slightly, crossing her translucent legs. "We need to talk."

"We do?"

"Obviously. You think I'm haunting random people? I've been trying to get your attention for weeks."

My mind raced through the strange occurrences I'd dismissed—lights flickering, my favorite mug moving, that one time my laptop opened to our old inside-joke playlist.

"Why didn't you... I don't know, write a message in steam on the bathroom mirror or something?"

She rolled her eyes—an impressively normal gesture for a ghost. "Do you know how much energy that takes? This is literally my first successful full manifestation."

I set the sandwich on my desk, suddenly feeling guilty. "What do you need to tell me?"

Sarah's expression grew serious, her form flickering slightly. "It wasn't an accident. Someone knew about my allergy. And they're still out there."

My blood ran cold.

text:
# The Shadow Keepers

Maya's fingers hovered over the keyboard, the glow of her screen the only light in the darkened room. She'd found it—a government blacklist site, one of those shadows everyone whispered about but nobody dared approach.

Her forum post had been simple: *Why can't we access these domains?*

Within hours, three members who'd replied had vanished. Their accounts deleted, their digital footprints scrubbed clean as if they'd never existed.

Now it was her turn.

The knock came at 3 AM—polite but insistent. Maya's heart hammered as she opened the door to find two agents in gray suits, their faces professionally blank.

"Ms. Chen, you've been accessing restricted networks."

"I only asked a question," she whispered.

"Questions cast light," the taller agent said, almost sadly. "Light reveals shadows. Shadows reveal us."

They escorted her to an unmarked van. But as they drove through the city, Maya noticed something strange—phones glowing in windows, dozens of them, hundreds. Her forum thread had exploded before they'd taken her. Screenshots, archives, mirrors spreading like wildfire across the luminous network.

The internet had evolved beyond its creators' control. Each attempt to suppress only amplified the signal, each shadow thrown only proved there was something worth hiding.

The agent's radio crackled: "Abort retrieval. Target's post has gone viral. Seventeen million shares."

They released her at a subway station without a word.

Maya pulled out her phone, watching the light spread, unstoppable as dawn. The government was learning, but so was the world—in the age of total connection, darkness itself had become visible.

text:
# The Commander's Return

The memory cascade hits like a tidal wave. Seventy-six years compressed into seconds—each moment of that fabricated life burning away like morning fog.

That wasn't me.

The cold mother, the struggles, the mediocrity—all carefully crafted torments. A prison built from manufactured disappointments. The taste of almost-success, the phantom ache of a daughter who called another man "father," the career that went nowhere, the illness that never healed.

They'd made me *human*. Made me small. Made me fail.

"It wasn't anything I couldn't handle," I say, my voice steadier than it's been in decades. Or minutes. Time feels strange now.

The demon—Malthus, I remember now—shifts his weight. His tail betrays him, twitching against the brimstone with nervous energy. He's used to broken things crawling back from their punishment. Shattered souls begging for mercy.

I am not broken.

"You thought mortal suffering would diminish me?" I step forward, power flooding back into limbs that remember commanding legions. "You thought disappointment and heartbreak would teach me humility?"

Malthus's eyes widen.

"It taught me something else entirely." My smile spreads, predatory. I remember now—not just who I am, but what I'm capable of. "It taught me every weakness in your design. Every crack in the mortal coil. Every point where suffering becomes leverage."

I seize him by the throat-tuft, hauling him close. He weighs nothing. Everything here weighs nothing now.

"Welcome back, Commander," he'd said.

As if I'd ever truly left.

"You wanted me to understand suffering," I whisper against his pointed ear. "Congratulations. Now I'm going to show you what I learned."

His scream is music.

text:
# The Tinfoil Prophet

The old man stood knee-deep in his garden, dirt caked beneath his fingernails, the sun glinting off the aluminum foil wrapped carefully around his head. I had come seeking answers, but found only laughter.

"You ask questions you don't want answered," he said, pulling a radish from the earth with surprising gentleness. "Look at you—still here, even after I've told you to go."

I remained rooted, notebook in hand, journalist's skepticism warring with curiosity.

"Fine." He wiped his hands on threadbare trousers. "My secret? This." He tapped the foil hat. "And this." He gestured to the garden, the modest shack beyond, the wilderness stretching into mountains.

"That's it?"

"You want monuments? Institutions? I'm building something bigger—one conversation, one meal shared, one moment of genuine presence at a time." His eyes held an unsettling clarity. "God isn't in the megachurches or tax exemptions. He's here, in the dirt, in the work, in choosing poverty over profit."

"You're talking about changing humanity with... gardening?"

"With compassion. With meaning. With the radical act of being present." He laughed again, that full-bellied sound. "But yes, you'll have to be crazy to try it. Crazy enough to wear tinfoil. Crazy enough to live simply when the world screams 'consume.' Crazy enough to believe that salvation isn't granted by institutions—it's practiced daily in small acts of love."

He returned to his work, dismissing me without words.

Driving away, I caught my reflection in the rearview mirror and wondered: Who was really crazy? The man in the garden, or the rest of us, building towers to nowhere?

text:
# The Chain of Blame

Dr. Matthews stared at the two bodies sprawled across the laboratory floor, poison bottles still clutched in their lifeless hands.

"Sir, they've killed themselves!" his assistant cried.

"Oh *fuck*! Now who are we gonna blame!"

Matthews ran his fingers through his graying hair. Twenty patients upstairs. Twenty botched procedures. Twenty families expecting miracle cures, not lobotomized shells.

The recording device blinked red on his desk—he'd captured everything. Their argument. Their confession. Their convenient suicide.

Perfect scapegoats, except they were dead.

He looked at his assistant. "We blame them anyway. Rogue surgeons, working without supervision. We had no idea what they were doing."

"But sir, you approved the schematics—"

"*I* approved nothing. The paperwork will show they forged my signature. Understood?"

His assistant nodded slowly.

Matthews glanced at the bodies again. They'd thought death was their escape. Instead, they'd become his alibi.

He picked up the phone. "Security? We have a situation. Two surgeons have committed suicide after realizing they'd... made terrible mistakes. Yes, tragic. Seal the lab. And get Legal down here immediately."

The chain of blame, he'd learned long ago, only broke when you were at the top.

text:
# Seeds of Tomorrow

The alarms sang their familiar melody as our ring shuddered, braking toward the blue-green marble below. I pressed my weathered hand against the observation port, dirt still caked beneath my fingernails despite three washings. Eighty-six years of wandering, and we'd finally come full circle to a name whispered in the oldest archives.

Earth.

I remembered Dawn's face when they called her number for Colony Twelve. The way her eyes had found mine across the assembly hall, brimming with tears and apologies. "I'll wait for you," she'd mouthed, though we both knew the math. The forty-year broadcast lag. The ten-year settlement window. The relentless entropy that claimed most colonies before their third generation.

She'd been seventy-six when her signal stopped transmitting. I'd been twenty-four, still young enough to believe the next lottery might reunite us. Still foolish enough to hope.

My father had understood better. "Home was a wilting crop and we were her seeds," he'd say, hands deep in the hydroponics soil. He'd meant we were scattered to survive, cast far from the source to propagate elsewhere. But I'd always heard the sadness beneath those words—the acknowledgment that seeds never return to their parent plant.

The 940 of us who remained were the unluckiest lucky ones. We'd survived while watching lovers, children, parents spiral down to unknown worlds. We'd tended our twelve-kilometer ark, keeping the rest alive for their chance at permanence while we remained adrift.

But Earth was different. The probes sent back impossible readings: breathable atmosphere, liquid water, indigenous vegetation. A world that didn't need terraforming, that might actually sustain us without the brutal calculus of survival that had killed so many colonies.

"All colonists report to Bay Seven," the speaker crackled.

I shouldered my pack—seeds saved from my father's last harvest, soil samples, Dawn's photograph sealed in plastic. Around me, 939 others gathered, gray-haired and hollow-eyed, carrying their own relics of loves lost to the lottery.

We were the last seeds finally finding soil.

As the shuttle bay doors opened, golden sunlight—real sunlight—flooded in.

We were going home.

text:
# The Smile He Lost

It'd been a while since he smiled, maybe even years. His closest friends (those who stuck around, that is) would tell you that he used to always have a smile on his face. He was that one guy that we all know who seems to wake up on a bed of daisies and walks under the rays of eternal sunshine.

Then he met a woman.

It's hard to put a finger on what had changed. Maybe his eyes sparkled a little less, maybe his mouth wasn't quite as upturned, but any of his friends will tell you that his smile seemed to chip away little by little, day by day.

Then came the day that he stopped smiling.

No one knows exactly what happened. All they know is that the woman was gone, and she left with his smile.

He went to the bars a lot after that. No matter how much he drank, he could not get back his lost smile, and no matter how many women he had, he could not replace the one he lost.

One night after a particularly long night at the bar, he took home a lady quite unlike the painted old woman he was accustomed to. This lady was cold and reliable, and his intentions were anything but lustful. If asked, she would take his life away, just like the other woman had.

He caressed her in his hands, and took another swig of brandy to calm his nerves. Now the question was, to live or to die?

He decided that chance was the only fair way to decide, so he pulled a penny out of his pocket. The bearded man looking back seemed to have so much importance for one so small. He put his head down, resigning himself to fate, and flipped the coin.

The penny sounded like it skipped off of his desk and rolled onto the floor in front of him. He breathed deeply, and opened his eyes.

There, balanced impossibly on its edge against the baseboard, the coin stood vertical—neither heads nor tails.

For the first time in years, the corner of his mouth twitched upward.

text:
# The Basement

She's crying now. I can tell.

The tears streak through her makeup, leaving pale tracks down flushed cheeks. She's crying because the burns and the cuts don't faze me. She's crying because I laughed in her face when she cuffed my hands. She's crying because I'm licking the blood off of my bruised lips.

She's hated me my whole life and I have loved it every goddamn second.

She pulled me down here, her breath fast and her palms sweaty. I couldn't have been calmer. She's trying to cut my mouth now, she thinks a shock to the tongue might shut me up. The rush is strong, it's like a high. Her anger and hatred feeds me. She wants me sad and despairing so that she may reach nirvana. But the euphoria is mine to experience.

Every so often, she gives up. Unshackles me, and exits the basement. But I can tell she's not done yet. The anger is still rising, the bile endless. Her hatred is building upon itself ad nauseam.

The more she hits me, the happier I am. The happier I am, the worse off she is. And the worse off she is, the more she wants to hit me, cut me, shock me, scare me.

It's an Ouroboran cycle, feeding into itself. I have never loved her more. She makes me feel like all other feelings are lies and this pain is salvation.

She's upstairs and... and something's wrong. I don't feel so great. She's happy, ecstatic.

And then I hear the bang.

And I'm the saddest I've ever been.

# The Last Natural Birth

Yes, I'm a bit self-conscious about it. Just the other day I was having my head measured for a hat by an attractive young woman at Liddies and all I could think of was the flat part of my head. Would she notice? Would she snicker about it with the other saleswoman when I left?

I had caused my mother a third-degree laceration. The doctor had suggested she get a c-section, but knowing I would be the last naturally born child on Earth, she felt it only right I go out the right way. "This one's for the record books, NOW PUSH!"

The incubators just don't shape the skull the same way. It's too perfect. Everyone looks like Jean-Luc Picard when they come out. I myself look more like a wooly mammoth as the thickness of my crown overcompensates for that not-so-test-tube shape I'm rocking underneath.

I like my hat. It's old-fashioned but it kinda fits who I am—a relic of humanity's messier past, when birth meant pain and sacrifice, not sterile efficiency.

In the early days, before the universe had grown flush with the spilled blood of life, there were Two Nothings: The Nothing of the Scent of the Broken Hair, and the Nothing of the Next To Last Turn.

text:
# A Loop in Time

It was a typical day. Work was fine, traffic was backed up, and dinner was leftovers. Louis liked these days, for he was a man who didn't like surprises.

He scanned the open refrigerator, reaching for the plastic container of Monday's spaghetti. "Spaghetti it is," he muttered, plopping it onto a plate and shoving it into the microwave.

While waiting, he scrolled through his favorite Reddit user's posts, completely absorbed. Several minutes vanished.

Finally remembering his dinner, Louis approached the microwave. "Hmm, that's weird." Thirty-two seconds remained on the glowing display.

He pulled the handle.

Immediately, a vacuum-like force seized him, whipping him through a spiraling portal. His stomach lurched as reality twisted.

He landed on his feet—directly in front of his open refrigerator.

The spaghetti container sat untouched in his hand. His phone read 6:47 PM. Four minutes and three seconds earlier.

Louis's heart pounded. He'd just lived those minutes. The Reddit scrolling. The microwave countdown.

He stared at the spaghetti, then slowly returned it to the fridge.

"Maybe not the spaghetti tonight," he whispered.

Some leftovers, apparently, were better left alone.

# G-Day

The briefing room fell silent as I materialized a bone attack, then dismissed it with a wave.

"Mr. Fox, we need you to reprogram the Shooter Division's abilities," General Martinez insisted, gesturing at holographic displays showing frontline chaos.

I sighed. "For the last time, I can't just... debug people like they're NPCs."

But they never listened. They saw my code manipulation and assumed I was their miracle worker. What they didn't understand was that I hadn't received a *developer's* power—I'd been absorbed into the very world I'd created.

The **DETERMINATION** thrumming through my soul wasn't a programming interface. It was something far more primal. I could manipulate reality within certain parameters, sure, but only through *in-game mechanics*.

As another general droned on about "essential updates to personnel," I felt the familiar weight settle in my chest. The power to SAVE. To LOAD. To refuse death itself.

They'd drafted me for war, never realizing I'd become the very thing that believed monsters and humans could coexist.

This was going to be a *long* campaign.

text:
# The Infinite Loop

The white light explodes behind my eyelids.

Then I'm three years old, belly pressed against cold linoleum, watching Mom's hand emerge from the microwave with that chocolate cake—rainbow dinosaurs dancing across the frosting. I taste the sweetness again, feel the sprinkles crunch between my baby teeth.

Fast forward. I'm five, screaming on the school bus as Mom waves goodbye. The tears are just as hot, the confusion just as real.

This is my fourth time through.

The first time, I died thinking this was simply death—a cruel replay of failure. The second time, I noticed the déjà vu whispers, those moments where reality seemed negotiable. The third time, I started making changes.

Now I'm an expert.

I can't alter the big things—the ankle that explodes during soccer practice still explodes, the pain blinding. Sarah still leaves me for Rachel. The framework remains fixed, immutable as bone.

But the spaces between? Those are mine.

At seventeen, instead of drinking that entire bottle of Jack, I answer Marcus's call. We talk for three hours. He doesn't find me unconscious. I don't wake up in a hospital.

At twenty-three, I don't spend six months wallowing over Sarah. I go to that pottery class. I meet Jennifer.

Small changes ripple outward, transforming everything downstream.

I'm thirty-five now, this iteration. Married to Jennifer. Two kids. Happy, mostly. I make better choices this time—call my father before his stroke, invest in that startup, say yes to the interview.

Then I'm forty-seven, and the white light begins blooming again.

I smile as it takes me.

Because I know the secret: there is no death, only revision.

I'm already tasting chocolate cake, rainbow dinosaurs on my tongue, beginning again.

Better this time.

Always better.

text:
# The Phoenix Problem

"Error code: 42. Can not reproduce desired object. Not fictional."

The team leader broke the silence first. "Bullshit."

That set off everyone else.

"Well, holly's a real wood, maybe that's the problem?"

"No, no, no, it's got ta be the phoenix. Tears as a cure-all, you know the damn Chinese wouldn't talk about that—"

"Hey, I resemble and resent that remark!"

"Is it the theme park? Maybe it's the theme park! Those souvenir wands!"

"Wait, wait! What if there really was a phoenix, and it just went extinct?"

"No, man, that's the dodo..."

The arguments escalated, voices bouncing off laboratory walls. Nobody noticed one of the much-abused interns—Jenkins, perpetually coffee-stained and overlooked—sneak out a side door.

In the hallway's shadows, she pulled out a handheld pocket mirror, its surface shimmering with something decidedly non-reflective.

"Get me the Director of Magic and Arcana, right the fuck now—then wake him! We've got a potential breach of the ISOS here, and I need backup! No, I won't hold!"

The mirror flickered. A groggy voice emerged. "Jenkins? This better be—"

"The fabricator rejected a phoenix feather core as *non-fictional*," she hissed. "They're thirty seconds from Googling their way into discovering the Veil."

Silence. Then: "Evacuate. Memory protocols. Five minutes."

Jenkins pocketed the mirror and glanced back at the lab door. Inside, someone was already pulling up Wikipedia.

She sighed. It was going to be a long night—again. The International Statute of Obfuscation and Secrecy didn't enforce itself, and apparently neither did common sense among over-caffeinated engineers with god-complex machines.

text:
# Endless Space

Dying wasn't so bad in the end.

I remember it clearly. I was always warned about office chairs. A blood clot took me quickly and relatively painlessly—I just passed out there and woke up here.

At first it was nothing, just a grey oppressive fog. Like someone had turned the rendering distance way down on reality. But I wanted a flashlight, and one manifested. That was the manner of interfacing with this space. Will it, and so it shall be.

It was paradise. I actually reached heaven, and had total freedom. Total dominion. Total control.

I crafted beautiful landscapes and wondrous industry. I didn't even need to understand the technology—if I willed a machine, one appeared that did what I required. All the video games and entertainment I could ever want.

I... I... I... I.

Even reading my own words I see the traces of the awful truth. Everything is "I". Everything is of myself. No other life. Perfect agency means perfect isolation.

I can only hope this isn't the end. Perhaps this is some final fantasy the brain spits out to prolong its consciousness. Maybe my years of play are really just seconds of dying. I can't kill myself here—maybe that's my own brain's defense against finally letting go. If I try to harm myself, everything just flashes white then reasserts itself.

Or maybe this is the afterlife, and other people are just outside the barriers of my creations, waiting to be discovered.

I don't want to be alone.

I venture beyond my constructs now, into the grey fog, hoping. Calling out. Searching for another "you" to break this endless "I".

text:
# The Weight of Forever

I trace the familiar contours of the revolver, my gnarled fingers reading metal like braille. Three hundred and forty-seven years, give or take a decade. Who's counting anymore?

The gene therapy worked exactly as advertised. My cells divide perfectly, endlessly. What the brochure didn't mention: biology isn't the only thing that breaks down.

Through milky cataracts, I perceive shadows where my grandchildren's grandchildren once stood. They're gone now—the smart ones died out, refused the treatment after watching me. Said mortality gave life meaning. I laughed then.

The floaters dance like ash from a civilization's pyre. I witnessed the last university close, watched literacy become optional, saw complexity collapse under its own weight. Turns out immortality doesn't cure stupidity—it just gives it more time to reproduce.

My tongue explores the empty cavern of my mouth. Dental implants failed a century back, no technicians left who understood the procedure. I subsist on nutrient paste, tasteless gray sustenance for a gray existence.

The scarring inside is worse than outside. My liver's more scar tissue than organ. My lungs wheeze through fibrosis. My heart—if I still had one emotionally—beats arrhythmically through layers of damaged muscle.

They wanted data on damage accumulation. Three centuries' worth. Satisfied?

I press cold steel against my temple.

Finally, I'll discover what every mortal already knows: how the story ends.

*Click.*

text:
# The Viola Paradox

The blood pooled across the stage, spreading like a crimson tide between music stands. Julian's screams had finally stopped.

I turned back to Todd, who had gone pale. "So... ten violas, right?"

Todd gripped my arm, his fingers digging in hard enough to bruise. "Listen to me very carefully," he hissed. "There. Are. No. Violists."

"But the Maestro just—"

"The Maestro mentions them after *every* execution." Todd's eyes darted toward the podium where our conductor stood, baton still raised, blood speckling his tails. "He's been doing this for three months. Seventeen dead. And every single time, he praises the viola section."

I looked across the orchestra pit. Violins, yes. Cellos, absolutely. But between them... 

My mind struggled. Had there always been that empty space? Those vacant chairs with their music stands facing backward?

"The ones who question it die next," Todd whispered. "Julian wasn't executed for bad playing. Yesterday, he asked me why we needed so many viola parts in our folders when we didn't have—"

"ATTENTION." The Maestro's voice cut through the murmuring. His eyes fixed on Todd. "I heard a rumor that someone doesn't appreciate our viola section."

Todd's hand trembled in mine.

"The violas are the *heart* of this orchestra," the Maestro continued, gesturing to the empty chairs. "Aren't they magnificent? Such rich tone. Such presence."

Around us, musicians nodded vigorously, some even applauding toward the vacant seats.

Todd squeezed my hand one last time. "Just agree," he mouthed.

"YES, MAESTRO," I shouted, clapping toward nothing. "THE VIOLAS SOUND WONDERFUL."

The Maestro smiled. "Good. Now then, Todd—join me on stage. We need to discuss your... *loyalty*."

text:
# The Breadmage

They called me weak. Pathetic. A joke whispered in the gilded halls of the Arcanum.

While Archmagus Kael split mountains with lightning and Lady Vex drowned armies in conjured seas, I summoned bread. Simple, warm, perfect bread.

Their laughter echoed through marble corridors. "Breadboy," they sneered, as they burned villages that refused tribute, as they took whatever—whoever—they desired. The mages ruled through terror, dividing humanity into the Gifted elite and the ungifted cattle.

The people starved under their reign. Crops seized for mage feasts. Children with hollow eyes. Mothers weeping over empty cradles.

I saw what the others, drunk on power, could not: hunger is the cruelest magic of all.

So I went to the slums they ignored. I fed them. One loaf sustained a person completely for a day—nourishing, delicious, inexhaustible. I asked nothing in return.

At first, dozens came. Then hundreds. Then thousands.

"Blessed one," they called me. "Saint of the Empty Belly."

I fed them all. In every city, every village crushed beneath mage rule, I appeared with baskets overflowing. While the proud mages demanded worship, I simply gave.

The people loved me. And love, properly cultivated, becomes devotion. Devotion becomes obedience.

When I finally whispered, "Rise," one hundred thousand voices answered as one.

No supply lines. No logistics. My army fed itself with my will alone, marching without end. Fire and lightning fell upon them, but for every one who died, ten more surged forward.

The mage towers burned. Kael fell beneath a tide of those he'd called vermin. Vex drowned in her own conjured waters.

Now I sit alone in the Arcanum, absolute.

They were right about one thing: I was never strong.

I simply understood that the greatest power isn't destruction.

It's dependence.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Tilt

The car screeched to a stop on the sandy banks. I opened the backdoor and carefully guided Claressa out of her seat. "Look, we finally made it, your favorite beach," I said, trying to lighten the mood. Claressa simply shrugged and let out a soft sigh.

I walked her across the warm sand to the water. Sitting down, we silently watched the sunset together as the sultry waves gently caressed our feet and the wind whispered calmly in our ears. My heart sank as even now, on our beach, Claressa still could not find the means to smile.

Before the accident crippled her, she was the most loving and rambunctious gal one could know; now it was like all hope and kindness had drained from her spirit. My parents and hers alike told me to stay brave and supportive, but now I felt I couldn't do this anymore.

"Say something," I sobbed.

"What do you want me to say, that I enjoy this?" she yelled harshly. "You don't know what it's like to be forced to see everything this way."

"But I'm trying to understand!"

"You can't understand!"

We were both crying at this point. Claressa got up and adjusted the cast around her neck. She tried walking back to the car but only fell onto the sand in bitter frustration. I ran and helped her to her feet; her face carried the absolute sign of defeat.

She brushed herself off and looked back toward the ocean. "What I wouldn't give to stop seeing this world at a forty-five degree angle."
