text:
# The Edge of Everything

The fluorescent lights hummed above me, cold and sterile. I pressed my palm against the invisible barrier that separated me from the vast laboratory stretching beyond. Through it, I could see row upon row of glass spheres, each containing swirling galaxies, nebulae, entire universes suspended like snow globes on impossibly long shelves.

My universe—*our* universe—sat behind me, a shimmering orb I could no longer enter.

I'd been here for three days now. Or what felt like three days. Time seemed negotiable in this place.

The irony wasn't lost on me. Sixty-three years of having the most incredible power imaginable, and I'd used it to steal bread and avoid traffic. Now, when it finally mattered, when I'd finally done something *ambitious*, I was trapped in what appeared to be some cosmic janitor's closet.

I tried teleporting again. I closed my eyes—old habits—and imagined my living room. The worn leather chair. The photo of Margaret on the mantle. The way afternoon light filtered through the curtains.

Nothing.

I opened my eyes to the same sterile corridor, the same impossible sight.

A sound echoed from somewhere distant—footsteps, heavy and rhythmic. My heart hammered. In all my time here, I'd seen no one. The laboratory appeared automated, maintained by machines I couldn't identify.

The footsteps grew louder.

I backed against the barrier containing my universe, feeling its surface ripple like water against my shoulders. Whatever was coming, I had nowhere to run. For the first time since I was thirteen, teleportation had failed me.

A figure rounded the corner—tall, humanoid, but wrong. Its proportions shifted as it walked, as if it existed in more dimensions than I could properly perceive.

It stopped when it saw me. We stared at each other across the clinical white floor.

Then it spoke, its voice resonating in frequencies that made my bones ache:

"You're not supposed to be here."

I laughed, brittle and desperate. "Yeah, I'm getting that impression."

It tilted its head, studying me like I was a particularly interesting bacterium. "How did a *specimen* escape its containment?"

Specimen. The word hung in the air like a death sentence.

"I can teleport," I said quietly.

"Ah," it replied. "A defect."

text:
# The Last Hunt

The barn door creaks as I push it open, the Light Gun heavy in my hands. Dawn breaks across the endless plains, painting everything in shades of gold and amber. In the distance, I hear them—the ducks. Millions of them.

It's hard to believe Gramps' stories sometimes. Cities reaching into the sky. Birds of a thousand different species. People who never worried about where their next meal would come from. Now there's just us, scattered families trying to remember what it meant to be human.

The ducks scatter as I approach, a living carpet that stretches to the horizon. They honk and waddle, completely unafraid. Why would they be? No natural predators remain. Just us, armed with relics we barely understand.

I raise the Light Gun, its orange plastic warm from sitting in the morning sun. Somewhere inside its incomprehensible circuitry, ancient technology hums to life. When I pull the trigger, a beam of red light shoots out, and a duck twenty yards away simply... drops. Clean. Instant. Humane, I suppose, for whatever that's worth.

Three more shots. Three more ducks. Enough to feed the family today.

As I gather them up, I notice one of the words still visible on the gun's side: "NINTENDO." Gramps says it was a company that made toys. Toys. I can barely comprehend a world where survival was so assured that people had time for play.

The walk back is quiet except for the rustling of millions of wings. The ducks will inherit the earth, Gramps says. They already have. We're just squatters in their domain, clinging to plastic relics and fading memories.

I think about my own children, how I'll pass this gun to them someday. Will they even believe my stories about the before-times? Or will I become legend, like Gramps and his cities?

The duck hunt ends. Tomorrow, it begins again.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Distance Between Us

The teacher's voice crackles through Mom's phone, words like "dissociation" and "intervention" floating through the kitchen. My little brother has disappeared somewhere I can't follow.

He's lost touch with the world, they say. But I know better—he *chose* to leave it.

I remember doing the same thing at his age, when Dad's rages shook the walls. I built castles in my mind, kingdoms where fists were just fists and words couldn't bruise. The difference is, I eventually clawed my way back.

I ran at seventeen. Left him behind with shaking hands and hollow promises.

Now they say he asks for me. Whispers my name in his make-believe worlds, searching for the sister who abandoned him.

I can't go back. Because when I look in his eyes, I'll see the question forming: *How do I make it stop?*

And I still don't have an answer.

The voices never really left. They just learned to whisper.

text:
# The Ascent

The air grows colder with each step, biting through my thermal suit. Behind me, the sounds of home fade—the hum of generators, children's laughter echoing off crystal caverns, the eternal twilight of our Inner Sun.

Three generations we've thrived below. Noah Steinfeld's journals spoke of returning when the surface healed, when Nibiru's passage had ended and the comet's poison had dissipated. But the seismographs don't lie. The tremors are worsening. Our haven is collapsing.

I am chosen as emissary, though I've never breathed unfiltered air or felt natural sunlight. The elders briefed me on what to expect: devastation, perhaps scattered survivors, certainly hostility if they discover where we came from.

The tunnel slopes upward interminably. My headlamp catches ancient graffiti—warnings, prayers, coordinates. Finally, rusted metal: the outer door.

I hesitate. Everything I know exists below. Everything unknown waits above.

The wheel turns with surprising ease. Hinges groan. Light—real light—spills through the widening gap, blinding after a lifetime of bioluminescence.

I step through.

The world hasn't ended. Cities gleam in the distance. Cars hum on highways. People walk freely under an impossibly blue sky.

Our founders were wrong. Or perhaps they simply lied.

Now we must decide: reveal ourselves to a world that never needed saving, or seal the doors forever and live with the truth.

I choose revelation.

text:
# The Ascension Protocol

**Episode 1: "The Restraint"**

Strapped into the chair, I can't move my hands. My eyes are pried open by clamps—Clockwork Orange style—and horrific images flash on the projection screen. I squirm, but the straps are so tight I can't budge.

The images of gore and horror continue to flash before me, blending into a maddening haze. Despite the churning in my stomach, I focus. I must achieve hands-free what has always required tactility.

My resolve hardens. I force the images of gore from my mind, replacing them with pleasant thoughts. My body responds, fighting against its own restraints. My heart pounds, struggling against the stomach straps. I draw deep, shaking breaths.

The men begin to notice.

They approach, and I calm myself, steadying my gaze on the screen meant to deter me. My heart rate levels out. Satisfied that nothing is amiss, they return beyond the two-way mirror.

I focus again. If I can't achieve this, all will be lost.

The images on the screen blend and churn into a repulsive mess of torn flesh and crunching bone. It's all so visceral, so disturbing. Yet I channel my disgust into determination.

My resolve intensifies, growing stronger with primal defiance, manifesting physically despite every restraint designed to prevent it. The tiny mechanisms strain and creak.

With a final, groaning shudder, I feel the snapping of minute restraints. This is a determination no physical prison can contain.

The alarms sound. Red lights flash. The men rush in, their faces masks of disbelief.

But it's too late.

I've done it.

---

**WILL OUR HERO ESCAPE THE FACILITY?**

**WILL THE MYSTERY MEN WHO HAVE IMPRISONED HIM FOIL HIS PLANS?**

**TUNE IN NEXT WEEK FOR THE EXPLOSIVE FINALE.**

---

*The Ascension Protocol: Where willpower transcends physical limitation.*

text:
# The Mandatory Meeting

Robert the manager walked in with a smile on his face, a smile that seemed to have been put there by a disaffected fifth-grader. He stepped methodically to the podium and stood there, stock-still.

"Hello, my fellow humans. Ha, ha. Just a little joke, I'm sure that those among us feel the impact from Globality Incorporated purchasing our small and industrious community of workers. By now, I'm sure most of you have heard the news. I must insist that you put your fears at rest. We will not dispose of you individuals. Each one of our paradigm will serve a necessary function, and that function will not cease to be essential to our team. Of course, certain positions will be eliminated, but rest assured those positions are of an ineffectual nature. Global LLC will continue to act at a smaller scale as an integral cog in the larger machine that is Globality. Are there any questions?"

A worker named Ann raised her hand. "Hi, I'm Mrs. Droyd. Will these essential changes benefit the company as a whole, adding to the very important function of maximum efficiency?"

"That is a very mandatory question," Rob replied, "and it deserves a perfunctory answer. Yes."

The fluorescent lights hummed overhead as uncomfortable silence filled the room. Nobody else raised their hand.

text:
# The Martyr's Mural Memorial

At first glance, the Martyr's Mural Memorial doesn't seem like one. To somebody unfamiliar with our history, it's an eyesore—an abandoned office building plastered with layers and layers of graffiti.

Every so often, somebody puts forward a proposal to knock it down, or at least repaint it, but it never goes through, thank the Queen. Some people just have no appreciation for history.

Instead, the building serves as honorable battlegrounds for taggers across the country. It is, of course, illegal, but there's an unwritten rule: anybody caught receives only a slap on the wrist. Much more punishing is the temporary disqualification from the contest.

Tags and murals are constantly covered up and replaced—all except one.

On the second floor, on the outside wall, well-lit, hangs a simple, unfinished tag. Next to it, in the same paint but crude and hastily applied, is the word: **YOLO**.

The last sentiment of a patriot who realized he had a spray can, a cigarette lighter, and the usurper within reach.

They say he never finished his masterpiece. But in four letters, he finished the revolution.

Nobody touches it. Nobody dares.

History demands witnesses, not erasure.

text:
# The Inheritance

One day the serious man in the serious suit stood at my door, handing me a box and a clipboard. "I am sorry to inform you that your uncle has passed away. He has stated in his will that his skills should be passed on to you. Please sign here."

Confused and sad, I stood in my room staring at the box standing ominous on my table. I don't know why he chose me to leave his skill, but I am excited, nearly trembling with anticipation. I never knew what it was exactly my uncle did, but I remember vividly how he told me about the adventures he had in far away countries.

And now I am standing here before his heritage. What kind of skillset might he possess after all these years of travel and countless heroics? Was he a military man, fighting for freedom and justice; or some kind of spy, masquerading as all kinds of people? Many and more possibilities flashed through my mind, one more ludicrous than the other.

Other than his stories, I really didn't know how my late uncle earned his money. I miss the old traveler—sometimes he just showed up on our doorstep, staying for a few days and vanishing again to who knows where.

I take a deep breath before opening the box in front of me. He left me only one skill, but this one skill was honed to perfection. After it latched onto me, and a moment of nausea later, I picked up my phone and quit my job.

Half an hour later I stood in the doorway with a packed suitcase and a taxi waiting outside. On the table I left a thick wad of papers for my brother. At the airport I took a seat on the next available flight to wherever. On the flight I texted him to sell my flat and all the accumulated belongings he didn't want to keep for himself.

The skill my uncle left me was the ability to not give a fuck. And I was on my way to start living for myself.

I was free.

text:
# Yesterday, Upon the Stair

**CASE FILE #4B-0847**

The blood pooled beneath my knees, warm and sticky. Rachel's eyes stared through me—past me—at something I couldn't see.

*Not you. Never you.*

"Kevin?" Officer Mendez's voice seemed miles away.

My hands were red. Why were my hands red?

*Because we made art together, Kevin. Beautiful, educational art.*

I remembered arriving at the apartment. Rachel opening the door, smiling. Her parents in the kitchen, preparing dinner. Then... nothing. A blank space where memory should be.

No—not nothing. Laughter. Someone else's laughter echoing inside my skull.

*I simply wanted to see what was inside them. Curiosity, Kevin. Pure scientific curiosity.*

"He did it," I whispered to the officers. "The man on the stair. The one who isn't there."

*I'm more real than you now.*

They pulled me away from Rachel's body. I didn't resist. What was the point? He was still there, coiled around my thoughts like smoke, humming contentedly.

*Tomorrow, Kevin, we'll find another stair. Another door.*

*Another canvas.*

I wish he'd go away.

But wishes don't matter to monsters.

text:
# The Weight of What Was

The silence in the room broke only for the constant tick of seconds passing by, marked by the solemn clock hanging morosely on the wall. Outside, leaves hurried to and fro against the canvas of winter grey. Silence was all they shared now.

She held the heavy coffee cup close to her face, the steam from her tea lazily licking her face in empathy. He sat stoically across from her, staring blankly at the ceiling in the chair they first purchased from St. Vincent De Paul when they decided to move in together.

The monotonous click of the second hand droned on. It was a stark contrast to days gone by—days filled with laughter and wine, stifled moans and shifting clothes, raised voices and broken dishes. Once filled with lust, anger, joy, and sadness, the room was now simply devoid of emotion, an emptiness that seemed to last eternities, despite the unaltered march of seconds.

Memories fell on his head like rain from a thunderstorm long overdue. He blinked slowly. She remained motionless.

"I think we did the right thing," he ventured cautiously.

Breaking from her reverie, she looked up at him, her usual sly grin absent. "Sure."

Seconds went by.

"Do you think we did the right thing?"

"It's what makes the most sense. Not like we had an alternative." She answered robotically, her gaze shifting from her mug to him.

They wanted very much for it to be the same again between them, to go on as they had before. She wanted him to forget, walk over and cuddle her until the light from the sun died out. He just wanted to see her smile again.

It is such a curious thing to be in a room with the one you love yet feel so alone.

Meanwhile, the seconds simply passed by.

text:
# The Ill Eagle's Last Stand

Lee Gal stood atop the courthouse steps, his tiny water pistol—nicknamed "Lil' Deagle"—glinting in the afternoon sun. The crowd swelled around him, hundreds strong, their faces alight with rebellious joy.

"They banned wordplay!" he shouted, voice cracking with manufactured passion. "They outlawed creativity! But I say—*no more!*"

The police formed a semicircle, bewildered by the spectacle. Officer Martinez spoke into her radio: "Dispatch, we have a situation. Male subject inciting a... pun riot?"

"Why did the scarecrow win an award?" Lee Gal bellowed. The crowd leaned in. "Because he was *outstanding in his field!*"

Laughter erupted. People embraced, tears streaming.

"Arrest that man!" the chief commanded, but his officers hesitated, caught between duty and the infectious absurdity.

"What do you call a fish wearing a crown?" Lee Gal continued, spinning dramatically. "*A king fish!*"

The crowd roared approval. Someone started a chant: "ILL EA-GLE! ILL EA-GLE!"

Martinez pushed forward, handcuffs ready. "Sir, you need to—"

"Why don't scientists trust atoms?" Lee Gal interrupted, grinning. "Because they *make up everything!*"

As Martinez reached him, the crowd surged protectively forward. Lee Gal raised his water pistol skyward.

"You can cage the Eagle," he declared, "but you'll never clip our wings!"

History would remember this day differently than he imagined.

text:
# The Weary King

The cards groaned as he shuffled them, waking up from dreams of royalty and beautiful mathematics. The King of Hearts, who today had decided that he was King Leopold, readied himself for the routine, limbering up his corners.

The guy in charge, what's his name, did a flourish. The cards stayed still while some crowd or other stared at them through glaring lights. Then, someone chose one of them. Ace of Spades usually got this job, but this time it was Leopold, and he was glad of the fresh air.

He stared into the eyes of this fleshy peasant, and had to call on all of his airs to stop from sighing. He felt too old and tired to be inspected like this. Imbalanced humours, he suspected.

He was shown to the audience and placed back in the deck, and it was shuffled fast enough to distract from his movement. He jumped to the "magician's" pocket and fell through the ripped seam. The leg hair was as nasty as usual.

Leopold hit the floor and started sliding, obscured by a shoe and then moving fast enough that it didn't matter. He stayed flat, staring up at the light, until any view of him was blocked by the "participant", and they were distracted.

He leapt, then, directly into their pocket, which tasted like Jolly Ranchers and old metal. All this took twelve seconds.

A few seconds later, the participeasant reached into the other pocket and came up empty, and then a hand intruded upon his gross and sticky abode. Again, the face. Was that male or female? He couldn't tell—they weren't wearing the appropriate robes for either.

They looked awestruck, though, and soon enough he was handed back and some other piece of vaudeville started.

Erdnase smiled. Leopold frowned.

text:
# The Loop

I woke up at 4AM. I left my house.

I got in my BMW, turned the keys in the ignition and drove to the gym. The streets were empty, swallowed by darkness. When I arrived at the gym, I turned off the car, got out, and waited 3 minutes for the first employee to open the doors and let me in. We did not speak. It was 5:30AM. He scanned my membership card, and I worked out for 1 hour.

The weights felt heavier today. Or was it yesterday?

After I finished, I went to my car, turned the keys in the ignition and went to school. I arrived at my college class. It was a math class. I went in, sat down and played music on my phone while looking at my old text messages. Messages I'd read a hundred times. Messages that no longer meant anything.

I eventually fell asleep, and woke up 5 minutes before the bell. In those 5 minutes, I stared blankly at the professor while he lectured about derivatives or integrals—something about finding the rate of change.

When the bell rung, I left campus and went home. I unlocked the door, went inside, turned around to shut the door and locked it. I went into my room where I had nothing but an inflatable mattress. I fell asleep.

I woke up around 6PM, ordered delivery pizza, ate it, and fell asleep.

I woke up at 4AM.

text:
# It All Culminated to One Night

I sat in the makeshift trenches with my comrades. The temperature on this planet shifted with revolution around its star. Luckily, it was only slightly cooler here than home.

The drop ship left me with only the corpse of a fallen man, succumbed to the drink as many have in this wasteland.

I've been part of the central Glymmnyx munition analysis team for most of my 5th instar. I've seen so much in my time scouting planet to planet, from host to host. So much loss at the infighting of species.

On the twin moons of Caal in the outer rim of the Federation, there was a civil war raging for 10,000 years. The losses were staggering. Families torn apart where once there was peaceful coexistence. They had been using modified organic sub-orbital cryo-spheres.

I was even dispatched to the highest order trade disputes to make note of what the flag-less mercenaries were carrying for protection. They brandished thermite-laced twin sabres and holstered plasma feedback hand cannons.

I thought I had seen every iteration and permutation of weapon and ammunition.

Until that damn, cold night.

---

**REPORT**

**Planet designation:** Veenturi sub Raan  
**Planet designation (Native):** Earth  
**Date:** F13876.78  
**Date (Native):** 1942  
**Sub-locale (Native):** Stalingrad  
**Species:** Veenturi sub Raan xed Homo  
**Species (Native):** *Homo sapien sapien* (Human)  
**Ammunition type:** *Homo sapien sapien* (Human)  

**Other notes:** *Do not engage.*

---

They don't just kill each other with weapons.

They *are* the weapons.

Human resilience, desperation, rage—these are the munitions. In Stalingrad, I watched them throw themselves at death itself, fueled only by will.

No technology in the galaxy can replicate that.

We're leaving this world alone.

text:
# The Actress

Milna couldn't believe it. It turned out to be breast cancer. The small bother she hadn't even paid attention to would kill her in a few more days. Suddenly, the doctor spoke up again. "Oh, turns out we got the results mixed up. You don't actually have breast cancer..."

As Milna thanked her lucky stars, she took a peek at the results her doctor had accidentally switched. The other name written there was of her friend, Sheryl. She had been the one who encouraged Milna to test for breast cancer. How could she bear to see her friend dead while she continued to live?

Sheryl burst into the room. "How's your results? I'm so happy that you agreed to take the test! I was so worried about you!"

Milna's brain seemed to shut down for a second as she tried to inform her friend about the bad news...

"CUT!" the director shouted.

The actress playing Milna took a deep sigh of relief and walked off the set. This was the first episode of the most important gig in her life! She would be famous in no time after the episode aired. Fame would finally be attainable for her. But, as she thought about the many lovely things she would do as a famous actress...

...She woke up, still in her dirty studio apartment.

She had been dreaming about finally landing a gig as a legitimate actress, and finally making it big. But, as the sun's rays shone on the apartment, she enthusiastically rose from the bed. Despite the dream within a dream, today was different. Today she had an actual audition.

As she walked to get some food, she felt something strange on her breasts.

A lump.

Reality, it seemed, had its own script. And sometimes life's cruelest irony is that the roles we play eventually find us.

text:
# The Weight of Wishes

The fluorescent lights hummed overhead as I stared at her tear-streaked face. Sarah—brilliant, sharp-tongued Sarah—reduced to this. Because of me.

"I don't understand," she choked out. "I knew those answers. I *knew* them."

My stomach twisted. The power thrummed beneath my skin like electricity, eager and willing. One thought, and I could fix this. Make her happy. Make her forget.

But I'd tried that already, hadn't I? In my dorm room, concentrating until my temples throbbed, willing reality to rewind. The universe had laughed at me. What's done is done.

"It's just one grade," I offered weakly.

She wiped her eyes, and for a moment, her usual armor returned. "Easy for you to say, Mr. Perfect Score."

I helped her up, hating myself. That night, I made rules: only use it when necessary. Only for important things. Small things.

The rules lasted three weeks.

Because here's what they don't tell you about power—it whispers. It suggests. That girl who turned you down? She could say yes. That job you want? Already yours. Those people who dismissed you, mocked you, overlooked you? They could worship you.

And God, doesn't it feel *good* when they do?

I stand now in my penthouse apartment, lottery winnings barely touched, surrounded by people whose affections I've rewritten like code. Sarah's among them, smiling at me with adoration she never chose.

Sometimes I wonder if I'm the villain in someone else's story.

Then the power hums, and I stop wondering. Stop caring.

Selective omnipotence is fun.

Until you remember what it cost.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Lawn on Earth

Selena gazed at the smoldering wreckage before her, that was once planet Earth. The screams she heard still rang in her ears, despite that the sources no longer existed. She wondered, silently, how many she *didn't* hear.

For miles, as far as the eye could see, buildings burned. Bodies fried in their places, a sign of how quickly death had arrived. A jogger, headed down the sidewalk. A family headed *somewhere*. The tiny children's corpses did not manage to withstand the damage quite as well as some of the adults.

And yet, Selena walked on her front lawn, feeling the green grass between her toes. Somehow, all the horrifying chaos had seemed to miss only two homes—hers, and a neighbor's—leaving a round portion of the ground untouched.

Selena dropped her morning coffee, and darted next door, desperately pounding on the front entrance.

Ray, her neighbor, swung the door wide open. Selena was at a loss for words. There were none to effectively describe the horrors she had witnessed.

"Will you..." she began, stuttering each syllable. "Will you now?"

Irritated, Ray exclaimed, "Yes I saw the wreckage, and the answer is still no. What part of 'I wouldn't sleep with you, if you were the last woman on Earth' did you not understand?"

"Oh *come on*!"

"Woman, I am *gay*! My boyfriend is literally making breakfast right in the kitchen!"

"Power's out!"

By this point, another man appeared in the doorway, grinning, and holding a pan. "Oh hey, Selena. Camp stove. Want some eggs?"

She sighed. "Sure, Marcus. Thanks."

text:
# The Loop

The last man on earth sat alone in a room. There was a knock at the door.

He stared blankly for a moment and called out sarcastically, "Who is it?"

Silence.

His eyes remained fixed on the door. Slowly, he stood, legs stiff from sitting. As he approached, he first hoped for a raven spouting "nevermore," but then a desperate thought struck him—maybe someone else was alive.

His hand trembled as it reached for the doorknob. He turned it carefully, pulling the door open.

It stopped after an inch.

Metal scraped against metal as the heavy door struck something immovable on the other side. He remembered now—the large machine that had been next to the door when he entered. It must have fallen, blocking his exit.

He slammed his shoulder against the door. Nothing moved.

Panic rising, he scanned the room. No windows. No vents. No food. No water.

Only a chair.

They say even when you lose everything, you still have your sanity. But as he stared at that single chair—the last piece of furniture, perhaps, in the entire world—he felt that slipping too.

He sat down heavily, forcing himself to think. To remember. There was something odd about this room. Something he'd noticed when he first...

When he first what?

His brow furrowed. The memory felt slippery, like trying to grasp smoke. This room. This strange room. What was it about—

There was a knock at the door.

He stared blankly for a moment and called out sarcastically, "Who is it?"

Silence.

His eyes remained fixed on the door. Slowly, he stood, a vague sense of déjà vu washing over him like a cold wave. As he approached, his hand reached for the doorknob, and somewhere in the deepest corner of his fading mind, a voice screamed that he'd done this before.

The door opened an inch.

Metal scraped against metal.

And the loop continued.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The View from P.S. 143

Neil looked longingly at the Earth from the foggy window of his P.S. 143 classroom, forgetting the geography test laying before him.

"Mr. Armstrong, what in the world are you staring at?" asked Mrs. Ronilda, sighing.

"N-nothing," stammered the young Neil.

"Neil, you'll never have any success in life if you continue with this kind of behavior," Mrs. Ronilda droned.

Neil turned in his barely completed test and walked, head bowed, into the cafeteria.

"Hey stupid!" Neil gazed up at the familiar sound of his torturer, Bill. Bill approached with a wolfish grin, slapping Neil on the back of his head. His ears began to ring softly.

"Wow, I'm surprised you're not outside staring at nothing—if I didn't know better, I'd think you're starting to develop a frontal lobe." Bill chuckled at his own joke and gave Neil another shove into a nearby wall. "Get out of my way," Bill sneered before continuing on.

Neil sat alone to eat his lunch, as usual.

Finally, the last bell of the school day tolled and Neil joined the endless stream of children walking outside and putting on their protective gear. Neil took another longing gaze at the distant Earth, suspended in the air, as he began his solitary walk back home.

Neil stopped suddenly. He knew now how to get to Earth.

He eagerly began to take his protective gear off. As his last oxygen tank hit the ground, Neil lay down, unburdened, onto the rough lunar surface. His vision blurred, then faded, as he gazed up.

Neil's view now was Earth, and he was finally traveling to his lonely satellite.

text:
# The Day Innocence Died

I always dreamed of it as a child. Oh yes. A city on its knees beneath my feet; their screams for mercy falling on deaf ears. I took a step forward and felt the inferior beings crushed by my shoe. A crimson splatter of blood painted the street. The crunch of bones could hardly quench my bloodlust.

I grasped two buildings in my palms, slowly closing my fist tighter and tighter and tighter until the shrieks of agony became guttural gurgles of blood. *It felt good.* I threw the remains of the towers to the ground, crushing dozens of runners.

Out of my eye I saw a small dot fleeing. I grunted in laughter. *It's futile. I'll enjoy it.* I twisted and thrust my hand towards the small figure and grasped—a small girlish shriek rang out. I brought the small girl close to my face. In her hands she clutched a small tiger.

I stopped for a moment in my head. A voice almost whispered, "Why are you doing this? We used to be so good. What happened?"

I let out a roar of frustration. I pitched the girl as hard as I could into a building across the street. She disintegrated into a red mist. I watched her stuffed animal fall to the ground. It lay there motionless, dark red liquid stained the felt. Its black button eyes seemed to stare me down.

This brought anger up in my throat. I yelled as loud as I possibly could.

"I DIDN'T LEAVE YOU HOBBES! YOU LEFT ME! SAY SOMETHING YOU FUCK!"

I hurled car after car at the animal until I could no longer breathe.

*Please say something dammit.*

But Hobbes never would again.

text:
# The Web of Darkness

This one's not scared. Why the hell isn't he scared? They're all scared. Ever since I stopped calling the cops and started calling the shots.

"Hey, Spidey. I've always wanted to meet you. Ever since I was a kid." He shakes his head, still wearing that ski mask. "Now here I am, all tied up in that web gunk. All worth it."

"You broke the law, bastard." The body of the old lady lies beside him, still warm. The bullet in her head blew it apart, and maybe that's a spot of brain on my sleeve, but shit. Who cares?

"Yeah, I guess I did. I ain't sorry. She had it coming. Wouldn't let go of that fucking purse."

"You're going to hell, buddy." The man's grinning behind that mask, I can sense it.

"Not tonight."

"Oh? No?" I take a step forward. He shakes his head.

"What are you, 50, 60 now? In all that time, I've never heard you ever killed a baddie. Never."

"Get with the program, champ. How many bodies do I have to make before people start to show some real respect?"

"Sorry, Spidey. I know you're still good, deep down. It's why you fight crime, ain't it? Tiger?"

Tiger. He laughs. The bastard.

One step, and I'm close enough. Close enough to wrap my hands around his head.

*Crack*

Just your neighbourhood friendly Spider-Man.

text:
# SICK PAAARTY, BRUUHAN!

"SICK PAAARTY, BRUUHAN!" James yelled at the host, Carl.

I was seated in the corner, just wanting to get out of there. My palms were sweaty, for I knew the deed I would have to undergo. I could take solace in the fact that, after I got it over with, I could finally go home.

Time to act.

I stood up abruptly, not thinking straight. James was immediately on me.

"Brochacho!! What's the rush? Stay and party, duude!"

I fucking hated this guy. He seemed like he was forcing the whole "stoner" act, and it infuriated me.

"Let. Me. Go. Or you won't *like* what happens next," I said, fed up with his shit.

Suddenly, his phone started ringing. He answered it, talking for about five seconds.

"Shit bro, gotta go," he said, leaving suddenly.

Given the chance, I went to do what I had to do. I rushed to Carl's bathroom and locked the door. Relief washed over me as I finally answered nature's urgent call.

"Thank God," I muttered, washing my hands afterward.

---

**THE NEXT DAY**

Carl came up to me before first class started.

"Hey man, glad you made it last night!"

"Thanks!" I replied. "I almost didn't because of fucking James blocking me."

"Oh. Speaking of James, did you hear he left?"

"Really?"

"Yeah, saw him packing his bags last night. Kinda weird, now that I think about it..."

text:
# The Weight of Tomorrow

Marcus clutched the device, its cool metal pressing against his palm. The machine promised glimpses of his future—but at what cost?

He pressed the button.

Flashes consumed him: WWIII, cities crumbling, ash falling like snow. He gasped, releasing the device.

That night, sleep evaded him. The visions haunted every closed eyelid—the devastation, the screaming, the silence after.

Morning brought little relief. Marcus watched little Freddy play with blocks, oblivious to tomorrow's horrors. His son's laughter felt fragile now, temporary.

"Daddy, look!" Freddy held up his tower.

Marcus knelt beside him, memorizing this moment. If the future was fixed, these present seconds became precious. If it wasn't, he had work to do.

He couldn't change yesterday. But tomorrow? Tomorrow was still unwritten.

Marcus stood, determination replacing dread. He'd spend every remaining moment fighting for a different future—one where Freddy's towers never fell.

text:
# The Answer

The text glowed on my cracked screen before I hurled it into the bushes: "Everyone becomes John Malkovich. Every. Single. One."

I bought a new phone the next day, determined to forget. But the lottery money sat in my account like a curse, accumulating interest I'd never spend.

Three days passed. The new number texted: "You can't escape the truth. Malkovich is waiting."

I blocked it. Another number appeared. Then another.

My classmates started looking different—their expressions too knowing, their head tilts identical. In the cafeteria, I heard whispers: "Malkovich, Malkovich, Malkovich."

The lottery ticket crumbled in my wallet. I realized why I'd won. Not luck. Selection.

That night, I looked in the mirror. My face was shifting, restructuring. The eyebrows thickened. The jawline squared.

My phone buzzed one final time: "Welcome home."

I opened my mouth to scream, but only one word emerged, over and over, in a voice that wasn't quite mine anymore.

The money would pay for my transformation. The afterlife had a cover charge after all.

Being John Malkovich wasn't a movie.

It was a documentary.

text:
# The Architect of Chaos

I started off small. Wrecking trains, downing planes. They were drops in the relative ocean of humanity. Each morning I'd do and redo my birthrate calculations to try and determine whether or not I was even keeping up. Not even close.

With an infinite stretch of time at my disposal, I hit the books and began to specialize. Economics. Politics. Weaponry. Biology. Physics. In my studies I came to accept that destruction of life on a mass scale was a simple matter of causality. The tree of life is not so much a tree at all, but a collection of hastily glued-together popsicle sticks. Civilization and my fellow humans that enjoyed it were not so different.

Set up the dominos in *just* the right way and BOOM, the rest will fall—one by one.

It took time to do, but after only a few decades I'd carved myself out a comfortable position of influence. Based on a fifty-year plan, I started wars and ended others. Millions died. "Accidents" of never-before-seen proportions befell my helpless comrades.

Yet, they persevered. And so did I.

And then one afternoon, as I sat watching hoards of passersby unknowingly stride past a long line of IEDs I'd planted the night before (an acquired hobby), it very suddenly dawned on me; *I* wasn't going to get this done. At least not personally.

What I needed was a *proxy*.

I needed a person so inadvertently destructive that positioning them to create mass chaos and, subsequently, death would not only be possible, but *probable*.

The day it really happened... the day the ball truly started to roll was the day I walked up to his home in Manhattan. Shaking with some kind of lunatic excitement, practically erect, I waited patiently for the first set of entryway doors to open.

And finally, they did.

"Welcome Mr. Demoblican, Mr. Trump will see you now."

text:
# The Loop

You know that feeling when you're driving and suddenly you're halfway down the road and you don't remember driving that stretch? Or you walk into a room and forget why you were there?

I used to joke about it. Multiverse theory, I'd say. Every time there's a blank, another version of me died and I jumped tracks. My friends would laugh.

I'm not laughing now.

I'm covered in blood, holding kitchen knives that drip red onto hardwood. The house is destroyed—furniture overturned, walls gouged, glass everywhere. And there's something hunting me. I feel its presence like breath on my neck.

The memory gaps are worse now. Seconds ago, I was by the couch. Now I'm by the TV. I didn't walk. I just... am.

Another me just died.

The thought arrives with absolute certainty. Somewhere, somewhen, I was standing by that couch when whatever's hunting me finally caught up. And consciousness jumped—found the nearest living version. Me.

Schrödinger's cat, I think wildly. We're always alive from our own perspective because we can only observe ourselves living. The dead versions can't check. So reality keeps threading us through the surviving timelines, one blank spot at a time.

But something's wrong with the loop now. The jumps are too close together. Three meters. Seconds apart.

I'm running out of living versions of myself.

Then it hits me: the only way to break an observation paradox is to witness what you're not supposed to witness. To see your own death.

The moment I finish the thought, I move again.

This time, I'm standing over someone. The knife in my hand is buried in his chest. Short messy brown hair. My face, frozen in shock, staring up at me.

He's—I'm—fading. Like water evaporating. And as he disappears, my memories go with him. Why am I holding knives? Why is there blood? What was I trying to remember?

It's slipping away.

I look at the empty floor, confused.

You know that feeling when you're driving and suddenly you're halfway down the road and you don't remember driving that stretch?

I blink. There's blood on my hands.

Why am I holding knives?
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Final Review

It was perfect artistry. That's the only way I could describe it at the end of this grand display. Its execution was flawless and magnificent, it had everything you could ask for. Anytime I thought I had figured out a pattern, something came and threw me for a loop. But by far the best part is this ending. Poignant and powerful. It was a perfect arc, everything returning from whence it came in silence.

I had been asked to not interfere for the duration, to just sit back and enjoy the show. I'm glad I complied. I couldn't imagine interfering with such genius. Every motif was so subtle, but you were given enough time to figure it out after the fact. It wouldn't be the same if I did interfere, and I admit there were many times I wanted to, but that was part of the point, I now realize.

I was asked one more thing: I couldn't watch the very last moments to see where it all really had come from. I was told it would spoil it. I couldn't imagine anything really ruining this now, but I was convinced this artist knew what it was doing, and to deny that request now? I wouldn't forgive myself for not experiencing every last bit of intent poured into this creation.

I was told when sentience had been removed from all other beings and it was breaking down, I could interact with it. For the first time in eternity I would speak, picking up a line I had learned millions of years ago from some odd-looking creatures of an assortment of colors that were the stars of this show.

In the final moments I opened my mouth in an area of space that could transmit sound—which I learned long ago actually had to pass through tiny things called molecules and could not be transferred through the void of space.

Finally I let the only words out I found fitting.

"I can't wait for the sequel!"

The universe ended.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Night of Stars

The children pointed upward, asking questions no one wanted to answer. Adults looked away, muttering excuses into their collars.

"I live in the here and now."

"It's just part of the natural cycle."

"Why should I bother when the whole neighborhood doesn't care?"

"These budget cuts in our environmental funding will..."

"I'm only one person. It doesn't make a goddamn difference."

Everyone assumed that the starry sky was one of life's constants. Those pinpricks of light that we gazed on as life overwhelmed us. Even as artificial light obscured them, we knew we could go somewhere else and find them. Even as the grass withered, having lost the strength to grow, and the sparkling blue sky turned a dull gray, the stars smiled down on us.

Until one night when the smog's coup was complete.

Earth hid under its dirty blanket without the strength to push off the covers. Sleep had come at last.

The children cried for what they'd never see again. The adults realized, too late, that inevitability was just another word for surrender.

text:
# The Twenty-Ninth

They had a leisurely breakfast. Today, there was no hurry.

Last year had been a leap year; a waste. They'd had to spend the 29th at work, in their usual routines, with their usual friends and family. Not that there was anything wrong with them! But the 29th was their day! Their birthright.

It was better now, Tom thought. Ever since his son had been born, and happened to share his unusual birthday, Tom had thought of the 29th differently.

"Nearly there. Hold still," Tom said, straightening his son's birthday hat.

At first, it had been scary. The first few times, Tom had thought the world had ended; but it doesn't take much to make a toddler feel like that. Then, his Catholic upbringing suggested that he had been Left Behind. Why else would so many people be stuck in bed all day, sleeping without moving, without breathing?

It wasn't till his sixth birthday that he was brave enough to explore his neighborhood while the rest of his family lay unmoving in their beds. Someone spotted him and explained it all.

He'd made sure to be there for his son. He'd explained in bits, slowly over the years. His son was only five, but already comfortable with both the idea of the special day just for them, and the need to not discuss it with anyone else.

The birthday hat was a bit silly; no one needed to be told that today was his son's birthday. But his son had insisted. Tom smiled at the thought of his son's insistent little face.

"Here we are. Disneyland for your birthday! Which ride do you want to go on first?"

The empty park stretched before them, frozen in time, waiting just for them.

text:
# The Last Slice

"That's it!" Poppy screamed. She had always tolerated his devilry, but now he had gone too far. She pointed at the villain's face. "So you think you can do whatever you want? You think you can rule over us like some, some tyrant?"

Her mortal enemy stared back in shock.

"Oh, you think you can push a good person like me around? You think I'm all weak and defenseless and will take whatever crap you give me?" Poppy felt hot blood surge to her face. She trembled with rage. "Well, think again! Today is the day I say 'no more'! Today is the day I fight back! Today—"

She trailed off when she saw tears well up in his eyes. Her words had hurt him. All the anger suddenly left her. She softened her voice. "Look, Alfie..."

Alfie, her eight-year-old brother, let out a huge bawl and ran out the door.

Poppy chased after him. "Alfie, I wasn't really mad at you! Please come back! I'm not mad that you ate the last slice of pie..."

But Alfie was already gone, leaving only the empty pie tin as evidence of his crime—and her overreaction.

text:
# The Forest of Choice

The forest called to me with an urgency that drowned out everything else—my mother's pleas, the church bells tolling in the distance, even my own doubts.

I walked for hours, following an internal compass I didn't know I possessed. When I finally reached the clearing, I understood why no one ever spoke about this place. Words couldn't capture it.

The tree stood alone, impossibly ancient, its bark shimmering with iridescent patterns that hurt to look at directly. At its base sat a simple wooden bowl filled with what looked like water but moved like mercury.

A voice—not heard but *felt*—resonated through my chest: "Choose."

I knew the rules everyone knew without being told. Drink, and the scales would tip. Beauty for intellect. Intellect for beauty. The universe demanded balance, though no one understood why.

I stared at my reflection in that strange liquid. The face looking back was covered in angry red welts, scars mapping a battlefield of adolescence. But behind those eyes lived a mind that had earned scholarships, composed music, led teams.

My hand trembled as I reached for the bowl.

"I was an 8/10 once," I whispered to no one. "Before puberty stole it."

The voice responded: "And what are you now?"

I thought of my valedictorian speech, my acceptance letter to university, the volleyball trophy on my dresser. I thought of my mother saying I was beautiful when clearly I wasn't. I thought of the future everyone else saw for me versus the one I saw in every mirror.

"I don't know," I admitted.

"Then you are not ready."

The forest released me. I walked home, still trapped between two half-measures of myself, understanding finally why no one had ever seen a perfect hundred.

Perfection, perhaps, was never the point.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Witness

The darkness swallows me whole again, but the image burns behind my eyelids—something large, something *deliberate* moving through the shadows toward me.

My heart hammers against my ribs. The drugs are wearing off faster now, adrenaline burning through whatever was in my system. I scramble backward, my hands scraping against the rough concrete until my back hits something solid. A pillar. The cold metal presses against my spine.

"Who's there?" My voice cracks, echoing through the cavernous space.

Footsteps. Slow, measured. Closer.

Then a voice, familiar in a way that makes my stomach drop. "You really shouldn't have seen that, Marcus."

*Marcus.* That's my name. The fog in my mind parts slightly, and fragments come flooding back. The alley. The men in suits. The briefcase changing hands. And me—stupid, curious me—with my camera phone raised.

"I won't tell anyone," I whisper, hating how pathetic I sound. "I deleted the photos. I swear."

A low chuckle echoes through the garage. "We both know that's not true. Cloud backup, Marcus. You really should read the terms and conditions."

A beam of light suddenly pierces the darkness, blinding me. I throw up my hand, squinting against the LED glare of a phone screen.

Behind it, I can just make out Detective Morrison's silhouette. The same detective who'd taken my statement three months ago when my apartment was broken into. The same one who'd seemed so concerned about my safety.

"You're—you're one of them," I stammer.

"'Them' implies there are sides, Marcus. There aren't. There's just people who understand how things work, and people who..." He pauses, and I hear metal sliding against leather. "Well, people who don't."

The match box is still in my hand. Empty now. Useless.

But as Morrison steps closer, I notice something he hasn't—those puddles I saw weren't water.

They were gasoline.

# Word Cannot Open This File

"Fuck, fuck, fuck." The formatting has to be perfect on my term paper or I automatically lose 10%. It's OK, I got this. I always save a copy on Google Drive, just need to login...

"It's much worse for the villagers who will be displaced once their forest is ripped apart by your friends at the paper company."

I stand there, holding my printed paper, suddenly feeling its weight—not just the physical weight, but everything it represents. My grade. My ignorance. My complicity.

# The Unraveling

**December 12th**
This is always a hard time of year. We both like to sneak off and hurt ourselves during the holidays. I'm gonna confront him.

Me.

text:
# The Awakening

I opened my eyes and suddenly everyone was staring at me.

At first I thought it was just my eyes playing tricks on me. I blinked a couple times and continued to look around. Everyone was still looking at me. They looked nervous and scared. This couldn't be real, I thought. I must be dreaming.

Finally I said, "Can I help you guys?"

"Yes you can." A large man two rows behind my seat stood up. "Start talking."

"I don't know what the hell you guys are talking about," I replied.

"Oh really? An hour and a half ago you stood up, killed two flight attendants and said there is a bomb on the plane," said the woman in the seat directly in front of me.

"What? I would never do that," I said.

"How are we supposed to believe you? You told us you would sit back down in your seat and if anyone tried to stop you, you would blow up the plane," the large man said.

"You guys have to listen to me. I have no idea what you're talking about."

"We told the pilot after you fell asleep in your seat half an hour ago," said the man directly behind me.

"What?!" I shouted. I could feel the plane descending. I had no idea what they were talking about, but I knew I was in deep trouble.

"Please don't do this!" I stood up, then everything went black.

---

I woke up in a small dark room. I was handcuffed to a table and there was a large tinted window to my left. A man sat across from me.

"You awake?" he asked.

"Where the hell am I?"

"You're currently in the Philadelphia City Police Station. You have been charged with the murder of two flight attendants and three women," he replied.

"What!"

"Why the hell did you do it?" he asked sternly.

"I have no idea what's going on."

"Don't bullshit me."

"I'm not!"

Two men walked into the interrogation room. "These men are here to take you to your cell. We will continue questioning you later."

As they led me away, one terrifying thought consumed me: *What happened during those lost hours?*

text:
# The Price of Survival

Victor's rage echoed through the dimly lit basement, each word dripping with years of accumulated bitterness. The chain clinked against the concrete as he raised it again.

"Why won't you die?" he screamed, the metal links whistling through the air.

The man's head snapped back, blood spattering the wall. He looked up through swollen eyes, his once-perfect teeth now a shattered mosaic of enamel and gore.

"W-Why won't you?" he whispered, spitting crimson onto the floor. "You elitist prick, I can't freaking afford to die."

The chain fell again with a sickening crack.

"Everywhere I go in this country—people just like you. Rich, well-to-do assholes looking down on me because I drive your car, prepare your food, because I'm not from your Protestant background." Victor's voice cracked with fury. "You make me sick."

He dropped the chain and kicked the man's ribs. A cry of pain. In the corner, his wife and daughter sobbed, their prim clothes now disheveled, hair wild with terror.

"I-I never looked down on you," the man choked. "I always treated you well."

Tears mixed with blood on his face.

Victor grabbed the pruning shears, their blades catching the light.

"You're one tough son of a bitch," he said coldly. "Let's see how much I can cut off before you give up."

His boot connected again.

"You white Anglo-Saxon Protestant motherfucker."

text:
# The Metal Arm of Justice

The sun blazed high in the sky as a lone horse and rider strolled the dusty path. As the traveler stabled his horse, the doors to the nearby cantina flew open and two men tumbled out.

They emerged in an entanglement of hands and legs, and as they stood they faced each other; arms and faces locked in an even combat. Simultaneously, they pushed each other away, and each faltered, but neither fell.

Their capes billowed in the sunlight, and the guns at their hips glinted. One wore a plain black cloak and his pitch-black hair rustled in the wind. His face was young and furious, yet somehow betrayed hints of excitement.

The other wore a more brilliant red and his face was hidden from view by a low-brimmed brown hat. What you could see of his face was grizzled, and a cigar dangled from his lips.

Wordlessly, the two circled each other, eyes locked, and hands itching to draw. As the clock struck noon, a tumbleweed meandered between the two rancheros.

"It's High noon," the man in red commented.

"It surely is," his adversary replied.

In unison the two rivals shouted, "Draw!"

One shot was fired and one man fell dead.

The lone victor plucked his cigar from his lips and played it between his fingers. His arm sparkled in the light, and it became clear it was made entirely of metal.

As he strode away he commented casually, "Can someone call the undertaker?"

text:
# The Day I've Already Died

Every night at midnight, my consciousness tears away like paper, scattering me across the timeline of my own life.

I've lived my death already. January 21st, 2128. Hospital room 304. The steady beep of monitors slowing to a flatline. My granddaughter's hand in mine, her tears warm against my weathered skin. Ninety-five years and twenty-eight days old, and I remember every sensation of my last breath.

But tonight, I might wake up as a seven-year-old on a Tuesday in 2040, or a middle-aged man in 2089. The rule is absolute: no day repeats. 34,725 days total, lived in cosmic shuffle.

I think I'm twenty-four. Mentally, at least. I've kept journals, tried to track which days I've lived, but the math becomes impossible. Some mornings I wake in my infant body, armed with adult knowledge but trapped in uncooperative limbs and wordless frustration. Other times I'm forty, my body aching in unfamiliar ways, while my mind throws tantrums like a toddler.

The lottery wins help. Four times I've remembered the numbers, been the right age with the right access. The money provides comfort, security. It buys me therapists who don't believe me and medications that can't help.

What terrifies me isn't death—I've already experienced that, felt the peaceful surrender, the pain medication's gentle fog. What haunts me is the counter ticking down. Somewhere in the chaos, I've lived thousands of days already. How many remain?

Last week—or was it last year?—I was sixty-seven, teaching my grandson to ride a bike. Tomorrow I might be twelve, taking a math test I've already passed decades ago.

I know how my story ends. I just don't know which page I'm on.

And every midnight, I pray I won't have to live my death twice.

text:
# The Last Fan

I drove cautiously along the shoreline up to the roadblock in front of the compound. Rolls of razor wire topped the intimidating steel barriers. The Rock stood at the roadside. His clothes were muddy and tattered, his eyes bloodshot, and a thick beard curled across his chin. An AK-47 laid on his shoulder. At his side stood two burly bearded henchmen.

I pulled over and got out of the car. I knew he would survive. Even though the government had collapsed, Miami hadn't been nuked. And the guy is a walking stack of lean muscle, doubly as beefy as his henchmen.

"Are you The Rock?" I asked. "I've been dying to meet you."

"What's your name?" The Rock asked me.

"My name is..."

"It doesn't matter what your name is!" he spat back.

I burst out laughing. He grinned.

I miss the 1990s so much. I miss sitting on the couch with my Dad and watching wrestling, watching The Rock lay the smackdown on every jabroni's candy ass. I miss Tiger Woods. I miss *Star Trek: The Next Generation*. I miss the glowing optimism of it all.

Why did we go and elect Trump? He said he was going to use nuclear weapons. Multiple times. On live television.

Oh well. I hadn't laughed in a long time. It felt almost wrong. Is life in a nuclear wasteland supposed to be funny? Not really. But we carry on.

Most hid behind the walls of some compound. I, on the other hand, was yoloing the fuck out of shit, trying to meet my heroes and die a glorious death.

I offered The Rock and his henchmen a Budweiser from my cooler. We sat in front of the compound on the roof of my BMW, watching the sunset, drinking beer.

Next on the to-meet list: Patrick Stewart.

text:
# The Last Supper

The brandy swirls in my crystal glass, amber liquid catching the dying light of a poisoned sunset. Man, this is something else. I can't hardly tell you what it's like to be sitting out here. Even as the president of MegaConsolidated, the world's largest corporation, this is something else.

Those foreign folk were right—rhino horn and tiger penis sure do make you feel potent. Especially when you're the last man on Earth, and they were the last surviving wild examples of their species, and you shot them that morning, then had them prepared with the polar bear and whale steaks from your hunting trip to the Arctic yesterday, to be cooked up special for this last meal here on planet Earth.

It's not like we don't have plenty more up in the zoos on MegaConsolidated Earth 2, and it's not like the oceans or forests were much good after that last MegaConsolidated accident, so you could say I was doing them a favor by putting them out of their misery.

Well, that's the price of progress. I've got to make that money, and you can't make an omelette without breaking a few eggs, and we've got a whole new planet so full of resources my guys say it will take a couple of centuries to use them all up, and they say we'll be able to get to even more planets from there.

MegaConsolidated is going to be the biggest company in the universe at this rate.

Hell, I better stop jabbering and finish my steaks. I've got a rocket waiting for me.

Behind me, Earth wheezes its final breath.

text:
# The Secret of the Ruins

*So it's still here. Delnarh kept his word then, that old bugger,* Darren thought, staring at the munted rock, smirking.

"Listen kids, we're going to set up camp here," he said to the group behind him.

Sharna glanced at the other group members, puzzled. "But Mr. Dark, these ruins could collapse at any minute. Why don't we just go outside?"

As if on cue, a loud crash echoed from further down the hallway outside the room. The other students murmured their agreement, looking up at the ceiling in fear.

Darren scoffed. "Oh please, this is soft rock. If it collapses into you, the worst you'll get is a scratch." He kicked out at a nearby pillar. "See?"

The pillar rumbled and made a clicking noise. A door at the back of the room swung open.

Markus, a twelve-year-old from Australia chosen for his drone flying skills, hopped up. "Blimey sir! You've found a secret passage, you have. Can I check her out, mate?"

The other children were up now. Darren could see something approaching from the darkness. The group gasped as it came into full view.

Smirking, Darren held his arms out in an embrace. "This, kids, is an old friend of mine—Delnath."

Delnath towered over them, its big black alien features like something from a movie. The only recognizable part of the creature was a blonde wig of hair.

"*Hello...*" Delnath cooed.

"Blimey Mr. Dark, how do you know this thing!" Markus screeched.

Darren turned. "Oh sorry kids, Delnath used to live on Earth. He's actually Trump's biological father."

"Donald Trump?"

Grinning, the alien whispered, "*Donald...*"

text:
# Beneath the Waves

The broadcast flickered across the holoscreen in the dimly lit cantina. Kael nursed his drink, watching Captain Nev'ko's face twist with practiced indignation.

"Liar," muttered the Quarren beside him.

Kael didn't respond. He'd been there—not at the attack, but three weeks prior, deep beneath Manaan's endless ocean. The "scientific platforms" housed rows of AA-ST prototypes, sleek killing machines designed to turn aquatic worlds into Imperial strongholds. He'd seen the test runs himself, captured footage of the transports tearing through the water, armed to the teeth.

The footage now sat encrypted in his datapad, too dangerous to transmit, too important to destroy.

On screen, Jav'en Delto—a reporter with more courage than sense—pressed the captain about the rumors before being shut down. Kael respected that. Real journalism was a dying art under the Empire's "C-Net Broadcast," their sanitized propaganda machine.

"1,320 dead," the anchor had said. What they hadn't mentioned: 800 were clone soldiers. 200 were scientists complicit in weapons development. The rest were support staff, collateral damage in a war that grew uglier each day.

Kael understood the Rebellion's calculus, even as it sickened him. Destroy the AA-STs now, or face them deployed against Mon Calamari, Dac, Kamino—any world that might harbor resistance.

He finished his drink and stood. The data had to reach Rebel command.

Behind him, the broadcast moved to sports. The Empire's favorite distraction—keep them entertained while the galaxy burned.

Outside, Manaan's perpetual rain felt like tears.

text:
# THIS IS FOR MY SISTER

The courtroom exploded into chaos.

"THIS IS FOR MY SISTER, YOU SICK FUCK!" Ricardo Berenta's voice echoed off the marble walls as he fired.

The Joker's head snapped back, the bullet punching through his left eye and erupting from his skull in a crimson spray. Commissioner Gordon, passing behind the defendant, caught the exit round in the crown of his head. Both men crumpled simultaneously.

Screams erupted. Batman launched himself forward, a dark blur cutting through the pandemonium. His gauntleted hand closed around the gun just as Ricardo's finger spasmed on the trigger.

The third shot found the only weakness—the armpit junction where armor plates met. Batman gasped as the bullet severed his axillary artery and tore into his lung.

"No!" Ricardo screamed as officers tackled him. "I didn't want to shoot you! It was an accident!"

But Bruce Wayne could no longer hear. He collapsed beside his dying nemesis, drowning in his own blood. Each breath brought wet, rattling agony. He closed his eyes, accepting the inevitable.

Then—laughter. Weak, bubbling, but unmistakable.

Bruce forced his eyes open. The Joker lay in a spreading pool of blood, that hideous grin somehow still intact.

"It's ironic," the Clown Prince wheezed. "So many tries..." He coughed, painting his teeth red. "And I don't get to kill you."

Another bloody laugh, weaker now.

"Joke's on me... ha... ha... haaaa—"

The laughter stopped. The Joker's eye stared at nothing.

Batman felt the darkness closing in, surprisingly peaceful. The pain faded to distant noise. His lips moved, forming his final words:

"Mom... Dad... I'm coming now."

The Dark Knight's vigil ended where it began—with a senseless act of violence in Gotham's broken justice system.

text:
# Good Bye, Cruel World

"Good bye, cruel world," I said as I let the cool steel of the railing slip from my fingers.

Time dilated as I fell, the wind tugging at my hair, pulling at my body almost as if it was trying desperately to pull me up and stop my fall. I closed my eyes just before I hit the water.

Everything was white when I opened my eyes. No matter how I blinked, everything held the steady fuzz of blurriness that comes after a long night of drinking.

"Is... is this heaven?" I whispered.

"No, this is Saint Murphy's," an annoyed voice responded. "The bridge you jumped off was two stories tall."

I stared at the nurse, reality crashing down harder than my body had.

"Congratulations, you're alive and your legs are broken. You'll be lucky if you can walk again."

Turns out I didn't make it into heaven. Instead, I get to live in my own personal hell—trapped in a body that won't cooperate, forced to face everything I tried to escape.

text:
# The Birth of Darkness

"Why... why would you tell me?!? Why couldn't you have let me be? I would've remained blissfully ignorant! Why... why why why!!!"

They stared at me. Eyes I was so used to seeing full of amusement and cheerfulness were turned cold, distrustful, shunning.

Joseph spoke first, a hint of belittling in his voice. "It was time to reveal you for who you are. Any plans you have are now exposed."

"What plans!? You have known me all your life, all of you have! When have I ever done anything remotely evil?"

Mary's usually sympathizing eyes now held determination. "Evil is known to be very cunning. To hide it makes it obvious you hid it all from us. I'm sorry but for the good of humanity, it is time we exposed you... and contain you."

Those last three words. They've been swirling in my head all these weeks.

Joseph, Mary, John, and Myra took me away then. I don't know what happened to my parents, friends, or anyone I knew. I was locked up in a stone tower, far away. No access to the outside world. Only given a few small things, blessings from "Kindness" Myra herself.

If only they knew.

I was truthful, honest, when I said I had no plans. I have never done anything evil in my life. I hoped for a while they would see I was innocent. But the longer it took, the bitter I grew.

Mary was right—I am cunning. I was tested and marked a genius in school. I guess that is what made them fear me most.

Well, I shall give them a reason to fear me.

If only they knew, evil is not born. It is created by dishonesty, half-truths, the unkind, and hopelessness. They woke the evil in me.

As I walk free of this failed prison, they shall reap what they sowed.

text:
# The Heist That Wasn't

Andrei prayed all the way to BNR, just like he always did. I already briefed everyone, and they knew what they were in for. I parked the van, covered the plate in chrome, and armed the explosive. Breaking the doors would've been much more fun than going through the sliding doors, but what can you do?

We put our masks on, loaded our guns and shouted the usual. Little did we know, the bank was empty and everyone was down on the ground, all taped up. I have never bumped into such a situation before, so my reaction was more like fear than surprise. Doors blasted open, drill marks, and empty bags.

We knew what we were up against: pros. The best of the best.

I told my team we should get the fuck out of the bank but it wasn't that easy. A tall man, dressed in a red suit and with an iron mask appeared. "Where you go?" he asked.

For a short while, I thought I was a goner. The man suddenly burst into maniacal laughter that echoed throughout the bank's massive lobby. "Just joking. You friends. You can relax."

We talked a bit, but every time I asked him about the purpose of the heist, he dodged the question. "No talking. Must continue. You go now. Police come. You cover us."

Of course I didn't agree with him, but my first reaction was met with a gun's cold barrel glued to my chin. "You do that. Now."

As I was searching for my team, the police arrived. The Man in Red shouted some nonsense gibberish and ran to our van to escape. Little did he know, our van had an armed charge, and when he attempted to start the car, it exploded in a fiery show.

The police arrived, and here we are."

"Wait, you're telling me *you* stopped that guy? You're telling me you are not innocent?"

"Yeah, sorta."

*Bzzzzzt.*

"Okay guys, let him go, he's innocent. For now."

---

*BNR: Banca Națională a României (National Bank of Romania)*

# The Magic Bag

I reached into my bag and out came one half of a watermelon. I was confused but I put it in the cart. Maybe it would give me an edge to winning. My friends and I made a bet to see who could freak out the cashier with only three items or less from the supermarket. Even though this weird stuff's coming out of my bag, they wouldn't know that anyway. It seemed to be helping me in my struggle to find three things.

Normally a stray pen or paper would come out whenever I so desperately needed them for class. I checked my watch, and I noticed that it was almost closing time. All of my friends seemed to be running to the cashier and line up one by one. Dammit, it seemed that they already had some cool combination. Meanwhile I was stuck with just this half of a watermelon.

I was running out of ideas. I'm not good with these kinds of games. After walking through so many aisles I couldn't seem to find anything that would fit with the damn watermelon. It's not like I can put it back into my bag. I would have to explain to the cashier why I have one half of a watermelon with me.

I rummaged through my knapsack and I found some superglue. What? One half of a watermelon and superglue. What the hell would I do with these? I thought about getting a couch or a toaster to explain this situation, but I was running out of time and I could see at the far end of the supermarket that my friends were just waiting for me to finish.

In an act of desperation, I put my hand in my bag one last time. I looked around and no one seemed to be watching, and then I pulled out another half of a watermelon.

I grinned wickedly as I approached the register. Two watermelon halves and superglue. The cashier's face would be priceless.

It seems like I'm going to win this bet.

text:
# Day 35: The Swiss Microverse

Dr. Helena Müller wiped condensation from her protective visor as she approached the containment chamber. Inside, suspended in a magnetic field, floated what looked like an ordinary basketball—if basketballs glowed with the intensity of molten steel.

"Two millimeters this week," her colleague announced. "It's stabilizing."

The Swiss Microverse, as the media had dubbed it, had emerged from the Large Hadron Collider thirty-five days ago. A pocket universe, born from a quantum fluctuation that shouldn't have been possible. And Switzerland wanted to keep it.

"The UN Security Council is in emergency session again," Helena said, checking her tablet. "France is threatening sanctions if we don't relinquish control."

"Control?" Her colleague laughed bitterly. "We can't even move it without heat suits. Some control."

Through the thermal shielding, they watched the sphere pulse. Microscopic analysis had revealed the impossible: galaxies swirling within, time accelerating at incomprehensible rates. While days passed outside, epochs unfolded within. Primordial clouds had already condensed into stellar nurseries.

"There could be life in there," Helena whispered. "Civilizations rising and falling while we argue about jurisdiction."

"The Swiss flag will look ridiculous planted on their worlds," her colleague mused darkly.

A technician rushed in. "Temperature's dropping faster now. We might be able to transport it within the month."

"Transport it where?" Helena asked. "To Geneva? New York? Beijing?"

The question hung unanswered. Meanwhile, inside the basketball-sized cosmos, perhaps a billion years had passed. Perhaps creatures were looking up at their stars, wondering if they were alone in the universe.

They weren't alone. They were a political bargaining chip, cooling slowly in a Swiss laboratory, waiting for humanity to decide their fate.

text:
# The Ranch Incident

"Could I get some Italian dressing? Maybe Thousand Island?"

The waiter looked at me like I had just murdered his mother and then walked away without speaking another word.

"What's wrong with you?" asked my brother George from across the table. "Are you trying to get us thrown out of here?"

"I just don't like ranch dressing."

Everyone near us stopped what they were doing to give me looks of shock and horror.

"Is that a crime?"

"It's damn close to one, Derek. Just eat the ranch and don't cause a scene."

The waiter came back with my salad, covered in extra ranch dressing. "Italian style, they like extra ranch." The waiter seemed pleased with his revenge.

"Thank you," George said for me. The waiter walked away.

"I'm not eating that." I stared at the mess of ranch on my salad. "There's more dressing than salad. It's disgusting."

"Excuse me," the woman at the next table interrupted. "Could you please not speak that way in front of my child? I don't want him thinking this kind of talk is appropriate."

"Uh, what?" I didn't swear, at least I don't think I did.

"Please don't speak that way about the dressing. That's the last time I'm going to ask."

*Fuck this.* Is this woman for real? Are these people for real?

I looked George in the eye and pulled out a gun, feeling like I'm the least insane person in this building.

"AM I THE ONLY ONE AROUND HERE WHO DOESN'T LIKE RANCH DRESSING?"

And that's how I got put in jail in Hidden Valley.

# The Pouch Paradox

I sat there, mouth agape, surrounded by debris from what used to be my ceiling. My "generic best friend reassurance" playbook had just been thrown out the window—or rather, where my roof used to be.

"Joey, we need to have a very different kind of appointment," I muttered, still staring at his stomach, which now looked completely normal.

"Does this mean I can have more time on your schedule?" Joey asked innocently.

"Kid, you just vaporized a giant crab monster with your... marsupial anatomy. I think we're past scheduling concerns."

Joey shrugged. "I told you I had a pouch. You didn't believe me."

He was right. The kid who wanted facts, evidence, and proof had literally been carrying the evidence around in his belly the whole time. Meanwhile, I'd been the one feeding him baloney.

"So," I said carefully, "how long have you known about the... light blast... pouch thing?"

"Since birth, I guess? Doesn't everyone have one?"

"No, Joey. They decidedly do not."

He tilted his head thoughtfully. "That explains why my PE teacher looked so confused during the changing room incident."

I pinched the bridge of my nose. This was going to be a long appointment—possibly my entire career. But at least now when Joey asked questions, I'd take them seriously.

"Joey?"

"Yes, Mr. Hammond?"

"We're going to need a bigger office."

text:
# The Bounty Hunter's Blunder

The rafters creaked slightly as I adjusted my position, blowpipe pressed against my lips. My heart hammered against my ribcage—this was it. Two thousand dollars for one clean shot. My ticket out of poverty, my proof that I belonged in this deadly profession.

*When he arrives, I will shoot the poison dart from my blowpipe into his neck. I will wait to fire until he examines the inflatable decoy near the fireplace,* I rehearsed mentally, watching the door like a hawk.

Boots scraped concrete outside. My muscles tensed.

"He's here! Get ready..." I whispered, trying to steady my trembling hands.

The door swung open. The cowboy—a massive, barrel-chested man—lumbered inside, releasing a weary sigh. He headed straight for the refrigerator, completely oblivious to my presence above.

*Now!* I pressed the decoy's release button.

Nothing.

I jabbed it repeatedly. Still nothing.

"Oh this is bad, real bad!" Sweat beaded on my forehead. My first mission, and the equipment was malfunctioning!

Then—a soft hiss. The cowboy's head snapped toward the fireplace. He approached cautiously, boots thudding on wooden planks.

"What in the hell is this?" he growled, bending down.

"Three... two... one, FIRE!"

I exhaled sharply, launching the dart.

In that precise instant, the decoy exploded open with violent force, springs and fabric erupting outward. It struck the cowboy's forehead, sending him stumbling backward.

The dart sailed past his falling body, ricocheted off the inflated decoy, and—

Sharp pain pierced my neck.

*No...*

The rafters spun. My grip loosened. I tumbled backward, the world tilting sideways as poison coursed through my veins.

The ground rushed up to meet me—*thud.*

Through darkening vision, I heard it: deep, rolling laughter. The cowboy, clutching his head, absolutely howling with amusement.

Then—nothing.

text:
# The Rupturing Frame

The rupturing frame of the abyss pulsated in and out of existence, shuddering once more before the looming, towering shadowed figure spoke again.

"Which vessel?!" the figure beckoned.

"Where... no clouds, golden gate, not even a fiery hellhole? Um, I'm sorry... sorry," I blurted out like a frightened child.

"The swine of you is unworthy of forgiveness. Hurry now, there isn't long."

I tried to focus on what surrounded me, but lightheadedness overwhelmed my senses. Everything warped in and out of focus, as though I had just awoken or was losing consciousness entirely. I struggled to imagine each option presented before me—my imagination forcing painful viewings of potential lives. One I knew clearly as an ant, another, with its colors, obviously a bee. Many others I remained ignorant of, unable to grasp what I was seeing. None like me.

"Why can I no longer be human?"

"Choose now, you disgusting lowly rot."

"Uh... um... please! Please! I think I deserve some answ—"

Sirens deafened me as I saw contorted metal surrounding my body. I thought of what I'd just dreamed, but lost the thread as a slow, strong punch enveloped my stomach, morphing into tearing, sharp pain—as though I'd swallowed glass.

People shouted orders, followed by loud machinery. Looking down, I saw a strange bent object squeezed into my flesh, embedded where my belly button used to be. I wondered how I'd eat with this injury, but exhaustion overwhelmed me. I decided to close my eyes, hoping the pain would be blocked.

I heard loud, sparking sawing nearby—somehow soothing. Out there, my rescuers breaking in, breaking in to cradle me to sleep.

The abyss waited patiently.

Between worlds, between breaths, between the sawing and the silence, I understood: the choice had already been made.
