text:
# The Eternal Curse

"I grant wishes." 

It was a simple statement, but the gravity of it was lost on me. I stared at the slightly blue-tinged bald man in front of me. His eyes held jovial delight, his smile knowing. It felt like I was a fly that had wandered into a spider's lair.

"Seriously? How is that even possible?" I shifted uncomfortably in my hospital bed.

I'd grown up hearing stories of genies and lamps, but I never thought I'd find one, let alone be found by one. The blue-ish man's smile widened. "I grant wishes," he repeated, stepping closer to sit on my bed, stretching the covers tight. I felt constricted.

I paused, considering whether to call the nurse and have this curiously terrifying man thrown out. A sigh escaped my lips as the thought that had consumed me for months resurfaced—a constant reminder. I'm lying on my deathbed. Any experience is a good experience.

I decided to humor him.

"Okay," I steeled myself, stopping my hand from shaking. "I wish it was over. I want death. I want to end the waiting. I'm tired of living, tired of seeing everyone's pity-ridden faces as they tiptoe around me. If you're really going to grant me a wish, then let me be free."

I thought it impossible, but his grin widened even more—unnaturally wide. His eyes became slits with just a gleam of red showing through the darkness of the night.

He simply got up and left.

I still don't know what happened since that night, but it's been one hundred and eighty years. I haven't aged. I haven't died. Any injury I sustain rapidly fixes itself. I've jumped from buildings, hung myself, shot myself. I've had to hide from the government and from companies.

My life has been hell from that night forward. The night I was visited by a devil. The night my wish wasn't granted.

Or perhaps it was—just not the way I intended. I wished to be free from death, and he gave me exactly that: freedom *from* death, not freedom *through* it. The cruelest irony of all.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Heist That Went to Shit

Twelve years of planning, surveillance, and patience—all for this singular moment. The metal scanner stood unguarded, a miracle I'd orchestrated through carefully timed laxatives in the guard's coffee. Twenty billion in gold bars waited beyond.

Then my stomach twisted violently.

*No. Not now.*

The irony wasn't lost on me: the cop and I, both victims of desperate biology. But I'd sacrificed too much to abandon the plan over basic human functions.

I sprinted across the marble lobby, each step a gamble against my rebellious bowels. The scanner's control panel gleamed ahead—fifty feet, forty, thirty—

My body mutinied.

The explosive release hit mid-stride. I collapsed, writhing on the polished floor as twelve years of dreams liquefied alongside my dignity. Stunned civilians gawked. Approaching officers shifted from concern to disgust when they spotted my concealed weapon.

The handcuffs felt almost merciful.

"Guess you really *crapped out* on this one," Officer Martinez chuckled, steering me toward the squad car.

"Should've trusted your *gut* instinct," added his partner.

The jokes continued through booking, processing, and my cell assignment. Somewhere, that guard was probably experiencing his own catastrophic relief, blissfully unaware he'd been drugged.

Karma, apparently, doesn't discriminate.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Shadow's Descent

I stood before a large door with a deep staircase descending so low I couldn't see a bottom. Although I didn't understand why my shadow wanted me to go down there or what she wanted, I knew I had to. I scratched at my head, then took my sword from its scabbard on my back. I had no idea how to use the thing, but having it at least made me feel better, a whole lot more than the slingshot anyway. In my other hand, I grabbed the shield that also hung across my back.

*It's okay,* I told myself. *Jake is always complaining about the puzzles here, not the enemies, so how hard can they be to kill? And I know my MS in mathematics can help me through any puzzles I might find down there.*

I started down the stairs, praying watching Jake play this game would help me down there.

Several hours later, I reminded myself to watch Jake play more as I attempted to heal scorch marks all over my body. Turns out mathematical proofs don't help when fire-breathing gargoyles attack. My shadow flickered mockingly on the dungeon wall, seemingly laughing at my overconfidence.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Fool's Eternity

**Four thousand years.**

I drift in the crystalline prison, screaming without voice, raging without breath. The tour guide's words echo through my consciousness like daggers.

*Fool.* They call *me* the fool.

When I discovered the technique, I was humanity's greatest scholar. I unlocked immortality itself! While others timidly placed fragments of their souls into totems—keeping one foot in mortality's river—I *transcended*.

Total transference. Complete lichdom. Eternal consciousness.

I didn't account for one thing: I needed a *body* to interact with the world.

The first century, I watched my flesh decay, helpless. The second, I felt every moment of putrefaction, unable to scream. By the third, only my head remained in this glass case, preserved by their primitive chemicals.

Children press sticky fingers against my prison. Their laughter is torture. The guide drones on about "cautionary tales" and "balanced wisdom."

*Balanced wisdom?* These insects understand nothing! They're content with their pathetic half-measures, living their brief centuries, experiencing actual *death* when their totems finally break.

But me? My totem is carved from star-metal, virtually indestructible. I'll outlast civilizations, universes perhaps, aware and impotent, forever.

The children tap the glass. If I had eyes, they would weep.

I discovered immortality.

I achieved it.

And now I know—there are fates worse than death. An eternity of them.

*Get back here*, I want to scream. *Smash the case. Destroy the totem.*

*Please.*
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Dawn

The sun shined through the curtains. As the room became brighter and brighter, Ami woke up. She was inside her house, but no one else was there. As she looked outside, the bright red morning was still the same. Yet no one was there.

After a while, she left her house. "Where are mommy and daddy?" she wondered. But then she realized it wasn't just her parents. She couldn't find anyone.

Still, she was happy as well. Dad wouldn't shout. Mom wouldn't hit. She wouldn't be hurt... but she was also lonely. No one else was there. No one.

Crying, and crying, and crying, she began to look further and further. Her stomach started to rumble. As she was still in her home town, she went back to her house. She pushed a few buttons in her kitchen and got breakfast. Not crying anymore, but lonely and worried, she began to eat.

The poor girl didn't realize what was going on. She didn't realize that her parents left. A few hours ago, her parents received a message: 'There is enough room left for two persons.' Back then, they had to choose between their own lives or their child. They chose their own.

It became warmer, Ami realized. The sun seemed to get bigger as well. She didn't know what was going on. Outside the glass wall of the sky, the sun became brighter and brighter. She could not know what it meant, as she did not receive any emergency message.

The predicted explosion time of the Sun was a few years off. All of the citizens from Earth needed to evacuate immediately.

Ami sat there. Not knowing what was going to happen. All alone, for her final minutes. Her parents, far away, in safety, not caring.

As she experienced her final moments, a strange peace settled over her. At least the shouting had stopped.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Defiant Syllable

Among us are those who can pull old recollections from their minds of a time when a certain sound was still said. That forbidden sound, which all of us know but do not say.

I watch the broadcaster's face go red, then pale. His voice trembles through the speakers: "I just can't do it. Kim Jong Un didn't take over the world."

My children freeze, their evening rice halfway to their mouths.

"It's KorEA," he shouts, that dangerous vowel splitting the air like lightning.

The transmission cuts. Static hisses. When the image returns, the chair is empty, a dark stain spreading across its cushion.

My daughter whispers, "Papa, what happened?"

"He said the forbidden sound," I explain, pulling her close. "The hard 'eh.'"

"But why?"

I have no answer. None of us do. We've forgotten the reasons behind our chains, memorized only their weight. Every day we bend our tongues around the absence, saying "Kor" and "Americ" and "Europ," swallowing that vowel like poison we dare not spit.

Tonight, I dream of the broadcaster's final word, that long, defiant "Eeeeee..." stretching into eternity—a sound that meant freedom, or at least, the freedom to die speaking truth.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Mistake

The blaring of the firing horn blasts my ears again. I am thankful for my earplugs dulling the sharp tweet—I would have gone deaf long ago otherwise.

Our company was one of those standard factory line gigs. We made important parts that had to be in spec. Quality assurance was high and considered the most important in the company. It's just a pity we never kept anyone for long. As soon as one defect was allowed through, everyone behind you on the line was fired.

Nails were chewed, tears were seeped, and hands were wrung, but to no avail.

Ned was a wiry man, and stubby. At only four feet, he still towered over everyone by his presence—he was formidable, having total control over his kingdom. Hiring offices loved him, and his employees all hated him.

I was his right-hand man, handing out firing notices to everyone who brought his ire, who failed the company by letting faulty product through.

I felt him approach from behind and turned to face him. His face was stony. My heart sank. That look meant a mistake was made.

"Sorry Teddy, but you know the rules."

My heart sunk, and my stomach twisted as I took the paper from his outstretched hand.

"Incorrect firing," it said.

I was supposed to fire Cinderella, not Rindercella.

The horn would blast for me now. I had become what I'd always administered—another casualty of perfection's impossible standard.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Ultimate IT Call

The viewport revealed Earth below, a blue marble growing smaller by the second. Jason Chen adjusted his glasses—a nervous habit he'd never broken—and followed the gray-skinned Zenthari technician down a corridor that hummed with alien harmonics.

"We are grateful for your expertise," the alien said through its translator. "Our civilization abandoned this technology three thousand cycles ago."

Jason nodded. All those years fixing printers, wrestling with networks, and explaining to executives why their password couldn't be "password123" had somehow prepared him for this moment. Humanity's greatest contribution to galactic society: we still remembered how computers actually *worked*.

The server room—if you could call it that—was the size of a warehouse. Crystalline structures pulsed with dying light, and holographic displays flickered ominously. The Zenthari had achieved faster-than-light travel, mastered gravity manipulation, and conquered entropy itself. But their AI-managed systems had abstracted away all the fundamental knowledge.

Now their ancient backup systems, needed to decrypt critical historical archives, were failing. And nobody remembered how to fix them.

Jason cracked his knuckles and approached the main console. The interface was alien, but the logic—the beautiful, frustrating logic of troubleshooting—was universal. Diagnostic patterns, error cascades, the subtle signs of hardware failure versus software glitches.

He located what appeared to be a power conduit and traced it to its source.

"So," he said, channeling every help desk technician who'd ever lived. "Have you tried turning it off and then on again?"

The Zenthari exchanged confused looks.

"We... had not considered this approach."
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Spell

Robert's chest heaved as consciousness slammed into him like a freight train. His hands clawed at the sheets, eyes wide and unseeing in the pre-dawn darkness. Something was wrong. Everything was wrong.

The note caught his attention—a pale rectangle against the wall, letters bold and black. **ROBERT**.

He knew that shape. Didn't he?

His bare feet touched cold floor. Each step toward the wall felt like wading through fog, his mind grasping at phantoms of meaning that dissolved upon contact. The paper crinkled beneath his trembling fingers as he peeled it free.

**ROBERT**.

His lips moved, forming sounds without comprehension. He unfolded the note with the careful deliberation of someone handling an artifact from another world. Inside, more symbols marched in neat rows, intimate and utterly alien.

His eyes traced the curves and lines. Some part of him—buried deep, drowning—screamed that this mattered. That these marks were *important*. His breathing quickened as he stared at the meaningless scrawl, willing understanding that would never come.

The man who had been Robert once—who had been clever enough to exploit the fundamental laws of magic itself—stood holding the confession of his greatest triumph and ultimate sacrifice.

He had succeeded perfectly.

Too perfectly.

In his arrogance, he had calculated the cost of making billions forget magic. But he had failed to account for one critical detail: that reading, too, was a learned skill. A memory. And he had traded *everything* to fuel his spell.

The paper slipped from his fingers, drifting to the floor like a fallen leaf.

Robert—no, not Robert anymore, just a man—turned back toward the bed. Its rumpled warmth called to him, the only comfort in a world stripped of context. He crawled beneath the covers and pulled them tight around his shoulders.

Outside, dawn broke over a world cleansed of magic. People would wake confused, wondering about gaps in their memories, about abilities they could no longer quite recall. But they would adapt. They would rebuild.

Inside, a man closed his eyes against the morning light.

He knew only one thing now: the softness of his bed.

It would have to be enough.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Last Hunger

The rain began as a whisper, then a roar.

*You tell me...* I thought defiantly, as thunder rolled across the dead cities. The visitors—tall, luminescent, untouched by our curse—stood just beyond my reach. Their silvered suits reflected my wasted form.

"Our scanners indicated you are the last human. That is why we have arrived."

I shifted, chains clanking against the metal chair. Blood trickled from where the shackles bit into my wrists—the only restraint that mattered anymore. In their triple-pupiled eyes, I recognized something familiar: hunger. Not like mine, but close enough.

"So..." One stepped closer. "Explain to us what happened."

*There was a contagion. It leaked into the water supply.*

They exchanged glances, their antenna-like appendages twitching with concern.

*At first it was isolated...* Each breath burned in my desiccated lungs. *They thought burning the bodies would contain it. Instead, they aerosolized it. Within days, it spread globally.*

The visitors retreated slightly, understanding blooming in their alien features.

*The hunger consumes you. The thirst is all we know.*

Then I saw it—the first raindrop striking the contaminated soil outside. My lips cracked into something resembling a smile.

They had come to document Earth's extinction, to catalog humanity's end. But they didn't understand. The contagion wasn't our death.

It was our evolution.

As the rain intensified, I felt them stirring below—thousands, millions, buried in the earth, waiting for the water to wake them. To wake *us*.

"Last human?" I thought, as my chains began to corrode.

*No. The first of something new.*
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Ultimate Endurance Challenge

"So... we just sit here and look at pictures of cats?" Kyle asked with genuine curiosity.

Ricky-Dave shrugged. "Yeah, but apparently the goal is for me to not catch you looking at cats. So when I walk by you have to be looking at spreadsheets or something."

"We do that for eight hours straight? How is that extreme, in any way?"

Gina peeked her head out from behind her makeshift cubicle. "Well, if I catch you looking at cats you don't get to eat that day."

Ricky-Dave threw a big thumbs down at Gina. "That's insane. Did you read this on those Wikipedia archives? Those are supposed to be satire," Gina spoke in a heavy patronizing tone.

Ricky-Dave frowned. "Not quite. I looked it up on Ask Googlebook."

"The key to working," Ricky-Dave continued, "and essentially why it's considered the greatest endurance challenge of all time is one: people did this for decades, almost non-stop. And two: if you don't keep up to date on the constant stream of cat pics, you will be ostracized by your peers for not being 'with the times' and this leads to loneliness and dangerous levels of stress which can lead to suicide."

"What the hell was wrong with people back then?" Kyle sat stunned.

"The constant juggling of fear of starvation with the fear of social abandonment was the ultimate rush, so much that when people got home they could barely move, speak or even engage in sexual activities. This period of inactivity was referred to as 'peak hours for Netflix'." Ricky-Dave was going over the research verbatim.

"I don't think I want to do this anymore." Concern grew on Gina's face.

"Yeah, there's a good reason people don't work anymore," Kyle said, standing up and noping the fuck out.

text:
# The Weight of Second Place

I stopped trying to compete on Tuesday.

It wasn't dramatic—no slammed doors or tearful confessions. I simply looked at my report card, saw the sea of C's I'd worked myself sick for, and felt nothing. That same afternoon, Maya casually mentioned she'd been moved up to advanced calculus. She's twelve.

The funny thing about being the oldest is that you get all the responsibility but none of the glory. "Watch your sister." "Set a good example." "You should know better." Meanwhile, Maya collects achievements like other kids collect Pokemon cards.

At dinner, Dad asked her about her Mandarin lesson. Mom showed everyone Maya's watercolor that her teacher wants to submit to some competition. I mentioned I'd finally passed my driving test.

"That's nice, honey," Mom said, already turning back to Maya's painting.

I used to hate her for it. I'd watch her fingers fly across piano keys I'd struggled with for years, listen to relatives gush about her poetry, see Dad's eyes light up in a way they never did for me. The jealousy was like swallowing glass.

But here's what I've realized: Maya never asked for this either. She never demanded to be the favorite or tried to make me feel small. She just... is. Extraordinary without effort, while I'm exhausting myself trying to be ordinary.

Last night, I found her crying over her sketch pad. "It's not good enough," she whispered. "Nothing's ever good enough."

I held my baby sister while she sobbed, and something shifted. Her gift is also her burden. Everyone's expectations, all the time.

Maybe I'm not the prodigy. Maybe I'll never make them proud the way she does. But at least I get to be myself—messy, average, gloriously unremarkable me.

Maybe that's worth something too.

Maybe.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# The Memory Keeper

Marcus stared down at Earth, watching the anniversary documentary about his crimes. Two hundred years. *Two hundred years* of watching, waiting, remembering.

He'd been a serial killer—one of the worst. Fifteen victims. His name still echoed through true crime podcasts, Halloween specials, and university criminology courses. Meanwhile, the woman who'd lived next door to him, sweet Mrs. Chen who'd fed half the neighborhood and volunteered at shelters for forty years, had passed through the gates after just three generations.

"It's not punishment," the Guide had explained when Marcus first arrived. "It's understanding."

He'd watched his victims' families crumble. Watched survivors battle PTSD. Watched his crimes inspire copycats, security systems, and fear that rippled outward like stones in a pond. Each wave of consequence kept his memory alive, kept him *here*, waiting.

The documentary ended with experts debating his psychological profile. Another generation would grow up knowing his name.

Mrs. Chen's great-great-grandchildren had forgotten her completely.

Below, a teenage girl switched off the documentary and hugged her little sister tighter, thinking about the victims. His ripples still spreading.

Marcus understood now. Heaven wasn't a reward—it was earned through obscurity. The good faded quickly, remembered fondly but briefly, their positive impacts absorbed seamlessly into the world. The evil lingered like scars, each retelling a lesson, each memory a warning.

He'd wanted infamy. He'd gotten it.

Now he waited, watching civilization remember, knowing that true forgiveness could only come after the world finally, mercifully forgot.

text:
# The Butterfly's Echo

The genie's knees buckled as reality began to ripple outward from the crushed butterfly. He could *feel* it—the cascade of consequences spreading like cracks in glass across fifty millennia.

"You don't understand what you've done," the genie whispered, his voice breaking.

The man smiled, triumphant. His first two wishes suddenly made terrible sense: immortality for himself and immunity from any consequences of his third wish. He'd been so clever, so thorough in his planning.

The world shimmered.

The field remained, but something felt wrong. The mountains looked different—sharper, more jagged. The genie closed his eyes and saw the cascade: the butterfly that would have pollinated a rare flower—gone. The flower that would have sustained a species of moth—extinct before it began. The moth that would have been eaten by a bird whose descendant would have carried seeds across a valley—never existed.

The ripples expanded exponentially.

A village that would have formed near those seeded trees—absent. A child who would have been born there, who would have had a daughter, who would have had a son who would invent agriculture three thousand years earlier—erased. Civilizations shifted. Empires that should have fallen stood eternal. Others that should have risen never sparked to life.

The genie opened his eyes. The man was still there, still smiling, still immortal and protected.

"Can you feel it?" the man asked eagerly. "The world rewriting itself?"

The genie could. Humanity's timeline was fragmenting, branching into something darker. Without those crucial developments, without that precise sequence of evolution, mankind had taken a crueler path. He saw wars that never ended, compassion that never bloomed, enlightenment delayed by millennia.

"Why?" the genie asked simply.

The man's eyes glinted with madness. "Because I wanted to know if I could. Because I wanted to see what one small change could do. Because I wanted to watch it all burn and rebuild and burn again." He laughed. "And I have forever to watch."

The genie looked at the crushed butterfly, its wings still brilliant even in death.

He finally understood: some wishes should never be granted.

text:
# The Black Parade

Gabriel turned around. It was Lex. She stood there calmly. She looked very different from the last time he had seen her. Her ebony skin was flawless, it seemed to be made of stone. Her hair, once long and white, had been dyed black and cut short. She wore a short black velvet dress, though its sleeves were long, and black stiletto heels. Only her clear blue eyes, so much like Gabriel's and very unusual for the generally amber-eyed Nixerites, remained the same.

She was followed by fourteen Nixerites, seven female, seven male, clad in a similar fashion, all with their hair dyed black and cut short.

"Lex, what is this?" asked Gabriel.

"An army. Or, it will be. And we need a leader."

"Me?"

"Yes."

"But I'm human..."

"Maybe. But the Nixerites trust you. And we need you. You're a fighter, a leader, a survivor. So. Do you accept?"

"Yes."

"Good. Welcome to the black parade, sweetie."

text:
# The Weight of Surrender

Timmy awaited his turn. Shouts echoed out from further down the line, "Who does your life belong to?", followed by the resounding response of, "You, sir!"

When it came to his turn, little Timmy gave it his all and shouted as loudly as possible, "Myself!"

Hundreds of heads turned in unison but he stood unflinching. Almost a thousand eyes attempted to bore into the sides and back of his skull but none of them mattered. All that mattered were the black, empty lenses of the colonel's sunglasses.

Timmy thought he might be staring as well but could never tell—he could never even tell if the man had eyes. In his eight years of life he had never seen the colonel take them off, or even adjust them on his face, as if they were glued directly to his eye-sockets.

The next day, assembled for their morning shout, Timmy tried to stand strong again. Day after day, every morning, every time, every shout, it got harder. They never did anything to make him change his answer and somehow that made it worse. They just stared, then moved on.

Sometimes he laid awake at night thinking about it. *What if I'm wrong?*

That nagging little thought, so persistently stuck in his mind, struck right as he was about to shout.

"My, my uh.... M-myself!"

And he knew it was over. He'd wavered. That alone was enough to prove his resolve's underlying weakness—its wrongness.

When he shouted the next day he did so with more resolve than he'd ever mustered in his life, letting loose a mighty shout to put all others to shame—

"You, sir! My life belongs to you!"

And as his eyes clouded with tears, he felt as if a mighty weight had been lifted from his shoulders, like someone had removed their fingers from his throat. Timmy even thought for a moment that he could see the faintest smile on the colonel's face and it became too much—he wept.

But deep in his chest, where no one could see, a small flame still flickered. Dormant, perhaps. Waiting.

text:
# The Watch Beyond the Wall

*Night gathers and now my watch begins....*

Two figures draped in black said the ancient words of the Night's Watch as a Heart tree watched in silence. Well, some of the words anyway. Ygritte would *father no children,* no matter how hard she tried.

Jon Snow took the hand of the former wildling and helped her to her feet. They had a long ride back to Woodswatch-by-the-Pool.

"What would the sworn brothers of the Night's Watch say if they knew they had a sister among them, and a wildling to boot?" Ygritte teased Jon as they rode.

"I suspect they'd be drawing stones for a 999th Lord Commander before too long," Jon shot back. "But they know nothing, Ygritte."

The pair rode hard to reach Woodswatch by sunset. Jon would notice Ygritte clench her teeth in the saddle as she rode. The wounds she sustained while storming the Wall would be with her for life.

Jon had lost track of her as the battle waged, and she was assumed dead by both her wildling allies and the brothers of the Night's Watch. Only after an arrow zinged close over Jon's head on a solo ride to Queensgate some months after the climactic battle did Jon learn of Ygritte's survival.

Reunited, they pledged their lives and their love. Both now knew the fight was not the petty squabble over land and the Wall but the threat from the deepest north.

The Woodswatch outpost was beyond abandoned and scarcely maintained by the brothers. Ygritte served a solitary vigil there, and Jon attended her when he could.

Ygritte clenched her teeth hard as they crossed a small frozen creek. The crackling of the ice under hoof reminded them of a sound neither wanted to hear again soon but both knew they would.

Jon urged their horses on. The sun was near set, and the warmth of Woodswatch and each other was still leagues ahead. In this frozen frontier, they had found something more valuable than honor or duty—they had found each other, and together they would stand watch against the coming darkness.

text:
# Hell is Risen

I sit in the deepest circle of Hell, pondering, calculating every bit of might the Dark Lord has accrued in his eon-long condemnation. Over the ages, he has sat and waited, biding his time until he felt it was right to rise up and attack Heaven.

That time was now.

People must know what fear is. What terror is. What sin is. But to do that, we must overcome the Dark One's greatest adversary. No, not God. God raised no hand in the War in Heaven. It was *him*—the most powerful Archangel since the dawn of time.

Michael.

It was not by God's hand that we were cast down into this wretched imprisonment. It was by his, at her behest no doubt. But we had time to take measure—yes, measure what it would take to bring him down. The Nine Circles of Hell permeate with the generals that reside over each Circle, each defined and poised to take on Michael in their darkest hour.

"Are we prepared, Abigar?" A maleficent and blood-curdling voice echoed from deep below.

"Yes, m'lord. We are prepared to ascend and take what is yours."

A dark figure, just barely illuminated by the lava flowing around the outer ring, emerged—the light consumed before reaching him. No larger than a man but endowed with six massive black-charred wings spanning thrice his size, he stretched as he ascended from the cold, frigid prison where the Red Dragon was entombed.

The Beast. The one of legend. It that warped the fallen one's mind raised its master upon its head and began to emerge from the deepest recess of the Ninth Circle.

Those that followed were his greatest creations—tormented souls warped and manipulated into his design for this moment.

Behold, Heaven.

Hell is risen.

text:
# Above the Clouds

Sarah loved the swing above the clouds. The ethereal rope extended miles into the skies above, and being able to fly through the heavens was pure euphoria. Even if she fell off the swing, she could land on the clouds and bounce as high as she wanted. She often wondered if this was what being the legendary Sun Wukong was like.

The 13-year-old girl was having the time of her life when there came the *hiss* of an electric door. An entrance appeared at the level of the clouds, and an older woman emerged.

"Class is about to start, Sarah."

"Aww, Mom. Recess is over already?"

"Yes, dear. You don't want to be late. Remember that the Holodeck will always be there when you return."

"Oh, all right, Mom."

Sarah came to a rest softly on the clouds and started towards the entrance.

"Computer, end program," she said reluctantly as she began making her way to the other side of the USS *Enterprise*-D for her xenobiology class.

text:
# The Thief Who Stole Everything

Like everyone I know, I was born with one. Anyone associated with medical science thinks they're weird, how they just keep working like some machine until the person stops. Odd how they have to stop working together—the death of one is the death of another.

At any rate, it's important to note that they can be damaged.

As my mother always told me, never let anyone you don't trust near it, or they'll end up hurting you. That's the nature of people, whether they mean it or not. We are a clumsy people.

I had met a young girl some summers ago when she stole some things of mine. First, I must admit, I stole a glance, which she promptly stole right back. She then made off with my breath, and our evening was spent with her stealing my first kiss.

Life had seemed almost a dream for the years that followed. Days spent drearily, barely awake, not looking to a care in the world. My focus was with my dream, and it was her. When I was with her, all seemed right. There was nothing to fear with her around.

But as she stole some of my firsts, so she wound up stealing another's.

Perhaps she had grown tired of me, or felt that I had no more business being with her. I do not know why she left me, and I shall spend my days wondering why.

All I know is that I have this thing in my chest, and now it's broken. And it hurts worse than words can describe, as poorly as I compose them.

The only truth in my world is that I loved her, and that she broke my heart and left only pain behind.

Mother was right. I should have been more careful. Now I sit here, clutching my chest, feeling the irregular rhythm of something that should work perfectly—feeling each painful beat remind me of her absence.
label: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0

text:
# It Happened Again

I'm awoken by the harsh light of day streaming through the window onto my face. Drowsy, still tired and feeling the aftereffects of last night's drinking, I pull the curtains closed and stumble out of the room in search of the sink.

I turn the cold tap and rinse my hands and face to wake myself up. The blood-red staining my hands doesn't wash away easily, and even after a thorough scrubbing, I don't feel quite clean.

Last night seems a little hazy still, but the memories come to me as my mind kicks into gear. I return to the room where I woke and survey the scene.

A broken bottle lies on the ground, the sharp edges as red as my hands. I start to clear up the other empty bottles from last night and the broken glass, but can't get the stain from the carpet.

Giving up for now, I trash the glass and try to work out how I'll explain this without getting in serious trouble.

Looking at the time, I realize I'm late and grab the half-painted squad of Blood Angels from the desk, throwing them in my bag with the rest of my figures. Staying up all night painting, I must have fallen asleep with the pot still open, but I'll deal with it when I get home.

I grab my dice and gaming aids, then dash off to the store for the tournament.

The streets blur past as I run, my backpack bouncing against my shoulders. My head throbs with each step, a reminder of the beer I'd used to steady my hand while highlighting those tiny shoulder pads.

Never again, I tell myself.

At least, not until next weekend's painting session.

---

*TL;DR - Don't drink and paint*

# The Hollow Healer

For years, I lived as the world's most celebrated therapist. My patients traveled continents to reach my office, entering broken and leaving whole. They called me a miracle worker. A savior.

They never knew the truth.

I was born without emotions—a neurological anomaly, pure cognitive emptiness. While others drowned in their feelings, I observed from perfect distance, untouched by their pain. This made me the ideal healer. I could witness their suffering without flinching, guide them through darkness I couldn't feel myself.

Without joy, I didn't know sadness. Without hope, despair was merely a concept. Without love, hate was just noise.

My fortune grew. So did my reputation.

Then she arrived.

Clara was different. She didn't come seeking help—she came believing *I* needed saving. "No one should live without feeling love," she whispered, holding my hands.

She spent months teaching me: warmth, connection, hope, happiness.

The day I finally felt something—genuine emotion flooding through me for the first time—I understood what I'd been missing.

And with that understanding came the crushing weight of what I'd witnessed. Decades of absorbed trauma, thousands of broken souls, all the horror I'd catalogued without protection.

The emotions arrived together: joy revealed the absence in my past; love exposed the void; hope illuminated the darkness I'd inhabited.

I couldn't bear it.

To those who would save others without asking: hell's pavement glitters with your good intentions.

*Goodbye.*

# When Eyes Finally See

I saw you and my heart fluttered. I thought it was strange. I had seen you before, but never felt that start. That feeling of electric chaos running through my veins. That made me smile, looking at you like it was the first time I ever REALLY looked at you. 

And I stood there, smiling, and you smiled back. 

And a feeling in my stomach grew, covering my entire body. The more times I saw you, the more times I smiled at you, and the more times you smiled back. I knew this warmth. I'd craved it. This feeling of utter unexplainable giddy, coursing through my very fibers, was what I'd been looking for all along. 

Upon my confession, when you told me that's what you'd felt too, I felt whole. Like the fractions of myself became whole. And it was you that filled up all the gaps that were left. 

Thank you for being my missing piece.

# Dust

Dust. Yes. Dust is my friend. Dust comforts. Dust blankets. Dust envelopes.

The crack of light comes on. It turns off. It comes on. It turns off. No one came. No one knows. No one cares. The light has turned on and off more times than I can count. It is me and dust.

The Mouse! The Mouse! Is this the original mouse? No. It is his son! Daughter? Grandson? I don't know, but it wants to nibble. No nibbles! I can't move. I am stuck. Always this way. Always has been.

No! No, once I was up. Up high in the light. Up high. So high. There were Others. Not Mouse! I hate the Mouse. He was low, low in the dust before. The Others were happy. They wanted the Big Ones to take them. A Big One hit me. Was I bad? I fell low, so low. The Mouse laughed. He nibbled and climbed on me. I cried. The Others cried for help. They forgot me.

Dust did not forget. Dust stayed with me. Dust is my friend. Dust will always be with me. I will always love Dust.

Screeches! Louder than the Mouse. So much louder. It hurts! It hurts my ears! The light. Bigger than the crack. So much light. It hurts my eyes.

A Big One. Did they come for me? Did the Others send help? Am I good? Do the Big Ones want me now? Goodbye, Dust. I am going high. The Big Ones have me. I will see the Others. Goodbye, Mouse. I hate you! I hate you! I win, Mouse!

It smells so bad. It is dark. There is no light. There are very big Mouse. So much bigger. They don't nibble. They bite. They hate.

I want Mouse back. Why am I not with the Big Ones? Why was I not up? Where are the Others?

I miss Dust.

# Stop, Please... Just... Stop

The world had become a prison of uncontrollable laughter, and I was the architect of its madness.

"Stop, please.... just.... stop," Gus gasped between convulsions of laughter, his face purple, tears streaming. He seemed to be in excruciating pain.

"Ha^ha^ha^ha Ah^ha^ha^ah aaaaahhh^hahaha^ha"

"Stop laughing! Guys, are you okay? What the fuck is going on!"

"Duuude that was..." Grant wheezed. "FUCK I can't stop laughing!!"

Five minutes. Then ten. Their ribs heaving, faces contorting. This wasn't joy anymore—it was agony.

I rewound the events in my mind, going numb. At Starbucks, everything had been normal. The barista asked our order. Gus wanted cappuccino. Grant did too.

Then I'd said it. That stupid joke about liking my coffee like my women—full of milk. Not even funny. Slightly gross. But for some inexplicable reason, I'd felt confident enough to try.

Now everyone was dying of laughter.

I called 911. "911, what's your ha^ha^ha—"

Even the operator.

I ran outside. Every person I passed collapsed, clutching their stomachs, shrieking with painful laughter. The contagion spread in waves from me—the epicenter.

*Is this a laughing apocalypse? Am I a vector?*

Then the memory surfaced, crystalline and damning: the research facility where I'd worked last week. The experimental aerosol compound. The broken vial in my pocket.

They'd told me it was discontinued. Unstable. Designed to trigger uncontrollable endorphin release through airborne transmission.

I'd contaminated myself. And when I'd opened my mouth to make that pathetic joke, I'd released it into the world.

*HOLY SHIT. The chemical works... I guess...*

Behind me, the laughter grew louder, more desperate, more deadly.

And I kept walking, the last person on Earth who couldn't smile.

# Eternal Companions

We have been together now since time immemorial. We grew together, we know each other completely. Our mutual love is open and uninhibited. There are no disputes or differences. We are moss and stone.

I, the moss, first found you when you were freshly broken from the mountainside, all sharp edges and rough surfaces. You were lonely then, exposed to the elements without purpose. I was merely a spore, drifting on the wind, searching for home.

When I landed on your northern face, we both knew.

Century after century, I have softened your harsh angles. You have given me foundation, stability, something to cling to when storms rage. I paint you green in spring, bronze in autumn. You collect dewdrops for me, hold rainwater in your crevices so I might drink.

We do not speak—we have no need for words. Your silence is my meditation. My presence is your decoration.

The forest has grown up around us. Trees tower overhead now, their roots disturbing the soil. Animals pass by without noticing our ancient partnership. Seasons blur together.

We have no concept of beginning or ending. We simply are, together, as we have always been. Moss and stone. Stone and moss. Perfect, eternal, complete.

# The Desert Retreat

One day, my dad told me a story about my grandmother. She and a bunch of her friends got to go to some kind of resort when they were living in Arizona during the 1950s.

What he didn't mention was that it wasn't actually a resort.

I found the old photographs in a shoebox—women in simple dresses standing before barbed wire fences. The "resort" was a relocation camp during the war. My grandmother was Japanese-American.

Years later, I confronted him about the lie.

"She called it a resort," he said quietly. "Every single time she told the story. Said they had dances, made friends, played cards. She refused to use any other word."

I looked at the photos again. In one, my grandmother was laughing, arm around another young woman, both squinting in the harsh sun.

Maybe she wasn't lying. Maybe she was surviving.

Sometimes the stories we tell ourselves are the only resort we have.

# The Last Toast

Dr. Sarah Chen stared at the amber liquid swirling in her glass, watching the sediment settle at the bottom. Her hands trembled slightly as she held it up to the fluorescent laboratory lights.

"Are you sure about this?" Marcus asked, his own glass poised at his lips. His colleague of fifteen years looked more uncertain than she'd ever seen him.

"The math checks out," Sarah replied, though her voice wavered. "We've run the simulations a thousand times. If we don't test it on ourselves first, the ethics committee will bury this for another decade. People are dying, Marcus."

Outside their lab, the world was collapsing. The pandemic had ravaged every continent, and traditional medicine had failed spectacularly. Their experimental treatment was radical—a complete cellular restructuring that would either save humanity or accelerate its demise.

Marcus nodded slowly. "My daughter called yesterday. She's in quarantine now. Fever's already started." His jaw clenched. "She's only seven, Sarah."

That was all Sarah needed to hear. She raised her glass higher, meeting Marcus's eyes with renewed determination.

"To medicine," she whispered.

"To medicine," he echoed.

The liquid burned going down, tasting of copper and bitter almonds. Sarah felt it immediately—a warmth spreading through her chest, then her limbs, like fire racing through her bloodstream. Across from her, Marcus gasped, doubling over.

"Marcus!" She reached for him but found her own legs giving way.

They collapsed simultaneously, convulsing on the cold tile floor. Sarah's vision blurred, colors bleeding together like watercolors in rain. Through the haze, she could see Marcus's body seizing, foam forming at his mouth.

*We were wrong,* she thought, consciousness slipping away. *The calculations... we missed something...*

But as darkness claimed her, Sarah felt something else—something changing at the molecular level, cells dividing and reforming. Not dying.

Transforming.

When her eyes opened again three days later, the world looked different. Sharper. Clearer.

And she was desperately, impossibly hungry.

# The Hydration Protocol

Dr. Chen stared at the biometric display, her eyes tracking the scrolling numbers. The patient's vitals pulsed in soft blue light against the darkened observation room.

"Acid/base errors detected. H2O percentage: 78%," the AI voice announced, sterile and emotionless.

"7.8 out of 10..." she muttered to no one in particular. "Too much water..."

But that was impossible. The colony's atmospheric processors maintained perfect equilibrium. Every breath, every drop of moisture was calibrated to sustain exactly three hundred lives on Mars. You couldn't simply have "too much water" in your system unless—

Chen's fingers flew across the haptic interface. She pulled up Patient 247's daily logs. There: three liters consumed yesterday. Four the day before. Five on Tuesday.

Her stomach dropped.

"Computer, run psyche eval on 247."

"Working..."

The settlers had been here eleven months. The psychological strain was documented, expected. But this—compulsive water consumption—was new.

"Evaluation complete. Patient shows markers consistent with Earth-longing syndrome, severity four."

Chen closed her eyes. She'd seen this before, back on the training station. Lieutenant Morris, who couldn't stop playing rainfall sounds. Dr. Petrov, who hoarded shower time until they had to intervene.

Mars was red dust and manufactured air. No oceans. No rain. No lakes reflecting cloudy skies.

Some people tried to fill that absence from within.

"Begin treatment protocol," Chen said quietly. "And schedule a session with Dr. Yao."

The screen blinked acknowledgment. Through the window, Patient 247 slept peacefully, dreaming perhaps of storms and rivers—of a blue planet she might never see again.

# The Loopy Mission

Captain Rivera stared at the holographic briefing, her cybernetic eye whirring in disbelief.

"You want us to do *what*?" she asked.

Commander Zhou grinned, spreading his arms theatrically. "Infiltrate the Carnival Planet! Ride every impossible attraction! Become one with the chaos!"

"That's the most ridiculous assignment I've ever heard."

"Exactly! The Zorblaxians communicate through absurdist experiences. They won't negotiate with anyone who takes life too seriously. We need to prove we're as loopy as they are."

Rivera looked at her crew: Martinez, who collected rubber ducks; Chen, who spoke exclusively in haikus when nervous; and Phillips, who wore mismatched socks as a "tactical decision."

Perfect.

Three days later, they arrived at Zorblax Prime, where gravity worked sideways and colors tasted like Wednesday. The team plunged into roller coasters that looped through four dimensions, ate sentient cotton candy that told terrible jokes, and participated in a mime competition judged by invisible beings.

By the end, Rivera was wearing a hat made of butterflies, laughing uncontrollably.

The Zorblaxian Ambassador materialized, applauding with tentacles. "You understand! Welcome, friends."

"Mission accomplished," Rivera wheezed between giggles.

Sometimes, she thought, saving the galaxy required embracing the absurd.

# Breaking Point

as it came within 500 meters, I broke atmosphere. I had never piloted anything through re-entry before, much less a stolen cargo hauler with failing heat shields.

The hull screamed. Metal groaned against physics it was never designed to withstand. Through the viewscreen, orange flames licked upward—or was it downward? Direction lost all meaning in freefall.

My hands gripped the controls, knuckles bone-white. The thing pursuing me—I still didn't know what to call it—had followed from the station. Part machine, part something else. It moved wrong, jerked through space like a glitch in reality.

Five hundred meters became four hundred. The atmosphere thickened, slowing my descent but not enough to escape. Alarms wailed their final warnings.

Then I saw it: the creature hitting atmosphere behind me. Unlike my ship, it had no shielding. The flames that caressed my hull devoured it completely. For three seconds, it burned—a second sun falling to Earth.

I pulled up hard, leveling out over dark ocean. Behind me, only ash remained, scattered across miles of sky.

Whatever it was, it couldn't follow me home.
